Conclusion
The brain tumor classification project achieved its goal by
developing and deploying deep learning models to accurately classify
brain tumors from MRI data. Various architectures, such as
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformer-based
models, were designed, trained, and evaluated for their effectiveness
in handling medical imaging data. The CNN models excelled in
feature extraction and classification tasks, reaching an accuracy of up
to 98.65%, making them valuable tools for medical practitioners in
detecting and diagnosing brain tumors. While Transformer models
showed potential, they required more computational resources and
fine-tuning to improve their efficiency for real-time deployment.
To ensure accessibility, the project deployed the best-performing
models through web interfaces using frameworks like Streamlit and
Gradio. These interfaces allowed for seamless real-time image uploads
and classification, providing an intuitive experience for users. The
deployment demonstrated the practical application of deep learning in
medical diagnostics, supporting radiologists and healthcare professionals
in identifying brain tumors early. The project highlights the potential of
deep learning in medical image classification and lays the foundation for
future advancements, evolving into a more powerful tool for early tumor
detection and diagnosis. Looking ahead, there are areas for improvement
and expansion in the brain tumor classification project.
Future work will involve refining advanced models with improved
attention mechanisms and feature extraction techniques, enhancing
the ability to detect subtle tumor features. An exciting prospect is the
integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) after the classification
stage, generating detailed diagnostic reports that summarize the
findings and provide insights into tumor characteristics and
recommended actions. This integration would enhance the
interpretability and usefulness of the model’s output, bridging the gap
between predictions and clinical insights.
Additionally, segmentation of brain tumors remains a key area
for future development. Using the BraTS dataset will improve
tumor boundary detection, aiding in assessing tumor growth and
response to treatment. Future research will focus on developing

title: Bridging the Gap: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor Detection and Diagnosis from MRI Images
authors: Wandile Nhlapho; Marcellin Atemkeng; Yusuf Brima; Jean-Claude Ndogmo
text:
Introduction
The field of medical imaging has experienced a transformative paradigm shift with
the emergence of deep learning (DL), unlocking unprecedented opportunities for accurate
disease classification and diagnosis, as discussed in [1–5]. In the area of brain tumor
classification using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scan images, these DL models
have shown exceptional promise [1,2]. The significance of brain tumor diagnosis from
MRI images lies in its pivotal role in modern healthcare, offering opportunities for early
detection and timely treatment, as is evident in [2,3,6]. DL models have demonstrated
significant promise in automating brain tumor classification tasks. However, their real-
world application and reliability, especially concerning accuracy and interpretability, are
still questioned [7].
Despite the impressive classification results produced by DL models, their “black-
box” nature impedes a comprehensive understanding of the decision-making rationale.
Also, their incorporation into clinical practice and decision-making needs adaptability, not
just in terms of classification performance, but also in interpretability and explainability.

title: Bridging the Gap: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor Detection and Diagnosis from MRI Images
authors: Wandile Nhlapho; Marcellin Atemkeng; Yusuf Brima; Jean-Claude Ndogmo

Information 2024, 15, 182
This study investigates the junction of medical image analysis and DL interpretability.
Brain tumors, characterized by their diversity and clinical significance as highlighted
in [2,3], demand precise classification for tailored treatment plans and improved patient
outcomes. While DL models have exhibited substantial prowess in this domain, their
inherent opacity presents a challenge, as discussed in [3,6]. The central issue revolves
around understanding how these models reach their conclusions, particularly crucial
in the context of medical decision-making. Today, interpretability techniques are used
to understand the decision-making processes of DL models in medical imaging. These
techniques aid in identifying crucial features and regions within images that impact the
model’s decisions, thus enhancing comprehension of the diagnostic process.
We conducted a broad performance evaluation of various state-of-the-art DL frame-
works with transfer learning such as AlexNet, DenseNet121, EfficientNetB0, GoogLeNet,
Inception V3, ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, ViT Transformer, and Xception for brain tumor
MRI classification. This evaluation encompasses not only the assessment of classifica-
tion accuracy, but also a focus on evaluating the interpretability of the models. Adaptive
path-based techniques, including Grad-CAM++ [8], Grad-CAM [9], and Integrated Gra-
dients [10], are used to understand what these DL models learn in MRI images. Other
methods exist in the literature for feature extraction, such as the Stationary Wavelet Trans-
form (SWT) [11] and optimized hybridization methods like Particle Swarm Optimization
(PSO) and Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) [11]. However, in this work, our primary focus is on
state-of-the-art CNNs using a gradient-based optimization method.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 discusses the literature review
on explainability in medical imaging, while Section 3 covers the attribution methods used
in this work and the transfer learning models. Section 4 presents the proposed method.
Section 5 presents the dataset and discusses the results, while Section 6 concludes the work.

Literature on DL Models’ Explainability in Medical Imaging
The input image is passed through the algorithm via one forward, as well as backward
propagation. The resulting score is then computed forward, and the dependency gradient
amongst the convolution layers is then determined to build an attribution map. This
process is known as the Vanilla Gradient explainability method. It is an easy-to-understand
attribution approach with few processing power requirements because of its simplicity.
Vanilla Gradient and other attribution-based graphic aids for MRI imaging of brain tumors
were evaluated using an attribution-based scheme named NeuroXAI [12]. Both feature
segmentation and classification were visualized using these techniques. Vanilla Gradient
produced noisier attribution maps than the other attribution techniques and had gradient
saturation, which means that a change in a neuron has no effect on the network’s output
and, so, cannot be assessed. Similar results were observed utilizing Vanilla Gradient
for feature visualization in [13], where the dissimilitude intensification juncture from
computed tomography (CT) images is anticipated. Furthermore, Vanilla Gradient is unable
to distinguish between classes (such as healthy and diseased) [14]. This demonstrates that
Vanilla Gradient is unable to produce attribution maps that are distinct based on class. The
deconvolution network (DeconvNET) is essentially comparable to Vanilla Gradient, with
the primary distinction lying in the computation of gradients over a Rectified Linear Unit
(ReLU) function [15].
The human brain’s artery segmentation was studied using different attribution tech-
niques for interlayer CNN visualization using TorchEsegeta, a structure for image-based DL
algorithms that can be understood and explained [16]. Since other techniques also indicated
non-vessel activation, their primary focus was on the vessels; Vanilla Gradient and Decon-
vNET produced results that were more comprehensible to humans than other attribution
techniques like Deep Learning Important Features (DeepLIFT) and Grad-CAM++.
Guided back-propagation (GBP) integrates both the DeconvNET [17] and Vanilla
Gradient. Comparing this approach to applying each technique separately yields less noisy
attribution maps as there are fewer active voxels. As compared to Vanilla Gradient, GBP

could furthermore produce attribution maps that are too sparse, which are unhelpful for
comprehensive image characterization [18]. Although they are not class discriminative, all
three of the gradient-based techniques are quite sensitive to the way the neural network
layers collect information. ReLU and pooling layers may also cause local gradients to
saturate. As a result, significant characteristics may disappear as the network’s layers
advance, which might lead to an inadequate model clarification or even a concentration on
unimportant features. Layerwise relevance propagation (LRP) is an Explainable Artificial
Intelligence (XAI) technique that employs principles unique to LRP to propagate the class
score backward through the neural layers to the input image [19]. The core idea of LRP is to
preserve inter-neuron interdependence, ensuring that information acquired by one layer of
neurons is equally transferred to the next lower layer. LRP addresses the challenges posed
by the saturation problem since the decomposition relies on propagating relevance scores
between neurons rather than gradients. In a study focused on the detection of abdominal
aortic aneurysms using CT images, LRP demonstrated a distinct class difference based on
activation differences in the aortic lumen [20].
Deep Learning Important Features (DeepLIFT) is an XAI technique that addresses
the saturation problem by employing a neutral reference activation, such as the neuron
activation in CT scans without pathology or disease [21]. The difference between a new
neuron’s activation and the reference activation is described by this reference activation. An
attribution map is generated by computing the contribution scores for each neuron based on
these differences. To discern individuals with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) using MRI, DeepLIFT
was compared to LRP and Vanilla Gradient [22]. Based on the quantitative evaluation,
DeepLIFT extracts target-specific characteristics much better than Vanilla Gradient and
marginally better than LRP. Gradient saturation is something that both LRP and DeepLIFT

Path-Oriented Methods and Transfer Learning Models
We explored the complexities of transfer learning models and path-oriented methods.
This investigation is essential because it offers a thorough grasp of the theoretical underpin-
nings of the models we trained and the attribution techniques used to ensure explainability.
Through providing in-depth analyses of these techniques, we want to provide clarification
on the fundamental ideas that underpin how they work. This theoretical foundation is
essential to understanding the subtleties of the models and their interpretability, which
is consistent with our goal of developing a deeper grasp of the theoretical foundations of
these approaches in addition to putting them into practice.

Transfer Learning Models
When faced with having a model excel in a related, yet slightly different challenge,
transfer learning (TL) becomes pertinent. Rather than training the model from the initial
stage, this approach involves leveraging the acquired knowledge, specifically the parame-
ters, from the initial task and applying it to the new, related task. This process facilitates a
more efficient adaptation of the model to the novel task by capitalizing on the previously
acquired expertise. The TL models under consideration include AlexNet, VGG16, VGG19,
GoogLeNet, ResNet50, Inception V3, DenseNet121, Xception, EfficientNetB0 and Vision
Transformer (ViT).

authors: Wandile Nhlapho; Marcellin Atemkeng; Yusuf Brima; Jean-Claude Ndogmo
text:
AlexNet
The deep CNN architecture AlexNet made significant contributions to the develop-
ment of DL and computer vision. By winning the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition
Challenge (ILSVRC) in 2012, it was first discussed in [53] and considerably advanced the
state-of-the-art in image classification problems. It contains 5 convolutional layers and
3 fully connected layers for a total of 8 layers. The convolutional layers are separated by
max-pooling layers, which are used to down-sample and capture important information.
3.2.2. VGG16
The contemporary transfer learning model VGG16, boasting sixteen weighted layers,
stands as a state-of-the-art solution. Demonstrating its power on the ImageNet dataset, the
model achieved an accuracy rate of 92.7% for the top-five test results. The VGG16 achieved
the top spot in the Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) organized by the
Oxford Visual Geometry Group (VGG) [54]. The increased depth of the VGG model enables
it to aid the kernel in capturing more intricate features.
3.2.3. VGG19
Within the VGG19 model, an extension of the VGG16 architecture with 19 weighted
layers, three additional fully connected (FC) layers contribute to a total of 4096, 4096,
and 1000 neurons respectively, as reported in [54]. This model encompasses a Softmax
classification layer alongside five max-pooling layers. The convolutional layers within the
architecture use the ReLU activation function.

title: Bridging the Gap: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor Detection and Diagnosis from MRI Images
authors: Wandile Nhlapho; Marcellin Atemkeng; Yusuf Brima; Jean-Claude Ndogmo
text:
GoogLeNet
The best-performing model, GoogLeNet, was presented by Google at the 2014 Ima-
geNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC14) [55]. The inner layers of the
neural network were expanded to output diverse correlation distributions, based on the
theory that achieving different probability distributions highly correlated with the input
data would optimize the efficiency of each layer’s neural network output.
3.2.5. ResNet50
The residual network ResNet50 is 50 layers deep [54]. The ResNet50 design integrates
a combination of convolution filters of various sizes to address the degeneration of CNN
models and shorten training times. A max-pooling layer, an average pooling layer, and a
total of 48 convolutional layers make up this architecture.
3.2.6. Inception V3
Inception V1 was the name given to Google’s initial proposal of GoogLeNets, which
was followed by Inception V2 and Inception V3 [56] the following year. To reduce the
size of the feature maps, Inception V3 employs convolutional layers with a stride of two
in combination with pooling layers. The first Inception module of Inception V3 replaces
the 7-by-7 layer convolutional layer with 3-by-3 layer convolutional layers, which is a
modification from Inception V2’s first Inception module. The network’s width and depth
are increased in Inception V3 with the aforementioned upgrades to enhance performance.

3.2.7. DenseNet121
The DenseNet model was proposed in [57]. Its primary components are the DenseBlock
(DB), transition layer, and growth rate. DenseNet121 has the advantage of requiring fewer
parameters, allowing for the training of deeper models during computation. Additionally,
the fully connected layer of the model also has a regularization effect, which can help
prevent overfitting on smaller datasets.

title: Bridging the Gap: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor Detection and Diagnosis from MRI Images
authors: Wandile Nhlapho; Marcellin Atemkeng; Yusuf Brima; Jean-Claude Ndogmo
text:
Xception
Inception V3 was updated by Google to create Xception [58], which split regular
convolution into spatial convolution and point-by-point convolution. Depthwise Separable
Convolution (DSC) was used in place of the original Inception module. While pointwise
convolution utilizes a 1-by-1 kernel to convolve point by point, reducing the number of
parameters and computations, spatial convolution is conducted on each input channel.
3.2.9. EfficientNetB0
The EfficientNetB0 CNN architecture was proposed in [59]. Enhancing accuracy and
efficiency through balanced scaling of the model’s depth, breadth, and resolution is the aim
of EfficientNet. The design presents a fixed-ratio compound scaling technique that scales
all three dimensions of depth, breadth, and resolution consistently.

Vision Transformer (ViT)
This architecture adopts the Transformer’s encoder component, revolutionizing im-
age processing by segmenting the image into patches of a specified size like 16 × 16 or
32 × 32 dimensions [60,61]. This patch-based method enhances training with smaller
patches. After flattening, the patches are fed into the network. Unlike traditional neural
networks, the model lacks positional information about the sequence of samples. To ad-
dress this, the encoder incorporates trainable positional fixed vectors, eliminating the need
for hard-coded positions.

Some of the most important performance measures frequently used are accuracy,
precision, recall, and the so-called F1 score. To describe these measures, let us denote by
TP, TN, FP, and FN the number of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false

the absence of the negative class. FPs are instances where the model predicted a positive

Method
This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for brain tumor classification while
integrating the model’s explainability. This approach comprises two phases: phase (a) for
classification and phase (b) for explainability, as illustrated in Figure 1.

Phase (a): This phase integrates a CNN model with TL for the classification of brain
tumor types based on MRI data. In this approach, the acquired features of a pre-trained
CNN model serve as an initial foundation, proving particularly advantageous in scenarios
involving sparsely labeled data. The data are fed into a CNN, which subsequently processes
the data through convolutional layers to capture intricate patterns and spatial hierarchies
within the MRI images. Following this, the pooling layer is employed to down-sample
and reduce the feature space, optimizing computational efficiency. Progressing along the
activation path, the dense layer plays a pivotal role in transforming high-level features
for effective classification. Finally, the model makes decisions about tumor types based
on the combination of these learned features. When the decision is made, a medical
expert becomes curious and seeks to understand how the model makes decisions based on
their expertise.
Phase (b): This phase uses explainability techniques, including Grad-CAM, Grad-
CAM++, IG, and Saliency Mapping. The explanation aims to shed light on how the
CNN model arrives at its classifications, providing valuable insights to the medical expert.
Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ offer the visualization of crucial regions in the MRI images
that contribute to the model’s decisions. IG provides a comprehensive understanding of
feature importance by perturbing input features, while Saliency Mapping highlights salient
features influencing the classification. Together, these explainability techniques bridge
the gap between the model’s predictions and human interpretability, fostering trust and
comprehension in the application of DL models to medical imaging. After the model is
explained, the focus shifts smoothly to the part where medical experts take over and make
sense of it. The explained visualizations and insights provided by techniques like Grad-
CAM, Grad-CAM++, IG, and Saliency Mapping serve as a bridge between the complex
nature of DL classifications and the expertise of medical experts.

text:
Dataset
For easy access and reference, the dataset used in this study is currently available on
Kaggle [62]. This brain tumor dataset comprises 3264 2D slices of T1-weighted contrast-
enhanced images, encompassing three distinct types of brain tumors—glioma, meningioma,
and pituitary tumors—along with images of a healthy brain. We allocated 90% of the
dataset for training and validation, reserving the remaining 10% for testing. We applied
various data augmentation techniques to further enrich the training and validation subsets.
The augmented subsets were subdivided into 90% for training and 10% for validation.
The original images, initially sized at 299 × 299, were resized to 150 × 150 to enhance
computational efficiency and facilitate model training. Figure 2 visually presents samples
from each of the four classes within the dataset, and Figure 3 illustrates the proportion of
each of the four classes in the dataset.
Gliomas are tumors derived from glial cells and can manifest as either benign or
malignant. Among them, glioblastoma multiforme stands out as a particularly aggressive
variant, posing significant challenges in terms of therapeutic intervention [3]. Pituitary
tumors arise in the pituitary gland; these tumors can disrupt hormonal balance. They
may present as growths that secrete hormones or as non-functioning growths. Common
sub-types include prolactinomas and growth-hormone-secreting tumors, each with its
distinct clinical implications. Meningiomas are generally benign, slow-growing tumors
originating from the meninges. The symptoms associated with meningiomas vary based
on the size and location of the tumor, making their clinical presentation diverse and often
dependent on individual cases [3].
Figure 2. Sample of each image in the dataset. A glioma tumor image typically exhibits abnormal
growth in the brain, indicating potential malignancy. No tumor images represent a healthy state
without any abnormal growth or lesions. Meningioma tumor images showcase tumors arising from
the meninges, the protective layers around the brain, and the spinal cord. Pituitary tumor images
depict tumors in the pituitary gland, influencing hormone regulation and potentially affecting various
bodily functions.

Training, Regularization, and Testing
As discussed in Section 5.1, 90% of the dataset was reserved for training and validation.
This 90 % dataset was then augmented and shuffled to ensure randomness before splitting
into 90% for training and 10% for validation. The hyperparameters, such as the number of
layers, filter sizes, and dropout rates, were optimized to enhance the model’s predictive
capabilities. This involved a systematic exploration of different hyperparameter combina-
tions using Grid Search. It took several days to run the Grid Search for hyperparameter
tuning. Throughout this process, we explored various combinations of hyperparameters,
such as learning rates ranging from 0.001 to 0.1, batch sizes from 16 to 32, epochs from 10
to 150, as well as filter sizes and the number of filters. After completing the search, the
best combination of hyperparameters was found to be a learning rate of 0.001, a batch size
of 32, and 10 epochs. We used the categorical cross-entropy as a loss function with the
Adam optimizer. The details of these hyperparameters are provided in Table 1. Figure 4
depicts the training and validation losses, as well as the training and validation accuracies
for the top-performing models. It is evident from this figure that the models did not exhibit
further learning beyond epoch 10, as indicated by the convergence of the training and
validation losses. Hence, we preferred to stop training at epoch 10. The testing phase
aimed to evaluate the trained model’s generalization to new, unseen data. The 10% test
dataset as discussed in Section 5.1, consisting of 327 images, was used for this purpose.
Metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and the so-called F1 score were computed to
assess the model’s performance. The model training and hyperparameter tuning of our
pre-trained models demanded substantial computational resources, and the efficiency of
the process hinged on the specifications of our Dell computer, featuring an Intel Core i7
processor. The use of a powerful GPU, specifically the P100 model, played a pivotal role in
accelerating the training speed. With 32 GB of system RAM, our system efficiently handled
the computational load, facilitated by the Kaggle kernel environment. The implementation
was carried out in Python version 3.9.7 and TensorFlow version 2.12.0.

Interpretability Results
In Figures 10–12, we present a detailed look into the explainability results of our
top-performing models: EfficientNetB0, DenseNet121, and Xception. Figure 10 provides
insights into the interpretability of EfficientNetB0, highlighting crucial image regions using
techniques such as Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, IGs, and Saliency Mapping. Moving to
Figure 11, we explore the explainability of DenseNet121, our second-best model, uncovering
the significant features influencing its predictions. Figure 12 reveals the interpretability
degrees of Xception, our third-best model, showcasing the impact of various image regions
on the classification decisions. These visualizations offer a transparent view into the
decision-making processes of our models, facilitating understanding and trust.
Based on our obtained results, both the Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ methods demon-
strated similar outcomes, offering visual explanations for the decision-making processes
of EfficientNetB0, DenseNet121, and Xception in predicting brain tumors. These methods
accurately pinpointed the exact location of the tumor, and the visualizations generated by
both approaches closely aligned, suggesting a consistent portrayal of the crucial regions
or features influencing the model’s predictions. However, it is essential to note that IG
faced challenges in precisely pinpointing the tumor’s location, and Saliency Mapping
exhibited some noise. Despite these challenges, both Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ consis-
tently provided excellent visual explanations for the decision processes of EfficientNetB0,
DenseNet121, and Xception, significantly enhancing our understanding of their predictive

how the deep learning model interprets images without tumors.

text:
Discussion
The findings of evaluating the performance of different DL models provide intriguing
new information on the relationship between total accuracy and model complexity, which
is reflected by the number of parameters shown in Table 2. EfficientNetB0, DenseNet121,
and Xception showed impressive accuracy values of 97-98% with much fewer parameters,
indicating how well they use information for the tasks at hand. On the other hand, the
accuracy was about 85% for VGG16 and VGG19, which have importantly greater parameter
counts of more than 138 million. There is a clear exchange between model accuracy and
complexity, highlighting the necessity of striking a balance. Interestingly, models with a
reasonable amount of parameters, such as AlexNet, ResNet50, GoogLeNet, and Xception,
achieved competitive accuracy in the 80-96% range, striking a medium ground. Even with
a low number of parameters, the ViT Transformer showed greater accuracy variability,
highlighting the impact of the architectural design on model performance.
Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, IG, and Saliency Mapping showed important areas that
matched the glioma, meningioma, and pituitary classifications. What stood out was
the remarkable similarity in the outcomes between the Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++
methods, precisely pinpointing tumor locations. This consistency paints a clear picture
of the essential regions influencing predictions across all three models; see Figures 10–12.
These visualizations played a crucial role, not just in making our models transparent, but
also in fostering a deeper understanding and instilling trust in how the decisions were
made. Our contributions are outlined as follows:
•
Model evaluation: The study comprehensively assesses various DL architectures,
providing valuable insights into which models are most effective for brain tumor
classification. This evaluation is crucial for guiding the selection of appropriate
models in real-world medical imaging applications.
•
Brain tumor diagnosis: Diagnosing a brain tumor is a challenging process that requires
the correct and rapid examination of MRI scan images. The study’s findings directly
contribute to enhancing the accuracy and reliability of DL models for identifying brain
tumors, focusing on this specific medical area. This is critical for early diagnosis and
treatment planning for patients.

text:
Conclusions
In essence, the objective of this investigation was to assess the proficiency of diverse
DL models in categorizing brain tumors. Following a series of comprehensive experiments
and detailed analysis, it became apparent that these models exhibited varying degrees of
competence for the assigned task. Models such as DenseNet121, EfficientNetB0, ResNet50
GoogLeNet, and Inception V3 distinguished themselves as top performers with almost
flawless levels of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores. For detailed classification
results, refer to Table 3. Conversely, AlexNet and the innovative ViT Transformer, a
recent contender in the field, displayed potential, but fell behind in terms of accuracy and
achieving an optimal equilibrium between precision and recall. This research accentuates
the significance of carefully selecting the most suitable DL model that aligns with the
specific requirements of the application. It further underscores how advancements in
neural network architectures, exemplified by the ViT Transformer, persist in shaping the
field of DL and computer vision, presenting captivating prospects for future advancements.
In summary, both Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ consistently provided a more accept-
able insight into model interpretability compared to other methods tested in our study. Put
simply, these methods precisely revealed the location of tumors, significantly enhancing our
understanding of how DL models make decisions in classifying brain tumors. Therefore,
it can be concluded that Grad-CAM’s and Grad-CAM++’s heatmaps have improved our
interpretative accuracy, playing a pivotal role in refining our understanding of DL model
decision-making processes. These methodologies have been instrumental in enhancing the
precision of our interpretations. This study contributes to selecting the correct DL model
for brain tumor classification tasks while shedding light on ongoing challenges in making
these models transparent and interpretable. However, further extensive work could be
carried out to compare correlation measures and feature localization precision among the
different studied models.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and large vision models (LVMs) have driven
significant advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV),
establishing a foundation for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to integrate
diverse data types in real-world applications. This survey explores the evolution of MLLMs
in radiology, focusing on radiology report generation (RRG) and radiology visual question
answering (RVQA), where MLLMs leverage the combined capabilities of LLMs and LVMs
to improve clinical efficiency. We begin by tracing the history of radiology and the devel-
opment of MLLMs, followed by an overview of MLLM applications in RRG and RVQA,
detailing core datasets, evaluation metrics, and leading MLLMs that demonstrate their
potential in generating radiology reports and answering image-based questions. We then
discuss the challenges MLLMs face in radiology, including dataset scarcity, data privacy
and security, and issues within MLLMs such as bias, toxicity, hallucinations, catastrophic
forgetting, and limitations in traditional evaluation metrics. Finally, this paper proposes
future research directions to address these challenges, aiming to help AI researchers and
radiologists overcome these obstacles and advance the study of MLLMs in radiology.

text:
Introduction
Radiology is essential in modern healthcare, serving as a primary diagnostic tool
for monitoring treatment and predicting outcomes. It encompasses diverse data sources
including electroencephalographs, laboratory tests, and demographic information. Clini-
cians rely on a combination of these modalities to diagnose and treat various conditions.
Imaging modalities (e.g., X-rays and computed tomography (CT) scans) make up a sig-
nificant portion of patient data and play a major role in diagnosis by clearly presenting
health conditions. Additionally, text data (e.g., radiology reports and clinical notes) are
also vital, capturing detailed medical information in natural language. Images and text
together support clinical diagnosis and treatment recommendations, with radiologists
summarizing imaging findings to guide physicians in patient management. However,
rising demand for radiological exams and a shortage of radiologists have led to delays,
forcing clinicians to make critical decisions without radiological opinions, which can lead
to different conclusions from those of experienced radiologists [1,2].
With advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision (CV) and natural
language processing (NLP) methods now enable multimodal learning by integrating and

analyzing diverse data sources [3,4]. Multimodal learning, which automates the processing
of varied medical data types, is increasingly adopted to enhance the affordability and
quality of patient care in radiology. Recently, large language models (LLMs) and large
vision models (LVMs) have gained significant interest, with prominent examples including
GPT-4V [5], LLaMA 3 [6], and DALL-E 3 [7]. Leveraging the capabilities of LLMs and LVMs,
multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in tasks like image captioning [8] and
multimodal dialogue [9]. Medical-specific LLMs and MLLMs, such as Med-PaLM 2 [10]
and LLaVA-Med [11], have shown notable progress in pharmaceutical development [12]
and clinical support [13].
Among multimodal tasks in radiology, radiology report generation (RRG) and radi-
ology visual question answering (RVQA) are particularly impactful due to their direct
support for clinical workflows and decision-making. Research on clinically relevant ap-
plications emphasizes these two tasks as they align closely with radiologists’ core needs
for documentation and interactive querying [14]. MLLMs for RRG synthesize visual and
textual data to create detailed, accurate reports, streamlining documentation and enhancing
clinical completeness [15,16]. Similarly, MLLMs for RVQA allow healthcare professionals
to interactively query imaging studies, such as CT scans, offering case-specific insights
that support diagnostic decisions [17,18]. By extending radiologists’ capabilities, reducing
workload, and supporting less experienced physicians, these applications hold significant
clinical value.
Prior reviews have explored the development and applications of LLMs and MLLMs
in medicine and radiology. For instance, Lin et al. authored the first medical VQA survey,
detailing its history and research directions [19]. Similarly, Demirhan et al. provided an
overview of medical VQA, covering methods, datasets, and potential business models [20].
Additionally, Sloan et al. analyzed automated RRG approaches, focusing on datasets, ar-
chitectures, techniques, and evaluation methods [21]. Meanwhile, Yang et al. discussed
LLM development for biomedical and clinical use, highlighting key challenges and limita-
tions [22]. Furthermore, D’Antonoli et al. reviewed LLMs in radiology, addressing their
history, technical basics, medical applications, and future directions [23]. Hartsock et al.

also contributed by examining advancements in VLMs, emphasizing datasets, architectures,

Finally, Xiao et al. outlined a comprehensive overview of the development, principles,
applications, challenges, and future directions of LLMs and MLLMs in medicine [25]. How-
ever, while these reviews address various aspects of LLMs and MLLMs in medicine and
radiology, they either primarily focus on LLMs without thoroughly examining MLLMs
or emphasize the applications and impacts of MLLMs in medicine, lacking detailed dis-
cussions specific to radiology. In contrast, this survey not only covers the background of
MLLMs but also explores their recent advancements in radiology, specifically tailored for
RRG and RVQA, with a clear structure and comprehensive coverage. In summary, our
contributions are as follows:
•
This survey provides a detailed overview of radiology’s evolution and advancements
in MLLMs, establishing a solid foundation for their application in RRG and RVQA. It
equips radiologists and researchers with essential knowledge about MLLMs.
•
This survey highlights key datasets, MLLMs, and evaluation metrics for RRG and
RVQA, offering radiologists and researchers valuable resources to innovate and seam-
lessly integrate MLLMs into radiology.
•
This paper summarizes the current challenges and potential solutions of MLLMs in
radiology, serving as a crucial guide for radiologists and researchers to drive future
research and development.

section_heading: Radiology in the Era of AI
text:
Radiology in the Era of AI
Radiology is a medical field dedicated to diagnosing and treating diseases using
imaging techniques. Over time, it has become a vital part of modern healthcare. Significant
advancements in radiology began in the late 19th century, notably with Wilhelm Roentgen’s
discovery of X-rays in 1895. This breakthrough laid the foundation for more advanced
imaging approaches such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), CT, and ultrasound [26].
In the late 20th century, medical imaging techniques progressed quickly. Picture Archiv-
ing and Communication Systems (PACS) greatly enhanced the acquisition, storage, retrieval,
and sharing of images [27]. Functional imaging techniques, such as positron emission
tomography (PET) [28] and Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) [29],
provided insights into cellular processes and offered vital information about organ function-
ality. Hybrid imaging technologies such as PET/CT combined PET’s metabolic data with
CT’s anatomical details, significantly improving the accuracy of lesion detection and charac-
terization [30]. The advent of three-dimensional (3D) and four-dimensional (4D) imaging
further enabled real-time monitoring of physiological activities [31]. Interventional radi-
ology, including image-guided biopsies, enhanced patient outcomes by offering real-time
visualization of targeted regions [32].
The use of virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) technologies has significantly
advanced radiology by enhancing the visualization of imaging data, improving diagnosis,
and optimizing treatment planning [33]. Machine learning has revolutionized radiology,
boosting image analysis accuracy and minimizing diagnostic errors [34]. Moreover, the per-
formance of computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) tools has been elevated through the integra-
tion of radiology, pathology, and genomics data, enabling more comprehensive diagnostic
services [35]. With the powerful reasoning and understanding capabilities of LLMs, their
application in radiology further strengthens efficiency and overall performance.

text:
Large Language Models
Transformers [36] are the backbone of modern natural language processing (NLP),
leveraging an encoder–decoder architecture and self-attention to capture contextual rela-
tionships. Multihead attention enables parallel processing, while feedforward networks
(FFNs) refine patterns. Built on this architecture, LLMs scale to hundreds of billions of
parameters. Trained on massive internet data, they excel in a wide variety of language
tasks, with a primary focus on text generation. Prominent examples include GPT-3 [37],
GPT-4 [38], PaLM [39], and LLaMA 3 [6]. LLMs exhibit a range of novel capabilities, in-
cluding in-context learning (ICL) [37], instruction following [40], and reasoning through
chain of thought (CoT) [41].
The advanced capabilities of LLMs are being increasingly applied to medical innova-
tions. Med-PaLM 2 uses CoT prompting to address medical queries, surpassing physicians
in several evaluations [10]. ChatGPT was employed by Ali et al. to generate clinical letters,
streamlining this otherwise time-consuming task for clinicians [13]. The vast knowledge
base in pretrained LLMs like LLaMA is also utilized to interpret patient inquiries more
effectively and offer accurate medical guidance [42]. Additionally, Liu et al. introduced a
GPT-4-based de-identification framework that integrates contextual information to auto-
matically detect and remove identifying details, demonstrating the potential of LLMs in
enhancing privacy protection [43].
The integration of LLMs into radiology is also advancing rapidly. Current research [44,45]
has explored how LLMs can enhance patient health literacy by providing timely, radiology-
specific responses to patient inquiries about their imaging results. These studies highlight the
impressive capabilities of LLMs such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing in offering relevant and
accessible information. Additionally, Fink et al. utilized the few-shot learning capabilities of
LLMs to efficiently extract and classify information from radiology reports [46].

title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology for Report Generation and Visual Question Answering
authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Large Vision Models
Similar to LLMs, LVMs are inspired by the Transformer architecture. The Vision
Transformer (ViT) [47] extends this architecture into CV, bridging the gap between text and
image domains and validating it as a unified framework. ViT captures intricate relationships
across an image by treating it as a sequence of smaller patches. Each patch is flattened into
a vector, embedded, and enriched with positional encodings to preserve spatial structure.
A key feature of ViT is a special token that captures global image information through a
unique and learnable embedding. Subsequent developments in CV have enhanced and
expanded the ViT model, including DeiT [48], Swin Transformer [49], TNT [50], MAE [51],
MoCo-v3 [52], and BeiT [53]. In 2023, Meta AI introduced the Segment Anything Model
(SAM) [54], a universal image segmentation model that employs prompt engineering as a
pretraining objective to tackle diverse downstream tasks. SAM consists of an image encoder,
a prompt encoder, and a mask decoder, which enhance its computational efficiency and
adaptability. The use of prompt engineering allows SAM to generalize effectively across
various segmentation tasks, including video object tracking [55–58], 3D reconstruction [59],
and image editing [60,61].
The concept of visual prompts in CV originated with interactive segmentation, where
user inputs like clicks [62–66] or bounding boxes [67–69] guided model segmentation.
This evolved to include task-specific vector prompts inspired by NLP, enabling models
to generate or analyze visual content effectively for tasks such as image classification,
detection, and generation. Notable models in this area include VPT [70], AdaptFormer [71],
and Convpass [72], which refine LVMs through adaptable prompts, enhancing task per-
formance without incurring high computational costs. Additionally, DAM-VP introduces

text:
Information 2025, 16, 136
diversity-aware meta-visual prompts to improve generalization across varied datasets,
optimizing models for specific tasks with enhanced adaptability and efficiency [73].
The advanced capabilities of LVMs are increasingly applied to medical innovations,
particularly in medical image analysis. Zhou et al. utilized SAM for polyp segmentation,
a crucial task in diagnosing and treating colorectal cancer, demonstrating SAM’s broad
generalization ability [74]. SAMAug enhances specialized medical segmentation models
by using SAM-generated masks and features as augmented inputs, eliminating the need
for direct fine-tuning of SAM [75]. Similarly, SAM-Adapter injects task-specific information
into SAM through lightweight adapters, significantly improving polyp identification [76].
Additionally, PRISM employs visual prompts to interactively refine 3D medical image
segmentation, achieving performance levels close to human experts across four tumor
segmentation datasets [77]. MedSAM adapts the original SAM model specifically for
medical image segmentation, fine-tuning it to address the unique characteristics of medical
images and meet the specific demands of this field [78].
The applications of LVMs in radiology are progressing rapidly. Shi et al. evaluated
SAM’s performance on three X-ray datasets, demonstrating its adaptability and efficiency
in X-ray image segmentation tasks with simple fine-tuning [79]. Ranem et al. fine-tuned
SAM to enhance segmentation accuracy and reliability, showing that providing just a few
points or a simple bounding box can yield precise results [80]. Additionally, a label-efficient
medical segmentation method was developed using a novel Meta-driven Visual Prompt
Selection (MVPS) mechanism. This method utilizes a prompt retriever from a meta-learning
framework to actively select optimal images as prompts, enhancing both computational
and label efficiency for X-ray segmentation tasks [81].

text:
Modality Fusion
In recent decades, a central focus in AI has shifted from unimodal to multimodal meth-
ods. Multimodal approaches leverage diverse data types, such as text, images, and audio,
to address real-world challenges [82]. Compared to unimodal methods, multimodal fusion
utilizes the complementary strengths of various data streams, reducing errors due to poor
data quality and cross-modal noise. Early research aimed to improve multimodal fusion ac-
curacy in tasks such as visual grounding and video captioning, often relying on rule-based
systems and manually designed features. For instance, the ‘Blocks World’ problem from
the 1970s and 1980s illustrated how early efforts connected vision (understanding block
arrangements) with language (interpreting commands), laying the foundation for modern
multimodal methods, even before the rise of deep learning techniques [83].
Based on different data fusion stages, there are four main multimodal fusion methods:
early fusion, deep fusion, late fusion, and hybrid fusion.
Early fusion occurs at the data level, typically in the input stage, where raw data from
different modalities are aligned and mapped into a common space. This approach combines
multimodal data to create richer and more expressive representations, establishing quick
correlations across modalities and maximizing the use of valuable information. However,
it demands more computational resources.
Deep fusion takes place during feature extraction, combining multimodal data in the
feature space to generate fused features. These features compensate for missing data across
modalities and are then used for classification or regression tasks in the prediction stage.
Deep fusion operates at a coarser granularity than early fusion [84], reducing computing
cost. However, it faces dimension explosion issues because as feature dimensions grow to
a specific scale, model performance declines and information loss increases.
Late fusion, a decision-level fusion, occurs at the prediction stage. Each modality has
its own decision branch, and the final output combines all these decisions. This approach

authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Information 2025, 16, 136
effectively leverages decision information from each modality without requiring raw data
fusion. However, relying on unimodal predictions can lead to missed or false detections
due to limitations in the data themselves.
Hybrid fusion combines decision-level information from one branch with data-level
or feature-level information from others, creating a cascade relationship across multiple
modalities. In cases where single-level fusion methods lack the accuracy and robustness
needed to handle data noise and loss, hybrid fusion leverages the strengths of early, deep,
and late fusion strategies. Although hybrid fusion addresses the limitations of unimodal
fusion, it increases model complexity and training difficulty.

authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Vision-Language Models
Recent advancements in multimodal models have been significantly influenced by
breakthroughs in deep learning for visual–language tasks. Recurrent Neural Networks
(RNNs) [85,86] established benchmarks for sequential data such as natural language,
while Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [87] became the preferred choice for image
and video analysis. This era saw the rise of popular tasks, such as image captioning
that generates detailed descriptions for visual content and VQA, where models answer
questions related to images and videos. Common vision–language models employ joint
embeddings to align visual features derived from CNNs with text features processed by
RNNs or Transformers [36]. This approach maps both modalities to a joint semantic space,
thereby boosting cross-modal learning [88–91].
Beyond vision and language, researchers proposed models for additional data types
such as 3D data and audio. Mroueh et al. proposed a deep learning multimodal approach
to integrate visual and auditory data in speech recognition tasks, utilizing CNNs to handle
visual data and RNNs to process sequential audio input [92]. Arandjelovi ́c and Zisserman
presented a self-supervised method that learns to recognize visual objects and align them
with their corresponding sounds in unlabeled videos, utilizing CNNs to process both visual
and audio data [93]. Moreover, Qi et al. explored two innovative approaches for classifying
3D objects. They applied volumetric CNNs to interpret 3D object data represented as
voxels and utilized multiview CNNs to analyze multiple 2D projections of the objects [94].
These contributions highlight how multimodal learning can uncover complex relationships
among various modalities, yielding representations that are both diverse and precise.

title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology for Report Generation and Visual Question Answering
authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Pretraining for Multimodal Transformers
Advancements in multimodal models have progressed as researchers investigate the
benefits of pretraining these models using extensive data before task-specific fine-tuning.
This strategy has significantly enhanced performance in diverse applications. Following the
successes of pretrained NLP models such as BERT [95], T5 [96], and various GPTs [37,97],
researchers have developed multimodal Transformers capable of processing cross-modal
inputs, including text, images, audio, and point cloud [98–100].
Noteworthy visual–language models, including ViLBERT [101], VisualBERT [102],
CLIP [103], SimVLM [104], Flamingo [105], and BLIP2 [8], have been pretrained on large-
scale visual and language data. Additional research has investigated multimodal models
for applications such as video comprehension [106], audiovisual scene analysis [107],
and the processing of 3D data [108]. Pretraining enables these models to align diverse
modalities and improve the encoder’s capacity for representation learning, with the goal of
generalizing across different tasks without requiring task-specific training data.
Moreover, the advancement of multimodal models has paved the way for novel
and intriguing potential uses. Motivated by GPT-3, Ramesh et al. introduced DALL-E,
a model capable of generating images from textual descriptions [109]. Meanwhile, Stable

authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Information 2025, 16, 136
Diffusion [110] and ControlNet [111] leverage a UNet-based diffusion model and CLIP to
create images based on textual prompts. These developments show the immense potential
of multimodal models across a range of applications including sports [112], art [113],
and autonomous driving [114].

title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology for Report Generation and Visual Question Answering
authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Multimodal Large Language Models
Research interest in MLLMs has been rising due to their ability to leverage the power
of LLMs (e.g., FLAN [115,116], OPT-IML [117], InstructGPT [40], and ChatGPT [118])
and LVMs (e.g., ViT, Swin Transformer [49], and SAM) to implement cross-modal tasks.
They demonstrate remarkable emergent abilities, such as storytelling based on images
and conducting mathematical reasoning. These abilities are uncommon in traditional
approaches, indicating a promising path toward achieving general-purpose AI.
MLLMs employ various key techniques, such as Multimodal Instruction Tuning, which
equips models with the ability to follow instructions across different modalities [119–121],
and Multimodal In-Context Learning, enabling models to gain insights from multimodal in-
puts [122–126]. Additionally, Multimodal CoT ensures the model sustains coherent reason-
ing across multiple data sources [127–131], while LLM-Aided Visual Reasoning leverages
the power of LLMs to boost performance in visual reasoning tasks [124–126,132–135].
MLLMs align more closely with human perception, offering a user-centric interface
and supporting a wider scope of tasks compared to LLMs or LVMs. Recent advancements
in MLLMs have been spurred by the development of GPT-4V [136], which has exhibited
outstanding capabilities. Researchers are making significant strides in developing powerful
and open-source MLLMs, showcasing impressive practical applications.

title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology for Report Generation and Visual Question Answering
authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Radiology Report Generation
RRG is a fundamental task in radiology, where medical images are analyzed to produce
detailed reports that highlight identified abnormalities, their specific locations, and poten-
tial differential diagnoses, all aimed at guiding patient treatment [137]. Figure 2 shows a
basic framework for RRG, utilizing an encoder–decoder model to generate reports. Typi-
cally, a CNN encodes the image into a fixed-length vector representation, while an RNN
decodes this representation to produce a descriptive caption. A standardized radiology
report typically includes several components: The examination refers to the type of exam
performed, while the indication provides the reason for the exam. The comparison notes
any references to prior exams, and the technique outlines the scanning method utilized.
Additionally, the findings section captures the radiologist’s observations, concluding with
an impression that summarizes the key findings [138]. The primary focus of RRG is on
drafting the findings and impression sections [18].
Figure 2. Architecture of RRG.

title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models in Radiology for Report Generation and Visual Question Answering
authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Datasets for RRG
Public datasets have been pivotal in advancing RRG. Key datasets include Indiana
University Chest X-Ray (IU X-Ray) [139], MIMIC Chest X-ray (MIMIC-CXR) [140], MIMIC-

text:
Multimodal Large Language Models for RRG
Leveraging MLLMs for RRG is a rapidly growing area of research. R2GenGPT [146]
employs Swin Transformer as a visual encoder and LLAMA2-7B as the LLM to effectively
align image features with language representations, enhancing performance on MIMIC-
CXR and IU-Xray. For the MIMIC-CXR dataset, 270,790 samples are used for training, 2130
for validation, and 3858 for testing. As for the IU-Xray dataset, it is divided into training,
testing, and validation sets in a 7:1:2 ratio. However, freezing the LLM improves efficiency
but limits adaptation to the medical domain and may reduce the accuracy of generated
radiology reports. Ji et al. introduced ClinicalBLIP [147], an MLLM tailored for RRG, build-
ing on InstructBLIP [148], which employs contrastive language–image pretraining [103]
and Flan-T5-XL [116] as the visual encoder and LLM. ClinicalBLIP uses a multistage fine-
tuning approach with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [149] to enhance its medical image
understanding, integrating Q-Former [8] to link visual and textual data. Through prompt
learning, ClinicalBLIP leverages prior knowledge for more precise, contextually accurate
reports. Tested on IU X-RAY and MIMIC-CXR, ClinicalBLIP outperformed other models,
demonstrating its effectiveness in high-quality RRG. For the IU X-RAY dataset, 2668 reports
are used for training and 669 for testing, while for the MIMIC-CXR dataset, 152,173 reports
are selected for training and 1196 for testing. Nonetheless, using both LoRA and Q-Former
for visual–textual alignment may introduce parameter redundancy by addressing simi-
lar tasks [147]. MAIRA-1 combines a specialized CXR image encoder with a fine-tuned
LLM based on Vicuna-7B, enhanced by text augmentation. This combination achieves
state-of-the-art (SOTA) RRG performance on MIMIC-CXR, utilizing 146,909 training sam-
ples, 7250 validation samples, and 2461 testing samples, while significantly improving
radiologist-aligned metrics such as RadCliQ. On the other hand, MAIRA-1 is limited by
noisy datasets that cause errors and ungrounded outputs as well as evaluation metrics that
penalize performance on incomplete reference reports [150].
Additionally, XrayGPT aligns a medical visual encoder (e.g., MedClip [151]) with a
fine-tuned language model (e.g., Vicuna) to generate concise, clinically relevant summaries
of chest X-rays, fine-tuned on high-quality data from free-text radiology reports in MIMIC-

reinforcement learning to produce accurate chest X-ray reports. LM-RRG includes an
LLM-driven visual feature extractor (e.g., BLIP-2) that captures features from both specific

pretraining. However, the paper does not offer concrete solutions to address the issue of

Traditional lexical metrics such as BLEU [156], ROUGE [157], METEOR [158], and
CIDEr [159] are commonly used to evaluate RRG based on textual similarity. However,
radiology-specific metrics like CheXbert vector similarity [160], RadGraph-F1 [161], and Rad-
CliQ [161] provide a more comprehensive evaluation of report quality in medical contexts,
focusing on the clinical accuracy and relevance of the generated reports.

match reference ones by analyzing the overlap of n-grams, where n-grams are sequences of
consecutive words of length n. We first compute the brevity penalty BP to punish the score

RadGraph-F1 [161] is a radiology-specific metric for evaluating the accuracy of clinical
information. It is based on the RadGraph model [162], which parses radiology reports
into graphs of clinical entities (references to anatomy and observations) and their relations.
RadGraph-F1 calculates the overlap of clinical entities and relations extracted from machine-
and human-generated reports. Entities match if they have identical text spans and assigned
types, while relations match if they have identical endpoint entities and relation types.
The final score is the average overlap.
RadCliQ [161] is a radiology-specific evaluation metric designed to assess the qual-
ity of RRG systems. It integrates multiple components to measure both textual simi-
larity and clinical relevance. RadCliQ combines BLEU for surface-level text matching,
BERTScore for semantic alignment, CheXbert vector similarity to evaluate clinical correct-
ness, and RadGraph-F1 to gauge clinical structure accuracy. This composite metric provides
a holistic assessment by focusing not just on lexical matching but also on the clinical fidelity
of the generated reports, making it particularly suitable for medical AI evaluation.

text:
Radiology Visual Question Answering
The goal of RVQA is to provide precise answers to image-based questions, thereby
reducing repetitive tasks and alleviating the workload of radiologists. Figure 4 depicts a
standard RVQA architecture, with components for image encoding, question encoding,
feature fusion, and answer generation. The image encoder may use a CNN model such
as VGG-16 [163] or ResNet-50 [164], while the text decoder can be an LSTM [85] or a
Transformer. Feature fusion between image and question vectors is achieved through either
simple concatenation or a Stacked Attention Network (SAN) [165], which employs multiple
attention layers to progressively refine attention distributions, focusing on the most relevant
image regions for the given question. Typically, RVQA questions can be divided into two
categories: open-ended, which generate detailed and free-form answers, and closed-ended,
which limit responses to predefined options such as yes/no, multiple-choice answers,
or numerical ratings [18,166]. RVQA is approached as either a classification task, where the

produces open-form text. Sometimes, both methods are combined to enhance results [19].

Multimodal Large Language Models for RVQA
Utilizing MLLMs for RVQA is becoming increasingly popular. ELIXR combines a
language-aligned image encoder via an adapter with the fixed PaLM 2 model, reaching
an overall accuracy of 58.7% in RVQA [175]. Ha et al. proposed a method combining a
radiology-specific LLM (e.g., RadBloomz-7b [176]) with a biomedical vision encoder (e.g.,
BiomedCLIP ViT [177]), using LoRA to reduce trainable parameters without compromising
performance. The model is pretrained on the image-captioning task for medical concept
alignment, then on a general MedVQA dataset for obtaining medical VQA knowledge.
Fine-tuned on downstream MedVQA tasks, it achieves leading accuracy on SLAKE and
competitive results on VQA-RAD [178].
LLaVa-Med adapts the VLM LLaVa to the medical field, utilizing a biomedical
language–image instruction-following dataset. It generates visual features using the
pretrained CLIP [103] encoder ViT-L/14 [47], which can also be replaced with Biomed-

CLIP [179]. Before being fed into the LLaMa-7B text decoder along with the tokenized
instructions, these visual features are processed through a linear projection layer. Another
option of the text decoder is Vicuna [180]. Fine-tuning LLaVA-Med outperforms previous
supervised SOTA on VQA-RAD [11]. MUMC is a novel self-supervised approach that
learns unimodal and multimodal representations of medical images and text using medical
image–caption datasets. It uses unimodal and multimodal contrastive losses, masked
language modeling, and image–text matching as pretraining objectives. The pretrained
model is then transferred to downstream medical VQA tasks, achieving SOTA accuracy on
three datasets with substantial performance gains [181]. PeFoMed is a parameter-efficient
framework used to fine-tune MLLMs specifically for medical RG and VQA tasks. Using the
EVA [182] as visual encoder and the LLaMA2-chat (7B) as text decoder, PeFoMed employs
LoRA for efficient fine-tuning while leaving the other components of the LLM completely
frozen, significantly outperforming GPT-4V on VQA-RAD [183].
Gu et al. introduced LaPA for medical VQA, which features a module to generate
the latent prompt, a multimodal fusion block with latent prompt fusion module to extract
clinical-relevant information, and a prior knowledge fusion module to integrate the re-
lationship between diseases and organs. LaPA outperforms the SOTA model ARL [184]
with a 1.83% improvement on VQA-RAD, comprising 315 radiology images, 3064 question–
answer pairs, and 451 testing pairs [185]. Ossowski et al. developed a generative model
enhanced by multimodal prompt retrieval (MPR) for medical VQA, which integrates
prompts and multimodal features to create free-text answers. This demonstrates promising
results in zero-shot and few-shot shift results among various datasets such as SLAKE [172]
and VQA-RAD [186]. M4CXR is another MLLM aimed at improving chest X-ray inter-
pretation, capable of supporting tasks such as RG, visual grounding, and VQA. It shows
exceptional performance in RVQA on MIMIC-CXR-VQA [174] by employing a CoT prompt-
ing strategy [187]. Kim et al. proposed CoQAH, a method using a series of QA interactions
between an LLM and a VQA model trained on synthetic data to generate logical answers
for human-written questions. CoQAH achieves SOTA performance on 3D-rendered and
chest X-ray datasets without fine-tuning [188].

text:
Discussion
The future of MLLMs in radiology is highly promising but also presents significant
challenges [190]. As technology advances, integrating MLLMs could revolutionize diagnos-
tics, treatment services, and patient support. Emerging MLLMs may enhance capabilities
in analyzing complex medical conditions, generating comprehensive radiology reports,
and improving communication between radiologists and AI systems. However, these
developments also introduce various hurdles that need to be addressed.
One of the key challenges in developing effective MLLMs in radiology is the scarcity of
diverse and publicly available datasets, which limits their ability to fully capture complex
and rare clinical scenarios [191]. Promising solutions involve using MLLMs with large
context windows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to enhance the model’s
contextual understanding by incorporating relevant information. Pretraining MLLMs
within the RAG framework could further improve their performance, especially in handling

unfamiliar medical cases [192]. Additionally, federated learning (FL) offers a way to address
data privacy concerns while expanding dataset access. By allowing models to be trained
across institutions without sharing sensitive data, FL facilitates collaborative learning while
maintaining patient confidentiality [193].
The privacy and security concerns are critical. Medical LLMs and MLLMs are often
trained on extensive datasets, including data that may contain personally identifiable infor-
mation. Patient information such as names and phone numbers can be extracted through
prompts, resulting in serious privacy and security risks [194]. Despite efforts to enhance
security through methods like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning
from human feedback (RLHF), sensitive data can still be exposed from training data using
techniques like multistep jailbreaking prompts [195]. To mitigate these risks, common
methods include removing personal information from datasets [42,196] or adding con-
trolled noise to the data [197]. Additionally, using high-quality synthetic data generated by
models like ChatGPT or GPT-4 can further reduce the risk [198]. Finally, strengthening legal
regulations and oversight on data acquisition and usage can help prevent unauthorized
access to patient information.
Large-scale corpora, particularly those sourced from the internet, often contain biased
viewpoints that LLMs and MLLMs may inadvertently learn [199,200]. These biases can
include disparities related to race [201], gender [202], and politics [203]. Additionally,
LLMs may generate toxic responses, exhibiting aggressive or harmful views that dispro-
portionately affect specific groups [204]. Such biases and toxicities pose significant risks to
patient safety, especially for individuals with mental health conditions. Mitigating these
issues requires addressing bias in training data through careful curation and screening
of diverse, balanced, and representative datasets, ensuring models learn from a broader
range of perspectives [199]. Utilizing empathetic data has also been shown to reduce
toxic content generation [205]. However, prescreening pretraining datasets and retraining
models to minimize bias and toxicity can be costly. A more cost-effective strategy is to
screen high-quality datasets for anti-bias and anti-toxicity measures during the SFT and
RLHF phases. Furthermore, enhancing evaluation methods for model bias and toxicity is

empathetic data has also been shown to reduce
toxic content generation [205]. However, prescreening pretraining datasets and retraining
models to minimize bias and toxicity can be costly. A more cost-effective strategy is to
screen high-quality datasets for anti-bias and anti-toxicity measures during the SFT and
RLHF phases. Furthermore, enhancing evaluation methods for model bias and toxicity is
essential. For instance, developing comprehensive benchmarks for model bias and toxicity
helps detection and allows developers to conduct regular model reviews [199,206].
The challenge of hallucinations in generative MLLMs significantly impacts their
reliability and usability [207]. Hallucinations occur when models produce outputs that
neither reflect the input images nor align with proven medical expertise. In radiology,
such errors can lead to serious consequences, like inaccurate diagnoses or inappropriate
treatment suggestions. A key factor behind hallucinations is the misalignment between
visual and textual data [208]. Addressing this issue requires better integration of these
modalities. For example, LLaVA-RLHF [208] effectively reduces hallucinations by using
RLHF to improve modality alignment. Further research is needed to develop MLLMs
rooted in factual radiology knowledge to minimize hallucinations.
Overcoming catastrophic forgetting presents another significant obstacle in developing
MLLMs for radiology. This challenge arises when a model inadvertently distorts or erases
previous knowledge while learning new information, thereby compromising its overall
performance. Striking the right balance in fine-tuning is crucial. Reasonable fine-tuning en-
hances the model’s ability to adapt to particular tasks, while overly fine-tuning can result in
catastrophic forgetting [209,210]. Leveraging techniques from continual learning [210–214],
which facilitates models to learn progressively and adapt to unseen data without losing
previously acquired knowledge, is particularly valuable for MLLMs in radiology [214].
Additionally, integrating adapters within the continual learning framework provides an
effective strategy for mitigating catastrophic forgetting [215].

Lastly, traditional evaluation metrics often fail to fully capture the intricate nuances
of clinical language, making it difficult to reliably assess the performance of MLLMs in
medical tasks [161]. This challenge is especially prominent when measuring the accuracy
of RRG or open-ended question answering in RVQA, where the metrics must differentiate
clinically relevant details. Developing customized metrics specifically for RRG and RVQA
is crucial. These metrics will both enhance the accuracy of model evaluations and measure
aspects such as generalization, efficiency, and robustness. Generating such metrics will be
key to improving MLLMs’ capabilities in radiology.

authors: Ziruo Yi; Ting Xiao; Mark V. Albert
text:
Conclusions
In recent years, the development of LLMs and LVMs has led to breakthroughs in NLP
and CV. Researchers have subsequently explored MLLMs to harness the complementary
strengths of multiple data streams, particularly visual and textual data, to mitigate errors
from poor data quality and cross-modal noise by combining the capabilities of both LLMs
and LVMs. These advancements have driven numerous applications in healthcare. To help
researchers and radiologists navigate the current technological landscape and development
of MLLMs in radiology, this survey highlights the paradigm shift introduced by MLLMs,
tracing the history of radiology and outlining the full scope of MLLM advancements. It also
serves as a comprehensive guide, covering essential medical datasets, MLLM applications,
and evaluation methods for RRG and RVQA tasks, examining the substantial potential of
MLLMs in radiology.
Despite the notable achievements of MLLMs in RRG and RVQA tasks, several chal-
lenges and limitations persist, hindering their practical deployment in clinical radiology
settings. This survey discusses these issues faced by current MLLMs in radiology, including
the lack of datasets, concerns with data privacy and security, model bias and toxicity,
hallucinations, catastrophic forgetting, and limitations in traditional evaluation metrics,
and also proposes potential solutions to address them. These insights aim to support the
future integration of MLLMs into practical radiology applications.

title: Utilizing Customized CNN for Brain Tumor Prediction with Explainable AI
authors: Md Imran Nazir; Afsana Akter; Md Anwar Hussen Wadud; Md Ashraf Uddin
text:
Abstract
Timely diagnosis of brain tumors using MRI and its potential impact on patient survival are
critical issues addressed in this study. Traditional DL models often lack transparency, leading to
skepticism among medical experts owing to their "black box" nature. This study addresses this gap
by presenting an innovative approach for brain tumor detection. It utilizes a customized Con­
volutional Neural Network (CNN) model empowered by three advanced explainable artificial
intelligence (XAI) techniques: Shapley Additive Explana-tions (SHAP), Local Interpretable Model-
agnostic Explanations (LIME), and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM). The
study utilized the BR35H dataset, which includes 3060 brain MRI images encompassing both
tumorous and non-tumorous cases. The proposed model achieved a remarkable training accuracy
of 100 % and validation accuracy of 98.67 %. Precision, recall, and F1 score metrics demonstrated
exceptional performance at 98.50 %, confirming the accuracy of the model in tumor detection.
Detailed result analysis, including a confusion matrix, comparison with existing models, and
generalizability tests on other datasets, establishes the superiority of the proposed approach and
sets a new benchmark for accuracy. By integrating a customized CNN model with XAI techniques,
this research enhances trust in AI-driven medical diagnostics and offers a promising pathway for
early tumor detection and potentially life-saving interventions.

The early detection of brain tumors is critical for saving lives and improv-ing patient outcomes. Brain disorders, including tumors
caused by abnormal cell growth, present significant challenges in modern medicine and pose serious risks to individuals of all ages [1].

However, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical imaging, particularly when using CNN, introduces the challenge

change observation. Grad-CAM is a visualization technique used to understand the decision-making process of a neural network,
particularly in image-classification tasks. It generates a heatmap that highlights the regions of an input image that contribute the most
to a specific class prediction. By understanding the complicated interactions between the input feature choices and model output, these
approaches can serve as interpreters.

Explainable AI techniques
Different XAI techniques were applied in this model to accurately un-derstand the internal working procedures of the model and
how it makes decisions using SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM.
SHAP: SHAP values are used to determine the complex decision-making process of the neural network. They are a computational
approximation of Shapley values, a method for assigning payouts to players in a cooperative game, or, in this case, contribution values
to features in a prediction task. Training examples that comprise a context set provide a benchmark for the feature contributions. The
trained model and backdrop data were used to ini-tialize the Deep Explainer, thereby making it possible to calculate the SHAP values
for certain test images. These numbers show how individual pixels affect the predictions, which makes it easier to understand which
features have a significant impact on the model’s output. The outcome images help to create a more transparent and understandable
neural system by providing detailed knowledge of the model’s decision boundaries.
LIME: This method uses a model-agnostic methodology to explain the behavior of local predictions. The local model behavior is
approximated around a set of test images using modified samples, which are defined as a prediction function and initialized as a LIME
explainer. The creation of an interpretable surrogate model makes it easier to pinpoint important features, and the resulting visual­
izations draw attention to the precise areas that influence the model predictions. LIME improves the transparency of individual
predictions by emphasizing local interpretability and providing important insights into the neural network’s decision-making at the
instance level.
Grad-CAM: In the field of image classification, in particular, the Grad- CAM technique is a useful method for improving the un­
derstanding of DL models. Grad-CAM generates informative heat maps that emphasize areas that are crucial to the decision-making
procedure of the model. Without specifically identifying the framework, the code utilizes a trained brain-tumor detection model.
After loading an image, preparing it, and running the Grad- CAM method, the last convolutional layer is used to extract the features.
Subsequently, the original image is layered with the generated heatmap, which shows the key regions that influence the predictions of
the modifications.

Proposed model
This study presents an innovative methodology for brain tumor detection employing the customized CNN model shown in Fig. 3,
enhanced by the integration of three advanced XAI techniques: SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM.
This research developed a customized CNN specifically designed to identify brain tumors. Customization involves designing the
architecture to enhance the feature extraction and classification accuracy specific to medical imaging challenges. The model begins
with an initial layer that has 32 filters and progresses through layers with 64, 128, and 256 filters using a 3 × 3 kernel size for each.
These layers are designed to incrementally capture more complex features in brain imaging data. To keep the model efficient and
focused on important features, including activation functions called ReLUs (Rectified Linear Units) and max pooling steps that help
reduce the size of the data passing through the network. After processing through these layers, the data are flattened and passed
through a series of dense layers with 128 neurons and 64 neurons to finalize the decision-making process of the model. In addition,
a dropout layer reduces the chance of overfitting, which means that the model is more reliable when analyzing new, unseen brain
images. The final decision of whether a tumor is present is made using a sigmoid function, which is well suited for binary classification

Limitation
Despite the significant advancements and high performance achieved by the proposed customized CNN model for brain tumor
detection, it is essential to acknowledge the inherent limitations of this study. These limitations provide context for the results and
highlight areas for future improvement and exploration.
• Trained the model using only one dataset, and for generalizability testing, used another dataset. This approach may limit the
robustness of the study’s findings because of the potential lack of diversity in the training data.
• The model’s current classification capability is restricted to binary outcomes (tumorous vs. non-tumorous), and it does not yet
differentiate between specific tumor types such as glioma, pituitary adenoma, and meningioma.
