authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
Abstract
Objectives Automatic data extraction from free-text radiology reports enables large-scale research, but few studies
assessed the performance of large language models (LLMs) on Dutch neuroradiology reports.
Materials and methods We analyzed 947 brain MRI reports from a tertiary memory clinic (2016–2021), authored by
consultant neuroradiologists. Trained medical students annotated thirty variables; 100 reports were double annotated
to assess inter-rater reliability. We evaluated the performance of the open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1 using different
languages (Dutch vs English translation) and few-shot prompting with different example selection strategies.
Performance was evaluated using balanced accuracy for categorical variables, accuracy and mean absolute error for
counts, and text similarity for free text. Metrics were computed across 10 random splits of the 947 reports.
Results LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated high zero-shot performance for visual rating scores (mean [95% CI]): medial
temporal atrophy: 0.90 [0.77–1.00] on the left and 0.96 [0.94–0.99] on the right, Global Cortical Atrophy: 0.87 [0.83–0.91],
and Fazekas: 0.94 [0.93–0.96]. Microbleed mentions were detected with 0.93 [0.92–0.95] accuracy, and infarct mentions
with 0.82 [0.80–0.84]. Text similarity for lesion location reached 0.95 [0.95–0.96]. Performance was lower for numerical
variables: 0.80 [0.78–0.82] for the number of microbleeds and 0.66 [0.63–0.68] for infarcts. English translation yielded
comparable results. Few-shot prompting improved performance for numerical variables, achieving 0.92 [0.90–0.93] for
microbleeds and 0.81 [0.77–0.85] for infarcts using structural similarity-based selection.
Conclusion LLaMA 3.1 shows strong potential for extracting data from Dutch neuroradiology reports. Few-shot
prompting enhances performance for numerical variables, whereas challenges remain for location-specific variables.
Key Points
Question The free-text format of radiology reports limits the accessibility of structured data; can LLM LLaMA 3.1
automatically structure free-text Dutch neuroradiology reports?
Findings LLaMA 3.1 accurately extracted 30 variables from Dutch neuroradiology reports, with few-shot prompting
significantly improving performance compared to zero-shot prompting, particularly with similarity-based example selection.

authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
Introduction
The rapid advancements of radiology techniques and their
growing accessibility have led to an increasing volume of
radiology reports, offering a rich resource for data-driven
medical research. However, their unstructured and free-
text format limits their usability, particularly in large-scale
analysis [1]. Although expert organizations such as the
European Society of Radiology (ESR) advocate for the
adoption of structured reporting (SR) in clinical practice,
its implementation remains limited [2]. This is primarily
due to technical barriers (e.g., incompatibility with radi-
ology information systems), challenges in documenting
complex cases, and resistance from radiologists to rigid
templates conflicting with their established workflow [3].
Currently,
extracting
structured
data
from
free-text
reports relies on manual annotation, which is time-
consuming and error-prone. This raises the need for
automated solutions, particularly for complex applica-
tions such as dementia, where reports often contain
detailed findings and specialized metrics [4].
Recently, ESR emphasized the potential of large language
models (LLMs), such as OpenAI’s Generative Pretrained
Transformer 4 (GPT-4), in automating the conversion of
free-text
reports
into
structured
formats
[5].
These
transformer-based models trained on extensive text corpora
can perform advanced language tasks with minimal anno-
tated data [6, 7]. Recent studies demonstrated their effec-
tiveness in extracting clinical information across diverse
languages and applications [4, 8]. For instance, Lehnen et al
[9] utilized GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to extract structured data
from stroke reports. Adams et al [10] evaluated GPT-4 for
standardizing German MRI/CT reports, and Sasaki et al
[11] applied GPT-4 to Japanese interventional radiology
reports. Cozzi et al [12] evaluated the performance of GPT-
3.5, GPT-4, and Bard in performing BI-RADS classification
in Italian, English, and Dutch reports. Despite their pro-
mising results, significant challenges remain in imple-
menting LLMs for
SR
[4]. Most
studies
relied
on
proprietary models like GPT-4, which require data transfer
to external servers, raising privacy concerns and limiting

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
clinical adoption [8]. Open-weight LLMs, which allow local
deployment, present a potential solution, though their
performance in specialized medical domains requires fur-
ther validation [13]. In this regard, Nowak et al [1] reported
that open-weight models achieve competitive performance
to private models in extracting variables from English chest
X-ray reports. Builtjes et al showed that open-weight
models outperform fine-tuned task-specific models on 28
extraction tasks from Dutch medical reports [14]. However,
benchmark analyses reveal that such models underperform
proprietary counterparts [15], particularly in non-English
languages and specialized domains, as their training pre-
dominantly relies on general-domain English data [16, 17].
While fine-tuning with domain-specific data can enhance
accuracy, hospital settings often lack the required compu-
tational resources and annotated datasets [13]. Few-shot
prompting, where models are given input-output pairs as
examples, emerges as a low-resource alternative that
showed promise in simpler tasks such as LI-RADS classi-
fication [18], yet its potential in radiology remains under-
explored [19, 20].
This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the
open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1 for structuring Dutch neu-
roradiology reports, encompassing 30 variables of diverse
types (categorical, numerical, and free-text). We first com-
pare its zero-shot performance to human raters using con-
sensus annotations and assess inter-rater reliability (IRR).
Next, we assess whether English translation of the input
reports improves performance. We also investigate few-shot
prompting as a resource-efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic
assessment of an open-weight LLM for structured radiology
reporting in Dutch using few-shot prompting, providing
critical insights into the feasibility of scalable, privacy-
preserving solutions for clinical deployment.

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
Materials And Methods
Dataset
The study was approved by the institutional Medical Ethics
Committee with a waiver of informed consent (METC-
2023-0569). It retrospectively included Dutch neuroradiol-
ogy reports from 947 patients who underwent brain MRI as
part of their diagnostic work-up at a tertiary memory clinic
between 2016 and 2021. We included all consecutive
patients with an MRI performed within three months of
their initial consultation. Reports were authored as part of
routine practice by different radiologists at the same clinic.
Of all 947 reports, 152 were drafted following a structured
template with predefined fields; the other 795 reports had
no predefined structure, leaving the outline of the report up
to the radiologist. Each report was manually annotated for
30 variables by one of three trained final-stage medical
students, using a structured template with standardized
guidelines that defined variable definitions, acceptable
values, and provided instructions for handling missing data
(See Appendix B for variable definitions and distributions).
The template included 24 clinical variables related to brain
atrophy and vascular lesions, and 6 internal quality control
(QC) variables. We applied Monte Carlo cross-validation
(MCCV) by generating 10 random splits of the dataset, each
with 50% training and 50% test data. Training sets were
used to select few-shot examples; test sets were used for
evaluation. To assess inter-rater agreement and compare
the model to human performance, a random subset of 100
reports was independently annotated by two raters, with
consensus reached in consultation with a neuroradiologist
(M.W.V., 15 years of experience).
LLM prompting
As LLM, we used LLaMA 3.1 (Meta, July 2024) [21], because:
(1) its open-weight nature allows local deployment, which
complies with hospital data governance requirements; (2) an
evaluation on a general-domain Dutch benchmark showed it
can process Dutch text, with no performance gain by fine-
tuning [22]; and (3) the availability of multiple model sizes
(8B, 70B, and 405B parameters) allows institutions to choose
models that fit their resources. We used the 8B and 70B

Comparison to human performance and inter-rater

examples), compared to human performance. Model
outputs and individual human annotations were
compared to consensus labels as reference standard.
In parallel, we assessed IRR between the two
annotators.

were back-translated into Dutch using LLaMA 3.1 to
maintain evaluation consistency. An author (K.M.)

Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis
Variable-specific performance metrics were used. For
categorical variables, we used balanced accuracy to
account for class imbalance; missing was treated as a
separate class. For count variables, we used accuracy (i.e.,
percentage of model outputs matching the reference
annotation) and mean absolute error (MAE). For MAE,
entries marked as missing by either the model or the
annotator were excluded. For free-text fields, semantic
similarity was computed between model outputs and
reference annotations by calculating the cosine similarity
of sentence embeddings generated using Sentence-BERT
[24], with RobBERT-v2 (a Dutch transformer model) as a
backbone
[25].

well-

used to evaluate whether the model and human annota-

comparisons. IRR was measured using Cohen’s Kappa for
categorical variables, inter-class correlation (ICC) for
count variables, and semantic similarity for text fields
[28]. Agreement levels for Kappa and ICC were defined
according to McHugh [29] and Koo and Li [30], respec-
tively. For text similarity, values above 0.9 were con-
sidered to indicate high agreement. A bootstrapping and
sensitivity analysis is presented in Appendix E to assess
the impact of inter-rater differences on the computed
metrics. In the remaining experiments, 95% confidence
intervals (CIs) were computed following the corrected
resampled t-test [31] to account for dependency between

Results
We evaluated the performance of LLaMA 3.1 in extract-
ing 24 neuroradiology report variables. For results related
to QC variables, see Appendix C. This section reports
results for the 70B version, which performs comparably or
significantly better than the 8B version for nearly all
variables (Appendix D). F1 scores for categorical variables
and Spearman’s correlation for numerical fields are pro-
vided as additional metrics in Appendix G. Tables in this
section are visualized as radar plots in Appendix J.
Comparison to human performance and IRR
Table 1 shows the results of the comparison with human
performance and IRR on the 100 double-annotated
reports.
LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated high performance on stan-
dardized visual rating scales, achieving balanced accuracy
of 0.98 for left medial temporal atrophy (MTA), 1.00 for
right MTA, 1.00 for Fazekas score, and 0.85 for overall
global cortical atrophy (GCA), all comparable to human-
level performance (p > 0.05). Detection of the mention of
brain infarcts (0.83) and microbleeds (0.86) was slightly
lower but remained on par with at least one annotator.
The model excelled in extracting lesion locations, with
high text similarities (0.95 for infarcts, 0.96 for micro-
bleeds). Numerical variables proved challenging, particu-
larly infarct counts, where extraction accuracy ranged
from 0.66 to 0.78, falling significantly below Annotator 1
(p < 0.05). The low MAE suggests that when numerical
values were extracted, they were mostly correct; and the
lower accuracy is due to confusion between true lesion
counts and cases where the count was missing from the
report. Performance was also lower for lobar GCA scores
and infarct subtypes. In 3 of the 24 variables (occipital
GCA, cerebellar infarcts, and splinter infarcts), the model
performed significantly worse than both human annota-
tors (p < 0.05). Notably, these variables were reported less
frequently (see Table S1). IRR varied, ranging from near-
perfect (κ = 0.99 for MTA) to poor agreement (κ = 0.39
for superficial siderosis). Considering variables with
moderate or higher agreement as reliable, most catego-
rical (15/17) and numerical (4/5) variables and both text
fields met this threshold, indicating satisfactory annota-
tion consistency. Bootstrapping results in Appendix E.1
further show that single-rater annotations yield compar-

detection of lesion presence, particularly using structural
similarity-based selection (balanced accuracy for cerebellar
infarcts: 0.85, 95% CI: 0.81–0.89; splinter infarcts: 0.86, 95%
CI: 0.82–0.89). Random and fixed selection increased the
extraction accuracy for three vascular lesion counts (cortical
infarcts, lacunes, cerebellar infarcts), and similarity-based
approaches yielded significant improvements across all
numerical variables. For instance, structural similarity-
based prompting yielded an accuracy of 0.81 (95% CI:
0.77–0.85) for infarct count, exceeding zero-shot perfor-
mance (0.66, 95% CI: 0.63–0.68). Accuracy for microbleed
counts using this method (0.93, 95% CI: 0.90–0.96) was also
higher than the zero-shot setting (0.80, 95% CI: 0.78–0.82).
Free-text variables showed no improvement.
We compared the examples extracted by the structural
and semantic similarity measures (Fig. S9) and found that
they extracted different examples for most test reports.
Table 4 shows that all methods require under 30 s for
inference. Few-shot prompting increases inference time
by 7%. Random selection is the fastest method at 0.30 ms,
while semantic similarity-based selection is the slowest at
170.43 ms.
In terms of format, all generated outputs across all
settings were syntactically valid JSON strings. The model
was instructed to return an empty JSON object if the
input did not correspond to a valid radiology report. We
quantified the number of empty JSON outputs per
experiment. The zero-shot setting produced 13.00 empty
JSON outputs per split on average. Few-shot prompting
reduced this number substantially: random selection
(9.80), fixed selection (5.10), structural similarity-based
selection (1.90), and semantic similarity-based selection
(2.00). In all non-empty JSON outputs, every key defined
in the template (Appendix A) was consistently included in
the generated JSON object.

showed
that
most

Discussion
This study evaluated the open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1
for extracting structured data from Dutch radiology
reports in a tertiary dementia clinic. We first assessed
model performance compared to two human raters using
100 consensus-annotated reports. We then used the full
dataset of 947 reports to examine the impact of input
language and evaluate few-shot prompting with different
example selection strategies as a resource-efficient alter-
native to fine-tuning.

authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated promising zero-shot cap-
abilities in extracting 24 variables from Dutch brain MRI
reports, performing overall comparably to human raters.
We observed that the model shows excellent performance
on simple variables (e.g. standardized visual scales). Per-
formance was lower when extraction concerns specific
locations in the brain (e.g. lobar GCAs) or specific lesion
subtypes. Numerical variables pose additional difficulties,
often demanding arithmetic operations (e.g., summing
numbers of infarcts across different locations). Perfor-
mance was also lower for variables that were less fre-
quently reported by radiologists. Most variables showed
moderate to near-perfect IRR, with only a few displaying
poor agreement. Stratified analysis (Appendix E) found no
link between agreement level and model performance,
likely to reflect the sensitivity of IRR to class imbalance in
rare findings such as superficial siderosis. However, lower
agreement may introduce noise into the reference stan-
dard, so results for individual variables with weak agree-
ment should be interpreted cautiously. Despite this,
manual annotations remain the reference standard in
radiological AI.
No significant performance gain was observed from
translating the reports to English. Notably, the findings
suggest that using the original Dutch reports yields more
reliable results than using translations. A key challenge
was handling local terminology. For example, the Dutch
term “splinterinfarcten”, referring to small, linear, streak-
like cortical cerebellar infarcts, has no direct equivalent in
the English literature and was therefore consistently
mistranslated, leading to extraction errors. These infarcts
are distinct from typical territorial cerebellar infarcts as
their linear or radial configuration is consistent with the
involvement of small penetrating vessels or distal emboli,
aligning them more closely with small cortical infarcts
and microinfarcts [34]. This morphological distinction
motivated their separate analysis in our cohort. We
addressed the mistranslation by including terminology-
mapping in the translation prompt. This straightforward
approach can be applied to other datasets but requires
prior knowledge of local terms. Parameter-efficient fine-
tuning methods could enable LLMs to learn local termi-
nology and improve their domain knowledge directly
from data, though current evidence suggests they under-
perform in limited-data settings [35]. We observed

mapping in the translation prompt. This straightforward
approach can be applied to other datasets but requires
prior knowledge of local terms. Parameter-efficient fine-
tuning methods could enable LLMs to learn local termi-

from data, though current evidence suggests they under-
perform in limited-data settings [35]. We observed
reduced performance in extracting free-text fields from
translated reports. Upon examination, this reduction was
primarily due to terminology discrepancies introduced
during the translation of extracted content back into
Dutch, which negatively impacted metric computations.
Overall, the model showed a strong ability to interpret
and process Dutch medical language, despite being pri-
marily trained on English data.
We explored few-shot prompting as a resource and
data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning, which is often
impractical in clinical settings due to high computational
and annotation costs. Our results show that few-shot
prompting with curated example selection can sig-
nificantly improve model performance. Variables that
initially showed low performance in the zero-shot setting
benefited most. Data extraction required less than 30 s
per report in our experimental setup using two NVIDIA
H100
GPUs,
corresponding
to
a
throughput
of
approximately 120 reports per hour. While such hard-
ware exceeds typical radiology workstation specifica-
tions, this configuration is feasible in centralized hospital
IT environments, academic medical centers, and cloud-
based infrastructures, where on-demand GPU instances
are available at moderate hourly cost. The primary
intended use case of large-scale registry generation and
retrospective structuring of reports is inherently batch-
oriented and does not require real-time processing; at
the observed throughput, hospital-scale datasets can be
processed in acceptable time frames. For prospective
picture archiving and communication systems (PACS)/
RIS integration, reports would be routed from the PACS/
RIS to the extraction service, with structured outputs
written back to the registry or electronic health record
for radiologist review; automated structuring would
occur in parallel with routine reporting and remain
substantially faster than manual template completion.

Several

can
further
reduce

and smaller model variants offer an alternative trade-off.
LLaMA 3.1 8B can be deployed on a single consumer-

most variables, indicating that the accuracy gain from
the 70B model is clinically meaningful (Appendix D).
The 8B variant nonetheless remains a viable option for
resource-constrained
settings.
Ongoing
advances
in
model compression and inference hardware are expected
to further narrow the gap toward seamless clinical
deployment. Beyond the retrospective analysis reported
in this work, real-world use would require a prospective
validation on locally collected reports, periodic expert
audits to detect drift, and confidence-based flagging of
uncertain extractions for targeted review. Structured
outputs should be treated as decision support rather
than final records, with radiologist review incorporated
for flagged cases and for variables with known weaker
agreement. The traceability of each structured field back
to specific text in the source report further supports
efficient human verification. Any application of auto-

authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
considered in the context of regulatory and safety fra-
meworks governing medical software. Tools that use
patient data or influence clinical workflows may be
subject to medical device regulations such as the Eur-
opean Union’s Medical Device Regulation [36]. Using
open-weight models that can be deployed on local
institutional hardware avoids sending protected health
information to external services and enables hospitals to
maintain control over data governance and audit logs,
potentially simplifying compliance with privacy and
security standards. Nonetheless, rigorous validation,
careful documentation of intended use, and adherence to
relevant regulatory requirements will be necessary for
any intended clinical deployment of LLM-based systems.
This study focused exclusively on extracting clinical
variables from Dutch radiology reports in a tertiary
memory clinic cohort using LLaMA 3.1. Although newer
open-weight LLMs exist, LLaMA 3.1 remains competi-
tive according to recent benchmarks (www.vellum.ai/
open-llm-leaderboard (Update of 19 November 2025)).
Medical-specialized LLMs can offer advantages in more
heterogeneous domains that require advanced clinical
reasoning, such as oncology, but evidence for their
consistent benefit in structured information extraction is
limited. For instance, Zhu et al showed that an oncology-
specific LLM outperformed LLaMA 3 in predicting
cancer progression [37], yet Liu et al [38] found that,
without
task-specific
fine-tuning,
general-purpose
LLaMA 3.1 8B outperformed Llama-3-8B-UltraMedical
on structuring radiology and pathology reports. In our
cohort, reports contained structured elements such as
visual rating scales, reducing the need for specialized
medical knowledge and making a general-purpose model
sufficient. A systematic comparison across newer general
and medical-domain LLMs for this specific task remains
an important direction for future work. The translation
quality assessment was limited by its single-rater design
and sample size (n = 50), although the consistency of the
observed differences and the downstream extraction
results support the reported conclusions. Our study also
lacked external validation, which limits its general-
izability beyond the present cohort. Future research will
extend to diverse and less standardized clinical domains
to broaden the impact of these results. We employed

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb; Amos Pomp; Antoine Manenti; Romy de Haan; Farog Faghir; Joy Martens; Harro Seelaar; Francesco Mattace-Raso; Meike W. Vernooij; Frank J. Wolters; Stefan Klein; Esther E. Bron
text:
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the potential of open-weight
LLMs for extracting structured clinical information from
radiology reports. Few-shot prompting with informed
example selection significantly improves performance,
approaching human-level accuracy for most variables.
Although challenges persist for complex or ambiguous
cases, the model’s effectiveness in processing Dutch
medical text underscores the promise of LLMs as scalable
tools for post-hoc structuring of free-text reports. Future
work should validate this approach across models, extend
it to other clinical domains, and explore multimodal
integration to enhance its applicability across different
research settings.

authors: Khalid M. Hosny; Mahmoud A. Mohammed; Rania A. Salama; Ahmed M. Elshewey
venue: Neural Computing and Applications, Volume 37, pages 1289–1306
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors are very dangerous as they cause death. A lot of people die every year because of brain tumors. Therefore,
accurate classification and detection in the early stages can help in recovery. Various deep learning techniques have
achieved good results in brain tumor classification. The traditional deep learning methods and training the neural network
from scratch are time-consuming and can last for weeks of training. Therefore, in this work, we proposed an ensemble
approach depending on transfer learning that utilizes pre-trained models of DenseNet121 and InceptionV3 to detect three
forms of brain tumors: meningioma, glioma, and pituitary. While developing the ensemble model, some changes were
made to the architecture of pre-trained models by replacing their classifiers (fully connected and SoftMax layers) with a
new classifier to adopt the recent task. In addition, gradient-weighted class activation maps (Grad-CAM) are an explainable
model to verify results and achieve high confidence. The suggested model was validated using a publicly available dataset
and achieved 99.02% accuracy, 98.75% precision, 98.98% recall, and a 98.86% F1 score. The suggested approach
outperformed others in detecting and classifying brain tumor MRI data, and verifying results using the explainable model
achieved a high degree of trust.

Introduction
Brain tumors are among the most severe types of malignant
tumors. These are abnormal tissue masses where cells
spread and replicate excessively, appearing unregulated by
the processes that manage usual cells. Tumors of the brain
can cause either focal or generalized neurologic symptoms
[1]. There are two types of brain cancers: primary tumors
and secondary tumors. Primary brain cancers arise in the
brain and may grow in any part of the brain or spinal cord.
Primary cancers can be malignant or benign. On the other
hand, secondary cancers form within different organs, such
as the lungs, breast, and kidneys, before spreading to the
brain.

The most frequent forms of brain tumors are menin-
gioma, glioma, and pituitary. Most commonly, gliomas are
brain tumors, though they can also occasionally be dis-
covered in the spinal cord. Gliomas are the predominant
type of brain cancer found in adults [2]. These cancers are
caused by the glial cells, which wrap and support neurons.
Meningioma originates in the meninges, the outer three-
level tissues that envelop the cerebral area immediately
beneath the skull. Meningiomas represent 53.9% of non-
malignant cancers, according to United States Central
Brain Tumor Registry statistics from 2013 to 2017 [3].
Tumors of the pituitaries are abnormal pituitary gland
evolution. The size of this gland is comparable to that of a
pea. It is placed behind the nose, near the base of the brain.
Some tumors cause the pituitary gland to produce exces-
sive amounts of certain hormones that control critical
biological functions.
A range of medical imaging modalities can be used to
diagnose brain tumors. Three of the most extensively used
technologies are ultrasonography (US), magnetic reso-
nance imaging (MRI), and computed tomography (CT).
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most frequently
used harmless imaging technology. Unlike X-ray and CT
imaging, it does not release dangerous ionizing radiation
and provides a clearer image. Furthermore, MR allows for
more freedom in imaging settings. Two kinds of imaging
sequences are frequently utilized. T1-weighted scans pro-
vide exceptional structural details; T2-weighted scans, on
the other hand, can distinguish between healthy and dis-
eased tissue [4].
In the early stages, accurate diagnosis and classification
of various types of cancer are critical. However, this task is
challenging because tumors differ in dimension, form, and
place. Many machine learning (ML) and deep learning
(DL) algorithms are applied for brain tumor classification.
ML approaches are time-consuming since they rely on
hand-crafted recognition of features for training before
categorization. Several studies employed ML approaches
to analyze medical images, such as support vector machi-
nes [5], k-nearest neighbors [6], and decision trees [7].
While DL techniques can extract features automatically
and have proven that they can be used to analyze images in
healthcare efficiently, the convolutional neural network
(CNN) is one of the most well-known models, as it can
distinguish both general and specialized features in medical

While DL techniques can extract features automatically

distinguish both general and specialized features in medical

Artificial intelligence is used in many fields, including
the medical domain. DL models are complicated and do
not interpret the obtained results; hence, increasing confi-
dence and trust in such models in the medical domain
should be implemented to remove the gap between AI
models and human understanding. Such models that are not
interpretable are known as ‘‘black boxes’’ [11]. Explainable
AI refers to methods and strategies for implementing
models that interpret and explain the produced results. In
CNN, the input image can be explained by obtaining
weighted gradients of the classification result for the final
convolutional layer, which allows us to identify the sig-
nificant parts with the highest impact on the predicted
class, which is then converted into a heat map overlay
along with the input image. Various studies have imple-
mented DL with explainable AI in the medical field
[12, 13].
DL has proved efficient in many fields, especially in the
medical field, which has increased recent research to
improve the performance of computer-aided diagnosis
systems. For example, Ghafourian et al. [14] presented an
ensemble model for brain tumor classification. Firstly, they
used the social spider optimization (SSO) segmentation
algorithm. Secondly, they employed an ensemble approach
comprised of three classifiers to diagnose brain tumors. The
three classifiers used were Naive Bayes (NB), support

Their proposed method was evaluated on two datasets,

acceptable accuracy of 98.61% and 99.13%, respectively.

and combining the most significant features extracted from
brain MR images. They also utilized nine ML classifiers to

Proposed methodology
This section introduces pre-trained networks, explains the
suggested methodology and the specific hyperparameters
employed, and emphasizes the explainable method.
3.1 DenseNet121
DenseNet121 [30] is an image classification convolutional
neural network (CNN) that evolved from earlier CNN
architectures like VGG and ResNet. It enhanced the
transfer of information and gradients across the network by
introducing different connectivity patterns so that each
layer directly connects to all subsequent layers. It consists
of multiple dense blocks comprising convolutional layers
of (1x1 and 3x3) filters. To decrease the size of input
feature maps, bottleneck layers (1x1 convolutional layer)
were used before each 3x3 convolution, which helped
boost computational performance. Moreover, it uses tran-
sition layers composed of a 1x1 convolutional layer and a
2x2 average pooling layer to control the growth of feature
maps and the number of parameters.
3.2 InceptionV3
InceptionV3 [31] is a convolutional
neural network
designed for image classification purposes and has proven
its efficiency in detecting complex image patterns. It uses
inception modules in which each module uses multiple
convolutional layers in parallel with varying kernel sizes
(1x1, 3x3, 5x5) and max pooling operations. Also, it
employed the idea of factorization by using a combination
of small convolutions (3x3, 1x7, and 7x1), which helped
reduce
the
number
of
parameters
and
computation
processing instead of using larger convolution filters. In
addition to combating the vanishing gradient problem, it
uses auxiliary classifiers at intermediate layers of the net-
work to push proper gradients to the lower layers, which
makes
them
immediately
helpful
and
improves
convergence.

Ensemble model
We proposed an ensemble model of DenseNet121 and
InceptionV3 based on transfer learning. The classifiers
(fully connected and SoftMax layers) were removed, and a
new one was introduced to be trained on the CE-MRI
dataset. After training the classifier for both pre-trained
networks, both models were combined using the soft voting
approach to get the predicted tumor class by computing the
mean probability of each class. The predicted class has the
highest mean probability. Figure 3 displays the diagram of
the suggested methodology.
To avoid overfitting, adopt a dropout layer [35] and L2
regularization [36]. The dropout layer can reduce overfit-

Explainable model
The proposed research employed the gradient class acti-
vation map (Grad-CAM) as the explainable model. Grad-
CAM is a method of differentiating locations that visual-
izes why a particular area is chosen or assigned. It can be
used for any CNN without further retraining or changing its
architecture. Grad-CAM is implemented on the last con-
volutional layer of DenseNet121 and InceptionV3, as
convolutional layers store spatial information missed in the
fully connected layer. Additionally, the final convolutional
layers have the most significant benefit of combining high-
level semantics and spatial data [32]. Grad-CAM can find
considerable parts of the input image by obtaining impor-
tance weights while backpropagating gradients concerning
activations. Furthermore, some modifications were made to
Grad-CAM to explain any convolutional layer.

confusion matrix is a standard method for assessing per-
formance in classification problems. It analyzes the clas-
sification model in a table of actual and predicted samples
from every class. The confusion matrix calculates the most
important measures: accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1-
score. As stated in [38], the classification metrics for multi-
class problems can be derived from binary classification
metrics.

samples for each class, whereas a standard k-fold does not.

Conclusions
This research article aimed to classify different brain
tumors effectively using ensemble learning based on
transfer learning with explainable AI. Preprocessing was
done on the dataset by extracting ROI through applying a
threshold, cropping, and resizing to remove the unneces-
sary black parts of the image. Two pre-trained models
(DenseNet121 and InceptionV3) were used with a new
classifier to adopt the recent task. The dropout layer and L2
regularization were
used to
overcome
the
overfitting
problem. Also, data augmentation was applied to make the
model more robust, expand the size of training instances,
and overcome imbalanced classes.
The model was evaluated against a publicly available
dataset using two methods: Train–test split and stratified
k-fold cross-validation to ensure that the model is reliable.
An explainable model was adopted to highlight the sig-
nificant parts, and testing was done on MR images obtained
on different planes. The ensemble model solves the
shortage in prior works, as combined models can perform
better in classification than single models by extracting
predictions or features from more than one model. The
explainable model can highlight the affected areas in MR
images, increasing the trust level of the model that neu-
rologists and surgeons can use.
In the future, we seek to develop a more efficient and
effective hybrid approach using DL and ML techniques
that can reduce the number of parameters, optimize
machine resources, and enhance the extracted feature
vector.

title: Automatic brain MRI tumors segmentation based on deep fusion of weak edge and context features
authors: Leyi Xiao; Baoxian Zhou; Chaodong Fan
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors pose a significant health risk to humans. The edge boundaries in brain mag­
netic resonance imaging (MRI) are often blurred and poorly defined, which can easily
result in inaccurate segmentation of lesion areas. To address these challenges, we pro­
posed an Automatic Brain MRI Tumor Segmentation based on deep fusion of Weak Edge
and Context features (AS-WEC). First, AS-WEC introduces the Otsu Double Threshold
Weak Edges Adaptive Detection (Otsu-WD), which focuses on tumor edge information
and differentiates between lesion edges and normal cerebral sulci and gyri. Second, an
edge branching network based on the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) is constructed to fully
preserve the edge context information of the lesion region. Finally, a maximum index
fusion mechanism has been designed to incorporate a multilayer feature map, preventing
the loss of edge details during the deep feature fusion process. The experimental results
demonstrate that the Otsu-WD method outperforms the Canny and TEED algorithms in
detecting brain MRI tumor edges. In brain MRI tumor segmentation, AS-WEC delivers a
clearer visual segmentation effect compared to the classical UNet++ network and recent
models like PVT-Former. On both datasets, AS-WEC demonstrated improvements across
multiple metrics. The Dice averaged 92.96%, and the mIoU reached 93.12%, effectively
validating the method’s efficacy in brain MRI tumor segmentation. Code and pre-trained
models are available at https://github.com/DL-Segment/AS-WEC.git.
Keywords Medical image segmentation · Edges detection · Deep learning · Brain MRI

text:
Introduction
Tumors are cancers caused by the formation of abnormal cells in the brain, characterized by
a high incidence and high mortality rate (Van Den Bent et al. 2023). As of 2023, there are
24,810 reported cases of brain tumors in the United States, accounting for 85% to 90% of all
primary central nervous system (CNS) tumors (Cancer.Net n.d). Brain tumors significantly
impact patients’ lives and pose a serious threat to their health. Most brain tumor character­
ization methods are based on biopsies or obtaining tumor information via MRI. Particularly,
brain MRI, being a safe and non-invasive detection method, effectively displays brain tissue
structures and lesion areas, making it a common tool in the early prevention and diagnosis
of brain tumors (Liu et al. 2024). Despite its convenience in diagnosing clinical conditions,
brain MRI can be affected by environmental and other factors during the imaging process,
leading to issues such as artifacts and blurred details (Malhotra et al. 2022). Additionally,
the brain tumor diagnosis process is highly subjective and reliant on the expertise of medi­
cal professionals, making it challenging to achieve accurate segmentation of brain MRI
tumor lesions through manual observation alone. This reliance often leads to low diagnostic
efficiency and other limitations (Ting and Liu 2024). Consequently, there is an urgent need
for a precise and efficient brain MRI tumor segmentation method to support and enhance
medical diagnosis.
In early research on region-of-interest segmentation, scholars sought to enhance segmen­
tation efficiency by leveraging the pixel-value transformation characteristics of images. This
led to the development of numerous segmentation algorithms grounded in mathematical
statistics, primarily focusing on region growth and edge features (Yu et al. 2023). These
algorithms perform region-of-interest segmentation based on features such as image gray
values, texture changes, and color differences (Chen et al. 2023). To efficiently determine
the initial threshold for segmentation, Guo et al. (2024) employed a region-growing algo­
rithm to aggregate points of interest, effectively reducing time complexity and enhancing
segmentation accuracy. Combining edge features from brain MRI, Aghazadeh et al. (2023)
utilized the Canny algorithm to detect initial edge profiles and proposed an edge region
level set image segmentation algorithm for brain tumor lesion segmentation. With advance­

text:
Medical image segmentation model
In deep learning-based medical image segmentation models, the encoding-decoding struc­
ture is commonly used to identify pixel points within the region of interest (Li et al. 2024).
The architecture of the image segmentation network based on the encoding-decoding struc­
ture is illustrated in Fig. 2.
(1) The encoder extracts and abstracts feature from the input medical image by building
a neural network structure, converting the image into a high-dimensional feature rep­
resentation. A typical encoder generally consists of various convolution and pooling
layers, which gradually reduce the spatial size of the image while increasing the depth
of the features.
(2) The decoder maps the high-dimensional features output from the encoder to form a fea­
ture map with the same size as the original input image, while preserving the semantic
information. It typically consists of an inverse convolution layer and an upsampling
layer, through which the spatial size and details of the image are gradually recovered.
Moreover, skip connections and attention mechanisms can be introduced into the
model.

Research motivation
After analyzing existing medical image segmentation methods, as depicted in Fig. 3, several
shortcomings were identified.
(1) The blurred and irregularly shaped edges of lesions in brain MRI scans lead to misclas­
sification of the segmentation results. Existing edge detection algorithms often lack sen­
sitivity to noise and fail to accurately recognize normal brain sulcus edges, as illustrated
by the yellow circle in Fig. 3. Traditional edge detection thresholds typically require
manual adjustment and exhibit limited adaptability to brain MRIs with color variations.
Moreover, concentrating solely on the strong edges of lesions during detection may
result in the neglect of detailed information, such as weak edges.Therefore, Otsu-WD
was developed to focus on the weak edge regions of brain MRI tumors, which are often
easily overlooked.

layers. Consequently, there is a more significant loss of information, such as texture
details, in the lower layers of the image (as indicated by the red circle in Fig. 3), which
adversely affects the model’s performance on complex image segmentation tasks.
Therefore, we proposed a GRU-based edge context branching structure that leverages
the ability of GRU neurons to capture contextual features and ensures the effective
propagation of detailed information through end-to-end edge loss training.
(3) During the fusion of semantic features at different levels, crucial lesion information is
often lost. Lower-level features typically emphasize image details and edge informa­
tion, whereas higher-level features focus on overall structure and semantic concepts.
Existing segmentation methods often lack an effective balancing mechanism to ensure
that key information, such as lesion edges, is preserved and highlighted effectively (as
shown by the segmentation results in Fig. 3). This deficiency compromises the accuracy
of medical image diagnosis. Therefore, we extracted and preserved the most representa­
tive features, such as edges and textures, within the encoder by merging the maximum
values at corresponding locations in the multilayer feature map, enabling the decoder to
access this detailed information more effectively during image reconstruction.

Proposed Method
To address these issues, we proposed the AS-WEC method for segmenting tumor areas on
brain MRI. The architecture of AS-WEC is illustrated in Fig. 4. Initially, brain MRI images
undergo Otsu-WD to extract weak edge features of the tumor. Subsequently, edge images
are input into GRU-EB, which integrates a two-branch network of gated recurrent units to
ensure the transmission of critical contextual semantic information. Finally, leveraging the
encoder features from the GRU and segmentation network, multi-layer feature map fusion
is performed using MF-Max, enabling the decoder to enhance semantic layer information
and edge features during image reconstruction.

Multi-layer feature channel max-index fusion mechanism
By utilizing edge detection and deep feature extraction methods in GRU networks, rich
semantic information about the edges of brain tumors is effectively captured. However, bal­
ancing underlying details with deep semantic information remains an area of consideration.
Typically, the lower layers of a deep learning network focus on learning features such as
image texture edges, while the middle layers learn the shape and structure of objects, and the
deeper layers represent high-level semantics (Agarwal et al. 2024c). However, a deeper net­
work structure does not necessarily yield better results, as excessively deep networks may
encounter issues such as gradient disappearance and increased computational complexity
(Xu and Zhang 2022). Therefore, to balance computational efficiency and segmentation per­
formance, a 4-layer encoder-decoder model based on the U-Net (Ronneberger et al. 2015)
network structure has been designed. Building upon this, a Multi-layer Feature Channel
Max-index Fusion Mechanism (MF-Max) has been designed, with the architecture of this
method illustrated in Fig. 7.
Typically, the largest values in the feature map correspond to the most significant
responses, such as edges and textures. Therefore, by retaining the maximum value in the
encoder feature map, these representative underlying semantic features are ensured to be
fully utilized during subsequent fusion and processing, preventing them from being lost
or weakened due to operations such as downsampling. This enables the decoder to better
utilize the detailed information during image recovery, allowing for a more accurate delin­
eation of the tumor edges.

Data sets and comparative models
The LGG Segmentation Dataset (Brain-MRI-segmentation n.d) and BraTS 2019 (Menze
et al. 2015) were initially selected for experimental evaluation in this study. The model pro­
cesses input brain MRIs resized to 224 × 224 pixels. Figure 8 displays brain MRI images
from the two datasets: colored images represent the LGG dataset, while grayscale images
correspond to the BraTS2019 dataset.
1) The LGG dataset was sourced from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) and cor­
responds to 110 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) low-grade glioma collec­
tion. It includes fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences and accompanying
genomic cluster data. The dataset comprises brain MRI scans and manual segmentation
masks.
2) BraTS2019 is one of the most extensively used datasets for brain cancer diagnosis.
The dataset is primarily employed to isolate heterogeneous brain tumors, which differ in
appearance, shape, and histology, using specialized multi-modal and preoperative MRI
scans. It includes multi-modal MRI scans of brain tumors and provides manually annotated
masks that correspond to the tumor lesions.
As illustrated in Fig. 8a, the first two images did not capture the lesion area due to angle-
related issues, despite having a clear internal structure. The brain structure details are blurred
in the third image due to an uneven magnetic field. The fourth image contains artifacts and
only displays bright or dark areas. Consequently, some of the aforementioned images were
excluded after screening, and only the brain MRI images shown in Fig. 8b were retained for
model training. Specifically, the first two images exhibit high color discrimination and more
prominent tumor regions, while the third image contains large lesion regions despite low
color saturation. The fourth image, although showing a clearer brain structure and higher
contrast, has a smaller lesion area. A total of 1,077 clear brain MRIs from the LGG dataset
and 18,626 images from the BraTS2019 dataset were utilized in this experiment. Both data­
sets were split into training and test sets with an 8:2 ratio.
We selected three classical segmentation models, including DeepLabv3+ (Chen et al.
2017) and Unet++ (Zhou et al. 2020), along with four recent models: TransDeepLab (Azad
et al. 2022), EGE-UNet (Ruan et al. 2023), MSFR-Net (Li et al. 2023b), and PVT-Former
(Jha et al. 2024), for comparative experiments. It should be noted that MSFR-Net is a 3D

1) Deeplab v3+: Deeplab v3+ designs dilated convolution based on an encoder-decoder
architecture to realize the fusion of feature information of different sizes. And depth

2) UNet++: The UNet++ network is an enhanced version of the UNet architecture.
It incorporates dense connections and a nested structure between the encoder and
decoder, while also introducing auxiliary supervised branches at various depth levels of
the network.
3) Trans Deeplab: Trans Deeplab introduces Transformer’s self-attention mechanism into
the Deeplab framework for better global information capture and long-term depen­

4) EGE-UNet: EGE-UNet significantly reduces the parameter and computational cost
while maintaining excellent segmentation performance by introducing Group multi-
axis Hadamard Product Attention (GHPA) and Group Aggregation Bridge module
(GAB).
5) MSFR-Net: MSFR-Net leverages both multi-modality and single-modality features of
brain MRI and introduces a dual recalibration module (DRM) to enhance features from
different dimensions, enabling 3D segmentation of brain tumors. The segmentation
results of the slices are primarily presented in the comparative experiments.
6) PVT-Fomer: PVT-Fomer combines the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer
model with the pyramid structure in the CNN model and captures features on different
scales of the feature map to improve the model’s performance in intensive tasks.

text:
Evaluation metrics
For the detection of tumor edges in brain MRI, Precision (P) (Soria et al. 2023), Recall (R)
(Soria et al. 2023), and the F1 score (Jing et al. 2022) are considered for the quantitative
comparison. For brain MRI tumor segmentation effect evaluation, we used the 95th per­
centile of the Hausdorff distance (HD95) (Li et al. 2023b), Dice Coefficient (Dice) (Li et al.
2023b), Sensitivity (Sen) (Li et al. 2023b), Mean Absolute Error (MAE) (Li et al. 2023a),
Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) (Li et al. 2023a), Mean Pixel Accuracy (MPA) (Cui
et al. 2024) and Accuracy (Acc) (Cui et al. 2024) to evaluate the models.
To assess the efficiency of models, we utilized three metrics: GFLOPs, Inference Speed,
and Params. GFLOPs represents the number of gigafloating point operations required by the
model for a single forward pass. Lower GFLOPs indicate greater computational efficiency
of the model. Inference Speed refers to the actual time taken by the neural network model
to perform a single inference task, typically measured in milliseconds. Shorter inference
times indicate that the model performs inference more rapidly. Params denotes the number
of parameters in the model, with fewer parameters signifying a more lightweight model.

title: Automatic brain MRI tumors segmentation based on deep fusion of weak edge and context features
authors: Leyi Xiao; Baoxian Zhou; Chaodong Fan
text:
Conclusion
To improve the accuracy in brain MRI lesion segmentation, we proposed a novel automatic
segmentation method. The AS-WEC emphasizes lesion edge information by employing
weak edge adaptive detection for brain MRI tumor regions. It constructs an edge branching
structure with gating loops to propagate edge context information and designs a maximum
index fusion mechanism for multi-layered feature maps to accentuate both edge and under­
lying detail features. Analysis of the experimental results demonstrates that the AS-WEC
method outperforms other models in metrics such as Dice, MAE, and mIoU, showcasing its
superior feature extraction and fusion capabilities.
While AS-WEC demonstrates robust overall segmentation performance, the effective­
ness of feature extraction and alignment in large-scale datasets with significant variability
remains to be fully assessed, owing to the limited sample size of the current dataset. Con­
sequently, there is a need to enhance the stability and robustness of the method. However,
with ongoing advancements in medical imaging technology and equipment, increasingly
available 3D brain MRI datasets may offer opportunities to further evaluate and refine the
method. This extension aims to further enhance segmentation performance and broaden the
application scope, thereby adding more value to related work in the field of medical image
processing.

authors: Khalid M. Hosny; Mahmoud A. Mohammed
text:
Abstract
Brain tumor detection and classification are critical for timely diagnosis and effective
treatment. The surge in demand for automated and accurate methods is driven by the
advancements in deep learning and the need for faster, more reliable diagnostic tools to
assist clinicians. Despite the current literature about brain tumor classification and detec­
tion, several limitations persist. This survey reviews and contrasts the state-of-the-art deep
learning diagnostic techniques that utilized brain tumor datasets such as Figshare and
BraTS. This study provides a technical analysis of research papers on brain tumor diagno­
sis techniques, covering the period from 2020 to 2024 from well-known databases such as
Scopus and Web of Science. Recent deep learning methodologies, including convolutional
neural networks (CNNs), transfer learning, vision transformers (ViTs), hybrid techniques,
and explainable AI, are explored regarding their performance, advantages, and limitations.
We examine various architectures, preprocessing techniques, and datasets commonly used
in brain tumor studies, focusing on multi-class classification, detection, and interpretabil­
ity. Furthermore, the survey discusses the challenges in deep learning-based approaches
related to brain tumor detection, including data scarcity and model interpretability, and
outlines future directions.

authors: Khalid M. Hosny; Mahmoud A. Mohammed
text:
Introduction
A brain tumor is an atypical development of cells within or next to the brain. These tumors
may be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). Brain tumors may arise within
the brain (primary brain tumors) or propagate to the brain from other regions of the body
(secondary or metastatic brain tumors). Malignant tumors have aggressive spread behavior,
affecting vital organs' normal functions. On the other hand, non-malignant tumors do not
spread to different parts of the body but can be life-threatening depending on their size, loca­
tion, and how they affect surrounding brain structures. According to Central Brain Tumor
Registry of the United States data from 2013 to 2017, malignant tumors form 29.7% of all
brain and central nervous system tumors, while non-malignant tumors preserve the remain­
ing 70.3% (Miller et al. 2021).
Malignant and non-malignant brain tumors present a significant risk of mortality and
necessitate early diagnosis and suitable treatment. The most frequent brain tumors in adults
are meningiomas, pituitary tumors, and malignant gliomas (McNeill 2016). Malignant
tumors such as glioma can lead to severe neurological deficits, including cognitive impair­
ment, motor dysfunction, and sensory disturbances (McKinnon et al. 2021). Non-malignant
tumors such as meningiomas may cause symptoms, for instance, headaches, seizures, or
vision loss (Nassiri et al. 2020). From 2014 to 2018, there were 83,029 deaths in the United
States because of malignant brain and central nervous system tumors (Low et al. 2022).
MRI is a prevalent scanning technology for diagnosing brain tumors, as it does not emit
harmful radiation (Panych and Madore 2018). Furthermore, it offers a wide range of adjust­
able parameters that enhance the visualization of specific tissues, highlight abnormalities,
and customize the imaging process to meet clinical needs. Nonetheless, the high cost of
MRI scans makes them less available in resource-limited environments. The lengthy acqui­
sition durations may pose challenges in emergencies and introduce variability in image
quality. Deep learning techniques such as image reconstruction have mitigated these issues

maintaining diagnostic precision.
Deep learning diagnostics in brain tumors can be divided based on the purpose of the task
into three categories: classification, detection, and segmentation. Classification techniques
aim to categorize features into a predefined class label (Chen et al. 2021). Object detection
techniques focus on defining the brain tumor's bounding box (Liu et al. 2020) without pre­
cisely defining the tumor boundary, limiting their use. For example, a classification model
might categorize the MRI scan as a tumor or non-tumor. On the other hand, the detection
model defines the tumor location by drawing a bounding box around it. Segmentation tech­
niques involve producing a binary mask (Minaee et al. 2021), where each pixel is classified
as either belonging to the region of interest (tumor) or not (skull or surrounding tissues),
thereby isolating the tumor from the skull. Figure 1 illustrates the different diagnostic tech­
niques in brain tumor detection, visually comparing classification, detection, and segmenta­
tion approaches.
Brain tumor detection and classification are critical for early diagnosis and treatment
planning, where any misdiagnosis can lead to severe effects. However, numerous chal­
lenges, such as the irregular shapes of brain tumors (Hamid and Khan 2020), differ in size,
texture, and location, making accurate classification challenging. The quality of MRI scans,
which can contain noise and artifacts, affects the effectiveness of AI models. Annotating
a brain tumor dataset is difficult as it requires much time and expertise from radiologists.
The rarity of certain brain tumor types makes the existing datasets suffer from imbalanced
classes that cause models to exhibit bias toward more prevalent tumor categories. Further­
more, deep learning models have an opaque decision-making process (Hassija et al. 2024)
because they have challenges defining the contribution of specific inputs to outputs. This
lack of interpretability in their outcomes makes them untrustworthy, as clinicians require
clear justifications for model predictions to ensure reliability.

This survey study analyzes the recent deep-learning approaches for classifying and
detecting brain tumors. Specifically, we address the following research questions: What
current state-of-the-art deep learning models are used? How do various architectures com­
pare regarding performance and computational efficiency? What datasets and preprocessing
techniques are commonly utilized? How can interpretability-based models enhance confi­
dence and facilitate understanding of the decision-making process? What are the existing
challenges and open research problems that require attention?
This survey reviewed and contrasted recent studies on classifying and detecting brain
tumors using an MRI modality from Figshare, BraTS, and other datasets. Different archi­
tectures and approaches, such as CNNs, transfer learning, ViTs, hybrid techniques, and
explainable AI, were explored to highlight their performance, advantages, and limitations.
The survey mentioned current datasets and preprocessing techniques. The survey offers sta­
tistical analysis to illustrate current and future trends in brain tumor diagnosis research. In
addition, we illustrated the challenges of deep learning-based methods. We outlined future
directions, such as using hybrid models that combine CNN with ViT to enhance the feature
extraction process or novel approaches that utilize GANs to eliminate data scarcity by gen­
erating new instances.
This study is organized as stated: Sect. 2 provides the related work and compares the
survey with related review studies. Section 3 demonstrates the systematic literature review
methodology. Section 4 discusses the results of the systematic literature review methodol­
ogy. Section 5 introduces different brain tumor datasets. Section 6 analyzes various deep-
learning brain tumor diagnostic approaches, including CNNs, transfer learning, ViTs, hybrid
techniques, and explainable AI. Section 7 gives a statistical analysis. Section 8 presents the
discussion. Section 9 states the limitations and future work. Section 10 outlines the research
recommendations and conclusions.

Related Work
Previous studies reviewed various brain tumor diagnostic techniques; for example, Jalali
and Kaur (2020) offered a survey focusing on feature extraction and classification tech­

is more common than deep learning and hybrid approaches. Additionally, they concluded
that feature extraction is a crucial phase that aids in effective classification and detection.
The survey focuses on machine and deep learning techniques for segmentation, feature
extraction, and classification while ignoring the recent methods that rely on ViTs. Al-Galal
et al. (2021) suggested a survey focus on deep learning-based approaches for segmentation
and classification tasks. The authors reviewed the research papers proposing various brain
tumor diagnosis methodologies from 2018 to 2020. Their survey addressed several chal­
lenges, such as the scarcity of dataset samples and the inherent complexity of deep neural
network models that make them black boxes. The survey has limitations, as it ignores ViT
models and interpretability-based techniques.
Nazir et al. (2021) reviewed the research studies from 2015 to 2020 that detect and clas­
sify brain tumors. The paper provides a quantitative analysis for each year separately, which
is helpful to highlight how the trend is changing. According to their qualitative analysis

brain tumor segmentation and classification. At first, they started to review brain tumor seg­

Results
In this section, we provide the generated results from the databases and clearly define the
process for identifying the final elected studies. One thousand one hundred forty-six stud­

After removing the duplicate records, we obtained 798 unique entries. After the first screen­

review studies. In the second screening process, based on the article abstract, we identified a
total of 338 studies, with 146 articles excluded because they focus on machine learning, are
not related to the reviewed techniques, or are not accessible through our institutional creden­

Datasets
This section overviews various brain tumor datasets suitable for binary- and multi-class
tasks. The datasets are named according to their original names.
Figshare (Cheng 2017) includes 3064 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI images from
233 patients. The dataset has three types of brain tumors distributed as follows: meningioma
(708 slices), glioma (1426 slices), and pituitary tumor (930 slices). The slices have a resolu­
tion of 512 × 512 and are obtained in three views: axial, coronal, and sagittal. The dataset
files are stored in a mat extension where each file includes the image, class, and binary mask
that can be useful for segmentation tasks.
BT-small-2c (Chakrabarty 2019) is considered a small binary brain tumor dataset. The
dataset comprises 253 MRI pictures, 155 designated for the tumor class and 98 for the
healthy class. The MRI slices have different resolutions, and most of them are stored in jpg
extensions.
Br35H (Hamada 2020) is a balanced binary-class dataset divided into two folders: 1500
images without tumor cases and 1500 with tumor cases. The dataset also includes a folder
containing MRI cases with bounding boxes, which can be helpful in detection tasks.
Sartaj (Bhuvaji et al. 2020) concatenates Figshare and Br35H into a single dataset that
contains 3264 MRI images categorized into four types: 937 meningioma, 926 glioma, 500
no tumor, and 901 pituitary. The images have different resolutions, but most are 512 × 512
and stored in jpg extensions.
BT-large-4c (Nickparvar 2021) is an extended Sartaj dataset containing 7023 scans split
into training and testing folders. The training set includes 1339 cases of meningioma, 1321
cases of glioma, 1595 cases of no tumor, and 1457 cases of pituitary. On the other hand, the
testing set includes 306 cases of meningioma, 300 cases of glioma, 405 cases of no tumor,
and 300 cases of pituitary.

on the target dataset. Transfer learning can be applied to custom CNN architectures as the

Asiri et al. (2023) proposed a fine-tuned ViT to detect various brain tumors. Several steps

transformer blocks, the hybrid module captures features at different window sizes, which
enables defining long-range dependencies while retaining local information.
Hameed et al. (2024) proposed ARiViT, a model that combines ViTs with residual con­
volutions. The model has an encoder and decoder that work together with RiT blocks. These
blocks act as an information bottleneck and use channel compression modules to reduce
feature size and enhance their quality through dimensionality reduction. Hong et al. (2024)
employed a modified VIT-B/16 model, incorporating residual architecture into a multi-
layer perceptron. They used image enhancement techniques to improve the quality of MRI
images, such as homomorphic filtering, contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization,
and unsharp masking. The authors used a residual multi-layer perceptron instead of the
traditional one to address the faster convergence issue, which led to local optimal learning

ViT-B/32, ViT-L/16, and ViT-L/32. The authors utilized versions of the pre-trained models

achieved the best performance due to the smaller patch sizes that can capture finer details.

text:
Hybrid techniques
Hybrid techniques aim to develop new approaches by combining various methods to attain
superior performance. Researchers combined CNN with machine learning algorithm clas­
sifiers to leverage CNN's robust feature extraction and the strong performance of machine
learning classifiers. Some research studies suggested merging CNN and LSTM (Islam et
al. 2024) to extract local features from CNN and long-range dependencies from LSTM.
Additionally, ensemble learning in many studies has achieved a remarkable classification
performance (Vaiyapuri et al. 2023; Natha et al. 2024; Archana and Komarasamy 2023).
Raja (2020) implemented a brain tumor classification technique based on Bayesian fuzzy
clustering-based segmentation. Due to the noise in the MRI images, the non-local mean
filter was utilized for denoising. Instead of training the autoencoder with the whole image,
they segmented the tumor through Bayesian fuzzy clustering. The authors enhance the fea­
ture extraction process using three techniques: information-theoretic measures, wavelet
packet Tsallis entropy, and scattering transform. The Jaya optimization algorithm fine-tuned
the deep autoencoder with SoftMax for classification. Deepak and Ameer (2021) suggested
a hybrid approach of CNN as a feature extractor and SVM as a classifier. The proposed
CNN architecture consists of five convolutional layers, each with a kernel size ranging from
3 × 3 to 9 × 9, to capture varying levels of detail. Furthermore, as the features progressed to
later layers, the depth of the feature maps doubled.
Kang et al. (2021) designed an approach based on an ensemble of deep features and
machine learning classifiers. The authors examined thirteen pre-trained models and com­
bined the features of the top three models based on the classifiers' evaluations. The deep
features are then fed into nine machine-learning classifiers. The SVM using the RBF and a
fully connected network outperformed all other classifiers. Majib et al. (2021) developed a
three-phase framework. In the first phase, they explored machine learning algorithms that
best detect brain tumors. Secondly, they developed fourteen different pre-trained models.
Finally, they proposed four hybrid models using four different algorithms: stacked classifier,
AdaBoost, CatBoost, and XGBoost. They achieved the best model by integrating a deep
CNN with VGG16 and a stacked classifier as their hybrid model.

Explainable AI
Deep learning models lack transparency in decision-making, making them opaque. In recent
years, researchers have widely used explainable techniques to interpret the model results
and answer the question, "Why did the model obtain these results?". Therefore, brain tumor
studies utilized various interpretability approaches (LIME, SHAP, and Grad-CAM) to high­
light the significant features and achieve high confidence in this crucial task. LIME (Ribeiro
et al. 2016) obtains local explanations by perturbing the input image to generate similar
versions by masking some parts. A simple interpretable model is trained on these perturbed
instances and the model predictions, which help observe how the predictions change and
track the relevant features. SHAP (Lundberg 2017) feeds the model with an input image
with a masked region (super pixel). If the masked region decreases the model's confidence,
it has a positive influence. The final heatmap comprised red (positive influence) and blue
(negative influence) colors. Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al. 2017) finds the important features
by computing the gradients of the class score concerning the last convolutional layer. Fig­
ure 8 shows different explainable AI techniques used in brain tumor diagnosis.

Zeineldin et al. (2024) introduced an explainable hybrid approach between ViT and CNN
to segment glioma scans. The authors implemented a modified CNN based on a U-shaped
encoder and decoder. The encoder implements transformer blocks that capture the features
and long-term dependencies. Conversely, the decoder employs 2 × 2-up convolutional layers
to upscale the encoded features into a segmentation map. Grad-CAM was deployed to the
last convolutional layer to provide a heatmap of the most significant features.
Appiah et al. (2024) investigated a proper orthogonal decomposition model in conjunc­
tion with CNN and pre-trained models such as MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, ResNet101, and
VGG19. The proper orthogonal decomposition was used to extract the scores of the pixels
that store high-intensity values. Furthermore, the authors employed SHAP to interpret the
results. The authors used SHAP to create a feature map of positive and negative values,
color-coded red and blue, respectively. The red pixels signify a high probability of a pre­
dicted class. In contrast, blue pixels indicate a low probability of a predicted class. Mahesh
and Guluwadi (2024) utilized ResNet50 with Grad-CAM to develop a transparent frame­
work for brain tumor classification. They integrated Grad-CAM into the final convolutional
layer of ResNet50. It generates a heatmap identifying the regions with the most significant
impact on the predicted class.
Krishnan et al. (2024) introduced a rotation-invariant ViT to improve the classification
accuracy of brain tumors. The authors resolved the issue of traditional ViT, which lacks rota­
tion invariance, by generating rotated versions of the images and defining unique rotation
embeddings. Moreover, they used Grad-CAM to provide visualizations that highlight tumor
regions. Mzoughi et al. (2024) proposed two models using ViT and CNN. The architecture
of the ViT model uses the traditional transformer encoder. On the other hand, the CNN
architecture uses four convolutional layers with a kernel size of 3 × 3. The authors enhanced
the interpretability of decision-making by using three techniques of explainable AI, includ­

edge detection techniques. Additionally, the overlap between the segments of the produced

corresponding importance to the segment. Hosny et al. (2025) developed an explainable
ensemble approach through transfer learning techniques. The authors used the soft voting
rule to average the classifier results of InceptionV3 and DenseNet121. They modified Grad-

could effectively highlight the tumor regions.

the model results. The most common explainability approach in brain tumor diagnosis is
gradient-based techniques, including Grad-CAM and its variants. Grad-CAM provides
model-specific global explanations, while other methods, such as LIME and SHAP, provide
model-agnostic local ones. The model-agnostic local explanations rely mostly on how the
model will interact with the input variations. Providing interpretability for deep learning

text:
Statistical analysis
This section presents a comprehensive statistical analysis to help you understand some cru­
cial aspects of brain tumor computer-aided diagnosis research. We conducted the statistical
analysis from the Scopus database solely on journal articles, excluding conference papers.
Figure 9 illustrates the published articles on brain tumor diagnoses per subject area from
2014 to 2024. The figure reveals that computer science, engineering, and medicine-related
journals contain the majority of journals concerning brain tumor diagnosis research. Given
the importance of the brain tumor topic, we are closely monitoring the impact factor of pub­
lished articles in these journals. We found that most of the articles included in this survey
are published in first- and second-quartile journals based on their impact factor, as shown
in Fig. 10.
Given the recent advancements in AI detection, classification, and segmentation, we
have observed a rapid increase in brain tumor diagnosis research over time, with 341 articles
published in 2024, as illustrated in Fig. 11. Furthermore, the utilization of new deep learning
techniques and recent disciplines such as ViT and explainable AI in brain tumor diagnosis
research has surprisingly increased. In Fig. 12a, the total number of articles using ViT to
detect brain tumors in 2024 has reached 22, marking a fourfold increase from 2023. In addi­
tion, Fig. 12b shows that the total number of articles that utilized explainable AI techniques
with brain tumor detection models in 2024 has reached 22, marking a seven-fold increase
from 2023.
Figure 13, which displays the accuracy curve of the studies reviewed in this paper, dem­
onstrates that transfer learning techniques achieved the highest performance compared to
other approaches. The ability to transfer learning from well-architectured models trained
on vast amounts of data to small datasets in brain tumors is still dominant in classification
performance. Hybrid techniques came in second place due to their combined approaches to
enhance the feature extraction process.

necessitating training from scratch and requiring significant data for better generalization

of the task and dataset, as deeper models may lead to overfitting on small datasets. They are
sensitive to hyperparameters in which a small change can influence the model performance
(Kandel and Castelli 2020).
Transfer learning is still dominating the performance of medical image analysis, espe­
cially brain tumor diagnosis. These approaches involve fine-tuning some or all model layers
to adapt to the target task. By training their weights on large amounts of data, transfer learn­
ing models address the issue of the limited size of medical images (Alzubaidi et al. 2021),
enabling their earlier layers to extract relevant features. Also, they require shorter training
times and fewer machine resources (Yu et al. 2022). However, fine-tuning pre-trained mod­
els can be challenging to select the correct learning rate and trainable layers. Incorrect fine-
tuning of the pre-trained models could lead to bias in certain situations.
ViT approaches address the limitations of CNN by capturing spatial relationships within
image parts. These models rely on self-attention mechanisms, which help the model focus
on the significant regions to decide. The most significant challenge is that their architecture
lacks inductive biases, resulting in poor generalization when trained on small datasets (Han
et al. 2023). Recently, researchers implemented pre-trained ViT models to solve the issue

significant computational complexity issues. Deploying these methods in real-world scenar­
ios will require longer inference times to obtain the results. However, researchers addressed
the computational complexity issue through various techniques, model pruning, and quan­
tization (Ozdemir and Dogan 2024; Singh et al. 2025). Model pruning removes redundant
or less important parameters from the network. Quantization techniques involve converting
high-precision values into lower precision. Additionally, there is a trade-off between the
complexity of the model and interpretability, as complex models will face challenges inte­
grating explainability methods.
Deep learning models exhibit an inability to provide reasoning for their decisions. How­
ever, integrating explainable AI techniques with deep learning models provides a more
transparent decision-making perspective. These strategies facilitate understanding how the
model attains its outcomes and the areas of concentration influencing its decisions. Fur­
thermore, autonomous medical agents can utilize these strategies to make decisions and
provide reasoning for clinical decisions (Ullah et al. 2024). Explainable AI enhances trust
and confidence in AI models while facilitating comprehension of their unethical or incorrect
behaviors.
