set. The proposed framework is designed to achieve a better segmentation and classification results by combining
diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foundation-driven feature extraction, and prompt-guided attention learning.
Moreover, an explainability module has been included for generating attention maps that are clinically meaning­
ful, and enhance the interpretability of the model. The framework simultaneously segments and classifies tumors
in a single model, to provide powerful and secure brain tumor intelligence.
The architectural novelty of the proposed framework does not arise from introducing diffusion models, foun­
dation encoders, prompt learning, or explainability as independent techniques. Instead, it lies in the task-coupled
interaction among these components. Unlike conventional sequential pipelines in which enhancement, segmenta­
tion, classification, and explanation are performed independently, the proposed framework introduces prompt–
image cross-attention before shared feature formation. The encoder-derived visual features and prompt-refined
representations are adaptively fused into a common tumor-aware representation that simultaneously supports
pixel-level segmentation and image-level classification. Joint optimization allows segmentation supervision
to reinforce spatially meaningful features used for classification, while classification supervision encourages
diagnostically discriminative representations within the shared feature space. Thus, the contribution is a unified
prompt-conditioned dual-task architecture in which enhancement, semantic guidance, localization, and diagnosis
interact during representation learning.
The study investigates whether diffusion-based MRI enhancement, prompt-guided semantic learning, and joint
segmentation–classification can improve tumour-boundary localization, diagnostic reliability, robustness under
degraded imaging conditions, and interpretability. By integrating these functions within a shared learning archi­
tecture, the framework aims to produce accurate and clinically meaningful tumour analysis while maintaining
performance across different MRI datasets.
The major contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
1. A diffusion-enhanced preprocessing module is introduced to improve MRI quality, suppress imaging artifacts,
and enhance tumor boundary visibility.

authors: Jeena Joseph

Review of literature
Recent studies show that deep learning has become central to MRI-based brain tumor analysis, particularly for
tumor detection, classification, and segmentation. Reviews by Bouhafra et al. [10], Dorfner et al. [11], Fahim et
al. [12], and Verma et al. [13] indicate that CNNs, hybrid CNN-transformer models, and attention-based segmen­
tation networks have improved automated tumor assessment, but challenges remain in boundary precision, model
explainability, robustness, and generalization.
CNN-based and hybrid deep learning approaches have achieved strong performance in classifying glioma,
meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor MRI classes. Ahmed et al. [14] proposed a hybrid ViT-GRU frame­
work for MRI brain tumor detection and classification, while Musthafa et al. [15], Disci et al. [16], Lu et al. [17],
Ali et al. [18], Gundogan et al. [19], and Younis et al. [20] further demonstrated the usefulness of pretrained and
hybrid deep models for multiclass brain tumor diagnosis. However, many of these studies mainly focus on clas­
sification accuracy and provide limited integration between segmentation, robustness, prompt-based learning,
and clinical explainability.
Recent advances in medical image segmentation have increasingly focused on improving boundary delinea­
tion, multiscale feature representation, attention-based feature selection, and robustness to subtle intensity varia­
tions. Arshad et al. [21] proposed RaNet, a residual attention network for prostate segmentation in T2-weighted
MRI, which integrates a DilatedContextNet encoder, Multi-Scale Attention Fusion (MSAF), and a Feature Fusion
Module (FFM) to capture hierarchical contextual information and refine spatially relevant features. Evaluations
on the PROMISE12 and ProstateX datasets demonstrated Dice scores of 98.61% and 96.57%, respectively, high­
lighting the benefit of residual learning, multiscale attention, and feature fusion for precise boundary delineation
and robustness to MRI variability.

the challenging problem of similar signal intensities and subtle textures in prostate MRI [22]. The framework
incorporates an Adaptive Boundary Fusion Module (ABFM), Dynamic Feature Injection Module (DFIM), and
Feature Enhancement Module (FEM) to integrate local details with broader contextual information and improve

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Proposed methodology
This section puts forward the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explainable
Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification. The proposed framework aims to tackle the major drawbacks
of the previous brain tumor analysis techniques, such as low robustness in MRI noise, inaccurate delineation
of tumor boundaries, low semantic understanding, and low clinical interpretability. This framework combines
diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foundation-driven semantic representation learning, prompt-guided cross-
attention refinement, and explainable dual-task intelligence, all within a single, end-to-end framework.
The proposed methodology starts with a preprocessing and diffusion enhancement of the MRI to enhance the
quality of the images and make the tumor visible. The enhanced MRI images are then fed into a pretrained medi­
cal foundation encoder to obtain powerful multi-scale semantic representations. A semantic attention mechanism
with prompt guidance is integrated into the framework to enhance adaptive localization and clinically relevant
feature learning. The semantic representations extracted are further refined by combining features together and
they are also used for tumor segmentation and multiclass classification. Furthermore, the explainability engine
creates attention visualization and saliency maps for enhancing transparency and clinical trustworthiness.
The proposed framework is tailored to optimise the segmentation accuracy, the classification reliability, the
robustness under degraded MRI conditions and the explainability performance simultaneously. The overall archi­
tecture and major components of the proposed framework are discussed in the following subsections.

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Overall framework architecture
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework aims to be a single multi-task framework
that segments and classifies brain tumors in MRI simultaneously. It integrates a diffusion-based enhancement, a
foundation-based semantic representation learning, a prompt-based cross-attention refinement, and explainable
prediction generation into a single end-to-end learning system. As shown in Fig. 1, the architecture is composed
of sequential stages such as MRI preprocessing, diffusion enhancement, foundation encoding, prompt-guided
semantic alignment, shared feature fusion, segmentation decoding, classification prediction, and explainability
generation.
The technical innovation of the proposed framework lies in the way semantic prompting and dual-task super­
vision are incorporated into shared representation learning. Unlike conventional pipelines that apply enhance­
ment, segmentation, classification, and explanation as independent stages, the proposed architecture introduces
prompt–image cross-attention before shared feature formation. The visual representation produced by the

localization and diagnostic discrimination to reinforce each other during training. Diffusion enhancement, foun­
dation encoding, and Grad-CAM are established techniques and are not claimed as individual innovations; rather,
the contribution is the prompt-conditioned, adaptively fused, dual-task learning mechanism that connects them
within a unified computational architecture.
Firstly, the input MRIs are preprocessed by normalizing, resizing, stripping the skull and correcting the intensi­

The preprocessed MRI images then go to the diffusion enhancement module, where latent diffusion learning is

The enhanced MRI images are then processed through a pre-trained medical foundation encoder which is
built based on MedSAM and DINOv2 architectures. Semantic representation learning is used by the foundation
encoder to learn both local tumor properties and global contextual relationships by contrast to the traditional con­
volutional models that mostly learned local spatial representations. The encoder can generate multi-scale feature
representations to keep fine-grained information of the tumor with different spatial resolutions.
A cross-attention mechanism is introduced in the framework to enhance the semantic understanding with
the help of prompts. Using a bio-clinical language encoder and cross-attention learning, clinically meaningful
prompts are encoded by a bio-clinical language encoder and aligned with image representations. This semantic
interaction allows for adaptive localization of clinically relevant tumor regions and better feature discrimination
and task-aware representation learning.

Experimental setup and performance evaluation
In this section, the experimental setup, the description of the dataset, the implementation details and the evaluation
metrics adopted to validate the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explain­

ability quality.

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Dataset description
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework was tested on the recently released expert-
annotated brain tumor segmentation and multiclass classification benchmark dataset named BRISC 2025. Some
of the most prominent shortcomings in earlier brain tumor MRI data sets were inconsistency in the way they
were annotated, lack of tumor diversity, class imbalance, and poor tumor segmentation quality, all of which were
addressed by the development of this data set. The BRISC 2025 database offers high-quality MRI scans along
with pixel-level tumor masks and multiclass diagnostic labels, which is ideal for assessing explainable dual-task
medical AI approaches.
The official BRISC 2025 partition contains 5000 training images and 1000 independent test images. To create
a validation set without accessing the official test data, 20% of the official training partition was selected through
stratified sampling based on tumour class and anatomical plane. Consequently, 4000 images were used for train­
ing, 1000 for validation, and 1000 for final testing. The same partitions were used for the proposed framework
and all comparison methods. The validation set was used for hyperparameter tuning, early stopping, and check­
point selection, whereas the test set was reserved exclusively for final evaluation. Data augmentation was applied
only to the training partition.
The data set contains two major tasks—Classifications and Segmentation. The subset of classification consists
of MRI images that are classified into four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Accurate
lesion localization and structural delineation is provided by the corresponding tumor masks in the segmentation
subset. The dataset contains various types of tumor appearances with significant differences in tumor size, shape,
texture, edema distribution, visibility of the contrast, and irregularity in the boundary. The variations make the
data appropriate for assessing the ability of the model to be robust and generalizable, further establishing the
complexity of automated tumor analysis.
The MRI scans have been acquired and annotated by experts in the medical field to maintain consistency in the
structures and to have reliable ground-truth labelling. The segmentation masks precisely localize tumor regions
and edema structures, which allows for a proper assessment of the segmentation performance. The previous

Implementation details
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework was put into practice with Python and
the PyTorch deep learning framework. All experiments were performed in a GPU-enabled environment with the
CUDA acceleration support to enable efficient training of the diffusion enhancement module, the transformer-
based foundation encoder and the prompt-guided semantic attention mechanism. The complete architecture was
trained in an end-to-end manner for simultaneous segmentation and multiclass classification.
First, all of the MRI images were resized to a fixed spatial resolution and normalized to achieve structural
uniformity in MRI acquisitions. After that, the normalized MRI representations were passed to the diffusion
enhancement module prior to the semantic feature extraction. Post diffusion reconstruction of the enhanced MRI
was then passed to the pretrained foundation encoder for hierarchical semantic representation learning.
The proposed framework employed a transformer-based semantic encoding that was able to model local tumor
structures and global contextual relationships. The semantic representations extracted were further improved by
the cross-attention learning strategies using prompts, and then fused into the shared feature fusion module. Both
the fused semantic representations were used concurrently for segmentation and classification.

The performance of the proposed framework was assessed based on standard classification and segmentation
metrics to fully cover the assessment of prediction accuracy, segmentation quality, robustness and semantic
consistency.
The accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under curve (AUC) were used for the classification evalua­
tion. Accuracy is the overall correctness of the predictions of tumors, while precision is the reliability of the posi­

Results And Discussion
The experimental results and detailed analysis of the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation
Framework for Explainable Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification is presented. The framework was
tested on the basis of classification accuracy, segmentation accuracy, explainability, robustness analysis, abla­
tion study, computational efficiency and cross-dataset generalization. The achieved performance of the proposed
technique proves that the combination of diffusion enhancement, pretrained foundation representation learning,
prompt-guided semantic attention, and explainable feature fusion has an extremely positive effect on segmenta­
tion and multiclass classification tasks.

The framework also shows enhanced uniformity of the segmentation in cases of low contrast and structurally
complex tumor images. Current segmentation methods based on standard segmentation strategies tend to have
diffuse segmentation margins and miss coverage when the appearance of the tumor is highly variable between
MRI samples. The proposed framework, on the other hand, maintains the structural continuity and generates
more prominent contours of the tumors by adaptive semantic alignment and multi-scale feature fusion.
To strengthen the comparison with contemporary medical-segmentation methods, nnU-Net [41], Swin UNETR
[42], and SAM-Med2D [43] were additionally evaluated. All methods were trained or adapted using the same
BRISC 2025 training, validation, and test partitions, input resolution, augmentation procedure, hyperparameter-
search budget, and evaluation metrics. The two-dimensional nnU-Net configuration was automatically adapted
to the BRISC images, while Swin UNETR was configured for single-channel MRI input. SAM-Med2D was
evaluated using the same prompt-generation procedure for all test images. This controlled evaluation allowed the
proposed framework to be compared with self-configuring segmentation, transformer-based medical segmenta­
tion, and promptable medical foundation-model approaches.
Among the recent baseline methods, SAM-Med2D achieved the strongest segmentation performance, with a
Dice score of 92.7% and an IoU of 88.8%, followed by Swin UNETR and nnU-Net. The proposed framework
achieved a Dice score of 93.2%, an IoU of 89.4%, and the lowest Hausdorff distance of 5.21. The improvement
suggests that diffusion-based refinement and prompt-conditioned shared feature learning provide complementary
benefits beyond self-configuring, transformer-based, and promptable segmentation baselines.
The segmentation results obtained from the proposed framework are also shown to be more stable over dif­
ferent types of tumors, such as glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor and small and difficult tumors. The frame­
work’s ability to incorporate explainable semantic attention allows it to reject unwanted background activations

work’s ability to incorporate explainable semantic attention allows it to reject unwanted background activations

the superior performance of the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework in reliably
delineating tumor structures with clinically relevant accuracy for heterogeneous MRI cases without compromis­
ing high-quality structural preservation and minimising segmentation uncertainty.
An additional error analysis was conducted to examine the principal failure conditions of the proposed frame­
work. Misclassifications occurred mainly between glioma and meningioma cases with similar intensity patterns
and between low-contrast pituitary tumours and no-tumour images containing high-intensity anatomical struc­
tures. For segmentation analysis, tumours were grouped according to their relative mask area as small (< 1% of
image pixels), medium (1–5%), and large (> 5%). The corresponding mean Dice scores were 88.4%, 93.0%, and
95.2%, respectively, indicating that small lesions were more difficult to delineate. Tumour size showed a moder­
ate positive correlation with Dice score (Spearman’s in l ine-eq-IEq119, in l ine-eq-IEq120). Peripheral tumours located close to the
skull achieved a lower mean Dice score of 90.6%, compared with 94.1% for centrally located tumours, while
low-contrast lesions achieved a mean Dice score of 89.8%. The principal failure modes were therefore small
lesion size, weak tumour-to-background contrast, irregular or infiltrative boundaries, peripheral location, imag­
ing artefacts, and visual similarity between tumour categories. These findings suggest that future improvements
should focus on scale-aware feature learning, boundary-sensitive loss functions, and stronger modelling of low-
contrast lesions.

Explainability analysis
In medical imaging systems, especially in the field of brain tumor diagnosis, reliability and transparency of the
system are crucial, and interpretability is an indispensable requirement in planning treatment. The explainability
capability of the proposed framework was assessed by using comparative analysis of the proposed visualizations:
Grad-CAM, transformer attention maps, localization consistency and semantic attention interpretability. The
results of the Explainability evaluation are presented in Table 6 below.
The proposed framework had the best tumor localization accuracy of 93.4% and attention consistency value of
91.7%, better than traditional explainability methods which showed interpretability and semantically meaningful
localization. In all cases the attention maps generated were tightly correlated to clinically relevant tumor regions
and attenuated irrelevant background regions.
The increased explainability performance can be explained by the incorporation of prompt-guided semantic
learning and explainable attention fusion. In contrast to the traditional Grad-CAM approaches that often result
in diffuse activation localization and low localization consistency, the proposed framework is able to provide
semantically informative distribution maps of attention regions that are coherent with tumor structures and edema
regions.

edema-rich lesions, low contrast tumors and small difficult lesions. Conventional Grad-CAM visualizations suf­

provide relatively more diffuse and less accurate attention regions.
The proposed explainability mechanism, on the other hand, yields more acute and focused attention maps to
diagnose important regions of tumors. The generated attention overlays exhibit better structural consistency, bet­
ter lesion boundaries and better semantic localization capability in all the evaluated tumor conditions.
This framework also exhibits better stability of explainability in difficult MRI environments. The proposed
attention mechanism maintains focused activations around clinically meaningful areas while reducing activations
that fall on non-relevant areas in healthy tissues, even for low-contrast lesions and structurally complex tumor

Discussion
The experimental results show the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework’s effec­
tiveness on various tasks of brain tumor MRI analysis, including classification, segmentation, robustness, and
explainability. By combining these components, the framework can overcome multiple challenges that traditional
CNN and transformer-based medical imaging models encounter, such as ambiguous object boundaries, noisy or
corrupted input data, and uncertainty regarding what to focus on.
The proposed framework shows superior explainability performance, semantic localization capability and seg­
mentation consistency when compared to the existing literature. It has been recently observed that the traditional
CNN architecture-based segmentation models tend to fail in capturing the irregular boundaries of the tumor, low
contrast lesions and in learning the contextual representation in the heterogeneous MRI environments [1, 44].
Recent explainable AI research also revealed that many deep learning models suffer from fragmented activations
and low interpretability of clinical actions, which hinders the real-world use of these models in medical deci­
sion support systems [45, 46]. Likewise, diffusion models have been recently found to benefit the preservation
of the structures and the refinement of their boundaries in complex medical imaging tasks [35, 36, 47]. These

robustness and explainability of segmentation in a single framework.
The applications of this research are of great importance for intelligent clinical decision support system. The
suggested framework can help radiologists to accurately segment tumors, reliably classify tumors into more than
one class, and generate attention visualizations that are clinically interpretable. Additionally, the explainability
mechanism enhances transparency by identifying diagnostically relevant regions of tumors, thereby boosting the
clinical trustworthiness and aiding in treatment planning. The framework’s performance in these MRI conditions
with noise and distortion also suggests it can be adapted to work well in a realistic clinical MRI setting with
acquisition artifacts and contrast variation.
The proposed framework also shows great potential to be adaptable to future medical AI applications like mul­
timodal MRI fusion, semantic-guided diagnosis, and explainable neuro-oncology systems. With prompt-guided
semantic learning, medical imaging workflows can be automated to incorporate clinical instructions and domain-
specific guidance flexibly. Moreover, the efficiency of the computations implemented with the framework sug­
gests potential for deployment in near real-time in hospital settings and intelligent radiology systems.
The external-dataset evaluation provides initial evidence that the learned representations can transfer beyond
BRISC 2025. Nevertheless, real-world performance may be influenced by differences in scanners, MRI acquisi­

authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Conclusion
This research presented a novel Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explainable Brain
Tumor Segmentation and Classification using MRI images. The proposed framework is built into the frame­
work of medical imaging, which incorporates diffusion-based MRI enhancement, pretrained semantic foundation
encoding, prompt-guided attention learning, explainable feature fusion, and dual-task optimization. The frame­
work was designed to overcome the major challenges of MRI analysis for brain tumors such as noisy imaging
conditions, low contrast, low visibility of the lesions, irregular boundaries of the tumor, variation of its structure,
and poor interpretability of traditional deep learning.
The experimental results on the BRISC 2025 dataset showed that the proposed framework outperformed
other compared methods in terms of segmentation and classification. Both the framework achieved a classifica­
tion accuracy of 98.1%, Dice score of 93.2%, and AUC value of 99.0%, surpassing the performance of tradi­
tional CNN architectures, Transformer models, and the latest foundation models for segmentation. The diffusion
enhancement module contributed greatly to the improvement of the MRI quality and structural preservation, and
the prompt guided semantic attention mechanism contributed to the adaptive localization of clinically relevant
tumor regions.

Abstract
Accurate diagnosis of brain tumors from MRI scans is crucial for effective treatment planning and patient outcomes. Deep
learning techniques have shown promise in automating this process, but the interpretability of their decisions remains a chal-
lenge. This paper introduces the Squeeze-and-Excitation Convolutional Neural Network-MobileNet (SECNN-MNet), a novel
deep learning model designed for precise and interpretable classification of brain tumors in MRI images. SECNN-MNet com-
bines the robust feature extraction capabilities of SE-CNN with the computational efficiency of MobileNet. By integrating SE
blocks, the model dynamically recalibrates feature maps to capture crucial tumor characteristics, enhancing diagnostic accu-
racy. MobileNet’s depthwise separable convolutions optimize computational resources while preserving image detail fidelity.
Our model achieves exceptional performance, demonstrating an accuracy of 99.6% in classifying brain tumors. Leverag-
ing explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), SECNN-MNet provides insights into decision-making processes, enhancing its
interpretability and utility for clinicians. This study underscores the potential of SECNN-MNet in advancing automated brain
tumor diagnosis, offering both high accuracy and interpretability crucial for clinical adoption and patient care.

convolutional neural network with MobileNet (SECNN-MNet) · Explainability analysis · Grad-CAM

Our proposed model analyzes BT image data (specif-

introduces the squeeze-and-excitation convolutional neural

enhance MRI image classification. It combines SE-CNN’s
dynamic feature recalibration with MobileNet’s efficient

and processed through dense layers with dropout regular-

via a softmax layer, enables robust multi-class classification.
Also, this paper produced a comprehensive and interpretable

Proposed model
The proposed model, termed squeeze-and-excitation con-
volutional neural network MobileNet (SECNN-MNet), is
meticulously crafted to elevate image classification perfor-
mance,particularlyforMRIimages.AsdepictedinFig.1,the
model comprises two synergistic components: the SE-CNN
and MobileNet, each contributing uniquely to the feature
extraction process.
Firstly, the preprocessed MRI images are inputted into
the SE-CNN, which functions as a powerful feature extrac-
tor. This network is architecturally enriched with several
convolutional layers; each layer followed by batch normal-
ization to stabilize the learning process and max-pooling
to down-sample the feature maps. A distinctive element of
the SE-CNN is the incorporation of squeeze-and-excitation
(SE) blocks. These blocks are pivotal in dynamically recal-
ibrating feature maps by emphasizing the most informative
features through adaptive channel-wise weighting. Strategi-
cally placed after specific convolutional layers, SE blocks
significantly enhance the network’s ability to represent cru-
cial features.
Simultaneously, the preprocessed MRI images are pro-
cessed by the MobileNet, another highly efficient fea-
ture extractor renowned for its lightweight architecture.
MobileNet utilizes depthwise separable convolutions, which
decouple the standard convolution operation into a depth-
wise convolution followed by a pointwise convolution. This
design dramatically reduces computational costs while main-
taining the network’s capacity to capture detailed image
features.
The SECNN-MNet architecture is optimized for MRI-
based tumor detection. The MobileNet backbone, using
depthwise separable convolutions, enables efficient feature
extraction while maintaining spatial granularity—crucial for
preserving subtle tumor edges. SE blocks recalibrate features
dynamically, allowing the model to focus on relevant areas
even when intensity varies across scans.
In this architecture, MobileNet’s top classification layers
are excluded, and the output from the global average pooling
layer is used as a high-level feature vector, representing a
compact and abstract summary of the image’s features. The
high-level features extracted by the SE-CNN and MobileNet
are then concatenated to form a unified and comprehen-
sive feature vector. This composite vector encapsulates a
broad spectrum of image characteristics, drawn from both
the detailed recalibration of the SE-CNN and the efficient

4.5.1 Experiment 1: the CNN model

Performance comparison with the existing

In our study, the performance of the proposed SECNN-
MNet model was rigorously compared with several existing
research works to evaluate its effectiveness in MRI image
classification. As shown in Table 8, a noteworthy com-
parison is with the work by P. Tiwari et al. [18], which
achieved an impressive accuracy of 99% using a deep convo-
lutional neural network (CNN) architecture. This model by
Tiwari et al. efficiently classified brain MRIs into four cate-
gories: no tumor, glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor.
In contrast, our SECNN-MNet model surpassed this perfor-
mance, achieving an outstanding accuracy of 99.6%. This
improvementcanbeattributedtotheinnovativeintegrationof
squeeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks within the CNN, which
dynamically recalibrate feature maps to emphasize crucial
details, and the use of MobileNet’s efficient depthwise sepa-
rable convolutions, which maintain high computational effi-
ciency while capturing intricate image features. Additionally,
the use of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques
enhanced the interpretability of the SECNN-MNet model,
providing valuable insights into the decision-making pro-
cess.

SECNN-MNet model, we employ gradient-weighted class
activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Grad-CAM provides a
visual explanation by highlighting the regions in the input
image that are most relevant to the model’s predictions. This
technique is instrumental in understanding and validating
the model’s behavior, especially in complex deep learning
architectures. This study utilized the Grad-CAM method to
explain the SECNN-MNet model prediction outputs.

Model performance and robustness in MRI brain
tumor classification
MRI scans often exhibit significant variability, resulting from
factors such as variations in scanner settings, patient move-
ment, and inherent anatomical differences among individ-
uals. The SECNN-MNet model effectively mitigates these
challenges through its innovative architecture, which com-
bines the advantages of MobileNet’s depthwise separable
convolutions and SE blocks. MobileNet ensures that spatial
sensitivity is preserved while maintaining computational effi-
ciency, which is critical when processing high-dimensional
MRI data. The SE blocks, on the other hand, provide dynamic
channel-wise recalibration, allowing the model to focus its
attention on the most discriminative tumor features, enhanc-
ing its diagnostic accuracy.

Furthermore, the model incorporates advanced data aug-
mentation techniques to simulate real-world MRI variability,
such as intensity shifts and structural distortions. This
improves the model’s robustness, enabling it to perform reli-
ably across diverse MRI scans. As shown in the previous
section Grad-CAM visualizations, SECNN-MNet accurately
localizes brain tumors, even in the presence of variations in
tumor morphology and intensity. This adaptability further
validates the architectural choices made during the model’s
development, confirming its capacity to handle MRI-specific
challenges in brain tumor diagnosis.
A distinctive feature of SECNN-MNet is its use of XAI
techniques, particularly Grad-CAM. This approach pro-
vides clinicians with greater transparency into the model’s
decision-making process, offering visual explanations of
how specific regions of an MRI scan contribute to the final
prediction. By generating heatmaps that highlight areas of
interest, Grad-CAM not only improves interpretability but
also fosters trust in the model’s predictions, which is essen-
tial for its clinical adoption.
Despite its strong performance, SECNN-MNet has cer-
tain limitations. The integration of SE-CNN with MobileNet
introduces additional complexity, which can increase the
computational resources required for both training and
deployment. This may present challenges for medical insti-
tutions with limited computational infrastructure, potentially
hindering the model’s widespread use in clinical practice. As
such, addressing the computational demands and optimiz-
ing the model for efficiency remains a key area for future
development. So, the SECNN-MNet model offers substan-
tial advantages in classification accuracy, interpretability, and
robustness, positioning it as a promising tool for brain tumor
diagnosis using MRI. However, future efforts should focus
on reducing its computational footprint and further enhanc-
ing its interpretability to ensure broader clinical applicability
and integration into healthcare systems.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the SECNN-MNet model represents a sig-
nificant advancement in automated brain tumor diagnosis
from MRI scans, achieving a remarkable accuracy of 99.6%.
By integrating squeeze-and-excitation convolutional neu-
ral network (SE-CNN) with MobileNet, our model effec-
tively balances feature recalibration and computational effi-
ciency, essential for real-world clinical applications. The
incorporation of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)
enhances interpretability, providing clinicians with insights
into decision-making processes crucial for accurate diagno-
sis.

Classification of brain tumor types
through MRIs using parallel CNNs
and firefly optimization
Chen Li 1,3, Faxue Zhang 1,3, Yongjian Du 2 & Huachao Li 1*
Image segmentation is a critical and challenging endeavor in the field of medicine. A magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) scan is a helpful method for locating any abnormal brain tissue these
days. It is a difficult undertaking for radiologists to diagnose and classify the tumor from several
pictures. This work develops an intelligent method for accurately identifying brain tumors. This
research investigates the identification of brain tumor types from MRI data using convolutional
neural networks and optimization strategies. Two novel approaches are presented: the first is a novel
segmentation technique based on firefly optimization (FFO) that assesses segmentation quality
based on many parameters, and the other is a combination of two types of convolutional neural
networks to categorize tumor traits and identify the kind of tumor. These upgrades are intended to
raise the general efficacy of the MRI scan technique and increase identification accuracy. Using MRI
scans from BBRATS2018, the testing is carried out, and the suggested approach has shown improved
performance with an average accuracy of 98.6%.
Keywords MRI image segmentation, Classification, Firefly optimization, Brain tumor, Convolutional neural
network
An abnormal and cancerous cell accumulation is called a brain tumor. The human skull is a strong and vital
organ that protects the brain. Any aberrant development of brain tissue within the skull’s constrained borders
might result in a variety of issues. There are two types of brain tumor classifications: benign and ­malignant1. The
primary functions of the human anatomy, including respiration, muscular and sensory function, are controlled by
the nerve cells and tissues that make up the ­brain2. Using MRI to detect and classify brain tumors is an essential
part of medical therapy. Information about anatomical structure is provided by this process for treatment plan-
ning. Brain atlas building and brain modeling may benefit from tumor segmentation. Despite the availability of
several technologies and their excellent results, precisely describing and segmenting abnormalities in medical

imaging may be challenging because to the variability of tumor location, intensity, and ­form3.
Image segmentation plays a crucial role in therapeutic picture evaluation and analysis, focusing on object rec-
ognition and region of interest (ROI) selection. As a result, it greatly aids in monitoring, diagnosis, and ­therapy4.
Different kinds of volumetric data are found using MRI segmentation. When compared to other medical images
that are available, it provides precise data and is beneficial for a variety of medical image applications. Compared
to other medical imaging, the contrast of an MRI provides the best results. Because an MRI represents an image
in its compressed form, extracting its features is essential. Various feature extraction techniques are applied,
enabling the classifiers to distinguish between normal and pathological ­tumors5. Many attempts have been made
recently in studies to use tumor segmentation from medical pictures to diagnose brain tumors. In the medi-
cal field, brain tumor segmentation using machine learning is crucial for accurate disease detection. Although
automated tumor segmentation has been shown to be effective, brain tumor segmentation is neither offered nor
used in clinical settings. The goal of the work is to use digital image processing methods to detect tumor areas
from brain MRIs. The region of the tumor is then calculated using symmetry analysis and a totally automated
­mechanism6. Medical imaging patterns may now be recognized and categorized thanks to recent advancements
in machine learning, particularly deep learning. One example of this field’s achievements is its capacity to collect
and extract information from data instead of depending on specialized expertise or academic ­publications7–9.

Remarkably, a wide range of deep learning and machine learning algorithms have been used for cardiovascular
stenosis detection as well as for the identification of malignancies, including lung tumors. Performance assess-

In this paper, an attempt has been made to identify the type of brain tumors from MRI scans using a com-
bination of optimization and an ensemble of convolutional neural networks. However, there is still room for
improvement with the present approaches. Two innovations that can be used to increase identification accuracy
have been described in this research. The first innovation consists of the introduction of a novel segmentation
technique that employs the FFO algorithm and multiple criteria to determine segmentation quality of images. In
order to classify the features of tumor areas and determine the type of tumor, the second innovation combines
two different forms of convolutional neural networks. When employing this mix of models instead of each one
independently, the accuracy is increased. Below is a summary of our main contributions.
• Combination of convolutional neural network and optimization techniques for tumor identification.
• Introduction of a novel segmentation technique using the FFO algorithm.
• Combination of two different forms of convolutional neural networks for tumor classification.

Using a dataset of 3064 MRI images of 233 individuals with brain tumors, Phaye et al.16 created diversified

layers. The model was 93.68% accurate and had a learning rate of 0.01 when compared to other methods. An
automated technique for classifying brain tumor kinds in radiologists and doctors was created by Gumaei et al.18.
With an accuracy rate of 94.23%, the research analyzed a collection of 3064 MRI pictures from 233 individuals.
Nevertheless, a comparison analysis using other methods was not carried out in this research.
Multi-CNNs, a hybrid of CNN and multimodal information fusion detection techniques, were created by Li
et al.19. This method enhanced the tumor detection process’s correlation coefficient, specificity, and sensitivity.
The Whale Hawks Optimization (WHHO) algorithm was presented by Rammurthy et al.20 as an efficient brain
tumor identification method that combines the Whale Optimization (WOA) and Harris Hawks Optimization
(HHO) methods. For tumor area segmentation on MRI images, it incorporates statistical and textural informa-
tion together with pixel data from the images using cellular automata and rough set theory. Even with low-quality
photos, this technique may enhance image quality.

To sum up, several recent studies applied deep learning to the classifying of brain tumors, and they achieved
good results (Phaye et al.16; Pashaei et al.17; Gumaei et al.18; Haq et al.21; Noreen et al.22; Hashemzehi et al.23;

remains in existing methods: proper tumor segmentation, which is usually performed as a manual process or by
less precise algorithms. It can be instrumental in the final decision-making process. In this regard, the innovative
FFO-based segmentation step is our solution to this problem. FFO offers a very profitable approach to segmenta-
tion which increases the accuracy of the segmentation of the brain tissue compared to the traditional methods.
In a nutshell, this result in addition to providing the foundation for the subsequent parallel CNN architecture
to extract meaningful features, can lead to higher tumor classification precision.

Classification
The pre-processing step is applied to each MRI image slice and during it, brain tissue regions are identified
in the image slice and the result is used as input to other steps of the proposed method. In the second step, the
FFO algorithm is used to segment MRI images. The objective of this study is to simplify the detection issue by
restricting the range of pixel colors in each section of the input picture and estimating the area of the lesion in
the image. Following the process of picture segmentation, a method based on thresholding is used to accurately
identify regions of interest (ROIs). The extracted regions form the input of the third step of the proposed method,
during which the existence of the tumor and its type in ROI is determined by a parallel convolutional neural
network (PCNN) model. This PCNN model consists of two 1D and 2D CNNs in which the 2D CNN model
is used for gray image processing of ROI and the 1D model to detect mass type through local binary patterns
(LBP) extracted from ROI. Each of these CNN models defines the features related to the mass type through its
last fully connected layer, and then the feature vectors extracted from these two models are combined based
on a concatenation layer to finally recognize the mass type based on the integration of the features of two CNN
models and using a SoftMax classifier.
Preprocessing
The first step in preprocessing database images is to remove the background of MRI images. The purpose of this
operation is to remove redundant information from the image and to eliminate data that may interfere with
the detection process. To remove the background from the images, the input image is first converted to binary
mode using the experimental threshold of 0.05. Thus, each image pixel with an intensity less than 0.05 × 255 is
replaced by 0, and each pixel with a higher intensity than this threshold is replaced by 1. Thus, a binary picture,

Segmentation and identification of the target region
In the second step of the proposed method, each image slice is segmented using a new approach. In the proposed
method, the combination of K-Means and FFO algorithms is used to segment images. The objective of this stage
is to simplify the problem by partitioning the brain area into its individual tissues. Through this procedure, it is
feasible to segregate the mass area in the picture as a distinct cluster from other regions. The choice of FFO for
segmentation on MRIs, offers several advantages over other optimization algorithms:
• Strong Exploration Capabilities: FFO is an innovative approach that is capable of a thorough search in the
problem space and locating the best segmentation parameters. This results in correct brain segmentation of
the tissue as compared to the other methods that may get trapped in local minimums.

• Balancing Exploration and Exploitation: FFO exhibits this balance through two methods: looking for new

continued exploration of diverse areas of the search space.
• Fewer Control Parameters: The FFO optimization algorithm does not need as many user-defined parameters
as several other algorithms. It is particularly simple and easy to adjust to different datasets.
The above-mentioned advantages of FFO are thus especially significant for MRI image segmentation pro-
cess where correct dissection of brain tissues is crucial for further tumor classification. Also, the comparisons
conducted ­in31 ­and32 demonstrate the superiority of FFO over other optimization algorithms for solving various
problems.
Brain images may be segmented by evaluating variations in brightness intensity to distinguish distinct areas
and tissues. Thus, through optimal adjustment of threshold values for each region, it is possible to determine
the correct separation of regions in the images. The proposed technique models this step in the form of an
optimization problem and uses FFO to solve it. The proposed method uses an approach similar to the basic
K-Means algorithm for image segmentation; however, the center of each region in the image is considered as an
optimization variable and its optimal value is determined using FFO. Additionally, to expedite the convergence
of the proposed segmentation algorithm, the initial FFO population is established using the K-Means algorithm.
In this section, firstly, the formulation of the segmentation process in the form of an optimization problem is
discussed, and then the method of solving it using FFO is explained.

Classification
In the third step of the proposed method, a parallel model of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) is used
to classify each ROI. The suggested parallel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model has two CNN com-
ponents that collaborate in the task of identifying the specific kind of lesion. Figure 3 illustrates this structure.
Based on the above diagram, the suggested model comprises of two components: a 1D Convolutional Neural
Network (CNN) and a 2D CNN. The CNN model attempts to perform pattern learning based on local binary
patterns extracted from ROI; while the 2D CNN model performs this operation based on the gray ROI matrix.
According to Fig. 3, the output of each CNN model is achieved through the weighted vector of the last fully
connected layer of that model. The feature vectors of two CNN models are joined together to combine the deci-
sion results of the two models using a SoftMax classifier and create the final output of the system. The first CNN
model in the proposed method is fed by LBP features, while the second CNN accepts ROI images with gray color
schemes. In the subsequent sections, the classification steps for each sample utilizing this model are detailed.

Uniform patterns refer to patterns that include a maximum of two transitions between 0 and 1, or vice versa,
when the bits are rotated. By saving consistent patterns, a novel operator is generated, including a total of 59
distinct patterns inside the 8-pixel region. The suggested approach utilizes an adjusted model that relies on
­methodology34 to extract LBP features. In the proposed method, the segmented image is divided into N non-
overlapping cells, and the LBP features of each image cell are extracted based ­on34. Then, the LBP features of
each cell are described as a histogram vector of length B. As a result, each image can be represented as a vector
with a length of N × B . It should be noted that in the proposed method, the LBP features of each image are
extracted using two radius values, R = 1, and R = 2, and the number of neighboring pixels is set to 8. As a result,
the resulting feature vectors to describe the LBP features of each segmented image have a length of 2 × N × B.
Training parallel CNN models. The CNN models used in the proposed method include input layers, convolu-
tion blocks for feature extraction, and necessary layers for feature classification. The general structure of these
CNN models is depicted in Fig. 4.
According to Fig. 4, both CNN models used in the proposed method include 3 convolution blocks. In the
first CNN model, 1D convolution and pooling layers are used to process the selected features, while the second
CNN model uses 2D pooling and convolution layers. Consequently, it is inherent that the input layer of the 1D
CNN model is one-dimensional, whereas the input layer of the 2D CNN model is in matrix form. The 1D CNN
model utilizes the sigmoid function as its activation function, while the activation function of the 2D CNN model
is uniformly set to the ReLU type in all convolution blocks. Both CNN models end with the layers necessary
to classify the samples. In this approach, the dimensions of the extracted feature maps are first reduced by two
consecutive fully connected layers with dimensions of 100 and 2, respectively. Subsequently, the classification of
the samples into the target classes is performed using a SoftMax layer. It should be noted that in the proposed

Implementation results
MATLAB 2020a software is used to implement the proposed technique. In addition to applying the cross-
validation methodology with ten iterations for the experimental setting, we tested the suggested method based
on the predefined criteria.
Metrics for performance evaluation
In the following, we will examine the criteria of Precision, Recall, F-Measure, Accuracy, Matthews correlation
coefficient (MCC), Critical success index (CSI). In this paper, we considered two categories of targets: LGG and
HGG. LGG was considered as negative category and HGG as positive category. After classification of samples,
each test sample may fall in the one of the following 4 groups:
• TP: The number of samples belonging to the HGG category and correctly identified.
• TN: The number of samples belonging to the LGG category and correctly identified.
• FP: The number of samples that were in the LGG category and were mistakenly placed in the HGG category.
• FN: The number of samples that were in the HGG category and were mistakenly placed in the LGG category.

weighting value may be calculated using accuracy and recall data. When assessing classification quality and
characterizing the weighted average of precision and recall, the F-measure is a useful metric. This measure’s

The obtained results show the higher level of accuracy compared to current methods ­(DACBT21, Rammurthy
et al.20), but computational efficiency and scalability are two other crucial things that need to be considered for
implementation in a real-world scenario.
The proposed parallel CNN architecture leverages two CNNs: a 1D CNN with 196,580 and a 2D CNN with
8,203,580 learnable parameters, for a total of around 8.4 million parameters. This particular parameter count
may directly determine the memory needs during training and inference.
The training model was based on a NVIDIA RTX 4050i GPU. During the training process, we employed the
Adam optimizer with batch size 32. The amount of memory for model parameters (running the trained model
on other machines) is about 33.5 MB. This value is considered low in terms of memory, allowing the model to be
used on machines with a wide range of memory capabilities compared to approaches with significantly higher
memory requirements. Also, for training the model, in addition to the mentioned required memory, about
3.5 MB is required for optimizer states. Additionally, considering batch size of 32, about 16.77 MB is required
for batch data. This means that the required Memory per batch in training the proposed model is about 53.8 MB
which is significantly lower that compared methods.
The present training results show good capacity on the dataset of 500 images in a batch size of 32. Neverthe-
less, in case of much bigger datasets, the memory footprint per batch is increased as the amount of data in the
batch is directly proportional to the memory footprint. This could make using training methods like gradient
accumulation or mixed-precision training necessary to achieve larger batch sizes on the same hardware. Fur-
thermore, a deep analysis with larger datasets is essential for the model’s further scalability in relation to the
increasing of input data. While training time increases linearly based on current observations, further investiga-
tion is needed.
The proposed model reaches high accuracy with a low number of parameters which seems to be a suitable
solution that preserves both accuracy and computational efficiency. The memory footprint during the training
can be controlled either using a right hardware or the training strategy. Nevertheless, for the biggest datasets,

Conclusion
In this paper, a hybrid model made up of quick optimization algorithms and parallel convolutional neural net-
works is used to examine the categorization of brain cancers in MRI data. Brain tumors have been successfully
classified by this model with high accuracy and low complexity. The model’s efficient optimization method and
use of parallel convolutional neural networks have contributed to enhancing the model’s performance and extrac-
tion of features. We used the criteria of accuracy, precision, recall, and f-measure to evaluate the acquired data.
Following 10 iterations, we evaluated the results using the cross validation methodology. When compared to
other methods currently in use, our performance was better. Accordingly, the testing findings demonstrate that,
with accuracy and precision of 1% and 0.03, our proposed approach outperformed the comparison methods.

Detecting brain tumours (BT) early improves treatment possibilities and increases patient survival
rates. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning offers more comprehensive information, such
as better contrast and clarity, than any alternative scanning process. Manually separating BTs from
several MRI images gathered in medical practice for cancer analysis is challenging and time-consuming.

learning of more robust representations without suffering from degradation in performance as the network
deepens. Additionally, ResNet50 has been widely validated in various image classification and feature extraction

presents superior performance in extracting meaningful features from high-dimensional data. Its pre-trained
versions also provide a crucial advantage in transfer learning (TL) scenarios, reducing the requirement for large

with BN, ReLU, and a shortcut link to acquire across a layer. This design permits a smoother data flow within the
network, making it simpler to train much deeper structures. Furthermore, ResNet50 utilizes bottleneck blocks
in its deeper layer to enhance model performance and computational efficacy. The design comprises a global
average pooling layer to collect spatial data from the feature map and an FC layer for classification.

title: Deep learning driven interpretable and informed decision making model for brain tumour prediction using explainable AI
authors: Khan Muhammad Adnan; Taher M. Ghazal; Muhammad Saleem; Muhammad Sajid Farooq; Chan Yeob Yeun; Munir Ahmad; Sang-Woong Lee
text:
Deep learning driven interpretable
and informed decision making
model for brain tumour prediction
using explainable AI
Khan Muhammad Adnan1, Taher M. Ghazal2, Muhammad Saleem3,
Muhammad Sajid Farooq4, Chan Yeob Yeun5, Munir Ahmad6 & Sang-Woong Lee1
Brain Tumours are highly complex, particularly when it comes to their initial and accurate diagnosis, as
this determines patient prognosis. Conventional methods rely on MRI and CT scans and employ generic
machine learning techniques, which are heavily dependent on feature extraction and require human
intervention. These methods may fail in complex cases and do not produce human-interpretable
results, making it difficult for clinicians to trust the model’s predictions. Such limitations prolong the
diagnostic process and can negatively impact the quality of treatment. The advent of deep learning has
made it a powerful tool for complex image analysis tasks, such as detecting brain Tumours, by learning
advanced patterns from images. However, deep learning models are often considered “black box”
systems, where the reasoning behind predictions remains unclear. To address this issue, the present
study applies Explainable AI (XAI) alongside deep learning for accurate and interpretable brain Tumour
prediction. XAI enhances model interpretability by identifying key features such as Tumour size,
location, and texture, which are crucial for clinicians. This helps build their confidence in the model and
enables them to make better-informed decisions. In this research, a deep learning model integrated
with XAI is proposed to develop an interpretable framework for brain Tumour prediction. The model
is trained on an extensive dataset comprising imaging and clinical data and demonstrates high AUC
while leveraging XAI for model explainability and feature selection. The study findings indicate that
this approach improves predictive performance, achieving an accuracy of 92.98% and a miss rate of
7.02%. Additionally, interpretability tools such as LIME and Grad-CAM provide clinicians with a clearer
understanding of the decision-making process, supporting diagnosis and treatment. This model
represents a significant advancement in brain Tumour prediction, with the potential to enhance patient
outcomes and contribute to the field of neuro-oncology.

healthcare, offering powerful tools to support disease diagnosis and treatment. Breakthroughs in deep learning

brain Tumours are particularly critical and rapidly progressing, posing serious challenges in timely and accurate
diagnosis. The increasing incidence of brain Tumours worldwide underscores the urgent need for innovative and
interpretable diagnostic models to improve early detection and guide effective clinical decision-making.

Literature Review
Numerous researchers have focused on leveraging artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, for medical
diagnostics due to its ability to analyze complex medical data with exceptional precision. Studies have extensively
explored its applications in brain Tumour detection, with an emphasis on enhancing diagnostic accuracy and
efficiency. Furthermore, the growing incorporation of Explainable AI (XAI) addresses the critical need for
model transparency, fostering trust and interpretability in clinical decision-making.
In21, the authors proposed a diagnostic approach based on transfer learning from a set of pre-trained CNN
models, including VGG19, InceptionV3, and ResNet-50. These models obtained features from MRI images and
were further trained through fully connected layers for multi-class Tumour differentiation, which yielded an
accuracy of 90% on average. Nevertheless, their work has a major disadvantage regarding data partitioning
as they used a very small proportion of the data for testing purposes, precisely 10%, which is a very serious
limitation since it offers a small and not necessarily accurate reflection of the overall population, to the test
sample. Furthermore, the information about the test data can be preliminarily obtained, which distorts the
evaluation, rendering the method non-generalizable.
Researchers in a recent study22 proposed a new approach called RanMerFormer for the classification of brain
tumours. This framework is based on a pre-trained vision transformer, with a merging strategy to increase
efficiency by removing unnecessary tokens. Moreover, a randomized vector functional link helps to train
models more quickly. The performance of RanMerFormer was evaluated on two public benchmark datasets,
and the results suggested the future possibility of using the model for the diagnosis of real-world brain Tumours.
However, the method faces criticism of high computational cost and system complexity as major drawbacks.
The research work23 developed a novel framework that combines deep learning techniques with evolutionary
algorithms for diagnosing brain Tumours. Their approach emphasizes the idea of automating the ResNet
architecture by creating an employment-based approach that goes by the name IACO-ResNet. This method
jointly learns the architecture of the model and the parameter settings of the model using differential evolution

The researchers in25 proposed the transfer learning model based on the MRIs for multi-class brain tumour

layer. In their study, they included experiments to assess the given model on the three-class and four-class
classifications of patterns, as their findings showed. Although the model was created with T1W MRI data derived
from one protocol, restricting the analysis to single protocol data is also a limitation.
Sharma et al.26 proposed a brain tumour detection technique using ResNet-50 with a transfer learning
approach. Their method was to decode the ResNet-50 architecture but strip off its last layer and add new
appropriate layers based on what is wanted to be achieved. These changes were supported by a performance
evaluation that showed higher accuracy in categorizing brain cancer. Some limitations of the work include the
unavailability of datasets and overemphasis on binary classification problems.

Limitations of the previously published work
In the rapidly evolving field of medical imaging, accurate and timely diagnosis is essential, particularly for
conditions like brain tumours, where early intervention can significantly impact patient outcomes. Despite
advancements in imaging technologies, traditional diagnostic models, as discussed in the references in Table 1,
still struggle with several inherent challenges. These limitations, outlined below, highlight the critical gaps
addressed by the proposed model:
• Data handling and scalability: Many existing models, such as VGG19, ResNet50, and CNN-based architec­
tures21,22, face challenges in handling small and noisy datasets effectively. Models like those discussed by26,28
suffer from sparse or unavailable datasets, affecting their robustness and reliability in real-world applications.
Moreover, models such as23 are time-consuming due to their optimization complexity, further limiting their
scalability.
• Unreliable predictions: Traditional models heavily rely on intensity data, leading to inconsistent results. For
example24,29, lacks uncertainty estimation and fails to detect subtle tumour regions. This limitation is com­
pounded in cases like27, where small datasets and computational complexity due to transfer learning hinder
their reliability in clinical decision-making.

To tackle the determined challenges posed by traditional models in brain tumour diagnosis, the proposed

not only accurate and reliable predictions but also transparency in decision-making, fostering trust and usability

techniques, robust data augmentation, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to deliver a reliable,

Cloud computing
Once the model has been trained and optimized, it is stored in a cloud environment. Cloud computing provides
scalability and enables the system to be accessed and utilized in real-time scenarios. By storing the model in
the cloud, healthcare professionals can access it from anywhere and use it to analyze new brain image data.
The cloud also supports updates and improvements to the model, ensuring that it stays effective as more data
becomes available.
Real-time validation phase
In the real-time validation phase, the trained model stored in the cloud is deployed to the testing dataset of brain
images. These inputs (testing dataset of brain images) are processed in real time, allowing the system to provide
instant predictions. Explainable AI techniques are also applied at this stage to maintain transparency, ensuring
that the results can be interpreted and trusted by medical professionals. This step tests the system’s ability to
perform in practical, real-world scenarios, confirming its utility in clinical settings.
Decision making
The final step involves making a decision based on the model’s prediction. If the system detects a brain tumour,
the information is forwarded to medical professionals for further analysis, diagnosis, or treatment planning. If
no tumour is detected, the data is discarded to avoid unnecessary storage and processing. This step ensures that
the system is efficient and the results are actionable, providing critical support for timely and accurate clinical
decision-making. Table 2 outlines the pseudocode detailing the step-by-step process of the proposed model.

of the proposed brain tumour prediction model. One of the primary challenges is handling variations in image

must be robust enough to perform accurately despite these inconsistencies. Additionally, the issue of class
imbalance is addressed by carefully analyzing the distribution of “Tumour” and “No Tumour” categories in the
dataset to prevent biased predictions.

While LIME and Grad-CAM enhance interpretability, they are sensitive to input variations and may produce
inconsistent results. A trade-off between transparency and accuracy also exists, which must be considered
in clinical applications. To address these interpretability challenges, the model further estimates predictive
uncertainty using Monte Carlo Dropout. By enabling dropout during inference and performing multiple forward
passes, it generates a distribution of predictions. The variance among these outputs is used as an uncertainty
score, reflecting the model’s confidence in its classification. This enables clinicians to identify low-confidence
predictions and prioritize them for expert review, thereby enhancing diagnostic reliability.

Effective treatment for brain tumors relies on accurate detection because this is a crucial health
condition. Medical imaging plays a pivotal role in improving tumor detection and diagnosis in the
early stage. This study presents two approaches to the tumor detection problem focusing on the
healthcare domain. A combination of image processing, vision transformer (ViT), and machine learning
algorithms is the first approach that focuses on analyzing medical images. The second approach is the
parallel model integration technique, where we first integrate two pre-trained deep learning models,
ResNet101, and Xception, followed by applying local interpretable model-agnostic explanations
(LIME) to explain the model. The results obtained an accuracy of 98.17% for the combination of vision
transformer, random forest and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization and 99. 67% for the
parallel model integration (ResNet101 and Xception). Based on these results, this paper proposed the
deep learning approach—parallel model integration technique as the most effective method. Future
work aims to extend the model to multi-class classification for tumor type detection and improve
model generalization for broader applicability.

LIME, Magnetic resonance imaging, Vision transformer

accurate identification of brain tumors is essential for the treatment and prognosis of diseases2. With the

accuracy. For instance, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have worked well with tumor detection in
medical images as an image classification tool. But these methods do require a lot of manually annotated data
and computational resources, which confronts their more broad applicability in a clinical setting9.
The systems for automated diagnosis of diverse medical conditions have been made more accurate and

Deep learning systems put some ease on the task involving the diagnostics classification by letting the deep
neural networks learn the features and patterns of the datasets on their own. The growing use of deep learning
as an approach for classification problems has an endorsement of powerful computing hardware architectures,
particularly GPUs and TPUs20. Also, some other free-source coding frameworks like Keras with TensorFlow
backend and PyTorch are contributing to this process. In addition, a variety of such neural network deep
architectures as VGG, AlexNet, Inception, ResNet, Xception and other models are available for incorporation in

MRI images aided in the construction of an advanced classification that supports recognizing brain tumors.
Tumor magnitudes such as VGG1623, ResNet50, DenseNet24 and VGG19 enabled the use of transfer learning
so as to efficiently identify most typical cases of brain tumors. The Deep Transfer Learning models were trained
and validated on 3,000 MRI scans available in the Figshare data repository. It achieved 99.02% accuracy, which
is very favorable when comparing it with results obtained from ResNet5025.
The described transformer architecture consists of an encoder that has multi-headed self-attention and
MLP26 components. To fit into the requirements of transformers, images must first be tokenized. So, the
input image of size 1024 × 256 × 3 is split into 256 patches of uniform size 32 × 32. These image patches
are transformed with linear layer projections, these patches are then fed into the model as fixed-sized 1-D
embeddings. One-dimensional positional embeddings are incorporated into the patch embeddings in order to
maintain spatial context. Furthermore, the model includes a class token that is appended to the beginning of the
patch embeddings set. In the end, the model output is taken from the MLP head and the dense layer. The weight
output layer that corresponds to the categories was also included27,28.

This set of works collectively makes the case for the paradigm shift deep learning introduces to the domain of
neuroimaging and patient care.
The ongoing increased adoption of deep learning (DL) approaches, and most specifically convolutional
neural networks (CNNs), has made many contributions to medical image interpretation. In contrast to the
traditional machine learning (ML) techniques, CNNs employ a top-down feature learning strategy that analyses
images in their natural form with no input on feature design33. This ability has tremendously enhanced the
accuracy and efficiency of brain tumor detection systems. Most of the studies have concluded that deep learning
algorithms outperform classical machine learning algorithms, particularly in image analysis involving complex
spatial features and tumor shape deformation. However, despite these achievements, the application of DL into
real-world clinical applications is hampered by large annotated data sets, high-performance computational
resources, and model explainability, among others, are required2.
Deep learning refers to a method that seeks a hierarchy of features from a given input through a neural
network with several layers. It is a popular method since, in contrast to traditional machine learning techniques
where features of an image are hard-coded, this one does it on its own. A variety of different deep-learning
algorithms have been used in order to achieve algorithms based on various objectives34. It is important to explain
that such architectures as ResNet101 or Xception, for example, are deep and good at capturing complex features,
so they are needed for complicated work such as the processing of medical images. As a starting point, the

makes the most impact. Using this advanced convolutional mechanism, the inputs information in the spatial

the amount of compute requirements while preserving the depth of representation. Xception on the other
hand, replaces standard convolutional layers with depthwise and pointwise convolutional layers and this way it
provides the opportunity for the model to learn even more complex patterns without any flattery55. Its distinct
advantage is that from large dimensional datasets it can obtain detailed information thus making it optimal

Self attention mechanism—
The self-attention mechanism technique has the potential to improve a model by emphasizing the most salient
parts of an input image through assigning importance to certain features. This technique therefore allows the
model to dynamically adjust the weighting of a feature in terms of its relevance to all other features and look
for significant areas or patterns within the image to make the required predictions accurately. Self-attention
processes the input by first generating query, key, and value representations from the input feature map and
use them to compute attention scores. These scores suggest the relative need of the strength of focus on a
feature as compared other features. The sounds have predictive implications therefore these predictive impli­
cations are used to alter the feature map. Features which are irrelevant or not predictive are suppressed. Such
a mechanism assists the model in capturing the long range interaction as well the contextual relationship
among the features within the image, important for recognition of both local and global structures such as
even small or faint elements in medical images. With self–attention it is expected that the model will perform
better for classifying images as it will concentrate more on the essential components of the image’s predicted
ones yielding more accurate and robust predictions.

Generalization enhancement
Parallel integration reduces overfitting by allowing diverse model perspectives during learning. As the two
networks process input images differently, the combined features act as a form of implicit regularization, leading

suggesting a moderate level of accuracy but indicating improved stability and consensus across predictions. The
Feature Fusion Technique underperformed relative to other models, achieving overall accuracy of 79.79%, thus
demonstrating a discrepancy in tumor recall 91.41% and no tumor recall at 68.18%.
Figures 14, 15 and 16 depict the learning progression of the three integration techniques over the epochs.
To ensure robustness and generalizability of the proposed model, 5-fold cross validation has been employed.
This method balances reliable performance estimation and workable computational efficiency within the system.
In this scenario, the dataset was divided into 5 partitions, also known as folds, or groups, of equal size. Each
subset works as a combination of both train and test data. For every pass, one subset is set aside as the validation
set, and the remaining four subsets serve as training data. While this step is necessary for optimization, it must
be done 5 times, allowing each subset to be used once for validation. These results from all of the folds worked
alongside each other to form new metrics for the model in question. The choice of five folds provides a practical
trade-off, reducing variance in performance estimation while keeping computational costs reasonable. The
detailed comparison of the results of all three techniques are displayed in Tables 9, 10 and 11.
The visualization of k-fold cross-validation with confusion matrix in Figs. 17, 18, and 19 demonstrates the
capacity of integrated models to extend across diverse datasets, where parallel model integration was superior
to other integration techniques. Therefore, confirming its applicability as a reliable solution in the real world.

Ethical considerations
Before clinical implementation, automated brain tumor classification systems require careful evaluation from
an ethical standpoint. The most important issue results from the potential for soft tissue brain tumors to be
misclassified as non-tumorous lesions (false negatives), which could slow down the necessary emergency
treatments and have dire health implications. On the other hand, these systems can also lead to false-positive
predictions which may increase unwarranted medical intervention alongside distressing emotions for patients.
Such consequences underscore the importance of developing AI systems designed to assist in decision-
making rather than acting autonomously as sole diagnosticians. Moreover, a lack of equity in the provision
of healthcare services may arise from bias in training data as well as opaque models. Therefore, incorporating
explainability methods, such as LIME, along with clinician-controlled validation, is crucial to establishing trust
and responsibility alongside safety for wider clinical use.

Conclusion
This study proposes a classification system for brain tumors that combines ResNet101 and Xception using
feature fusion, self-attention mechanism, and parallel model integration. Out of all the methods, the parallel
model integration method exhibited better results because it used the benefits of both architectures for enhanced
feature discrimination and classification robustness. The test results confirm that this method outperforms
traditional approaches by effectively capturing the complex spatial and semantic patterns present in medical
images. To overcome the inherent challenges presented by deep learning models, the use of explainable AI, like
the LIME algorithm, has been applied to enhance model transparency. LIME, like other XAI techniques, sheds
light on the components that ensure the model is free from bias and is reliable during clinical sessions. Such
methods demonstrate the expected competencies of advanced medical imaging understanding integrated with
the fusion of the interpretability components within deep learning models.
Future directions
Looking ahead, we plan to focus on expanding our efforts to a multi-class classification problem for differentiating
distinct subtypes of brain tumors. Also, the addition of cross-modality MRI data (T1, T2, FLAIR) will increase
the diagnostic utility even further. Moreover, semi-supervised and self-supervised paradigms can alleviate
the problem posed by too few labeled data. Also, further investigation may be conducted on strong domain
adaptation techniques for generic use on different MRI scans from varying sources. Another direction that holds
potential is treating tumor segmentation and tumor classification as interdependent, which could improve the
accuracy of the diagnosis.
