Abstract
Purpose Accurate brain tumor grade classification from magnetic resonance imaging is essential for diagnosis, treat-
ment planning, and prognosis assessment. Although deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance,
many lack clinical validation, robustness across datasets, and interpretability for decision support. This study proposes
an explainable hybrid deep learning framework that integrates tumor segmentation, feature optimization, grade clas-
sification, and model attribution for high-grade and low-grade gliomas, with evaluation across multiple MRI datasets
under controlled experimental conditions.
Methods The proposed framework, Towards Interpretable Multiclass Semantic Intelligence: Explainable Brain Tumor
Segmentation and Automated Grade Stratifi cation, integrates brain tumor segmentation, optimized feature selection,
and discriminative classifi cation to support automated tumor analysis and grade stratifi cation. Tumor regions are segmented
using a Path Aggregation Network (PANet) integrated with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) and ResNet-50
to preserve relevant structural characteristics. From the segmented tumor regions, shape, texture, and Histogram of Oriented
Gradients (HOG) features are extracted to characterize morphological and visual patterns. A modified Reptile Search Algo-
rithm (RSA) is then employed to select discriminative features, aiming to reduce feature redundancy and mitigate over fitting.
The selected features are subsequently classified using DenseNet-201 within a Siamese architecture to enhance robustness
to inter-patient variability. Model interpretability is incorporated through Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-
CAM), which provides visual explanations of the regions contributing to model predictions. The framework is evaluated using
the BraTS 2019, BraTS 2020, and BraTS 2021 datasets, together with additional MRI datasets.
Results The proposed model achieved classification accuracies of 99.12%, 99.23%, and 98.86% on the benchmark
datasets. The average precision, sensitivity, and specificity exceeded 98% across datasets, demonstrating strong
discrimination between tumor grades and consistent generalization across imaging protocols. Visualization analysis
highlighted tumor regions contributing to classification decisions.

Introduction
Brain tumors are among the most life-threatening dis-
eases and represent a significant cause of cancer-related
mortality worldwide [1]. According to the American
Cancer Society, approximately 25,400 new cases of
malignant brain and spinal cord tumors were diagnosed
in the USA in 2023, with nearly 18,760 associated deaths
reported during the same year [2]. Accurate identifi-
cation and classification of brain tumors are therefore
essential for effective treatment planning, prognosis esti-
mation, and improvement of patient survival outcomes in
clinical practice [3–5]. Advances in computer vision and
machine learning have significantly transformed medical
image analysis, enabling the early detection of diseases
and improving diagnostic accuracy.
Brain tumor classification (BTC) aims to categorize
tumors based on grade and severity. According to the
World Health Organization (WHO) grading system, glio-
mas are classified into Grades I–IV, where Grades I and
II correspond to low-grade gliomas (LGGs), and Grades
III and IV correspond to high-grade gliomas (HGGs)
[6]. Accurate differentiation between LGG and HGG
is crucial for treatment planning, chemotherapy and
radiotherapy selection, and predicting patient survival
[7]. Although LGG tumors generally grow more slowly,
delayed treatment may lead to malignant progression
into HGG.
Deep learning (DL) has significantly advanced brain
tumor classification (BTC) using magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), consistently outperforming traditional
machine learning approaches by automatically learn-
ing hierarchical and discriminative features from raw
data. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been
extensively employed for BTC, with architectures such
as DenseNet, ResNet, and custom CNN variants achiev-
ing strong performance on benchmark datasets. Recent
explainable CNN-based frameworks further enhance clini-
cal interpretability by highlighting tumor-relevant regions
using techniques such as Grad-CAM and SHAP, thereby
supporting clinical decision-making. However, purely
CNN-based models often exhibit limited generalization
across heterogeneous MRI datasets due to variations in
tumor appearance, size, and acquisition protocols [8].
DL techniques have demonstrated effectiveness across
multiple medical imaging applications, including brain
tumor classification and skin cancer detection [9, 10].

such as texture and descriptor methods [11], DL mod-

Methodology
The suggested methodology is comprised of five phases,
namely preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction,
feature optimization, and classification. Figure 1 illustrates
the overall architecture of the brain tumor classification
model. Multimodal MRI images are gathered and split into
training, validation, and testing datasets. Next, the images
are preprocessed through augmentation, resizing, and bias
field correction (BFC). Further, the tumor is segmented
by means of the proposed Panoptic Tumor Segmentation
Network that incorporates the use of PA-Net, GCNN, and
ResNet-50. The output obtained from the process is used
to segment the tumor region. Afterward, Radiomic fea-
tures such as shape-based and texture-based features are
extracted from the segmented tumor region. Statistics of
mean, entropy, and kurtosis are later on analyzed to find dis-
criminative tumor properties. The modified reptile search
algorithm (mRSA) is used to remove any redundant infor-
mation from the features obtained. The selected features are
provided to the classifier called DenseNet-201. Lastly, the
DenseNet-201 classifies tumors according to their grades
and, in other words, divides the MRI images into low-grade
glioma (LGG) and high-grade glioma (HGG).
Dataset description
The publicly available multimodal MRI brain tumor data-
sets BraTS 2019 [29–31], BraTS 2020 [32], BraTS 2021
[33, 34], and Brain Tumor MRI Dataset [35] were used to
train and assess the technique. The MRI sequence for the
LGG and HGG is illustrated in Fig. 1. The MRI images
of the LGG and HGG from the BraTS 2019 dataset are
illustrated in Fig. 2. The datasets used for development
and independent evaluation are summarized in Table 1.
The available evaluation includes public benchmark MRI
datasets and additional MRI data described in Table 5.
These datasets provide useful evidence of performance
across the evaluated cohorts, but they should not be
interpreted as equivalent to prospective multicenter clin-
ical validation.

Tumor regions are segmented using a hybrid deep learn-

effective boundary localization while preserving spatial

that subsequent classification focuses only on clinically

Patient‐level cross‐validation strategy
To prevent data leakage and ensure a fair evaluation, all
dataset partitioning procedures were performed strictly
at the patient level. Since each BraTS subject consists of
a complete 3D MRI volume containing multiple 2D slices
across four modalities (T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR), all
slices belonging to a given patient were treated as a single
entity during data splitting.
For the tenfold cross-validation experiments, patients
rather than individual slices were randomly assigned to
one of the tenfold. Consequently, all slices from a par-
ticular patient were included exclusively in either the
training or validation fold during each iteration and
never appeared simultaneously in both sets. This patient-
level stratification ensured that no information from a
patient’s MRI volume was shared across folds.
Furthermore, the class distribution of low-grade glioma
(LGG) and high-grade glioma (HGG) cases was main-
tained across folds to preserve class balance throughout
the cross-validation process. This evaluation protocol
eliminates inter-patient data leakage and provides a real-
istic estimate of the generalization performance of the
proposed framework.
Data partitioning and model validation procedure
In order to carry out a strict assessment and avoid data
leakage, all data partitioning steps were done in the con-
text of patient-level splitting. All slices from one BraTS
subject were included exclusively in one dataset parti-
tion. BraTS 2019 dataset was used to develop our model,
which included training, validation, feature selection, and
hyperparameter tuning. In BraTS 2019 dataset, patients
were split into train (70%), validation (15%), and test
(15%) sets via patient-level stratified sampling in order to
maintain the proportion of low-grade glioma (LGG) and
high-grade glioma (HGG).
In order to check the stability of our model, tenfold
patient-level cross-validation was performed using BraTS
2019 development dataset. In each fold, preprocessing,
feature extraction, mRSA-based feature selection, and
classification model training were done using only the
training part of this fold. Validation set from each fold
was used for performance estimation purposes only. Fol-
lowing the completion of the model development phase,
the proposed framework was tested on BraTS 2020 and

Performance evaluation
Statistical analysis and uncertainty
The evaluation was performed at the patient level to
avoid treating multiple slices from the same subject as
independent observations. Accuracy, sensitivity, speci-
ficity, precision, F1-score, AUC/ROC, and confusion
matrices were used as primary performance measures.
Where patient-level prediction outputs were available,
uncertainty should be summarized using patient-level
resampling rather than slice-level resampling. Formal
comparisons with selected baseline methods should use
paired patient-level predictions and a predefined sig-
nificance threshold. The manuscript does not introduce
numerical confidence intervals, calibration estimates,
decision-curve results, or ROC-comparison statistics
that are not explicitly supported by the source data sup-

Also, a major limitation of this study is that prospective

validation and workflow integration studies are required
before routine clinical deployment.

vide sufficiently detailed scanner-vendor, magnetic-

information to support a comprehensive multicenter

Conclusion and future work
In this study, an explainable hybrid method incorporat-
ing multiclass semantic segmentation, enhanced rep-
tile search algorithm-based feature selection, Siamese
DenseNet-201 classification, and Grad-CAM++ visuali-
zation was developed for classification of gliomas grades
from multimodal MRI images. The experimental analysis
revealed high classification accuracy and good perfor-
mance on the benchmark datasets evaluated.
The proposed hybrid method can be considered com-
petitive compared to a number of recent deep learning
methods while offering increased explainability of the
model. It can be potentially applied as a decision-support
tool in the diagnosis of brain tumors for radiologists.
Nevertheless, the results of this study can be only gen-
eralized to the datasets used in the study and cannot be
extrapolated onto other cases.

Abstract
Brain tumor detection remains a critical focus in neuro-oncology, requiring precise and efficient diagnostic methods
to support timely clinical decisions. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for this task, owing to
its exceptional soft tissue contrast and spatial resolution. Recent advancements in deep transfer learning have driven
transformative progress in automating tumor detection, achieving notable improvements in accuracy, scalability, and
computational efficiency. This paper systematically reviews state-of-the-art transfer learning techniques, including pre-
trained neural networks, domain adaptation approaches, fine-tuning methodologies, and ensemble learning frame-
works. It also provides an in-depth analysis of widely used MRI datasets, highlighting persistent challenges such as data
imbalance, overfitting, and variability across imaging domains. Emerging trends in model optimization, architectural
innovation, and generalization strategies are discussed, offering a forward-looking perspective on the future of auto-
mated tumor detection. Through a detailed comparative evaluation, this review identifies the strengths and limitations
of existing methods, while outlining potential directions for research aimed at developing robust, interpretable, and
clinically deployable systems for brain tumor diagnosis.
Keywords Brain tumor detection · Attention mechanisms · Deep learning · Segmentation · Classification · Transfer
learning · Medical imaging · Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) · And magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

The brain, a marvel of complexity and indispensability, governs the nervous system through an intricate interplay of
neurons and glial cells [1]. However, its susceptibility to pathological conditions, particularly brain tumors, presents
profound clinical and scientific challenges. Brain tumors, classified into benign (non-cancerous) and malignant (cancer-

implications. These tumors are often accompanied by severe neurological symptoms, including cognitive impairment,
persistent headaches, and motor dysfunctions. In the United States, the National Brain Tumor Society estimates over
787,000 individuals live with brain tumor diagnoses, with the five-year survival rate for malignant cases standing at a
mere 36% [2]. On a global scale, brain tumors rank as the tenth leading cause of death, emphasizing the urgent need for
improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

2.4 Brain tumors’ grade
The human brain is anatomically segmented into three primary regions: the brainstem, cerebrum, and cerebellum [7].
The cerebellum, the second-largest brain structure, is essential for coordinating motor functions, including equilibrium,
postural control, gait, and fine motor coordination. It is located posteriorly and connected to the brainstem. Both the
cerebellum and cerebrum contain internal white matter, deep gray matter nuclei, and a superficial gray matter layer
known as the cortex [8]. The brainstem, positioned at the base of the brain, serves as a conduit to the spinal cord and
regulates vital autonomic functions, encompassing motor and sensory path- ways, cardiovascular and respiratory con-
trol, and reflexive actions. It is comprised of the medulla oblongata, pons, and midbrain. According to the World Health
Organization (WHO), brain tumors are classified into four grades, ranging from I to IV. Tumors classified as Grade I and II
are typically characterized by slow proliferation and a relatively favorable prognosis. In contrast, Grade III and IV tumors
exhibit more aggressive growth patterns and are associated with a substantially poorer prognosis [9]. A detailed exami-
nation of these tumor grades and their clinical implications follows below.
Grade I: Tumors grow gradually and do not spread rapidly. Meningiomas and pitu- itary tumours, for example, have
a higher likelihood of long-term survival and are frequently totally eradicated through surgery.
Grade II: Tumors develop slowly but can infect neighboring tissues and advance to higher grades. They may return
following surgery. Oligodendroglioma is one such case.

2.5 Imaging modality: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
MRI is a sophisticated imaging method commonly used in medicine to visualize the inside components of the body,
particularly soft tissues such as the brain, muscles, and organs. MRI uses powerful magnetic fields and radio waves to
produce detailed pictures, giving it significant benefits over other imaging modalities such as X-rays and CT scans [10].
A big, strong magnet—typically a superconducting magnet—in the MRI equipment creates a static magnetic field.
When a patient enters the MRI scanner, the magnetic field aligns the protons in the body’s hydrogen atoms along the
field direction. The Short bursts of radio-frequency energy are applied, typically in the form of RF pulses at a specific
frequency. These pulses knock the aligned protons out of their alignment with the magnetic field. Once the RF pulse is
turned off, the protons begin to realign with the magnetic field. As they realign, the protons emit energy in the form of
radio waves, which are detected by the MRI sensors. The emitted signals are converted into digital images by the MRI
computer. The most commonly used sequences include T1-weighted, T2-weighted, Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recov-
ery (FLAIR), and Short Tau Inversion Recovery (STIR) [11]. Each sequence has unique characteristics and applications in

into two categories: supervised and unsupervised learning. Supervised learning trains models using labeled datasets,
where each input has a known output, enabling precise predictions. In contrast, unsupervised learning finds patterns
and relationships in unlabeled data without predefined categories. In brain imaging, ML has shown great potential for
tumor classification [15]. The process typically involves image preprocessing, feature extraction, feature selection, and
classification—each step playing a crucial role in improving accuracy. These techniques help refine the data, extract
meaningful information, and enhance diagnostic performance. Several ML classifiers, including Support Vector Machines

using kernel functions, effectively differentiating normal and abnormal tissues. Additionally, integrating SVM with

Domain adaptation involves modifying machine learning models so that they can perform well on different datasets,
even when there are variations in imaging protocols or equipment [77]. In the context of brain tumor detection, domain
adaptation techniques work by aligning the feature distributions between the source and target datasets, ensuring the
model maintains consistent performance despite differences in MRI scan characteristics. Techniques like adversarial

5.3.2 Variability across imaging domains
Differences in MRI scans, caused by variations in imaging protocols, hardware set- tings, or patient demographics, can

Longitudinal studies and the broader application of transfer learning and pretrained models could offer valuable
insights into tumor progression and treatment responses, further enhancing model performance across diverse clinical

title: Explainable artificial intelligence for brain tumor classification via fine-tuned transfer learning
authors: Essam H. Houssein; Amr M. Gamal; Eman M. G. Younis; Ebtsam Mohamed
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors remain one of the most life-threatening diseases worldwide, marked
by the abnormal and aggressive proliferation of cells within the brain. Accurate and
early detection is critical to improving treatment outcomes and reducing patient
mortality rates. However, manual analysis of brain MRI scans is often time-consuming,
prone to inter-observer variability, and lacks scalability. To address these challenges,
this study proposes an efficient and interpretable deep learning (DL) model for brain
tumor classification, utilizing transfer learning with the ResNet50 architecture. The
model is trained to distinguish among three tumor types—glioma, Meningioma, and
pituitary tumors, and normal brain MRI scans, using a fine-tuned network combined
with extensive data augmentation strategies to mitigate overfitting and enhance
generalization, particularly on limited-size medical datasets. The proposed model was
trained and evaluated on three publicly available multiclass brain tumor MRI datasets
comprising multi-planar MRI scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal) collected from patients
with diverse ages, tumor grades, and demographic backgrounds. In particular,
the BT-large-4c dataset from Kaggle includes 3264 MRI scans of brain tumors and
healthy controls across four classes (395 normal, 827 pituitary, 826 glioma, and 822
Meningioma). The proposed system achieved outstanding performance, attaining
99.41% accuracy, 99.15% precision, 99.09% sensitivity, 98.18% specificity, and a
98.91% F1-score on the test dataset. Unlike conventional black-box models, this work
emphasizes interpretability by integrating SHAP (Shapley Additive explanations), an
Explainable AI (XAI) technique that visualizes and quantifies feature importance at
the pixel level. This transparency facilitates greater clinical trust and understanding
by elucidating the rationale behind model predictions. Moreover, the proposed
ResNet50-based model consistently outperformed other established transfer learning
architectures, including VGG16, MobileNet, and DenseNet201, across key evaluation
metrics. By combining high diagnostic performance with SHAP-based interpretability,
the system provides transparent and trustworthy predictions that can meaningfully
support radiologists and healthcare professionals in routine clinical practice and the
early diagnosis of brain tumors.
Keywords Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), Brain tumor, Deep learning,
ResNet50, Transfer learning

Introduction
The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) applications across various sectors
makes their integration into healthcare inevitable and essential, particularly in disease
detection using diverse medical imaging modalities. Among the many health challenges,
brain tumors are among the most prevalent, devastating, and life-threatening condi­
tions, frequently associated with high morbidity and mortality. These tumors originate
from abnormal cell growth within the brain or surrounding tissues and can be either
malignant or benign. They can originate within the brain (primary tumors) or result
from metastasis from other parts of the body (secondary tumors). Regardless of type,
brain tumors disrupt normal brain function by exerting pressure on adjacent tissues,
leading to neurological deficits and potentially fatal outcomes if untreated.
Brain tumors represent a significant and growing global health concern. According to
the National Brain Tumor Society (2024), more than 700,000 individuals in the United
States are living with a primary brain tumor, with approximately 94,000 new cases diag­
nosed annually, indicating a steady rise in incidence. Complementary data from the
American Brain Tumor Association confirm that brain tumors affect all age groups and
remain a major cause of cancer-related mortality. Recent advancements in neuroimaging
and computational methods, particularly in AI, have opened new frontiers in the early
detection, segmentation, and classification of brain tumors, significantly improving clin­
ical decision-making and patient outcomes [1].
According to the previous classification, benign brain tumors are typically non-inva­
sive, grow slowly, and do not spread to surrounding tissues, thereby posing relatively
lower health risks. In contrast, malignant tumors are aggressive and often infiltrate
adjacent brain structures. Moreover, according to the Moffitt Cancer Center, the sur­
vival rate for malignant brain tumors remains alarmingly low, ranging between 6% and
9%, reflecting the aggressive nature and limited treatment success associated with these
tumors. Accurate differentiation between tumor types—such as gliomas, meningiomas,
and pituitary adenomas—is crucial, as each requires a distinct clinical approach and
treatment regimen [2].

The adoption of AI systems for brain tumor diagnosis also raises several important ethi­
cal considerations that extend beyond dataset bias. Public MRI datasets, while essential
for reproducible research, may not fully represent the demographic, clinical, or scan­
ner variability seen in real clinical settings, potentially introducing fairness concerns that
affect model generalizability. Moreover, medical imaging data inherently carries sensitive
patient information, underscoring the need for strict adherence to data privacy and gov­
ernance standards when utilizing publicly available datasets. Another ethical challenge
arises from the risk of over-reliance on automated predictions in high-stakes environ­
ments such as oncology, where diagnostic errors can have severe consequences. There­
fore, AI-based systems must remain decision-support tools rather than replacements for
clinical judgment. Additionally, the opaque nature of deep learning models poses risks
related to accountability and trust, as clinicians must understand the rationale behind
algorithmic outputs before integrating them into clinical workflows. To mitigate these
concerns, this study incorporates SHAP-based explainability to provide transparent,
clinically meaningful visualizations of model reasoning, thereby enhancing interpretabil­

Related works
The accurate and early identification of abnormal tissues within the brain has become a
critical priority in modern competent healthcare, as it directly impacts the survival and
quality of life for millions worldwide. As brain tumors often pose life-threatening risks,
timely diagnosis is essential for initiating appropriate clinical interventions. To support
radiologists and reduce diagnostic delays, a substantial body of research has been dedi­

clinical workflow efficiency.

With advancements in medical imaging, particularly MRI, automated brain tumor
detection frameworks have emerged as valuable tools for aiding clinical decision-mak­
ing. Leveraging DL, ML, and advanced image processing techniques, these systems
can accurately analyze complex brain scans, detect tumors, and classify them based on
type and severity. The integration of XAI further enhances these approaches by offering
transparency and interpretability, which are crucial for building clinical trust and ensur­
ing the safe adoption of medical practices.
This section is organized into two parts to systematically explore the evolution of brain
tumor diagnosis using AI. The first part highlights prominent studies utilizing traditional
AI techniques, including DL and ML, to detect and classify tumors based on MRI data.
These models primarily focused on improving classification accuracy, segmentation pre­
cision, and computational efficiency. The second part presents a selection of more recent
research that integrates XAI into the diagnostic process, demonstrating how transpar­
ency and interpretability can support clinicians in understanding model predictions and
improving trust in AI-driven medical imaging applications.
In the broader context of medical imaging, numerous studies have emphasized the
benefits of transfer learning for scenarios involving limited or imbalanced MRI datas­
ets. Pretrained convolutional models such as ResNet, VGG, and Inception have demon­
strated the ability to reuse rich, generic feature representations learned from large-scale
natural image datasets like ImageNet, thereby significantly reducing the amount of
domain-specific labeled data required for training [13, 14]. This capability is particularly
valuable in neuroimaging, where acquiring large and diverse MRI datasets is challenging
due to privacy constraints, high annotation costs, and clinical heterogeneity. Transfer
learning not only mitigates overfitting but also accelerates convergence and enhances
generalization, making it a widely adopted strategy in brain tumor classification tasks.

Beyond predictive performance, recent literature increasingly highlights the essential

“black boxes,” posing challenges for clinical acceptance because radiologists must
understand the rationale behind algorithmic decisions before integrating AI outputs
into patient care. Explainable AI (XAI) methods such as SHAP and Grad-CAM have
therefore become central to building clinical trust, as they provide interpretable visual
or quantitative attributions that help clinicians validate model reasoning and identify
potential failure points [15, 16]. These techniques serve as a bridge between high-accu­
racy DL systems and real-world medical decision-making standards, where transparency
and accountability are paramount. Recent architectures integrating Vision Transform­
ers (ViT) with convolutional networks have also shown promising results across several
medical imaging domains, including brain MRI classification [17, 18]. Hybrid ViT-CNN
models leverage the global self-attention capabilities of transformers alongside the
local feature extraction strength of CNNs, and in some cases, achieve superior accu­
racy. However, these models typically require larger datasets and more computational
resources than pure CNNs, and many existing transformer-based studies still provide
limited interpretability. As a result, CNN-based transfer learning combined with explicit
XAI mechanisms continues to offer a more balanced trade-off between data efficiency,
interpretability, and clinical practicality, particularly in settings where dataset diversity
is limited.

3.4 eXplainable artificial intelligence (XAI)
XAI is a vital subfield within AI that aims to develop models and algorithms capable
of producing human-understandable explanations for their predictions or decisions. In
high-stakes areas like medicine, where model transparency and reliability are impera­
tive, XAI provides essential interpretability to otherwise opaque ML systems [46]. Tra­
ditional DL and ML models often function as “black boxes,” offering high predictive
performance while obscuring the internal decision-making process. In such models,
users, even developers,typically have limited insight into how inputs are transformed
into outputs. This lack of interpretability is particularly problematic in critical domains
such as healthcare, where understanding the rationale behind a model’s decision is as
important as the decision itself [47]. XAI addresses this challenge by making ML predic­
tions more transparent, comprehensible, and justifiable to end-users.
By offering interpretable outputs, XAI empowers users to better understand the rea­
soning behind AI decisions, detect potential biases, and refine model performance. In
clinical applications such as brain tumor classification, integrating XAI enhances diag­
nostic confidence and fosters collaboration between AI systems and medical practitio­
ners [48].
Several XAI techniques have been explored in this context, including SHAP, Anchors,
and CEM (Contrastive Explanation Method). SHAP, based on cooperative game theory,
interprets model output by assigning each feature an importance value (Shapley value)
for a given prediction. It provides local explanations tailored to individual predictions, as
well as global interpretations across the entire dataset [49]. Anchors, in contrast, gener­
ate intuitive if-then rules that serve as high-precision conditions under which a model’s
prediction is invariant, making them especially accessible for users without deep ML
expertise. Meanwhile, CEM provides contrastive explanations by identifying the features
that must be present for a prediction and those that must be absent, offering a dual-
perspective insight into model reasoning.

brain tumor classification to visualize and validate model attention. This helped assess

reflects the degree of differentiation between the brightest and darkest areas within

making structural details more prominent. In this study, the enhancement techniques
employed are primarily based on histogram modification methods, which are designed

3.5.4 Phase 3: explainable AI using SHAP
To enhance the interpretability of the classification model, we employed SHAP, a model-
agnostic framework for explainability introduced by Lundberg and Lee [52]. SHAP is
grounded in cooperative game theory and offers a unified approach to interpreting pre­
dictions made by complex ML models, including deep neural networks and ensemble
methods. The core idea of SHAP is to assign each feature an importance value that rep­
resents its contribution to a particular prediction. This is achieved through the compu­
tation of Shapley values, which consider all possible combinations (coalitions) of input
features. The final explanation is derived by aggregating the marginal contributions of a
feature across all possible subsets of features in the dataset.
The SHAP Python library was utilized to generate local and global explanations of our
model’s predictions. These explanations enabled the visualization of feature importance,
allowing for the interpretation of how each input feature influenced the output class in
the context of brain tumor classification.

rather than non-pathological background tissues.

explanation fidelity, enabling the generation of stable and interpretable attribution maps

Explainability of the proposed model using SHAP
SHAP was utilized to analyze MRI samples across all brain tumor classes, thereby pro­
moting interpretability and trust in the proposed classification model. By leveraging
SHAP with the fine-tuned ResNet50 architecture, this study provided detailed insights
into the model’s decision-making process, enabling clinicians to better understand and
validate the classification outcomes. SHAP assigns an importance score to each input
feature, in this case, each image pixel, by evaluating its contribution to the model’s out­
put. These values are derived using a game-theoretic approach that considers all possi­
ble combinations of features, generating visually interpretable heatmaps. In these maps,
red pixels signify a positive contribution toward a particular class prediction, while blue
pixels reflect features that reduce the likelihood of that class. This pixel-wise attribution
enhances the transparency of the model’s predictions, allowing more informed assess­
ments in clinical settings.

four classes: glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor. Each row corresponds
to a sample image, accompanied by SHAP heatmaps for all possible classes. A strong
diagonal activation pattern is observed, i.e., SHAP maps highlight the correct class while
suppressing irrelevant ones, demonstrating the model’s ability to learn class-specific
features effectively. In the first row, red regions are prominently highlighted only in
the glioma SHAP map, indicating correct classification and strong feature importance.

Conclusion
This research presents a robust and interpretable DL framework for classifying brain
tumors using MRI. By fine-tuning the ResNet50 architecture through transfer learning
and integrating SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), the proposed model effectively
balances high predictive performance with explainability, an essential requirement for
clinical adoption.
The system achieved outstanding classification results, with accuracies of 99.81%
(training), 99.55% (validation), and 99.30% (testing). It also maintained excellent preci­
sion (99.15%), sensitivity (99.09%), specificity (98.18%), and F1-score (98.91%). These
metrics confirm the model’s ability to accurately differentiate between glioma, menin­
gioma, and pituitary tumor classes. The low disparity between training and valida­
tion accuracy further indicates strong generalization capability and reduced risk of
overfitting.
SHAP-based explanations provided pixel-level interpretability by highlighting the
regions contributing most strongly to a specific tumor prediction. This integration
enhances transparency and fosters clinician trust, providing a reliable foundation for
informed clinical decision-making. The proposed model was also rigorously compared
with established DL architectures such as VGG16, MobileNet, and DenseNet201, con­
sistently outperforming them across all evaluation metrics.

clinical variability. Second, the model operates exclusively on 2D MRI slices without
leveraging multimodal or volumetric (3D) information, which limits its ability to capture
richer anatomical context.
Although the model demonstrates strong generalization performance, the learning
curves reveal a slight but consistent gap between training and validation accuracy, indi­
cating mild overfitting. This behavior is expected in deep learning models trained on
highly discriminative datasets and does not significantly affect overall classification qual­
ity. Data augmentation, transfer learning, regularization, and early stopping were applied
to minimize overfitting. The final confusion matrix and per-class metrics confirm bal­
anced performance across all tumor classes and the Tumor-less category. Nonetheless,
future work may further mitigate this effect by incorporating stronger regularization
strategies, expanding the datasets, or utilizing cross-institutional validation cohorts.
While Table 12 provides a broad comparison between the proposed method and prior
brain tumor classification studies, it is important to note that several of the cited works
were conducted on datasets with different sizes, imaging protocols, preprocessing pipe­
lines, and evaluation splits. These variations inherently limit the direct comparability
of accuracy values across studies. Although such comparisons remain useful for high­
lighting general performance trends, the reported differences should be interpreted cau­
tiously. Future work will therefore focus on harmonized cross-dataset evaluation and
benchmarking to enable more rigorous and externally valid comparisons.
Additionally, while SHAP provides fine-grained interpretability, the system has not
yet been validated on external multi-center datasets, raising the possibility of dataset-
specific bias. Finally, real-time performance constraints and hardware limitations were
not explicitly benchmarked, leaving the feasibility of deployment in time-critical clinical
environments open to question.

Future Work
To address the identified limitations and further advance the clinical applicability of the
proposed framework, several targeted directions are planned:
1. Extension to 3D and multimodal data: The current 2D slice-based approach will be
extended to process full 3D MRI volumes using architectures such as 3D ResNet or
nnU-Net. Additionally, fusion of multiple MRI sequences (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) will
be explored through late or early fusion strategies. These extensions are expected to
enhance tumor boundary delineation and reduce false positives in complex cases, as
demonstrated through quantitative evaluation on the BraTS challenge datasets.
2. Enhanced external validation: The model will be rigorously evaluated on independent,
multi-center datasets (e.g., BraTS 2020–2024 cohorts and TCIA collections) to assess
generalizability and detect potential dataset-specific biases. Cross-institutional testing
will include harmonization techniques, such as ComBat or histogram matching, to
enable a fair performance comparison.

4. Deployment optimization and efficient learning: Model compression techniques (e.g.,

Furthermore, active learning frameworks will be incorporated to iteratively select

These focused extensions aim to bridge the gap between the current research prototype
and a robust, clinically deployable tool, ultimately strengthening its potential impact in

The proposed framework offers two key advantages over prior work. First, it not only
achieves superior predictive performance, with an accuracy of 99.41% compared to the
typical 97–98% reported in recent studies, but also maintains consistently high preci­
sion, sensitivity, and specificity, as summarized in Table 10. Second, by integrating SHAP
to generate pixel-level attribution maps directly overlaid on MRI scans, the model moves
beyond black-box predictions and provides clinically meaningful visual evidence of its
decisions. This combination of state-of-the-art accuracy and fine-grained interpretabil­
ity enhances the model’s suitability for real-world clinical decision support, where both
reliability and transparency are essential.

title: A deep transfer learning and ensemble learning framework for brain tumor detection and classification in MRI images
authors: Md. Abdul Alim Sheikh; Abhijit Dey; Alok Kole
text:
Abstract
This study proposes a novel framework that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) and
Ensemble Learning (EL) for multi-class classification of brain tumors using Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI) images. The classification targets four categories: glioma,
meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Several state-of-the-art deep learning
architectures from the VGG, Inception, ResNet, and DenseNet families were analyzed
and compared. Based on their performance, six Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs)—VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201—
were selected for transfer learning to perform the classification task. To enhance
classification accuracy, ensemble learning was applied using a weighted voting
strategy, where the accuracy of each model served as its weight. The four top-
performing models VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were combined
in this ensemble. To further interpret the model’s decisions, Explainable Artificial
Intelligence (XAI) technique, specifically Grad-CAM, was employed to highlight
key regions in the MRI images that influenced the classification outcomes, thereby
improving model transparency. The models were trained and evaluated on the
publicly available BT-7023 dataset from Kaggle, consisting of 7,023 MRI images
(5,712 for training and 1,311 for testing). Performance was assessed using accuracy,
precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed ensemble method achieved excellent
results, with 99.28% accuracy, 98.62% precision, 99.56% recall, and a 98.58% F1-score.
To verify the robustness of the approach, cross-dataset validation was conducted
using an external dataset from Figshare. The proposed ensemble outperformed
existing models on this dataset, achieving 98.80% accuracy. Overall, the ensemble
framework demonstrated a 5%–13% performance improvement over existing
methods, underscoring its effectiveness and reliability for early detection and
classification of brain tumors. Additionally, the XAI-based analysis confirmed the
model’s focus on clinically relevant tumor regions, enhancing interpretability and
trustworthiness in medical applications.
Keywords Brain tumor, CNN, Deep learning, Transfer learning, Ensemble learning, MR
images

​1 Introduction
Brain tumors result from abnormal and uncontrolled cell growth in different brain
regions, leading to severe neurological impairments and reduced quality of life [1].
Owing to their clinical severity and diagnostic complexity, they remain a major medi­
cal challenge [2]. Brain tumors commonly include glioma (GL), meningioma (ME), pitu­
itary (PT), and no-tumor (NT) cases, with gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors
being the most prevalent primary brain tumors [3, 4]. Meningiomas typically originate
from the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord and are generally benign [5],
whereas gliomas arise from glial cells, account for nearly one-third of brain tumor cases,
and exhibit the highest mortality rates [6]. Pituitary tumors develop within the pituitary
gland and are usually less aggressive [7].
Brain tumors can cause significant physical and neurological impairments, often
necessitating intensive treatment. The severity of symptoms depends on tumor type,
size, and location. Accurate tumor classification using MRI is critical for diagnosis, treat­
ment planning, and improved patient outcomes. Early detection enhances survival rates
and quality of life; however, manual image interpretation is time-consuming and prone
to human error [8, 9]. Medical imaging, particularly MRI, plays a central role in brain
tumor diagnosis due to its high spatial resolution and non-invasive nature [10, 11].
Despite technological advances, the diagnostic process [128] remains complex and
heavily reliant on radiologist expertise. Increasing imaging volumes and inter-patient
variability in tumor characteristics reduce efficiency and increase diagnostic cost [8].
Automated classification systems address these challenges by enabling objective, repro­
ducible, and efficient image analysis, thereby improving diagnostic reliability [12, 129].
The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Deep Learning (DL),
has significantly advanced medical image analysis [13]. DL-based methods, particularly
convolutional neural networks (CNNs), demonstrate strong capability in learning com­
plex patterns from large datasets, making them highly effective for brain tumor classi­
fication [14, 15]. AI-assisted diagnosis has improved neuropathological confidence and
clinical decision-making [16, 17].
Nevertheless, challenges such as dataset imbalance, high computational requirements,

rely on single CNN architectures or unweighted ensembles, our method integrates (i)
the unified integration of transfer learning, ensemble learning and explainable AI within
a single pipeline, (ii) performance-guided weighted voting, (iii) cross-dataset evaluation
to demonstrate generalization.

limited interpretability, and variability in imaging. By incorporating XAI and leveraging
diverse data sources, the model demonstrates improved generalizability across different
populations and imaging conditions, making it a more adaptable and clinically relevant
solution for brain tumor diagnosis.

field of medical imaging. DL has emerged as a powerful alternative, offering improved

of DL technologies has fueled growing interest in their application to brain tumor analy­
sis. Several works [25, 33–35] have employed both machine learning (ML) and DL meth­
ods for tumor classification, demonstrating promising results. This section presents a
review of notable research contributions that apply ML and DL models for the detection
and classification of brain tumors from a medical imaging perspective.

the automated segmentation of brain tumors in MRI scans. Their architecture com­
prises two core components: an encoder, which utilizes a CNN to extract both spatial
and semantic features from the input images, and a decoder, which reconstructs a prob­
ability map to delineate tumor regions. The study further explored the use of ResNet and
DenseNet architectures, incorporating ResNet-50 within a TL paradigm for enhanced
tumor identification. The proposed model achieved a segmentation accuracy of 95% in
experimental evaluations. In a related effort, Sarmad Maqsood et al. [37] proposed a
hybrid technique integrating fuzzy logic with a U-Net-based CNN to perform binary

The workflow of the proposed model, illustrated in Fig. 1, employs six widely recognized

This study investigates deep transfer learning architectures to improve brain tumor
classification accuracy. Four CNN families—VGG, Inception, ResNet, and DenseNet—
were evaluated using RGB images resized to 224 × 224 pixels. Six pre-trained models
(VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet152, and DenseNet201) were selected
due to their robustness, high accuracy, and complementary feature-learning capabilities.
All six CNNs were pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset prior to task-specific fine-
tuning. Next, the front-end layers of the trained models in these six CNNs are frozen
to preserve the learned features and prevent any loss of information during subsequent
training. Subsequently, the augmented brain Tumor images and their corresponding
labels are used to fine-tune the fully connected layers at the back ends of the six net­
works. This allows the classification knowledge gained from ImageNet to be effectively
transferred to the target test data. The following sub-sections provide a brief overview of
the CNN models employed for TL in this study.
3.1.1 Visual geometry group 16
VGGNet ranked among the top two performers in the 2014 ImageNet Large-Scale
Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) [18, 92]. Introduced by Simonyan and Zisser­
man in 2014 [18], the VGG16 model is a widely used variant within the VGG network
family. Similar to AlexNet [18, 95, 96], VGG16 is a deep CNN designed for image classi­
fication and object detection. One of its key strengths lies in its ability to effectively man­
age large-scale datasets and handle complex visual recognition tasks [93].
The VGG16 architecture is composed of 16 layers, including convolutional layers with
3 × 3 receptive fields that enable fine-grained feature extraction. It incorporates five max-
pooling layers with 2 × 2 filter sizes, which gradually downsample the spatial dimensions
of the feature maps. These are followed by three fully connected layers that refine the
learned features for final classification. ReLU activation is used in the hidden layers to
introduce non-linearity, while the SoftMax function in the output layer enables multi-
class classification [94]. The VGG16 architecture is shown in Fig. 2.

VGG19 is a deep CNN architecture that extends the original VGG16 model [95]. It com­

extracts complex patterns and features from image data using its deep architecture,
which relies on 3 × 3 convolutional filters for effective feature extraction [95].
Max-pooling operations are used to progressively reduce the spatial dimensions of the
feature maps, thereby lowering computational complexity. The fully connected layers
at the end of the network utilize the high-level features learned by the preceding con­
volutional layers to make final predictions. Non-linearity is introduced using the ReLU
activation function. Renowned for its simplicity and effectiveness, VGG19 has become a
widely adopted benchmark in computer vision tasks, particularly in image classification.
However, despite its deep and straightforward design, it has been outperformed by more
recent architectures such as ResNet and Inception in terms of accuracy and computa­
tional efficiency. Figure 3 illustrates the VGG19 architecture. Both VGG16 and VGG19
are known for their structural simplicity, but they are resource-intensive, requiring sig­

consisting of 152 layers [96]. Its standout feature is the use of residual or skip connec­

Data preprocessing and augmentation
To standardize the input data for brain tumor classification, a series of preprocessing
steps were applied. All MRI images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels to ensure uniformity
across all models. RGB images were converted to grayscale, followed by Gaussian blur
filtering to reduce noise and enhance image quality while preserving essential features.
High-pass filtering was then used to sharpen the images and emphasize fine details.
These preprocessed images, along with their corresponding labels, served as input for
model training and evaluation.
To address limited data availability and improve generalization, data augmentation
was performed using Keras’ ImageDataGenerator. Techniques such as rotation, zoom,
flipping, and shifting were applied to synthetically expand the dataset and simulate vari­
ability in real-world medical imaging. This not only enhanced model robustness and
reduced overfitting but also balanced class distributions [106, 107]. This augmenta­
tion-based strategy has proven effective in improving the overall performance of deep
learning models, resulting in higher accuracy [106, 107]. In total, data augmentation
increased the training dataset from 10,087 to 35,583 images. Data augmentation was
applied exclusively to the training set. No augmented samples were used in validation or
testing, thereby fully preventing data leakage. In particular, we have applied augmenta­
tion before dataset splitting can lead to data leakage, where augmented variants of the
same image may appear across training and testing sets, resulting in overly optimistic
performance estimates. To mitigate this risk, dataset splitting was performed prior to
augmentation, and all augmented samples were derived solely from the original train­
ing images. Additionally, all images were normalized to ensure consistent pixel value
distribution. Figure 10 illustrates examples of original and augmented MRI images, and
Table 3 summarizes the dataset composition.

Although Table 4 reports the use of five-fold cross-validation, the model was not

was repeated five times so that each fold served as the validation set exactly once. The

clarity, references to a “single training session” indicate one complete training run per

Evaluation metrics
The performance of the proposed transfer learning models is assessed using a confusion
matrix, which enables the calculation of key evaluation metrics such as precision, recall
(sensitivity), F1-score, AUC and accuracy [15]. Structured as an n × n square matrix for
n-class classification problems, the confusion matrix provides a comprehensive view of
the model’s prediction outcomes [91]. Table 5 presents an example of a confusion matrix
for a binary classification task, where TP (true positives), FP (false positives), FN (false
negatives), and TN (true negatives) represent the four fundamental prediction catego­
ries. Specifically, TP refers to tumor cases correctly identified by the model, FP denotes
non-tumor cases wrongly classified as tumors, FN accounts for tumor cases missed by
the model, and TN indicates non-tumor cases correctly predicted. The F1-score, defined
as the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
These evaluation metrics are computed by applying the model to a dataset of 7023
MRI images and counting the occurrences of TP, FP, FN, and TN. Equations (1)–(4) [15]
are used to calculate the accuracy, precision, recall (sensitivity), and F1-score of each
model. Accuracy represents the proportion of correctly classified instances relative to
the total number of samples. Overall, the confusion matrix serves as an essential analyti­
cal tool for measuring and interpreting the classification performance of the proposed
models.

Ensemble learning
Ensemble learning is a powerful machine learning paradigm where multiple models
are combined to solve a particular problem e.g., classification, regression with better
accuracy, robustness, and generalization than any single model [28]. Ensemble pruning
is a technique used in ensemble learning to select a subset of trained individual learn­
ers rather than utilizing the all-ensemble learners [91]. This approach offers two key
advantages. First, it enables ensemble predictions with a reduced network scale, which
lowers both storage requirements and computational costs associated with processing
each learner’s output, thereby enhancing overall model efficiency. Second, by eliminat­
ing redundant or less effective models, ensemble pruning can improve the generalization
performance compared to using all available learners.
In this study, two classifiers with comparatively lower performance were pruned from
the six TL-based CNN models. The remaining four VGG16, Xception, ResNet152, and
DenseNet201 were selected as the final individual learners for further analysis. Since
classification accuracy was the primary evaluation criterion, each model’s accuracy was
used as a weight in the ensemble’s voting mechanism. In this method, first, each weight
is quantized using a step size of 0.01, forming a discrete set inl ine-eq-IEq 1

Qualitative evaluation
To complement the quantitative evaluation of our proposed brain tumor detection
technique using MRI, we conducted a qualitative analysis. For this purpose, six repre­
sentative MRI images were selected from our dataset. As illustrated in Fig. 14, the pro­
posed EL model delivered consistent and reliable results across all tumor categories.
The selected cases reflect a broad spectrum of brain tumor scenarios, highlighting the
model’s robustness under diverse clinical conditions. This consistent performance sug­
gests the model’s potential for effective monitoring and detection of brain tumors in
MRI scans.
Accurate identification of small brain tumors has remained a challenge in prior
research. To address this, we expanded our dataset to include tumors of varying
sizes, thereby improving detection accuracy. Figure 17 displays examples of small
brain tumors included in our study. Drawing inspiration from previous work [14], we
employed a technique designed to enhance the detection of small objects while preserv­
ing fine-grained details. This approach involves fusing a low-resolution feature map with
a higher-resolution map from deeper layers. The larger feature map benefits from both
the spatial information captured in lower layers and the rich semantic information from
higher layers, enabling more precise identification of tumors across different size scales.
Figure 18 presents the images that were misclassified by the proposed model. The
numerical values within the matrix offer valuable insights into the model’s performance
in accurately distinguishing between various tumor classes.

Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence
Explainable AI (XAI) [29] is essential for transparency in AI systems, especially in health­
care where model decisions directly affect patient outcomes [108]. In brain tumor clas­
sification, methods like CAM, Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, and Attention Maps improve
deep learning model interpretability [31]. We incorporated XAI into our proposed
model to provide insight into its decision-making process and enhance clinical trust.

Specifically, Grad-CAM [30] was employed for its strong spatial localization, enabling
clear visualization of tumor regions in MRI scans.
Grad-CAM [30], an extension of CAM, is a widely used XAI technique for visualiz­
ing CNN decision processes. It generates class-specific heatmaps by computing the gra­
dients of the predicted class with respect to the final convolutional layer’s activations,
thereby highlighting the most influential regions in MRI images for brain tumor classifi­
cation. In our XAI-integrated CNN architecture, Grad-CAM was applied by performing
a forward pass to obtain predictions, followed by a backward pass to compute impor­
tance weights from the gradients. These weights were used to create activation maps,
emphasizing regions critical to the model’s decision. ReLU was applied to retain only
positive contributions, and the resulting maps were overlaid on the original images,
offering interpretable visualizations of model focus across different layers.

Slice-level analysis and patient-level decision making
In this study, model training is performed at the 2D slice level, while diagnostic deci­
sions are derived at the patient level. It is acknowledged that MRI slices acquired from
the same subject exhibit strong inter-slice correlation, particularly among adjacent axial
planes. To prevent bias caused by such correlation, data partitioning was conducted
strictly at the patient level, ensuring that all slices from a given subject were assigned
exclusively to either the training, validation, or test set, thereby eliminating cross-set
leakage.

Comparisons with previous research
To assess the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, a comparative analysis was con­
ducted against existing deep learning models using the Kaggle Brain Tumor dataset. The
performance of recent state-of-the-art methods in image classification is summarized
in Table [11] . As illustrated, our approach achieved a superior accuracy of 98.90%, out­
performing previous studies such as Z. Ren et al. [109], who reported an accuracy of
approximately 96%, and H. H. Sultan et al. [65], who achieved 96.13%. Table [13] also
presents the performance of other artificial neural network (ANN) models on various
classification tasks, with all methods evaluated using the Tumor dataset (refer to column
3 of Table 11). It is important to note that while some studies addressed both binary
and multi-class classification, only the results for multi-class tasks are considered in this
comparison. Furthermore, few studies reported metrics beyond accuracy. In cases where
additional metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score were provided, the proposed
method consistently demonstrated superior performance. For the sake of consistency
in statistical comparison, the focus here is primarily on accuracy. Overall, the proposed
method exhibits a notable improvement in accuracy, ranging from 0.13% to 19.4% com­
pared to other algorithms.

To evaluate the generalizability and robustness of the proposed method, we conducted
cross-dataset validation using an external brain tumor dataset from the publicly avail­
able Figshare collection [105]. As this dataset lacks normal brain images, the “no tumor”

Among all fine-tuned transfer learning models, the proposed ensemble learning (EL)
approach achieved the highest performance, attaining an accuracy of 98.80%, F-score of
98.11%, recall of 98.17%, and precision of 98.06%, highlighting its effectiveness in accu­
rately classifying brain tumors. ResNet152 also performed well, with 97.69% accuracy,

achieving 94.41% and 95.67% accuracy, respectively. DenseNet201 also yielded strong
results with an accuracy of 97.24%. A summary of all performance metrics for the indi­
vidual CNN models and the proposed ensemble method on the test set is provided in
Table 13. To provide a more intuitive visualization of these classification results, a histo­
gram summarizing the evaluation metrics was constructed and shown in Fig. 21.

training from scratch and transfer learning approaches were applied independently on
each model using the pre-segmented Kaggle Brain MRI dataset to compare their perfor­
mance. Confusion matrix analysis was used to evaluate and visualize the strengths and
limitations of each architecture.
To further improve classification accuracy, ensemble learning was implemented
using a weighted voting strategy. The four top-performing models VGG16, Xception,
ResNet152, and DenseNet201 were selected through ensemble pruning to serve as indi­
vidual classifiers. Based on extensive experimentation, a weighted voting mechanism,
where each model’s weight corresponded to its accuracy, was used to combine their
predictions effectively. Extensive experimentation confirmed that our ensemble method
significantly outperformed individual models, achieving outstanding metrics: 99.285%
accuracy, 98.619% precision, 99.558% recall, and 98.586% F1-score. Compared to indi­
vidual transfer learning models, the proposed method improved accuracy by 0.1% to
5.25%, recall by 0.09% to 8.93%, and F1-score by approximately 0.3% to 5%. To validate
model interpretability, we employed XAI technique such as Grad-CAM to visualize
attention maps, highlighting tumor-affected regions in MRI scans. This explainability
supports clinical transparency and aligns model predictions with medical reasoning,
thereby improving its applicability in real-world healthcare settings. Although promis­
ing results are achieved, this study is limited to single-center data and basic geometric
augmentations. Future work will explore more realistic disturbance models and multi-
center datasets to better evaluate robustness under domain shifts and enhance clinical
generalization.
Although the proposed framework operates on 2D MRI slices, the final diagnostic out­
come is determined at the patient level. It is acknowledged that adjacent slices from the
same subject exhibit a high degree of correlation. To prevent information leakage aris­

ensuring that all slices belonging to a given subject appear exclusively in either the train­

and confidence-weighted averaging strategy. This aggregation emphasizes consistent
patterns across the full image volume and reduces the influence of redundant or highly
similar slices.
While 3D CNN architectures can explicitly model volumetric spatial dependencies,
a 2D slice-based approach was adopted in this study due to limited availability of fully
annotated volumetric datasets and computational constraints, which remains a com­
mon practice in brain MRI analysis. To enhance robustness and generalization, data aug­
mentation was applied exclusively to training slices, and patient-level aggregation was
employed to mitigate slice redundancy. Nevertheless, we recognize that 2D methods do
not fully capture inter-slice contextual information. Future work will investigate 3D and
hybrid 2.5D architectures to better exploit volumetric continuity and further improve
patient-level diagnostic performance.
The overarching goal of this work is to assist clinicians in accurately diagnosing brain
tumor types while improving computational efficiency, reliability, and transparency.
Nevertheless, there remains room for further development. Future work may explore
alternative ensemble strategies, more refined weighting mechanisms, and the inclusion
of additional tumor subtypes beyond the four classes studied. Moreover, the framework
can be extended to 3D imaging data for better spatial feature extraction and diagnos­
tic accuracy. The integration of transformer-based architectures could further elevate
performance by leveraging their capability for sequential and contextual data process­
ing. Ultimately, developing a real-time, user-friendly application would bridge the
gap between research and clinical practice, making advanced diagnostic tools widely
accessible.

Abstract
Hierarchically organised report generation from high-dimensional 3D inputs is a central yet underexplored capability of
multi-task vision–language models (VLMs), obstructed by three problems: unifying report generation with structurally
incompatible auxiliary heads under one weight-shared backbone, natively handling partially available modalities, and
providing axiomatically grounded, numerically verifiable attributions for multi-output predictions. We propose MT-
BrainVLM, an end-to-end multi-task 3D VLM coupling a modality-aware 3D U-Net encoder and mask-gated fusion, a
BLIP-2-style Q-Former with three levels of learnable query tokens, a hierarchical autoregressive decoder, a disease head and
an InfoNCE vision–text pathway under a joint objective, so that lesion segmentation across three incompatible taxonomies,
three-level report generation and patient-level classification are emitted by one forward pass from any subset of the acquired
sequences. Over it we develop a dual-path Shapley framework: data-prior KernelSHAP on 25 report-derived descriptors
through a Random Forest surrogate, and model-prior exact ModalitySHAP enumerating all 2M modality coalitions through a
task-wise value multiplexer. On a held-out split of 92 cases spanning five cohorts the network attains a mean Dice of 0.325
with HD95 21.0 mm, both scored in the original voxel grid at native spacing, an impression-level BLEU-4 of 0.032 with
clinical-efficacy F1 0.312, and a disease micro-F1 of 0.351, against fifteen baselines trained under an identical budget. The
outcome is stated plainly: MT-BrainVLM leads none of the three tasks, trailing the strongest task-specialised segmentation
network by 0.118 Dice, the expected cost of a shared backbone devoting 5.9% of its parameters to the visual path; the
contribution claimed is the joint capability and the attribution pathway over it. The enumerator reproduces a closed-form
ground truth to order 10−16 and, on the trained network and real volumes, satisfies efficiency to 2.22 × 10−16 over 120
modality attributions. We also quantify the framework’s own limits: an exact grouped (Owen) reformulation retains
exactness at 2G rather than 2M cost; a surrogate’s predictive fidelity (R2 = 0.9995) does not imply agreement with the target

tocol combining structural sequences (T1-weighted pre- and

coefficient (ADC) maps, each exposing a distinct tissue
property and disease signature (Ghadimi et al. 2025). On
this volumetric, multi-channel input a neuroradiologist
performs several interdependent tasks: delineating lesions at
the voxel level, synthesising a hierarchically organised
report in which per-modality findings are consolidated into
a global finding and distilled into a diagnostic impression,
and assigning disease labels consistent with downstream
management (Alameddine et al. 2026). The workload is
substantial and subject to inter-reader variability while
demand grows faster than the neuroradiology workforce
(Barnard et al. 2025), which motivates decision-support
systems that emulate the full reporting pipeline rather than
one sub-task in isolation (Räz et al. 2025), under realistic
conditions in which the acquired sequence set is hetero-
geneous across institutions and indications. Progress in 3D
segmentation, multi-modal fusion and vision–language
models puts a unified framework producing voxel-level
masks, hierarchical text and patient-level predictions in a
single forward pass within reach (Nasir et al. 2025). For
such a system to be trustworthy, accuracy alone is not
sufficient: it must expose which modalities, which textual
cues (Fang et al. 2025) and which structured descriptors
drove each decision, so that experts can audit and contest its
outputs (Herrera et al. 2026), and it should evidence its own
internal consistency through numerically verifiable attribu-
tion rather than visual heuristics (Jin et al. 2022).
The existing literature falls short of such a system along
three axes (Hasan et al. 2026). First, brain-MRI pipelines
are specialised: segmentation networks excel on a single
cohort with a single taxonomy, report-generation models
are trained on 2D or single-sequence inputs, and disease
classifiers are decoupled from both spatial and linguistic
supervision, so the mutual regularisation available from co-
training across structurally incompatible tasks is left on the
table (Zhan et al. 2025). Second, vision–language approa-
ches rarely respect the hierarchical structure of neuror-
adiology reports and typically assume a fixed, fully
available modality set (Lai et al. 2025), which is incom-
patible with protocols where sequences are routinely miss-
ing, substituted or re-encoded (Havaei et al. 2016). Third,
explainability for medical deep networks is dominated by

section_heading: A unified multi-task vision–language architecture for
text:
A unified multi-task vision–language architecture for
multi-parametric 3D brain MRI. We design an end-to-
end network that integrates a shared modality-aware
3D U-Net encoder, a BLIP-2-style Q-Former bridging
module, a hierarchical autoregressive report decoder, a
multi-label
disease
classification
head,
and
a
vision–text contrastive pathway, so that lesion seg-
mentation across three incompatible labelling taxo-
nomies
(BraTS,
ISLES22,
WMH),
three-level
hierarchical report generation (modality/global/impres-

authors: Haitao Wu; Tingxuan Wang; Mingchen Xie; Xiaodong Chen; Jian Xu
venue: Journal of King Saud University – Computer and Information Sciences, Volume 38, Article 899
section_heading: Native support for heterogeneous and partially available
text:
Native support for heterogeneous and partially available
MRI protocols. By coupling an explicit binary modality
mask with learnable modality-type embeddings and a
mask-aware cross-modality fusion mechanism, the
proposed architecture allows any subset of the up-to-
eight clinical sequences (T1c, T1n, T2w, T2f/FLAIR,
ADC, DWI, etc.) to be provided at training or inference
time without architectural changes. This is a claim about
behaviour, not only about admissibility, and it is tested
here: one trained network is evaluated under every non-
empty subset of the sequences each cohort provides, at
inference time and without retraining (Section 4.1.6).

title: MT-brainVLM: a multi-task 3D vision–language model for hierarchical report generation with dual-path Shapley explainability
authors: Haitao Wu; Tingxuan Wang; Mingchen Xie; Xiaodong Chen; Jian Xu
venue: Journal of King Saud University – Computer and Information Sciences, Volume 38, Article 899
section_heading: A dual-path Shapley explainability framework, and an
text:
A dual-path Shapley explainability framework, and an
explicit account of where it is exact and where it is not.
We develop a data-prior path based on KernelSHAP
over a Random Forest surrogate that operates on
25 structured descriptors derived from the three-level
reports and modality metadata, and a model-prior path
based on exact enumeration of all 2M modality
coalitions (M ≤8) through a task-wise value multi-
plexer. The two paths are complementary rather than
redundant, and we characterise the guarantees of the
framework and its limits by measurement: the exact
enumerator reproduces a closed-form linear ground
truth on a synthetic scoring head to a maximum
deviation of order 10−16 and satisfies additivity exactly;
exact enumeration is tractable only for small M, for
which we derive an exact grouped (Owen) reformula-
tion costing 2G rather than 2M evaluations; and we show
that a surrogate’s predictive fidelity (R2 = 0.9995) does
not imply agreement with the target model’s own
attributions (Spearman 0.60 against an estimator ceiling
of 0.99), which is in fact the quantity on which a
surrogate must be selected. The framework thereby
provides an auditable attribution pathway for a multi-
task VLM, together with an explicit account of where
that pathway is exact, where it is only approximate, and
where it does not yet reach.

Multi-task deep learning for brain MRI analysis
Lesion segmentation from 3D MRI has been driven by
public benchmarks such as the BraTS series, the ISLES
challenges and the WMH challenges (Alshomrani 2025).
Encoder–decoder architectures of the 3D U-Net family,
augmented with residual connections, attention gates or
dense aggregation, are the de facto backbone for volumetric
delineation, extended with self-configuring pipelines and
hybrid CNN–Transformer designs for cross-dataset robust-
ness (Zhu et al. 2026). A complementary line couples
segmentation with disease classification, survival prediction
or lesion counting through weight-shared backbones and
per-task heads, improving sample efficiency and partially
regularising the shared representation, but typically trained
on a single cohort under a single labelling taxonomy
(Karabağ et al. 2026). Modality-aware fusion for multi-
sequence MRI has in parallel been explored through early
channel concatenation, late fusion with per-modality enco-
ders, mixture-of-experts gating and learnable missing-
modality imputation (Han et al. 2024; Kashyap et al.
2022). Existing pipelines nonetheless remain narrow: they
specialise in one lesion category on one dataset, or handle
several tasks on homogeneously labelled data (Ottoni et al.
2025), and very few unify structurally incompatible seg-
mentation taxonomies, multi-label classification and free-
text report generation in one end-to-end framework driven
by an arbitrary subset of the available sequences (Zhang
et al. 2025).

Vision–language models and radiology report
generation
Radiology report generation has progressed from template-
filling and retrieval systems, through encoder–decoder
Transformers attending over CNN feature maps, to large-
scale VLMs aligning dense visual embeddings with long-
form clinical narrative (Chen et al. 2020; Kotsiantis et al.
2026). One influential paradigm introduces learnable query
tokens that interrogate a visual encoder by cross-attention
(Li et al. 2023a), yielding a compact text-aligned context for
an autoregressive decoder, progressively adapted from
natural-image captioning to chest X-ray, dermatology,
ophthalmology and pathology reporting (Fang et al. 2025).
Parallel work has proposed hierarchical decoders separating
findings from impression, clinical-entity and knowledge-
graph priors, and contrastive vision–text pre-training (Jiao
et al. 2026). Several gaps remain pronounced in brain MRI:
volumetric multi-sequence data are high-dimensional and
protocol-dependent, so 2D recipes transplant poorly; reports
are intrinsically hierarchical, with modality-wise findings, a
consolidated global finding (Panayides et al. 2026) and an
impression each carrying a distinct level of abstraction; and
segmentation, classification and generation are seldom co-
trained under a shared representation. A directly relevant
development
is
the
emergence
of
MRI-specific
vision–language foundation models: Decipher-MR couples
self-supervised volumetric representation learning with
report-guided text supervision over 200,000 MRI series and
exposes a frozen encoder to which lightweight task heads
are attached (Yang et al. 2026). That work establishes the
transferability of a shared 3D MRI representation but treats
the downstream heads as separate adaptations of a frozen
encoder; we instead co-train voxel-, sentence- and patient-
level supervision end to end, and add an axiomatic attri-
bution pathway over the resulting joint output space (Moor
et al. 2023).

Shapley-based explainability for medical AI
Explainability for deep medical models follows two broad
lines (Jin et al. 2022). The first comprises saliency methods
—class-activation
mapping,
gradient-based
attributions,
perturbation and occlusion analyses (Liu et al. 2024)—
which yield visually compelling heatmaps but suffer from
instability under small input perturbations, architectural
sensitivity and a lack of axiomatic grounding; a systematic
review of explainability for visual affordance recognition
documents the same pattern outside medicine, finding that
deep detectors are explained almost exclusively by post-hoc
saliency and that the explanations are consequently hard to
interpret or act upon (Bhattacharyya et al. 2024). The sec-
ond line uses cooperative game theory, and in particular
Shapley values, to redistribute a model’s output across its
inputs in the unique way satisfying local accuracy, sym-
metry (Li et al. 2024), the null-player property and addi-
tivity; kernel-based surrogate regressions and tree-specific
exact algorithms have enabled attributions on tabular clin-
ical variables (Aravindkumar et al. 2026), genomic features
and health records, while deep-learning variants extend the
idea to super-pixels, concept bottlenecks and tokens (Tan
et al. 2024). In medical imaging these tools have been
applied mostly to single-task binary classifiers, whereas
modality-level attribution—treating each sequence as an
atomic player whose coalition with others determines the
prediction—has only recently attracted attention despite its
clinical relevance in multi-parametric MRI (Ghadimi et al.
2025). Two limitations are salient (Zhao et al. 2024): most
pipelines target a single task rather than the joint output
space of a multi-task VLM (van der Velden et al. 2022), and
data-prior attributions from report metadata are rarely
combined with model-prior attributions from the network
itself (Covert et al. 2021), though the former captures
dataset-level regularities and the latter the model’s internal

Overall model architecture
MT-BrainVLM jointly performs lesion segmentation, hier-
archical report generation and multi-label disease classifi-
cation end to end. As Fig. 1 shows, it comprises a multi-
modal input stage, a shared 3D vision encoder, a segmen-
tation decoding branch, a vision-language bridge, a hier-
archical autoregressive report decoder, a disease head and a
vision-text contrastive pathway, optimized jointly through a
weighted aggregation of their task-specific losses.
The input stage ingests the volumes together with a
binary modality mask recording which sequences are pre-
sent, so partially observed protocols are admitted at training
and inference alike without an architectural change, and a
learnable modality-type embedding is added as a channel-
wise bias to the shallow features, giving each sequence a
distinct representational prior on a fully weight-shared
backbone. Features flow to two consumers: a U-Net decoder
terminating in
dataset-specific heads, because
BraTS,
ISLES22 and WMH define incompatible label taxonomies;
and a Q-Former compressing bottleneck features and
modality tokens into three sets of query tokens, one per
report level, which drive the shared decoder, the disease
head and the contrastive pathway. One forward pass yields
the segmentation map, the three-level report and the disease
predictions together; Section 3.2 specifies each component
formally.
