This stores the feature vectors and class labels of the training
samples in the training phase, and the unlabeled sample is
categorized in the classification phase by assigning the class
label based on the most frequent of the k training samples
closest to the query point, where k is a defined constant.

Oxford in the paper ‘‘Very Deep Convolutional Networks for

top-5 test accuracy in ImageNet, which is a dataset of over
14 million images belonging to 1000 classes. It was one of
the famous models submitted to ILSVRC-2014. It improves
AlexNet by replacing large kernel-sized filters (11 and 5 in
the first and second convolutional layer, respectively) with
multiple 3 × 3 kernel-sized filters one after another. The

of medical data. Because of the high death rate linked with
brain tumors, it is critical to diagnose them early to treat
them and reduce mortality. Manual diagnosis of the brain and
tumor tissues is time-consuming and operator-dependent due
to the intricacy of brain tissue. Therefore, in this research,
an effective transfer learning-based SC model, which was
named VGG-SCNet, was proposed to classify brain tumors
from MRI Images. The F1 score obtained by the proposed
classifier shows the efficacy of the approach followed by this
study.

authors: Hamail Ayaz; Esra SÃ¼mer-Arpak; David Tormey; Ian McLoughlin; Esin Ozturk-Isik; Thomas C. Boothe; Saritha Unnikrishnan
text:
Abstract
Deep learning (DL) has shown promise in glioma imaging tasks using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and
histopathology images, yet their complexity demands greater transparency in artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
This is noticeable when users must understand the model output for a clinical application. In this systematic
review, 65 post-hoc eXplainable AI (XAI), or interpretable AI studies, have been reviewed that provide an
understanding of why a system generated a given output for tasks related to glioma imaging. A framework of
post-hoc XAI methods, such as Gradient-based XAI (G-XAI) and Perturbation-based XAI (P-XAI), is introduced
to evaluate deep models and explain their application in gliomas. The papers on XAI techniques in gliomas
are surveyed and categorized by their specific aims such as grading, genetic biomarker detection, localization,
intra-tumoral heterogeneity assessment, and survival analysis, and their XAI approach. This review highlights
the growing integration of XAI in glioma imaging, demonstrating their role in bridging AI decision-making
and medical diagnostics. The co-occurrence analysis emphasizes their role in enhancing model transparency
and trust and guiding future research toward more reliable clinical applications. Finally, the current challenges
associated with DL and XAI approaches and their clinical integration are discussed with an outlook on future
opportunities from clinical users’ perspectives and upcoming trends in XAI.

Introduction
Gliomas are infiltrative primary intracranial tumors accounting for
about 24.5% of all primary brain and other central nervous system
(CNS) tumors, and 80.9% of malignant brain tumors [1]. According
to the latest World Health Organization (WHO) CNS tumor classifica-
tion, adult-type gliomas have been classified into three main groups
according to their genetic and molecular features, which are astrocy-
toma (isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant, 1p/19q non-codeleted),
oligodendroglioma (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) and glioblastoma
(IDH wild-type) [2]. IDH mutant (IDH-mut) gliomas have been reported
to have a better treatment response and overall survival [3–5]. On the
other hand, IDH-wildtype (IDH-wt) gliomas with telomerase promoter
(TERTp) mutation (TERTp-only) have been reported to have the worst

led to converting medical images into quantifiable representations.
Radiomics is an emerging field that converts medical images into high-
dimensional mineable quantitative data and can be used to improve the
predictive accuracy of diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment outcome in
oncological studies [19,20]. The radiomics process consists of acquiring
the imaging data, identifying region of interests, feature extraction, and
predictive model building. The radiomics features can be categorized
as first-order statistics, shape descriptors, and texture features [19].

learning (ML) techniques. Deep Learning (DL) is the subset of ML
that has been increasingly applied to glioma research. Compared to
classical ML methods, DL does not require manual feature extraction to
identify underlying complex information in MR images [18]. The appli-

text:
h as IDH mutational status [22], with the help of machine
learning (ML) techniques. Deep Learning (DL) is the subset of ML
that has been increasingly applied to glioma research. Compared to
classical ML methods, DL does not require manual feature extraction to
identify underlying complex information in MR images [18]. The appli-
cations of different DL architectures in glioma research have emerged
and shown impressive performances on automatic glioma segmenta-
tion [23], subtype classification [24], mutation detection [25], and
survival prediction [26]. Although a significant amount of ML and
DL models have been applied for glioma imaging, many of the high-
performing models have failed to provide a clear explanation of the
reasoning behind the decision-making process, as shown in Fig. 1.
This notion of black-box models has been strongly challenged by
novel XAI studies, which have aimed to shed some light on the decision-
making process of the many deep non-linear ML models [27,28]. Ex-
plainability, interpretability, and transparency of DL models are crucial
for clinical end-users to understand the rationale behind the model’s
predictions and interpretations of a disease. XAI approaches have been
broadly classified as ante-hoc and post-hoc based on their nature
of explanation. Ante-hoc methods represent intrinsically explainable
machine learning methods including supervised learning techniques
such as linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, and in
some cases, rule-based learners [29], as well as unsupervised clustering
techniques such as k-means, fuzzy C-means, and Gaussian Mixture
Models [30]. Such methods are primarily specific to a single model
or a group of similar models and are called model-specific. Post-
hoc techniques, on the other hand, refer to explainability approaches
developed to interpret black box model predictions post-training or
post-deployment and are mostly model-agnostic. The goal of model-
agnostic methods is to interpret the predictive contribution of input
features irrespective of the model architecture.
One of the most common post-hoc XAI approaches is to derive
transparent surrogate models in the form of decision trees, attention-
based networks or linear models to explain the predictions, of a deep
neural network, locally or globally [32–34]. Post-hoc approaches are
quite broad in scope and may vary between text, image, and tabular
data types. Examples of post-hoc XAI approaches include gradient-

authors: Hamail Ayaz; Esra SÃ¼mer-Arpak; David Tormey; Ian McLoughlin; Esin Ozturk-Isik; Thomas C. Boothe; Saritha Unnikrishnan
text:
e of the most common post-hoc XAI approaches is to derive
transparent surrogate models in the form of decision trees, attention-
based networks or linear models to explain the predictions, of a deep
neural network, locally or globally [32–34]. Post-hoc approaches are
quite broad in scope and may vary between text, image, and tabular
data types. Examples of post-hoc XAI approaches include gradient-
based techniques (G-XAI) which highlight the relevant pixels in the
input image that contribute most to the output of a deep neural
network [35]. G-XAI approaches include saliency maps [36], class
activation maps (CAM), layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) [37],
Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) [38], Guided
Backpropagation (Guided Backprop) [39], Integrated gradients [40],
and SmoothGrad [41] as well as feature importance layer-wise rele-
vance propagation (LRP) [37] and perturbation-based (P-XAI) methods
(SHAP, Occlusion, LIME) for generating explanations by manipulating
or masking parts of an input image [42,43].
XAI has been increasingly used to explain the results of DL models.
Furthermore, within the glioma imaging domain, there is an increasing
demand for explainability to develop transparent DL models capa-
ble of describing their decision-making processes in a comprehensible
manner. Therefore, this systematic review aims to explore the current
literature on the utilization of DL applications in conjunction with post-
hoc XAI techniques within the field of glioma localization, grading,
detection of genetic biomarkers, differential diagnosis, and survival
estimation. To the best of our knowledge, no systematic review has
been conducted to explain the usage of post-hoc XAI techniques in
glioma imaging. This systematic review focuses on identifying the most
commonly explored XAI approaches and their findings in interpreting
MRI and histopathological whole slide images (WSI) of gliomas. Fur-
thermore, we perform an inductive analysis of the relevant keywords
to highlight research trends in brain tumor imaging and to point
out what XAI categories people have focused on in the last several
years including the gaps associated with it and potential future work.
Additionally, we discuss the challenges and limitations associated with
the XAI models and future work to integrate machine learning models
with XAI into the clinical workflow.

Search strategy
A manual search was conducted by two independent reviewers
using two search strings: (1) (‘glioma’ OR ‘glioblastoma’) AND ‘Deep
learning’ AND (‘XAI’ OR ‘interpretable’) AND (‘MRI’ OR ‘WSI’ OR
‘pathology’); (2) ‘Glioma’ AND ‘eXplainable AI’ AND ‘interpretable’
AND ‘Artificial Intelligence’ AND ‘MRI/WSI’. Four electronic databases
– PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Science Direct were searched
and articles published between 1st January 2019 and 31st Dec 2024
were cited in this review. Since explainable AI is an evolving field
of study, only 65 studies were identified that used XAI methods for
understanding glioma biology.

text:
Study selection
This review investigates studies that explore post-hoc eXplainable
artificial intelligence (XAI) methods in interpreting DL models for clin-
ical glioma applications. The primary tasks in these applications involve
glioma grading and localization through AI techniques such as image
classification and segmentation. This review specifically encompasses
image-based studies utilizing XAI techniques.
The inclusion criteria required selected articles to have at most
one grade of glioma, while excluding non-imaging studies, non-English
articles, reviews, and non-peer-reviewed articles. Additionally, only
the publications that employed DL models providing G-XAI and P-XAI
based explanation were included, ignoring classical machine-learning
and ante-hoc explainability approaches. Fig. 2 illustrates the article

authors: Hamail Ayaz; Esra SÃ¼mer-Arpak; David Tormey; Ian McLoughlin; Esin Ozturk-Isik; Thomas C. Boothe; Saritha Unnikrishnan
text:
Foundational concepts of post-hoc XAI
The core principle of post-hoc XAI approaches involves interpret-
ing the decisions made by deep neural networks, either locally or
globally [33]. Gradient-based XAI approaches highlight the relevant
information in the input data that contributes most to the output. Class
activation Maps (CAM) are heatmaps that highlight the spatial average
of the output feature maps from the last convolutional layer, weighted
by the connections to the output class. When superimposed onto the
original image, this heatmap draws attention to crucial regions for
classification, offering a visual representation of the model’s decision-
making process. [44]. CAM is widely used for explaining CNN-based
models however, CAMs work only for CNNs which use global average
pooling. To address this issue, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Map-
ping (Grad-CAM) were introduced. Grad-CAM computes the gradients
of the target class with respect to the feature maps of the chosen layer
which is then globally averaged for each feature map finally producing
a set of weighted scores [45]. The Grad-CAM approach is easy to gener-
alize across different CNN models. However, there are two significant
issues with Grad-CAM methods: (1) Noisy gradient signal: The gradient
signal is difficult to interpret and results in visually noisy saliency map
explanations [41]; and (2) The resolution of the heatmap is limited by
the size of the feature maps in the selected convolutional layer, which
may not match the original image size. [46]. To overcome the noisy
gradient issues, the Guided Backprop approach is used, which analyzes
the gradient of the output for the input of the DL model, with the posi-
tive gradients backpropagated and negative gradients set to zero [47].
Grad-CAM and its variants, such as SmoothGrad, Guided Grad-CAM,
and Integrated gradients, have been used in several studies to interpret
automatic tumor localization and grading of gliomas. However, they
still lack layer-specific relevance distribution and often produce false
positives for complex non-linear models. Therefore, to overcome these
issues, LRP functions by computing gradients during backpropagation,
assigning relevance scores to each neuron, and evaluating each neu-
ron’s contribution to the final decision [48]. LRP overcomes the issue
of shattered gradients, which is a problem particularly at the depth of
each layer.
Although G-XAI methods explain model predictions very quickly

on-linear models. Therefore, to overcome these
issues, LRP functions by computing gradients during backpropagation,
assigning relevance scores to each neuron, and evaluating each neu-
ron’s contribution to the final decision [48]. LRP overcomes the issue
of shattered gradients, which is a problem particularly at the depth of
each layer.
Although G-XAI methods explain model predictions very quickly
with minimal computation, there are various prerequisites for each
method to apply the gradient-based explanation [49]. They are lim-
ited to very well-designed model architecture, sensitive to input data,
producing complex gradient calculations, and limited to explaining the
importance of individual features [50]. To overcome these limitations,
P-XAI approaches are used, which focuses on the entire model layers
of input data to see how changes affect the output of a deep network,
helping to pinpoint which features are most influential. Occlusion-
based saliency maps use a sliding window approach to remove the
irrelevant image features covered by the window region to explain the
model’s learning [51]. For more detailed, instance-level explanation
using complex models, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations
(LIME) are used. The LIME method creates local surrogate models to
approximate specific predictions of the original model by changing
the input parameters and analyzing how the output of the model
changes accordingly based on local features [52]. The LIME approach
is easy to implement to learn more about local features within the
model; however, for a global explanation of the deep model, SHAP
(SHapley Additive exPlanations) is used. SHAP [53] uses the concept of
gamification to calculate the contribution of each feature between the
actual prediction and the average prediction across all possible subsets
of features.

Deep learning and XAI in glioma imaging
DL models have been found capable of automatically extracting
multidimensional radiomic features from medical images effectively
classifying glioma grades [54–56]. However, in clinical settings, physi-
cians often seek not only disease predictions but also comprehensive
explanations of how these models arrive at their conclusions. To meet
this need, explainability approaches that incorporate graphical and
visual representations, along with analyses of local and global feature
significance, prove invaluable. These approaches explain the reasons
behind a model’s specific outputs, such as the localization and grading
of gliomas. Additionally, various XAI approaches, such as layer-wise
relevance propagation (LRP), counterfactual explanations, and textual
explanations, are adaptable across different model architectures and
have applications in natural language processing. [57]. Table 1 sum-
marizes DL studies in glioma diagnostics using MR images, highlighting
how a combination of graphical, visual, and diverse XAI techniques
can deepen insights into model decisions, thereby enhancing clinical
decision-making.

text:
Gradient based (G-XAI) in glioma:
This section is based on the clinical application of DL methods
in gliomas, which is further subdivided into the gradient-based XAI
approaches used by similar studies. Each study explains the clinical
question followed by the deep models used for solving the question and
the XAI approach used to interpret the deep model and the associated
limitations.
Tumor grading and localization with G-XAI in gliomas:. One impor-
tant question in glioma research has been pre-operatively predicting
tumor grade based on imaging data. Additionally, the clinical ex-
plainability of intra-tumor localization to differentiate between various
tissue types inside the tumor region, such as necrosis, edema, and
solid tumor has been of interest. DL models such as U-Net, Vision-
Nets, and many more have been experimented with for tumor grading
and sub-tumoral region definition; however, due to their very complex
framework, explainability is still a challenge.
• Class activation mapping (CAM): One explainable technique
to understand the visual representation of the feature-relevant
regions in an image is CAM [88,99]. Glioma studies have reported
tumor grading and localization using the CAM method [93]. Quon
et al. 2020 [59] examined a ResNet-50 model for brain tumor
detection and pathology classification. To explain the model per-
formance, CAM identified influential regions in the images for
accurate predictions, particularly near solid tumors. However,
some incorrect predictions showcased scattered, unrelated pivotal
regions, even prioritizing tumor-free areas as important in some
cases. Aboussaleh et al. 2021 [65] constructed a CNN model
that performs both grading and localization of gliomas. The CNN
model was trained for classification first, and further in the testing
phase, CAM from the last convolution layer was used to extract
features and their gradient to predict the tumor segmentation.
Similarly, Ozbay et al. 2023 [81] reported glioma grading and
localization using interpretable feature fusion of a DenseNet201
model. The interpretable binary mask was used from the global
network by computing a CAM of the last convolutional layer
and further adopted as input to the DenseNet201 Model. CAM
illustrated the details of the interpretable mask to highlight the
salient regions for the tumor area. Finally, they concluded that
an interpretable binary mask could accurately localize the lesion
region.

Accurate grading of glioma tumors is essential for the diagnosis,
treatment planning, and prognosis prediction of gliomas [100].
Five studies have explored clinical explanations of model classifi-
cation in gliomas using the Grad-CAM method [79,80]. Maqsood
et al. 2022 [70] proposed a method to develop an automated
system for classifying glioma sub-grades (I–IV). The pipeline of
the proposed method involved linear contrast stretching for edge
detection, a custom 17-layer deep neural network for segmenta-
tion, a modified MobileNetV2 architecture for feature extraction
using transfer learning, and an entropy-based feature selection
method with a multi-class support vector machine (M-SVM). To
explain the model’s performance, the Grad-CAM method was
employed to provide unique visualizations for each glioma grade.
The result of the Grad-CAM visualization marked features rele-
vant to the tumor area as red and the background information
as blue. The proposed method and XAI provided reliable and
accurate classification of brain tumors.

• Variants of Grad-CAM: Three glioma studies have reported for
tumor grading and localization using the Grad-CAM variants. In
a study, Zeineldin et al. 2022 [42] proposed explainability of
deep models for intra tumor localization using a NeuroXAI frame-
work. The proposed framework implemented several state-of-
the-art XAI methods (Vanilla gradient, Guided backpropagation,
Integrated gradients, guided integrated gradients, SmoothGrad,
Grad-CAM, and Guided Grad-CAM) to provide visualization maps
explaining (ResNet-50) model, as shown in Fig. 3. All seven
explainability methods for grading and localization highlighted
the contributing features irrespective of the selected class. Despite
the mentioned limitation of Grad-CAM, the proposed work stated
that Grad-CAM and Guided-Grad-CAM localized the most crucial
input regions for network decisions.
Saleem et al. 2021 [63] introduced a novel 3D visual explanation
method for glioma localization using a 3D Dilated Multi-Fiber
Network (DMFNet). DMFNet model incorporated interpretabil-
ity techniques and compared with gradient-free explainability
methods. Higher quality visual explanations were achieved by
integrating activation maps with the prediction layer. The study
also used deletion metrics to evaluate the model’s interpretability,
where important features’ removal led to a measurable drop in ac-
curacy. The proposed approach provides interpretability in deep
models with higher predictive accuracy. However, the proposed
study investigated only 2D images and it is yet to be examined
if this approach would improve visual interpretability for 3D
MR image inputs. Additionally, Wood et al. 2022 [77] reported
a smooth guided Backprop technique to investigate the perfor-
mance of the Densenet121 model for T2-weighed MR images.
They reported that smoothly guided backpropagation demon-
strated accurate tumor localization, and the model prediction was
robust to extract the presence of moderate image artifacts.

• Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP): Two studies have
employed LRP for glioma grading and localization so far. Sefcik
& Benesova, 2021 [64] reported a fused CNN-ML technique to
improve the explanation of convolutional layers for classifying
gliomas through an explanation-guided training process. To better
understand the model behavior through feature relevance, the 2D
CNN model using three convolutional layers was used for LGG
and HGG classification. The proposed model inner activations on
hidden layers were further passed to k-nearest neighbor to predict
the feature relevance of an image. Finally, the model employs the
Bi-Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (BiLRP) approach to pro-
vide a higher-level explanation. Based on neuron activity in the
hidden layers and varied TumorLRPScores in the loss function, the
model focuses on tumor regions and learns the most significant
characteristics for glioma classification.
Coupet et al. 2022 [76] proposed a computer-aided system ca-
pable of helping experts to classify healthy brain against brain
with glioma. To better understand the XAI approaches VGG19, In-
ceptionV3, Resnet50, DenseNet, and EfficientNet-B6 models were
used for training. Further, to interpret these models, LRP, Deep
Taylor decomposition, and Guided Backprop were used to ex-
plain the visual difference between models feature maps. They
explained LRP method could highlight the parenchyma and the
cerebral periphery region for DenseNet and ResNet50 CNN. Deep
Taylor explained the outer bounds of the edema region and
performed very well for all networks; however, VGG19 and Incep-
tionV3 networks better detected the borders of cerebral ventricles.
Similarly, Guided Backprop explained the result to identify large
structures between cerebral hemispheres, ventricles, and other
tumor tissue.

Survival prediction of gliomas:. DL frameworks have increasingly
been employed for survival prediction in gliomas. DL models analyze
various patient data, including genetic, molecular, and imaging data, to
forecast patient survival outcomes. The prediction models are intended
to find relationships and patterns that physicians might not notice
right away. This information can be crucial for clinicians to make
personalized treatment plans and improve overall patient care. Two
studies have been reported for glioma survival prediction using XAI
methods.
• Class activation mapping (CAM) Yan et al. 2021 [67], intro-
duced a deep learning signature (DLS) derived from diffusion
tensor imaging (DTI) to forecast survival probabilities in patients
with infiltrative gliomas. The DLS was intricately linked with
significant pathways (e.g., synaptic transmission, calcium signal-
ing, glutamate secretion, axon guidance, and glioma pathways),
and further passed to a residual network. To explain the model’s
performance, CAM was used to visualize the neuron activation.
CAMs indicated that the proposed network model could highlight
certain risky regions that may be relevant to tumor prognosis
while suppressing other less relevant regions.
• Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM):
Malhotra et al. 2023 [82] investigated overall survival predic-
tion of high-grade gliomas through several attention maps and
fused feature-learned models. This study used a customized CNN
model to perform glioma survival prediction on BraTS 2018
and BraTS 2019 datasets. The model integrated four blocks,
pre-processing modules, glioma detection, an overall survival
classification pipeline and a visual interpretability pipeline. The
pre-processing block convert the 3D MRI volumes to 2D array
to parallel process the survival data array. Further, age for each
subject is also added in the last layer for final classification. To
explain the model performance, the Grad-CAM function extracted
the visual interpretability of last layers within the network. Grad-
CAM represented the color code sequence with the maximum
influence in predicting the survival class (Short, Medium, and
Long). Blue signified low survival, and Red corresponded to high
survival.

The proposed experiment concluded that multimodal medical

be challenging in clinical settings.
• SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP): SHAP have been re-
ported in several studies to explain glioma localization and grad-
ing [91,92]. Saueressig et al. 2021 [58] proposed a graph-based
neural network for automatic tumor localization. The proposed
model used graph data by aggregating information over con-
nected nodes, which allows them to capture relative information
between data elements. The model used 3D MRI scans to build a
graph, with nodes representing distinct regions in the images and
edges connecting nearby regions. The proposed method achieved
reasonable performance with significantly less computational cost
and time than state-of-the-art segmentation models. Additionally,
SHAP-based Shapley value contribution scores were calculated to
explain the model segmentation performance to identify relevant
input features. The proposed method demonstrated the poten-
tial for automatic medical image segmentation and reduced the
need for manual evaluation. Gaur et al. 2022 [71] proposed an
explanation-driven CNN model using LIME and SHAP features
to classify brain tumor subtypes (meningioma, glioma, and pi-
tuitary). Three different brain tumor subtypes were used for a
dual-input CNN approach to achieve higher classification results.
To explain the model performance, SHAP method ensured local
accuracy for interpreting all future predictions by applying all
possible combinations of inputs as Shapley values. In compari-
son, LIME created sparse linear models around each prediction
to highlight how the model works in the immediate neighbor-
hood. The proposed model emphasized interpretability and high
accuracy in predictive performance for future possible clinical
translation.

vital features for grading gliomas. SHAP demonstrated 20 most

Glioma-Histopathology and XAI
The pathological examination of gliomas is crucial in providing
diagnostic, phenotypic, and prognostic information about the disease
[123]. The application of AI on WSI has enabled the development of
more precise disease characterization by providing intense and complex
information in histopathological examinations [123]. Nevertheless, the
application of DL techniques on digital pathology has suffered from
the absence of an understanding of the underlying information flow in
decision-making [124]. Accordingly, 20 studies that have attempted to
fill this gap in model interpretability using G-XAI and P-XAI approaches
are listed in Table 2. Three of the reviewed articles encompassed both
G-XAI and P-XAI methods; however, we chose to list them under G-XAI,
as they were not applied directly to WSIs, one of the primary focuses
of our investigation. All reviewed articles in this section did not mainly
focus on XAI methods, but used them superficially or as a sanity check
for their results.

Gradient based (G-XAI) in pathological examination:
This section focuses on the application of DL methods in WSIs
of gliomas, which is then subdivided into various G-XAI approaches
utilized by similar studies. Each study is characterized by its specific
aim, such as classification, genetic biomarker detection, tumor grading,
assessment of intra-tumoral heterogeneity, and survival analysis. This
is followed by the deep models employed to address the research
question, the XAI approach used for interpreting the deep model, and
a discussion of the associated limitations, if applicable.
Classification, genetic biomarker detection, and tumor grading:. Out
of the 20 studies identified for the use of DL on WSIs in gliomas,
10 of them used XAI methods combined with DL models to differ-
entiate gliomas from other tumors [103], predict molecular biomark-
ers [106,108,111,116–118,120], subtyping [122] and estimate tumor
grades [112,117].
• Class activation mapping (CAM): Glioma subtyping (glioblas-
toma, oligodendroglioma, astrocytoma, necrosis, normal tissue)
was performed with the pre-trained models in a two-step semi-
supervised learning approach [122] and using data collection
from the National Center of Pathology, Luxembourg National
Health Laboratory. They provided superior performance com-
pared to baseline transfer learning models with a balanced accu-
racy of 96.91% and an F1-score of 97.07% from weakly annotated
WSIs. The proposed visualization tool generated heatmaps to
highlight significant areas on which the model’s prediction relied
on, providing understanding of how DL model made decisions.
IDH mutation is the most critical genetic biomarker to predict
prognosis in gliomas, but there is no standard method for detect-
ing IDH status from routine histomorphology alone, even though
histological features correlate with IDH status. Thus, Liechty et al.
2022 created a hybrid approach that integrated the assessments
of a pathologist and a DL model to detect IDH mutation from

proach. Along with heatmaps, UMAP was used as coordinates
to show ground truth and predicted IDH status and enabled
insight into whether these decision-related morphological fea-
tures, e.g., microcysticity, hypercellularity characteristics, etc.,

Karim et al. 2019 performed differentiation of 33 tumor types,

posed approach, OncoNetExplainer, trained CNN and VGG16

Through G-XAI integrated weakly supervised learning algorithms,
researchers could reach successful results in developing objec-
tive prognostic models from histology images [109,113]. Chen
et al. 2022 developed a multimodal DL model for jointly using
the WSIs and molecular data from 14 cancer types to predict
patient prognosis [109]. Patient stratification (low and high risk)
in Kaplan–Meier curves was improved with the multimodal DL
model and tested with a log-rank test (p < 0.05). The attention
and gradient-based interpretability elaborated how input features
were used to predict prognosis. They visualized the attention
weights on WSIs using heatmaps; high attention regions identified
the dense immune cell infiltrates in low-risk patients, and nuclear
pleomorphism and atypia in high-risk patients. SHAP was applied
for molecular features’ interpretability and identified the most
important prognostic markers, such as IDH, ATRX, and epidermal
growth factor (EGFR) in LGG. Similarly, Liu et al. 2023 developed
a dual-stream network with cross-attention (DSCA) to estimate
cancer prognosis. The network was evaluated on the LGG dataset,
which resulted in a prediction performance of a mean C-index
of 0.70 ± 0.04 [113]. To enhance the model’s interpretability,
cross-attention pooling provided the most informative regions on
which the model focused. The visualization result indicated that
DSCA could identify the parts (highly differentiated and irregular
cells showing poor survival) with a high correlation to cancer
prognosis.

prognosis prediction using WSIs. They achieved superior results
for prognosis estimation with a C-indices range of 0.71–0.86
using TCGA dataset. The proposed strategies aimed to detect
learnable features to identify clinical patterns related to patients’
survival using the attention modules. Visualizing the attention
maps enhanced interpretability by capturing different morpholog-

made on the key clinical histological features such as the immune
and tumor cells and their interactions with surrounding benign
cells. Additionally, multi-head attention mechanism [114] could
capture the regions characterized by high nucleus density and
active angiogenesis, which are prognostically relevant. While the
multi-head attention mechanism can capture influential regions
related to a patient’s prognosis, the overlapping contributions of
multiple heads may make it challenging for clinicians to interpret
the overall decision-making process.

Challenges and limitations
Artificial Intelligence applications with explainability components
have shed some light into better understanding glioma tumor biology.
However, AI models face many issues apart from explainability, causing
challenges for efficient implementations on gliomas applications. The
current challenges associated with DL and XAI approaches, particularly
focusing on their integration into clinical settings are discussed in this
section.
Clinical Integration: Several challenges remain to be addressed
for widespread clinical adaptation of AI and its explainability. Firstly,
the integration of AI in diagnosis and management of glioma requires
it to be integrated into the existing clinical workflow. Secondly, the
translation of AI into clinical practice could be accelerated by the
use of user-friendly AI software and effective collaboration between
scientists and clinicians. Currently, clinicians generally have limited
understanding of data science, while scientists lack knowledge about
the complex clinical practice of glioma management [126]. Moreover,
challenges in the use of AI models create technical and ethical political
barriers. Medical data is accounted for privacy and safety issues and
requires legal permission to collect clinically available data. Due to
the risk of compromising patient’s privacy data, AI is subjected to
regulations such as Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
of 1996 (HIPAA) in the United States, and the General Data Protection
Regulation (GDPR) in Europe.To share research data with the scientific
community, obtaining consent from participants is essential; the Open
Brain Consent initiative addresses challenges by offering information,

Furthermore, highly accurate models are often more complex and
challenging to understand. A primary limitation of XAI is a need for
standardization and clear definitions. Since XAI is a recent trend in in-
dustrial and clinical applications, more research needs to be conducted
to define explainability parameters properly, and there has been no
agreement on a specific definition. Therefore, many works have focused
on the feature importance with visual and graphical approaches of XAI
and their limitations so far.
Visualization Limitations: This section highlights some critical
shortcomings of model interpretability, including (1) the failure to
interpret XAI explanation maps for decision-making, and (2) the lack
of a quantifiable measure of the explanation map’s completeness and
accuracy. As an example, G-XAI-based approaches have their limita-
tions, as, Ghorbani et al. 2019 [128] explained that small perturbations
on an input generate significant changes in the output interpretation.
Their work explained that adversarial examples such as GAN and au-
toencoders failed to produce the interpretable heat maps generated by
the DeepLift and integrated gradient. Kindermans et al. 2017 [129] de-
termined that explanations of deep models generated using integrated
gradients and Deep Taylor Decomposition were easily manipulable
by minor alterations, and these models relied on reference images to
determine the network predictions. Also, the gradient-based methods
do not work well when the input data contains constant vector changes,
so these methods may not provide appropriate explanations for specific
changes in the input data. Zhou et al. 2018 [130] implied that G-XAI
methods are inherently dependent on the model and data-generating
process. The authors presented two randomization tests for gradient-
based approaches, which were model parameter randomization and
data randomization. The output of these approaches for gradients,

changes in the input data. Zhou et al. 2018 [130] implied that G-XAI
methods are inherently dependent on the model and data-generating
process. The authors presented two randomization tests for gradient-
based approaches, which were model parameter randomization and
data randomization. The output of these approaches for gradients,
GradCAM, passed the sanity checks; however, Guided Backprop and
Guided-GradCAM, failed these tests.
Similarly, several P-XAI limitations have been reported for SHAP
and LIME algorithms. Weerts et al. 2019 [131] studied the SHAP
explanations for increasing human performance in alert processing
tasks. To determine whether giving decision explanations could im-
prove some decision-making conditions, the results showed that adding
more SHAP justifications to the class output probability did not help
people make better decisions. Mohseni et al. 2018 [132] built a user-
centered evaluation benchmark and assessed the performance of the
LIME algorithm by comparing the explanation map created by LIME
to a weighted explanation map containing ten human annotations. Ac-
cording to the findings, LIME generated some attributions irrelevant to
human explanations, resulting in low precision compared to a weighted
explanation map generated by human annotators.
Although G-XAI methods explain the model prediction very fast
with minimal computation, there are various prerequisites for each
method for applying the gradient-based explanation [49]. G-XAI meth-
ods are limited to very well-designed model architecture, sensitive to
input data, limited to explaining the importance of individual features,
and produce complex gradient calculations [50]. P-XAI methods do
not require access to the model’s internal parameters. However, the
heatmap generated by P-XAI methods can be affected by factors such
as the perturbed data, hyperparameters of the models, and several sam-
ples of input–output pairs [69]. Finally, P-XAI can be computationally
expensive, especially for high-dimensional inputs [133].
Feature Importance and Relevance Limitations: One of the sig-
nificant limitations is the statistical need for evaluation metrics of the
explainable features. An explainability score is required for each XAI
technique to measure the performance of the classifier or the model
itself. The XAI score may determine a close relationship between the

Feature Importance and Relevance Limitations: One of the sig-

explainable features. An explainability score is required for each XAI
technique to measure the performance of the classifier or the model
itself. The XAI score may determine a close relationship between the
actual ground truth and the XAI technique. Another main challenge is
no clear standard use of XAI techniques, because of diverse users such
as the AI-researchers, clinicians, software developers, policymakers,
and industrial consumers. AI-researcher implement several AI models
for different challenges and generate some explainability based on their
personal standards [134].
Furthermore, while data is usually labeled for training purposes,
ground-truth explanations are rarely provided. In such cases, XAI re-
sults will lack a standard for comparison. Another notable limitation for
explainable AI is information security under GDPR rules [135]. When
employing the XAI technique, data confidentiality is very important
and may be jeopardized. As a result, any knowledge revealed by the
XAI method can be used to generate hostile or adversarial attacks to
mislead the model. Another major limitation of current XAI methods is
that these techniques provide explanations designed specifically for ML
experts to understand and deploy the models, which creates a handicap
for the clinical translation.[64].

text:
Discussion and future directions:
In this paper, we discuss post-hoc XAI methods and their implemen-
tation in gliomas, addressing clinical challenges, DL algorithms, and
the associated limitations. The performance of DL models is improving
day by day, and have attained saturation on traditional benchmarks.
Current research in DL focuses on the interpretability/explainability of
the model framework; however, these methods are yet to be applied
in real-world patient care settings. To this end, our review foresees
greater interest in highlighting the latest trends to interpret deep model
performance using XAI. The review also explains some challenges that
need to be addressed by XAI studies in glioma imaging, in order to
develop clinical decision support systems (CDSS).

text:
Clinical users’ perspective:
Deep learning models are expected to complement clinician’s work,
the interpretability of these models becomes essential for their uti-
lization and acceptance in the clinics. For instance, a CNN learns
fixed weights deterministically, whereas a Bayesian neural network
learns parameters from random variables used to sample weights. These
parameters could be used to show the uncertainty of the model’s predic-
tions and, consequently, help clinicians comprehend the limitations of
the model [136]. Keyword co-occurrence analysis from Fig. 6 highlights
the dominance of Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME techniques that focus
on enhancing AI interpretability in medical imaging while maintaining
diagnostic accuracy. However, our systematic review found no peer-
reviewed clinical usability evidence regarding explainable AI models
for brain tumor analysis in hospital settings.
Further, the integration of XAI methods into existing clinical work-
flow is another critical aspect, which requires being sure about the
adaptation and trustworthiness of XAI methods. The integration process
can be divided into several steps: A discussions should be carried
out with healthcare professionals to design XAI system based on their
clinical requirements. In this step, design principles of a user-friendly

text:
and user-centric XAI system should be emphasized, which enables
physicians to easily interpret and proceed with the information gen-
erated by an XAI system. Then, the specific use of the XAI system,
such as assistance in glioma diagnosis, giving insight about optimal
treatment options, or prognosis prediction should be determined. Fur-
thermore, the implemented XAI system should take advantage of new
data samples and continuously update the model to improve its pre-
dictive performance. Promoting educational programs for clinicians is
another vital step in understanding the capabilities and limitations of
integrated XAI systems. Moreover, establishing feedback mechanisms
between clinicians and AI developers would make it easier to refine
the implemented system and contribute to iterative improvement of
the XAI models. Additionally, the ethical considerations related to
integrating XAI into clinical settings should be addressed. Achieving the
above-mentioned steps will require close collaboration between data
scientists, AI experts, and user interface designers.
Future research is essential to determine how clinicians use and
interpret the different explanations presented in this review. Associated
with this is the need to understand safety and efficacy of explanations in
the clinic (including inadvertent behavioral change in diagnosis). There
is also a need for health economic analyses to determine whether there
is overall clinical time and cost saving. Future research would subse-
quently benefit from exploring how explanations – and the software
that produces the explanations – can be optimized to be beneficial in
the clinic.

Future trends in XAI:
XAI is a rapidly growing field that aims to create transparent and
interpretable AI-based systems. Aside from the extensive needs of the
technical and ethical aspects, XAI has the power to revolutionize the
management of glioma by providing more quantitative and under-
standable information about the disease. XAI on gliomas predominantly
provides medical imaging explanations, including digital pathology and
multi-modality MRI scans. The weak associations in Fig. 6 between
XAI, pathology and multi-modal imaging underscore a research gap,
suggesting the necessity for integrative frameworks that enhance model
generalizability and clinical trustworthiness.
In the field of digital pathology, there are significant opportunities
to conduct XAI. Firstly, future research could focus on developing
accurate and transparent DL models for improved glioma diagnosis
and treatment planning by handling large amounts of WSI data, which
is often difficult to interpret. Moreover, interactive XAI models may
assist pathologists in clinical decision-making with more accurate and
reliable diagnosis, selecting the optimal treatment, and monitoring
glioma patients over time. Finally, the application of XAI may be
further expanded to eliminate inter-pathologist variations with collab-
orative XAI models that integrate the computational power of AI into
human expertise. Overall, the development of safe and standardized
XAI approaches should be carried out in the field of glioma digital
pathology.
The integration of XAI in advanced MRI holds immense promise for
revolutionizing medical imaging interpretation. Recent advancements
in DL models such as, attention mechanisms, gradient-based visual-
izations, and feature attributions can effectively interpret advanced
MRI [137]. This fusion of XAI and advanced MRI not only enhances
the accuracy of diagnosis and prognosis but also empowers clinicians
with insights into the reasoning behind AI-generated results. A new era
of transparent, interpretable, and trustworthy medical imaging CAD
systems is underway, which will ultimately advance patient care and
clinical decision-making.

robust visual heatmaps. Moreover, feature importance and visualization
of XAI techniques like Grad-CAM and Guided Backpropagation help

Conclusions
The recent advancements in large-scale annotated glioma datasets,
innovative DL architectures, open access to source codes, and increas-
ing computational power have accelerated the growth of DL application
on gliomas. Recent studies have shown that DL models might provide
significant contributions to glioma diagnosis, patient care, and prog-
nosis. This review covered the existing applications of XAI methods
on glioma studies that incorporated MRI or pathology images. More-
over, the co-occurrence keyword analysis highlighted emerging XAI
techniques applied to brain tumor imaging to develop trustworthy DL
models for this domain. In addition, the analysis identified gaps in brain
tumor imaging, particularly the limited exploration of multi-modal
deep learning approaches for gliomas, presenting valuable opportuni-
ties for future research. This review highlighted the main limitations of
current XAI methods applied in gliomas, including the lack of clarity
of the interpretability maps and the lack of quantitative evaluation of
both the explanation maps of the model and the explainable features.
All aside, XAI could be identified as an urgent need for transferring
DL architectures into clinical practice. Our review has demonstrated
that interpretable DL methods have begun to be demanded to enhance
the transparency and confidence in decision-making, for an easier
integration into routine clinical practice while complying with the
GDPR regulations. Significant works that focus on the development of
more robust and well-explained XAI methods are necessary to conduct
trustworthy XAI applications. Subsequently, these advances should be
integrated into clinical practice.

Abstract
Brain tumors (BT) constitute significant diseases that require an early diagnosis with accurate assessment to plan appropri­
ate treatment strategies. MRI scans are utilized extensively to diagnose BTs;however, manual examination is both tedious
and prone to inconsistencies. In the past few years, significant advances have been made in BTC using DL models, which
have shown exceptional efficacy.Unfortunately, the black box problem associated with DL models prevents their wider
implementation in healthcare institutions.The current review aims to explore recent developments in MRI-based BTC
through the use of transfer learning and hybrid deep learning algorithms combined with XAI technologies.This review
also explores recent developments in this field, identifies existing gaps in current research,and provides a conceptual model
to advance BT identification systems.

T1-weighted scans typically indicate active tumor tissue.
T2-weighted imaging (T2) Provides strong contrast for
edema, cystic changes, and necrotic regions within or around
tumors. Tumors usually appear hyperintense in T2, helping
to differentiate between solid tumor mass and peritumoral
edema.Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) sup­
presses cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signals, improving the
visibility of peritumoral edema and infiltrative tumor mar­
gins. FLAIR is particularly sensitive for detecting low-grade
gliomas and tumor spread into white matter.
Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) measures water
molecule motion within tissues, enabling identification of
hypercellular tumors or restricted diffusion areas. Appar­
ent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) maps derived from DWI
are valuable for differentiating tumor grades, distinguish­
ing tumor recurrence from treatment-related necrosis, and
identifying highly cellular tumor cores. Perfusion-Weighted
Imaging (PWI) assesses tumor vascularity and hemodynam­
ics by measuring cerebral blood volume (CBV), blood flow,
and mean transit time. High-grade gliomas typically show
elevated CBV due to angiogenesis, whereas low-grade glio­
mas exhibit lower perfusion values. Perfusion imaging is
critical in tumor grading, treatment monitoring, and differ­
entiating pseudoprogression from true progression.
These MRI sequences provide a comprehensive multipa­
rametric view which includes structural, physiological, and
molecular view. This makes MRI the cornerstone for non­
invasive brain tumor classification and treatment planning.
Computed Tomography (CT) is often used in emergen­
cies because of its speed and effectiveness in detecting cal­
cifications, hemorrhage, and bone involvement. Positron
Emission Tomography (PET), often combined with CT
or MRI, provides metabolic and molecular information,
helping differentiate tumor recurrence from treatment
effects. DL algorithms are essential for assessing medical
images in the context of grading and categorizing BT. DL
models can identify important features and patterns in medi­
cal pictures, increasing the precision and reliability of BTC
as well as categorization [7, 8].

Motivation
The reason why DL models have been widely used to clas­
sify BT is because they give high accuracy. However, the
“black box” nature of the model itself hinders one from
gaining confidence in the results. Another thing to keep in
mind is that model precision and interpretability should be
balanced. While it is true that XAI applications in the classi­
fication of BT are increasingly prevalent, no systematic lit­
erature review and design of the framework have been done.
Some of the recent works have shown promising results in
classifying brain tumors using the integration of deep learn­
ing and transfer learning approaches. For example, a recent
work [9] suggests a computer-aided diagnosis system that
employs CNN-based feature extraction along with the use
of transfer learning for multiclass classification of brain
tumors. This work emphasizes the efficiency of applying
the concepts of transfer learning to achieve better classifica­
tion results using MRI data. In another study [10], the need
for accurate classification and segmentation of brain tumors
to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis and treatment. Even
though CNN, U-Net, transformers, and hybrid approaches
have achieved better results, certain issues related to varia­
tion in datasets, insufficient annotations, and lack of inter­
pretability remain. Motivated by these gaps, this survey
provides a comprehensive analysis of existing methods to
identify reliable and clinically applicable solutions for brain
tumor analysis.

Although existing surveys on the topic of XAI in medi­

give guidelines, frameworks, and cross-domain perspec­

ets and improving classification performance.

●
ResNet50
ResNet adds residual connections, which prevent the
vanishing gradient issue and enable the model to learn
deeper and more abstract features from MRI scans. This
is very useful in capturing the fine texture and patterns
in various types of brain tumors. ResNet is very good at
preserving spatial information from layer to layer and
has excellent generalization even on small data. It also
gets along very well with explainability methods such as
saliency maps. ResNet is, however, GPU-intensive and
consumes more GPU memory, particularly in its deeper
variants (e.g., ResNet101 or 152). It is one of the most
stable architectures for high-accuracy tumor classifica­
tion [24–26].
●
EfficientNet (B0 to B7)
EfficientNet balances scaling depth, width, and resolu­
tion with a compound scaling strategy and is highly ef­
ficient with fewer parameters. It uses mobile inverted
bottleneck convolution (MBConv) blocks with squeeze-
and-excitation layers to pay attention to important spa­
tial features and enforce feature channel interdependen­
cies. It doesn’t employ conventional skip connections
like ResNet, yet preserves spatial information well
among layers. The EfficientNet architecture is ideal for
classifying brain tumors where computational power is
limited, but accuracy remains the priority. However, the
network relies on proper preprocessing of inputs to an
adequate size [23, 27–29].

sophisticated tumor features. It can be used in real-time
systems or portable diagnosis devices, like onboard
screening machines in rural locations. The accuracy of

●
DenseNet
The model DenseNet employs dense connectivity. In
DenseNet, the subsequent layers get inputs from all
preceding layers, which allows dense feature reuse and
gradient stability. This makes it possible to retain both
high- and low-level spatial features necessary for clas­
sifying tumors with slight differences in MRI scans. The
architecture is highly efficient, even with small medical
datasets, minimizing overfitting and making it more in­
terpretable. DenseNet is easy to deploy in a multimodal
system, such as using MRI along with patient data. The
problem with DenseNet is that its dense connections
lead to high memory consumption and training times
[32–34].
●
InceptionV3
InceptionV3 is an advanced version of GoogleNet that
utilizes factorization of convolutions and better incep­
tion blocks, allowing for more effective feature extrac­
tion. This architecture can extract global and local spatial
features using various convolutional filters. Although
there are no classic skip connections, it uses auxiliary
classifiers and batch normalization, providing better sta­
bility and information flow during training. InceptionV3
is suitable for classification tasks of brain tumors be­
cause of its ability to represent multiscale features. It
demonstrates good performance for large images. The
model’s complexity is not flexible, and it requires exten­
sive computational power during training [8].

Ensembled Model
Ensemble model integrate the best features of several mod­
els, therefore they improve accuracy, resilience, and gen­
eralization, making them very useful for classifying brain
tumors. Accurately identifying various tumor types in
MRI scans requires the capacity to handle data variability
and minimize overfitting, which is achieved by employing
strategies like bagging, boosting, and stacking. Ensembles
can help improve the model’s classification of uncommon
tumor types and generalization on unknown data. They
are more resource-intensive, nevertheless, because of their
drawbacks, which include higher memory usage, more
complicated setup, and higher processing demands. Despite
these difficulties, they are a useful tool in medical imaging
because they can produce predictions that are more accurate
[8, 35–38]. The heterogeneous predictions can be calculated
by majority voting, weighted averaging and meta-learning
techniques. Ensemble models provide precise tumor diagno­
sis and help in early diagnosis. Figure 9 illustrates the basic
structure of ensemble learning for brain tumor organization.

2.3 CNN + Transformer Based Hybrid Models
Transformers improve our understanding of the structure of
the brain by capturing global context and long-range depen­
dencies, whereas CNNs are excellent at retrieving local data
from MRI scans, such as tumor boundaries. This combina­
tion enables the model to concentrate on both specific tumor
locations and more general contextual data, resulting in a
classification that is more thorough and accurate. Although
these models increase performance, their complexity and
computational costs are higher. Transformers improve fea­
ture extraction and classification accuracy by focusing on
key regions of the image using self-attention techniques.
With the help of this hybrid technique, the model may con­
centrate on various MRI scan regions both locally (using
CNNs) and globally (using Transformers), resulting in more
thorough and accurate tumor detection and classification
[39–41]. In Vision Transformers, the input image is initially
split into patches of fixed size, which are each flattened and
linearly embedded together to create a sequence of vectors.
Positional embeddings are appended in order to preserve
spatial information regarding where each patch originally
was. This sequence goes through a transformer encoder,
where self-attention mechanisms are used to capture global
relationships among the patches. In addition, a classification
token that can be learned is added to the sequence and its
output upon encoding is utilized by a linear classification
head to predict the final image class [8, 29, 42]. Figs. 10

2.4 CNN + Attention Based Hybrid Models
CNNs excel in identifying spatial patterns in MRI scans,
such as tumor edges and textures. However, attention mod­
ules assist the model in focusing on the most pertinent areas,
usually the tumor, while disregarding less significant back­
ground data. This increases the model’s resilience to changes
in tumor location, size, and form while also improving clas­
sification accuracy. Furthermore, by producing visual expla­
nations such as heatmaps, attention processes improve the
model’s interpretability, which is advantageous in medical
settings [31, 43–45]. A self-attention image classification
model employs a self-attention mechanism to comprehend
the interaction between various parts of an image and is
very efficient at capturing global context and long-range
dependencies for precise classification. As shown in Fig. 11,
it begins with an input image as a matrix of pixel inten­
sities, from which features are learned through a CNN or
transformer-based structure such as ResNet or Vision Trans­
former (ViT). These are then passed through the self-atten­
tion layer, where they are converted into queries, keys, and
values. The model determines attention weights by match­
ing every query against all the keys to find their similarity,
and utilizes these to calculate a weighted sum of the val­
ues, allowing it to focus on the most important information.
Lastly, this attention-augmented representation, together
with the raw input, is fed into a feed-forward neural network
to generate the classification outcome.
Table 2 shows the pros and cons of DL methods for
EBTC.For brain tumor classification, transfer learning is
fast and effective on small datasets but may overfit and
lack MRI-specific features. Ensemble learning improves
accuracy and robustness but is computationally expensive.
Transformer + CNN hybrids capture both local and global
features, performing well on large datasets but are complex
and resource-intensive. Attention + CNN hybrids efficiently
focus on tumor regions, suitable for small datasets, though
they may miss global context and occasionally highlight
artifacts. The choice of method depends on dataset size,
computational resources, and the desired balance between
performance and interpretability.

sis accuracy [28, 43]. Researchers are confident that the
identification and categorization of BT using XAI form a
potent combination for improved diagnostic accuracy and

Intelligence (XAI) encompasses a set of methodologies
and frameworks aimed at making the internal mechanisms
and decision-making processes of complex deep learning
models interpretable to human users. XAI facilitates under­
standing, debugging, validation, and regulatory compliance
of human-centric models, which are especially critical in
medical diagnosis and finance systems. It also plays a cru­
cial role in ensuring fairness and improving the robustness
and trustworthiness of the model.
The integration of explainable artificial intelligence
(XAI) in brain tumor classification systems is crucial
because medical decision-making is of high stakes. Black-
box AI models, which tend to be highly accurate, are not
transparent, which means clinicians cannot trust or rely on
their predictions. XAI focuses on important brain scan fea­
tures which lead to classifier’s decision. This interpretability
is important not only for the belief of medical profession­
als, but also to determine whether decisions are grounded
in clinically relevant patterns, rather than irrelevant or
deceptive data artifacts. XAI also enables legal and ethical
demands for accountability and transparency in healthcare,
allowing clinicians to clarify AI-based diagnoses to patients,
crucial for shared decision making and informed consent.
XAI bridges the gap between advanced AI systems and the
realistic, ethical, and regulatory needs of modern medicine.
This connection is essential for effectively using AI in diag­
nosing brain tumors [46–48].

Taxonomy and Categorization of XAI Techniques
In the literature, Explainable AI (XAI) methodologies are
commonly categorized along several technical dimensions
such as model transparency, scope of explanation, expla­
nation technique, and model type [47]. In Fig. 6 we have
shown all types of XAI and its purpose.
●
Based on model transparency, approaches are divided
into intrinsically interpretable models (e.g., linear re­
gression, decision trees) that are self-explanatory by
design, and post-hoc explainability methods that are ap­
plied to complex, opaque models to derive interpretabil­
ity (e.g., LIME, SHAP).
●
Based on the scope of explanation, methods are classi­
fied as global explanations, which aim to describe the
overall behavior and logic of the model, and local expla­
nations, which focus on interpreting individual predic­
tions or decisions.
●
Based on explanation technique, categorization includes
feature attribution methods, example-based explana­
tions, rule-based methods, and visualization techniques.
These define how the rationale behind predictions is pre­
sented to users.
●
Based on model type, XAI methods are differentiated
by whether they are designed for white-box models (in­
terpretable by nature) or black-box models (requiring
post-hoc interpretation), and further tailored to specific
architectures such as deep neural networks, ensemble
models, or probabilistic frameworks.
XAI is important in medical applications like brain tumor
identification and classification since it improves algorithm
transparency and interpretability. Current research efforts
are focused on developing AI models with explainable
outputs, which will assist healthcare practitioners in under­
standing decision-making processes and establishing trust
in automated systems.Various XAI techniques are investi­
gated in Fig. 12
These strategies were investigated to improve the inter­
pretability, trustworthiness, as well as explainability of brain
tumour categorization systems [49, 50]. These strategies are
divided into five categories: feature importance, model-spe­
cific interpretability, visualization-based, attention-based,
and example-based. These methods are meant to explain
complex ML models’ decisions, increasing transparency
and reliability for patients, radiologists, and neurologists.

LIME explains the classifier’s predictions by approximately

relevance of a feature by measuring the increase in predic­

that assigns every characteristic’s impact on the forecast
using cooperative game theories [52, 53].
Model specific interpretability is a model-specific tech­

based are intrinsically interpretable models where features
lead directly to predictions with transparent paths [47] Lin­

their coefficients, indicating the influence of each feature
[54]. Surrogate models are interpretable and simple models
that mimic predictions of more complex models, providing
insight into their decision-making process [55].

terfactuals explain solely the classifiers’ positive outcomes
rather than the negative outcomes. The counterfactual local

Prototype-based approaches use prototype examples to
explain predictions, displaying instances from training data
that are most relevant to the present input [60].

Pre-Processing Techniques in EBTC
Pre-processing is an efficient and effective technique for
accurate analysis of medical images. There are numerous
challenges in datasets for brain tumor classification, which
encompasses several critical aspects. Class imbalance, lim­
ited dataset size, lack of comprehensive annotations and
data collection variability are key challenges. Pre-process­
ing methods like data augmentation, intensity normaliza­
tion, noise removal methods as well as image synthesis
techniques are used to solve these problems. Collaboration
with multiple institutions is necessary to solve limited data­
set size issues
In the study [77], Grad-CAM was applied to draw atten­
tion to areas in the images of interest or regions of interest.
Those regions were resized to 224 × 224 pixels. The pictures
were further segregated into smaller pixels of 28 × 28 to ease
handling. In order to avoid overfitting, the paper [7]. used
z-score normalization with rotation, random flipping, and
intensity modification to extract valuable features. Paper
[46, 78]. examined MRI images from various sources using
z-score normalization to ensure uniformity. Data augmenta­
tion strategies such as cropping, flipping, and dynamic patch
cropping all helped to introduce variations, which increased
the model’s generalizability [35]. New MRI images of vari­
ous types were generated in the study [28] using conditional
Generative Adversarial Networks (cGAN). By forcing
the model to learn from a variety of samples, this strategy
helped to alleviate issues with overfitting and data imbal­
ance. Table 5 shows the commonly used pre-processing
techniques in EBTC.

Skull Stripping
Skull stripping is one of the most common techniques in
medical imaging, particularly brain imaging using MRI
scans. The technique is extracted from head images to isolate
non-brain tissues and concentrate only on the brain struc­
ture. Some of the techniques used are thresholding, where
the boundaries of brain and non-brain tissue are defined;
watershed segmentation is done to demarcate clearly dif­
ferentiated regions within an image; and morphological
operations can be carried out to improve further on the
segmentations. These methods have significantly enhanced
MRI data interpretation and evaluation, as well as the treat­
ment of patients with brain tumors [79].

Intensity Normalization
MRI images are known to differ in intensity because of the
type of MRI scanner used, the protocols employed during
acquisition, and even the patient themselves. Such differ­
ences are detrimental to deep learning models because the
system starts to focus on irrelevant changes instead of mean­
ingful features such as the tumor itself. Intensity normal­
ization aims to resolve the problem by ensuring all images
have the same range and distribution by harmonizing their
pixel intensity values. This enables the model to concentrate
on the real structural and anatomical patterns aligned with
the tumors instead of being skewed by brightness or con­
trast differences. Intensities must be normalized since this
is essential in making sure that there are consistent intensity
values when it comes to different samples. This is especially
true in medical images where the values of intensities mean
a great deal. This process is needed, and some common
processes include min-max scaling where intensity values
are normalized within a given range, such as 0 to 1 and 0
to 255.-Z scores: Intensity values are normalized based on
standard score and contrast stretching. These methods are
important when it comes to measuring intensities and ensur­
ing precise measurement through visual analysis of tumors
or lesions in the images [39, 74].

Contrast Enhancement
However, distinguishing brain tumors is complicated by the
high similarity of the characteristics of brain tumors and
healthy brain tissue. Thus, the boundaries between these
two types of tissues can be barely noticeable to the eye.
Contrast enhancing techniques allow for highlighting small
differences in tissues, thus making the boundary between
healthy tissue and the tumor clearer. In turn, it facilitates the
diagnosis process by providing an opportunity to recognize
brain tumors more effectively, as well as making the clas­
sification process easier for deep learning methods. Further­
more, enhanced contrast helps detect more relevant features
that will contribute to increasing the accuracy of recognition
and classification. The histogram equalization results in the
uniform distribution of the intensities throughout the histo­
gram. CLAHE technique uses adaptive histogram equaliza­
tion for small regions of image, which constrains contrast
amplification. Such methods help visualize and provide
opportunities for visual interpretation of images; therefore,
they are highly beneficial for brain tumors classification due
to its dependence on feature visibility [22, 80].

Image Synthesis
Image synthesis is a central aspect of brain tumor classifi­
cation since it generates realistic medical images, primar­
ily using techniques like Generative Adversarial Networks
(GANs). Its main strength is that it can address the lack of
data, which is common in medical imaging due to privacy
issues and the cost of specialized annotation. Through gen­
erating synthetic MRI scans that are indistinguishable from
real ones, image synthesis makes training sets larger and
more diverse so deep learning models can learn more and
generalize better [28].

XAI as Pre-Processing Techniques
During preprocessing, XAI methods like saliency maps,
Grad-CAM [77], or Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
(LRP) can highlight what areas of an MRI scan are most rel­
evant to making model predictions. This can be utilized for
region-of-interest (ROI) extraction guidance, e.g., cropping
out and highlighting tumor regions and removing distract­
ing background.In this way, XAI helps to enhance the input
data, and hence the training process becomes more interpre­
table and efficient. It also helps researchers and clinicians to
ensure that the model is not relying on misleading features,
for instance, image artifacts or non-tumor regions.

Evaluation Metrics for XAI
Fidelity (or faithfulness) captures the quality of how closely
the explanation mimics the actual decision-making process
of the model. High-fidelity explanations are close to what
the model is actually doing. Interpretability captures how
easy it is for a human to understand the explanation.Shorter,
simpler explanations are typically more interpretable. Sta­
bility or consistency measures whether small variations in
the input lead to comparable explanations, which is impor­
tant for establishing user trust. Usefulness captures the
value of the explanation to users, e.g., whether it improves
decision-making or helps with model confidence building,
typically measured by human-in-the-loop tests such as user
studies. Lastly, ground truth alignment evaluates expla­
nations against known or expert-labeled salient features,
which enables to verify whether the explanation points to
actually salient features. Collectively, these metrics ensure
XAI methods provide insights that are not only technically
valid but also actionable and relevant to human users

occurs in the range of about 0.5% to 1.5%, but it can be

techniques enable complementary feature learning from dif­
ferent models, thus ensuring reduced variance and low risk
of overfitting. Even a minor improvement like this can be
quite crucial in healthcare imaging since it adds reliability
to clinical diagnostics. At the same time, ensembles have a
major disadvantage – higher complexity and slower infer­
ence time in comparison to single model systems. On the
other hand, hybrid networks combining convolutional neu­
ral networks (CNN) with Vision Transformer (ViT), atten­
tion, and recurrence have shown more reliable and better
results. Networks like ViT-GRU and self-attention-based
CNN networks can provide up to 99.81% accuracy [19, 57],
whereas EfficientNetV2 with attention blocks performs well
in competitive ways [44]. The capacity to understand local
as well as global features increases classification effective­
ness. Also, XAI methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and
LIME are extensively applied by both, with the former
being better in providing interpretations using multi-layer
explanations. Overall, hybrid deep learning models are
better than transfer learning in handling EBTC in terms of
accuracy and robustness. On the other hand, the latter two
are efficient and competitive.

In this section, the gaps in research and future areas in
Explainable Brain tumor classification are explored. There
are various challenges that come with medical image clas­
sification, especially when applied to brain tumor detection.

Challenges in Dataset
●
Limited number of multimodal datasets: Most re­
search relies only on MRI, while the availability of com­
bined MRI, CT, PET, clinical, biomarker, and genomic
data is scarce.
●
Restricted generalization: Datasets typically represent
only one imaging technique, which reduces the model’s
ability to generalize across different modalities.
●
Class imbalance: Tumors often belong to minority
classes, leading to biased predictions toward majority
classes and degraded performance.

●
Small dataset size: Many publicly available datasets
are not large enough to support the training of robust
deep learning models.
●
Institutional variability: Differences in scanners, ac­
quisition protocols, and annotation standards introduce
inconsistency in data quality.
●

Challenges in Multimodal Integration
●
Underutilization of multimodal approaches: Most
existing work relies solely on MRI, while multimodal
fusion with CT, PET, clinical data, and genomic infor­
mation remains underexplored.
●
Limited access to genomic and biomarker data: Re­
stricted availability of such data limits the development
of multi-omics models that could enhance diagnostic
accuracy.
●
Complexity of multimodal data fusion: Integrating
heterogeneous data types requires sophisticated fusion
architectures and standardization.

Computational Constraints
●
High computational cost: State-of-the-art deep learn­
ing models require high-end GPUs/TPUs, making train­
ing and deployment expensive.
●
Real-time deployment challenges: Large and complex
models struggle to meet low-latency requirements in
clinical workflows.
●
Scalability issues: Efficient on-device or edge-based
processing approaches are still underdeveloped.

title: Deep Learning Meets Explainability in MRI Brain Tumor Analysis: A Review and Future Research Framework

text:
Explainability and Interpretability Gaps
●
Accuracy vs. interpretability trade-off: Highly inter­
pretable models often sacrifice accuracy, while high-
performing models lack transparency.
●
Overreliance on visual interpretability: Methods such
as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME generate visual expla­
nations useful for experts but not accessible to patients.
●
Lack of user-centric explanations: Patients and non-
technical users require textual or descriptive explana­
tions rather than heatmaps.
●
Unexplored multimodal XAI: Most existing explain­
ability methods focus on image-only models, leaving
multimodal XAI significantly underdeveloped.
●
Inadequate XAI evaluation metrics: Few studies em­
ploy standardized metrics to assess explanation quality
or clinical utility.

Deployment and Clinical Integration Challenges
●
Limited real-time validation: Few models have been
tested in real clinical environments to assess practical
performance.
●
Workflow integration: Incorporating DL models into
existing radiology workflows requires addressing com­
patibility constraints, regulatory approval, and usability
issues.
●
Interoperability issues: Variations in clinical systems
across institutions create challenges for consistent mod­
el deployment.

Privacy and Security Concerns
●
Patient data protection: Sensitive medical and genom­
ic data must remain secure throughout multi-institution­
al collaborations.
●
Underuse of privacy-preserving learning: Federated
learning, homomorphic encryption, and other priva­
cy-preserving training techniques are not yet widely
adopted.
●
Domain mismatch: The majority of pretrained mod­
els are trained using natural images, such as ImageNet,
which differ greatly from MRI/medical images in terms
of their features. Features may become less relevant as
a result.
●
Overfitting on small datasets: If the pretrained model
is very deep, fine-tuning on small datasets of brain tu­
mors may result in overfitting.
●
Restricted support for 3D: Most standard transfer
learning models are 2D, and it is difficult to extend them
to volumetric MRI data.
●
Explainability problems: XAI techniques may draw
attention to unimportant characteristics that are passed
down from pretrained weights, making them harder to
understand.
