Future Directions in EBTC
A future study of brain tumor classification should be based
on large, standardized multimodal datasets. Enhanced aug­
mentation may mitigate challenges regarding limited and
imbalanced annotations. Development of efficient models
to deploy in real-world scenarios is needed, including mul­
timodal fusion and lightweight architectures for edge AI.
Improvements in explainability are expected through user-
oriented multimodal XAI. Moreover, privacy needs to be
guaranteed with federated learning or other forms of secure
collaboration. Hybrid models shall include 3D adaptation,
integrated XAI, and automated hyperparameter tuning to
regularize overfitting and further improve reproducibility.

Proposed Conceptual Framework for
Multimodal EBTC
Figure 16 shows the proposed Conceptualframework that
aims to perform a complete diagnosis of brain tumors by
combining different sources of heterogeneous patient data
using a deep learning model that applies a late fusion strat­
egy based on hierarchical decision making and a logical rea­
soning algorithm.
The multimodal brain tumor study frameworks com­
bine information sources like clinical data and MR images.
Each information source can be processed through separate
hybrid DL models. The predictions from these models can
be fused through late fusion, where higher-level informa­
tion or predictions or decisions are combined and work
well when modalities are missing. A hierarchical decision
approach is used where classification related to tumor type
are done first, and then glioma grading is done. To ensure
explanation and understanding for specific tasks in brain
tumor analysis, recent architectures have embraced the
implementation of explainable AI tools such as saliency or
activation maps.

Conclusions
This research, therefore, underlines the transformative
effect of various deep learning models on explainable brain
tumor classification, including transformer-based architec­
tures, attention mechanisms, transfer learning strategies,
and ensemble learning approaches. By integrating these
advanced DL models with explainable AI techniques, it
bridges the gap between predictive power and interpret­
ability, enabling clinicians to trust and act upon model out­
puts. Hybrid deep learning architectures, particularly those
integrating CNNs with transformers and attention mecha­
nisms, achieve the best performance for EBTC tasks, while
EfficientNet-based transfer learning models provide an
effective and computationally efficient alternative.The com­
prehensive review of the datasets, preprocessing methods,
and classification strategies based on DL lays the founda­
tion for further innovations in the field of EBTC and opens
up perspectives toward multimodal, interpretable, and clini­
cally impactful solutions.

title: A contrastive learning framework with adaptive feature fusion for brain tumor classification
authors: Yating Peng; Song He; Lingle Chang
text:
A contrastive learning framework
with adaptive feature fusion for
brain tumor classification
Yating Peng1,2, Song He3 & Lingle Chang4
Accurate classification of brain tumors from MRI scans is critical for diagnosis and treatment planning,
yet remains challenging due to high intra-class heterogeneity and subtle inter-class differences. While
deep learning has shown promise in automating this task, existing models often lack the discriminative
power to reliably capture fine-grained pathological features. To address these limitations, we propose
a novel contrastive learning framework with adaptive feature fusion (AFF-CL). Our method introduces
a dynamic label queue that stores historical labels, enabling the construction of multiple positive
pairs from different images of the same class. This design injects explicit supervision into contrastive
learning, where the multiple positive pairs provide comprehensive intra-class variation coverage,
directly facilitating feature representations that minimize intra-class distance while maximizing inter-
class separation. Furthermore, to capture multi-scale contextual information, we augment the model
with a local input stream and design an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module to intelligently integrate
localized features with global representations. Extensive experiments on the public figshare dataset
demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming
existing methods. The proposed approach shows strong potential for enhancing the precision of
computer-aided diagnosis in clinical practice.
Keywords Deep learning, Contrastive learning, Brain tumor classification, Adaptive feature fusion
Brain tumors represent one of the most formidable challenges in modern oncology, characterized by the
uncontrolled proliferation of cells within the cranial cavity. The growth of these abnormal masses can impose
mechanical pressure on vital neural structures. This leads to a spectrum of neurological impairments, including
severe headaches, seizures, and sensory-motor deficits1. Clinically, tumors range from benign (slow-growing)
to malignant (aggressive). To standardize diagnosis and prognosis, the World Health Organization (WHO)
has established a comprehensive grading system2. In clinical practice, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
serves as the cornerstone for brain tumor detection and evaluation, providing exceptional detail of soft tissue

to malignant (aggressive). To standardize diagnosis and prognosis, the World Health Organization (WHO)
has established a comprehensive grading system2. In clinical practice, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
serves as the cornerstone for brain tumor detection and evaluation, providing exceptional detail of soft tissue
anatomy. However, the diagnostic process remains heavily reliant on manual interpretation by radiologists. This
practice is inherently subjective, time-consuming, and prone to inter-observer variability3,4. These challenges
are particularly acute when distinguishing between common tumor types, such as meningioma, glioma, and
pituitary tumors. The difficulty arises from their often overlapping radiographic appearances and significant
intra-class heterogeneity.
The advent of deep learning, encompassing convolutional neural networks (CNNs)5–8, has heralded
a new era in medical image analysis, promising to automate and augment diagnostic workflows. Moreover,
significant advancements have been achieved in discriminative feature learning, particularly for fine-grained
image recognition, retrieval, and robust generalization9–13, providing valuable methodological inspirations for
capturing subtle pathological variations. These models excel at learning hierarchical feature representations
from vast amounts of imaging data14–17. Nevertheless, prevailing deep learning models frequently struggle with
the specific complexities of brain tumor MRI analysis. While strategies like the integration of attention modules
and graph structures have been employed to boost performance, existing models still exhibit non-trivial error
rates18–20. These errors frequently stem from the model’s failure to capture the nuanced pathological distinctions
between tumor categories. This limitation is exacerbated by two inherent characteristics of brain MRI data. First,

and morphological presentations across different imaging perspectives. Second, discriminative features between
tumor classes often reside in subtle variations in spatial distribution, morphological structure, and boundary
characteristics rather than conspicuous visual differences. This presents challenging fine-grained inter-class
variations that conventional models struggle to resolve.
To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel contrastive learning framework with adaptive feature fusion, named
AFF-CL, for brain tumor classification. Our method leverages a dynamic label queue and a corresponding
feature queue. Unlike conventional contrastive learning that primarily relies on self-augmentations to form
positive pairs21, our framework capitalizes on the stored label information in the queue. This allows us to
dynamically construct multiple positive sample pairs from different images belonging to the same class. This
mechanism injects explicit supervisory signals directly into the contrastive learning process22. Effectively, it
guides the model to learn more discriminative and semantically meaningful representations by pulling features
of the same tumor type closer in the embedding space while pushing others apart. Furthermore, to capture
richer, multi-scale representations that are crucial for discerning subtle pathological details, we augment the
standard global encoding pipeline with an additional local input stream. These local inputs are derived from
focused regions of the original MRI scans, forcing the model to scrutinize fine-grained patterns. A critical
component of our architecture is the designed adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module. This module is responsible
for intelligently and dynamically integrating the global contextual information with these localized details. It
allows the model to automatically perceive and emphasize the most salient features across different scales for
the final diagnosis. Extensive validation on the public Figshare brain tumor dataset, encompassing Meningioma,
Glioma, and Pituitary tumors, confirms the efficacy of our proposed framework. Our model achieves state-of-
the-art classification accuracy, demonstrating its strong potential for clinical decision support.

text:
Related Work
Current research on brain tumor classification from MRI scans can be broadly categorized into traditional
machine learning methods and deep learning approaches. Due to the limitations of traditional techniques in
feature representation and generalization23,24, deep learning has gradually become the dominant paradigm. It
has demonstrated superior performance in handling complex medical imaging data25,26. Recent studies have
explored various deep learning architectures to improve classification accuracy. Hasan et al. proposed SSPANet,
an explainable attention-based framework. It integrates channel and spatial attention mechanisms to enhance

In this section, we provide a detailed description of the AFF-CL framework and its components.
AFF-CL framework
The proposed AFF-CL is an end-to-end contrastive learning framework designed to learn discriminative
representations for brain tumor classification. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the framework primarily consists of a main
dual-encoder and a momentum encoder. The main encoder takes an input image and its cropped local patch
to extract complementary global and local features. Simultaneously, a differently augmented view of the same
input is processed by the momentum encoder to produce a consistent feature representation. A core innovation
of our framework is the introduction of a label queue, which stores historical features from the momentum

the framework employs two AFF modules. Unlike a simple unidirectional integration, these modules operate
collaboratively to enable mutual adaptive fusion between the global and local feature streams. This bidirectional
cross-talk allows contextual information from the global view to refine the local features, while simultaneously
injecting fine-grained details from the local view into the global representation, achieving a more powerful and
multi-scale feature synthesis. Finally, refined fused representation is then directed to the classifier for tumor type
prediction.
Contrastive learning framework with a label queue
Brain tumor classification from MRI scans faces two inherent difficulties. The routine acquisition of images
from multiple anatomical planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) introduces significant intra-class variation, as the same
tumor type can exhibit diverse appearances. Concurrently, inter-class differences are often subtle, primarily
defined by variations in tumor location and morphology rather than distinct visual features. To directly address
this issue and learn a more structured and discriminative feature embedding, we introduce a contrastive
learning framework augmented with a label queue. The core of this framework operates with two encoders:
a main encoder and a momentum-updated encoder. The momentum encoder serves as a consistent feature
extractor for a dynamically updated queue. As shown in Fig. 1, for an input image, the main encoder produces
a global feature representation, termed the query. A strongly augmented version of the same image is processed
by the momentum encoder to produce a key feature. Unlike the standard instance discrimination approach
that forms a single positive pair (query and its own key), our key innovation lies in leveraging a label queue.
This queue maintains a first-in-first-out buffer of the most recent key features encoded by the momentum
encoder, with each feature stored alongside its associated class label. This design enables the global query
feature to be compared against both its immediate augmented key and a large set of stored keys. Specifically,

Adaptive feature fusion
While the contrastive learning framework effectively narrows intra-class differences and amplifies inter-class
separation, it primarily operates on global feature representations. However, discriminative clues for brain
tumor classification often reside in fine-grained regional characteristics, including variations in tumor location,
morphological shape, and local texture. Global contrastive learning alone may struggle to capture these subtle
yet decisive features. To address this limitation, we enhance our framework with multi-scale representation
learning through an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module. Our approach introduces an additional local input,
generated by cropping random regions from the original image, which is processed in parallel with the global
input by the main encoder. This design yields multi-scale outputs that capture both comprehensive contextual
information and detailed local patterns. The core of our solution is the AFF module, which performs adaptive
bidirectional integration of these complementary representations. Rather than simply combining features, the
module employs a spatial attention mechanism to dynamically recalibrate both feature streams, allowing detailed
local characteristics to enhance the global representation and semantically rich global features to enhance local
representations. This adaptive fusion creates enriched feature maps that embed crucial fine-grained details
within a semantically rich global context. The resulting multi-scale representations not only provide more
discriminative features for the final classifier but also create a more structured feature space for contrastive

Dataset
The experiments in this study are conducted on the publicly available Figshare brain tumor dataset32. This
comprehensive collection contains 3,064 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced axial, coronal, and sagittal MRI slices
obtained from 233 patients, with each image having a resolution of 512×512 pixels. The dataset encompasses
three major brain tumor categories: meningioma (708 images), glioma (1,426 images), and pituitary tumor (930
images). To ensure rigorous evaluation, the dataset is randomly partitioned into training, validation, and test
sets with a ratio of 8:1:1. Specifically, 2,451 images (80%) are used for model training, 305 images (10%) for
hyperparameter tuning and validation, and the remaining 309 images (10%) are reserved as the test set for final
performance assessment. The detailed distribution is summarized in Table 1.
Regarding data preprocessing, although the original MRI scans are single-channel grayscale images, we
convert them to three-channel RGB format to maintain compatibility with prevalent deep learning architectures
that are typically pre-trained on color image datasets. Sample images from each tumor category after
preprocessing are visualized in Fig. 3, illustrating the characteristic appearance and structural variations among
different tumor types.

Impact of label queue length
The length of the dynamic label queue determines the number of available positive and negative pairs for
contrastive learning, which directly influences feature representation. To justify our selection of 8192 as the
default queue length, we conducted an ablation study comparing it with alternative lengths of 4096 and 16384.
As demonstrated in Table 8, the model achieves its peak accuracy of 99.35% and highest stability (lowest standard
deviation) at a queue length of 8192. When the queue is shortened to 4096, the accuracy drops to 99.03%.
This indicates that a smaller queue provides an insufficient number of positive pairs to fully capture the rich
intra-class diversity present in brain tumor MRI. Conversely, expanding the queue to 16384 results in a slight
performance degradation to 99.16%. This decline can be attributed to the momentum update mechanism: an
excessively large queue inevitably retains older, outdated feature representations generated by earlier iterations
of the momentum encoder. These outdated features act as noise and interfere with the contrastive optimization.
Therefore, a queue length of 8192 strikes the optimal balance between sample diversity and feature consistency.
Impact of local view size

influencing the effectiveness of the AFF module. To evaluate this impact and justify our chosen size of 96 × 96
pixels (derived from the 224 × 224 global input), we conducted experiments using alternative cropping sizes
of 64 × 64 and 128 × 128. As shown in Table 9, the 96 × 96 crop yields the highest accuracy of 99.35% and the
most stable performance across all metrics. When the crop size is reduced to 64 × 64, the accuracy decreases to

and boundary characteristics of larger tumors. On the other hand, expanding the crop size to 128 × 128 results
in a slight accuracy drop to 99.29% and higher variance. This is because a larger local view incorporates more

Evaluation on another brain tumor dataset
To further substantiate the robustness and clinical relevance of our proposed framework, we extended our
evaluation to a second independent brain tumor MRI dataset55. This dataset is notably larger and more diverse
than the previous benchmark. It comprises 7,023 images across four distinct categories: No Tumor with 2000
images, Glioma with 1621 images, Meningioma with 1645 images, and Pituitary Tumor with 1757 images. The
data was partitioned into training, validation, and testing sets using the same 8:1:1 ratio to ensure experimental
consistency. As presented in Table 10, AFF-CL achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy of 99.00% and outperforms
competitive methods such as FHD-HybridNet with 98.78% accuracy and TUMbRAIN with 97.94% accuracy.
The ability of our framework to maintain exceptional performance on this larger dataset strongly validates its
generalization capability. This is particularly evident with the inclusion of a “No Tumor” class. These results
confirm that the discriminative features learned via the contrastive label queue and adaptive fusion are robust
to variations in imaging protocols and data distributions. This effectively mitigates concerns regarding dataset-
specific overfitting.

Limitations
Despite the promising performance of the AFF-CL framework, two potential limitations should be
acknowledged. First, the introduction of the dual-encoder architecture and the adaptive feature fusion module
inevitably increases the computational overhead. As indicated in the ablation study, the additional branches and
attention calculations lead to a rise in model parameters and floating-point operations (FLOPs) compared to a
standard single-stream backbone. While this trade-off is justified by the significant gains in diagnostic precision,
it requires higher hardware resources during the training phase. Second, regarding the experimental validation,
this study followed the prevalent protocol in current literature by employing a random slice-level split on the
figshare dataset. Since the dataset originates from 233 patients, a slice-level split carries a risk that different MRI
slices from the same patient may appear in both the training and testing sets. Adopting a strict patient-wise
split, in which no data from a test patient is seen during training, would likely result in lower classification
accuracy compared to the reported 99.35%. This is because the current slice-based approach may allow the
model to leverage patient-specific anatomical features, whereas a patient-wise split would demand a higher level
of generalization to completely unseen subjects. Future work will focus on validating the framework on strictly
patient-isolated datasets to further assess its clinical robustness in more challenging scenarios.

title: SYNAPSE-X: a calibration-aware vision transformer framework for selective referral in multi-class brain tumor MRI classification
authors: Sadaf Tabatabaee; Mohammad T. Khasawneh
text:
Abstract
Brain tumor MRI classification models can achieve high aggregate accuracy, but reliable decision support also
requires calibrated confidence estimates, transparent handling of uncertain cases, and careful evaluation under
external data shift. This study presents SYNAPSE-X, a calibration-aware Vision Transformer framework for
multi-class brain tumor MRI classification with uncertainty-guided selective referral. The framework classifies
contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI images into glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor catego­
ries while explicitly evaluating prediction reliability beyond accuracy alone. The corrected experimental cohort
included 7,023 images, with 5,712 training images and 1,311 held-out test images; augmentation was applied
only to the training subset to reduce leakage risk. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, macro-F1,
weighted-F1, expected calibration error, Brier score, negative log-likelihood, confidence-stratified accuracy,
and risk-coverage analysis. Post hoc temperature scaling was applied to improve probability calibration without
changing predicted labels. On the held-out test set, SYNAPSE-X achieved 98.41% accuracy, 98.2% macro-
F1, and 98.4% weighted-F1. Temperature scaling reduced expected calibration error from 0.041 to 0.018 and
Brier score from 0.036 to 0.021. Using a confidence threshold of 0.85, the selective-referral strategy deferred
6.7% of cases for expert review, while retained high-confidence cases achieved 99.12% accuracy. External
direct-transfer testing on an independent external brain MRI cohort of 3,264 images achieved 97.86% accuracy,
97.7% macro-F1, 97.9% weighted-F1, and an expected calibration error of 0.026 without retraining, fine-tun­
ing, external recalibration, or threshold re-selection. These findings position SYNAPSE-X as a research-stage
reliability-assessment framework for calibrated brain tumor MRI classification, supporting uncertainty-aware
referral while acknowledging limitations related to public image-level datasets, unavailable patient-level identi­
fiers, and the need for prospective clinical validation.

Scaling · Selective Referral · Confidence Reliability · Risk-Coverage Analysis · External Direct-Transfer
Testing · Medical Decision Support · Uncertainty-Aware AI

Introduction
Brain tumors are among the most clinically significant neurological disorders because their diagnosis influences
surgical planning, oncology referral, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surveillance, and long-term patient manage­
ment, and they remain a substantial contributor to cancer-related morbidity in population-based cancer registries
[31]. Glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor cases may present with heterogeneous morphology and
overlapping image characteristics, making reliable classification clinically important; a diversity now formally
reflected in the histological and molecular criteria of the fifth-edition World Health Organization classification of
central nervous system tumors [18]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains central to brain tumor assess­
ment because it provides high soft-tissue contrast and supports noninvasive visualization of intracranial struc­
tures. Recent reviews emphasize the growing role of machine learning and deep learning in MRI-based brain
tumor detection, classification, segmentation, and decision support [23, 33], building on community benchmarks
such as the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) challenge that catalyzed much of this methodologi­
cal progress [21]. In adolescent and young adult populations, gliomas remain a clinically important tumor group,
further supporting the need for accurate and reliable imaging-based tools [7].
Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in brain tumor MRI classification. Conventional con­
volutional neural networks and transfer-learning models remain widely used, with recent pipelines built on pre­
trained backbones such as VGG, ResNet, and Inception reporting accuracy above 97% on public four-class brain
MRI datasets [1, 29, 36]. More recently, Vision Transformer models have gained increasing attention because
they represent images as patch sequences and use self-attention to model spatial relationships across the image.
Foundational Vision Transformer work showed that a pure transformer applied to image patches can perform
effectively for image recognition when pretrained and transferred to downstream tasks [8]. Recent brain tumor
MRI studies have further demonstrated that fine-tuned Vision Transformer models can perform multi-class tumor
classification across glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor categories [2, 25, 32], consistent with

broader evidence that transformer architectures can match or exceed convolutional networks across diverse medi­
cal imaging tasks once adequately pretrained and fine-tuned [3, 20, 35].
However, high aggregate accuracy alone is not sufficient for reliability-sensitive medical decision support. A
model may achieve strong overall accuracy while still producing overconfident errors, poorly calibrated prob­
abilities, or uncertain predictions that should not be treated as equally reliable. Calibration is therefore impor­
tant because predicted confidence should correspond to the observed likelihood of correctness. Guo et al., [12]
showed that modern neural networks can be poorly calibrated and that temperature scaling can improve prob­

important because confidence scores may influence whether a prediction is accepted, questioned, or referred for
expert review [16, 34]. This concern becomes even more important when models are evaluated beyond their
development data, because deployed models can behave unpredictably under distributional shift. For example,
hospital-specific acquisition patterns have been shown to degrade cross-site generalization [40], and distribu­
tional shift can affect the reliability of predicted confidence values themselves, not only classification accuracy
[28]. Begoli et al., [4] further argue that machine-assisted medical decision making requires a principled uncer­
tainty-quantification discipline rather than reliance on point predictions alone.

calibration metrics, confidence-stratified behavior, selective-referral performance, and external direct-transfer
stability. Expected calibration error, Brier score, negative log-likelihood, and confidence-stratified accuracy are

●A calibration-aware Vision Transformer framework for four-class brain tumor MRI classification.
●A consistency-corrected experimental design with standardized dataset size, train/test counts, and external

architecture, calibration procedure, selective-referral protocol, external evaluation design, and evaluation met­
rics. Section 4 presents classification performance, calibration results, selective-referral analysis, error-profile
findings, and external direct-transfer results. Section 5 discusses the implications, limitations, and future direc­
tions of SYNAPSE-X.

section_heading: Deep learning and vision transformers for brain tumor MRI classification
text:
Deep learning and vision transformers for brain tumor MRI classification
Brain tumor MRI classification has been widely studied using deep learning. CNN-based models have been used
for tumor detection, grading, and classification because they can learn local texture, boundary, and intensity pat­
terns from medical images. Saeedi et al. [33] reviewed MRI-based brain tumor detection using convolutional
deep learning and selected machine-learning techniques, supporting the continued relevance of deep learning in
this area. Comparable transfer-learning pipelines built on pretrained CNN backbones have reported strong aggre­
gate performance on public four-class brain MRI datasets similar in composition to the one used here [1, 29, 36],
reflecting rapid progress in classification accuracy even as calibration and referral behavior remain comparatively
underreported in this literature. Broader reviews have also emphasized that machine learning and deep learning
are increasingly used across brain tumor detection, segmentation, classification, and clinical decision-support
tasks [23].
Vision Transformers provide a different modeling approach by processing images as patch embeddings and
using self-attention to learn relationships among image regions. This approach is based on the broader Vision
Transformer paradigm introduced by Dosovitskiy et al., [8], in which images are divided into fixed-size patches
and processed through transformer encoders. In brain MRI classification, this design can be useful because tumor
discrimination may depend not only on local texture but also on lesion shape, spatial arrangement, and surround­
ing anatomical context.
Recent studies have applied Vision Transformer models directly to brain tumor MRI classification. Asiri et al.
[2] proposed a fine-tuned Vision Transformer for brain tumor detection in MRI scans. Reddy et al. [32] evalu­
ated fine-tuned Vision Transformer variants for multi-class brain tumor classification and used a 7,023-image
MRI dataset categorized into glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor classes. Murala and Rao [25],
also proposed a Vision Transformer model for classifying a Kaggle brain tumor MRI dataset into no-tumor,
meningioma, pituitary tumor, and glioma categories. These studies support the suitability of transformer-based
models for multi-class brain tumor MRI classification [2, 25, 32]. This pattern is consistent with broader surveys

Despite these advances, many high-performing studies still emphasize aggregate classification metrics such

text:
Calibration and probability reliability in medical image classification
Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities reflect observed correctness. For example, if a model assigns
90% confidence to a group of predictions, a well-calibrated model should be correct approximately 90% of the
time. Calibration is therefore different from accuracy. A model can be accurate but poorly calibrated, especially
if it is overconfident in its errors.
Guo et al. [12] showed that modern neural networks are often miscalibrated and that post hoc calibration meth­
ods can improve the reliability of predicted confidence values. Their work identified temperature scaling as a
simple and effective calibration method for many neural-network classifiers, building on an earlier methodologi­
cal tradition of post hoc probability correction that includes Platt scaling for support vector machine outputs [30],
comparative evaluations of calibration methods across supervised learning algorithms [27], and histogram-bin­
ning approaches such as Bayesian binning into quantiles [26]. More recent work has revisited these questions for

non-convolutional models, tend to be comparatively well calibrated relative to earlier CNN generations, while
Kull et al. [15] showed that Dirichlet calibration can outperform single-parameter temperature scaling for multi-
class probability correction. Temperature scaling rescales logits before the softmax operation and can improve
probability calibration without changing the predicted class label.
Medical image classification studies have increasingly emphasized calibration. Sambyal et al. [34] investi­
gated calibration of deep neural networks for medical image classification and emphasized that confidence scores
are important for identifying cases requiring attention and for establishing trust in model predictions. Kurz et al.
[16] systematically reviewed uncertainty estimation in medical image classification and reported that uncertainty
estimation, network calibration, and out-of-distribution detection are important topics for real-world medical
imaging systems [16, 34]. Begoli et al. [4] frame this more broadly, arguing that machine-assisted medical deci­
sion making cannot rely on point predictions alone and instead requires a principled discipline for quantifying
and communicating predictive uncertainty.
In SYNAPSE-X, calibration is evaluated using expected calibration error, Brier score, and negative log-like­
lihood. Expected calibration error summarizes the gap between confidence and accuracy across confidence bins.
Brier score measures the squared difference between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes and is a
long-established probability forecast evaluation metric [5]. Negative log-likelihood penalizes confident incorrect
predictions and is useful for identifying overconfident errors. Together, these metrics allow the model to be evalu­
ated not only by how often it is correct, but also by whether its confidence is reliable.

text:
Temperature scaling and confidence correction
Post hoc calibration methods are useful because they can be applied after model training. Temperature scaling is
one of the most commonly used post hoc calibration approaches. It introduces a scalar temperature parameter that
rescales model logits before computing softmax probabilities. Guo et al. [12] showed that this method is simple
and effective for improving calibration in modern neural networks.
More recent work has extended temperature scaling by allowing sample-dependent temperature adjustment.
Joy et al. [13] proposed sample-dependent adaptive temperature scaling, showing that per-input temperature
values can improve expected calibration error while adding negligible computational overhead. Although SYN­
APSE-X uses standard post hoc temperature scaling rather than adaptive sample-dependent scaling, this work
supports the broader methodological rationale for confidence correction in neural networks [13].
For this manuscript, temperature scaling is used cautiously. It is not described as making the model clinically
validated. Instead, it is presented as a method for improving probability calibration in a research-stage classifier.
This wording is important because calibration improves confidence reliability but does not solve all limitations
related to image-level splitting, scanner variation, external dataset shift, or prospective clinical validation.

Uncertainty-guided selective referral
Selective prediction allows a model to abstain from making predictions when uncertainty is high. This is espe­
cially relevant in medical decision support, where forcing predictions on ambiguous cases can increase the risk
of overconfident errors. In selective classification, the model trades coverage for lower risk: stricter confidence
thresholds reduce the number of retained cases but may improve accuracy among retained cases.
Geifman and El-Yaniv [10], introduced selective classification for deep neural networks, showing that a clas­
sifier can reject uncertain instances to achieve a target risk level. They later proposed SelectiveNet, a deep neural
network with an integrated reject option, formalizing selective prediction as an end-to-end framework [11]. These
studies provide a methodological foundation for selective referral in reliability-sensitive classification settings. A
complementary line of work has developed uncertainty-estimation techniques for deep networks more generally,
including Monte Carlo dropout as an approximate Bayesian method [9], deep ensembles that estimate uncertainty

temic uncertainty in computer vision tasks [14]. Although SYNAPSE-X relies on calibrated softmax confidence
rather than ensembling or explicit Bayesian approximation, these methods provide complementary evidence that
predictive uncertainty can be estimated and operationalized in deep learning systems.
In medical image classification, uncertainty estimation has been linked to human-machine collaboration. Kurz
et al. [16] noted that when an AI system provides uncertainty estimates, predictions with high uncertainty can be
treated with extra care by medical experts, while low-uncertainty predictions may be trusted more appropriately.
This idea aligns directly with selective referral: uncertain model outputs should be referred for expert review
rather than treated as equally reliable.
SYNAPSE-X uses confidence-based selective referral to identify cases requiring expert review. Rather than
reporting only overall accuracy, the framework reports retained-case accuracy and referral rate. This makes
the evaluation more informative for decision-support settings because it shows how the model behaves when
uncertain cases are deferred. Complementary explainability techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations
(SHAP), which attribute individual predictions to input features [19], are outside the primary calibration-and-
referral focus of this study but represent a natural extension for future interpretable versions of SYNAPSE-X.

section_heading: External direct-transfer validation and dataset limitations
text:
External direct-transfer validation and dataset limitations
External testing is important for assessing whether model performance remains stable beyond the primary devel­
opment dataset. In radiology AI, internal test performance may not fully reflect generalization because datasets
can differ in patient population, scanner type, acquisition protocol, labeling process, and disease prevalence.
Yu et al. [39] showed that many radiology deep learning models experience performance reduction on external
datasets, supporting the need for external testing beyond internal holdout evaluation. This concern is well docu­
mented outside neuro-oncology as well: Zech et al., [40] found that pneumonia-screening CNNs trained on chest
radiographs from one hospital system performed inconsistently when applied to radiographs from other institu­
tions, in part because models could learn site-specific acquisition signatures rather than genuine disease features.
Distributional shift can also degrade the reliability of predicted confidence values themselves and not only classi­
fication accuracy, further motivating calibration-aware external testing rather than accuracy-only external testing
[28]. However, external testing should not be overstated as proof of prospective clinical validity or deployment
readiness.
Transparent reporting is also essential. CLAIM and CLAIM 2024 recommend clearly describing data sources,
partitioning level, and whether testing is performed at the patient, series, or image level [24, 37]. TRIPOD + AI
similarly emphasizes complete reporting for prediction models using machine learning, including model devel­
opment, evaluation, and validation procedures [6, 38]. These guidelines are especially relevant for public brain
MRI datasets, where patient identifiers, scanner metadata, acquisition parameters, and institutional information
may be unavailable. When such metadata are missing, patient-level independence cannot be fully verified, and
image-level splitting may overestimate generalization.
In the revised SYNAPSE-X framework, external evaluation is described as direct-transfer testing rather than
prospective clinical validation. The trained model was applied to an independent external brain MRI cohort of
3,264 images without retraining, fine-tuning, recalibration on external labels, threshold re-selection, or model
re-estimation. This design was used to reduce optimistic external performance estimates and to evaluate whether

Materials And Methods
The revised SYNAPSE-X methodology was designed to evaluate brain tumor MRI classification beyond aggre­
gate accuracy by incorporating calibration assessment, confidence reliability, uncertainty-guided selective refer­
ral, and external direct-transfer testing. Because Vision Transformers have already been applied to brain tumor
MRI classification, the methodological contribution of this study is not the use of a Vision Transformer alone.
Instead, SYNAPSE-X introduces a reliability-centered framework that evaluates whether model confidence is suf­
ficiently calibrated to distinguish high-confidence predictions from uncertain cases requiring expert review. The
revised framework directly addresses key methodological concerns raised during review, including dataset-size
inconsistency, unclear split reporting, leakage risk, calibration terminology, external validation ambiguity, and
overly strong clinical claims. The workflow is organized into four main components: dataset preparation, Vision
Transformer model development, calibration and selective-referral analysis, and internal/external evaluation.

title: SYNAPSE-X: a calibration-aware vision transformer framework for selective referral in multi-class brain tumor MRI classification
authors: Sadaf Tabatabaee; Mohammad T. Khasawneh
text:
SYNAPSE-X workflow and dataset preparation
SYNAPSE-X follows a four-stage workflow. First, public contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI images are stan­
dardized through deterministic preprocessing, image-level partitioning, and training-only augmentation. Second,
a compact Vision Transformer classifies each image into one of four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary
tumor, or no tumor. Third, model confidence is evaluated using calibration-sensitive metrics, and temperature
scaling is applied to recalibrate predicted probabilities without changing predicted labels. Fourth, confidence-
based selective referral separates high-confidence retained predictions from low-confidence cases requiring
expert review, followed by internal held-out testing and external direct-transfer testing (Fig. 1).
The corrected primary dataset contained 7,023 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI images across four
classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The dataset was partitioned into 5,712 training
images and 1,311 held-out test images, corresponding to an image-level split of 81.33% training and 18.67%
testing. The training set included 1,321 glioma, 1,339 meningioma, 1,595 no-tumor, and 1,457 pituitary tumor
images. The held-out test set included 300 glioma, 306 meningioma, 405 no-tumor, and 300 pituitary tumor
images (Fig. 2).
As illustrated in Fig. 3, all images were cropped to remove noninformative margins, resized to 224 × 224
pixels, and intensity-normalized to the [0,1] range. Data augmentation was applied only after the train/test split
and only to the training subset. Augmentation included random rotation, horizontal flipping, translation, and
brightness variation. The held-out test set and external test set were not augmented and underwent deterministic
preprocessing only.
Because the public dataset lacked complete patient-level identifiers, scanner metadata, acquisition parameters,
and institutional information, patient-level independence could not be verified. Therefore, all results are inter­
preted as public image-level evidence rather than confirmed patient-level clinical generalization.

Overall, the methodological novelty of SYNAPSE-X lies in advancing brain tumor MRI classification from
a conventional single-output classification task toward a calibrated reliability-assessment and selective-referral
framework. While Vision Transformers have previously been used for brain tumor MRI classification, SYN­
APSE-X extends this direction by jointly evaluating classification accuracy, probability calibration, confidence-
stratified correctness, risk-coverage behavior, and external direct-transfer stability. This design enables the model
to distinguish high-confidence predictions from uncertain cases requiring expert review, providing a more cau­
tious and operationally meaningful evaluation than aggregate accuracy alone.

The compact Vision Transformer was evaluated on the internal held-out test set of 1,311 images, which was not

macro-F1, and 98.4% weighted-F1, demonstrating strong four-class discrimination across glioma, meningioma,
pituitary tumor, and no-tumor categories.
As shown in Fig. 5, training and validation curves followed a stable convergence pattern. The absence of large
divergence between training and validation performance suggests that regularization strategies, including drop­
out, weight decay, and training-only augmentation, helped limit overfitting. However, the model’s final reliability
cannot be inferred from training curves alone; therefore, performance was evaluated on the untouched held-out
test set.
The confusion matrix in Fig. 6 shows that most predictions were concentrated along the diagonal, confirming
strong class-level discrimination. The no-tumor and pituitary tumor classes showed particularly stable classifica­
tion behavior, while the remaining errors were concentrated mainly between visually overlapping tumor classes.

Error profile of referred and misclassified cases
The distribution of referred and misclassified cases was reviewed to better understand where the model was
uncertain. Most errors occurred between tumor classes with overlapping imaging appearance, particularly glioma
and meningioma, followed by meningioma and pituitary tumor. No-tumor cases had the lowest referral burden
and the strongest high-confidence classification behavior.
At the primary threshold of 0.85, the model referred 6.7% of internal test cases. Meningioma showed the
highest referral tendency, suggesting that this class contained more borderline or visually overlapping cases.
This pattern is clinically plausible because meningioma can share enhancement patterns, lesion boundary char­
acteristics, or slice-level appearance with other tumor categories depending on tumor location and image plane.
This uncertainty profile supports the value of selective referral. The model did not simply refer cases at random;
rather, referrals were concentrated in categories where visual overlap and classification ambiguity are expected.
Such analysis is important because it helps identify where additional training data, expert review, or class-specific
refinement may be most useful. It also prevents overgeneralization by showing that reliability is not uniform
across all tumor categories.

title: SYNAPSE-X: a calibration-aware vision transformer framework for selective referral in multi-class brain tumor MRI classification
authors: Sadaf Tabatabaee; Mohammad T. Khasawneh
text:
External direct-transfer testing
External direct-transfer testing was performed on an independent external brain MRI cohort of 3,264 images. The
trained SYNAPSE-X Vision Transformer was applied to this cohort without retraining, fine-tuning, architecture
modification, external recalibration, threshold re-selection, or model re-estimation. The same deterministic pre­
processing pipeline, calibrated model, and primary referral threshold were used to reduce the risk of optimistic
external performance estimates.
As shown in Table 5, SYNAPSE-X achieved 97.86% external accuracy, 97.7% macro-F1, and 97.9% weighted-
F1 under direct transfer. These results indicate that the model maintained strong classification performance when
applied to an independent external cohort without additional model adaptation. The external expected calibra­
tion error was 0.026, suggesting that probability calibration remained acceptable under dataset transfer. At the
same referral threshold of 0.85, the external referral rate was 8.4%, and retained-case accuracy remained high at
98.74%, indicating that the selective-referral strategy continued to identify a high-confidence subset with stron­
ger reliability than the overall external cohort Fig. 10.
The external results show a modest reduction compared with internal held-out performance, which is expected
under dataset shift. Importantly, the external cohort was not used for training, calibration fitting, threshold selec­
tion, or model tuning. Therefore, the findings provide a conservative estimate of external direct-transfer behavior.
The results support the stability of SYNAPSE-X across datasets, while still requiring cautious interpretation
because public external testing does not replace prospective, patient-level, multi-institutional clinical validation.
Overall, the external direct-transfer analysis strengthens the reliability-centered contribution of SYNAPSE-X.
The framework maintained high external classification performance, acceptable calibration, and strong retained-
case accuracy without adapting to the external cohort. This supports the use of calibration-aware selective referral
as a more informative evaluation strategy than accuracy-only reporting.

assigns excessive confidence to incorrect predictions. For this reason, calibration and selective-referral analyses
were treated as central components of the evaluation rather than secondary additions.
The calibration results support this reliability-centered interpretation. Before temperature scaling, the model
achieved high classification performance but showed moderate calibration error. After post hoc temperature scal­
ing, expected calibration error decreased from 0.041 to 0.018, Brier score decreased from 0.036 to 0.021, and
negative log-likelihood decreased from 0.092 to 0.061, while accuracy remained unchanged. This finding is
important because it shows that classification discrimination and probability calibration are distinct properties.
The model did not become more accurate after calibration; instead, its confidence estimates became more consis­
tent with observed correctness. This directly addresses the need to evaluate whether reported confidence values
are meaningful, rather than assuming that high accuracy implies trustworthy probabilities.
Confidence-stratified accuracy further demonstrated that calibrated confidence was informative. Higher-con­
fidence predictions were more accurate than lower-confidence predictions, supporting the use of confidence as
an operational reliability signal. This finding justifies the selective-referral component of SYNAPSE-X. If con­
fidence values did not correspond to correctness, threshold-based referral would provide little practical value.
Instead, the observed pattern showed that lower-confidence predictions contained a larger share of uncertain or
incorrect cases, making them appropriate candidates for expert review.

The selective-referral analysis represents the main methodological distinction of SYNAPSE-X. At the primary
confidence threshold of 0.85, the framework retained 93.3% of internal test cases and referred 6.7% for expert
review. Among retained predictions, accuracy increased to 99.12%, and retained-case risk decreased to 0.88%.
Threshold sensitivity analysis across 0.70 to 0.95 further showed the expected risk-coverage trade-off: as the con­
fidence threshold became more conservative, retained-case risk decreased while the referral rate increased. This
allows the model to be evaluated across possible operating points instead of relying on a single fixed accuracy
value. In this way, SYNAPSE-X converts brain tumor MRI classification from a conventional single-output clas­
sification task into a reliability-aware selective-referral framework.
The uncertainty and error-profile analysis also supports the practical relevance of selective referral. Referred
and misclassified cases were concentrated primarily in tumor categories with visually overlapping features, par­
ticularly glioma-meningioma and meningioma-pituitary patterns. This suggests that uncertainty was not randomly
distributed across the dataset, but was more common in categories where image-level ambiguity is clinically
plausible. Such information is useful for future dataset curation, targeted model improvement, and prospective
expert review. It also prevents overgeneralization by showing that model reliability is not necessarily uniform
across all tumor categories.
External direct-transfer testing provided additional evidence of public cross-dataset stability. When applied to
an independent external brain MRI cohort of 3,264 images without retraining, fine-tuning, architecture modifica­
tion, external recalibration, threshold re-selection, or model re-estimation, SYNAPSE-X achieved 97.86% accu­

remained high at 98.74%, with an external referral rate of 8.4%. The modest decrease in external performance

Despite these encouraging findings, the results should be interpreted cautiously. Both the primary and external
cohorts are public image-level datasets with incomplete patient-level identifiers, scanner metadata, institutional
source information, and acquisition parameters. Therefore, patient-level independence could not be verified, and
the findings should not be interpreted as definitive clinical validation. The results provide evidence of image-
level classification and public cross-dataset reliability, but they do not establish prospective multi-institutional
generalization or clinical deployment readiness. This distinction is important because medical AI systems require
additional validation under real clinical conditions, including patient-level splits, scanner- and institution-level
diversity, prospective testing, and radiologist-in-the-loop assessment.
Overall, the revised results support the central objective of SYNAPSE-X: to move beyond accuracy-only brain
tumor MRI classification by evaluating calibrated confidence, uncertainty-aware referral, and external direct-
transfer behavior. The framework identifies high-confidence predictions that can be retained for decision-support
reporting and low-confidence predictions that should be referred for expert review. This provides a more opera­
tionally meaningful evaluation than aggregate accuracy alone and directly addresses reviewer concerns regarding
calibration, external testing, leakage risk, dataset transparency, and clinical overclaiming.

framework using patient-level multi-institutional datasets, scanner-diverse cohorts, prospective clinical evalua­

title: CMDA-Net: Auditable SHAP-based brain-tumor MRI classification, with a cross-modal dynamic-attention design for modality-robust segmentation
authors: Mingchen Xie; Xueyan Li; Xia Liu; Xiaodong Chen; Peng Lun
venue: Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences
text:
Abstract
Reliable computer-aided analysis of brain-tumor MRI must be accurate, robust to the imaging conditions encountered in
practice, and interpretable in a form that can be documented and reviewed. We present CMDA-Net, a framework built around
two contributions. The first, which we validate experimentally, is an auditable classification pipeline: a 2D residual–CBAM
classifier (CMDA-Cls) coupled with a SHAP-based interpretation layer that goes beyond heatmaps to emit a centre-versus-
periphery separability metric and an attribution-weighted confusion matrix, archived in a versionable multi-sheet report to
support post-hoc auditing. On the four-class Brain Tumor MRI benchmark, CMDA-Cls attains 99.47% accuracy and 99.44%
macro-F1 on the full held-out test set (N=1311), with 97.09%±0.55% accuracy under stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and
the centre-to-periphery attribution ratio exceeds one for every class (from 1.17 on pituitary to 2.94 on meningioma), excluding
peripheral-shortcut behaviour. The second contribution is architectural: a 3D multi-modal segmentation network (CMDA-Seg)
that couples Cross-Modal Attention Fusion (CMAF), a survival-constrained Modality-Dropout (MoDrop) regularizer and a
FiLM-conditioned decoder to fuse MRI modalities adaptively and to degrade gracefully when modalities are missing. Because
a multi-parametric segmentation cohort was not available for this study, CMDA-Seg is presented as a design contribution
whose four-modality evaluation is left to future work.
Keywords Brain tumor MRI classification · SHAP interpretability · Auditable explainable AI · Shortcut-learning diagnostics ·
Cross-modal attention fusion · Modality-dropout regularization · CBAM attention

authors: Mingchen Xie; Xueyan Li; Xia Liu; Xiaodong Chen; Peng Lun

section_heading: Brain tumor segmentation on multi-parametric MRI
text:
Brain tumor segmentation on multi-parametric MRI
Early brain tumor segmentation pipelines relied on hand-
crafted intensity and texture descriptors fed into atlas-based
registration or classical discriminative classifiers, and were
typically tuned on a single MRI modality at a time. The
advent of fully convolutional networks shifted the field
to end-to-end learnable encoders and decoders, with the
U-shaped encoder-decoder topology Azad et al. (2024)
rapidly becoming the de facto backbone thanks to its
skip connections, which preserve high-frequency anatomical
detail across resolution scales. Subsequent work extended
this template along three complementary axes. The first
axis pursued increasingly aggressive volumetric process-
ing, replacing slice-wise 2D operators with 3D convolutions
in order to exploit the through-plane continuity of tumor
sub-regions Hatamizadeh et al. (2022b); this line of work
established that voxel-level inference benefits substantially
from full 3D context but inherits a steep memory cost Ma
et al. (2024a); Xing et al. (2024). The second axis pursued
self-configuring pipelines that automatically adapt prepro-
cessing, patch size, batch composition and post-processing
to the dataset at hand, and that quickly emerged as strong
reference baselines on community benchmarks Isensee et al.
(2024); Ferreira et al. (2024). The third axis introduced
Transformer blocks into the encoder, the bottleneck or the
decoder Hatamizadeh et al. (2022,b); Lin et al. (2023);
Ma et al. (2024b), motivated by the observation that purely
convolutional receptive fields struggle to capture the long-
range relationships needed to separate diffusely infiltrative
gliomas from focal lesions. A recurring assumption across
these methods is that all expected MRI modalities are
available at both training and inference time, an assump-
tion that is routinely violated in real clinical workflows
where one or more sequences may be missing, artefacted
or non-coregistrable Zhang et al. (2022); Liu et al. (2023);
Shi et al. (2024). Our CMDA-Seg branch builds on the
volumetric U-shaped tradition but explicitly relaxes this
assumption through a Modality-Specific Stem, a Modality-
Dropout regularizer and a content-adaptive Cross-Modal
Attention Fusion module that downweights uninformative
streams on a per-sample basis, rather than concatenating all
modalities up-front.
An orthogonal and increasingly popular way to cope

An orthogonal and increasingly popular way to cope
with absent sequences is explicit modality synthesis: rather
than making the task network robust, a generative model
first hallucinates the missing sequence(s) so that a down-
stream segmentation or classification pipeline can be run
on a nominally complete four-modality input. Conditional-
GAN and representation-disentangling synthesizers Authors
(2021), latent-diffusion imputation models Authors (2024),
and unified synthesis-segmentation frameworks that jointly
reconstruct and delineate within one network Authors (2025)
have been shown to recover a large part of the full-modality
accuracy from partial inputs, and thus constitute a direct alter-
native to the Modality-Dropout strategy proposed here. We
regard the two families as complementary. Synthesis restores
the missing signal and can feed any off-the-shelf downstream
model, but it requires an additional generative network (typ-
ically tens of millions of parameters), a separate or joint
reconstruction objective, and a correspondingly higher infer-
ence cost, and it may propagate synthesis hallucinations into
the diagnostic decision. MoDrop instead makes the fusion
mechanism itself degrade gracefully at negligible extra cost
and with no generator to train or store, at the price of not
reconstructing the absent modality for human inspection. A
like-for-like efficiency comparison against these synthesis
pipelines is part of the multi-modal validation left to future
work (Section 4).

authors: Mingchen Xie; Xueyan Li; Xia Liu; Xiaodong Chen; Peng Lun

text:
Brain tumor classification from MRI
Parallel to the segmentation literature, a separate body of
work has targeted slice-level diagnostic categorization, most
commonly on a curated four-class corpus consisting of
glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumors and tumor-free con-
trols Tummala et al. (2022); Reddy et al. (2024). The domi-
nant recipe in this strand of research transfers an ImageNet-
pretrained 2D backbone—residual, dense or efficient Aamir
et al. (2022); Pacal et al. (2024); Mehmood and Bajwa
(2024)—to brain MRI slices, fine-tunes it under standard
cross-entropy with rotation and flip augmentation Saurav
et al. (2023); Asiri et al. (2023), and reports macro-averaged
accuracy. Refinements have included custom-designed shal-
low networks tailored to the relatively limited dataset
size Nazir et al. (2024); Aamir et al. (2022), ensembles of
complementary backbones Tummala et al. (2022); Reddy
et al. (2024), and hybrid pipelines that prepend a region-of-
interest crop or a coarse mask to the classifier. While these
efforts have steadily pushed reported accuracies upward,
they suffer from two limitations that our work addresses
directly. First, the classification head is almost always devel-
oped in isolation from any segmentation branch, so that
the underlying anatomical priors learned for delineation are
not reused for diagnosis, and the two tasks end up being
optimized on disjoint architectures with disjoint training
schedules. Second, the reported metrics are typically opaque:
a high macro-F1 is taken at face value without an audit of
where the classifier actually looks, even though several pub-
lished brain MRI corpora are known to contain peripheral
artifacts—scanner watermarks, framing letters or institu-
tional banners—that a network can exploit as shortcuts Ong
Ly et al. (2024). CMDA-Cls shares its residual–CBAM build-
ing blocks with the segmentation branch, so that both net-
works are governed by the same methodological primitives,
and is paired with a structured SHAP audit that quantitatively

title: CMDA-Net: Auditable SHAP-based brain-tumor MRI classification, with a cross-modal dynamic-attention design for modality-robust segmentation
authors: Mingchen Xie; Xueyan Li; Xia Liu; Xiaodong Chen; Peng Lun
venue: Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences
text:
Cross-modal fusion and attention mechanisms
How to combine multiple MRI modalities into a single rep-
resentation has been a long-standing question Liu et al.
(2022); Azad et al. (2024). Early-fusion strategies con-
catenate all modalities along the channel axis at the input
level, leaving the network entirely responsible for discover-
ing modality-specific features, and tend to be dominated by
the modality with the highest contrast. Late-fusion strate-
gies process each modality with a dedicated branch and
merge only the final predictions, at the cost of duplicated
parameters and limited cross-talk between branches. An
intermediate family of approaches injects fusion at one or
several encoder scales, often through simple addition or
weighted average, and has empirically proven more flex-
ible than either extreme Lin et al. (2023); Huang et al.
(2023). Orthogonally, the attention literature has equipped
convolutional features with the ability to recalibrate them-
selves both channel-wise and spatially: squeeze-and-excite
blocks introduced channel reweighting Pacal et al. (2024),
convolutional block attention modules extended this idea to
a sequential channel-then-spatial refinement Rasheed et al.
(2024), and self-attention—first popularized in language
modelling—enabled global token interaction at the cost of
quadratic complexity. Within the medical imaging commu-
nity, these primitives have been progressively combined:
CBAM modules placed after each residual stage, Trans-
former encoders inserted at the bottleneck of U-shaped
backbones Hatamizadeh et al. (2022b,?), and softmax-gated
fusion of parallel modality streams Huang et al. (2023); Shi
et al. (2024). Our Cross-Modal Attention Fusion module sits
in this intermediate-fusion family but differs in two practi-
cal respects. It computes modality importances from a global
descriptor rather than from spatially indexed tokens, which
keeps the fusion cost negligible compared to the encoder;
and it is paired at training time with Modality-Dropout, so
that the gating is forced to remain useful even when one or
more streams are entirely zero-masked, a property that con-
ventional attention-based fusion does not guarantee.

section_heading: Post-hoc explainability of medical image classifiers
text:
Post-hoc explainability of medical image classifiers
The fourth and most recent thread relevant to our work
is the post-hoc explanation of deep medical image clas-
sifiers. Vanilla saliency maps, guided backpropagation,
class-activation mappings and their gradient-weighted exten-
sions Nazir et al. (2024); Chaddad et al. (2023) provide
visually intuitive heatmaps but offer no additivity guarantee:
the per-pixel scores cannot be summed to recover the model’s
output, and their magnitudes are not directly comparable
across inputs or classes. Shapley-value-based attribution
methods Patrício et al. (2023) address this gap by satisfying
local accuracy, missingness and consistency simultaneously,
at the cost of an exponential combinatorial complexity that
has motivated a family of approximations—kernel-based,
deep-network-aware and gradient-based Muhammad and
Bendechache (2024); Patrício et al. (2023). Among these,
gradient-style approximations are particularly attractive for
high-resolution medical inputs because their cost scales lin-
early in the number of background references rather than
exponentially in the number of features. Despite this method-
ological progress, two recurrent shortcomings limit the clini-
cal utility of existing explainability work Velden et al. (2022);
Muhammad and Bendechache (2024). First, explanations are
typically produced for a handful of cherry-picked images and
displayed as standalone figures, with no archival counterpart
that a regulator or an auditor could inspect. Second, when
the classifier exploits non-anatomical shortcuts—peripheral
watermarks, framing artefacts or field-of-view borders Ong
Ly et al. (2024)—a single qualitative heatmap is rarely suffi-
cient to diagnose the failure mode, and quantitative shortcut
diagnostics remain under-developed. Our SHAP-based inter-
pretability framework is designed explicitly with these two
shortcomings in mind: every visual claim is backed by a
tabular counterpart in a multi-sheet auditable Excel report,
and a dedicated centre-versus-periphery separability met-
ric, complemented by an attribution-weighted confusion
matrix, turns the qualitative inspection of heatmaps into a
quantitative trustworthiness assessment that can be archived
alongside the trained model.

bution that we build on, a more recent strand of medical-
imaging XAI moves from purely gradient-driven pixel

Despite the rapid progress of medical-imaging deep learn-

only partially and rarely in a unified fashion. Volumetric seg-
mentation networks based on the U-shaped encoder–decoder
templateHatamizadehetal.(2022);Isenseeetal.(2024);Roy

unprecedented levels, but typically assume that all expected
MRI modalities are simultaneously available at both training
and inference time, and rely on early-concatenation fusion
strategies that are dominated by the highest-contrast chan-

Overall model architecture
To address the heterogeneous appearance of gliomas, menin-
giomas and metastases across multi-parametric MRI, we
propose a unified deep learning framework, named CMDA-
Net, which couples a 3D multi-modal segmentation network
(CMDA-Seg) with a complementary 2D four-class clas-
sification network (CMDA-Cls). The two networks share
a common methodological backbone built from residual
convolutions and CBAM-style channel–spatial attention,
but operate at different spatial dimensionalities and serve
complementary clinical purposes: voxel-level delineation of
tumor sub-regions on the one hand, and slice-level diagnos-
tic categorization on the other. The complete architecture is
illustrated in Fig. 1.
The 3D segmentation branch, CMDA-Seg, takes as input
a stack of four co-registered MRI modalities (T1, T1ce, T2
and FLAIR) and produces a dense four-class label map cov-
ering background, peritumoral edema, non-enhancing tumor
core and enhancing tumor. To explicitly preserve modality-
specific low-level texture before any cross-modal interaction
occurs, the input volume is first passed through a Modality-
Specific Stem (MSS): each modality is processed by an
independent shallow 3D stem composed of a 3 × 3 × 3
convolution, instance normalization, leaky activation and
a residual block. To improve robustness against missing
or corrupted modalities at inference, a Modality Dropout
(MoDrop) regularizer is applied during training only, ran-
domly zero-masking entire modality channels at the input
level while guaranteeing that at least one modality is always
retained.

residual block and a CBAM3D attention module that sequen-

At every encoder scale, the per-modality feature maps are
merged by a Cross-Modal Attention Fusion (CMAF) mod-

descriptor obtained from per-modality global average pool-

authors: Mingchen Xie; Xueyan Li; Xia Liu; Xiaodong Chen; Peng Lun
venue: Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences
text:
Experimental results
This section reports the experimental verification of the
proposed CMDA-Net framework on a publicly available
2D brain tumor MRI benchmark. Because the voxel-level
segmentation branch (CMDA-Seg) and the slice-level clas-
sification branch (CMDA-Cls) operate on different data
dimensionalities, we focus the present section on a com-
prehensive empirical study of CMDA-Cls, which is the
component that directly interfaces with the SHAP-based
interpretability framework introduced in Section 2.4. The
experimental study is organized around four progressively
detailed views. We first document the dataset statistics and
the preprocessing pipeline that condition every downstream
measurement (Sections 3.1–3.2). We then present a class-
balanced SHAP audit of the trained classifier, in which the
spatial pattern of the network’s reliance on different image
regions is quantified at three increasingly fine-grained lev-
els: a global per-class importance heatmap (Section 3.4), a
centre-versus-periphery spatial decomposition (Section 3.5),
and an attribution-weighted confusion analysis backed by a
complete per-image audit trail (Section 3.6). Throughout the
section, every reported number is also archived in a struc-
tured Excel report so that all figures can be cross-checked
against tabular evidence.

All experiments are conducted on the public Brain Tumor
MRI Dataset assembled by Nickparvar on Kaggle, which
aggregates and harmonizes images from three widely used
sources (figshare, SARTAJ and Br35H) into a single four-
class corpus covering glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor
and no-tumor. The dataset is supplied with a fixed train/test
split that we use without modification in order to remain
directly comparable to prior work. The total corpus contains

The class distribution is approximately balanced, with the
no-tumor class being the largest (about 28.5% of the cor-

between 23.1% and 25.0% of the samples. The test-to-train
ratio fluctuates only mildly across classes, from 0.206 (pitu-

a size-preserving downscale of the training partition. This
mild imbalance is well within the regime where standard
cross-entropy training with label-smoothing remains effec-
tive without resorting to oversampling or class-weighted
losses, which we therefore deliberately omit from our default
configuration.
A representative slice from the training and test partitions
of each of the four classes is shown in Fig. 3. The grid
visually confirms that the dataset spans a wide variety of
acquisition planes (axial, coronal), field strengths and con-
trast settings (T1-weighted post-gadolinium, T2-weighted,
FLAIR), as well as a non-trivial amount of inter-source het-
erogeneity. In particular, several no-tumor slices originate
from a re-distributed Br35H subset that retains an explicit
Medscape watermark along the upper border, a cue that
we will explicitly diagnose in the interpretability analy-
sis of Section 3.5. Glioma and meningioma cases display
strongly variable lesion location, size and enhancement pat-
tern, while pituitary cases predominantly use a coronal plane
that exposes the sellar region near the centre of the field of
view; this acquisition-protocol regularity will be reflected in
the spatial concentration of the SHAP attributions for the
pituitary class (Fig. 4).

Image-level statistics
A second source of heterogeneity in the dataset is purely
image-level: the native resolution and the pixel-intensity
statistics differ markedly between sources. We summarize
these statistics in Table 3, which reports for each class the
modal native resolution H×W, the corresponding raw pixel
count Npx = H · W and aspect ratio W/H, the central
moments of the raw pixel intensities (mean μI, standard
deviation σI, coefficient of variation CV = σI/μI, dynamic
range), and the empirical minima and maxima on the [0, 255]
grayscale grid. Three of the four classes (glioma, menin-
gioma, pituitary) are predominantly acquired at 512×512
resolution, whereas the no-tumor class is dominated by a sub-
stantially smaller 251×201 resolution that betrays its mixed
origin: the per-image pixel count drops from 262 144 for
the three high-resolution classes to a mere 50 451 for no-
tumor, a 5.2× reduction, and the aspect ratio likewise departs
from 1 to 0.80. The pixel-intensity distributions are simi-
larly disparate: the meningioma subset has the lowest mean
intensity (μI ≈27.6) and the largest coefficient of varia-
tion (CV = 130%), the glioma subset is moderately bright
(μI ≈34.5, CV=106%), the pituitary subset is brighter still
(μI ≈58.4, CV = 81%) and the no-tumor subset exhibits
both the highest mean (μI ≈76.0) and the highest absolute
standard deviation (σI ≈67.4), although its relative spread
CV = 89% is intermediate.

these contrasts visually explicit. All four classes share a dom-

reflects the proportion of black padding and air in each sub-

with a low-intensity sub-peak that we attribute to the dural
and cerebrospinal-fluid surroundings of the sellar region, and
the no-tumor class exhibits the broadest tissue distribution,
with non-negligible mass all the way up to 150. These pixel-

Preprocessing and augmentation pipeline
The full preprocessing pipeline that turns a raw native MRI
slice into the 3×224×224 tensor consumed by CMDA-
Cls is summarized in Table 4 and visualized in Fig. 6.
For each step we report not only the operation and its
parameters but also the output tensor shape, the under-
lying torchvision class used in the implementation,
and whether the step is active during training, evalua-
tion, or both. Concretely, every slice is first bilinearly
resized to 224×224 in order to align with the receptive
field of the 2D backbone, then converted from grayscale
to a three-channel tensor by simple channel replication so
that ImageNet-pretrained statistics remain meaningful. Dur-

online—a random horizontal flip with probability 0.5 and a
random rotation drawn uniformly from [−10◦, +10◦]—and
a ±10% photometric brightness/contrast jitter is additionally
applied to mitigate inter-source intensity drift. The ten-
sor is then converted to a float32 representation in the
[0, 1] range and finally normalized using the standard Ima-
geNet mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406) and standard deviation
(0.229, 0.224, 0.225) on a per-channel basis. The augmen-
tation block is disabled at evaluation time, so that test
predictions are deterministic and the SHAP analysis of the
next subsection operates on a fully reproducible input distri-
bution.

meningioma→no-tumor case. The attribution-weighted con-

that does contain errors, but on a saturated model such as ours

Per-image stability
Table 13 reports, per class, the mean per-image attribu-

Unliketheearlier draft—whichclaimedanear-constant mag-
nitude with coefficient of variation below 6%—the real audit
shows a moderate per-sample spread (CV between 24.8%
for no-tumor and 51.7% for meningioma), reflecting genuine
slice-to-slice variability in how much evidence the network
commits. The class-level means are nonetheless well sepa-
rated and their ordering is stable, which is what the spatial
(centre–periphery) analysis relies on; we accordingly inter-
pret the audit-subset statistics as class-characteristic rather
than as sample-invariant.

Audit-report storage and scalability
Regarding the practicality of archiving one report per subject,
a complete per-subject numeric audit record (the multi-sheet
workbook containing the summary, region, boundary, confu-
sion and per-image sheets) occupies approximately 11.3KB
when written as .xlsx, and less when stored in a columnar
binary format. For the full 1311-image test set the tabu-
lar audit trail is therefore on the order of 10–15MB; only
the optional high-resolution overlay PNGs are large, and in
deployment these are regenerated on demand from the stored
attributions rather than archived. The audit layer thus intro-
duces no meaningful storage bottleneck at scale.

Conclusion
In this work, we have presented CMDA-Net, a framework
that pairs a 2D four-class brain-tumor classification net-
work (CMDA-Cls) with a structured SHAP-based inter-
pretability layer, and that additionally contributes a 3D
multi-modal segmentation architecture (CMDA-Seg)—with
content-adaptiveCross-ModalAttentionFusionandsurvival-
constrained Modality-Dropout—as a design whose four-
modality validation is left to future work. On the Brain Tumor
MRI corpus, the classification branch attains 99.47% accu-
racy and 99.44% macro-F1 on the full held-out test set,
with 97.09%±0.55% accuracy under stratified 5-fold cross-
validation (statistically indistinguishable from a no-attention
baseline, p = 0.23), while the post-hoc attribution anal-

attention for all four classes. Quantitatively, the centre-to-

class (from 1.17 on pituitary to 2.94 on meningioma), which
excludes peripheral-shortcut behaviour; we note that this
spatial-concentration signal, rather than the global sign frac-
tion ρ+ (which is close to 0.5 for all classes in the real attri-
butions), is the diagnostically meaningful quantity. Beyond
these numerical results, the contribution of our work is

design for modality-robust segmentation, and we validate
the classification instantiation (CMDA-Cls) of this shared
backbone experimentally; clinically, every visual claim pro-
duced by the framework is backed by an auditable tab-
