covering summary, per_image, region_importance, confu-
sion_attribution and config—thereby turning interpretability
from a one-off illustration into a versionable, audit-oriented
artifact intended to facilitate the documentation and audit-
ing that regulatory frameworks increasingly call for (though
not, by itself, to establish regulatory compliance); and
methodologically transferable, the centre-versus-periphery
separability diagnostic and the attribution-weighted confu-
sion matrix introduced here form a reusable template for the
trustworthiness assessment of related medical-imaging clas-
sifiers. Several limitations delimit these findings. First, the
quantitative validation concerns the 2D classification branch
(CMDA-Cls) and its interpretability layer on a single, single-
sequence public corpus; the multi-modal machinery (CMAF,
MoDrop, the FiLM-conditioned CMDA-Seg) is presented
as a design contribution and its four-modality experiments
(missing-modality robustness, fusion and loss-weight abla-
tions) should be regarded as pending full validation on a
multi-parametric cohort such as BraTS. Second, the SHAP
audit is computed on a small class-balanced subset; although
class-level means are stable, the per-sample coefficient of
variation is moderate (25–52%) and the absolute attribu-
tion magnitudes are explainer- and background-dependent,
so they should be read as relative, within-model diagnostics.
Third, because the model is highly accurate the balanced
audit subset is error-free, so the attribution-weighted confu-
sion matrix reduces to its diagonal there and error analysis
relies on the full-test confusion. Fourth, our interpretability
artefacts are designed to support auditing, but their clini-
cal value has not been established through a reader study,
so “auditable” should be read in a methodological rather
than regulatory sense. Finally, the centre–periphery metric
assumes an approximately centred field of view; strongly off-
centre acquisitions would require an anatomy-aware region
definition.

on a multi-parametric cohort such as BraTS, compris-

that both removes and replaces each block (CBAM→SE,

framework to larger and more diverse multi-institutional
cohorts and lifting the SHAP audit to a fully volumet-

branch; incorporating additional imaging modalities such
as diffusion-weighted and perfusion MRI, together with
non-imaging data including radiomic descriptors and clin-

mechanism; coupling the attribution maps with calibrated,
uncertainty-aware confidence estimates so that clinicians are

real-world impact on radiologists’ diagnostic workflow and

title: Explainable Hybrid Deep Learning Framework Integrating MobileNetV2, EfficientNetV2B0, and KNN for MRI-Based Brain Tumor Classification
authors: Mohammed Jajere Adamu; Li Qiang; Charles Okanda Nyatega; Muhammad Fahad; Ayesha Younis; Adamu Halilu Jabire; Rabiu Sale Zakariyya; Halima Bello Kawuwa
text:
Abstract
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is central to noninvasive brain tumor assessment, yet clinical uptake of artificial intel­
ligence depends on both accuracy and transparency. This study presents a lightweight and interpretable hybrid framework
that fuses features from two efficient convolutional backbones, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetV2B0, using late fusion with
global average pooling and vector concatenation. Classification is performed with a K‐Nearest Neighbors (KNN) head
configured with k = 5, Euclidean distance, and distance‐based weighting. The dataset contains 7,023 MRI images drawn
from Figshare, SARTAJ, and BR35H. Data were split with a 20% held‐out test set and a validation set equal to 20% of
the remaining training pool, yielding 64%/16%/20% train/val/test. Four diagnostic categories were evaluated: Glioma,
Meningioma, Pituitary, and Notumor. The confusion matrix shows a compact diagonal, and class‐wise precision, recall,
and F1 are consistently high on the test set. A 5‐fold cross‐validation with normality assessment and paired significance
testing supports robustness across folds. On the held‐out test set, class‐wise ROC–AUC was 1.00 for all four classes, and
overall accuracy was 99.69%. Results should be interpreted in light of the unified dataset; external validation is warranted.
Clinical interpretability is supported by class‐wise Grad‐CAM overlays and SHAP analyses, including waterfall plots that
quantify individual feature contributions. These findings indicate that a dual‐backbone late‐fusion design coupled with a
simple nonparametric classifier delivers strong, balanced performance while providing anatomically plausible case‐level
insight into model decisions.

Automated MRI classification has therefore become

is difficult because tumor phenotypes vary widely in size,

because imaging artifacts and site differences add distri­

and neurological conditions and similarly motivates robust

well suited to MRI because they learn hierarchical features
that capture both local textures and higher‐level semantic

angiogenesis, mass effect, and infiltrative growth produce
spatial–textural signatures that deep networks can exploit
(Singh 2023).
Among efficient CNN families, MobileNetV2 and Effi­
cientNetV2B0 offer complementary strengths: depthwise
separable convolutions and inverted residuals for light­
weight feature extraction in MobileNetV2, and compound
scaling with modern MBConv blocks and Swish activation
in EfficientNetV2B0. Leveraging both can improve repre­
sentational diversity without incurring the cost of very deep
models. For the final decision layer, non‐parametric K‐Near­
est Neighbors (KNN) is attractive because it makes mini­
mal distributional assumptions and performs excellently on
fused feature spaces with nonlinear class boundaries.

hybrid framework that:

●

Literature Review
Deep learning for MRI brain tumor classification has pro­
gressed along three main lines: (i) classical feature–engi­
neering with machine‐learning classifiers, (ii) end‐to‐end
CNN models including transformers, and (iii) fusion strate­
gies that combine complementary information.
Early pipelines extracted hand‐crafted texture or fre­
quency features and used classical classifiers. Examples
include fuzzy optimization for network design (Narmatha
2020), hypercolumn or multi‐layer feature aggregation in
BrainMRNet (Toğaçar et al. 2020), deep feature selection
and texture fusion (Sharif 2020), and multi‐sequence fusion
with wavelet representations (Amin et al. 2020). Hybrid
classifiers and ensembles, CNN‐SVM thresholding (Khai­
randish 2022), majority‐voting ensembles with KNN, RF,
and DT (Garg 2021), and multi‐modal DNN with multiclass
SVM (Maqsood et al. 2022), reported solid accuracy but
required careful feature curation and tended to be less scal­
able across datasets.
With the rise of transfer learning, single‐backbone CNNs
achieved strong performance on tumor classification, seg­
mentation, or detection tasks. Prior work spans differential
CNN variants (Kader et al. 2021; (Singh et al. 2025), U‐NET
with fuzzy logic (Maqsood 2021; Yadav et al. 2025; Yadav
2025), transfer learning from VGG-ResNet family models
(Singh 2023; Yadav et al. 2025; Yadav 2025; Mavaddati
2024; Ghosal 2019; Abbood et al. 2021; Siar 2019), and
hybrid deep learning tailored to three class tumor problems
(Raza et al. 2022). Deep feature fusion methods further
improved robustness by combining multiple learned repre­
sentations (Mavaddati 2024), while GAN pre‐training has
been explored to regularize feature learning on MR images
(Ghassemi et al. 2020). These CNN approaches generally
deliver high accuracy but may involve heavier fully con­
nected heads or extensive fine‐tuning, which can increase
complexity and overfitting risk on modest datasets.
Vision Transformer (ViT) variants have shown competi­

regularization. Ensemble strategies for grade classification
also illustrate gains from combining diverse learners (Bv et

Preprocessing and Data Augmentation
This is an essential procedure that adjusts the dataset to
suit the model during training better and enhances its gen­
eralization capability. This study applied several data aug­
mentation techniques to introduce variability and improve
the model’s robustness. All images got resized to 224 × 224
pixels to match the input dimensions of the deep learning
models, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetV2B0. The follow­
ing augmentation techniques were applied:
(i) Random Rotation: Images were randomly rotated
within a range of ± 10 degrees to simulate positional
variations and improve the model’s robustness to orien­
tation changes.
(ii) Random Scaling: Images were randomly scaled within
90% to 110% of their original size to ensure robustness
to scale changes.
(iii)
Horizontal Flipping: Images were horizontally
flipped with a probability of 50% to introduce spatial
diversity and account for symmetry in brain structures.
(iv) Random Brightness and Contrast Adjustments: The
brightness of images was randomly adjusted by a factor
of ± 20%, and a factor of ± 15% adjusted the contrast to
account for variations in imaging conditions.
(v) Random Translation: Images were randomly translated
by up to 10% of their width and height to simulate
minor shifts in the field of view.
(vi)
Random Zoom: Images were randomly zoomed in
or out by up to 10% to simulate variations in the dis­
tance between the MRI scanner and the subject.

Complementary post hoc explanation methods are employed
to analyze model behavior at both class and case levels.
i.
Grad‐CAM: Grad‐CAM heatmaps were computed
from the last convolutional block for each target class

ii. SHAP: DeepSHAP was used on the auxiliary softmax

Model Architecture
Our model extracts complementary features using two
ImageNet pretrained backbones, MobileNetV2 and Effi­
cientNetV2B0, followed by late fusion and non‐parametric
classification. Figure 2 shows the complete architecture.
For each input image, both backbones process the image
in parallel to produce convolutional feature maps. Global
average pooling (GAP) is applied to each backbone’s final
convolutional output to obtain compact feature vectors.
These vectors are concatenated into a fused representation
and regularized with dropout (rate 0.5). The fused feature
vector is classified using K‐Nearest Neighbors (KNN; k = 5,
Euclidean distance, distance weighting). Because KNN is
non‐differentiable, a small auxiliary softmax head is trained
on the fused features solely to compute Grad‐CAM and
SHAP explanations; all reported performance metrics are
derived from the KNN classifier.
Feature Fusion and Classifier
Feature fusion is performed after global average pooling
(late fusion). Specifically, the two pooled vectors, one from
MobileNetV2 and one from EfficientNetV2B0 are concate­
nated without additional weighting to preserve contributions
from both backbones. A dropout layer (rate 0.5) is applied
during auxiliary‐head training for regularization. The result­
ing fused feature vector is passed to a KNN classifier con­
figured with k = 5, Euclidean distance, and distance‐based
weighting. The fusion schematic is shown in Fig. 3.

Model Efficiency Analysis
To evaluate the practicality of the proposed model for real-
world clinical deployment, we measured its computational
efficiency in terms of inference time, memory usage, and
model size. The inference time was calculated as the aver­
age time to classify a single MR image. Memory usage was
measured as the peak RAM consumption during inference,
and the total number of parameters determined the model
size. All experiments were conducted on a system with an
NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, 32 GB RAM, and Python 3.8
with TensorFlow 2.6. The results were compared with other
state-of-the-art models to assess the efficiency of the pro­
posed approach.

Representative misclassifications from the test set are shown

Why Fusion and KNN Worked Well
Late fusion after global average pooling retained comple­
mentary information learned by two diverse but efficient
backbones, producing a compact fused representation. Clas­
sifying this representation with KNN (k = 5, Euclidean, dis­

ease of calibration and ablation when probing what the
features capture. In practice, this design yielded balanced

Limitations and Future Directions
Though our current study demonstrates excellent per­
formance on the unified dataset, the combined Figshare,
SARTAJ, and Br35H dataset is known to be relatively easy
and has produced near-ceiling metrics in prior studies. For
reliable clinical translation, prospective multi-center vali­
dation on diverse cohorts such as BraTS, TCIA, and multi-
site hospital data is essential. Future work will include: (i)
External validation on independent datasets from different
institutions and scanner manufacturers to assess generaliz­
ability and explanation stability across acquisition settings;
(ii) Integration of clinical metadata (age, sex, presentation
symptoms) to enable multi-modal prediction; (iii) Extension
to 3D volumetric analysis to capture spatial relationships
more comprehensively; (iv) Investigation of the relation­
ship between SHAP-derived feature importance and known
molecular markers such as IDH mutation status and 1p/19q
co-deletion to bridge radiological and molecular character­
ization. Additionally, clinician ratings of explanation plausi­
bility will be collected to ensure clinical usefulness.

Conclusion
Detecting a tumor might be extremely difficult due to the
sophisticated nature of the brain. The brain ultimately con­
trols all physiological activities in the body. Machine and
Deep learning technologies can automatically categorize
brain cancers in their early stages. Nevertheless, there is a
growing prevalence of brain tumors worldwide, resulting
in shorter lifespans and the possibility of death. Inaccurate
identification often leads to superfluous medical interven­
tions, reducing opportunities for those affected. Hence,
medical assessments are crucial for enhancing the progno­
sis of individuals with brain tumors. The effective use of
computer-aided diagnostic tools has led to notable prog­
ress in machine and deep learning, explicitly aiding medi­
cal practitioners in establishing accurate diagnoses. This
study presented a fused hybrid framework of state-of-the-
art convolutional neural network (CNN) models designed
to increase feature extraction and better classification
performance.
The proposed technique uses a lightweight, interpre­
table hybrid framework for MRI-based brain tumor clas­
sification that fuses features from MobileNetV2 and
EfficientNetV2B0 via late fusion (global average pooling
and concatenation) and performs final classification with a
KNN head. Using a stratified split (64% train, 16% valida­
tion, 20% test) across four classes (Glioma, Meningioma,

These observations point to practical avenues for

provide complementary cues for challenging sellar and dural
cases. Radiologist‐guided hard‐negative mining, curating

uch as controlled variations in edge sharpness, local
texture, and contrast may help disambiguate look‐alike pre­
sentations. Incorporating additional MRI sequences when
available, such as T1, post‐contrast T1, T2, FLAIR should
provide complementary cues for challenging sellar and dural
cases. Radiologist‐guided hard‐negative mining, curating
confounders that commonly trigger spurious saliency can
steer the model away from misleading patterns. Additional
safeguards include harmonized intensity normalization
to reduce site effects, region‐of‐interest cropping to focus
attention, and uncertainty estimation to flag borderline cases
for human adjudication.
The interpretability artifacts are directly actionable in a
clinical viewer: alongside the predicted class, a Grad‐CAM
overlay and a SHAP‐based, case‐level rationale can support
rapid verification of anatomical plausibility and focused
review of difficult cases. Although the auxiliary head used
for explanations is not identical to the KNN decision rule,
the observed concordance between Grad‐CAM and SHAP
across correct and incorrect cases suggests that the expla­
nations reflect the underlying fused features. Together, the
interpretability results and error patterns provide a coherent,
clinically meaningful picture of model behavior and clear
guidance for the next iteration of improvements.
Clinical Implications
The pipeline’s outputs can be integrated into a viewer to
display: (i) the predicted class with confidence, (ii) a Grad-
CAM overlay indicating suspected regions, and (iii) a SHAP
explanation showing feature contributions for the specific
case. The proposed hybrid model, with Grad-CAM and
SHAP visualizations, has potential clinical utility in triage,
second-opinion support, and resident training contingent
upon local institutional validation and robust clinical gover­
nance. The model’s simplicity and small footprint also make
it suitable for constrained compute environments, pending
external validation.

title: Exploring the value of peritumoral brain zone for classification of two malignant brain tumors based on the MRI interpretable models
authors: Endong Zhao; Yun-Feng Yang; Hao Zhang; Yuan-Yuan Yang; Yutong Shi; Beibei Li; Xuelin Song; Shiyun Lou; Chao Yang
text:
Abstract
Objectives This study aims to develop and validate a novel multimodal interpretable artificial intelligence model
capable of fusing radiomics features and imaging features to accurately classify primary central nervous system
lymphoma (PCNSL) and glioblastoma (GBM), and to explore the impact of including the tumor and different
peritumoral brain zones (PBZs) on the diagnostic performance of the model.
Materials and methods A retrospective cohort of 242 patients with PCNSL or GBM, along with their multi-sequence
MRI scans and clinical data, was enrolled from two medical centers. After image preprocessing, tumor and PBZ
regions were segmented as volumes of interest (VOIs), and imaging features were evaluated. Based on different
combinations of three image sequences and four VOIs, a total of seven models (T1WI-Tumor-Model, T2WI-Tumor-
Model, T1CE-Tumor-Model, T1CE-Tumor-Edema-Model, T1CE-Tumor-PBZ10mm-Model, T1CE-Tumor-PBZ20mm-Model,
and Multimodal-Radiomics-Model) were established. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, sensitivity,
specificity, calibration curves, and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) were used to assess the models’ performance
and clinical application value. Additionally, the best model was analyzed for interpretability using SHapley Additive
exPlanations (SHAP).
Results The T1CE-Tumor-Edema-Model and Multimodal-Radiomics-Model demonstrated superior predictive
performance among the seven models, with AUCs of 0.91 and 0.94 in the external validation cohort, respectively. The
SHAP interpretation of the results revealed that the Rad-Score and Clinical-Rad-Score features contributed the most to
the models’ decision-making process.
Conclusion A radiomics framework based on interpretable machine learning is proposed. Based on this framework,
models combining different ranges of peritumoral brain regions with tumors were constructed for the first time,

​Introduction
PCNSL is a rare extranodal non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
primarily affecting the brain, spinal cord, meninges,
or eyes, accounting for approximately 7% of all malig­
nant brain tumors [1]. Its incidence has been increas­
ing in recent years with approximately 0.3–0.6 cases per
100,000 people [2], while GBM is the most common
malignant brain tumor in adults [3], representing around
49% of all cases, with an incidence rate of about 3–4 cases
per 100,000 people [1]. Surgical resection of PCNSL
does not confer a survival benefit, and patients are typi­
cally treated with high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX)-
based chemotherapy [4], which is pivotal in achieving
long-term disease control [5]. Conversely, the standard
of care for GBM involves maximizing the safe resection
of the tumor, which significantly impacts patient survival
and quality of life [6, 7]. Therefore, accurate non-invasive
identification of these two conditions plays a crucial role
in guiding clinical treatment decisions and improving
prognosis.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating
brain tumors. However, MRI still has limitations in dif­
ferentiating between PCNSL and GBM, as they often
exhibit atypical characteristics [8–12]. Atypical PCNSL
presents as a tumor with interior necrosis, hemorrhage,
cystic changes, or heterogeneous contrast enhancement
[13–15]. On the other hand, atypical GBM manifests as a
solid-enhancing lesion without visible necrosis [16–19],
making it challenging to distinguish from PCNSL based
on typical imaging features alone. Several advanced MRI
techniques [15, 16, 20–22] show promise in differentiat­
ing PCNSL from GBM by utilizing quantitative param­
eters. However, further validation is needed to determine
the optimal parameters, thresholds, and their consis­
tency in identifying atypical tumors. Since not all physi­
cians and patients opt for advanced MRI techniques, it
becomes crucial to extract and quantify a large number
of features that describe tumor heterogeneity between
PCNSL and GBM. This enables accurate and robust
tumor classification using radiomics models constructed
from available conventional MRI sequences.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad conceptual frame­
work encompassing methods that simulate human cog­
nition [23]. Within this domain, machine learning (ML)
provides a data-driven approach, automatically extract­
ing patterns from data to perform tasks like classifica­

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad conceptual frame­
work encompassing methods that simulate human cog­
nition [23]. Within this domain, machine learning (ML)
provides a data-driven approach, automatically extract­
ing patterns from data to perform tasks like classifica­
tion and prediction. Furthermore, deep learning (DL),
an advanced subset of ML, utilizes multi-layered neural
networks to autonomously extract high-dimensional fea­
tures from complex data, such as medical images. Despite
their impressive performance, the increasing complex­
ity of these ML and DL models often turns them into
“black boxes.” This lack of transparency makes it difficult
to explain the clinical reasoning behind their predictions,
raising trust concerns. In response to this issue, inter­
pretable machine learning methods have emerged [24].
Interpretable machine learning aims to elucidate model
decisions, enabling users to understand how the model
arrives at specific decisions. With the increasing demand
for model transparency and interpretability, interpretable
machine learning methods will play an important role in
fields such as radiomics [24, 25]. Additionally, validating
model performance using multicenter data can compre­
hensively evaluate the model’s robustness, generalization
capability, and adaptability to different population data
distributions [26, 27].
The peritumoral edema in PCNSL and GBM is charac­
terized by different pathological attributes. GBM tends
to exhibit invasive growth, with peritumoral edema areas
featuring both vasogenic edema [28] and infiltrative
edema due to tumor cells infiltrating into the periphery
[29]. The concept of peritumoral brain zone (PBZ) was
introduced in the current study. It was defined as the
tumor’s peripheral brain area without contrast enhance­
ment on MRI images with a gadolinium contrast agent
[30]. Peritumoral edema is only the PBZ in a narrow
understanding. In contrast, the broader PBZ delineates
a region several centimeters wide around the tumor,
including the site of tumor invasion, specific molecules,
radiological information, and cellular alterations [31]. The
usefulness of detailed segmentation of the peritumoral
brain region and its impact on the performance of mod­

remains unexplored. Given the gradual reduction phe­

Materials And Methods
Patients
This retrospective study was approved by the Ethics
Committee of the participating medical centers and
adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of
Helsinki throughout the research process.
Patients with PCNSL and GBM who were treated at
two medical centers between November 2010 and June
2023 were retrospectively enrolled through the Picture
Archiving and Communication System (PACS). The
inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Complete imag­
ing data and clinical history; (2) No prior interventions
such as biopsy, surgery, or other treatments, before the
MRI examination; and (3) Histopathologically confirmed
primary PCNSL or GBM (IDH-wildtype), diagnosed
according to the 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors
of the Central Nervous System [3]. The exclusion cri­
teria were: (1) Poor image quality, significant artifacts
hindering the delineation of the region of interest; (2)
Tumors without contrast enhancement; and (3) A his­
tory of hematological or immune system diseases. A total
of 242 patients were ultimately enrolled in the study.
Specifically, 138 patients from Medical Center 1 were
assigned to the training cohort, while 104 patients from
a fully independent institution, Medical Center 2, consti­
tuted the external validation cohort. The overall cohort
included 104 cases of PCNSL (19 atypical cases) and
138 cases of GBM (26 atypical cases). The flowchart for
patient enrollment is shown in Fig. 1.

Based on previous studies [13, 17, 32–34], the follow­

the maximum diameter of the tumor was measured on

Tumor volume: the tumor VOI volume parameter was

Tumor and edema volume: the volume parameter for the
combined VOI of the tumor and edema was calculated,
as above; (4) Localization: supratentorial, infratentorial;
(5) Tumor number: single, multiple; (6) Tumor compo­
nent: defined as solid (80–100% solid component), cystic
(80–100% cystic component), or cystic and solid (oth­

(8) Enhancement characteristics: mass, nodular, patchy,

The edema index (EI) was calculated as (V edema + V
tumor)/V tumor. 1 < EI < 1.5 indicates mild edema,
1.5 ≤ EI < 3 indicates moderate edema, and EI ≥ 3 indicates

glia involvement: yes, no; (12) Corpus callosum infiltra­

A radiologist manually modified the registered VOIs to

respectively. The expanded ROI area was strictly confined
to the brain parenchyma, and the radiologists manually

Feature screening and fusion
Each feature was normalized using the Z-score normal­
ization, and the values of each radiomics feature column
were tested for normality. Redundant features were then
removed using Pearson or Spearman correlation analy­
sis. An ElasticNet regression model was trained on the
remaining features, and the Rad-Score was calculated
based on the regression coefficients. The mRMR algo­
rithm was then used to select the radiomics features with
the highest predictive value.
For clinical and MRI imaging features, univariate anal­
ysis was performed to compare PCNSL and GBM in the
training set. Variables with P < 0.05 were selected for sub­
sequent model construction.
Radiomics model construction and evaluation
The SMOTE algorithm [37] was used to balance the class
distribution within the training set. The Random Forest
algorithm, which can adapt to high-dimensional feature
data and has strong resistance to overfitting [38], was
employed as the classifier. Three stages of experiments
were designed to address the main tasks. In the first stage,
three single-sequence tumor models (T1WI-Tumor-
Model, T2WI-Tumor-Model, and T1CE-Tumor-Model)
were built to identify the optimal MRI sequences. In
the second stage, based on the optimal sequences, three
new models incorporating different PBZ ranges were
developed (T1CE-Tumor-Edema-Model, T1CE-Tumor-
PBZ10mm-Model, and T1CE-Tumor-PBZ20mm-Model)
to explore the impact of different VOIs. In the third stage,
the Multimodal-Radiomics-Model was constructed by
integrating clinical factors, imaging features, and multi-
sequence radiomics features to evaluate the added value
of multimodal data.
For the first two stages, the selected radiomics fea­
tures and Rad-Score were inputted into the RF algorithm
for model training. For the multimodal model, a new
fusion feature, the Clinical-Rad-Score, was generated
using LASSO regression to integrate radiomics features,
imaging features, and clinical factors. Finally, the mRMR
algorithm selected the top 10 most predictive features to
train the multimodal radiomics model, aiming to cap­
ture complementary information across modalities and
improve classification accuracy.

Statistics
Clinical information and macroscopic imaging features
were statistically analyzed using R version 4.3.0. Con­
tinuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard
deviation (SD) if normally distributed, or as median
(interquartile range, IQR) if non-normally distributed.
Group comparisons were performed using the indepen­
dent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continu­
ous variables, and the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact
test for categorical variables. P < 0.05 was considered sta­
tistically significant. The “sklearn.metrics” Python library
was used to calculate the AUC metrics of the model. The
“sklearn.calibration”, “sklearn.metrics,” and “matplotlib.
pyplot " libraries were used to calculate and plot calibra­
tion curves and decision curves for the model.

built on three independent predictive factors (tumor
number, enhancement characteristics, and basal ganglia

of cases where the model failed in prediction were con­
centrated in atypical tumors, indicating limitations in the
diagnostic value of MRI macroscopic features. Radiolo­
gists may struggle to accurately differentiate them based
on past experiences alone, highlighting the importance of
significantly improving diagnostic performance through
alternative means. In a previous study, Suh HB et al.
[19] constructed a model only for patients with typical
PCNSL and atypical GBM. However, its diagnostic sta­
bility and clinical applicability for typical GBM are ques­

lymphomas were included for training, the diagnostic
performance of the model decreased considerably in the
external validation set.
In the multimodal radiomics model proposed in this
study, the training set and external validation set contain­
ing typical and atypical tumors still maintained a high
AUC (0.94), demonstrating that the model has strong
generalization capability and clinical utility. In addition,
we compared the predictive efficacy of models based on
separate T1WI, T2WI, and T1CE sequences. We found
that the diagnostic effectiveness of the radiomics model
based on T1CE was always superior to that of the models

another challenge in modeling T1CE radiomics, namely

another challenge in modeling T1CE radiomics, namely
the selection of the coverage of VOIs, which determines
the inclusion range of imaging features related to tumor
pathology heterogeneity. We introduced the PBZ in a
narrow and broad sense [30, 31], where peritumoral
edema and peritumoral brain parenchyma regions both
provide potential radiological information. Therefore,
we uniformly expanded 10 and 20 mm from the enhanc­
ing tumor margins as the region of interest. An autopsy
study by Yamahara et al. [40] revealed that tumor cells
are densely present within 1 cm from the tumor margin
in GBM patients. Hochberg FH et al. [41] described that
90% of GBM recur within 2 cm of the primary site on
imaging. Specifically, the 10-mm margin was established
as an internal boundary to divide the peritumoral space
into proximal and distal zones. The proximal zone (within
10 mm) captures the region with the highest tumor cell
density, while the 20-mm margin aligns with the clinically
high-risk zone for infiltration and recurrence. Intermedi­
ate distances or dynamic margins were not considered
to uphold the principles of methodological robustness
and model parsimony. Narrow bands (e.g., 5 mm) are
highly susceptible to partial volume effects, which com­
promise feature reproducibility, whereas further subdivi­
sion (e.g., 15 mm) would unnecessarily increase feature
dimensionality. In our study, we found that the com­
bined tumor and peritumoral edema model achieved the
highest AUC (0.91), followed by the combined tumor
and PBZ 10 mm model, the combined tumor and PBZ
20 mm model, and finally the tumor model. This sug­
gests that peritumoral edema contains more biologically
heterogeneous information, and GBM and PCNSL have
different vascular properties. The microenvironment
of edema in GBM and PCNSL suggests the emergence,
aggregation, and alteration of neuroglia cells, vascular
endothelial cells, astrocytes and microglia, and tumor
cells to varying degrees. In addition, the role of some
inflammatory changes remains to be further explored

A recently published study by Yu et al. [43] evaluated
radiomics models for differentiating PCNSL and GBM.
While they appropriately recognized the diagnostic
value of both contrast-enhancing and peritumoral edema
regions, their framework evaluated individual modalities
independently. Consequently, their highest-performing
model remained constrained to a single sequence (CE-
T1WI total region), achieving an AUC of 0.917 in the
external validation set. The performance of such single-
sequence radiomics models is inherently limited because
they cannot capture comprehensive information from
the overall imaging data. In contrast, the core advan­
tage of our study lies in true multimodal integration. We
explicitly fused high-dimensional multimodal radiomics
features with clinical semantic features to construct the
Clinical-Rad-Score. This comprehensive fusion captures
a more holistic tumor profile, allowing our model to

individual-level predictions. It should be noted that the
initial extraction of 5,286 features relative to the sample
size introduces a potential risk of overfitting. Although
we mitigated this concern by implementing a rigorous
step-by-step dimensionality reduction pipeline to select
only 10 key features and validating the model on an inde­
pendent external cohort, nested cross-validation can be
employed to more effectively minimize feature selection
bias and further ensure model stability. Furthermore,
MRI images with different field strengths were included
in both the training and external validation sets, which
not only broadens the diversity of the data but also more
closely resembles real-world clinical scenarios, thereby
providing the trained model with stronger generalization
ability.
A recent comprehensive meta-analysis on AI-based
brain tumors confirmed the highly robust diagnostic
capabilities of various ML and DL algorithms [44]. How­
ever, a persistent challenge in the broader field of AI-
driven neuro-oncology is that the “black-box” nature of
many high-performing models often limits clinical trust
and translation. To address this critical trade-off between
high performance and transparency, the SHAP approach
applied in this paper is a standard interpretable machine
learning method. Based on Shapley values from game
theory, this method can quantify the impact of each fea­
ture on the prediction results and generate SHAP sum­
mary plots to show the contribution and importance of
different features. The SHAP analysis of the multimodal
radiomics model reveals the underlying drivers of the
model’s predictions and suggests which features are of
great value for the prediction. Moreover, the feature
fusion technique proposed in this study introduces new
features (Rad-Score and Clinical-Rad-Score) for model
training, capturing more complex feature relationships
and further helping the model better understand the
data. The Random Forest algorithm can further combine
these fusion features when integrating multiple decision
trees to improve the model’s performance [45]. Addi­
tionally, we observed that among the selected radiomics
features in the multimodal model, there were four fea­
tures describing the distribution of voxel intensities (First

data. The Random Forest algorithm can further combine
these fusion features when integrating multiple decision
trees to improve the model’s performance [45]. Addi­
tionally, we observed that among the selected radiomics
features in the multimodal model, there were four fea­
tures describing the distribution of voxel intensities (First

ing the gray level of the images (Gray Level Run Length
Matrix and Gray Level Dependence Matrix). This sug­
gests that subtle differences in voxel intensity distribution
and grayscale changes can help to better predict hetero­
geneity within the tumor and in the peritumoral region.
There are a few limitations to this study that should
be noted. Firstly, this study lacked a comparative trial
of diagnostic performance by expert radiologists, ide­
ally both with and without AI assistance, to observe the
incremental clinical benefits of using the model in a real-
world setting. This limits our current ability to directly
quantify the model’s added clinical value. Secondly, the
model developed in this study is only applicable to tumor
binary classification tasks. Further development of a
stable multi-class tumor classification model is needed
for real-world clinical scenarios. Thirdly, although our
multimodal model demonstrated strong overall perfor­
mance, the sample size of atypical cases in our cohort
remains relatively small. This limits the robustness of
subgroup analyses specifically targeting these subtypes.
Future multi-center studies with larger, dedicated cohorts
of atypical cases are necessary to further validate our
model’s performance in these complex clinical scenarios.
Finally, manual VOI segmentation is labor-intensive,
which limits large-scale clinical scalability. Given that
automated methods, particularly deep learning-based
segmentation, have demonstrated high feasibility for
brain tumor delineation, integrating these tools into
future clinical workflows is essential to overcome effi­
ciency bottlenecks and ensure rapid, reproducible results.

Conclusion
This study proposes a multimodal interpretable machine
learning radiomics research framework, explores the
impact of multimodal information on model predic­
tion performance, and investigates the performance
of radiomics models based on the tumor and differ­
ent peritumoral inclusion ranges for discriminating
between lymphomas and gliomas, two types of malig­
nant brain tumors. By providing clinicians with a clearer
understanding of the model’s decision-making process,
this framework can increase its clinical acceptance and
usefulness.

imaging (MRI) scans have improved significantly, but their clinical deployment

exclusion criteria for MRI-based brain tumor studies addressing deep learning,
explainability, privacy, or Federated Learning, resulting in 147 initially retained
studies for the final screening set. One study was subsequently identified as
formally retracted and excluded from the final synthesis, resulting in 146 included

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Introduction
Despite achieving high performance on benchmark datasets in brain tumor
segmentation and classification, many deep learning (DL)-based neuro-oncology systems
remain insufficiently validated for routine clinical deployment. The major barriers limiting
clinical translation include poor interpretability, weak external generalization, dependence
on centralized datasets, and increasing concerns regarding patient data privacy under
regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. Consequently, recent neuro-oncology research has
gradually shifted from performance-oriented AI toward the development of trustworthy
AI frameworks capable of ensuring transparency, robustness, privacy preservation, and
clinically reliable decision support.
Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a critical component of trustworthy neuro-
oncology systems because clinicians require biologically meaningful reasoning rather than

(SHAP), and saliency-based visualization are increasingly used
to identify whether neural networks focus on clinically relevant
pathological regions such as enhancing tumor cores, necrosis, and
peritumoral edema instead of imaging artifacts. Simultaneously,
Federated Learning (FL) has gained considerable attention as a
privacy-preserving collaborative learning paradigm that enables
multi-institutional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis
without direct data sharing. The convergence of XAI and FL
therefore represents an important step toward secure, transparent,
and clinically adaptive neuro-oncology AI systems. In parallel,
recent advances in architectural design have accelerated the
evolution of brain tumor analysis frameworks from conventional
neural network-based models toward Vision Transformers (ViTs)
(Dosovitskiy, 2020), hybrid attention-driven systems, and State
Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba, which are capable of
modeling long-range spatial dependencies in high-dimensional
multi-modal MRI volumes (Gu and Dao, 2023). Moreover, the
increasing integration of multimodal MRI, radiogenomics, digital
pathology, and clinical metadata has expanded the role of AI
beyond tumor detection toward prognosis prediction, treatment
planning, and personalized neuro-oncology.

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Research gap and open problems
Despite substantial progress in brain tumor MRI analysis,
the reviewed literature reveals several specific open research
problems that remain insufficiently addressed. First, explainability
is predominantly implemented through post-hoc visualization
methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and saliency maps, while
quantitative
evaluation
of
explanation
reliability,
biological
plausibility, and agreement with clinical experts remains limited.
Second, XAI and Federated Learning are rarely integrated into
a unified framework, leaving a methodological gap between
interpretable prediction and privacy-preserving multi-institutional
learning. Third, federated approaches remain challenged by
non-independent
and
non-identically
distributed
(non-IID)
data arising from differences in scanners, acquisition protocols,
patient populations, missing modalities, and annotation practices,
while privacy-preserving mechanisms may introduce additional
performance degradation and communication overhead. Fourth,
the strong dependence on benchmark datasets limits assessment of
robustness under real-world domain shifts, external institutions,
and heterogeneous clinical conditions. Fifth, multimodal and
multi-omics approaches remain computationally demanding and
are not yet consistently evaluated for calibration, interpretability,
and clinical usefulness.
These gaps motivate future XAI-FL frameworks that jointly
address explanation validity, privacy preservation, heterogeneous
data distributions, and clinical robustness. Such frameworks could
incorporate quantitatively evaluated XAI with clinician-informed
and
biologically
grounded
explanations,
adaptive
federated
optimization for non-IID clients, privacy mechanisms with explicit
utility monitoring, multimodal fusion capable of handling missing
modalities,
and
standardized
evaluation
protocols
covering
predictive
performance,
calibration,
uncertainty,
explanation
quality, robustness, and clinical utility. The resulting research
direction is therefore not simply to improve predictive accuracy,
but to develop integrated and externally validated trustworthy AI
systems capable of supporting privacy-preserving and clinically
interpretable brain tumor analysis across institutions. Hence, the
current survey provides a focused systematic synthesis of 146
studies from 2020 to 2026 related to trustworthy AI for brain
tumor MRI analysis. The contributions made by this systematic
review can be listed as follows:

• Thematic synthesis of deep learning, explainable AI, Federated

• A focused cross-paradigm evaluation of CNNs, transformers,

• Detailed analysis of translational barriers that hamper real-

The rest of the paper is outlined as follows. In Section II, the
background and preliminaries of trustworthy AI-based brain tumor
detection using technologies such as explainable AI, Federated
Learning, and multimodal MRI analysis are presented. Section III
outlines the method for literature review, specifically the study
selection criteria following the PRISMA guidelines and the thematic
evaluation criteria adopted for this survey. In Section IV, a detailed
thematic analysis is provided about deep learning approaches for
brain tumor analysis including CNN, transfer learning, explainable
AI, multimodal/radiomics frameworks, robust learning techniques,
workflow-based clinical solutions, and optimization-based neuro-
oncology solutions. In Section V, we discuss some of the major
barriers to the adoption of trustworthy AI-based brain tumor
detection, whereas emerging research directions are discussed in

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Explainable AI (XAI)
Conventional deep learning models often operate as black-
box models, limiting clinical confidence despite achieving high
predictive
performance.
In
brain
tumor
segmentation
and
classification, XAI methods such as Gradient-weighted Class
Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) (Selvaraju et al., 2017), SHapley
Additive exPlanations (SHAP) (Lundberg and Lee, 2017), Local
Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) (Ribeiro et al.,
2016), and saliency mapping are increasingly used to associate
model activations with anatomically meaningful tumor regions.
Such
explainability
mechanisms
are
particularly
important
for differentiating true tumor progression from treatment-
related pseudoprogression and for improving clinician trust in
automated neuro-oncology systems. However, many current
explainability approaches remain post-hoc visual approximations
without biologically validated causal interpretation. To maintain
conceptual consistency throughout the review, explainability-
related methods are distinguished according to the type of
information they provide and the degree of validation they receive.
Feature attribution refers to methods that estimate the contribution
or importance of input features to a model prediction, including
SHAP and LIME. Saliency visualization refers specifically to
spatial or feature-level visual representations of model sensitivity,
such as Grad-CAM, CAM, saliency maps, and attention maps.
These visualizations indicate regions or features associated
with a prediction but do not, by themselves, establish that the
highlighted regions are biologically causal. Intrinsic interpretability
refers to models whose decision mechanism is designed to
be interpretable as part of the model architecture or learning
process, rather than applying an explanation after prediction. In
contrast, post-hoc explanation refers to methods applied after a
model has generated a prediction to approximate or visualize the
factors associated with that prediction. Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME,
and conventional saliency-based methods are therefore treated
primarily as post-hoc explanation or attribution approaches unless
the reviewed study explicitly integrates them into the learning
process. Counterfactual explanation considers how a prediction
would change under a specified change in the input or relevant
feature, thereby providing an alternative form of explanation
based on hypothetical modifications. Causal explanation requires

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
herefore treated
primarily as post-hoc explanation or attribution approaches unless
the reviewed study explicitly integrates them into the learning
process. Counterfactual explanation considers how a prediction
would change under a specified change in the input or relevant
feature, thereby providing an alternative form of explanation
based on hypothetical modifications. Causal explanation requires
stronger evidence than attribution or visualization because it
seeks to establish whether a feature or biological characteristic
has a causal influence on the prediction, typically requiring an
intervention-based, mechanistic, or otherwise causally grounded
evaluation. Consequently, an attention map, saliency map, or
feature-attribution score is not interpreted as evidence of biological
causality unless such causal validation is explicitly demonstrated.
Finally, clinician-validated explanation refers to explanations that
have been evaluated by domain experts, such as radiologists,
pathologists, or neuro-oncology specialists, for clinical relevance,
anatomical plausibility, or agreement with established diagnostic
evidence. Clinical trust is treated separately from these explanation
types because it represents a broader outcome or property of an
AI system rather than a specific explanation mechanism. Similarly,
visualization describes the presentation format of an explanation
and should not be treated as synonymous with explainability
or interpretability.
Accordingly, throughout this review, XAI methods are
described using the most specific applicable category: feature
attribution, saliency visualization, intrinsic interpretability, post-
hoc explanation, counterfactual explanation, causal explanation,
or clinician-validated explanation. This taxonomy is used to
distinguish what an explanation method computes from how the
explanation is presented and whether its clinical or biological
validity has been demonstrated.

Federated Learning (FL)
Large-scale centralized collection of MRI data is generally
hindered by stringent healthcare data protection policies such
as General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Federated
Learning provides an opportunity for collaborative learning in
multiple institutions through sharing model updates rather than
patient images. In such a decentralized approach, access to
diverse neuroimaging data is ensured without compromising data
ownership at institutions. However, federated approaches are still
plagued by several problems of non-IID (non-independent and
identically distributed) data distribution, communication costs,
utility-privacy trade-offs, and robustness issues in a heterogeneous
clinical setting. Decentralized privacy-preserving techniques and

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Synergy of multi-modal MRI sequences
Multimodality is an intrinsic quality of brain tumor analysis
with MRI. For example, T1-weighted (T1), T1 contrast-enhanced
(T1c), T2-weighted (T2), and fluid attenuated inversion recovery
(FLAIR) images are indispensable in order to have an adequate
characterization of a tumor. More specifically, FLAIR is more
prone to detecting peritumoral edema, whereas T1c images
are more informative in identifying the core and necrosis
of enhancing tumors. Thus, contemporary trustworthy neuro-
oncology systems tend to incorporate image fusion approaches into
their algorithms.

primary research themes: (i) Explainable AI (XAI), (ii) Deep

Advanced Architectures (Transformers/Mamba), and (v) Multi-
modal MRI Integration. The process of literature search entailed
several stages including database searching, filtering based on
metadata, logical screening and manual verification of articles.
All retained studies were manually reviewed to confirm thematic

trustworthy brain tumor detection using AI systems.

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Research questions
To guide the systematic synthesis, this review addresses three
research questions:
• RQ1: What are the major methodological trends in brain
tumor MRI analysis using deep learning, Explainable AI
(XAI), Federated Learning (FL), advanced architectures, and
multimodal approaches?
• RQ2: How are explainability and privacy-preserving learning
addressed in the reviewed literature, and to what extent are
XAI and FL integrated within the same brain tumor MRI
analysis frameworks?
• RQ3: What are the major limitations and research gaps
concerning
interpretability,
privacy,
data
heterogeneity,
validation, evaluation, and clinical applicability of trustworthy
AI for brain tumor MRI analysis?
The intersection of XAI and FL is examined by distinguishing
studies that address XAI and FL separately from studies that
incorporate both components within the same framework. For
studies involving both components, the review considers how
interpretability and privacy-preserving collaborative learning are
jointly addressed, together with the reported challenges related to
data heterogeneity, robustness, and clinical validation.

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Explainable and interpretable deep learning
models
In order to boost the level of trust in clinicians and enhance
decision-making, the latest research has adopted an approach
involving the incorporation of XAI methods like SHAP, LIME,
Grad-CAM, CAM, and neuro-fuzzy reasoning in deep learning
workflows. The goal was to detect biologically relevant tumor areas
and generate explainable interpretations along with predictions.
These studies, (Saeed et al., 2023; Hardani et al., 2024; Zheng et al.,
2023a; Valerio et al., 2025; Šefˇcík and Benesova, 2023; Gaur et al.,
2022; Mayeta-Revilla et al., 2025; Mazhar et al., 2026; Jahan et al.,
2025; Gao et al., 2025) together show that there is an increasing
trend toward moving away from accuracy-driven deep learning
models for the application of brain tumor detection using AI
toward explainable and biological models. Many of these papers
adopted techniques like Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, CAM, neuro-
fuzzy reasoning, or explanation-guided learning methods to ensure
better explainability and provide better insight into tumor-related
areas of interest. Although the MGMT methylation paper cast
serious doubt on the explainability techniques used today due
to the poor correlation of model attention with biologically
interesting tumor characteristics, frameworks like CSF-Glioma
and explanation-guided learning tried to achieve explainability
during the model learning process itself rather than relying
on post-hoc techniques. At the same time, segmentation-to-
explanation models extended explainability further by integrating
large language models for human-comprehensible reporting,
while histopathology-based frameworks like PGE-Net and diffuse

Bridging the trust gap: Explainable AI
(XAI) in brain tumor detection
Approaches such as the combination of convolutional neural
networks and explanation methods like Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME,
and attention visualization aim to highlight tumor-relevant areas
and help clinicians better understand the decisions made by the
models (Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2025; Pongphaw and Buaphan,
2026;
Srinivas and Parvathi,
2025;
Shaheema et al.,
2025;
Samara and Harry, 2025), Saleem et al. (2021), and Safarpour et al.
(2026). Though these approaches improve the interpretability of
the diagnostic results, many of these approaches are still based
on saliency map-based methods, which are not always reliable.
Other approaches focus on the development of hybrid approaches
for feature engineering and explanation methods, where machine
learning classifiers are combined with feature selection methods
and explanation methods like Boruta, LASSO, and SHAP to
improve the selection of clinically meaningful radiomic features
(Rohan et al.,
2025;
Hosny et al.,
2025;
Rahman et al.,
2024;
Song et al., 2022; Hosny and Mohammed, 2025; Mushgil et al.,
2025; Aksoy et al., 2025). Though these approaches improve
the interpretability of the diagnostic results, they are still based
on carefully curated data, which may not be applicable to all
situations. Recent approaches have been made to improve the
interpretability of the diagnostic results by developing explanation
methods for segmentation and multi-task approaches, where
tumor localization, segmentation, and classification are combined
to improve the interpretability of the results for better tumor
characterization in MRI scans (Andrianos et al., 2025; Ali et al.,
2025; Cao et al., 2023; Dasanayaka et al., 2022; Ayaz et al., 2024;
Bhaskaran and Datta, 2025). These methods have shown better
interpretability of the diagnosis but often come with the cost of
higher computational complexity and large amounts of annotated
data like BraTS. Another direction that is currently being explored
is the fusion of explainable AI with more powerful deep learning
architectures like ensemble methods, transformer networks, and
multimodal methods for more reliable predictions (Gagliardi et al.,
2025;
Alyatimi et al.,

section_heading: Privacy risks beyond federated data locality
text:
Privacy risks beyond federated data locality
Although Federated Learning avoids direct exchange of raw
MRI data, it should not be regarded as a complete guarantee of
patient privacy. The model updates exchanged during federated
optimization may themselves contain information about local
training samples. Gradient leakage or gradient inversion attacks
can exploit shared gradients or model updates to reconstruct
sensitive characteristics of training images, while model inversion
attacks can use model outputs or updates to infer representative
features of the underlying data (Zhu et al., 2019). Membership
inference attacks pose a different risk by determining whether a
particular patient or MRI sample contributed to model training
(Shokri et al., 2017; Nasr et al., 2019). These threats are particularly
relevant in neuro-oncology because MRI data contain highly
sensitive patient-specific anatomical and pathological information.
Therefore, privacy protection in federated brain tumor analysis
requires safeguards beyond data locality.
Additional
privacy-preserving
mechanisms
can
be
incorporated to mitigate these risks. Differential Privacy (DP)
limits the contribution of individual records by perturbing model
updates or gradients with controlled noise, thereby reducing the
risk of information disclosure (Abadi et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2020).
However, excessive noise may reduce the sensitivity required for
detecting subtle tumor characteristics and can introduce a privacy–
utility trade-off. Secure Aggregation can further protect client
updates by ensuring that the aggregation server receives only an
aggregate of participating updates rather than directly inspecting
individual client updates (Bonawitz et al., 2017). Consequently,
future XAI-FL frameworks for brain tumor MRI analysis should
evaluate not only whether raw data remain decentralized, but
also the resistance of shared model updates to gradient leakage,
model inversion, and membership inference attacks, together
with explicit assessment of differential-privacy parameters and
secure-aggregation mechanisms.

Data heterogeneity and domain shift in federated
learning
A major challenge in federated brain tumor MRI analysis
is the non-IID nature of institutional data. Differences in
scanner manufacturers and field strengths, acquisition protocols,
voxel spacing, MRI sequences, patient demographics, disease
distributions, and annotation practices can cause substantial
variation in the local data distributions across participating
institutions.
Such
heterogeneity
can
produce
client-specific
optimization objectives and gradient divergence, causing a globally
aggregated model to perform inconsistently across institutions.
Domain shift can further arise when a model trained collaboratively
across participating centers encounters an unseen institution with
different imaging characteristics or patient populations. Therefore,
evaluation of federated brain tumor models should extend
beyond aggregate global performance and include client-level
performance, cross-institutional validation, and explicit assessment
of robustness under domain shift. Approaches such as FedProx,
adaptive client selection, personalized Federated Learning, and
other non-IID-resilient optimization strategies may help reduce
the effects of distributional divergence, but their effectiveness
should be evaluated under realistic multi-institutional MRI
heterogeneity rather than only under artificially homogenized
data splits.

Multimodal and multi-omics
frameworks
In brain tumor research, multimodal learning has gained
popularity as a result of its capacity for integrating complementary
features extracted from different imaging sequences, heterogeneous
clinical data, and multi-omics data sources. As opposed to
traditional monomodal models, multimodal techniques seek
to increase accuracy, improve segmentation quality, enhance
interpretability, and boost robustness by fusing distinct feature
spaces into one coherent learning framework. Nevertheless,
although multimodal methods have achieved impressive results
in many recent publications, significant variation exists in aspects
related to the fusion mechanism, architectural design, explanation
capacity, computational considerations, and experimental validity.
This paper therefore provides a critical evaluation of the discussed
multimodal and multi-omics research papers by contrasting
their methodologies, interpretability techniques, computational
challenges, and generalizability problems instead of merely
highlighting their results.

computational efficiency
The studies reviewed here show an evident compromise

and the ability to computationally optimize them. Coupet et al.

Explainability and clinical interpretability
challenges
sExplainability remains one of the most important unresolved
issues across the reviewed studies. Kesav and Rajini (2024) apply
the Class Activation Mapping (CAM) technique for pointing
out relevant tumor locations, and Coupet et al. (2022) rely on
three techniques including LRP, Deep Taylor decomposition, and
Guided Backpropagation for visualizing the feature relevance. In
this regard, both methods increase explainability because they
show the relevance of predictions to particular image areas.
Nevertheless, due to their mathematical complexity, visualization
techniques need further explanation, and it is not easy to
provide a clinical understanding of the generated explanations
through the heatmaps. To solve this problem, Rawas and Samala
(2024) implement a novel approach for linking the CNN
model and ChatGPT to create a conversational explanation
tool based on human-language input and output. Although this
method increases usability and also interactive experience, the
study fails to prove causality between the chatbot responses
and the operations of the neural network. This introduces
an important clinical concern. Large language models can
generate fluent but potentially inaccurate explanations, creating
a risk of overreliance by clinicians. Therefore, although the
integration of generative AI is innovative, the interpretability
benefits remain preliminary and require stronger validation before
clinical deployment.

Data scarcity, validation limitations, and
generalizability
One of the consistent drawbacks found in almost all reviewed
papers is the lack of validation scale and poor proof of
clinical applicability. This issue is addressed by Kesav and Rajini
(2024). Despite the fact that the model is described as having
a 98.99% accuracy and a specificity of 99.76%, it was tested
on just 32 patients and evaluated through just five images
for assessing features. A study of this small size cannot
provide sufficient statistical evidence to claim robustness or
applicability. Coupet et al. (2022) clearly state the problem of
overfitting with regard to limited training data in medicine.
The authors prove the fact that deep learning approaches
may fail under such conditions without proper regularizing

challenges
One of the key insights derived from the above analysis is that
AI research in brain tumor detection is moving beyond simple
accuracy-driven learning models to more trustworthy intelligent
systems for clinical use. Although previous research efforts focused
mostly on achieving high accuracy results by using neural networks
for segmentation purposes and optimizing Dice-score values,
today’s research tends to pay more attention to explainability,
data privacy protection, multimodal reasoning capabilities, and
distributed learning strategies. As depicted in our framework of
the systemic architecture transition (Figure 9), it appears that
improvements in architectural design have been outpacing those in
other areas significantly.

literature in this area is the reliance on post-hoc interpretability
frameworks such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, LayerCAM, Guided

Moreover, the review emphasizes the methodological gap
between the centralization of explainability studies and the
development of privacy-preserving approaches to collaborative
learning. While most of the relevant research is dedicated to
the topic of explainability, less attention is paid to the topics of
Federated Learning (FL), differential privacy, or decentralization
of the optimization process. The problem under consideration
highlights one of the critical deployment issues faced by clinical
brain tumor detection. Since the disease under study implies
multi-institutional learning because of the rarity and diversity of
patients’ cases, centralized training is limited by GDPR, HIPAA,
and the principle of institutional data sovereignty. One important
trade-offthat emerges frequently in the FL body of work is the
one between protecting privacy and ensuring feature sensitivity.
Methods like differential privacy and adding noise improve privacy
protection but can potentially hinder the identification of fine
imaging markers required to classify lesions with poor contrast,
predict MGMT methylation, and subtype gliomas. This trade-off

configurations, voxel spacing, missing modality information, and
variable annotations. While methods like FedProx, dynamic
collaboration schemes, adaptive client selection strategies, and

of brain tumors. Indeed, image sequence fusion of T1, T1ce, T2,
and FLAIR images has been widely used in the segmentation and
classification of brain tumors since different images reveal different
features. Furthermore, novel paradigms based on genomics,
transcriptomics, and radiomics try to go beyond anatomy and
develop biologically-driven predictive models. Yet, despite these
advancements, the current multimodal models are computationally
costly and rely significantly on properly curated pre-processing
pipelines. Additionally, very few multimodal studies have been
externally validated. The review also highlights a basic conflict
between the computational efficiency and clinical reliability.

Classical deep learning models ensure high prediction quality
but are poorly interpretable. Explainable AI models increase the
level of interpretability but are rarely subjected to strict biological
validation. Federated Learning reduces direct exposure of raw
patient data but does not inherently eliminate privacy risks,
as shared model updates may remain vulnerable to gradient
leakage, model inversion, and membership inference attacks.
Transformer and Mamba models enable good representation
learning but are computationally expensive and require validation
on large samples. Multi-modal frameworks allow complete tumor
characterization due to integration of diverse data sources; however,
they create significant problems related to data standardization
and workflow organization. Overall, this review indicates that
future applications of AI in neuro-oncology would result from
the combination of explainability, privacy protection, improved
representation learning, and multi-modality rather than from one
specific paradigm.

each paradigm, the table summarizes its primary strengths, key
limitations, emerging research directions, and current level of
clinical readiness. This synthesis provides a focused overview of the
evolution of the field while highlighting the remaining challenges
and future opportunities for clinically deployable trustworthy
AI systems.

studies could report multiple datasets, dataset frequencies were not

survival prediction, and multi-omics studies. Unlike BraTS, which

provides complementary genomic, transcriptomic, and clinical
data, allowing the design of predictive models. Less number
of research studies use Figshare datasets, Institutional cohorts,
and multi-center clinical datasets. These datasets are primarily
used for tumor classification and diagnostic decision support.

authors: B. Uthra; R. Sivashankari
text:
Trustworthiness and clinical validation
gap
In addition to being effective predictors, trustworthy AI
needs to be reliable, well-calibrated, robust, and clinically useful.
Yet, the evaluation of the reviewed papers shows an obvious
disparity between performance-related and trustworthiness-related
approaches to assessing these models.
As seen from Table 19, traditional performance indicators
like accuracy, Dice, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-scores prevail
in research; calibration indicators, metrics related to uncertainty
estimation, and clinical usefulness criteria are mentioned quite
rarely. Calibration measures like Brier Score, Expected Calibration
Error (ECE), Maximum Calibration Error (MCE), and Negative
Log-Likelihood (NLL) can be found in less than 7% of the reviewed
works. This problem is especially pertinent since the accuracy of a
model does not imply its trustworthiness. A system can have great
benchmark scores but at the same time can have poor-calibrated
confidences or be unreliable in distribution shift situations. Thus,
performance scores alone are not enough for assessing the
clinical readiness of a model. Fortunately, some promising recent
works started to use the analysis of the calibration, uncertainty
quantification, external validation cohorts, and decision-curve
analysis which shows that there is already a move toward the
trustworthy evaluation of AI. However, these approaches still are
exceptions rather than the rule.
Overall, these results expose an underlying imbalance within
modern neuro-oncology AI research. As is clear from the extensive
use and reporting of performance metrics, there has been far less
focus on developing reliable evaluation methodologies. Thus, many
state-of-the-art algorithms show excellent performance metrics but
lack adequate validation for their calibration, uncertainty handling,
robustness to distributional shifts, or practical applicability in
clinical settings. It is therefore imperative that future research
efforts emphasize both innovative validation methods along with
algorithm design.

Open challenges
However, despite all the advances in brain tumor detection
research that can be considered trustworthy, there is still a
set of crucial obstacles impeding the reliable implementation of
such technologies in practice. For instance, one of the major
drawbacks of neuro-oncology AI is its high dependence on
benchmark datasets such as BraTS, TCGA, TCIA, and Figshare.
As a result, models trained on such datasets may demonstrate
their inefficiency in real-life settings due to lack of generalization.
Furthermore, despite the availability of explainable AI technologies
(Grad-CAM, SHAP, and saliency mapping), the biologically causal
explanation and physician-oriented assessment of AI frameworks
remain problematic.

robust Federated Learning, variability in images, and translating
regulations. These limitations illustrate how the aforementioned

In terms of trustworthy brain tumor detection using AI,
future research directions include improving the clinical utility,
robustness, and biological plausibility of DL methods. The
potential approach that could address these needs is developing
the concept of radiology foundation models using large pre-

reliance on benchmark datasets, like BraTS. Moreover, combining

an effective privacy-preserving way of distributed learning while
preserving clinically useful explanations of the decision process.
Multimodal and radiogenomic intelligence can be considered
as another key aspect of future developments as they may allow

reported in 73.8% of the representative studies analyzed, while
F1-score and Dice-based measures were reported in 27.9% each. In
contrast, calibration, clinical utility, and uncertainty measures were
comparatively uncommon, reported in 6.6%, 3.3%, and 1.6% of
the representative studies, respectively. This quantitative evidence
indicates
that
predictive
performance
remains
substantially
more established than systematic evaluation of calibration,
uncertainty, and clinical usefulness. Overall, the reviewed evidence
demonstrates measurable progress toward trustworthy AI for
brain tumor MRI analysis, particularly in explainability and the
adoption of emerging architectures. However, the relatively limited
representation of Federated Learning, multimodal integration, and
trustworthiness-oriented evaluation, together with dependence
on benchmark datasets, highlights persistent gaps in privacy-
preserving collaboration, external validation, clinical validation,
and robust assessment. These findings support the need for future
studies to complement predictive performance with externally
validated,
clinically
grounded,
and
quantitatively
assessable
measures of trustworthiness.

This research explores the use of gated recurrent units (GRUs) for automated brain tumor detection
using MRI data. The GRU model captures sequential patterns and considers spatial information
within individual MRI images and the temporal evolution of lesion characteristics. The proposed
approach improves the accuracy of tumor detection using MRI images. The model’s performance is
benchmarked against conventional CNNs and other recurrent architectures. The research addresses
interpretability concerns by employing attention mechanisms that highlight salient features
contributing to the model’s decisions. The proposed model attention-gated recurrent units (A-GRU)
results show promising results, indicating that the proposed model surpasses the state-of-the-art
models in terms of accuracy and obtained 99.32% accuracy. Due to the high predictive capability of
the proposed model, we recommend it for the effective diagnosis of Brain tumors in the E-healthcare
system.

(CAD) system for the detection of brain tumors. The AI-based CAD system extracted more deep features from
data for target production. The AI techniques particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) tech-
niques have been used by various researchers in designing CAD diagnosis systems for brain tumor detection.
However, these methods still have the problem of lack of prediction accuracy according to the literature review.

The brain tumor’s accurate and on-time detection is important for effective treatment and recovery at an early
stage in the E-healthcare system. Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques particularly machine learning (ML) and
deep learning (DL)-based computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems play important roles in the detection of
critical diseases. The AI-based CAD system effectively interprets the MRI images of brain tumors as compared
to medical doctors. However, AI-based CAD system predictive accuracy of interpreting the images is still not
enough to accurately detect the brain tumor. To tackle the accurate detection problem of brain tumors various
researchers proposed different methods using machine learning deep learning techniques. In this research work,
we have explored various brain tumor detection methods to find the research gap in the domain and designed a
new method to accurately detect brain tumors using machine learning and deep learning techniques.
Haq et al.4 proposed a new automated diagnostic framework for accurate brain cancer diagnosis, utilizing
deep learning techniques in an intelligent integrated model (CNN-LSTM) on BTDS, MBNDS, and BMIDS

novel method using brain imaging to identify brain cancers, utilizing equalization of histograms and methods
for opening, followed by a convolutional neural network for classification, achieving high accuracy. In another
study, Jia and ­Chen6 proposed a novel approach called fully automatic heterogeneous segmentation using sup-

Gated recurrent unit (GRU)
The gated recurrent unit (GRU) is an architecture within the realm of recurrent neural networks (RNNs)24 that
has been devised for the purpose of handling and modeling sequential data. It addresses certain limitations
that are encountered in conventional RNNs, particularly the issues of vanishing gradients and the complexities
associated with capturing long-range dependencies within sequences. It was also presented as a modification
of the conventional long short-term memory (LSTM)25 model. Both the GRU and LSTM architectures are for-
mulated to tackle the challenge of the vanishing gradient problem that can occur during the training of deep
networks involving sequential data, like text or time series. But GRU is a more straightforward design featuring
just two gates: reset and update. This leads to quicker training and inference processes as a result of having fewer
parameters. This design works particularly well for smaller datasets and tasks that involve simpler relationships.
However, it might not be as effective in capturing complex, long-range dependencies. The distinctive feature of
GRUs lies in their incorporation of gating mechanisms, which serve as controls governing the flow of informa-
tion throughout the network. The GRU model structure is given in Fig. 2.

Attention mechanism
The reduction in prediction accuracy for the output sequence within the GRU network is observed when employ-
ing a more extensive input sequence. This occurs because the network treats all input variables uniformly, over-
looking potential variations in their correlations with the forecasting task. To mitigate this issue, an attention
mechanism can be implemented to highlight more pertinent input variables.
The attention mechanism is composed in the form of an attention vector-generating encoder based on the
encoder output as input for a decoder that creates a hidden state based on the input. Each step of hidden state
is given an attention score by the encoder, which uses the hidden state of the previous view decoder to divide
the hidden states. After that, a soft-max operation is used to the attention scores to create an attention vector.
Consequently, during the prediction of the output value by the decoder, the encoder directs attention towards
input variables that are similar to the predicted value.
The attention mechanism functions by assigning weights or conferring significance to each lower level during
the assessment of the higher-level representation, ultimately concentrating on a pivotal segment of the textual
content. Equations (5), (6), and (7) describe the attention mechanism ­mathematically27.
Here, H symbolizes a matrix comprising hidden output vectors (h1, h2,...hN) N specifies the count of hidden
layers generated by GRU, C denotes the attention model’s contextual word, w represents the trained vector, and
wT stands for its transpose. The attention weights (α1, α2, . . . αN) are employed to create the vectors C as well
as the output sentence representation h∗ for a provided input, as shown in Eq. (8).
