In the current hybrid CNN-Transformer methods, the encoding of the Transformer is the only part where
tokens are not explicitly removed such as background tokens.The current hybrid CNN-Transformer models are
mostly feature fusion, instead of explicitly removing the background tokens before the Transformer encoding.
Swin Transformer architectures reduce interactions to a specific window, and standard ViT models attend to all
image patches equally which can result in diminishing attention to smaller areas in tumors. EfficientNet-based
methods are capable of effectively extracting local spatial information, but fall short in incorporating mechanisms
to represent global, contextual dependencies. Furthermore, most explainable AI methods are retrospective,
giving visualizations of the model only after it has been trained, but don’t modify the optimization process of
the parameters. XAI-BTNet introduces three key innovations to rectify these drawbacks: (i) filter tokens and
introduce attention masks using segmentation, before the multi-head self-attention blocks; (ii) hybrid CNN–
ViT architecture, which learns jointly local and global representations; and (iii) explainability-aware composite
loss that constrains attention maps to pay attention to tumor-specific regions during the training process. This
design provides enhanced interpretability for diagnosis and at the same time preserves good classification of the
tumor.
This paper’s organization continues below. Section 2 discusses innovative brain tumour detection, hybrid
deep learning models, Vision Transformers, and explainable AI in medical imaging. Section 3 describes the
segmentation-guided CNN–ViT architecture and explainability-aware training method of the XAI-BTNet
system. Experimental setup, datasets, evaluation measures, and outcome analysis are in Sect. 4. Section 5
concludes the work and suggests future research.

The existing literature has revealed the effectiveness of hybrid CNN–Transformer and explainability-aware
deep learning approaches for analyzing brain tumors from MRI. Previous research has demonstrated that
architectures of transformers achieve better global contextual learning, and CNN-based architectures achieve
better local spatial feature learning and tumor localization. Additionally, explainable AI technologies have been
developed in recent years that enhance the transparency of the AI model and its reliability in diagnosis by
visualizing its attention and explaining its features. To date, however, there are still many methods that depend
on post-hoc explainability, and most of them are not supported by the integration of segmentation-guided
attention optimization, which motivates the development of the proposed XAI-BTNet framework.
Proposed methodology
The proposed XAI-BTNet (Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based Brain Tumor Network) is a two-step,
segmentation-directed hybrid deep learning architecture, which will overcome three fundamental weaknesses
of existing brain tumor analysis systems: uniformity of feature extraction, which does not identify pathologically
relevant areas, the lack of a coherent multi-stage pipeline that jointly trains segmentation and classification, and
the use of post-h XAI-BTNet combines a UNet segmentation block based on Convolutional Neural Network
(CNN)-based Stage 1 with a hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer (ViT)-based Stage 2 backbone. The two phases
are closely intertwined with a segmentation-directed token-suppression framework and a new Grad-CAM
consistency loss that incorporates explainability as an objective to training, achieving competitive performance
compared with recently reported methods under comparable evaluation settings. This integrated architecture
will guarantee that localization of the tumor, multi-class classification and interpretability are collectively
optimized in a single end-to-end pipeline, indicating the potential applicability of the framework for interpretable
computer-aided brain tumor analysis.

The segmentation-guided token filtering process aims to suppress irrelevant background information prior
to transformer-based feature learning. Initially, the CNN–UNet module predicts a binary tumor mask for each
MRI image. The mask is subsequently divided into patches corresponding to the Vision Transformer input
tokens. For each patch, the proportion of tumor pixels is estimated and compared with a predefined threshold.
Patches containing sufficient tumor content are preserved, while those dominated by background regions are
assigned lower attention weights using a soft masking mechanism. The filtered token sequence is then forwarded
to the transformer encoder, enabling the self-attention layers to concentrate on clinically meaningful tumor
regions and enhancing explainability.

The UNet architecture is a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture that has skip connections that maintain
spatial context lost during downsampling. The encoder uses a sequence of convolutional blocks with batch
normalization and ReLU activations and max-pooling operations to sequentially abstraction of the spatial
features into a small latent representation. The decoder uses bilinear upsampling combined with convolutional
blocks with the aid of skip connections between the respective encoder levels to retrieve fine spatial detail and
generate a complete-resolution segmentation map. To have proper delineation of the clinically heterogeneous
tumor subregions, the segmentation module is trained with a hybrid loss function that consists of a combination
of Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and Dice loss. The BCE metric punishes pixelwise misclassification by
capitalizing on the task as independent binary predictions. In contrast, the Dice loss encourages the agreement
between the predicted mask and the ground-truth annotation, and is in effect directly maximising region-level
correspondence. The composite loss is given as:

Implementation details and training configuration

RTX 4090 GPU. CNN-UNet used four encoder-decoder layers, each having 3 × 3 convolution kernels, batch

training was done over 100 epochs and a batch size of 16, with an AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of
0.0001 and weight decay of 0.01. Optimization was stabilized by cosine annealing and by gradient clipping.
Data augmentation techniques used were rotation, flipping, normalization, scaling and noise injection. In all
experiments, the stratified five-fold cross-validation (5 F-CV) technique was adopted to provide a reproducible
evaluation. All the implementation parameters, configuration and training methods were kept the same for all
the experiments to ensure the repeatability and a fair comparison of their performance.

Transformer used input patches of 16 × 16, resulting in 196 patches was embedded along with an embedding

with a dropout rate of 0.1. The training was performed on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU using AdamW optimizer,
cosine annealing scheduler and stratified 5-fold cross validation for 100 epochs.

NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The CNN–UNet module consisted of four layers of the encoder–decoder network with

rate: 0.0001, weight decay: 0.01), and cosine annealing scheduling. Augmentation techniques employed were

The ablation experiments show that the performance boost of XAI-BTNet is not just due to the growing
complexity of the CNN–ViT backbone architecture, but also due to the coordinated ablation operation of
segmentation-guided token suppression and explainability-aware optimization. The overall accuracy result of
the XAI-BTNet was 98.6% while the CNN–ViT baseline got 96.8%. Without token suppression, the accuracy
drops to 97.3%, showing that the transformer attention is more likely to suffer from irrelevant background
information. The Grad-CAM consistency loss is shown to be important to accuracy, as ablation reveals a drop
to 97.7% when it is removed. Removing both components resulted in performance drops to 96.8%, which is the
CNN–ViT baseline. The results show the complementary nature of token-level background suppression and
explanation learning that is spatially consistent.
The spatial overlap between the explanations and the tumor regions was quantitatively assessed in addition
to the qualitative visualization using Grad-CAM. Dice and intersection-over-union (IoU) scores were used
to compare the normalized Grad-CAM maps with the corresponding CNN–UNet tumor masks. The Dice
agreement of 0.91 ± 0.02 and the IoU of 0.84 ± 0.03 showed that there was a high spatial overlap between the
tumor regions segmented and the discriminative regions of the model. These results indicate that the use of the
Grad-CAM consistency objective during optimization is effective and not merely as a post hoc analysis.

explainability regularization, but in case of segmentation failure, it can be propagated to the stage of classification

Conclusion and future work
The study introduces XAI-BTNet, an explainable hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer model to detect and classify
brain tumours across multiple stages using MRI, that overcomes the three key limitations of uniform feature
extraction, disjointed multi-task pipelines, and post-hoc explanations found in current deep learning models.
XAI-BTNet developed an interpretability-conscious diagnostic pipeline through the addition of a CNN-UNet
segmentation module to extract tumor-specific ROI, a masked token attention mechanism to inhibit non-tumor
patch tokens before ViT self-attention, and a new Grad-CAM consistency loss that makes interpretability a
proactive training constraint and not a post-hoc visualization. Tested on the Figshare brain tumor MRI data
with cross-validation of five-folds and tested on the BraTS 2021 dataset on robustness, the framework achieved
a classification accuracy rate of 98.6%, sensitivity of 97.8% and specificity of 98.9%, demonstrating competitive
performance relative to recently reported approaches under similar experimental conditions. The present study
has certain limitations. All steps of the framework were tested on publicly available data, but external clinical
validation was not conducted on multi-institutional MRI data. Furthermore, the explainability assessment
was restricted to the overlap-based localization measures. Work with larger heterogeneous datasets and, in
conjunction with radiologist guidance, will follow.
Future directions include the extension of XAI-BTNet to three-dimensional volumetric MRI inputs in order
to capture tumor morphology in axial, coronal and sagittal planes and the incorporation of multi-modal MRI
sequences such as T1CE and FLAIR as part of a single feature fusion approach. Furthermore, the concept of
federated learning will be explored to enable privacy-preserving multi-institutional training on heterogeneous
clinical data, and future clinical validation trials will be conducted to evaluate the diagnostic utility of the
proposed framework in practice, its acceptance among radiologists, and its applicability to regulatory standards.

authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors are among the most life-threatening neurological conditions, and effective therapy and patient
outcomes depend on accurate and timely diagnosis. This study proposes an interpretable and deployment-
oriented deep learning framework for multi-class classification of brain tumors using magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI). The framework employs a carefully designed lightweight CNN configuration that prioritizes
computational efficiency and robustness for practical clinical use. Evaluations on a publicly available MRI
dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving a classification accuracy of
99.54%. To enhance clinical trust, Grad-CAM visualizations were integrated to highlight class-discriminative
regions within MRI scans, providing transparent and interpretable predictions. In addition, the framework
was deployed within a user-friendly desktop application, enabling real-time diagnostic support. Comparative
analysis with state-of-the-art models shows that the proposed system achieves competitive or superior
performance while maintaining efficiency, making it a promising candidate for clinical decision support, subject
to further validation in real-world settings.

Introduction
Brain tumors, which are characterized as a collection of abnormal
cells that develop within the brain’s tissues, are one of the main
causes of illness and death globally. The World Health Organization
(WHO) reports that brain tumors rank as the second most common
cause of death globally [1]. Brain tumors are generally classified into
two broad categories: benign and malignant. Benign tumors typically
develop more slowly and neither invade nor spread to neighboring
tissue. Malignant tumors, such as gliomas, on the other hand, have
the ability to spread into nearby tissues and organs, which can lead
to serious health problems. Early detection of brain tumors is crucial
to improve patient survival rates and outcomes [2,3].
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the primary imaging modality
for brain tumor detection due to its superior ability to visualize soft
tissue structures. However, manual interpretation of MRI scans is still
highly dependent on radiologists’ expertise and is prone to human
error, fatigue, and variability in judgment. Furthermore, brain tumors
often exhibit heterogeneous appearances in MR images, with over-
lapping morphological features that complicate accurate classification.
Biopsy procedures, although definitive, can be invasive and risky,
especially during the early stages of diagnosis [4].

authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
This study introduces an interpretable and deployment-oriented
deep learning framework for multi-class brain tumor classification us-
ing MRI scans. While several existing approaches focus on architectural
complexity or transfer learning, the proposed framework emphasizes
a balanced design combining accuracy, interpretability, and practical
usability. The key contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
• A carefully designed lightweight CNN configuration for four-class
brain tumor classification, achieving high diagnostic accuracy
while maintaining low computational complexity compared to
transfer learning and transformer-based approaches.
• A multi-level explainability strategy using Grad-CAM, including
layer-wise visualization and analysis of misclassified cases, pro-
viding deeper insight into the model’s decision-making process
beyond standard post-hoc explanations.
• The development of a fully offline, real-time desktop applica-
tion that integrates classification and visual explanation, facili-
tating practical deployment in clinical environments with limited
computational or network resources.
• Experimental evaluation demonstrating that a carefully designed
lightweight CNN can outperform or match more complex models
while offering improved interpretability and deployment readi-
ness.
By bridging the gap between research innovation and clinical ap-
plicability, this work contributes a significant step forward in making
AI-assisted brain tumor diagnosis more reliable and potentially useful
for clinical decision support.
This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work.
Section 3 details the proposed methodology. Section 4 presents experi-
mental results and clinical evaluation. Section 5 discusses key findings,
and Section 6 concludes the paper with future directions.

Related Work
This section reviews prior work on brain tumor classification, cov-
ering traditional machine learning methods, deep learning approaches,
and recent explainable AI techniques used in medical imaging. From a
clinical and imaging perspective, brain tumors present significant chal-
lenges in medical image analysis due to their varying types, locations,
and sizes [9]. Brain tumors must be classified accurately to prepare
a proper diagnosis and treatment plan. Researchers have employed
different techniques to enhance the performance of classifiers, such as
traditional machine learning and deep learning.
Traditional machine learning approaches have built on the founda-
tion of handcrafted features and standard classifiers. Gumaei et al. [10]
proposed a hybrid feature extraction technique combined with a Regu-
larized Extreme Learning Machine (RELM), achieving 94.23% classi-
fication accuracy. Similarly, Kaplan et al. [11] utilized Local Binary
Patterns (LBP and nLBP) with K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) for classifi-
cation, achieving 95.56% accuracy. Although these early approaches
demonstrated promise, their dependence on manually crafted features
restricted their scalability and ability to adapt to diverse datasets.
Deep learning methodologies, especially Convolutional Neural Net-
works (CNNs), have revolutionized medical image analysis and brain
tumor detection due to their automated feature extraction and superior
performance. CNNs excel in learning features directly from imaging
data, bypassing the need for manual feature design. Afshar et al. [12]
introduced a modified Capsule Network (CapsNet), emphasizing spatial
relationships among features and achieving 90.89% accuracy. Rasheed
et al. [13] proposed a CNN-based framework that incorporated Gaus-
sian blur-based sharpening and Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram
Equalization techniques, yielding a classification accuracy of 97.84%
across four brain tumor classes. Furthermore, data augmentation tech-
niques, such as scaling and rotation, have been incorporated to improve
the performance of deep learning models [14].
Transfer learning has further advanced this field by enabling the
reuse of powerful pre-trained models. Architectures such as VGG19,
ResNet-50, InceptionV3, and DenseNet have been fine-tuned on
domain-specific brain MRI datasets to achieve strong classification
performance. Zhu et al. [15] demonstrated the effectiveness of transfer

Transfer learning has further advanced this field by enabling the

randomized neural network as the classifier. Sharma et al. [16] mod-

proposed a framework combining deep learning and evolutionary
algorithms to optimize ResNet architecture, achieving an accuracy of
98.69%. Deepak and Ameer [18] proposed a brain tumor classifi-
cation system using transfer learning with a pre-trained GoogLeNet,
achieving 98% accuracy on the Figshare MRI dataset using five-fold
cross-validation.
While substantial progress has been achieved, challenges remain,
particularly with respect to interpretability in CNN-based systems. To
address this, several recent studies have integrated explainability tech-
niques such as Grad-CAM to enhance transparency and facilitate clini-
cal validation [19,20]. Li and Dib [9] applied Gradient-weighted Class
Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to assess the interpretability of mul-
tiple pre-trained CNN models, including ResNet-50, Xception, and In-

Similarly, Musthafa et al. [21] proposed a brain tumor detection frame-
work based on ResNet-50 integrated with Grad-CAM visualizations to
support explainable decision-making.
Beyond CNN-based approaches, Vision Transformers have emerged
as an alternative deep learning paradigm capable of capturing long-
range dependencies within medical images [22]. Elhadidy et al. [23]

ciency. Wang et al. [24] proposed a transformer-based architecture
that combines token representations to enhance classification perfor-

example, Aloraini et al. [25] combined convolutional feature extrac-

that combines token representations to enhance classification perfor-

in resource-constrained clinical environments. Moreover, their explain-

favorable trade-off between accuracy, computational efficiency, and
interpretability, making it better suited for real-time clinical decision
support. In parallel, recent studies have investigated federated and
distributed learning paradigms to support multi-institutional collabo-
ration while preserving data privacy, highlighting both opportunities
and practical challenges for clinical translation of medical imaging AI

Recent studies have explored optimization-assisted and robustness-
oriented deep learning frameworks to improve convergence stability
and generalization in complex medical imaging tasks. Hybrid bio-
inspired optimization strategies and adaptive learning mechanisms
have been reported to enhance training robustness and mitigate sen-
sitivity to initialization and data variability, particularly in deep and
transformer-based architectures [28–31]. More recently, uncertainty-
aware and adaptive learning strategies have been proposed to im-
prove robustness and interpretability under data variability, reinforc-
ing their relevance to explainable AI in medical image analysis [32,
33]. While these approaches provide valuable insights into stability-
aware learning, they often introduce additional architectural and op-
timization complexity, motivating the exploration of lightweight and
deployment-oriented alternatives such as the framework proposed in
this study.

Materials And Methods
This section describes the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, model
architecture, and explainability strategy adopted in this study. Each
component is designed with consideration for classification accuracy,
interpretability, and practical usability.
While recent studies have explored optimization-assisted and
uncertainty-aware learning frameworks to enhance robustness, the
proposed methodology emphasizes training stability and generaliza-
tion through architectural design choices, regularization strategies,
and explainable visualization, prioritizing computational efficiency and
deployment simplicity.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Brain tumor MRI dataset
The dataset employed in this study is a publicly available image-
level brain tumor MRI dataset obtained from Kaggle and curated by
Kadam et al. [34]. It integrates MRI scans from several publicly ac-
cessible repositories, including Figshare, SARTAJ, and Br35H, thereby
ensuring a diverse and representative collection of imaging data. It
consists of 7023 MRI images, divided into four categories: normal (no
tumor), pituitary tumors, meningioma tumors, and glioma tumors.
The dataset does not provide patient-level metadata (e.g., age,
sex, clinical history, scanner manufacturer, magnetic field strength, or
acquisition protocols), and subject identifiers are unavailable. Conse-
quently, annotations are provided at the image level rather than the
patient level. Labels were assigned by the dataset curators based on
expert-reviewed sources and have been widely used in prior brain
tumor classification studies. A sample of images from the dataset is
shown in Fig. 1.
The dataset was systematically partitioned into training, validation,
and testing subsets to ensure effective model development and evalua-
tion. Specifically, 4569 images were allocated for training, 1143 images
(20% of the training set) for validation, and 1311 images for testing.
This split preserves the overall dataset composition across the four
classes: no tumor (2000 images, 28.5%), pituitary tumors (1757 im-
ages, 25.0%), meningioma tumors (1645 images, 23.4%), and glioma
tumors (1621 images, 23.1%). The dataset exhibits mild class imbal-
ance, with the ‘no tumor’ class exceeding the smallest class (glioma)
by approximately 5.4 percentage points. To mitigate potential bias,
stratified splitting was employed to maintain class proportions across
all subsets. Macro-averaged evaluation metrics were used to ensure
balanced performance assessment, and data augmentation was applied
uniformly to the training set without introducing artificial rebalanc-
ing techniques such as oversampling or class weighting. The class
distribution and its preservation across splits are illustrated in Fig. 2.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Data preprocessing
Effective image preprocessing plays a vital role in enhancing the
performance of deep learning models, especially in medical imaging
applications. To get the dataset ready for training, it is subjected to
various preprocessing steps. All images are resized to 125 × 125 pixels
in the first step. In the next step, pixel values are normalized by
dividing them by 255. This normalization step helps stabilize training
and improves optimization efficiency. The training data were ran-
domly shuffled to reduce sampling bias and improve generalization.
Class labels were one-hot encoded, which is required for multi-class
classification.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Data augmentation
The specialized nature of medical imaging datasets gives them high
value but also comes with several challenges. Accurate annotation
requires domain-specific expertise, while labeling inconsistencies can
result in negatively influence model training and predictive perfor-
mance [35]. In addition, when it comes to data privacy, the sensitive
nature of the data limits the accessibility and sharing of data. As
a result, it complicates the data gathering of sufficiently large and
representative datasets.
The limited size of labeled medical image datasets creates a se-
vere bottleneck to effective deep learning model development. To
avoid this problem, the image augmentation techniques have been
widely used to increase data diversity to improve model generalization
synthetically [36]. Consistent with prior brain tumor classification
studies, data augmentation has been extensively employed to mitigate
overfitting and enhance model robustness when training on publicly
available MRI datasets. Commonly adopted strategies in the litera-
ture include geometric transformations such as rotation, flipping, and
translation [37,38], while more advanced approaches have explored
GAN-based synthesis to generate realistic tumor variations [39,40].
Compared to these methods, our augmentation strategy prioritizes
computational efficiency and anatomical preservation. In this study,
data augmentation was employed to enhance robustness and improve
generalization under real-world variability. The augmentation strategy
included controlled geometric transformations with the following pa-
rameters: rotation range = 10, width shift range = 0.05, height shift
range = 0.05, and horizontal flipping. The rotation range introduces
random rotations up to ±10 degrees, while the shift parameters apply
minor horizontal and vertical translations of up to 5% of the image
dimensions. Horizontal flipping was applied with a probability of 0.5,
further increasing sample diversity. All augmentation operations were
applied exclusively to the training set, while validation and test data
were kept unchanged to ensure unbiased performance evaluation.
Fig. 3 illustrates the impact of data augmentation by presenting a
visual comparison between original and augmented MRI scans. The top
row displays four representative training images in their original form,
while the bottom row depicts the corresponding images following the
application of augmentation transformations.

identify complex image patterns makes them particularly effective for

In this work, a custom lightweight CNN architecture is adopted. This
design provides explicit control over feature hierarchies and activation
behavior, reduces computational and memory overhead, and supports

The proposed approach employs a custom-designed Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN) architecture tailored for brain tumor classifica-
tion, as depicted in Fig. 4. Each convolutional block within the model
comprises a Conv2D layer with a 3 × 3 kernel, followed sequentially
by batch normalization and a ReLU activation function to ensure stable
and non-linear feature transformation.
The model architecture begins with an input layer that specifies
the dimensionality of the input data without performing any feature
extraction. In this study, the input consists of grayscale MRI images
with a fixed resolution of 125 × 125 pixels. The images are then passed
through a number of hidden layers that learn to represent features in
a hierarchy to facilitate correct classification. The feature extraction
process consists of five convolutional blocks. The first block consists
of two Conv2D layers with 64 filters each, followed by batch normal-

Training configuration
The model’s hyperparameters were selected to balance classifica-

Hyperparameters were selected empirically through iterative experi-
mentation, where candidate configurations (learning rate, batch size,
dropout rates, and optimizer) were evaluated based on validation per-
formance and training stability. The reported settings represent the
best-performing combination among the tested configurations. The fi-
nal training configuration, chosen to facilitate exact replication, is
summarized in Table 1. The Adamax optimizer was selected for its
adaptive learning rate behavior in complex classification tasks [8]. The
dropout rates (0.25, 0.3, 0.4) and the 50-epoch training limit were

stable training given the dataset size. Data augmentation was applied

validation and test splits. All hyperparameters were kept fixed across
the cross-validation experiments and ablation studies to ensure a fair
and reproducible evaluation of the proposed architecture. Using this
fixed configuration, the final model was trained for a total duration
of approximately 32.5 min (1948 s) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU, with an

Visualization of model decision-making using Grad-CAM
To examine model interpretability, Gradient-weighted Class Activa-
tion Mapping (Grad-CAM) was employed to visualize regions of the in-
put MRI scans that most influenced the model’s predictions. Grad-CAM
produces class-discriminative heatmaps that highlight salient image
regions without requiring architectural modifications. Fig. 9 illustrates
the evolution of model attention across multiple convolutional layers
for a correctly classified meningioma sample. Early layers exhibit dif-
fuse responses to general anatomical structures, while deeper layers
progressively focus on the tumor region. This coarse-to-fine local-
ization behavior is consistent with the hierarchical feature learning
characteristics of convolutional neural networks.
To further assess model explainability, Figs. 10 and 11 present Grad-
CAM overlays for both correctly classified and misclassified samples
across the four tumor classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and no
tumor. The top row in each figure illustrates accurate predictions, where
attention heatmaps are well aligned with the tumor mass. In contrast,
the bottom row highlights misclassified cases, revealing that the model
occasionally focuses on irrelevant anatomical structures (e.g., ventricles
or image borders), which may contribute to confusion between tumor
types. For instance, in Fig. 10, several no tumor cases are misclassified
as glioma, with Grad-CAM activations concentrated near artifact regions
or ambiguous tissue boundaries. Similarly, Fig. 11 shows that pituitary
tumors are misinterpreted as glioma or meningioma when the model’s at-
tention drifts toward peripheral features rather than the central lesion.
These observations demonstrate the utility of Grad-CAM not only for
validating correct predictions but also for diagnosing common failure
modes and potential model biases.
A layer-wise Grad-CAM analysis was further conducted on repre-
sentative correct and misclassified cases (Fig. 12). In the correctly
classified example, deeper-layer activations accurately localize the tu-
mor region, while earlier layers exhibit broader responses. In contrast,
misclassified cases show diffuse or misplaced activations and insuf-
ficient focus on diagnostically relevant regions at deeper layers. For

trustworthy predictions. However, standard localization metrics such as
Dice or Intersection over Union (IoU) cannot be computed in this study
due to the absence of pixel-level tumor annotations. Consequently,
unlike Dice or IoU, the proposed metrics do not quantify overlap
with precise tumor boundaries, but instead evaluate attention at the
organ level (brain) rather than at the lesion level. These metrics are
therefore not intended to replace segmentation-based evaluation, but
to provide complementary insight under weakly supervised conditions.

direct comparison with Dice/IoU and a more fine-grained assessment

Real-time brain tumor detection application
To demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed model, we
developed a user-friendly desktop application using Python, Tkinter,
and CustomTkinter for real-time brain tumor detection. The application
allows healthcare professionals to upload MRI scans, initiate model
inference, and receive classification results instantly—streamlining the
diagnostic workflow.
The system supports classification into four categories: no tumor,
pituitary, meningioma, and glioma. It provides both the predicted class
and the associated confidence score. To enhance interpretability, Grad-
CAM visualizations are incorporated to highlight the image regions
most influential in the model’s decision.
Fig. 13 illustrates the application interface. In Fig. 13a, the user has
uploaded an MRI scan and is prompted to classify it. Upon clicking
the ‘‘Classify Image’’ button, the application displays the predicted
tumor type (e.g., pituitary), the confidence score (e.g., 99.98%), and
a Grad-CAM overlay highlighting the tumor region (Fig. 13b).
To support interpretability and streamline clinical workflows, the
interface employs a color-coded scheme—green for no tumor, yellow
for pituitary, orange for meningioma, and red for glioma—allowing rapid
visual assessment. The design prioritizes simplicity and accessibility,
ensuring usability even for non-technical users. Additionally, the sys-
tem operates entirely offline, making it suitable for clinics with limited
internet connectivity or heightened data security requirements.
This application functions as a real-time decision support tool, help-
ing radiologists review cases efficiently and confidently, particularly in
resource-constrained or high-demand clinical settings.

The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of
99.54% while maintaining a lightweight design (5.37M parameters),
enabling real-time inference at approximately 0.66 ms per image
(pure model forward pass). Beyond accuracy, Grad-CAM visualizations
provided clinically meaningful validation through anatomically plau-
sible attention patterns, addressing the critical need for transparency
and interpretability in medical AI systems. Together, these results
demonstrate a strong balance between performance, efficiency, and
explainability, representing a practical step toward clinical integration.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Clinical translation
The framework is designed as an offline decision-support tool,
supporting data privacy and usability in resource-limited clinical envi-
ronments. Its integrated explainability mechanisms facilitate clinician
trust and align with emerging regulatory expectations for transparent
AI-assisted diagnostics.
In real-world clinical settings, MRI data exhibit substantial vari-
ability due to differences in scanner manufacturers, magnetic field
strengths (e.g., 1.5T vs. 3T), and acquisition protocols (e.g., T1, T2,
FLAIR sequences). In addition, patient-specific factors such as age,
tumor characteristics, and anatomical variability further contribute to
data diversity. These factors can introduce domain shifts that may
affect model performance when deployed outside controlled experi-
mental conditions. For example, a model trained predominantly on
T1-weighted contrast-enhanced images may exhibit reduced sensitivity
when applied to non-contrast T2-weighted sequences. Furthermore,
real-world clinical populations may exhibit class distributions that
differ from those in benchmark datasets, which may influence model
calibration and decision thresholds.
Future multicenter validation and prospective clinical studies are
essential to address real-world challenges such as scanner variabil-
ity, protocol heterogeneity, and patient-level diversity, and to support
regulatory approval and clinical adoption.

authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Limitations and future work
A key limitation of this study is the reliance on a single publicly
available dataset, which may not fully capture the diversity and vari-
ability encountered in real-world clinical environments. In particular,
the dataset is curated at the image level and lacks subject-level iden-
tifiers and detailed acquisition metadata (e.g., scanner type, imaging
protocols, and patient demographics), which prevents direct assessment
of cross-institutional generalization.
Although the proposed framework demonstrates strong and con-
sistent performance, including under stratified cross-validation, this
evaluation remains confined to a single data distribution. Consequently,
performance may vary when the model is applied to external datasets
with different imaging characteristics and acquisition conditions. Given
the high classification accuracy achieved, particular care was taken to
minimize the risk of overfitting and data leakage. The model exhibited
consistent performance across cross-validation folds, suggesting stable
learning behavior rather than overfitting to a specific data split.
To mitigate this limitation, strict experimental protocols were
adopted, including complete separation of training, validation, and test
sets, stratified cross-validation, and controlled data augmentation to
simulate real-world variability. Nevertheless, these strategies cannot
fully substitute for true external validation. The held-out test set was
fully isolated and was not used during preprocessing, augmentation, or
hyperparameter tuning. However, due to the absence of subject-level
identifiers, potential hidden correlations cannot be entirely ruled out
and should be considered when interpreting the results.
Future work will therefore focus on external validation using inde-
pendent and multi-institutional MRI datasets to assess robustness under
domain shifts. In addition, federated learning and domain adaptation
strategies will be explored to enable generalization across heteroge-
neous clinical settings while preserving data privacy.
Furthermore, robustness-enhancing strategies such as class-weighted
loss functions and imbalance-aware training schemes will be inves-
tigated to improve performance on rare tumor subtypes and highly
imbalanced data. Future work may also investigate the integration
of uncertainty-aware or adaptive optimization strategies to further
enhance robustness and interpretability under increased data variability,

authors: Helala AlShehri; Luluh Almogbil; Jiyan Alrajhi; Lama Alosaimi; Jawlan Almarri
text:
Conclusion
This study presents an interpretable deep learning framework for
multi-class brain tumor classification from MRI scans. The proposed
model achieves high classification accuracy while maintaining compu-
tational efficiency suitable for practical clinical decision-support sce-
narios. Multi-level Grad-CAM analysis provides clinically meaningful
transparency, while the fully offline desktop implementation supports
potential use in resource-limited settings. While results under stratified
cross-validation demonstrate robust performance, external multicenter
validation remains necessary to further assess generalization across
diverse clinical imaging environments.

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny
venue: Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Volume 322, pages 10â€“22
text:
lead to devastating neurological consequences. In order to preserve vital neurological
function located near the tumor, it is important for the neurosurgeon to be able to identify the
anatomical location of the eloquent cortices, either pre- or intraoperatively.
Traditionally, the eloquent cortices, such as the motor cortex, are identified by direct cortical
stimulation. More recently, blood-oxygen-level-dependent functional MRI (BOLD fMRI)
has been used successfully in planning and carrying out the resection of brain tumors [3,4].
However, it has been found that BOLD maps adjacent to brain tumors have limited accuracy
[5–9]. BOLD fMRI is based on the premise that there is a coupling between neuronal
activity and blood flow. However, the neovasculature of malignant tumors is known to be
abnormal both structurally and functionally [8], including changes in vascular reactivity
[10–14]. Since BOLD fMRI measures the vascular response (rather than neuronal
activation), in patients with malignant brain tumors the abnormal tumor neovascularity does
not respond as vigorously to increased neuronal activity, which leads to a muted BOLD
response [15]. A number of recent studies have correlated the anatomical location of
neurovascular uncoupling, defined by quantitative measurements of cerebrovascular
reactivity, with false negative BOLD fMRI results [7,16–18]. Consequently, models
assuming a uniform rather than an abnormal hemodynamic response function over the whole
brain may not be sufficient to detect activation in an eloquent cortex influenced by the
tumor. Data analysis based on the uniform hemodynamic response functions may lead to
missed activation (or false negative errors) in the BOLD statistical parametric maps.
A possible way to overcome the limitation of false negative results caused by the presence of
abnormal tumor neovasculature and resultant neurovascular uncoupling is to measure
vasoreactivity and to incorporate these data into the BOLD fMRI analysis. One way to
independently measure vasoreactivity is by breath-holding, which leads to hypoxia and
hypercapnia, which under normal circumstances leads to vasodilatation of the cerebral
vasculature [14,17,18]. These changes in vasodilatation can be measured by fMRI in the
same way as BOLD fMRI responses to routine task paradigms are measured. The
assumption is that the hemodynamic response function of abnormal neovasculature is altered

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny
venue: Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Volume 322, pages 10â€“22
text:
oreactivity is by breath-holding, which leads to hypoxia and
hypercapnia, which under normal circumstances leads to vasodilatation of the cerebral
vasculature [14,17,18]. These changes in vasodilatation can be measured by fMRI in the
same way as BOLD fMRI responses to routine task paradigms are measured. The
assumption is that the hemodynamic response function of abnormal neovasculature is altered
from the norm in the same way irrespective of the stimulus (breath-holding or task fMRI). If
this assumption holds true, then one should be able to detect BOLD activation even in areas
of abnormal neovasculature by searching for coherence between the hemodynamic response
function in the breath-holding and routine task fMRI paradigms.
The purpose of this study is to derive a voxel-specific model that takes into account altered
hemodynamics by comparing BOLD response maps obtained during motor and language
tasks with and without the incorporation of a breath-holding task. It is based on the
observation that the response to breath-holding and tasks shows a statistical dependency that
is described here for the first time. We hypothesize that BOLD response maps of motor and
language tasks computed by using this dependency will be overall similar to standard
activation maps based on uniform hemodynamic response models but will also show new
areas of activation that accurately reflect increase in neuronal activity due to altered
hemodynamics of the tumors.

Materials And Methods
The research performed was in full compliance with the Code of Ethics of the World
Medical Association (Declaration of Helsinki). The institutional review boards of Memorial
Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medicine approved the study. Informed
Consent was not obtained on patients, as the study was a retrospective review.
Patient information
Each patient underwent an anatomical brain MRI and an fMRI as part of their routine
preoperative care. All underwent resection of the tumor within two days of the MRI.
Pathological examination of the resected tumors revealed the diagnosis of glioblastoma
multiforme (N = 9), anaplastic astrocytoma (N = 1), low-grade glioma (N = 5), or metastasis
(N = 1). See Table 1 for demographic data.
fMRI and anatomical MRI scanning
Patients—In total, 18 fMRI scans were performed on 16 patients on a 3.0 Tesla GEMS
(Waukesha, WI) clinical MRI system with an 8-channel head coil. Breath-hold and task-
specific fMRI were performed using echo-planar fMRI (TR = 4 s; TE = 40 ms; 90° flip
angle; 128 × 128 matrix; 240 mm FOV; 4.5 mm slice thickness). Patients also underwent an
anatomical brain MRI. The fMRI paradigms performed by patients were dictated by the
clinical scenario. In the present study, we analyzed the most relevant fMRI paradigms. For
example, if the tumor was in close proximity to the pre-central gyrus, we analyzed the motor
fMRI.
Six off/on blocks of 15 samples each were used in both breath-holding and task fMRI: 5
samples on (corresponding to inhalation and breath-holding, or task, respectively), and 10
samples off (corresponding to normal breathing or resting/no task, respectively). During
fMRI, patients either performed a motor and/or a language task, following aural instructions.
See Table 1 for all tasks performed. Motor tasks consisted of bilateral finger tapping, foot
and hand tapping, and tongue curling. In the finger tapping task the patient was asked to
touch with the thumb consecutively the other four fingers in succession and start over again.
It was self-paced at a rate of approximately two fingers per second, and had been practiced
before the fMRI session. In the tongue curling task, patients were asked to make a small
lateral movement of the tongue without opening the mouth. In the “foot and hand tapping”
task, the finger tapping task was combined with foot-tapping. Language tasks consisted of

fMRI data analysis
All analysis of fMRI and breath-hold echo planar imaging (EPI) data was done with AFNI

Preprocessing was performed as follows: Motion correction, thresholding of brain versus
background, voxelwise linear detrending of time series, and in-plane spatial smoothing with
a Gaussian kernel of full-width-half-maximum of 3 voxels.
The severity of head motion in the breath-holding and the task scans was quantified by using
the six rotational and translational parameter time series resulting from the three-

mean squared sum of the three translational parameters was added to the mean squared sum

scans (rank 1 corresponding to strongest motion) and are provided in Table 1.

section_heading: Task response maps based on correlation
text:
Task response maps based on correlation
A task indicator function It consisting of the numbers 1 and 0 was used to describe the
timing of the motor and language paradigms, as well as the identical breath-hold timing. It is
defined as It = 1 for breath-holding or task samples and It = 0 for normal breathing or rest
samples. It was also used as an approximation for the hemodynamic response function
template, or ideal function, ht. The task response maps were defined by correlating the signal
in each voxel, yt, with the task-indicator function, yielding a Pearson’s linear correlation
coefficient R(It, yt). A significant positive task response was defined as R(It, yt) > 0.55. This
value corresponds to an average p-value of p = 10−5, set as an ad-hoc threshold in numerical
simulations in order to compare with the coherence (see below). The one-sided tail
probability for Pearson’s linear correlation of R(It, yt) = 0.55 is, however, p = 1.3 × 10−8 for
the used sample size. In other words, the latter p-value determines single voxel significance.
This is a quite conservative threshold even if the multiple testing problem is taken into
account. In addition, a simple cluster-wise threshold was used; only clusters with at least two
adjacent voxels of activation were retained in the final maps of correlation coefficients. An
example for this map is shown in Fig. 5C.

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny
venue: Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Volume 322, pages 10â€“22
section_heading: Task response maps based on coherence
text:
Task response maps based on coherence
The spectral coherence between two signals is smaller than or equal to 1 and equals 1 for
linear dependence. The maximum value of the coherence between It and yt, C(It, yt), in an
interval [0.006 Hz, 0.028 Hz], centered at the block design task frequency of 0.017 Hz, was
used as test statistics. The significance threshold corresponding to an average p-value of p =
10−5 was determined by Monte-Carlo simulations, and found to be C(It, yt) = 0.79. Only
clusters with at least two adjacent voxels of activation were retained in the final coherence
maps. An example for this map is shown in Fig. 5D.

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny
venue: Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Volume 322, pages 10â€“22
text:
Vasoreactivity-informed response map
The conventional assumption in the most basic linear modeling of BOLD responses is the
model
yt = aht + εt,
(1)
in which ht is the hemodynamic response, a is a coefficient to be estimated from yt, and εt is
noise not captured by the model. The hemodynamic response usually is considered
independent of location, or uniform, throughout the brain. To take into account the possible
dependence of ht on location in the brain, which is necessary to assess the impact of altered
vascular reserve by the presence of tumors, here we assumed that ht varies depending on
brain location. Specifically, we assume that ht can be modeled from measuring the
vasoreactivity xt, obtained from breath-holding scans on the same patient and with the same
timing as the task scan. This assumption was motivated by the observation that the task
response yt and the breath-hold response xt were very often simultaneously correlated or
anti-correlated to It in voxels in which significant task activation was observed (see Figure 2
and Results section). We call this observation the “vaso-task dependency.” The breath-hold
response is known to be significantly different from task responses [20]. Modeling the

between these responses. Therefore, for this unknown dependence between task and breath-

ht = L0 Xt ,
(2)
where Xt is a local vasoreactivity template derived from the breath-hold signal xt as defined

yt = L Xt + εt,
(3)
with again an unknown general linear dependence L. The degree of dependency can thus be
estimated by the coherence between Xt and yt [21]. The regional vascular response template
Xt was computed by averaging the breath-hold signal xt over the six repetitions per
experiment, for each voxel independently. The resulting signal of length corresponding to
one breath-hold repetition was then concatenated six times to obtain a template time series

used. The same statistical thresholds for coherence as determined in the second step were
used. Only clusters with at least two adjacent voxels of activation were retained in the final
maps of coherencies. A pictorial representation of this method is shown in Fig. 1, and an

The vasoreactivity maps were computed only for illustration and are provided in the

A vaso-task dependency map was computed by correlating the task response signal in each

simultaneously correlated or anti-correlated to It in voxels in which significant task
activation was observed (Figs. 2, 3, and S1). The degree of this dependency has been
estimated by the coherence C(Xt, yt) between Xt and yt above (“Vasoreactivity-informed

Specifically, when R(Xt, yt) < 0, breath-hold and task response are anti-correlated (upper left

Comparison of patient activation maps with control activation maps
In order to compare the degree of change in activation maps for the coherence-based
standard analysis and the coherence based vasoreactivity-informed response map, we
performed a concordance analysis of activation maps by using the Dice similarity coefficient
[22], a spatial overlap index. Such an analysis has been used before for comparing activation
maps of presurgical fMRI experiments [23]. The Dice coefficient is defined as D = 2 |P ∩C|
|P| + |C|,
where P and C are the sets of significantly activated patient and control subject voxels,
respectively, and | . | is the cardinality of the set, i.e. the number of elements in the set. The
Dice coefficient takes on values between 0 and 1, where 1 is attained for maximum
concordance. Dice coefficients for motor tasks were computed for patient IDs 1 to 10 in
Table 1, and control subject IDs 1b to 6b (Supplementary Figure 3). Dice coefficients for
language tasks were computed for patient IDs 11, 12a, 13, 14, 15, 16a, and control subject
IDs 1a to 6a. The second language tasks for subjects 12 and 16 were not included to avoid

assess the difference between control and patient groups. When the second language tasks

result of statistical significance did not depend on this selection.

Dependency between the task response and the breath-hold response
We found that very often a significant positive task response was associated with either a

Comparison of the standard method of analysis and the proposed vasoreactivity-informed
method
For control subjects, the coherence-based standard analysis and the coherence based
vasoreactivity-informed method yielded overall very similar results. These are shown for all
of the control subjects in Supplementary Figure S3, columns 2 and 5.
For patients, review of the fMRI scans superimposed on the anatomical images
demonstrated similar results between the standard method of analysis and the proposed
vasoreactivity-informed method. The main difference was that the coherence maps including
the vaso-task dependency showed more areas of activation adjacent to the tumor. This was a
retrospective study and in the actual clinical presentation of each specific case, the standard
method was used; the vaso-task dependency analysis was performed after surgery on pre-
surgical data. Hence, we could estimate the clinical utility of the proposed vasoreactivity-
informed method in a retrospective manner only. Nevertheless, we judged that the new
information made available from coherence analysis and particularly when vaso-task
dependency was incorporated (information which was not appreciated using the standard
method) would have been clinically meaningful in 9 of 16 cases. Our results are illustrated
by the following three examples.

than during task. Whereas for the cases with the strongest motion in the breath-hold scan or
the task scan no change was observed, a further relationship between the degree of motion

Comparison with healthy control group
As already mentioned, all of the control subjects showed the same nontrivial dependency
between task and breath-hold responses as the patient group (Supplementary Figure S1), and
the coherence-based standard analysis yielded overall very similar results as the coherence
based vasoreactivity-informed response map (Supplementary Figure S3, columns 2 and 5). It
remains to be shown that the application of the proposed methods to control subjects yields
fewer changes in activation maps than in the presence of tumors. The rationale is that tumors
change vascular response, which can then be picked up by the proposed methods, but in
control subjects the vascular response should have a more static dependence on breath-
holding, and less additional information can be extracted from the data. Computation of the
Dice coefficient D, which measures the similarity of sets (see Methods), to the coherence-
based standard analysis and the vasoreactivity-informed response map, yielded the following
mean values (standard deviations) and statistical differences. For the motor tasks,
D(patients) = 0.61 (0.17), D(controls) = 0.93 (0.02), p = 0.0005 (t = 4.5). For the language
tasks, D(patients) = 0.59 (0.11), D(controls) = 0.85 (0.04), p = 0.0003 (t = 5.3). Overall, the
application of the proposed method yielded significantly smaller changes in activation maps
for control subjects when compared to patients.
Summary
In summary, we found significant changes in activation in about half of the subjects when
including information from the vaso-task dependency. This finding may potentially lead to
altering the neurosurgical decision-making process, which would require a larger clinical
trial to decide.

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny

Discussion
To map eloquent cortical areas in patients with brain tumors more precisely and to limit false
negative BOLD fMRI results, we attempted to correct for altered hemodynamic response,
which is characteristic of malignant tumors, by performing a simple breath-hold task and
incorporating this information into the modeling of the BOLD fMRI response. The breath-
hold BOLD response was often positively or negatively related to the motor or language task
BOLD response in the same patient, depending on the region, as illustrated by scatterplots of
correlation coefficients of both responses with the task indicator function (Fig. 2). A closer
investigation of the BOLD response near a tumor in case examples showed various origins
for altered hemodynamics, such as delays and shortened duration of responses.

authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny
venue: Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Volume 322, pages 10â€“22
text:
Breath-hold hypercapnia
We have based our analysis on the well-known vasodilatory effects of CO2 in brain
vasculature, which may be observed with BOLD fMRI imaging. We used the relatively
crude and not well-controlled method of breath-holding to induce hypercapnia and measure
vasoreactivity. The effectiveness of the proposed vasoreactivity-informed method relies on
the compliance of patients with both the breath-hold and the performed motor or language
tasks. Breath-hold compliance can be very low in the clinical setting [4].Therefore, care had
to be taken to ensure breath-holding. In our study, we believe that all 16 patients indeed did
perform a satisfactory breath-hold, based on the vaso-task dependency data (Fig. 2). Another
problem was head motion, often enhanced in tumor patients, by difficulties in performing
motor tasks with keeping the rest of the body perfectly still, or language tasks without
unwanted talking. Motion may affect both task response and vaso-task dependency mapping,
either causing false-positive or false-negative activations. In our study, motion was
summarized as the relative rank of severity of motion for each patient in Table 1. We would
not exclude the possibility that motion caused false activations in particular for patients with
a low rank in Table 1.
Whereas breath-holding is very easy to apply in the clinical population without the need of
additional equipment and personnel, other more direct methods of hypercapnia, for example
by delivering pre-mixed gas [24], may be better controlled.
BOLD normalization
The vasodilatory effects of varying CO2 content may be utilized in various ways to calibrate
and improve functional BOLD detection [25,11,5,6]. Other hypercapnia-based fMRI task-
response normalization methods [26–28] are usually based on a local re-scaling of the task
response by the hypercapnic response amplitude or parameters derived from it. They have
proven to be useful in particular to control inter-subject variability among healthy subjects
[29–32]. The method proposed here differs from this approach by utilizing our observation
that vasoreactivity and task response have a typical statistical relationship (“vaso-task
dependency”). Thus, the method proposed here can be seen as a generalization, as a local
linear relationship between hypercapnic and task response is estimated by the coherence.
This relationship includes signal changes over time such as hemodynamic delays [33] and
paradoxical BOLD response [34,35].

aiming at separating response from the capillary bed from venous response for the tumor

Whether the observed vaso-task dependency in healthy control subjects and subjects with
brain tumors could be of use in other cerebrovascular diseases such as arteriovenous
malformations or cavernomas, which are known to affect the BOLD signal as well [36–38],
requires further research.
Clinical utility
The apparent ability of the proposed vasoreactivity-informed method to identify eloquent
cortices adjacent to brain tumors not seen with the standard method allows us to postulate
the clinical utility of the proposed approach. We were able to perform the vasoreactivity-
informed method retrospectively only. However, our preliminary results in this study are
convincing enough to pursue a future prospective study that would compare the standard
method to our proposed vasoreactivity-informed method and would use intra-operative
cortical stimulation as the gold standard. For example, in Fig. 5, using the standard method,
we were unable to define the language laterality to the operating neurosurgeon and we were
unable to define the relationship of the tumor to the adjacent eloquent cortices (Wernicke’s
area). However, when we retrospectively re-analyzed the case (after the operation had been
performed) using the proposed vasoreactivity-informed method, not only Wernicke’s area
became clearly visible, but we were also able to unambiguously identify Heschl’s gyrus.
Had this information been available to the operating neurosurgeon prior to the operation, it
would have proved invaluable by clearly identifying the language lateralization (in this case,
ipsilateral to the tumor) and the exact anatomical relationship between the tumor and the
functional language area to be avoided during tumor resection. This information would have
indicated the necessity for “awake mapping” during the operation, which would have
required awakening the patient for anesthesia and asking the patient to perform various
language paradigms during direct cortical stimulation to identify Wernicke’s area. The
accurate localization of Wernicke’s areas in the vasoreactivity-informed response map would

anatomical relationship of the tumor to Wernicke’s area was clearly displayed and the
possibility of cortical reorganization was discounted.
In one case, we were able to identify activation in an eloquent cortex contralateral to the
FLAIR-defined tumor (Fig. 7). Analysis of the bilateral finger-tapping task using standard
methodology failed to elicit activation in the expected location of the finger homunculus in
the pre-central (motor) gyrus. However, analysis using the proposed vasoreactivity-informed
method was able to accomplish this task. Since pathologically defined malignant tumor cells
and abnormalities in MRI breath-hold characteristics extend large distances past the borders
of the MRI-defined gliomas [29], the case examples in this study raises the intriguing
possibility of the correction of false negative BOLD fMRI results using the here proposed
vasoreactivity-informed method even at a distance from the MRI defined borders of the
tumor.
Subject 12 performed two different language tasks, “Categories” (Fig. 6) and “Letters” (Fig.
S2). Substantial changes in the vasoreactivity-informed response map were only seen for the
former but not the latter task. Whether this difference was caused by the involvement of
different language areas, one of which was not affected by the tumor, differences in task
attention, head motion, or other unknown factors cannot be assessed based on the available
data.
In this study, we did not investigate whether altered hemodynamics correlated with
proximity to the eloquent areas of the tumor, the pathology, or the related task. All analyses
were performed retrospectively; therefore, we were not able to correlate the results obtained
to direct intraoperative cortical mapping of eloquent cortices. More experiments are
necessary to investigate these concerns. However, overall, our results suggest that our way of
including vasoreactivity information may enhance functional mapping in patients with
compromised hemodynamics secondary to tumor pathology. Our future prospective study
will include deriving heuristic methods to assess improvement in sensitivity or specificity.

Statistical thresholds
In presurgical planning fMRI, as in any other fMRI study, it is imperative to use an adequate
statistical threshold for the statistical parametric maps. Whereas in neuroimaging studies
with normal subjects statistical thresholds are often set to a fixed value for all subjects
encountered in a group study, for clinical patients with brain tumors an adequate choice of
thresholds requires more thought. One reason is that often a considerably altered
hemodynamic response weakens the BOLD signal observed, as has been demonstrated
recently in pre-motor areas of clinical patients performing a motor task [7]. Another reason
is that there is an on-average stronger head motion, which reduces signal, since clinical
studies cannot be performed in the same controlled way as research studies. They also have
to take disease-related task performance limitations such as fatigue into account. Whereas
this does not mean that statistical thresholds can be set arbitrarily, often in clinical practice
thresholds are chosen less conservatively than in research studies. In order to provide an

title: A vascular-task response dependency and its application in functional imaging of brain tumors
authors: Henning U. Voss; Kyung K. Peck; Nicole M. Petrovich Brennan; Eduard L. Pogosbekyan; Natalia E. Zakharova; Artyom I. Batalov; Igor N. Pronin; Alexander A. Potapov; Andrei I. Holodny

text:
Conclusion
Preoperative BOLD fMRI is limited by a muted BOLD response caused by abnormal
vasoreactivity and resultant neurovascular uncoupling adjacent to malignant brain tumors.
We proposed to overcome this limitation and more accurately identify eloquent areas near
brain tumors by independently assessing vasoreactivity using breath-holding. The observed
relationship between task and breath-hold response, the vaso-task dependency, was then
incorporated into the BOLD standard method of analysis using coherence. The coherence
maps demonstrated clinically meaningful areas of activation that were not seen using the
standard method of analysis in 9 of 16 cases. This included localization of language areas
adjacent to brain tumors. The present preliminary results demonstrate the principle that the
neurovascular uncoupling known to affect the accuracy of BOLD fMRI adjacent to brain
tumors may be, at least partially, overcome by incorporating an independent measurement of
vasoreactivity into the BOLD standard method of analysis. These initial, limited results need
to be substantiated by further, prospective studies.

Fig. 1: A schematic demonstrating the method used to incorporate breath-holding data into the
BOLD fMRI analysis.
“A” represents the standard method of analysis of a language fMRI data set, where the
BOLD fMRI data is compared to a standard ideal hemodynamic response function (HRF).
The fMRI data in Broca’s area (green) and Wernicke’s area (red) matches the standard HRF
(in black), but the fMRI data in the occipital lobe (blue; not related to language function)
does not match the standard HFR. This method results in “activation” in Broca’s area and
Wernicke’s area but not in the occipital lobe. In “B”, the shaded area represents a tumor with
abnormal neurovascular reactivity (neurovascular uncoupling), which leads to a muting of
the BOLD HRF. Consequently, the HRF in Broca’s area no longer matches the ideal HRF
and Broca’s area is no longer “activated”. “C” demonstrates the HRF in each region during
breath-holding. In Wernicke’s area and in the occipital lobe, the breath-holding HRF
remains normal, but in Broca’s area, the breath-holding HRF is muted. In the enhanced
vasoreactivity-informed method described in the present paper, instead of comparing the
HRF obtained during the fMRI examination to an ideal, we compared it to the breath-
holding HRF–an independently obtained measure of the HRF. In the illustration, both
Broca’s and Wernicke’s area now demonstrate “activation”.

authors: Alberto G. Valerio, Katya Trufanova, Salvatore de Benedictis, Gennaro Vessio, Giovanna Castellano
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, Volume 270, Article 108922
text:
Abstract
Background and Objective: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly advanced medical imaging, yet the
opacity of deep learning models remains challenging, often reducing the trust of medical professionals towards
AI-driven diagnoses. As a result, there is a strong focus on making AI models more transparent and interpretable
to boost healthcare providers’ confidence in these technologies.
Methods: This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance AI explainability in critical medical tasks
by integrating state-of-the-art semantic segmentation models with atlas-based mapping and Large Language
Models (LLMs) to produce comprehensive, human-readable medical reports. The proposed framework ensures
that the generated outputs are factual and contextually rich. Our anti-hallucination design, which combines
structured JSON with prompt constraints, is a critical innovation compared to most naïve LLM report
generation methods, thereby enhancing the transparency and interpretability of AI systems.
Results: Experimental results show that the SegResNet model achieves high segmentation accuracy, while
LLMs (Gemma, Llama, and Mistral) demonstrate diverse strengths in generating explanatory reports. Numerous
metrics have been employed to assess the quality and effectiveness of generated textual explanations, such as
lexical diversity, readability, coherence, and information coverage.
Conclusions: The method has been specifically tested for brain tumor detection in glioma, one of the most
aggressive forms of cancer, and subsequently applied to multiple sclerosis lesion detection to further validate
its generalizability across various medical imaging scenarios, thereby contributing to the trustworthiness of
healthcare AI applications.
Reproducibility: The complete source code for implementing the framework and reproducing the results is
publicly available, along with full pipeline examples demonstrating each step – from segmentation to report
generation – at the following repository: https://github.com/albertovalerio/from-segmentation-to-explanation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly prominent role
in healthcare, particularly in medical imaging, where deep learning
models have achieved remarkable performance in tasks such as disease
detection, classification, and segmentation. However, despite these ad-

adoption. The inability to understand how and why a model arrives
at a particular decision raises concerns among healthcare profession-
als, especially when diagnostic decisions can directly affect patient
outcomes [1,2].

aiming to enhance transparency and foster trust in AI-assisted diagnos-

While visual and textual explainability have often been treated as
separate modalities, their integration holds the key to more compre-
hensive and clinically useful AI explanations. Visual cues can guide
attention to relevant image regions, while text can convey diagnostic
reasoning and contextual interpretations. When appropriately com-
bined, these two modalities can complement each other, reflecting the
way clinicians interpret and report findings.
This paper presents a novel framework that integrates visual expla-
nations and LLMs to generate clinically interpretable reports from 3D
brain MRI segmentations automatically. Unlike traditional approaches
that rely on pre-existing text corpora or external knowledge bases, our
methodology generates explanations from scratch, grounded directly in
the model’s outputs and anatomical context.
The framework is applied primarily to the detection of glioma
tumors in adult brain MRIs, and its generalizability is further evaluated
on a separate dataset focused on multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation.
The process begins with the application of state-of-the-art deep learning

segmentation maps are then enriched with anatomical context through
a mapping module based on the Julich Brain Atlas, which localizes each
detected region within specific brain structures.
These anatomically grounded maps are transformed into structured
intermediate representations – formatted in JSON – that encode spa-
tial and diagnostic attributes in a format interpretable by LLMs. This
structured input constrains the language model’s generative process,
ensuring that the final textual reports remain factually consistent and
clinically relevant. The generated explanations are designed to emulate
the style and reasoning found in radiology reports, making the outputs
directly useful for medical professionals.

assessment strategy that combines quantitative metrics – such as read-
ability, coherence, and lexical diversity – with domain-specific criteria
related to diagnostic completeness and clinical accuracy. Through this
multi-faceted evaluation, we aim to validate both the interpretability
and the practical utility of the generated reports.

Background and objective
Explainable AI has gained significant traction in healthcare, par-
ticularly in medical image analysis. XAI techniques aim to enhance
the transparency and interpretability of deep learning models, enabling
medical professionals to understand the decision-making process and
build trust in AI-based systems [6].
A substantial body of research in XAI for medical imaging fo-
cused on generating visual explanations that elucidate the model’s
decision-making process. Common approaches include saliency maps,
gradient-based methods (e.g., Grad-CAM [3]), and relevance propa-
gation techniques (e.g., Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, LRP [7]).
These methods visually represent which regions of an input image are
most influential in the model’s predictions.
Specifically, in brain tumor detection and segmentation from MRI
data, several studies have integrated XAI techniques with deep learning
models to enhance trust in AI-based computer-aided diagnostic systems.
Zeineldin et al. [8] proposed the NeuroXAI framework, which combines
deep neural networks with various XAI methods to generate visual
explanation maps for brain tumor classification and segmentation tasks.
Similarly, different studies have also integrated XAI techniques to
provide visual explanations in the context of multiple sclerosis lesion
segmentation from MRI data. Sadeghibakhi et al. [9] utilized M3d-CAM
to generate 3D attention maps, visually highlighting the regions in the
input images that are most influential in the model’s predictions.
While these visual explanation methods have proven useful, they
have limitations in providing comprehensive clinical explanations. As
discussed in the introductory section, heatmaps and similar visual-

decision-making [4].

in generating textual explanations in natural language for medical

Framework overview
We propose an innovative and explainable approach that combines
advanced deep learning techniques with Large Language Models to gen-
erate interpretable medical reports in natural language. The proposed
approach differs from conventional techniques in the scientific litera-
ture, as it generates textual explanations without relying on existing
text related to medical images or external knowledge sources.
An essential advantage of LLMs, in fact, lies in their ability to
leverage the extensive knowledge gained through pre-training on vast
textual corpora. This training equips LLMs with a comprehensive un-
derstanding of medical knowledge, encompassing disease pathologies,
clinical manifestations, and treatment methods. Such a rich foundation
enables LLMs to effectively apply this understanding to specific med-
ical image-processing tasks, provided they are supplied with accurate
factual data. By utilizing this rich pre-trained knowledge, LLMs can gen-
erate accurate, relevant, and contextually appropriate textual explana-
tions that reduce hallucinations commonly associated with generative
models, thereby enhancing the overall interpretability and usefulness
of AI-generated insights in medical imaging and assisted diagnostics.
The proposed methodology comprises four stages, as shown in Fig.
1:
• Semantic segmentation: A segmentation model processes 3D brain
MRI volumes to segment pathological regions such as gliomas.
• Brain atlas mapping: The segmented tumor regions are registered
to the MNI152 standard space and mapped onto the Julich Brain
Atlas to determine the most affected anatomical areas.
• JSON construction: The extracted spatial and quantitative
information – including affected regions, tumor distribution, seg-
mentation confidence, and model metadata – is encoded into a
structured JSON file.
• LLM prompting: The JSON file is used to prompt advanced LLMs
(Gemma, Llama, Mistral), which generate natural language med-
ical reports describing the tumor’s location, extent, and potential
clinical relevance.

and then to multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation in 3D brain MRI.
