title: From segmentation to explanation: Generating textual reports from MRI with LLMs
authors: Alberto G. Valerio, Katya Trufanova, Salvatore de Benedictis, Gennaro Vessio, Giovanna Castellano
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, Volume 270, Article 108922
text:
Data
We used the dataset associated with the first task of the BraTS 2023
challenge, organized by the Radiological Society of North America
(RSNA), the American Society of Neuroradiology (ASNR), and the
Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Interventions (MIC-
CAI) society. Specifically, the dataset comprises scans from 1470 adult
patients affected by brain glioma tumors [15–19].
Each MRI scan in the BraTS 2023 dataset is provided as a NIfTI file
and includes the following four MRI modalities:
• Post-contrast T1-weighted (T1Gd): T1 scan taken after a contrast
agent injection.
• Native (T1): Captures the brain’s natural state.
• T2 Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (T2-FLAIR): Suppresses
the signal from free water, making it easier to see lesions and
other abnormalities.
• T2-weighted (T2): Highlights fluid-filled areas.
The imaging data underwent preprocessing steps, including co-
registration to a standard anatomical template, interpolation to a uni-
form resolution of 1 mm3, and skull stripping [15]. An example of the
MRI modalities in the BraTS 2023 dataset is shown in Fig. 2.
One to four expert raters have manually annotated all images in
the dataset following a standardized annotation protocol, with anno-
tations approved by experienced neuroradiologists. The annotations
include the GD-enhancing tumor (ET), the peritumoral edematous/in-
vaded tissue (ED), and the necrotic tumor core (NCR). The sub-regions
considered for evaluation were defined as follows:
• Enhancing tumor (ET): Areas showing hyper-intensity in the T1Gd
modality compared to T1 and healthy white matter in T1Gd.
• Tumor core (TC): Comprises the ET and NCR parts of the tumor,
typically resected during surgery.
• Whole tumor (WT): The complete extent of the disease, including
the TC and ED, typically represented by a hyper-intense signal in
the FLAIR modality.

Semantic segmentation
The first stage involves preprocessing the imaging data and per-
forming data augmentation to enhance the quality and diversity of the
training dataset. Intensity normalization was applied to mitigate differ-
ences in intensity distributions across scanners and imaging protocols.
The image intensities were normalized based on the mean and standard
deviation of the non-zero voxel values within each channel using the
formula:
Normalized Intensity = Image Intensity −Mean
Standard Deviation
.
(1)
Inspired by previous approaches in the literature [20,21], we also
applied data augmentation techniques, including random flipping along
the three spatial axes, random spatial cropping, and random intensity
scaling and shifting. These techniques increase the diversity of the
training data and improve the model’s generalization ability.
We explored different state-of-the-art deep learning models for se-
mantic segmentation:
• Residual U-Net [22]: This model enhances the classic U-Net archi-
tecture by incorporating residual units in both the encoding and
decoding paths. It uses parametric rectified linear unit (PReLU)
activations and instance normalization. The encoding path em-
ploys residual units with varying strides for downsampling, while
the decoding path uses transposed convolutions for learnable
upsampling.
• SegResNet [23]: Designed for 3D medical image segmentation,
SegResNet is a 3D CNN based on the residual network (ResNet)
design. It features an encoder–decoder structure with four down-
sampling blocks in the encoder and three upsampling blocks in
the decoder.
• SwinUNETR [24]: This model combines a hierarchical Swin
Transformer encoder with a CNN-based decoder in a U-shaped
architecture. Developed for multi-modal 3D brain tumor segmen-
tation, it achieved top performance in the BraTS 2021 challenge.
SwinUNETR processes 3D MRI data by dividing it into non-
overlapping patches and employs a shifted windowing approach
for efficient modeling of long-range dependencies.
To prevent data leakage, a stratified subject-wise splitting of the
dataset was employed, ensuring data from the same patient was present
in either the training or testing set but not in both [25,26].

Brain atlas mapping
In the second stage, we mapped the segmented ROIs (i.e., the tumor
core) to specific brain areas using the Julich Brain Atlas [27], a unique
and comprehensive three-dimensional atlas resulting as a culmination
of 25 years of research. It provides detailed probabilistic maps of
over 200 cortical areas and subcortical nuclei in the human brain,
all based on cytoarchitectonic differences. This atlas stands out for
its ability to represent the structural and functional organization of
the brain, capturing inter-individual variations through the mapping
of postmortem brains.
The mapping process involved overlaying the ROIs onto the stan-
dard MNI152 brain space. From there, we generated a point set rep-
resentation of the tumor core voxels, which were then assigned to
the corresponding brain regions in the labeled atlas map. An example
of this brain atlas mapping process for brain tumor segmentation is
illustrated in Fig. 3.
Through this process, we identified the top five most affected brain
regions and quantified the tumor volume in each region. This stage is a
significant step in understanding the impact of pathological conditions
on specific brain areas.

JSON construction
We constructed a structured JSON file in the third stage to encapsu-
late the relevant information extracted from the semantic segmentation
and brain atlas mapping stages. This step is crucial for providing the
LLM with structured, factual information, thereby mitigating the risk of
hallucinations—a common issue language models face when generating
text without a factual basis. The JSON file serves as a source of truth,
ensuring that the LLM’s outputs remain consistent with the quantitative
analysis and do not deviate into unreliable or fictional content.
The JSON file contains comprehensive information extracted from
the previous stages for the brain tumor segmentation task. Specifically,
it includes:
• The top five affected brain regions as determined during the brain
atlas mapping stage, along with their respective percentages of
tumor occupation and the percentage of each region affected.
• The color-coding scheme used for the semantic segmentation
masks, associating specific colors with the tumor core, peritu-
moral edema, and GD-enhancing tumor.
• Performance metrics for the semantic segmentation, including
Dice scores and Hausdorff distances for enhancing tumor, tumor
core, whole tumor, and their averages.
• The name of the model used for semantic segmentation.

prompting stage can access accurate, quantitative data derived from the
image analysis, facilitating the generation of factual and trustworthy

Textual explainability
The LLMs employed in our framework – Gemma, Llama, and Mistral
– exhibited varying performance levels in generating textual expla-
nations for the segmentation task. Each model demonstrated unique
strengths across different aspects of text generation. We evaluated the
performance of these LLMs using several metrics: lexical diversity,
readability, coherence, and coverage of information. We recognize the
critical importance of refining prompt engineering to ensure consis-
tent and reliable report generation across different LLMs. To address
this concern, we emphasize that an empirical selection process was
conducted, prioritizing a prompt design that optimizes coherence and
comprehensive coverage while minimizing inter-model performance
differences. Table 6 summarizes the evaluation results for the brain
tumor segmentation task. For each LLM, we report the average perfor-
mance across all generated reports in the test set, along with the stan-
dard deviation of each metric, to provide insight into the consistency
of the outputs.
The results in Table 6 highlight the diverse strengths among the
models. Gemma demonstrated superior lexical richness, achieving the
highest Type-Token Ratio of 0.351 and the lowest Maas’ Index of 0.023,
indicating a rich and diverse vocabulary. Mistral led in coherence with
a score of 0.357. Llama slightly outperformed the other models in read-
ability with a Flesch Reading Ease Score of 37.204, Embedding-based
Coverage (0.433) and Token-based Coverage (0.305). An example of
the output generated by Llama for the brain tumor segmentation is
shown in Fig. 6.

title: From segmentation to explanation: Generating textual reports from MRI with LLMs
authors: Alberto G. Valerio, Katya Trufanova, Salvatore de Benedictis, Gennaro Vessio, Giovanna Castellano
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, Volume 270, Article 108922
text:
Error evaluation
Although this approach offers substantial benefits, it has shortcom-
ings and could be further refined. For instance, our top-performing
model achieves an average Dice Score of 0.90 for segmentation mask
generation in the brain tumor task. Nevertheless, even minor inaccura-
cies in these masks can lead to ambiguous visual explanations. These
imprecisions can also cascade into subsequent analyses, potentially
leading to misinterpretations of the tumor’s dimensions, shape, spread,
and potential effects on brain functionality. The model’s segmentation
errors, whether over-segmentation (excessive marking of tumor area)
or under-segmentation (omitting tumor parts) are distributed across
the entire tumor region. In our framework, we introduced a specific
mitigation strategy to reduce the impact of such errors on the report
generation process. By deliberately restricting the input to the five
brain areas most significantly affected by the disease, the pipeline limits
the propagation of false positives and false negatives to the textual
output. This targeted filtering is a purposeful design choice within
our framework and should not be considered an inherent property
of all segmentation-to-report pipelines. This constraint, while limiting,
safeguards against propagating segmentation errors.
To quantitatively assess the impact of segmentation inaccuracies
and further validate the applied mitigation strategy, we conducted a
comparative analysis across the entire test set. Specifically, we exam-
ined the brain regions extracted using the segmentation masks gener-
ated by the SegResNet model against their corresponding ground truth.
We then progressively reduced the number of regions considered for
medical report generation, starting from a maximum of 30 (the highest
value observed in the test set) down to a single region.
The results, presented in Fig. 7, show the percentage of test set
examples containing at least one region that would not have been af-
fected by the tumor if identified using the corresponding ground truth.
Notably, by setting a threshold of five regions for medical report gener-
ation, we achieve a 96.6% reduction in error propagation, decreasing
from 53.1% to 1.8% for cases with at least one incorrect region out
of five. Furthermore, for cases with two incorrect regions out of five,
the error is reduced by 98.3%, from 23.5% to 0.4%. Importantly, no
instances were found with more than two erroneous regions out of five,

Statistical analysis
To determine whether observed differences in report quality are
statistically meaningful across the evaluated LLMs (Gemma, Llama,
and Mistral) we conducted pairwise statistical comparisons on the
six text quality metrics: Type-Token Ratio (TTR), Maas’ Index, Flesch
Reading Ease Score (FRES), Coherence Score (CohS), Embedding-based
Coverage Score (ECS), and Token-based Coverage Score (TCS). Given
that each LLM generated reports for the same test set instances, we
employed paired statistical tests, ensuring that comparisons were made
on a per-sample basis.
For each metric, the choice of statistical test was guided by the
distribution of paired differences. When the normality assumption held,
verified using the Shapiro–Wilk test [40], we applied a paired t-test;
otherwise, we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, a non-parametric
alternative suitable for skewed or ordinal data.
The results of the pairwise comparisons are summarized in Ta-
ble 7. Significant differences (with p< 0.05) were found between
Llama and Mistral for all six metrics. Llama outperformed Mistral in
vocabulary diversity (TTR and Maas’), readability (FRES), coherence
(CohS), and both coverage metrics (ECS and TCS), with all p-values
indicating strong evidence of difference. Comparisons between Llama
and Gemma also revealed significant differences across all metrics.
These results indicate that Llama consistently produced outputs with
statistically distinct linguistic and semantic characteristics compared
to Gemma, suggesting meaningful performance differentiation between
the two models. In contrast, the comparison between Mistral and

Data
For the MS lesion segmentation task, a separate dataset was used,
comprising three distinct subsets: MSSEG-1 [41], ISBI [42], and
PubMRI [43]. This dataset is part of the 2022 Shifts challenge [44] and
focuses on white matter MS lesion segmentation in 3D MRI of the brain.
Each sample in the MS dataset consists of a 3D brain scan captured
using both FLAIR and T1 contrasts. These scans have undergone several
preprocessing steps to enhance their quality and consistency, including
denoising to reduce noise and improve image clarity, skull stripping
to remove non-brain tissues and focus the analysis on brain matter,
and bias field correction to address intensity non-uniformities in the
images. The combination of FLAIR and T1 provides complementary
information, with FLAIR being particularly sensitive to white matter
lesions and T1 offering detailed anatomical structure.

Method adaptations
The methodology is the same as that applied for brain tumors,
described in Section 3, with a few adaptations to make it suitable for
MS lesions.
A similar JSON file was constructed for the MS lesion segmentation
task. The main difference from the brain tumor JSON file is the absence
of color coding. Unlike the brain tumor JSON, which includes color
information for different lesion types, the MS lesion JSON does not, as
MS lesions are typically represented as a single class.
For the MS lesion segmentation task, the performance was evaluated
using the metrics suggested by the Shifts challenge:
• Normalized Dice Similarity Coefficient (nDSC) [45]: It provides
an unbiased metric for evaluating model performance in identify-
ing lesions, regardless of the lesion load across different patients.
It normalizes the precision for each patient while keeping the
recall fixed, allowing for fair comparison across different patients.
The nDSC is defined as:
nDSC = 2 (2 + κp+ n)−1 ,
κ= h(r−1 −1) ,

where p= FP

the positive to the negative classes in the predicted mask ̂Y, and
0 < r< 1 is a reference value that denotes the mean fraction of the
positive class in ̂Y across a large number of subjects, indicating
the average occurrence rate of the positive class.
• F1 Lesion Score: It assesses the lesion detection quality and is
defined as:
F1 =

(11)
where TP (true positives) is when the detected lesion matches the
actual lesion well (IoU > 0.5), FP (false positives) is when the
predicted lesion does not match any actual lesion closely (IoU
< 0.5), and FN (false negatives) is when an actual lesion is not
detected correctly (IoU < 0.5).
• Robust Area Under the Curve (R-AUC) [44,46]: This metric jointly
assesses the model’s robustness to distributional shifts and the
quality of its uncertainty estimates. It is calculated as the area
under error-retention curves, plotting the mean error against
the fraction of retained predictions. Lower R-AUC indicates bet-
ter performance, achieved by improving prediction accuracy or
better correlating uncertainty estimates with errors.

Discussion and conclusion
This paper presented an innovative framework to enhance the ex-
plainability of AI systems in medical imaging, specifically for brain seg-
mentation tasks. By integrating state-of-the-art semantic segmentation
techniques, brain atlas mapping, and Large Language Models, our ap-
proach generates comprehensive, clinically meaningful textual reports
that align with physicians’ diagnostic reasoning and reporting prac-
tices. Unlike conventional explainability methods that rely on heatmaps
or concept attribution, our framework offers structured, anatomically
grounded, and linguistically validated explanations – marking a step
towards clinically deployable AI transparency.
A distinctive aspect of the framework is its anti-hallucination design,
which incorporates structured data extraction and a JSON-based inter-
mediary combined with constrained prompts to ground LLM outputs in
factual, quantitative information. This approach addresses a common
limitation in naïve LLM-based report generation, significantly reducing
the risk of hallucinated content. Furthermore, by bridging visual and
textual modalities, the framework provides a more holistic explanation,
improving the interpretability of segmentation outputs for medical
professionals.
To ensure robustness and flexibility, we conducted multi-model
validation using different segmentation models and multiple LLMs,
demonstrating consistent performance across architectures and con-
firming the model-agnostic applicability of our method. The SegResNet
model emerged as the top performer for semantic segmentation, achiev-
ing high Dice Scores and low Hausdorff Distances for brain tumor
segmentation, as well as competitive performance in MS lesion seg-
mentation. Using a comprehensive set of metrics, we evaluated three
state-of-the-art LLMs (Gemma, Llama, and Mistral) in the textual ex-
planation generation phase. The results revealed that each model had
unique strengths in different aspects of text generation, such as lexical
diversity, readability, coherence, and information coverage. Llama con-
sistently performed well across both tasks, excelling in lexical diversity
and coverage metrics.

brain tumors in magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, its versatility
allows for broader applications. The underlying principles of this ap-
proach can be easily adapted and applied to the segmentation of various

the ongoing efforts to make AI systems in healthcare more transparent,
interpretable, and trustworthy. By providing medical professionals with
detailed, context-rich explanations of AI-driven analyses, our approach
has the potential to support clinical decision-making and increase
confidence in AI-assisted diagnoses.
While this approach offers significant benefits, it has limitations
that warrant further refinement. Our top-performing model achieves

inaccuracies can lead to ambiguous visual explanations and misinter-

mitigate their impact on report generation, our framework includes a

managing potential domain shifts remains an important considera-

healthcare environments.

Abstract—Radiologists face increasing workloads that
make accurate and timely report generation both critical
and challenging. This paper presents a novel system for
grounded automatic brain MRI report generation, with con-
tributions in three key areas: First, we release RadGenome-
Brain MRI, a benchmark dataset featuring multi-modal
scans, expert-annotated abnormality masks, and radiol-
ogy reports with region-level grounding to support fine-
grained, explainable report generation. Second, we pro-
pose AutoRG-Brain, the first brain MRI report generation
framework that combines automatic anomaly segmentation
with a visual prompting-based language model to produce
structured, anatomically grounded findings. Third, we con-
duct extensive quantitative and expert evaluations across
segmentation and reporting tasks, and demonstrate in real
clinical settings that our system significantly enhances ju-
nior radiologists’ ability to detect subtle abnormalities and
compose high-quality reports, narrowing the gap with se-
nior doctors. All code, models, and datasets will be publicly
released to facilitate future research and development.
Index Terms—3D medical imaging analysis, grounded
report generation, medical imaging segmentation.

This often results in vague or incomplete descriptions, especially
regarding localized findings, thus limiting the clinical utility and
interpretability of generated reports [2]. Efforts to generate more
structured and region-specific reports have emerged, such as
region-guided methods for chest X-rays [3], which leverage
annotated bounding boxes and structured templates. However,
these resources are not widely available for more complex imag-
ing modalities such as MRI. In brain imaging, prior works in CT
report generation [2], [4] have explored knowledge-guided and
attention-based methods to improve spatial-textual alignment.
Yet, the subtle and diffuse nature of brain MRI abnormalities,
combined with the multi-modality nature of the data, necessi-
tates accurate segmentation to support fine-grained, explainable
report generation. Several region-aware CT report generation
methods assume the availability of accurate, general-purpose
anatomical segmentation models [5]. However, such models are
scarce for multi-modality brain MRI due to the variability in
contrast, resolution, and acquisition protocols across institutions
and scanners.
To address these challenges, we propose a novel two-stage
system for regionally grounded brain MRI report generation.
Our framework decomposes the task into: (1) a region of in-
terest (ROI) detection and segmentation stage, and (2) a visual
prompting-based report generation stage. As a proof of con-
cept, we focus on brain MRI due to its clinical significance
and complexity, and we contribute in three key areas: dataset
construction, model design and training, and comprehensive
evaluation.
First, in terms of dataset construction, we curate two comple-
mentary datasets: (i) A large-scale pre-training dataset compris-
ing 30,793 multi-modal brain MRI scans and radiology reports
from Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital (referred to as SSPH).
(ii) A benchmark dataset for grounded report generation, named
RadGenome-Brain MRI, which includes 3,408 multi-modal
scans, paired reports, and expert-annotated abnormality masks.

Related Work
The growing adoption of deep learning-based methods has
heightened the demand for model explainability, especially
in high-stakes fields such as medical image analysis. Within
this context, visual interpretation methods, which identify the
image regions that influence model predictions, have attracted

interpretation methods for 3D medical imaging, with an empha-
sis on applications in disease diagnosis, medical segmentation,
and radiology report generation.
A. Disease Diagnosis
Recent advances in medical imaging diagnosis increas-
ingly emphasize the identification of clinically relevant regions
within whole-body or organ-level scans, often leveraging atten-
tion mechanisms to guide image classification. For example,
LEAR [12] improves Alzheimer’s disease (AD) diagnosis by
using a GAN to generate a counterfactual map conditioned on
the diagnostic label. This map highlights anatomical regions
associated with AD in an interpretable manner and is fused
with the original image to refine classification. In a similar
vein, DeepSC-COVID [13] presents a joint deep learning model
that performs simultaneous 3D lesion segmentation and classi-
fication for COVID-19 diagnosis. The architecture comprises
three subnetworks: a cross-task feature extraction module, a
3D segmentation subnet, and a classification subnet. A task-
aware loss function explicitly models the interaction between
segmentation and classification, leading to improved diagnos-
tic performance. Within oncology, Cho et al. [14] propose a
deep learning-based computer-aided detection (CAD) system
for automated identification of brain metastases and assessment
of treatment response. Accurate lesion detection is shown to
substantially enhance diagnostic reliability. Another notable
contribution comes from Sarabian et al. [15], who introduce
a deep learning framework for real-time velocity quantification
using Transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound. By integrating
velocity measurements from multiple cerebral locations with
baseline vascular geometry from 3D angiography, the system
reconstructs high-resolution maps of hemodynamic parame-
ters across the cerebral vasculature. This method significantly
advances the diagnosis of cerebral vasospasm (CVS) by pre-
dicting changes in vessel diameter from sparse velocity inputs.

this research gap by bridging visual analysis with narrative

abnormalities but also generates detailed, free-text reports to

B. Medical Segmentation
Accurate segmentation of organs and lesions is essential
for medical image interpretation. Early breakthroughs like U-
Net [16] established the encoder-decoder architecture with skip
connections as a standard framework for localized feature ex-
traction. Building on this foundation, nnU-Net [17] advanced the
field by automating dataset-specific preprocessing and network
configuration, achieving state-of-the-art performance across di-
verse segmentation tasks. Subsequent hybrid models, such as
SwinUNETR [18], have further enhanced segmentation accu-
racy by integrating transformer-based mechanisms into U-Net
architectures to capture long-range contextual dependencies. In
parallel, registration-based methods, including EasyReg, Trans-
Morph, and ANTsX, have specialized in segmenting anatomi-
cal structures through deformable image registration, aligning
volumetric scans with standardized anatomical atlases. Despite
these advances, the simultaneous segmentation of brain abnor-
malities and anatomical structures—a task of significant clinical
relevance—remains underexplored.
Despite their significant achievements, current segmenta-
tion models lack the capability for simultaneous segmentation
of anatomical structures and abnormalities. This capability is
crucial for comprehensive clinical image analysis, particularly
when interpreting multi-sequence MRIs. To address this gap,we
introduce a two-stage training strategy. This approach equips our
model to jointly segment both anatomies and anomalies within
multi-sequence MRI data,thereby substantially improving the
performance of subsequent radiology report generation.

B. Segmentation Module Training
The segmentation module aims to perform segmentation for
both anomaly and brain structures for the scan in any of the
four common brain MRI modalities: T1-weighted, T2-weighted,

both hospital healthy samples and public segmentation datasets.

mentation module is trained from scratch using unlabeled

the ‘a01’ sample from Hammers-n30r95 [26] as the reference
image to obtain the backward deformation field. Subsequently,
we apply this field to the ‘a01’ segmentation, resulting in the
registered segmentation of the healthy sample.

C. Report Generation Module Training
Upon completing segmentation module training, we freeze its
parameters and train the report generation module. This stage
employs supervision from both global and regional ground-truth
reports, training the model to produce multi-granular reports
conditioned on visual mask prompts from the ROI selector.
1) Training Data Preprocessing: An ideal training sample
would require (X, M, T), denoting the original MRI scan, the
regional mask prompt, and the ground truth report describing the
region. Our curated RadGenome-Brain MRI can satisfy such
condition, with the anomaly annotation mask as M and the
corresponding radiologist-written report as T. While the other
in-house hospital dataset only has (X, Tg) pairs, where Tg is the
global report. We first compensate for these by leveraging the
trained segmentation tool and GPT-4 [28]. In detail, we decom-
pose Tg into modal-wise regional descriptions Tr for different
brain structures by GPT-4. To ensure the reliability of training
labels derived from GPT-4-based global report decomposition,
we implemented a rigorous three-stage quality control pipeline:
(i) Structured Prompt Engineering: We designed specialized
prompts that constrained GPT-4 to function as an information
extractor, strictly instructing it to reassemble phrases from the
original global report into regional descriptions. This method
minimized the risk of fabricating content not present in the
source report. (ii) Automated Rule-Based Filtering: Raw GPT-4
outputs were automatically filtered using predefined rules (e.g.,
JSON schema validation, approved MRI sequence checks),
discarding approximately 0.12% of anomalous entries. (iii)
Expert-Led Random Sampling Audit: A board-certified radi-
ologist blindly reviewed 300 samples. The audit revealed a low
error rate of 1.3% , with no instances of clinically significant
hallucinations, confirming the high fidelity of the decomposed

We present the evaluation results of two key sub-modules of
our system: the segmentation module included in the automatic

report generation module. Lastly, we showcase the efficiency
of integrating AutoRG-Brain into a real clinical scenario.
A. Evaluation on Segmentation
We first present quantitative results for anomaly and structure
segmentation, comparing zero-shot and supervised performance
against baselines, followed by human evaluation of structural
segmentation robustness in abnormal scans.
Brain Anomaly Segmentation: AutoRG-Brain demonstrates
superior anomaly segmentation performance versus existing
methods on BraTS2021 and ISLES2022 datasets (Table IV). In
zero-shot evaluation, AutoRG-Brain outperforms state-of-the-
art unsupervised models, achieving 75.69% DSC on BraTS2021
(+9.25% gain over nearest competitor) and 38.66% DSC on
ISLES2022 (+14.82%). While Sim2Real showed the highest
sensitivity among unsupervised methods, its significantly lower
precision indicates clinically problematic false-positive over-
segmentation as shown in Fig. 7. After second-stage training,
AutoRG-Brain achieves further substantial gains (90.10% DSC
on BraTS2021, 71.14% DSC on ISLES2022).
Brain Structure Segmentation: While existing methods seg-
ment brain structures primarily in healthy anatomy, our model
addresses the critical challenge of lesion-induced deforma-
tions. Benchmarking on Hammers-n30r95 and a novel synthetic
test set (simulating pathology-induced distortions), AutoRG-
Brain showed greater resilience than registration methods
in zero-shot ’lesioned’ brain tests (DSC decline: 1.18% vs.
EasyReg’s 1.39%). After second-stage training, it achieved
80.22% mean DSC (+5.03% over nearest competitor), 80.52%
PRE (+2.49%), and 81.31% SEN (+5.69%) for pathologic
cases while maintaining healthy-brain segmentation parity with
nnU-Net (DSC 81.29% vs. 81.85%). In blind radiologist eval-
uations across real pathology datasets, namely ISLES2022,
BraTS2021, RP3D-Brain, and SSPH, AutoRG-Brain achieved
top-ranking segmentation quality in ≥80% of cases as shown
in Fig. 8.

Discussion
A. Effectiveness of Key Method Components
Results (Table V) demonstrate that region-based report gener-
ation outperforms global methods, primarily due to: (i) capturing
fine-grained details to avoid lesion-report mismatches; (ii) fo-
cusing attention on relevant regions via segmentation masks;
(iii) enabling enhancement through radiologist prompting or
segmentation refinements; and (iv) maintaining robustness to
scale disparities (e.g., small lesions in large anatomical masks)
through training on diverse pathologies and explicit region-
grounded supervision, ensuring effective feature extraction for
subtle abnormalities (qualitatively validated in Fig. 13). Ad-
ditionally, our approach leverages partially labeled data via
synthetic supervision, with RadGenome-Brain MRI integration
during pretraining further boosting performance (Table VII).
B. Clinical Impact
Results demonstrate AI-assisted junior radiologists produce
higher-quality reports, attributed to: (i) Reduction of false neg-
atives through automatic abnormal region segmentation, pre-
venting critical findings from being missed. (ii) Comprehensive
reports with detailed information, including characteristics such
as signal, shape, location, deformation, displacement, and other
relevant features of identified regions. These findings highlight

rationales and human-AI collaboration, advancing trustworthy
clinical assistive systems.
C. Limitations and Failure Case
Our framework’s performance is inherently influenced by the
accuracy of the segmentation module, as errors in this initial
stage can propagate to the report generation phase. Through sys-
tematic failure analysis, we identified four primary error patterns
that illustrate both the challenges and the practical boundaries
of current cross-sectional AI systems: (i) Sequence-Dependent

tions may be highly conspicuous on diffusion-weighted imag-
ing (DWI) but nearly isointense on T1-weighted MRI. When

Conclusion
In this paper, we propose the first brain MRI interpretation
system, termed AutoRG-Brain, capable of analyzing brain MRIs
through brain anomaly segmentation, brain structure segmen-
tation, and report generation, closely following radiologists’
workflow. We also build RadGenome-Brain MRI, a new bench-
mark dataset for grounded report generation on brain MRI with
anomaly segmentation and report annotations, encompassing
3,408 images across 6 modalities and 5 disease types. Exper-
imentally, we demonstrate the superior performance of each
system sub-module and the effectiveness of RadGenome-Brain
MRI as a pre-training dataset. Lastly, we show that integrating
AutoRG-Brain into clinician workflows can provide educational
benefits for junior radiologists and enhance overall work effi-
ciency. All resources (AutoRG-Brain, RadGenome-Brain MRI,
evaluation platform) are open-sourced to advance research.

text:
Abstract
The opaque nature of deep learning models remains a significant barrier to their clinical adoption in medi­
cal imaging. This paper presents a systematic empirical benchmark of visual saliency attribution, atlas-based
visualisation, and LLM-based reporting for brain tumour MRI classification, integrated into a unified pipeline,
leveraging large language models (LLMs) to deliver human-interpretable diagnostic narratives. The proposed
framework operates through three coupled stages. First, nine CNN architectures are extended with a dual-output
hybrid formulation that simultaneously optimises a classification head and a segmentation head, enabling spa­
tially richer feature learning. Second, visual saliency attribution methods, namely Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++,
and ScoreCAM, are applied to generate class-discriminative heatmaps, which are subsequently refined into
coarse binary masks via an adaptive percentile thresholding pipeline. Third, the resulting masks are projected
onto the Harvard–Oxford cortical atlas as an illustrative anatomical overlay, offering an approximate visual
reference for the tumour’s cortical neighbourhood, and the extracted findings are encoded into a structured
JSON file that conditions three LLMs (Grok3, Mistral, and LLaMA) to generate coherent, radiological-style
diagnostic reports. Evaluated on a dataset of 4,834 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI images spanning
three tumour classes, InceptionResNetV2 achieved the highest classification performance, and Grad-CAM++
yielded the best segmentation overlap. Among the language models, Grok3 led in lexical diversity and coher­
ence, while LLaMA achieved the highest readability score. By integrating visual, anatomical, and linguistic
modalities into a unified pipeline, the framework attempts to produce technically grounded and meaningfully
interpretable explanations, offering a step toward more transparent artificial intelligence-assisted brain tumour
diagnosis.

tumour classification

title: From visual saliency to anatomical explanation: generating textual diagnostic reports from brain MRIs with saliency-grounded LLMs
authors: Paul Valery Nguezet, Elie Tagne Fute, Yusuf Brima, Benoit Martin Azanguezet, and co-authors
text:
Introduction
Brain tumours represent a significant challenge in neuro-oncology, owing to their heterogeneity, variable malig­
nancy, and significant impact on patient prognosis [1]. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective treat­
ment planning, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains the modality of choice due to its high-resolution,
non-invasive imaging capabilities [2]. However, interpreting MRI scans, especially in complex tumour cases,
can be time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability, underscoring the need for automated and reliable
decision-support systems [3].
To address these diagnostic challenges, deep learning (DL) methods, and convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) in particular, have emerged as usefull tools for automated medical image analysis [4]. These computa­
tional models excel at automatically learning hierarchical feature representations from voluminous and multi-
parametric MRI data, capturing intricate patterns that may elude conventional analysis [5]. DL-based models
have demonstrate considerable potential in performing critical tasks such as tumour detection, segmentation into
distinct sub-regions (e.g., enhancing tumour, peritumoural edema, necrotic core) [6], and non-invasive differen­
tial diagnosis and genomic characterization. These models offer a potential avenue for supporting radiological
diagnoses. Despite their growing adoption, the opaque nature of these models often raises concerns about trust
and clinical acceptance [7]. Medical professionals require not only accurate predictions but also transparency and
justification for those predictions.
To address this, various explainability techniques, predominantly in the domain of visual saliency, have been
introduced into diagnostic pipelines. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), its enhanced
variant Grad-CAM++, and Score-weighted Class Activation Mapping (ScoreCAM) generate spatial heatmaps
that highlight the image regions most influential to the model’s prediction, offering a visual explanation of the
network’s internal reasoning without modifying its architecture or training procedure [8]. Although these meth­
ods have shown clinical utility in identifying diagnostically relevant regions, they carry important limitations.

Furthermore, bridging the translational gap between computational outputs and actionable clinical intelligence
requires moving beyond purely visual explanations. The emerging integration of natural language generation
(NLG), facilitated by large language models (LLMs), presents a perspective shift towards this goal [11]. These
models offer the potential to synthesize complex, multi-modal data; including quantitative imaging features,
segmentation masks, and saliency maps into coherent, narrative-style reports articulated in clinically relevant
terminology [12]. However, hybrid systems introduces significant challenges. Paramount among these is the
imperative to ensure the factual accuracy and ontological consistency of generated text, preventing misrepre­
sentation of model confidence [13]. Moreover, achieving robust cross-modal alignment where the generated
narrative is precisely and reliably correlated with the visual evidence is non-trivial and necessitates sophisticated
architectures capable of joint representation learning to maintain a verifiable link between image features and
their descriptive linguistic counterparts.
In response to these limitations, this work introduces a unified component-integrated pipeline, designed to
set a link between opaque model predictions and human-interpretable medical reports. The proposed system is
designed to integrate three distinct explanation modalities tightly: computational visual saliency mapping, an
illustrative anatomical contextualization, and natural language-based interpretation. Throughout this paper, mul­
timodal refers to the integration of these explanation modalities rather than to multiparametric MRI acquisition.

lished CNN models, enabling each network to perform tumour-type classification and spatial mask estimation
during training.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section “Related works” presents a review of prior

Finally, Sect. “Conclusion” concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.
Related works
Explainability has become a critical focus in the development of AI systems for medical imaging, with research­
ers exploring both visual and textual methods to increase transparency and user trust. In particular, efforts have
intensified around generating human-interpretable insights that align model predictions with clinically relevant
cues. This section reviews prior research in three main domains: visual saliency methods, language model-based
explanations, and integrated multimodal approaches that bridge the gap between image-based and language-
based reasoning.
Visual saliency techniques have been widely adopted as a means of elucidating the internal decision-making
processes of CNNs in medical applications. Brima and Atemkeng [10] proposed a saliency-driven framework
that leverages Grad-CAM to highlight predictive regions in brain tumour MRI scans, while quantitatively corre­
lating these highlighted areas with statistical measures to validate clinical relevance. Similarly, Mahesh et al. [15]

scope of our single-site benchmarking design, but a natural extension if this framework adopts multi-center use.

inclusion mechanism respectively; both report substantial gains over standard CNN segmentation baselines.

reasoning is the goal, rather than as a substitute for accurate tumour delineation.

Dataset and methods
The proposed method has three main stages as summarised in Fig. 3. Stage 1 is the dual-head CNN training
step, which takes the data as input and outputs the classification results and the saliency heatmap. These are then
passed as input to Stage 2, which is the segmentation step that outputs the mask highlighting the tumour bound­
ary. Stage 3 then takes place following the methodology in [11]. However, the work in [11] presents a methodol­
ogy using the Julich Brain Atlas, a unique and comprehensive three-dimensional atlas, to output a medical report
from a given mask as input. In contrast, we adopt this methodology using the Harvard-Oxford cortical atlas [14],
which is appropriate for 2D images and in line with our dataset. The stages are discussed in detail in the follow­
ing subsections.
Dataset
The dataset used in this study is a curated and enhanced version of brain tumour MRI images derived from two
publicly available datasets. The first source dataset merges three publicly available collections (figshare/Cheng
et al., SARTAJ, and Br35H); the figshare component is documented to contain multiple slices per patient (3,064
images from 233 patients). The second dataset from the Kaggle platform. The two datasets were merged into one
after eliminating duplicate segmentation masks, which were identified through a visual inspection of the masks.
The resulting dataset comprises 4,834 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI images with paired binary
segmentation masks, distributed across three tumour classes: 1,203 Gliomas, 1,707 Meningiomas, and 1,924
Pituitary tumours. Table 1 summarizes the composition of each source dataset. Figure 1 shows representative

All MRI images were subjected to a standardized preprocessing pipeline prior to model training. First, a con­

regions and focus the field of view on the anatomically relevant brain tissue. Both the cropped image and its mask
were then resized to a uniform resolution of 225 inline-eq-IEq3 225 pixels. Images were normalized to the range [0, 1] using
min-max normalization. Masks were kept in their original 8-bit grayscale scale [0, 255] and subsequently bina­

Dual-head CNNs training strategy
Nine CNN architectures were employed as classification backbones: Densely Connected Convolutional Net­
works (DenseNet) [35], Visual Geometric Group (VGG16 and VGG19 [36]), DL with Depthwise Separable
Convolutions (Xception) [37], Deep Residual Network (ResNet50, ResNet50V2) [38], a hybrid deep Inception
and ResNet and EfficientNet [39], and Going deeper with convolutions (Inception) [40]. These architectures were
selected for their established performance in computer vision and medical image analysis tasks and to enable a
comprehensive comparative evaluation across a diverse range of network designs. All models were implemented
in TensorFlow and Keras, and initialized with ImageNet pre-trained weights to leverage transfer learning from
large-scale visual representations
Rather than employing each backbone as a single-output classifier, we extend all nine architectures with a
dual-output hybrid formulation, wherein a shared encoder extracts a common feature representation that simulta­
neously feeds two independent decoding heads: a classification head and a segmentation head. The classification
head consists of a global average pooling layer followed by a fully connected layer with softmax activation, pro­
ducing a probability distribution over the three tumour classes. The segmentation head is a lightweight decoder
comprising four successive transposed convolutional layers with filter sizes of 256, 128, 64, and 32, each using

Conclusion
This paper discussed the integration of explainability components into a unified pipeline for brain tumour clas­
sification from MRI scans, designed to bridge the gap between opaque DL predictions and medical interpretable
reports. The framework integrates four coupled components: a dual-output hybrid CNN backbone for simulta­
neous classification and spatial mask estimation, visual saliency attribution refined into coarse attention masks,
illustrative anatomical atlas mapping, and a structured LLMs reporting module. Together, these components pro­
vide an end-to-end pathway from raw MRI input to a human-readable diagnostic narrative, offering a transparent
view into what the classifier attended to and why.
The atlas mapping step successfully translated pixel-level saliency evidence into named neuroanatomical struc­
tures using the Harvard–Oxford cortical atlas, providing an illustrative anatomical reference layer that purely
visual explanations do not offer. The three evaluated LLMs, Grok3, Mistral, and LLaMA, demonstrated comple­
mentary strengths in generating structured diagnostic narratives from the JSON-encoded findings, with Grok3
leading in lexical diversity and coherence, and LLaMA achieving the highest readability score. Taken together,
these results show that the proposed framework produces multimodal explanations that are technically coherent
and meaningfully interpretable for clinical practitioners.
Several limitations of the present study must be acknowledged. The absence of prospective clinical validation
means that the clinical utility of the generated reports has not been assessed by radiologists or neuro-oncologists
in a real diagnostic workflow. The segmentation head, while effective as an auxiliary training signal, is not
designed to replace dedicated segmentation architectures, and its spatial precision is likely insufficient for surgi­
cal planning applications. The fixed threshold of in l ine-eq-IEq11 4 was the most consistent deployable strategy across all
three saliency methods, but this value was selected empirically on the present dataset and may require recalibra­
tion when the framework is applied to tumour populations with substantially different size distributions or imag­
ing characteristics.
The atlas mapping step carries two limitations of its own. First, it relies on a single, fixed reference slice rather

opercula, respectively, and are involved in various higher-order cognitive functions, including aspects of lan­
guage, sensorimotor integration, and possibly taste. Tumors here could affect speech production, sensorimotor
functions, or gustatory perception.
●Heschl’s Gyrus (includes H1 and H2): This region is primary auditory cortex and is essential for basic sound
processing. A tumor in this area could significantly impact auditory perception.

The presence of a tumor in these regions could have varied and potentially significant impacts on cognitive,

A.5 Discussion
The results presented in this appendix complement the quantitative trade-off established in Table 3 with three
concrete, qualitative observations that merit explicit discussion.
Despite a substantial difference in mask precision between the two methods (DSC: 0.9135 vs. 0.5537 for the
Meningioma case), both pipelines converge on the same two similar neuroanatomical structures: the Insular
Cortex and Heschl’s Gyrus. This convergence suggests that the deployable saliency-based approach correctly
captures the primary anatomical findings even in the absence of mask supervision. The additional regions identi­
fied exclusively by the Grad-CAM++ mask are attributable to known boundary imprecision of class activation
mapping methods rather than genuine tumour involvement, and should be interpreted accordingly.

segmentation models that mean DSC alone does not capture: on individual samples, a separately trained seg­
mentation network can fail entirely, yielding no usable mask, no atlas mapping, and consequently no meaningful
report. Unlike the UNet baseline, the saliency-based visualisation will generally produce some non-zero activa­
tion for any confidently classified sample, since it is derived directly from the classifier’s gradient signal rather
than from an independently thresholded segmentation decision. This does not guarantee the resulting visualisa­
tion is anatomically meaningful, only that a visualisation is produced.
The Grad-CAM++-derived report marginally outperforms the UNet-derived report across all four linguistic
metrics (Table 7). However, this difference should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical content:
it is primarily driven by the greater number of identified regions (7 vs. 3), which produces a longer and more
lexically varied report regardless of whether the additional regions reflect genuine tumour involvement. This is
a known artifact of TTR, Maas’ Index, FRES, and coherence scores when comparing texts of substantially dif­
ferent lengths. The more clinically meaningful observation is that both reports correctly identify the same domi­
nant anatomical structures and produce comparably structured narrative output, suggesting that the framework’s
descriptive content is robust to the segmentation method used, within the limits of the cortical atlas employed.

text:
Abstract
The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various fields has prompted growing interest in their
application within the healthcare ecosystem. In particular, Vision Language Models (VLMs) offer potential for
generating radiology reports. This study aims to perform a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art VLMs
with varying sizes and domain specializations to determine their effectiveness in generating radiology reports
for MRI scans of brain cancer patients. We conducted a comparative analysis of several open-source VLMs,
including Qwen2-VL, Meta-Vision 3.2, PaliGemma 2, DeepSeek-VL2, Nvidia open-source models, and medical-
specific VLMs. Each model family was assessed across small, medium, and large variants. A benchmark dataset
comprising multisequence brain MRI scans of cancer patients was curated with expert annotation and guidance
from board-certified radiologists. The models were evaluated on their ability to generate complete radiology
reports, using objective metrics, reasoning models (R1 and o1 models that judged the AI generations based on
completeness, conciseness, and correctness), and human experts. Model performance varied significantly across
size and type. Among large-scale models, Meta-Vision 3.2 90B achieved the highest scores with o1 of 70.19%
and R1 of 68.09%. In the medium category, Meta-Vision 11B and DeepSeek-VL-2-27B outperformed others,
achieving o1 scores of 57.56% and 53.44%, and R1 scores of 51.06% and 52.75%, respectively. For smaller
models, Qwen2-VL-2B demonstrated the best performance (o1: 23.88%, R1: 23.25%). To our knowledge, this
is the first study evaluating VLMs for generating comprehensive radiology reports for brain cancer diagnosis
using multisequence MRI. Our findings reveal substantial performance differences based on model size and
specialization, offering important guidance for future development and optimization of medical VLMs to
support diagnostic radiology workflows.

For instance, in the context of brain tumors, precise and detailed

must ensure accuracy and thoroughness in their assessments. According
to the International Agency for Research on Cancer, the number of
brain cancer patients is growing rapidly, which will increase to more
than 200 K in 2030, and annual radiotherapy for brain cancer affects
approximately 90 K patients in the US [12].
Automated report generation in the medical domain has been an
active area of research, focusing on enhancing diagnostic efficiency
and reducing the workload of healthcare professionals [16]. Structured
reporting systems like BT-RADS and automated tools are being inte-
grated into clinical practice to streamline the reporting process and
improve diagnostic accuracy [17–19]. Recent advances in LLMs and
VLMs have enabled significant progress in radiology report generation.
A cross-modal context module was proposed to facilitate alignment and
interaction between distinct modalities [20]. This effectively bridges
the gap between the extensive visual sequences of radiographic images
and corresponding highly summarized reports. This approach enhanced
alignment with human assessments by incorporating radiologists’ ex-
pert evaluation criteria. A longitudinal image-report alignment-guided
model was developed for longitudinal mammogram generation using
cross-modality radiology reports [21]. They guaranteed alignment be-
tween generated images and textual diagnostic insights, demonstrating
improved predictive performance. LLMs, such as ChatGPT, have been
used to summarize radiology reports, making them more comprehen-
sible for patients and healthcare providers. This can improve patient
education and healthcare outcomes [22,23]. LlaVA-Med [24] is cur-
rently the state-of-the-art medical model, which was created based
on the architecture of the LlaVA model [25] and was trained by
Microsoft using the PMC-45 dataset [26]. This model was developed
by training the LlaVA-Med using the ChatGPT responses on medical
questions and medical image descriptions. To the best of the authors’
knowledge, there is no specialized LLMs or VLMs that address radi-

rently the state-of-the-art medical model, which was created based
on the architecture of the LlaVA model [25] and was trained by
Microsoft using the PMC-45 dataset [26]. This model was developed
by training the LlaVA-Med using the ChatGPT responses on medical
questions and medical image descriptions. To the best of the authors’
knowledge, there is no specialized LLMs or VLMs that address radi-
ology reports solely for brain tumors. This is a rather complicated
problem due to the requirement of processing several image volumes
that are difficult to handle efficiently. Instead, current models are either
generalized for multiple medical applications or designed for broad
purposes, negatively impacting the quality of the generated radiology
reports. While some earlier investigations might seem analogous to
our study at first glance, important divergences exist; for instance,
the study of Park et al. [27], the researchers tackled the use of LLMs
in automatically extracting diagnostic labels from spinal MRI reports
using Large Language Models (LLMs) that processed only the text,
avoiding direct image analysis. These text-derived labels were then
used to successfully train separate image classifiers to detect conditions
like spinal cancer in MRI scans, achieving performance comparable to
models trained with manual annotations. Another interesting study is
the one proposed by Shi et al. [28], where they used Llama 3 70B
for inference and training on the comprehensive dataset from Mas-
sachusetts General Hospital covering 2008–2018. The authors report
starting from more than 6.5 million raw radiology reports and – after
regex de-identification (removing names), whitespace/format cleaning,
and filtering out reports lacking findings/impressions or with very short
findings – using approximately 4,354,321 findings, impression pairs for
training and 2,114 held-out reports for testing. The corpus includes
multiple modalities (CT, MRI, X-ray, fluoroscopic). While the dataset
is comprehensive, it is not publicly available. In this study, they again
used LLMs in a text-to-text setup (using the impressions to generate
the radiology reports), leaving the medical images outside the LLM
workflow.
Given the highlighted studies in Table 1, the novelty of our study is
in the use of the state-of-the-art new large vision language models to
compare their performance on writing full, comprehensive radiology
reports for brain MRIs.

Dataset curation
Most of the available open-access datasets with attached medical
reports are based on two-dimensional (2D) imaging modalities, such
as chest X-ray radiographs [33,34]. In contrast, open-access datasets
for brain tumor MRI are typically accompanied by annotation labels
and, in some cases, limited clinical data. However, to the best of
our knowledge, no publicly available dataset includes comprehensive,
clinical-style diagnostic reports associated with brain MRI. The pro-
posed dataset curation process involved slicing 3D images into 2D
slices, which were then arranged in a multisequence montage for-
mat. This format enables VLMs to access multisequence information
from different slices within a single image. The slices are arranged
in columns, and each sequence occupies a separate row, as illustrated
in Fig. 2. Each patient case could include between 4 and 9 batches,
with up to 10 slices per one montage image. These montage images
were accompanied by a structured prompt template and submitted to
ChatGPT-4o. In particular, the use of ChatGPT-4o to generate the initial
radiology reports was intended to reduce the time that radiologists
would otherwise spend drafting reports from scratch.
A template prompt was used to generate the reports, under the
supervision of a medical radiologist. This template was designed to
guide the model in producing radiology reports that follow a format
similar to those used by medical professionals. It is important to note
that the use of AI for report generation was intended solely to facilitate
the dataset creation process, with oversight from medical experts. A
sample of the comprehensive diagnosis report used in the dataset,
initially generated by ChatGPT 4o and revised and edited by medical
experts, is shown in Fig. 3.

Vision language models
The selection of VLMs was based exclusively on top-performing
models according to the latest available benchmarks. We specifically
focused on VLMs capable of processing images or videos as input
and generating textual output. Accordingly, we used only the vision
models listed in Table 2. To enable a fair comparison across different
capacities, the models were classified as small, medium, and large
based on model size. Although this study adopts a broad perspective,
it aims to highlight that larger models do not necessarily yield better
performance. Additionally, large models require more than seven times
the computational power of small models, highlighting the trade-off
between size and efficiency. The performance of each model is cru-
cial within its respective category, as this helps assess which model
performs best and whether scaling up in size is worthwhile. The same
prompt template was used to create the proposed dataset and applied
uniformly across all vision models to ensure consistency. Furthermore,
all models were run with identical hyperparameter values to maintain
a fair comparison, as illustrated in Table 3.

Evaluation and assessment
The results of this comparative study were evaluated using three
methods: (1) static evaluation metrics, which compare the similarity
between the model’s text and the radiology report of the dataset; (2)
the use of LLMs as judges to compare the model-generated radiology
reports with those in the dataset; and (3) human evaluation using three
experienced radiologists.

Evaluation metrics
As listed in Table 4 one of the used metrics was the Recall-Oriented
Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROGUE) [42]; two types of ROGUE
were applied in our study, which are ROGUE 1 (UNIGRAM) and
Longest Common Subsequence (Rogue L). In our case, ROGUE 1 would
measure single words overlapping between the model’s generated and
reference radiology reports. ROGUE-L would measure the longest over-
lapping sentences between the two reports. Another used metric was
the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) [43]. Evaluation is done
by measuring how closely the generated radiology report is to the
reference one through n-gram overlapping and brevity penalty (BP),
which adds a penalty if the generated text is significantly shorter than
the reference. Cosine similarity [44] is a metric that can measure
the angle between two text vectors in a multi-dimensional space to
determine if both vectors have the same direction.

LLMs as judge
Investigating the two current state-of-the-art reasoning models,
ChatGPT o1 and DeepSeek R1, was motivated by the previously men-
tioned metrics, which are effective for evaluating textual similarity but
are insufficient for assessing such a sensitive task. Medical terms may
appear similar but can have different clinical implications. Reasoning
models are ideal for this task, as their chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning
enables them to assign scores based on a deeper understanding of
the radiology report. A prompt template used with the reasoning
models, along with the AI-generated radiology report and the reference
radiology report, was designed to assign scores ranging from 0 to 10
for four criteria: correctness, conciseness, completeness, and medical
image analysis of the model following the evaluation study in [45].
The reasoning models were used through APIs to send the AI-generated
and ground truth reports using the prompt template. The parameters
given to the model for evaluation were meant to aid in the complete
assessment of correctness, conciseness, completeness, and the medical
image description of the model. These parameters were meant to
evaluate if the model is writing a complete radiology medical report
or it is trying to make things up to generate a report that ‘‘looks like a
realistic one’’.

Ethical approval
Our study did not require new ethical clearance. All analyses were
carried out on the RHUH-GBM dataset [29], an openly available re-
source of fully anonymized brain-tumor images accompanied by min-
imal, non-identifying clinical details. The dataset’s original curators
collected the material under the Declaration of Helsinki and stripped
it of any information that could link back to individual patients. Be-
cause we are performing a secondary analysis of this de-identified,
public data, the work is not classified as human-subjects research and
therefore falls outside the scope of institutional review board (IRB)
oversight.

Results
The model’s ROUGE and Cosine similarity performance metrics are
very close to the general scores given by the o1 and R1 reasoning
models (Table 4). Although these evaluation metrics provide a useful
general overview, they are highly sensitive to syntax similarity and
structure. This is evident in the case of the PV04 model, which is one
of the smallest models with weaker performance compared to others.
However, it is the best model based on ROUGE and Cosine’s similarities.
This discrepancy arises because the radiology reports generated by this
model are primarily empty due to hallucination. The model struggled
with the complexity of the prompt and the medical images, leading it
to generate only the report structure – such as section titles – before
leaving the content blank and simply commenting that it had processed
the photos. However, models like LM07 and MV11 experienced the op-
posite issue. Their responses occasionally included the prompt template
before generating the actual answer. Furthermore, the high sensitivity
of these metrics to structure and syntax contributed to inconsistencies
in evaluation.
The results of the O1 and R1 judge models are slightly different
in some scoring; however, the difference never exceeds more than one
point in any of the comparison criteria as shown in Table 5. It is
also worth noting that none of the models surpassed a score of 6/10
in image description, indicating that even large models struggled to
provide accurate medical descriptions. This reinforces the difficulty of
handling such a task using a zero-shot approach, suggesting that better
results would require fine-tuning the models or providing a detailed
image description to aid prediction.
The overall scores are shown in Fig. 4, which shows that a larger
model size does not always guarantee better performance. MV90 out-
performed QW72, but the trade-off was an additional 18B parameters
requiring over 20% more computational power. The MV11 is the fourth
model on the list with just 11B parameters, rivaling a model like DS27,
which is more than 2.5 times its size. Also, LM07, the only medically
specialized VLM on the list, struggled with poor performance, as it was
surpassed by QW07 (a generalized model of the same size) and nearly
matched by QW02, with less than a 3% difference.

Iterative inference approach
As previously discovered, the MV11 and DS27 models were iden-
tified as the best options, not solely due to their performance but
because of the trade-off between performance and the computational
power required to run these models. These models offer the best cost-
effective value, which motivated a deeper comparison using slightly
different techniques. To enrich the comparison, we employed an infer-
ence technique to evaluate the models better and push each to its limits.
As shown earlier in Fig. 2, we utilized all five modalities alongside
the segmentation mask for the MRI multi-sequences, with each image
containing 10 sequences. In this approach, we split each image into
two parts: the first part contained the ADC and FLAIR modalities
alongside the segmentation mask. In contrast, the second part included
the T1, T1c, and T2 modalities alongside the segmentation mask.
This allowed the models to focus more effectively on the brain MRI
slices, providing a better zoomed-in view of the images and enabling
improved recognition of brain image details. Additionally, the models
were exposed to the images through multiple inference requests. The
model was asked to generate an initial report based on the first batch of
images and modalities during the first request. In subsequent requests,
the model was presented with additional modalities of the same slices
or the remaining multi-sequences, allowing it to refine the initial report
iteratively. This iterative approach enabled the model to improve the
generated radiology report progressively, rather than processing all the
data simultaneously as was done in previous experiments.
It is worth noting that the system prompt was only provided to
the model during the first request to avoid overloading it with a large
prompt, which could lead to hallucinations. Instead, the system prompt
was used initially. For subsequent requests, the model was instructed
to refine the previously generated report based on the newly presented
images. The results, as shown in Table 6, indicate that the performance
of DS27 and MV11 remains very close. The newly adopted technique in
this comparison enabled the models to achieve results around the 65%

Discussion
Our benchmarking of Vision Language Models (VLMs) for generat-
ing brain MRI radiology reports revealed significant performance vari-
ations. While the large Meta-Vision 3.2 90B model scored highest (o1:
70.19%), medium-sized models like Meta-Vision 11B and DeepSeek-VL-
2-27B, especially with an iterative inference approach, offered a strong
balance of performance and efficiency, rivaling larger counterparts.
Qwen2-VL-2B led the smaller models. These results imply that model
size alone is not determinative; strategic model selection and inference
methods are crucial. The study also highlighted current VLM limitations
in detailed zero-shot medical image analysis but showed that itera-
tive techniques can enhance report quality, with DeepSeek-VL-2-27B
notably improving descriptive detail with this approach.
The proposed study encountered several noteworthy challenges.
First and foremost were model hallucinations; both LLMs and VLMs
experienced hallucinations when the provided prompt was too complex
or lengthy. This was the primary reason why, for some patients, smaller
models, some medium-sized models, and the Paligemma2 models suf-
fered hallucinations, responding to the prompt with a single repeated
word or an empty radiology report structure. According to this study,
although VLMs are currently dominating the field with impressive
results, they appear to lack the ability to attend to small details crucial
for this clinical procedure. Such details include the size of the tumor
and its precise location within the brain, especially considering that
each medical image provided contained 50 brain MRI 2D slices, each
representing a different modality. It is important to note that our novel
approach to creating the multi-sequence dataset by combining these
sequences and modalities into a single 2D montage image was primarily
motivated by the fact that most VLMs used in this study can only handle
a single image. Moreover, even models capable of processing multiple
images suffered from the model hallucinations mentioned earlier. For

Unexpected behavior
There was an unexpected behavior by the model Deepseek-VL2-
27B during the iterative inference approach, which was that the model
started giving extremely detailed medical descriptions for the MRI
slices, as illustrated in Fig. 5. The model’s answers are on the top side of
the figure, and at the bottom is our reference report that was created by
ChatGPT-4o and modified by the medical experts for our dataset. This
indicates that during the iterative inference approach, the DeepSeek-

generation. This was revealed during the evaluation scoring being
conducted by o1 and R1 judgments, as both were penalizing the models
for the image descriptions with the complain that the model is writing
detailed image descriptions that are not written in the reference report.

text:
Conclusion
Brain radiology reporting is one of the unexplored areas in gen-
erative AI, particularly in applying LLMs, which unlocks the poten-
tial to improve the efficiency of brain radiotherapy and alleviate the
enormous workload on radiologists. The lack of available datasets
containing medical brain images alongside radiology reports motivated
the creation of the proposed dataset, which was developed under the
supervision and review of professional radiologists for this compara-
tive analysis. VLMs vary in size, architecture, and the data on which
they were trained, which could explain why some models outperform
others on benchmarks but fail in specialized case studies like this one.
The comparison results indicated that Meta-Vision 3.2 90B was the
best among the large models, achieving a 70.19% o1 score and a
68.09% R1 score. Among the medium-sized models, Meta-Vision 11B
and DeepSeek-VL-2-27B performed best, with o1 scores of 57.56% and
53.44% and R1 scores of 51.06% and 52.75%, respectively. Qwen2-
VL-2B was the best among the small models, with an o1 score of
23.88% and an R1 score of 23.25%. Also, with the iterative inference
approach, medium-size models like Meta-vision 11B and DeepSeek-VL-
2-27B were able to achieve a performance close to the performance
of big models like Qwen2-VL-72B. Also, after a close inspection turns
out that DeepSeek-VL-2-27B has outperformed ChatGPT 4o in the AI
radiology report generation before the medical expert’s inspections.
The study concludes with the observation that larger models do not
necessarily guarantee superior performance; in some instances, more
compact and specialized models can deliver better accuracy and effi-
ciency, challenging the conventional notion that size alone determines
success.

title: Enhancing brain tumor detection in MRI images through explainable AI using Grad-CAM with Resnet 50
authors: Mohamed Musthafa M, Mahesh T. R., Vinoth Kumar V., and Suresh Guluwadi
text:
Abstract
This study addresses the critical challenge of detecting brain tumors using MRI images, a pivotal task in medical diag-
nostics that demands high accuracy and interpretability. While deep learning has shown remarkable success in medi-
cal image analysis, there remains a substantial need for models that are not only accurate but also interpretable
to healthcare professionals. The existing methodologies, predominantly deep learning-based, often act as black boxes,
providing little insight into their decision-making process. This research introduces an integrated approach using
ResNet50, a deep learning model, combined with Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to offer
a transparent and explainable framework for brain tumor detection. We employed a dataset of MRI images, enhanced
through data augmentation, to train and validate our model. The results demonstrate a significant improvement
in model performance, with a testing accuracy of 98.52% and precision-recall metrics exceeding 98%, showcasing
the model’s effectiveness in distinguishing tumor presence. The application of Grad-CAM provides insightful visual
explanations, illustrating the model’s focus areas in making predictions. This fusion of high accuracy and explainability
holds profound implications for medical diagnostics, offering a pathway towards more reliable and interpretable brain
tumor detection tools.
Keywords Explainable AI, Brain tumor detection, MRI images, Deep learning, Grad-CAM, ResNet50, Medical image
analysis

Brain tumors, comprising a range of neoplasms within

which metastasize from other body parts. The global

precise diagnostic tools. Brain tumors exhibit heteroge-

neurological impairments, necessitating early and accu-
rate detection to optimize treatment outcomes [1].
Moreover, the overlapping symptoms of brain tumors
with other neurological disorders necessitate a diagnostic
tool that offers both high sensitivity and specificity. Tra-
ditional diagnostic methods, while effective, often require
invasive procedures or can be limited in their ability to
detect small or early-stage tumors.

a cornerstone in the non-invasive diagnosis of brain
tumors [2], offering detailed images of the brain’s anat-

detailed and high-contrast images. Various traditional
image processing techniques, including segmentation
and feature extraction, have been employed to differen-
tiate between normal and abnormal brain tissues. How-
ever, these methods often require manual intervention
and are limited by their reliance on predefined features,
which may not capture the full complexity of brain tumor
characteristics.

Deep learning, particularly convolutional neural net-

small datasets [8].
Despite these advancements, a critical limitation of

Training, validation and testing process
The training process for the ResNet50 model in brain
tumor detection entails a meticulous sequence of steps
aimed at optimizing its performance and robustness.
Commencing with model initialization, pre-trained
weights from datasets like ImageNet are often leveraged
to kickstart the learning process, facilitating transfer
learning and expediting convergence towards task-spe-
cific objectives. Subsequently, a suitable loss function,
typically binary cross-entropy for binary classification
tasks, is selected to quantify the disparity between pre-
dicted outputs and actual labels. An optimizer, such
as SGD or Adam, is then chosen to iteratively update
the network’s weights based on feedback from the loss
function.
Batch processing is employed to partition the training
dataset into manageable subsets, enabling incremental
weight updates and enhancing computational efficiency.
During each training iteration, a forward pass propa-
gates data through the network, generating predictions.
Following this, a backward pass, known as backpropaga-
tion, computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the
network weights, facilitating weight updates by the opti-
mizer to minimize the loss.
The training process unfolds over multiple epochs,
with each epoch representing a complete pass through
the entire training dataset. Techniques like dropout or L2
regularization may be employed to mitigate overfitting,
ensuring the model generalizes well to unseen data.
Concurrently, the validation process occurs at the end
of each epoch, where the model’s performance is evalu-
ated on a separate validation set. This assessment offers
insights into the model’s generalization capabilities and
informs hyperparameter tuning decisions. Hyperparam-
eters such as learning rate and batch size are adjusted
based on performance metrics such as accuracy, preci-
sion, and recall. Furthermore, early stopping criteria
may be implemented to halt training if the model’s per-
formance on the validation set deteriorates, mitigating
overfitting by preventing the model from learning noise
from the training dataset. Through this iterative training
and validation regimen, the ResNet50 model is honed to
achieve optimal performance and reliability in the task of
brain tumor detection.

complex patterns in data, their performance is inherently
tied to the quantity and quality of the training data. The
size of the dataset limits the model’s exposure to the wide
range of variations that occur in brain tumors, poten-
tially hindering its predictive performance in clinical sce-
narios that are not represented in the training data. The
dataset predominantly includes MRI images from a lim-
ited demographic and may not adequately represent the
diversity seen in the global population. Brain tumors vary
significantly in their appearance, not only due to biologi-
cal factors but also due to demographic variations. There-
fore, a dataset with greater demographic diversity would
likely improve the model’s generalizability and reliability
across different populations. These limitations under-

findings to the general population. The high accuracy and
precision demonstrated by our model may not fully pre-

and incorporating a more diverse and extensive dataset

tumors. This would enable the development of a model

environments.
