Conclusion
This study presents the promising application of a deep
learning model, particularly ResNet50 augmented with
Grad-CAM, for brain tumor detection in MRI images.
Achieving a testing accuracy of 98.52% alongside high
precision and recall metrics underscores the model’s
efficacy in identifying brain tumors accurately. Leverag-
ing data augmentation techniques significantly bolstered
the model’s robustness and generalization capabilities
across diverse imaging scenarios. Moreover, the integra-
tion of Grad-CAM provided valuable insights into the
model’s decision-making process by highlighting relevant
areas within the images that influenced its predictions,
crucial for building trust and interpretability in medical
AI applications. Despite these promising results, several
limitations and areas for improvement are recognized.
Firstly, the study acknowledges the relatively limited
dataset size and diversity, emphasizing the need for
larger and more varied datasets encompassing a broader
spectrum of tumor presentations. Exploring alternative
architectures like EfficientNet or DenseNet could offer
insights into optimizing model complexity and compu-
tational efficiency. Additionally, future research direc-

expert assessments and integration into real-world clini-
cal workflows to evaluate diagnostic impact and patient
outcomes. Refining explainability methods such as Grad-

further enhance the model’s diagnostic capabilities and
foster trust among medical professionals. Overall, while
this study marks a significant advancement in AI-driven
brain tumor detection in MRI images, ongoing research
efforts aim to enhance accuracy, interpretability, and
clinical applicability, paving the way for improved patient
care in medical imaging analysis.

An explainable hybrid CNN–vision

using MRI
S. R. Sowmiya & N. Sabiyath Fatima
Despite the significant strides towards exploiting deep learning in medical image analysis for
diagnostic purposes, the diagnosis of brain tumors is still a challenging task where the localization,
multi-class classification and explainability of brain tumors are not fully included in a single deep
learning model. Current methods treat both tumor and non-tumor areas equally, potentially
contributing to an underrepresentation of discriminative information and the ideas of explainability
are typically used as a post hoc visualization method. To tackle these problems, this work proposes
an Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based Brain Tumor Network model (XAI-BTNet), which is a
segmentation-guided hybrid architecture by combining CNN and Vision Transformer (ViT) with EAI. A
CNN–UNet model trained with BraTS 2021 data is designed to generate tumour masks to reduce the
background noise patch tokens before the self-attention stage of ViT, allowing the model to learn the
tumour-relevant features. In addition, a consistency mechanism based on Grad-CAM is embedded in
the training process for the consistency of the attention maps generated with the tumors areas, in
order to improve interpretability. Thereafter, the proposed framework was tested on the MRI dataset
from the Figshare database for multi-class brain tumour detection and validation of the segmentation
results using the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2021 dataset. Experimental results show that XAI-
BTNet has a classification accuracy of 98.6%, a sensitivity of 97.8% and a specificity of 98.9%. These
insights reveal the capability of XAI-BTNet in accurate and explainable brain tumor classification and
its potential applications in computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support.

deep learning, Vision transformer, Convolutional neural network, Multi-class classification, Grad-CAM, Image
segmentation

• To develop the XAI-BTNet framework incorporating a CNN–UNet-based segmentation module for accurate

• To design the XAI-BTNet hybrid architecture by integrating convolutional neural networks (CNN) and Vi­

• To integrate an explainability-aware training mechanism within XAI-BTNet using Grad-CAM consistency

• To evaluate the performance of XAI-BTNet on benchmark datasets (Figshare and BraTS 2021) using

Brain tumor classification methods based on CNN have proven to be effective in learning local spatial patterns;
however, they have limitations in learning long-range dependencies between two anatomically distant regions.
In contrast, Vision Transformer (ViT)-based methods can incorporate all contextual information around the
image using self-attention, but the attention mechanisms might assign large weights to regions that are not
tumor and background regions. CNN–ViT hybrid models partially overcome these drawbacks by integrating the
local and global feature representations, but these models typically lack explicit constraints on the tokens in the
transformer, and often explanations are produced after training. To address this drawback, XAI-BTNet proposes
a segmentation-based token suppression strategy to control the background and tumor-related tokens prior to
transformer self-attention using tumor masks generated by the CNN–UNet. Additionally, a consistency loss
with Grad-CAM is added to the optimization goal to learn consistent regions across different spatial locations
while training, which is a desirable property when segmenting tumors. Therefore, the proposed framework
tackles representation learning, suppression of irrelevant backgrounds, and alignment of explanations in a single
framework.

while training, which is a desirable property when segmenting tumors. Therefore, the proposed framework
tackles representation learning, suppression of irrelevant backgrounds, and alignment of explanations in a single
framework.
In the current hybrid CNN-Transformer methods, the encoding of the Transformer is the only part where
tokens are not explicitly removed such as background tokens.The current hybrid CNN-Transformer models are
mostly feature fusion, instead of explicitly removing the background tokens before the Transformer encoding.
Swin Transformer architectures reduce interactions to a specific window, and standard ViT models attend to all
image patches equally which can result in diminishing attention to smaller areas in tumors. EfficientNet-based
methods are capable of effectively extracting local spatial information, but fall short in incorporating mechanisms
to represent global, contextual dependencies. Furthermore, most explainable AI methods are retrospective,
giving visualizations of the model only after it has been trained, but don’t modify the optimization process of
the parameters. XAI-BTNet introduces three key innovations to rectify these drawbacks: (i) filter tokens and
introduce attention masks using segmentation, before the multi-head self-attention blocks; (ii) hybrid CNN–
ViT architecture, which learns jointly local and global representations; and (iii) explainability-aware composite
loss that constrains attention maps to pay attention to tumor-specific regions during the training process. This
design provides enhanced interpretability for diagnosis and at the same time preserves good classification of the
tumor.

deep learning models, Vision Transformers, and explainable AI in medical imaging. Section 3 describes the
segmentation-guided CNN–ViT architecture and explainability-aware training method of the XAI-BTNet
system. Experimental setup, datasets, evaluation measures, and outcome analysis are in Sect. 4. Section 5
concludes the work and suggests future research.

The existing literature has revealed the effectiveness of hybrid CNN–Transformer and explainability-aware
deep learning approaches for analyzing brain tumors from MRI. Previous research has demonstrated that
architectures of transformers achieve better global contextual learning, and CNN-based architectures achieve
better local spatial feature learning and tumor localization. Additionally, explainable AI technologies have been
developed in recent years that enhance the transparency of the AI model and its reliability in diagnosis by
visualizing its attention and explaining its features. To date, however, there are still many methods that depend
on post-hoc explainability, and most of them are not supported by the integration of segmentation-guided
attention optimization, which motivates the development of the proposed XAI-BTNet framework.
Proposed methodology
The proposed XAI-BTNet (Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based Brain Tumor Network) is a two-step,
segmentation-directed hybrid deep learning architecture, which will overcome three fundamental weaknesses
of existing brain tumor analysis systems: uniformity of feature extraction, which does not identify pathologically
relevant areas, the lack of a coherent multi-stage pipeline that jointly trains segmentation and classification, and
the use of post-h XAI-BTNet combines a UNet segmentation block based on Convolutional Neural Network
(CNN)-based Stage 1 with a hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer (ViT)-based Stage 2 backbone. The two phases
are closely intertwined with a segmentation-directed token-suppression framework and a new Grad-CAM
consistency loss that incorporates explainability as an objective to training, achieving competitive performance
compared with recently reported methods under comparable evaluation settings. This integrated architecture
will guarantee that localization of the tumor, multi-class classification and interpretability are collectively
optimized in a single end-to-end pipeline, indicating the potential applicability of the framework for interpretable
computer-aided brain tumor analysis.

The segmentation-guided token filtering process aims to suppress irrelevant background information prior
to transformer-based feature learning. Initially, the CNN–UNet module predicts a binary tumor mask for each
MRI image. The mask is subsequently divided into patches corresponding to the Vision Transformer input
tokens. For each patch, the proportion of tumor pixels is estimated and compared with a predefined threshold.
Patches containing sufficient tumor content are preserved, while those dominated by background regions are
assigned lower attention weights using a soft masking mechanism. The filtered token sequence is then forwarded
to the transformer encoder, enabling the self-attention layers to concentrate on clinically meaningful tumor
regions and enhancing explainability.

The UNet architecture is a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture that has skip connections that maintain
spatial context lost during downsampling. The encoder uses a sequence of convolutional blocks with batch
normalization and ReLU activations and max-pooling operations to sequentially abstraction of the spatial
features into a small latent representation. The decoder uses bilinear upsampling combined with convolutional
blocks with the aid of skip connections between the respective encoder levels to retrieve fine spatial detail and
generate a complete-resolution segmentation map. To have proper delineation of the clinically heterogeneous
tumor subregions, the segmentation module is trained with a hybrid loss function that consists of a combination
of Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and Dice loss. The BCE metric punishes pixelwise misclassification by
capitalizing on the task as independent binary predictions. In contrast, the Dice loss encourages the agreement
between the predicted mask and the ground-truth annotation, and is in effect directly maximising region-level
correspondence. The composite loss is given as:

evaluation. All the implementation parameters, configuration and training methods were kept the same for all
the experiments to ensure the repeatability and a fair comparison of their performance.

Implementation details and training configuration
The proposed XAI-BTNet framework was coded in Python, with the utilization of PyTorch and trained with an
NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The CNN–UNet module consisted of four layers of the encoder–decoder network with
3 × 3 convolutions, batch normalization, ReLU activation and bilinear upsampling. The Vision Transformer used
a patch size of 16, an embedding dimension of 768, a number of attention heads of 12, and a number of encoder
layers of 12. The training was done for 100 epochs with a batch size of 16, with the AdamW optimizer (learning
rate: 0.0001, weight decay: 0.01), and cosine annealing scheduling. Augmentation techniques employed were
rotation, flipping, normalization, noise injection and scaling. Stratified five-fold cross-validation was adopted

The ablation experiments show that the performance boost of XAI-BTNet is not just due to the growing
complexity of the CNN–ViT backbone architecture, but also due to the coordinated ablation operation of
segmentation-guided token suppression and explainability-aware optimization. The overall accuracy result of
the XAI-BTNet was 98.6% while the CNN–ViT baseline got 96.8%. Without token suppression, the accuracy
drops to 97.3%, showing that the transformer attention is more likely to suffer from irrelevant background
information. The Grad-CAM consistency loss is shown to be important to accuracy, as ablation reveals a drop
to 97.7% when it is removed. Removing both components resulted in performance drops to 96.8%, which is the
CNN–ViT baseline. The results show the complementary nature of token-level background suppression and
explanation learning that is spatially consistent.
The spatial overlap between the explanations and the tumor regions was quantitatively assessed in addition
to the qualitative visualization using Grad-CAM. Dice and intersection-over-union (IoU) scores were used
to compare the normalized Grad-CAM maps with the corresponding CNN–UNet tumor masks. The Dice
agreement of 0.91 ± 0.02 and the IoU of 0.84 ± 0.03 showed that there was a high spatial overlap between the
tumor regions segmented and the discriminative regions of the model. These results indicate that the use of the
Grad-CAM consistency objective during optimization is effective and not merely as a post hoc analysis.

explainability regularization, but in case of segmentation failure, it can be propagated to the stage of classification

Conclusion and future work
The study introduces XAI-BTNet, an explainable hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer model to detect and classify
brain tumours across multiple stages using MRI, that overcomes the three key limitations of uniform feature
extraction, disjointed multi-task pipelines, and post-hoc explanations found in current deep learning models.
XAI-BTNet developed an interpretability-conscious diagnostic pipeline through the addition of a CNN-UNet
segmentation module to extract tumor-specific ROI, a masked token attention mechanism to inhibit non-tumor
patch tokens before ViT self-attention, and a new Grad-CAM consistency loss that makes interpretability a
proactive training constraint and not a post-hoc visualization. Tested on the Figshare brain tumor MRI data
with cross-validation of five-folds and tested on the BraTS 2021 dataset on robustness, the framework achieved
a classification accuracy rate of 98.6%, sensitivity of 97.8% and specificity of 98.9%, demonstrating competitive
performance relative to recently reported approaches under similar experimental conditions. The present study
has certain limitations. All steps of the framework were tested on publicly available data, but external clinical
validation was not conducted on multi-institutional MRI data. Furthermore, the explainability assessment
was restricted to the overlap-based localization measures. Work with larger heterogeneous datasets and, in
conjunction with radiologist guidance, will follow.
Future directions include the extension of XAI-BTNet to three-dimensional volumetric MRI inputs in order
to capture tumor morphology in axial, coronal and sagittal planes and the incorporation of multi-modal MRI
sequences such as T1CE and FLAIR as part of a single feature fusion approach. Furthermore, the concept of
federated learning will be explored to enable privacy-preserving multi-institutional training on heterogeneous
clinical data, and future clinical validation trials will be conducted to evaluate the diagnostic utility of the
proposed framework in practice, its acceptance among radiologists, and its applicability to regulatory standards.

title: BTReport: A Framework for Brain Tumor Radiology Report Generation with Clinically Relevant Features
authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Dickson T. Chen, Tianyi Ren, Daniel K. Low, Jacob Ruzevick, Asma Ben Abacha, Alberto Santamaria-Pang, Mehmet Kurt
venue: Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL); Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 315, pp. 1445â€“1472
text:
Abstract
Recent advances in radiology report generation (RRG) have been driven by large paired
image-text datasets; however, progress in neuro-oncology RRG has been limited due to a
scarcity in open paired image-report datasets. Here, we introduce BTReport, an open-
source framework for brain tumor RRG that constructs natural language radiology re-
ports using reliably extracted quantitative imaging features. Unlike existing approaches
that rely on general-purpose or fine-tuned vision-language models for both image inter-
pretation and report composition, BTReport performs deterministic feature extraction of
clinically-relevant features, then uses large language models only for syntactic structuring
and narrative synthesis. By separating RRG into deterministic feature extraction and re-
port generation stages, synthetically generated reports are completely interpretable and
contain reliable numerical measurements, a key component lacking in existing RRG frame-
works. We validate the clinical relevance of BTReport-derived features, and demonstrate
that BTReport-generated reports more closely resemble reference clinical reports when
compared to existing baseline RRG methods. To further research in neuro-oncology RRG,
we introduce BTReport-BraTS, a companion dataset that augments BraTS imaging with
synthetic radiology reports generated with BTReport, and BTReview, a web-based plat-
form for validating the clinical quality of synthetically generated radiology reports. Code
for this project can be found at: https://github.com/KurtLabUW/BTReport.
Keywords: Brain MRI, Radiology report generation, VASARI, Midline shift, Open dataset,
Multimodal learning, Neuro-oncology

radiology services is expected to increase between 16.9% to 26.9% by 2055, while attrition
in radiology also continues to increase (Christensen et al., 2025). As the gap between physi-
cian workload and available workforce widens, assisted radiology report generation (RRG)
is positioned to help address this unmet clinical need.
RRG leverages advances in artificial intelligence (AI) to extract quantitative imaging
markers from raw unstructured data in an automated manner. In clinical workflows, RRG
promises to improve data quality, repeatability, factual completeness, and timeliness of
radiology reporting.
The adoption of vision-language models (VLMs) in RRG has led
to substantial advances, allowing models to jointly reason over medical images and textual
findings (Liu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Sellergren et al., 2025). These developments have
been primarily driven by large-scale chest X-ray datasets such as MIMIC-CXR (Johnson
et al., 2019) and IU X-ray (Demner-Fushman et al., 2016), which provide over 300,000 chest
X-ray images paired with clinical reports. However, accessible image-report datasets across
other radiology specialties are limited. For instance, in neuro-oncology, large neuroimaging
datasets are made openly available through efforts such as BraTS (de Verdier et al., 2024),
but paired text reports for VLM training remain lacking.

as subregion involvement and midline shift (MLS) measurements, among others. Together,
these descriptors provide comprehensive brain tumor characterization, and improve risk

framework is directly interpretable and reduces the likelihood of critical detail omission (Wu

title: BTReport: A Framework for Brain Tumor Radiology Report Generation with Clinically Relevant Features
authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Dickson T. Chen, Tianyi Ren, Daniel K. Low, Jacob Ruzevick, Asma Ben Abacha, Alberto Santamaria-Pang, Mehmet Kurt
venue: Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL); Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 315, pp. 1445â€“1472
text:
Related Work
A variety of approaches have been proposed for the task of image-paired RRG and gen-
erally fall into one- and two-stage frameworks. The leading paradigm for RRG involves
training monolithic VLM foundation models to extract image features and generate re-
ports in one step, such as in MedGemma (Sellergren et al., 2025) and MedPaLM-2 (Singhal
et al., 2023). Approaches in neuro-oncology following this paradigm include TextBraTS (Shi
et al., 2025), which directly prompts GPT-4 models (Achiam et al., 2023) with videos of
2D mpMRI axial slices alongside tumor segmentation masks derived from FLAIR imaging.
Radiologists refine these annotations into structured textual labels, which are then used to
guide tumor segmentation models toward clinically relevant regions, improving segmenta-
tion performance. Although these annotations improved segmentation performance, they
do not contain quantitative measurements typically reported by radiologists.
Other image-paired RRG frameworks adopt a two-stage design.
For example, From
Segmentation to Explanation (Seg-to-Exp) (Valerio et al., 2025) first establishes descriptive
tumor-ROI relationships based on the co-registration of tumor segmentation masks to an
anatomical atlas. These relationships are extracted as structured features that describe
the percent overlap of the brain tumor with ROIs it occupies, and then provided to an
LLM for report generation. The generated reports provide details about regional tumor
impact and offer insightful clinical implications based on the functional role associated
with identified tumor-ROI relationships. However, generated reports do not resemble the
standard narrative structuring of radiology reports authored by fellowship trained neuro-
radiologists. Additionally, Seg-to-Exp reports do not describe additional clinically-relevant
imaging observations beyond anatomical tumor location.
AutoRG-Brain (Lei et al., 2024) also adopts a two-stage framework. In the first stage,
anomaly ROI masks are generated and mapped to specific ROIs based on anatomical seg-
mentations. In the second stage, a fine-tuned VLM takes embedded anomaly ROI masks
as visual prompts for RRG. This approach uses deterministic features to focus the VLM,
generating region-specific findings grounded in areas of the image where anomalies were
detected. Based on this design, generated reports are largely descriptive, with findings ex-

Data
This study uses two complementary datasets to support radiology report generation and
validation of BTReport-derived features. First, the HuskyBrain dataset is a retrospective
cohort of fully de-identified pre-operative mpMRI studies paired with radiologist-authored
reports, serving as the primary resource for training and evaluation of neuro-oncology RRG
frameworks. The second dataset is a subset of BraTS’23 cases, which enable survival anal-
yses with imaging and clinical metadata. Together, these datasets support the evaluation
of synthetic report clinical quality and the use of deterministic neuroimaging features for
survival outcome prediction.

title: BTReport: A Framework for Brain Tumor Radiology Report Generation with Clinically Relevant Features
authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Dickson T. Chen, Tianyi Ren, Daniel K. Low, Jacob Ruzevick, Asma Ben Abacha, Alberto Santamaria-Pang, Mehmet Kurt
venue: Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL); Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 315, pp. 1445â€“1472
text:
HuskyBrain Dataset
We collected pre-operative mpMRI scans and radiology reports from a retrospective co-
hort of GBM patients (n=184) treated at the University of Washington Medical Center
(UWMC), an academic medical institution serving patients across the WWAMI region
(Washington, Wyoming, Alaska, Montana, and Idaho). Inclusion criteria were: 1) con-
firmed histopathologic diagnosis of GBM; 2) availability of pre-operative mpMRI sequences
including T1, T2, T1c, and T2-FLAIR; and 3) a corresponding pre-operative diagnostic
radiology report. Images were pre-processed using CaPTk (Davatzikos et al., 2018; Pati
et al., 2020), following BraTS 2017-2023 procedures: DICOM to NIfTI conversion, SRI24
co-registration, 1 mm isotropic resampling, and skull-stripping.
Reference reports were
authored by fellowship-trained radiologists and selected as the clinical reference standard.
For each case, the HuskyBrain dataset contains de-identified MRI sequences, radiologist-
authored reports stripped of protected health information, and tumor masks.

Survival Analysis Dataset
From the BraTS’23 dataset (Adewole et al., 2023), a smaller cohort of mpMRI cases (n=461)
was used for survival analyses. Cases were selected based on the availability of five minimum
metadata entries: (1) age at initial diagnosis, (2) biological sex, (3) confirmed methylation
status of O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), (4) mutation status of isoci-
trate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1), and (5) overall survival or equivalent survival quantification
representing the number of days between radiological diagnosis and reported days to known
death. We collected these demographic and genomic features from multiple publicly avail-
able collections of GBM cases, including those from the University of California San Fran-
cisco (UCSF-PDGM) (Calabrese et al., 2022), University of Pennsylvania (UPenn-GBM)
(Bakas et al., 2021), Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC-GBM) (Na-
tional Cancer Institute Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC), 2018),
and The Cancer Genome Atlas from the Cancer Imaging Archive (TCGA-LGG & TGCA-
GBM) (Pedano et al., 2016) (Scarpace et al., 2016).

text:
BTReport Framework
BTReport is a two-stage approach for neuro-oncology RRG that first deterministically ex-
tracts interpretable and clinically relevant neuroimaging features from mpMRI, then uses an
LLM for syntactically structured narrative construction and report generation. Since quan-
titative measurements are central to radiological evaluation, BTReport relies on validated
open-sourced algorithms to derive descriptors of anatomy and tumor pathology, rather than
performing end-to-end medical inference with a VLM.
Figure 1: BTReport Overview: Interpretable, clinically meaningful variables are determin-
istically extracted for each case, including demographics, VASARI features, and
3D midline shift measurements. These features are utilized by context-guided
LLMs for clinically grounded radiology report generation.
For a given case, the BTReport framework (Figure 1) consists of four steps:
1. T1-weighted scans and tumor masks are used to generate tumor-robust anatomical
segmentations, from which regional volumetric statistics are computed (Section 4.2).
2. Midline shift is quantified by propagating a hand-annotated MNI152 midline into
subject space using the MNI152-to-subject deformation field (Section 4.3).

Segmentation Statistics
BTReport Inputs:
For a given case, inputs to the BTReport framework include their
T1 sequence and corresponding tumor segmentation masks. Tumor segmentation masks
are derived from manual annotation or automated segmentation, and tumor sub-region
annotations (necrotic core, edema, enhancing tumor) follow BraTS convention.
Robust Anatomical Segmentations & Volumetric Statistics:
Anatomical segmen-
tations provide tumor-ROI relational context by localizing tumors with respect to critical
brain structures. However, many automated methods assume near-normal anatomy and
can fail when large tumors deform tissue and obscure boundaries. Prior work improves
tumor-robust segmentations either by training with synthetic tumor-mask augmentation
(Lei et al., 2024), or by synthesizing pseudo-healthy structural images that suppress tumor
appearance, increasing the reliability of established segmentation pipelines (Iglesias et al.,
2023). Our approach closely resembles the latter.
First, we register the MNI152 atlas (Collins et al., 1999; Fonov et al., 2011, 2009) to
subject space using SynthMorph (Hoffmann et al., 2024). The resulting warped atlas, re-
ferred to as MNI152-to-subject, provides a pseudo-healthy anatomical representation of the
brain. Next, we obtain anatomical segmentations by running SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023)
on the MNI152-to-subject volume. As SynthSeg operates on the tumor-free brain repre-
sentations, anatomical segmentations remain robust when tumors deform native anatomy.
Finally, anatomical labels are merged with the tumor and midline segmentations, to produce
a unified mask that jointly represents normal neuroanatomy and pathological structures.
With this joint segmentation, we can reliably extract quantitative features including tumor
and ventricle volume, lesion count, tumor sub-region proportions, and tumor-ROI overlap.

text:
VASARI Feature Extraction
To standardize neuroimaging-derived glioma characterization and improve repeatability,
the VASARI (Visually AcceSAble Rembrandt Images) feature set was developed by The
Cancer Imaging Archive. The VASARI feature set uses controlled vocabulary to quantita-
tively describes anatomical relationships between GBM tumors and clinically relevant brain
structures established in the literature. Furthermore, these relationships are also routinely
included in neuroradiology reports and used by neurosurgeons to assess whether patients
are candidates for surgical intervention. VASARI features have been used to accurately pre-
dict tumor histological grade (WHO I-IV grade), disease progression, molecular mutation
status (e.g., IDH1 WT/mutant, MGMT un/methylated), risk of recurrence, and overall
patient survival (Jain et al., 2014; Nicolasjilwan et al., 2015; Peeken et al., 2019; Setyawan
et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2017). Here, we employ a modified variant of
VASARI-auto (Ruffle et al., 2024), an automated labeling tool, which has been validated as
non-inferior to radiologist VASARI annotations, and can be used to reduce inter-rater vari-
ance. The included variations use the subject-space anatomical and midline segmentations
extracted in Sections 4.2 and 4.3 to improve feature accuracy.

BTReport Feature Validation
To determine whether extracted imaging features are clinically relevant, we assessed them
based on two criteria: (1) whether features correspond to commonly reported radiological
concepts (Section 4.5.1) and (2) by modeling their prognostic value with respect to patient
survival (Section 4.5.2). To validate the accuracy of extracted features, we assess the quality
of feature extraction in generated reports to those found in associated radiologist-authored
ground truth reports, assessing categorical and numerical feature precision and error.

section_heading: Semantic Clustering of Common Radiology Findings
text:
Semantic Clustering of Common Radiology Findings
Here, we derived a ranked list of the most frequently included topics in real radiology
reports. First, we extract all discrete factual claims across all reports in the HuskyBrain
dataset using the method proposed in TBFact (Blondeel et al., 2025). TBFact uses an
LLM (in this case DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025)) to divide each clinical report into
independently verifiable factual claims. Next, we embedded each extracted claim using a
lightweight sentence-transformer model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019))
to obtain dense semantic representations.
All embedded claims were pooled across the
dataset and clustered using hierarchical agglomerative clustering (cosine distance, average
linkage) without specifying the number of clusters a priori, allowing groups of semantically
related statements to emerge from the data in an unsupervised manner.
We then use a pre-trained Gemma 3 27B LLM (Gemma Team et al., 2025) model to
summarize claims in each cluster into representative topic sentences. For example, a cluster
containing claims such as: [“The lesion measures 4.0 x 3.5 cm”, “The lesion measures 3.9
x 2.0 x 2.1 cm.”, ...], is summarized by the topic sentence “Lesion size and measurements
reported.”
The number of claims assigned to each cluster serves as an estimate of the
frequency of the corresponding topic. The 35 most frequent cluster descriptors, along with
representative example claims for each cluster, are reported in Appendix A.
Collectively, the resulting set of cluster descriptors and frequencies provides an inter-
pretable, data-driven view of radiological concepts based on real-world reporting. We use
these concepts to validate the clinical relevance of deterministically extracted features found
in BTReport and assess their alignment with findings in real radiology reports.

Survival Outcome Modeling
To assess whether BTReport-extracted features were predictive of clinical outcomes, we
evaluated their association with overall survival measured from diagnosis. This analysis
used the dataset described in Section 3.2, which provides survival outcomes and patient
metadata for a subset of BraTS cases. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan–Meier
estimators implemented with the lifelines library (Davidson-Pilon, 2024), with curves
reported in Appendix B. Differences between survival groups were assessed using the log-
rank test, and relative risk was quantified using Cox proportional hazards models, reporting
hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was determined from
p-values derived from both the log-rank tests and Cox models.

text:
Clinically Relevant Features Included in BTReport
Table 1 summarizes the quantitative imaging features used by BTReport for automated
report generation. Each feature was evaluated according to two clinically motivated cri-
teria: 1) whether it corresponded to at least one of the top 35 radiological concepts most
frequently documented in reference reports from the HuskyBrain dataset (Section 4.5.1),
and 2) whether it was a statistically significant predictor of patient survival time based on
the survival analysis described in Section 4.5.2. We found that 21/22 of the BTReport fea-
tures are commonly reported in clinical reports, and 11/22 are predictive of overall patient
survival. This analysis highlights the clinical relevance of extracted features, motivating
their use as inputs for downstream RRG.

authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Dickson T. Chen, Tianyi Ren, Daniel K. Low, Jacob Ruzevick, Asma Ben Abacha, Alberto Santamaria-Pang, Mehmet Kurt

section_heading: Structured Synthetic Report Generation Using LLMs
text:
Structured Synthetic Report Generation Using LLMs
The BTReport framework generates the Findings sections of radiology reports in a style
that mimics a target institution through an in-context learning prompt to provide stylistic
guidance and emphasize the relevant radiological facts which should be included in generated
reports (Appendix C). Some facts in reference reports (e.g., diffusion characteristics, vascu-
lar features) cannot be derived from standard structural mpMRI modalities used for tumor
segmentation (T1w, T1c, T2w, T2-FLAIR). Therefore, the LLM is explicitly instructed to
exclude these findings in generated reports to prevent unsupported claims.
Report generation is conditioned on the BTReport feature set and prompt instructions
that restrict the LLM to narrative synthesis and stylistic alignment, enabling tighter control
over report content and structure without task-specific fine-tuning. This prompting strategy
improves interpretability by allowing reported findings to be directly traced to deterministic
features.
For RRG with BTReport, we experiment with two open-source pre-trained LLMs with
reasoning capability:
gpt-oss:120b (Agarwal et al., 2025) and Llama 3.1 70B Instruct
(Grattafiori et al., 2024). These models were selected based on their strong reasoning and
instruction-following capabilities. To avoid cloud sharing of medical data, only local offline
models were used. Examples Findings sections from synthetically generated reports across
the different BTReport variants and other RRG frameworks can be found in Appendix F.

text:
Automated Evaluation of Generated Radiology Reports
Generated radiology reports were evaluated using RadEval (Xu et al., 2025), a unified
open-source framework that evaluates radiology text based on:
• N-gram-based lexical similarity: BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), ROUGE (Lin, 2004)
• pre-trained contextualized embeddings: BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020)
• clinically grounded scores: RaTEScore (Zhao et al., 2024)
To assess the clinical correctness of content in generated reports, we used TBFact (Blon-
deel et al., 2025), an LLM-based factuality metric that evaluates reports based on factual
inclusion, distortion, and omission. These metrics are presented in Tables 3 and 4.

Reliability of Extracted Features
We evaluated the reliability of BTReport-extracted clinical features by comparing them with
the same features extracted from ground-truth radiology reports in the HuskyBrain dataset.
Using LangExtract (Goel, 2025), we decompose radiology reports into class-attribute pairs,
where each class represents a clinically defined radiology concept, and their associated
attribute(s) specify the characteristic linked to the concept. For example, the text [“arising
in the right parietal lobe...”] is decomposed into the “side of tumor epicenter” class and
the “right” attribute (See Appendix E for a complete example). We present the accuracy
of categorical features and the error of the numerical features in Table 2.

title: BTReport: A Framework for Brain Tumor Radiology Report Generation with Clinically Relevant Features
authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Dickson T. Chen, Tianyi Ren, Daniel K. Low, Jacob Ruzevick, Asma Ben Abacha, Alberto Santamaria-Pang, Mehmet Kurt
venue: Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL); Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 315, pp. 1445â€“1472
text:
Discussion
We present BTReport, a framework for brain tumor RRG grounded in clinically relevant
quantitative imaging features. Overall, our findings support the two-stage report generation
paradigm for neuro-oncology RRG, suggesting that in medical imaging domains with limited
data, adding quantitative features to prompts is an efficient way to generate reports and
improve factual consistency.
BTReport enables accurate measurement-grounded report-
ing without requiring task-specific fine-tuning of vision encoders or VLMs, and generates
interpretable reports by using modular, reliably-extracted features.
We presented novel pipelines for midline shift measurement and tumor-robust anatom-
ical segmentation for deterministic feature extraction, and showed that these features had
strong agreement with expert annotation. Additionally, other quantitative features were
selected based on clinical guidelines such as VASARI and validated to be significant predic-
tors of survival time using KM-analysis. By clustering concepts frequently reported in real
radiology reports, we validated that the included features were clinically relevant. When
compared with existing neuro-oncology RRG approaches, BTReport generated reports are
superior in terms of lexical similarity and factual accuracy. We believe this improvement
is due to the clinically-relevant features used for generation and the in-context learning
prompt which allows reasoning LLMs to predict the most relevant features for RRG.
To facilitate further research in neuro-oncology RRG, we provide BTReport-BraTS, an
open-source companion dataset containing anatomical descriptors, metadata, and BTRe-
port generated reports for mpMRI cases in the BraTS’23 dataset. To assess the clinical
applicability of BTReport, we have developed BTReview, a survey tool for radiologist as-
sessment of generated neuro-oncology radiology reports (Appendix H). Future work will
obtain radiologist feedback with BTReview, incorporate additional features such as white
matter hyperintensities and basal cistern status, handle additional mpMRI imaging modal-
ities, and include descriptions of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke findings.

Despite rapid advances in radiology report generation (RRG), there remains a lack of accessible,

venue: Image and Vision Computing, Volume 161, Article 105629
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors pose a significant medical challenge, characterized by high incidence and mortality rates, which
underscore the critical need for accurate and early diagnosis using minimally invasive techniques such as
magnetic resonance imaging. In this context, Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a promising tool to enhance
diagnostic precision and efficiency. However, its widespread adoption in clinical practice remains limited due to
the opacity of Artificial Intelligence-driven decision-making processes. To address this challenge, we introduce
BrAInVision, a hybrid and doubly explainable AI framework for brain tumor detection. The novelty of our
approach is the integration of both deep learning and traditional machine learning techniques, combining deep-
extracted features with hand-crafted features to create a more robust and interpretable classification system.
In contrast to conventional single-explanation methods, our framework provides comprehensive explainability
through a multi-level analytical approach, enhancing both interpretability and transparency. The first level
employs Grad-CAM to visualize regions of interest identified by the deep feature extractor, while the second
level utilizes Permutation Feature Importance and Partial Dependence Plots to understand and quantify the
contribution of specific image characteristics to diagnostic decisions. The proposed framework achieved an
F1-score of 97% on the four classes (Glioma/Meningioma/Pituitary/NoTumor) and an average 99% in binary
classification (Glioma/NoTumor), outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach has
been validated on both the original dataset and an independent dataset with radiologist-annotated tumor
masks, demonstrating strong generalizability. Designed for seamless integration into radiologists’ workflows as
a decision support system, BrAInVision ensures a high degree of explainability, thereby fostering greater trust
in AI-assisted medical decision-making.

Introduction
The detection and classification of brain tumors remain among
the most critical tasks in neuro-radiology, carrying significant im-
plications related to patient survival and quality of life. Globally,
approximately 347.992 new cases of brain cancer were recorded in
2019, with 187.491 males and 160.501 females diagnosed [1]. About
24.820 malignant tumors of the brain and spinal cord are expected
to be diagnosed in 2025 in the United States only, which can lead
to approximately 18.330 deaths [2]. Unfortunately, despite great ad-
vances in treatment modalities, the five-year survival rate for malignant
brain tumors remains below 36%, clearly evidencing the paramount
importance of early and accurate diagnosis. These statistics obviously
underline the urgent need for accurate and early diagnosis to improve

However, the adoption of AI in clinical practice is not without

process. Indeed, traditional AI models often operate as ‘‘black boxes’’,
providing almost no insight into their decision-making process [5]. This
lack of transparency is a significant challenge and barrier in clinical

into their processes to enlarge trust in AI [6,7].
The understanding of AI decisions is a key factor for clinical adop-
tion [8]; XAI systems receive significantly higher acceptance rates
among healthcare professionals compared to non-explainable counter-

Incorporating XAI into brain tumor diagnostics could help to en-
hance the trustworthiness of AI-assisted decisions, while also could
facilitate better communication between clinicians and patients. In
addition, regulatory frameworks increasingly require explainability for
AI systems, particularly in healthcare settings, making transparency not
only a clinical necessity but also a legal and ethical requirements.
This paper has two main objectives: build an AI framework, aiming
at the widest possible explainability, and increase the trustworthiness
towards healthcare AI. The implementation of two complementary
layers of explainability is the main innovation of our approach. The first
layer offers visual interpretations of how the deep learning component
analyzes MRI images, whereas the second layer provides feature-level
explanations of the classification decisions. This strategy performs a
dual-explanation approach that addresses the ‘‘black box’’ problem
of AI systems from multiple perspectives, and helps in making the
framework’s decisions transparent and trustworthy for clinical use.
Thereby, we involve both machine and deep learning pipelines proposing
BrAInVision, a hybrid and dually explainable framework for brain tumor
detection. In the proposed solution, two kinds of feature extraction,
and consequently two levels of explanation, were implemented: deep-
based and hand-crafted. The deep features are exploited to conduct an
image visual analysis; Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation
Mapping, a technique that highlights regions in images that influence
model predictions) is applied to explain what areas are considered
relevant by the framework for diagnosis. The hand-crafted features
are extracted without the need for a segmentation pipeline and they
are merged with deep features to create a new numerical and inter-
pretable dataset. The better-evaluated machine learning model was
choose to produce the final classification. After this step, the second

Related works
Numerous studies have explored different approaches to classify
tumors in MRI scans enhancing AI and medical image processing. On
the other hand, the challenge remains due to solutions interpretability
and dataset limitations. This section reviews key contributions in the
field highlighting recent advancements and their impact. We organize
our review focusing on three main methodological approaches: deep
learning-based techniques, textural feature extraction methods and
explainable AI frameworks.

Deep learning approaches
The most widely used approach in the literature concerns feature
extraction using stand-alone deep learning algorithms. For example,
Montalbo et al. [12] utilize the Vision Transformers and Convolutional
Neural Networks. The authors investigate ViT, MobileViT and Swin
Transformers benchmarking them against a ConvNeXt CNN model.
The dataset consists of 7.023 MRI images with four classes: no tu-
mor, glioma, meningioma and pituitary tumor. Results indicate that
transformer-based models outperform CNNs in terms of tumor de-
tection accuracy (95%) but face challenges related to computational
complexity and data requirements. An improvement regarding the data
privacy is implemented by Albalawi et al. [13] which use a tuned
VGG16 architecture in a federated learning-based architecture. Unlike
conventional methods, federated learning enables decentralized model
training ensuring data privacy across multiple institutions. The model is
trained on the Msoud dataset, ensuring robust feature extraction across
various tumor types. The approach achieves high precision with an
overall accuracy of 98%.

Textural feature extraction methods
While deep learning approaches show impressive performance, tex-
tural feature extraction methods often require fewer computational
resources and offer greater interpretability. In this review, we take
into account the works that do not use segmentation, therefore the
hand-crafted features will refer to the whole magnetic resonance image.
Selvy et al. [14] use Histogram Equalization for image enhancement
followed by feature extraction using the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix
(GLCM, a statistical method that examines texture by analyzing spatial
relationships between pixel intensities). The extracted features are then
fed into a Probabilistic Neural Network classifier to distinguish between
normal and glioma-affected brain MRI scans. The dataset consists of
150 MRI images divided into training and testing sets. The proposed
model achieved an accuracy of 90,9%. Kaplan et al. [15] introduce a
Pyramid and Fixed-Size Patch approach integrating Histogram of ori-
ented gradients (HOG) features and a k-Nearest Neighbor classifier (KNN).
This study extends beyond brain tumors, incorporating Alzheimer’s
Disease classification. The proposed model achieves high accuracy,

Explainable AI frameworks
As interpretability becomes increasingly crucial in medical appli-
cations, numerous researchers have intensively worked on developing
explainable frameworks. Saaed et al. [17] introduce Neuro-XAI, a deep
learning framework based on two deep feature extraction modules.
The study utilizes pre-trained models with integrated a XAI technique,
Grad-CAM (which produces visual explanations for CNN decisions by
highlighting important regions in the input image), to enhance model
interpretability. The experimental results indicate a 97% of accuracy,
showing the fact that the deep extraction modules, based on DarkNet53
and MobileNet, are not worthy to classify brain tumor despite the
computational effort. Appiah et al. [18] integrates Proper Orthogonal
Decomposition with deep learning techniques for brain tumor detec-
tion. The method extracts essential spatial features before feeding them
to a fine-tuned CNN and uses SHAP to provide a visual diagnosis. This
pre-processing step mitigates the computational complexity. The study
evaluates its approach using the BraTS 2016 dataset and achieves a
92,78% in classification accuracy, surpassing traditional deep learning
models that rely solely on raw MRI images.

Research gaps and our contribution
Based on the performed literature review, we have identified several
significant gaps in the current state-of-the-art. First, there is limited
use of hand-crafted features in brain tumor classification, and when
employed, they are rarely utilized for enhancing the interpretability
of the diagnostic process. Second, deep features though extensively
employed, are often underutilized, particularly when accuracy is low,
when only binary classification is performed, or when it is not ap-
plied to XAI methods. Third, most existing approaches just implement
single-level explanations, which offer limited insight into the model’s
decision-making process.
Initially, our study aimed to enhance the existing literature using
the widely adopted dataset [19], improving it with the accuracy of the
deep features, the interpretability of hand-crafted features and incor-
porating visual explainability techniques. However, we decided to use
a recently published medical dataset on Mendeley Data [20] to train
and test the framework. Furthermore, the proposed methodology was
validated using the first dataset enhanced with radiologist-validated
segmentation [21] to ensure a rigorous analysis. Although the dataset
used to train the model was introduced in early 2024, so the amount
of existing literature is scarce, consisting of only two studies.
The first one by Mohan and Ramkumar [22] used MobileNet, a

which includes rotation (20 degrees), scaling, shear transformation
and horizontal/vertical flips. Additional layers were introduced, includ-

Background
This section provides an overview of the fundamental techniques
and algorithms that form the backbone components of our brain tumor
classification framework (BrAInVision). Understanding these building
blocks is essential for appreciating the hybrid and explainable approach
presented in this work.
3.1. VGG16
VGG16 [24] is a deep CNN architecture developed by the Visual
Geometry Group (VGG) at the University of Oxford. The name VGG16
refers to the 16 weight layers which consist of 13 convolutional layers
and 3 fully connected layers. The convolutional layers use small 3 × 3
filters with a stride of 1 and padding to maintain spatial dimensions.
These layers extract features from the input image, followed by a
Rectified Linear Unit activation function that introduces non-linearity.
Additionally, max pooling layers with 2 × 2 filters and a stride of 2 are
used to downsample feature maps and reduce computational complex-
ity. After the convolutional and pooling layers, the network includes
three fully connected layers. The first two fully connected layers con-
tain 4096 neurons each, while the final output layer contains neurons
corresponding to the number of classes in the dataset or the number
of features extracted. Feature extraction in VGG16 occurs through
convolutional layers, which apply filters to detect edges, textures and
complex patterns across different depths of the network. One of the
advantages of VGG16 is its simple and uniform architecture, making
it easy to implement and adapt for transfer learning applications in
medical imaging.

Machine learning models
Our framework employs several machine learning algorithms for
final classification task based on the extracted features:
• Support Vector Machines (SVM) [25]. SVM is a supervised
learning algorithm used for classification and regression that finds
the optimal hyperplane that separates data points belonging to
different classes in a high-dimensional space. The optimal hy-
perplane is determined by maximizing the margin, which is the
distance between the nearest data points (support vectors) from
each class to enhance generalization. Common kernel functions
include linear, polynomial, and radial basis function (RBF), each
suited for different types of data structures. Despite its ability to
rigorously manage large dimension dataset, SVM can be compu-
tationally intensive and requires careful selection of parameters
to achieve optimal performance.
• Random Forest Classifier (RF) [26]. RF is an ensemble learn-
ing method primarily used for classification and regression tasks
which operates by constructing multiple decision trees during
training and aggregating their predictions to improve accuracy
and reduce overfitting. The algorithm is an extension of bagging
(Bootstrap Aggregating), where each decision tree is trained on
a random subset of the data sampled with replacement. The
effectiveness of Random Forest is attributed to its ability to han-
dle high-dimensional datasets, robustness to noise, but can be
computationally expensive, particularly with large datasets.
• K-nearest neighbors (KNN) [27]. KNN is a simple yet powerful
supervised learning algorithm used for classification and regres-
sion tasks. Unlike many machine learning models, KNN does not
build an explicit mathematical model during training, but instead
perform a ‘‘lazy’’ learning, where it simply stores the training
data and makes predictions by comparing new data points to
existing ones. While KNN may be a lightweight and easy-to-
implement solution, it can be computationally expensive for large
datasets since every prediction requires measuring distances from
all training points. Additionally, KNN is sensitive to irrelevant or
highly imbalanced features, making feature scaling an important
preprocessing step.
• Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) [28]. XGBoost is a highly
efficient and scalable machine learning algorithm based on gradi-
ent boosting, an ensemble learning technique. It is widely used for

Grad-CAM
Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) is a tech-
nique used to visualize the regions of an image that are important for
a CNN in a classification task [29]. This technique is central to our
framework’s first layer of explainability, providing visual insights into
the deep extractor focus area. Grad-CAM is largely used for interpreting
CNN results, increasing explainability and improving debugging pro-
cesses. The algorithm operates as follows: firstly, the network produces
class scores through its layers for a given input image, then the gradi-
ents of the target class score are computed with respect to the feature
maps of a convolutional layer via backpropagation. These gradients are
then averaged over width and height dimensions to obtain importance
weights for each feature map channel. These weights highlight the
significance of each feature map for the target class and they are
used to perform a weighted combination of the feature maps from the
convolutional layer. The result is a coarse localization map highlighting
the important regions of the image. This map is then passed through a
ReLU function to ensure only positive influences on the class score are
considered. The final class activation map is upsampled to the size of
the input image and superimposed on the original one. The output is
a heatmap showing the image regions most influential to the model’s
prediction, providing radiologists with visual confirmation of the areas
influencing the diagnostic decision.

Permutation Feature Importance
Permutation Feature Importance (PFI) is essential to our frame-
work’s second layer of explainability, revealing which features most
significantly influence classification decisions. The importance of a fea-
ture is determined by measuring the increase in the model’s prediction
accuracy after permuting its values. A feature is considered important if
shuffling its values results in a significant increase in model error, indi-
cating that the model relied on that feature for prediction. Conversely, a
feature is deemed unimportant if permuting its values has no impact on
the model error, implying that the model did not utilize that feature for
prediction. PFI metric was introduced by Breiman [26] for its random
forests model. Expanding on this idea, Fisher et al. [30] proposed a
model-agnostic version, referred to as model reliance. Following Fisher’s
approach, let ̂f be the trained model, X the feature matrix, y be the target
vector, and L(y,̂ f) the error measure.
Permutation feature importance offers several advantages. One of
its key aspects is interpretability because the importance measure is
directly related to the increase in model error (or accuracy, in our case).
This makes easy to understand the impact of each feature on model
performance. In this sense, it provides global insight of the model’s
behavior, helping to identify which features contribute the most to
predictions. Comparability is another key aspect since permutation
feature importance relies on an error ratio rather than an absolute error
difference. Another benefit is that no retraining is required. Unlike
methods that remove features and retrain the model, permutation
feature importance evaluates features within a fixed model [31].

Partial Dependence Plot
Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) complements PFI in our framework
by visualizing how specific features affect the model’s predictions, fur-
ther enhancing the interpretability of our classification results. PDP is a
global and model-agnostic XAI technique [32]. This method provides a
comprehensive interpretation by analyzing the influence of one or more
features on the target variable across all observations. In contrast, local
interpretability techniques focus on assessing the impact of individual
features at the observation level. The model-agnostic nature of PDP
allows it to be applied to any predictive model, regardless of its
underlying architecture. PDP allow us to examine the marginal effect
of specific features on the model’s predictions, thereby offering insights
into their contribution to the overall decision-making process of the
black-box model.

Architecture
BrAInVision stems from the critical need to develop an AI framework
that ensures high diagnostic accuracy and transparent decision-making
in the challenging domain of brain tumor diagnostics. Our approach
embraces four conceptual phases, each designed to progressively trans-
form raw images into a clinically relevant decision:

• Data Preprocessing: this initial phase, handles MRI images as
raw material to be refined. More in details, images belonging
to four classes (Glioma, Meningioma, Pituitary tumor, or NoTu-
mor) are loaded and preprocessed to standardize their format
and dimensions. Image normalization, resizing, and color space
transformations are applied in order to guarantee consistent input
representation regardless of acquisition parameters. The aim of
this phase is to create a clean, standardized dataset ready for
analysis.
• Deep Feature Extraction: deep features are extracted using a
custom deep features extractor based on an VGG16 network to
capture complex visual patterns which are not immediately visi-
ble in the images. This phase applies transfer learning by utilizing
pre-trained ImageNet weights, allowing the network to extract
rich hierarchical features despite limited domain-specific training
data.
• Feature Engineering: this phase represents the core of our hybrid
approach. BrAInVision involves not only features extracted by
the neural network in the precedent step, but enrich them with
additional hand-crafted features, derived from Hu moments and
GLCM. These traditional features are extracted and merged with
deep features in order to obtain a complex representation vector
for each original image. These combined features are normalized
using Z-Score Standardization [33]. Above the technical details,
the merging of these two features types intuitively ensure the di-
alogue between two relevant domain nuances: the computational
intuition encoded in features extracted by deep neural networks
and the soundness of traditional clinical analysis encoded in
hand-crafted features.
• Classification: in the final phase, a machine learning model
performs the final classification, receiving the combined features
array, and providing a clinical decision, corresponding to one of
the four tumor categories. In the proposed architecture, we delib-
erately separate feature extraction from classification to enhance
explainability at multiple levels of the framework.

tween deep learning’s predictive power and traditional machine learn-
ing’s interpretability, therefore offering a unique solution to medical
image analysis challenges. More specifically, our framework addresses

BrAInVision implements a hybrid approach that bridges the gap be-
tween deep learning’s predictive power and traditional machine learn-
ing’s interpretability, therefore offering a unique solution to medical
image analysis challenges. More specifically, our framework addresses
the crucial requirement for explainability in medical AI systems by
incorporating different explanation techniques at multiple levels of the
classification pipeline:
• Grad-CAM is used in the first framework phase to visualize how
the deep extractor focused on images and then extracted the most
important features, making the extraction process clearer.
• PFI and PDP are used in the final framework phase to fully under-
stand how hand-crafted features contributed in the classification
process, firstly assessing the impact of each feature on the model’s
prediction and then analyzing the relationship between specific
features and the model’s output. These techniques guarantees
transparency as they provide quantitative evidence of feature
relevance and their influence on specific diagnostic decisions.
The proposed hybrid approach enhances accuracy while ensuring
explainability, making the solution’s insights more accessible to domain
experts and facilitating practical clinical applications.
Our architectural design supports radiological expertise as it pri-
oritizes both diagnostic accuracy and clinical workflow integration
by offering visual analysis alongside feature-level explanations. A de-
tailed description of used hand-crafted features is proposed in the next
subsection of this work. The proposed hybrid explainable framework,
BrAInVision, is reported in Fig. 1, while the methodology phases are
formalized in Algorithm 1.
Algorithm 1 formalizes the training workflow of our framework,
illustrating the sequential processing steps from image preprocessing

Hand-crafted features
Hand-crafted features are a critical component of our explainable
framework as they provide objective evidence, such as domain specific
measurement, that are inherently interpretable to clinical experts. In
the following section, we formally introduce the hand-crafted features
used in the classification process: Hu Moments [34] and GLCM [35].
The idea behind the combination of these features was twofold: pro-
viding a system that employs reproducible techniques which are in-
terpretable and model-agnostic, while leveraging their complementary
properties in characterizing both the morphological aspects (shape and
geometry) and textural patterns of brain tissues, which are known to be
particularly relevant for distinguishing between different types of brain
tumors.

These moments are particularly useful in pattern recognition and shape

orientation or positioning within the scan while maintaining their

Datasets
For this study, we carefully selected two complementary brain MRI
datasets to rigorously evaluate our framework’s performance and gen-
eralizability. The first dataset served as our primary training and testing
resource, while the second dataset provided additional validation with
expert-annotated tumor masks. The first dataset, namely Brain Tumor
Data dataset [20], is a rigorously curated collection of grayscale MRI
images of brain tumors organized in two main sets: one dedicated to
training and the other for independent testing. Each set is divided into
four categories, corresponding to the different types of tumors: glioma,
meningioma, pituitary and a further class called no tumor which includes
images of healthy brains. (see Fig. 2).
For the first experimental evaluation, the training section of the
dataset contains 1.321 images of glioma, 1.339 of meningioma, 1.457
of pituitary and 1.595 images of no-tumor brains, making a total
of 5.712 images. The testing part, designed to provide an unbiased
assessment of model performance, includes 300 images of glioma, 306
of meningioma, 300 of pituitary and 405 of healthy brains which brings
the total number to 1.311 images. Overall, the dataset comprises 7.023
images. The dataset exhibits a well-balanced distribution across the
different classes, (approximately 25% per class), which is particularly
important for avoiding class bias during training and ensures that the
model learns to discriminate equally well between all tumor types.
The second dataset, namely Brain Tumor Segmentation Dataset, is
a well-known selection of brain tumors grayscale MRI images [19]
segmented afterwards by radiologists [21]. Both images and masks
folders are divided into the four upcited categories, glioma, meningioma,
pituitary and no tumor. The second experimental evaluation consists in
testing the framework on the Brain Tumor Segmentation Dataset. This
cross-dataset validation approach provides a more stringent test of
the framework’s robustness and generalizability beyond the training
distribution. This type of testing is made to provide an additional proof
of the model’s robustness. The dataset includes 649 glioma images, 999
of meningioma, 994 of pituitary, which are all provided with tumor
masks, and 1.595 of healthy brains where masks are null. The dataset
exhibits balanced distribution across the different classes.

The choice of using VGG16 as the deep feature extraction net
stems from the results obtained from recent works [43–46], where re-
searchers have compared various state-of-the-art pre-trained networks
in brain tumor classification task. These comparative studies showed
that VGG16 consistently outperforms other architectures in terms of
Accuracy and F1-score for this specific domain, despite newer architec-
tures often showing superior performance in general computer vision
tasks.
Our custom deep features extractor is constructed using a VGG16
network as base model, leveraging the imagenet pre-trained weights
through transfer learning technique without fine-tuning the original
architecture. The output of the VGG16 base model is passed to a
GlobalAveragePooling2D type level, which effectively reduces the spa-
tial dimensions (height and width) to a single value per channel.
Subsequently, a Dense layer with 256 neurons processes the output and
performs the final feature selection, using a ReLU activation function.
To facilitate access to the extracted features, this layer was specifically
labeled with the name ‘‘features_layer’’. This architectural design bal-
ances network depth and feature dimensionality, producing a rich yet
manageable set of 256 deep features that capture complex MRI visual
patterns.
Table 2 provides a concise overview of the deep feature extractor
architecture.

Limitations and future perspectives
While our framework demonstrates significant advancements in
both classification performance and explainability, several limitations
should be acknowledged and addressed in future research.
First, a more systematic feature selection methodology could poten-
tially further optimize the model. The current framework utilizes all 27
hand-crafted features and 256 deep features without a formal feature
selection process. Implementing techniques (such as recursive feature
elimination or LASSO regularization) could identify the most discrimi-
native subset of features, potentially improving both performance and
computational efficiency.
The deep feature extraction process could be improved helping
the model to achieve better performance and results interpretation,
for example introducing the use of layers incorporating spatial atten-
tion mechanisms [48]. These attention mechanisms could enhance the
model’s focus on tumor regions, addressing the limitations observed in
our Grad-CAM analysis where the network sometimes fails to precisely
localize tumor boundaries.
Second, BrAInVision uses transfer learning on VGG16 for deep
feature extraction without fine-tuning it or re-training it due to lack
of computational power. In future developments, the training of a
convolutional neural network from scratch on domain-specific 2D
MRI images could enhance predictive performance by better captur-
ing modality-specific features. Third, the model’s capacity to gener-
alize across different datasets requires further validation on multi-
institutional data. While our cross-dataset validation provides initial
evidence of generalizability, testing on more diverse datasets with vary-
ing acquisition parameters, scanner types, and patient demographics
would provide stronger evidence of the framework’s robustness in real-
world clinical settings. Future research should focus on integrating
multi-modal data from complementary imaging techniques (such as
CT or PET scans) and exploring federated learning approaches to
improve robustness and address privacy problems in medical data
sharing. Moreover, future perspectives should include prospective vali-
dation in clinical environments confirming the framework’s robustness,
generalization qualities, and practical utility in real-world diagnostic
practice.

Conclusion
The early and accurate diagnosis of brain tumors remains a crit-
ical challenge in modern neurology, with direct implications for pa-
tient survival. Despite significant advances in imaging techniques, the
interpretation of MRI scans requires specialized expertise, is time-
consuming, and can lead to diagnostic delays. AI-powered systems
offer promising solutions, but their widespread adoption in clinical
practice has been hindered by the ‘‘black box’’ nature of conventional
approaches. This study introduced BrAInVision, a hybrid and explain-
able AI framework designed for brain tumor classification on MRI
images. Our approach uniquely combines the predictive power of deep
learning features with the interpretability of traditional hand-crafted
features (Hu moments and GLCM), creating a balanced solution which
ensures high level of explainability without sacrificing performance.
BrAInVision demonstrated high performance across multiple evaluation
scenarios, achieving an F1-score of 97% in the four-class classifica-
tion task (Glioma/Meningioma/Pituitary/NoTumor) and 99% in binary
classification, outperforming current state-of-the-art approaches. Im-
portantly, these results were validated not only on the original test set
but also on an independent validation dataset with expert-annotated
tumor masks, confirming the framework’s generalizability. The dual-
level explainability approach represents a significant advancement for
clinical adoption. Visual explanations allow radiologists to verify how
neural network look at MRI images, while feature-level interpretations
provide quantitative evidence of which imaging characteristics drive
the classification decisions. Together, these complementary explana-
tions transform the diagnostic process from an opaque prediction to
a transparent, verifiable analysis. BrAInVision is designed as a decision
support system that augments radiological expertise rather than replac-
ing it. By providing both accurate classifications and clear explanations
for those classifications, our framework has the potential to enhance
diagnostic confidence, reduce interpretation time, and ultimately im-
prove patient outcomes through earlier and more accurate diagnoses.
While our current implementation has demonstrated promising re-
sults, future research will focus on enhancing region-specific attention
mechanisms, incorporating multi-modal imaging data, and conducting
prospective clinical validation studies.

localization at an anatomical granularity that is consis-
tent with radiology reports. Most vision-only methods ad-
dress localization and classification as separate label-
prediction tasks, and therefore provide limited alignment
with the fine-grained anatomical semantics used in rou-
tine reporting. To address this limitation, we propose
LIGHT (Learning Image-text Grounding for Hierarchical Tu-

multimodal MRI inputs, LIGHT retrieves coarse anatom-

563 fine-grained subregions, and 5 tumor subtypes; (2)
large-scale foundation pretraining on a curated patient-
disjoint in-house dataset of 99,813 MRI-report pairs; and (3)
grounded task fine-tuning that uses segmentation-guided
tumor crops and multi-template prompt supervision to im-
prove tumor-prompt alignment. Across 11,034 annotated
3D brain tumor MRI cases from in-house, external clinical,
and public datasets, LIGHT achieved 72.1% accuracy for
coarse-grained localization, 70.1% top-1 accuracy for fine-
grained localization, and 76.0%, 83.7%, and 84.6% accuracy
for subtype classification on three 3D datasets, respec-
tively. Additional public 2D subtype-classification experi-
ments provide further evidence of cross-setting subtype
recognition. These results suggest that report-grounded

Introduction
Brain tumors remain a major neurological disease burden,
causing an estimated 248,000 deaths worldwide annually [1]
and approximately 17,600 deaths in the United States [2]. The
5-year survival rate for adults with malignant central nervous
system tumors remains low at 34.8% [2]. Accurate MRI-based
assessment requires joint understanding of tumor identity
and anatomical context to support diagnostic interpretation,
surgical planning, and treatment selection [3]–[5], motivating
methods that combine subtype prediction with report-aligned
localization.
Brain MRI reports translate imaging observations into clini-
cally structured descriptions. They typically comprise findings
(e.g., tumor appearance, anatomical location, and imaging
characteristics) and impressions (e.g., diagnostic interpreta-
tion and differential diagnoses) [6], as illustrated in Fig. 1.
These reports provide a natural source of semantic supervision
by linking visual tumor appearance to anatomical locations
and diagnostic categories. Fine-grained anatomical locations
are hierarchically organized under coarse brain regions, which
makes report-derived location descriptions compatible with
coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Existing vision-only methods usually split into segmen-
tation for tumor delineation and localization [7]–[12], and
classification for subtype, molecular status, or grade predic-
tion [13]–[15]. Segmentation models identify tumor extent
but do not directly express report-level anatomical phrases,
such as "left cerebellar hemisphere near the
fourth ventricle" in Fig. 1, whereas classification
models predict diagnostic categories without linking them to
anatomically meaningful locations. Thus, vision-only pipelines
have limited ability to jointly model MRI appearance, fine-
grained anatomy, and tumor subtype semantics.
Vision-language foundation models provide a suitable for-
mulation by aligning medical images and text in a shared
semantic space [16]–[19]. With contrastive image-text pre-
training, anatomical locations and diagnostic concepts can
be represented as textual prompts and matched with image
features, allowing downstream tasks to be treated as retrieval.

However, current medical vision-language models remain in-
sufficient for report-aligned multimodal brain MRI analysis.
Many studies focus on 2D images, CT, or chest X-ray, leaving
large-scale 3D multimodal brain MRI-report pretraining less
explored [19]. Existing approaches also often underuse report-
derived fine-grained anatomical phrases and lack retrieval
mechanisms that respect the hierarchy between coarse regions
and fine locations [16]–[18].
To address these gaps, we propose LIGHT, a 3D vision-
language framework for hierarchical image-text retrieval in
brain tumor analysis (Fig. 3). LIGHT learns a shared em-
bedding space between multimodal brain MRI and structured
reports, and uses a report-derived hierarchy of 21 coarse-
grained regions and 563 fine-grained subregions (Fig. 2) to
retrieve coarse region(s) before fine-grained subregions. Tumor
subtypes are represented as diagnostic prompts in the same
space, enabling localization and subtype prediction through
one matching framework. During fine-tuning, segmentation-
guided tumor crops and multi-template prompts improve
tumor-centered alignment. Across 11,034 annotated 3D brain
tumor MRI cases, LIGHT achieves 72.1% coarse localization
accuracy, 70.1% top-1 accuracy for fine-grained localization,
and 76.0%, 83.7%, and 84.6% subtype accuracy on three 3D
datasets.
The main contributions are: (1) hierarchical joint re-
trieval, which unifies coarse localization, fine localization,
and subtype classification as image-text retrieval; (2) large-
scale foundation pretraining on 99,813 patient-disjoint MRI-
report pairs covering T1w, T2w, FLAIR, DWI, and ADC;
and (3) grounded task fine-tuning, which uses segmentation
priors and multi-template prompts to improve lesion-prompt
alignment.

and broader biomedical image-text pretraining has produced

and MedCLIP [17] mainly use chest X-rays and reports, while
