2) Prompt-Conditioned Grounded Vision-Language Models:
Prompt-conditioned grounding models match visual regions
with text queries. GLIP [27], for example, formulates object
detection as vision-language pretraining by aligning image
regions with natural-language prompts. This text-conditioned
matching motivates our use of fixed anatomical and subtype
prompts; unlike natural-image grounding, LIGHT matches
tumor-centered 3D MRI crops with a curated clinical vocab-
ulary of regions, subregions, and tumor subtypes.
B. Brain Tumor Segmentation and Localization
1) Brain Tumor Segmentation: CNN-based models, espe-
cially U-Net and nnU-Net [8], have been widely used for brain
tumor segmentation. Transformer-based networks, including
SwinBTS [9] and Swin UNETR [10], further model long-
range 3D dependencies in multimodal MRI. These methods
provide useful tumor masks, but masks do not directly map to
the report-level anatomical vocabulary needed for fine-grained
localization.
2) Coarse-grained Localization: Coarse localization is often
achieved by registering scans to standardized atlases such
as MNI152 [28] or Desikan-Killiany [29] and assigning tu-
mor voxels to atlas regions. Earlier methods use affine or
deformable registration [11], [30], while later approaches
restore anatomy before registration to reduce tumor-induced
distortion [12]. Atlas-based localization supports outcome and
tumor-burden analyses [31], [32], but atlas labels may not
cover descriptive report phrases.
3) Fine-grained Localization: Fine localization has recently
been studied with CLIP-style image-text matching. Uni-
Brain [16] aligns multimodal brain MRI with clinical reports,

3) Fine-grained Localization: Fine localization has recently
been studied with CLIP-style image-text matching. Uni-

H-CLIPs [18] performs hierarchical retrieval from coarse to
fine anatomical levels, and SeLIP [19] strengthens contrastive

this direction to 3D multimodal brain tumor MRI and jointly
handles coarse localization, fine localization, and subtype

C. Brain Tumor Subtype Classification
Most subtype classification methods are vision-only mod-
els. GLI-3D-DenseNet [13] integrates multimodal MRI with
a 3D DenseNet, Hy-3D-UNet [14] combines segmentation
and classification layers, and Hy-Transformer [15] combines
convolutional and transformer components. These methods are
useful baselines, but they do not ground subtype predictions
in anatomical text prompts. LIGHT instead retrieves subtype
and location prompts from the same embedding space.
III. METHOD
LIGHT contains three stages: large-scale foundation pre-
training (Sec. III-A), grounded task fine-tuning (Sec. III-
B), and hierarchical joint retrieval (Sec. III-C). The first
stage aligns 3D multimodal MRI volumes with structured
radiology reports. The second stage adapts this embedding
space to tumor-centered anatomical and subtype prompts using
segmentation-guided crops. The third stage performs inference
by matching one tumor-centered image embedding with pre-
computed text prompt embeddings.
A. Large-scale Foundation Pretraining

For downstream learning, LIGHT aligns a tumor-centered
MRI embedding with fixed anatomical and subtype prompts.
The tumor crop is generated by a frozen lightweight 3D tumor
segmentation model (Eseg, Dseg) based on RTP-Net [7]. This
segmentation model was pretrained before this study on an
independent patient-level separated brain tumor segmentation
dataset. It remains frozen during fine-tuning and inference,
and no downstream test case from Datasets 1–3 was used to
train, fine-tune, select, or evaluate it. The model predicts a

merged before bounding-box extraction:
Mseg = Dseg(Eseg(ximg)) .

(5)

MRI modalities with the tumor mask within the same field of
view, providing a spatial prior that directs the image encoder

A. Experimental Setup
1) Materials:
After excluding tumor-related cases and
patient-level duplicates overlapping with Dataset 1, we cu-
rated 99,813 patient-disjoint multimodal brain MRI image-
report pairs from Huashan Hospital for foundation pretraining
(Fig. 5). This dataset provided broad image-report supervision
rather than tumor-specific downstream supervision.
Downstream evaluation included 11,034 annotated 3D
brain tumor MRI cases from Dataset 1 (Huashan Hospital),
Dataset 2 (two external clinical centers), and Dataset 3 (BraTS-
derived public benchmark), plus two public 2D subtype-
classification datasets (Table I). Dataset 1 labels were reviewed
by two senior radiologists; Datasets 2–5 used original annota-
tions. Dataset 1 used the five-subtype vocabulary, Datasets 2–3
used mapped labels, and public 2D datasets followed native
labels including PIT. All downstream splits were patient-level.
All 3D volumes were resampled to 1.0×1.0 mm2 in-plane
resolution with native through-plane spacing preserved, then
center-cropped or zero-padded to 224 × 224 × 18. Intensities
were clipped to the [0.5, 99.5] percentile range and normalized
to [−1, 1] per modality [39], [40]. Skull stripping was omitted
for Datasets 1–2 to preserve skull and meningeal structures;
Dataset 3 followed BraTS preprocessing.
Available modalities and segmentation priors were concate-
nated by early fusion. Each dataset was trained independently
with an input stem matching available channels; T1c was
treated as a separate contrast, and no synthetic missing-
modality channels were introduced. For 3D LIGHT, T2w-
available datasets were co-registered to T2w space before
mask generation. For LIGHT-2D, released masks were used
only in Dataset 4, and Dataset 5 was evaluated without masks
or the 3D segmentation model. Quality control excluded 15%
of Dataset 1 and 17% of Dataset 2 candidates, with no
exclusions from Datasets 3–5.

Discussion
LIGHT formulates brain tumor localization and subtype
classification as unified hierarchical image-text retrieval, im-
proving localization on Dataset 1 and subtype classification
across in-house, external clinical, and public datasets. The
public 2D validation in Table IV further supports subtype
recognition beyond the 3D setting. Unlike conventional task-
specific classifiers, LIGHT produces scores over human-
readable anatomical and subtype prompts, making its outputs
inspectable as clinical hypotheses.
The main advantage of LIGHT is that localization and
subtype classification share one semantic space rather than
separate task-specific heads. The coarse-to-fine retrieval pro-
cedure also matches the structure of radiology descriptions,
where broad regions often constrain the interpretation before
detailed subregions are specified. Subtype prompts further
allow the same retrieval space to support diagnostic prediction
alongside anatomical localization.
We evaluated two reliability-sensitive components. All
Dataset 1 downstream labels were manually reviewed before
training, and Qwen3-14B was validated on 932 randomly
sampled reports (30%) with consensus labels from two senior
radiologists (Fig. 10). It achieved 96.8% valid structured out-
puts, 94.8% coarse localization accuracy, 90.9% subtype ac-
curacy, 91.7% fine-grained extraction F1, and 86.2% strict all-
fields-correct rate. Errors mainly involved ambiguous subtype
wording, multifocal tumors, or vocabulary merging, and were
corrected or filtered before training. The frozen segmentation
module was evaluated separately (Table V), supporting its use
as a cropping prior.
Several limitations remain. First, fine-grained localization
is constrained by the curated 563-subregion vocabulary and
cannot cover every free-text anatomical expression. Second,
boundary-spanning, diffuse, multifocal, or very small tumors
may reduce confidence when multiple subregions are plausi-
ble. Third, the pretraining reports are mainly in-house Chi-
nese reports; broader validation is needed across languages,

Conclusion
We presented LIGHT, a 3D brain MRI image-text retrieval
framework for hierarchical tumor localization and subtype
classification. By combining large-scale MRI-report pretrain-
ing, segmentation-guided tumor cropping, and prompt-based
task fine-tuning, LIGHT retrieves coarse anatomical regions,
fine-grained subregions, and tumor subtypes from a shared
embedding space. At inference, the model requires only mul-
timodal MRI inputs, because report parsing is used offline
and prompt embeddings are pre-computed. Across multiple
datasets, LIGHT improves localization and classification per-
formance over the evaluated baselines and provides inter-
pretable prompt-level outputs for future radiologist-centered
validation.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Abstract
Detection of brain tumors through MRI scans is a difficult and crucial process since medical
imaging is complex and there are not enough experts to analyze these images in many
countries. The timely detection of diseases such as gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary
tumors is critical because delayed detection may have adverse impacts on the patient’s
condition and result in incorrect treatment. These difficulties are why automated deep
learning models were introduced to help diagnose brain tumors. In this research, we
introduce a multi-stage sequential pipeline for brain tumor classification, localization,
explainability, and report generation in a radiologist-style structured format based on MRI
imaging data, with each stage trained and evaluated independently on its respective dataset.
Specifically, an Xception-based classifier was used to classify MRI images into one of four
classes, achieving 98.96% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.9876. To enhance interpretability,
the Grad-CAM technique was used to visualize image patches the model used during
prediction. If the tumor was present, U-Net was used to perform localization, giving a
Dice score of 0.7835 and an IoU of 0.6919 with the use of T1-weighted MRI images. Finally,
the obtained features were passed as input to a QLoRA fine-tuned language model that
generates structured radiology reports, including such components as Technique, Findings,
and Impression.The proposed framework was evaluated on a hold-out subset of publicly
available T1-weighted MRI data, achieving LLM-as-a-Judge scores of 4.92/5 for accuracy
and 4.95/5 for fluency. These results suggest that the proposed approach is promising
and provide an initial proof of concept. However, additional validation on independent
multi-center datasets and multimodal MRI data is still needed before considering its use in
clinical practice.
Keywords: brain tumor detection; deep learning; fine-tuning for generative model; medical
image classification; generative AI; radiology report generation; QLoRA; U-Net

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Introduction
Brain tumors are among the most dangerous oncological problems in the world, with
a high mortality rate and rapid development. More than 80% of brain tumor types are
considered the worst types of cancer [1,2]. The most commonly diagnosed variants are
gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors, each with a distinct therapeutic pathway
ranging from surgical resection to targeted radiation. Gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary
tumors are the most common diagnoses, and each has its own unique therapeutic path
from surgical resection to targeted radiation [1]. MRI is the gold standard for non-invasive

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
assessment because of its superior soft-tissue contrast and multi-planar capabilities, espe-
cially by T1-weighted sequences [3]. But manual interpretation of these complex medical
images is a notorious bottleneck. It is an inherently time-consuming process, subject to
inter-observer variability and critically limited by a worldwide shortage of specialized
neuroradiologists, especially in developing and underserved countries [4]. In such cases,
delayed or incorrect diagnostic triage can lead to sub-optimal treatment planning, with
irreparable compromise to patient prognosis.
The detection method of choice for brain tumors is MRI because of the excellent spatial
resolution and contrast offered by the imaging modality. Nevertheless, image analysis is
tedious and requires an experienced radiologist because of the large variety of tumors. Deep
learning techniques have improved automated image analysis tasks tremendously. For
example, deep neural networks based on convolutional layers have achieved impressive
results in brain tumor classification [5], while U-Net architectures have allowed accurate
segmentation of brain tumors [6,7]. Furthermore, transformer models based on language
processing allow for automatic report generation in radiology [8].
Despite these advances, most existing systems treat classification, localization, and
report generation as separate processes, with computational efficiency typically treated as
secondary to accuracy [9,10].
While the deep learning technique has been successful in the analysis of brain tumors,
most research has concentrated only on classifying brain tumors with few efforts towards
localizing and clinically understanding their nature. Clinically, the categorization of brain
tumors is rarely adequate, as radiologists will want to determine its localization, size, and
whether it fits clinical visualization. It is also evident that segmentation and classification
are always taken separately; hence, the spatial information between both steps is not
adequately utilized. As a result, the process of segmentation occurs despite the input scans
not having brain tumors, leading to an increase in computation costs, especially when
analyzing scans from large-scale screenings. Recent advances have begun challenging the
traditional separation of these tasks. Sultan et al. [11] proposed a deep learning fusion-
based pipeline that explicitly integrates classification and segmentation of brain tumor

not having brain tumors, leading to an increase in computation costs, especially when
analyzing scans from large-scale screenings. Recent advances have begun challenging the
traditional separation of these tasks. Sultan et al. [11] proposed a deep learning fusion-
based pipeline that explicitly integrates classification and segmentation of brain tumor
progression using generative artificial intelligence, achieving strong performance on multi-
class tumor analysis. The proposed model classifies brain tumors into early-stage brain
tumor (EBT) and progressive brain tumor (PBT) to help neuro-oncologists accurately track
longitudinal disease dynamics and optimize personalized treatment planning without
requiring separate pre-processing networks. Then the model segments the tumor using
deep learning networks with DFB and HFUB modules. After segmentation into EBT and
PBT, the model utilizes an AI generative LLaMA language model paired with clinical
in-the-loop feedback to generate reports that describe the tumor’s morphology. The model
achieves strong performance on multi-class tumor analysis. A lightweight hybrid network,
TumorNet, was presented by Wang et al. [12] for efficient brain tumor classification, which
integrates multi-scale convolutional filters, a Squeeze-and-Excitation attention module,
and a transformer backbone MobileViT-XXS. The model employed a two-phase freeze-
then-fine-tune strategy, reaching 99.85 % accuracy on its primary clinical dataset and
99.91–100% on two public datasets, using diffrent parameters, and incorporated a Gemini
API based module to generate explanatory reports. Similarly, recent studies have shown
that multistage processing can address the challenges of intraprostatic tumor localization
in MRI. Specifically, cascaded architectures that incorporate initial ROI detection and
slice filtering prior to 3D segmentation such as the framework proposed using Swin-
UNETR backbones have demonstrated significant performance gains, improving cancer
segmentation Dice scores from 55.03% to 67.11% on T2-weighted MRI scans [13].

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
While existing models often treat classification, segmentation, and reporting as entirely
separate processes, recent work has begun exploring integrated pipelines [11,13]. However,
these approaches typically require multi-modal MRI inputs or lack automated report
generation. In this work, we address the gap of accessible, single-modality sequential
integration by proposing a modular pipeline that chains independently trained components
classification, conditional segmentation, and report generation into a clinically interpretable
workflow. For the tumor classification, we use transfer learning architectures, namely
Xception, ResNet50 and EfficientNet-B3, initialized with pre-trained ImageNet weights.
To improve the efficiency of resource consumption, we suggest a conditional mechanism,
where we perform segmentation only when a tumor is detected in the first classification
step. This prevents unnecessary downstream processing for healthy scans. Finally, for scans
flagged as pathological, a QLoRA fine-tuned large language model automatically generates
a structured Technique-Findings-Impression report directly from image data, achieving
strong performance for each individual task. We emphasize this is a proof-of-concept
sequential architecture with each component trained and evaluated independently, rather
than a jointly trained end-to-end system.
The contribution of this study is to introduce a multi-stage sequential pipeline ad-
dressed by existing integrated frameworks that combine (Xception, U-Net, Grad-CAM,
QLoRA). This work contributes:
1.
A conditional, resource-aware pipeline design in which segmentation and report
generation are triggered only when the classifier detects a tumor, rather than being
run unconditionally on every scan as in prior integrated pipelines;
2.
A single T1-modality integration spanning classification, localization, explainability,
and automated structured report generation, addressing a gap left by prior inte-
grated pipelines that either require multi-modal MRI input (e.g., Swin-UNETR-based
frameworks) or stop short of automated report generation;
3.
An empirical comparison against existing integrated and single-task pipelines.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Brain Tumor Classification
Cheng et al. [16] proposed a method based on a classification algorithm on the Figshare
dataset and employing data augmentation to increase the size of the training set and mit-
igate the problem of overfitting, resulting in 91.28% accuracy. Nevertheless, the use of
artificial data augmentation and testing on the relatively clean dataset limits its generaliz-
ability to real clinical data.
A lightweight CNN structure designed specifically to decrease computational com-
plexity for brain tumor classification was used in Abiwinanda et al. [17], yielding 84.19%
accuracy. Although the simplicity of the neural network architecture is its main advantage,
the poor result indicates that simplification negatively affects performance, especially in
cases where more classes are involved.
The combination of feature extraction with CNNs and classification with an SVM was
applied in Pashaei et al. [18], leading to 90.89% accuracy. This approach exploits the benefits
of both approaches but requires the use of multiple algorithms and cannot be considered
end-to-end.
The specific multi-class CNN designed by Sultan et al. [19] achieved 96.56% accuracy
in detecting brain tumors in MRI scans, showing that task-oriented architectural design
may be highly beneficial; nevertheless, the model’s evaluation was done in a consistent
train/test split setting that lacks replication throughout other papers.
Srinivas & Parvathi [2] showed that a lightweight four-layer CNN architecture, backed
up by explainability techniques such as Grad-CAM and LIME, was able to deliver 95.86%
accuracy on a four-class classification task. It is crucial to highlight that the research by

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Srinivas & Parvathi [2] shows that the interpretability of a model does not need to be at
odds with its accuracy, even when using rather shallow network architecture.
Anand et al. [20] proved this by achieving 98.5% accuracy with the use of a specifically
designed four-block CNN architecture, optimized using the Adam algorithm and cross-
entropy loss function. Farooq and Jing [21] managed to push the performance of image
classification models even further by achieving 99.66% accuracy with an F1 score of 1.00
in an ensemble of EfficientNet-B4 trained using aggressive data augmentation techniques.
Even though the results are remarkable, they have been achieved on a relatively small clean
dataset and involve significant overhead.
More recent works comparing models include testing ConvNeXt, DenseNet, Swin
Transformers, and EfficientNet-B3 on Kaggle datasets; EfficientNet-B3 managed to achieve
around 94.5% accuracy. Using ensemble approaches managed to push accuracy up to
98.66%, yet those models were trained on rather small, clean datasets.
A common problem across all the reviewed research is the inconsistency between the
datasets, methods, and metrics used throughout papers, leading to an inability to make
reliable judgments concerning the best way of doing brain tumor classification.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Brain Tumor Segmentation
U-Net [22] still remains one of the most commonly used deep learning frame-
works in brain tumor segmentations due to its encoder-decoder architecture and skip
connections, allowing highly accurate localization with a small number of training
images. The problem with the use of only convolutional operations lies in its restricted
receptive field, leading to incorrect tumor borders segmentation, especially in cases of
diffused and irregular boundaries.
Vision Transformer [23], a newer architecture, have also been used for tumor seg-
mentation tasks, yielding competitive accuracy; however, ViT architectures’ ability to
globally analyze input images via their attention layers is countered by the need for
large datasets of labeled images, which is impractical due to the shortage of clinical
annotations in MRI scans.
The use of the Swin Transformer in place of the U-Net encoder makes it possible to
capture long-range spatial relationships between voxels via shifted-window self-attention
mechanisms [24]. The evaluation of the Swin-UNETR framework on the BraTS 2020 dataset
showed Dice scores of 91.95% for the whole tumor, 82.80% for the tumor core, and 81.70%
for the enhancing tumor, placing it among the best-performing methods in the BraTS 2021
challenge. Nevertheless, Swin-UNETR requires substantial computational power and much
time for training.
Similar to our approach, TransUNet [25] incorporates transformers into a CNN archi-
tecture for segmenting images through the fusion of local and global contexts. Although
the model is effective, TransUNet and Swin-UNETR make an assumption regarding access
to all four MRI modalities, namely T1, T2, FLAIR, and T1ce; unfortunately, in practice, this
constraint does not hold true.
Atiea et al. [26] explored a contrasting approach by performing a systematic review
of more than a hundred AI-driven brain tumors studies published between 2020 and
2025. They note an important trend emerging in the literature, namely that of inadequate
interpretation and inability to generalize to actual medical data sets, noting that current
algorithms still lack significant clinical utility.
Another study by Aksoy et al. [27] could be considered a prototype for the proposed
solution, with MobileNetV2 used for classification, SegResNet for segmentation, and XRAI
for explanation in a Gradio-based application. Their model reaches a Dice score of 68–70%,
which is effective but definitely has room for improvement.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
A limitation common among all three models discussed herein lies in their indepen-
dent nature in that these networks attempt to solve the problem of segmentation without
any prior step of classification determining whether segmentation is required at all. Such a
drawback directly influences the efficiency of computations when working with scans that
lack tumors since the majority of cases prove negative for the presence of lesions. Here, we
introduce a solution to the issue by applying segmentation only after classifying a scan as
positive and achieve the results of 78.35% Dice and 69.19% IoU using a simple one-channel
2D U-Net.

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Automated Radiology Report Generation
Chen et al.’s [28] research is devoted to applying memory transformers for solving
the task of structured radiology report generation based on the images that are received
through chest X-rays. The authors suggest implementing memory into neural networks
in order to store information on popular diagnoses from radiology reports. However, it
should be noted that this approach works only for chest radiology and does not include
any other type of data, such as classification or localization.
Meanwhile, Nicolson et al.’s [29] article concentrated on warm-starting models and
explored whether previous experience can improve their effectiveness. In fact, it was

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
proven that warm starting was an effective solution. However, as previously mentioned, it
is suitable only for chest radiology and cannot be used in other areas, including brain MRI.
Similarly, Tanida et al. [30] presented a report generation model that operates on
region-level analysis and creates reports for each salient region. Although this makes
the report generator more transparent and interactive, this technique is limited to chest
radiography analysis and cannot be extended to other imaging modalities to include
classification and localization results.
Following the same line of thought, Kanzawa et al. [31] showed that large lan-
guage models can be fine-tuned for classifying brain MRI reports into pretreatment,
post-treatment, and non-tumor classes. Nonetheless, this paper is concerned with the
classification of existing reports and not generating structured reports using image data.
One common thing in all these papers is that none of them offers any way to address
the issue of the classification of brain tumors with structured brain MRI reports.
The proposed research aims to solve the identified research problem through an
integrated framework that combines the three stages above to enhance brain tumor anal-
ysis. The previous methodologies have always separated the three stages in different
frameworks, but the proposed research methodology aims at integrating the three stages
in one architecture using deep learning methodologies such as Xception, ResNet50, and
EfficientNet-B3, among others. It employs conditional segmentation, which is conducted
after tumor classification to avoid wasting computational power. Once the segmenta-
tion process is complete, clinical report generation is performed through the creation of
techniques, findings, and impression based on the segmented information using QLoRA
fine-tuned language model.

Methodology
The proposed pipeline integrates three sequential components: classification, segmen-

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Input (Datasets)
In this study, three different datasets were employed, each at a different stage of the
proposed pipeline: a dataset for brain tumor classification, a dataset for tumor segmentation
and a dataset for radiology report generation. This ensured that each model was trained
and evaluated independently for its specific task, consistent with the modular, non-jointly-
trained nature of the proposed framework. The proposed pipeline relies on open source
datasets that are extensively used in the literature and constitute the standard benchmark
for the validation of the model. All experiments were performed on these public datasets
and no external validation was performed on data from independent hospitals, scanners
or clinical sources. Hence, the present study should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept
evaluation, and not as a clinically validated assessment of generalizability.

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Classification Dataset
The brain tumor classification dataset was sourced from Kaggle and contains different
combinations of the Figshare, SARTAJ, and Br35H datasets [29]. In total, the dataset has
7023 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI images which are categorized into four classes
including glioma (1621), meningioma (1645), pituitary tumor (1757), and no tumor (2000),
as shown in Figure 2. The training set originally provided in the dataset was entirely used
to train our models, while the test set was further partitioned using stratified sampling
per class. Particularly, 20% of the images from each class in the test set were sampled
for validation purposes, and the rest were used as the final test set.Dataset splitting was
performed at the image level, as the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI Dataset [32] does not provide
patient-level identifiers or metadata.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Synthetic Dataset for Report Generation
As the availability of publicly available radiology reports is limited due to privacy
concerns [35], the dataset was obtained through the use of AI Studio on Google, with the
Gemini 3 Flash model trained to generate datasets in the medical field. The 1100 samples
consist of structured information regarding the tumor. With a sampling temperature
value of 1.0, it was ensured that the generated data would be balanced with linguistic
diversity as well as clinical relevance. Restrictions on prompts ensured consistency with
tumor types, generation of realistic numerical values, and avoidance of directly copying
any numbers. As a result of preprocessing, 1051 samples were retained for training.
The AI model was tasked with generating a structured input-output dataset in Newline
Delimited JSON (NDJSON) format, with the input consisting of a structured summary
of the tumor type (glioma, meningioma, pituitary, or no tumor), tumor detection status,
tumor size in pixels, tumor area in cm2, and bounding box coordinates, while the output
included the tumor report, similar to a radiology report, with three sections: TECHNIQUE,
FINDINGS, and IMPRESSION. In cases where the tumor is absent, the input values are
fixed (detection = No, size = 0 px, area = 0.0 cm2, bounding box = None); however, in cases
where a tumor is present, the size and area input values are limited to a reasonable range
(500–5000 px and 1.0–25.0 cm2, respectively), with a four-coordinate non-empty bounding
box. The AI model was specifically designed not to reproduce input values in the output,
in order to obtain qualitative descriptions in natural language that would not be a literal
reproduction of the input values. The resulting output obtained from the NDJSON was
later refined to create a nested JSON structure, in which the output column is divided
into its corresponding technique, findings, and impression columns. The structured data
thus obtained served as the training objective for the report generator model, following
the adaptation of LoRA. The generated reports were not independently validated by an
authorized radiologist from a clinical accuracy perspective; instead, their quality was
indirectly determined through the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm (Section 4.4), whose focus
is on fluency and semantic coherence but not clinical accuracy. The resulting synthetic
dataset does not necessarily reflect actual radiology terminology, diagnostic uncertainty,

authorized radiologist from a clinical accuracy perspective; instead, their quality was
indirectly determined through the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm (Section 4.4), whose focus
is on fluency and semantic coherence but not clinical accuracy. The resulting synthetic

Preprocessing
As the proposed pipeline includes three different modules: tumor classification, tumor
segmentation, and radiology report generation, various preprocessing techniques have
been employed on each dataset depending on the needs of the particular module. Image
standardization and augmentation were the focus of the preprocessing steps taken in regard
to the classification dataset to facilitate improved generalization capabilities of the model in

goal of maintaining consistency between MRI and corresponding masks while improving
dataset diversity using synchronized augmentation techniques. As for the radiology report
synthetic dataset, text-based preprocessing techniques were necessary.

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Synthetic Data Preprocessing
To ensure that the integrity and quality of data remained acceptable, various pre-
processing procedures were applied to the generated radiology reports, including the
following: first, elimination of possible errors related to the Markdown and JSON formats
to provide the plain text format for the input data; second, elimination of all quantitative
information about the number of pixels in the radiology reports, retaining only clinical
data; third, verification of the correctness of the ground truth labels associated with the
tumor class inside the dataset structure; and fourth, dividing the reports into three typical
clinical parts: technique, findings, and impression. In this way, it was possible to preserve
the semantic integrity of the generated reports.

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Model Architecture
Classification Models. Four architectures were used: CNN, ResNet [36], Efficient-

The choice of these models was done with a view to providing an analysis of the com-
parative performance of traditional Convolutional Neural Networks and more advanced
Deep Learning architectures with diverse design philosophies. In particular, CNN was cho-

and pooling layers to classify inputs. ResNet50 was chosen because it makes use of skip
connections that allow for efficient training of deeper networks without succumbing to the
vanishing gradients problem. Thus, it is very reliable in image classification tasks, includ-
ing those involving medical images such as the case at hand. EfficientNet-B3 was added
because of its compound approach to scaling network size through balancing of depth,
width, and resolution to provide optimal performance with minimal computation costs.
Finally, Xception was selected as the main model because of the ability of its depth-wise
convolutional layers to reduce computations and complexity without impairing feature
extraction [38].

Classification Performance
The following proposed system assesses the performance of the four deep learning
networks, such as CNN, ResNet50, Xception, and EfficientNet-B3 in MRI brain tumor
classification. All the above-mentioned neural networks were chosen due to their efficiency
in brain tumors detection and ability to discover complex structures within MRIs. The
basic CNN model is applied to estimate its performance compared to the other models
applied for the same purpose. ResNet50 is chosen due to the fact that residual learning
helps solve the problem of gradient vanishing during training deep neural network models.
EfficientNet-B3 is chosen due to its scalable properties making feature extraction more
effective while using fewer resources for calculations. Finally, Xception was chosen for its
efficient depthwise separable convolution.

Comparison with Brain Tumor Segmentation
To further evaluate the segmentation component of the proposed framework, a com-
parative analysis was conducted against related benchmark methods using available Kaggle
notebooks that performed brain tumor segmentation on the same dataset. As presented
in Table 11, the key metrics and characteristics of each approach alongside the proposed
integrated U-Net module.
It can be observed from Table 11 that the proposed model obtains the highest Dice
Score of 0.7835 amongst all other benchmark experiments segmentation benchmarks based
on our experiments, which obtained Dice Scores between 0.3499 and 0.7682. The key
difference between the proposed framework and the existing models lies in the fact that
while the existing literature only considers standalone segmentation models for brain tumor
detection and segmentation, the proposed model utilizes the U-Net segmentation model
in the overall classification-gating pipeline. In particular, the segmentation phase takes
place only when there exists an indication of tumor detected by the Xception classifier, thus
avoiding unnecessary computations in cases where no tumors exist.
In order to further evaluate the robustness of the proposed segmentation framework,
an enhanced variant of the U-Net architecture, namely U-Net++ [45], was trained using
the same data split, preprocessing pipeline, and training configuration (25 epochs) as
the original U-Net model. As shown in Table 12, U-Net++ achieved only marginal im-
provements across most evaluation metrics. Specifically, the Dice score increased from
0.7835 to 0.7846, the IoU improved from 0.6919 to 0.6959, and the F1-score increased from
0.8064 to 0.8190, while the recall remained unchanged. These results indicate that the
original U-Net already provides competitive segmentation performance on the employed
dataset. Following the same logic, the Kaggle-based segmentation techniques that have
been described in Table 11 can be regarded as informal, unreviewed applications, not as
scientifically based benchmarks; therefore, the comparisons that have been made can be
considered as indicative, not scientifically proven. For corresponding epoch-by-epoch loss
curves, see Figure 28; for detailed Dice score and IoU progressions across 25 epochs, see
Figures 29 and 30.

Computational Efficiency Evaluation: Methodology
In order to assess the quantitative gains from using the proposed conditional seg-
mentation algorithm, it was compared to a baseline scenario where the segmentation
step is executed irrespective of the classification result for each input image. Both sce-
narios were tested using a test set containing 95 MRI images representing all four cat-
egories (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and non-tumor). For each image, we

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
obtained (1) the actual latency of the classification and segmentation stages, measured
with torch.cuda.synchronize() -bounded timers; (2) the peak memory consumption
on GPU, measured with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(); and (3) the theoretical
computational complexity of the models in GFLOPs, calculated using the thop library. To
ensure there was no systematic bias in timing due to GPU warm-up (e.g., CUDA kernel
compilation and caching), a warm-up period of five runs was conducted prior to time mea-
surement, and the order of running the two methods on each test image was randomized
rather than sequential.

text:
Latency, Compute, and Memory Results
Figure 32 and Table 15 present the latency analysis, demonstrating a critical design
aspect of the proposed pipeline: post-classification segmentation reduces computational
load without compromising the responsiveness of the overall system. Latency is reduced
from 49.98 ms to 36.05 ms (a 27.87% reduction) through the use of conditional segmentation,
where the classification stage itself takes only 14.3 ms. This demonstrates that the computa-
tional benefits gained by avoiding segmentation on scans predicted to be tumor-negative
substantially outweigh the additional overhead of the classification decision. When the
full pipeline is considered including the LLM-based report generation stage (≈22.55 s)
the relative reduction drops to 0.06%. This is because report generation dominates the
end-to-end latency by three orders of magnitude. This asymmetry should not be perceived
as a flaw of the proposed approach; rather, it highlights precisely where the strength of
the approach lies: in deployment settings where vision-pipeline processing is separated
(either fully or partially) from report generation. In other words, the 27.87% reduction in
vision-pipeline latency leads to reduced GPU time and increased throughput without any
risk to report-generation quality.

Limitations and Generalization
This research work must be considered a proof of concept and not a clinically tested
system. All the tests in this experiment have been conducted using publicly available bench-
mark datasets (Figshare/SARTAJ/Br35H for classification and a separate Kaggle dataset
for segmentation) without being validated through external datasets that are obtained from
an independent hospital, scanning center, or any other clinically sourced data. Besides,

authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery

both the classification and segmentation systems use only T1-weighted contrast-enhanced
MRI while, in actual clinical scenarios, the process of assessing the brain tumors utilizes
several sequences (T1, T2, FLAIR, T1ce).

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Automated Brain Tumor Diagnosis and Clinical Report Generation
authors: Mohamed Eassa, Nagwa Yaseen Hegazy, Hussam Elbehiery
text:
Conclusions
This study established an optimized, sequential, automated AI modular pipeline
framework brain tumor analysis. This approach includes the processes of brain tumor
classification, segmentation, explainability, and even generating a report for the radiologist
from MRI images. For the tumor classification task, four deep learning models were used,
which include CNN, ResNet50, EfficientNet-B3, and Xception. Xception performed best,
producing results with 98.96% accuracy, 98.83% precision, 98.75% recall, and a 98.76% F1-
score. Xception also produced a low validation loss, indicating that it can be used efficiently
for classifying brain tumors. In the context of tumor localization, the U-Net segmentation
model scored a Dice score of 0.7835 and IoU of 0.6919. Radiology report generation was
performed by fine-tuning the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5 Bmodel via QLoRA based
on a synthetically generated dataset of structured radiology reports. In evaluations done
under the “LLM-as-a-Judge” setup, very high scores were obtained, specifically an average
score of 4.92 out of 5 for accuracy and 4.95 out of 5 for fluency.
Qwen-1.5B was fine-tuned for generating radiology reports by QLoRA training with a
synthetic dataset of 1,051 structured radiology reports. The Qwen-1.5B model was tested
using the LLM-as-a-Judge framework, where the Mistral 7B-Instruct-v0.2 served as an
independent judge on 100 unseen examples from the hold-out set. The fine-tuned model
received an average accuracy of 4.92/5 and a fluency rating of 4.95/5 with 100 successful
evaluations. This indicates that the fine-tuned model can generate clinically meaningful,
fluently written radiology reports following the structure of the Technique, Findings, and
Impression sections on affordable consumer-level hardware.
This work presented an integrated method for brain tumor analysis using a three-
component architecture: classification, segmentation, and automated radiology report
generation. The model demonstrates that the Xception classifier is capable of detecting
the presence of tumors with accuracy in terms of per-class prediction. On the other hand,
the U-Net is capable of localizing tumors within the brain image based on the single-
modality input. The combined application of classification followed by segmentation is
computationally efficient in case there are no tumors found within the brain image. QLoRA
fine-tuned language model is capable of producing coherent radiology reports.

For future research studies, MRI imaging techniques can be applied with multimodal-

authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
Abstract
Objectives Automatic data extraction from free-text radiology reports enables large-scale research, but few studies
assessed the performance of large language models (LLMs) on Dutch neuroradiology reports.
Materials and methods We analyzed 947 brain MRI reports from a tertiary memory clinic (2016–2021), authored by
consultant neuroradiologists. Trained medical students annotated thirty variables; 100 reports were double annotated
to assess inter-rater reliability. We evaluated the performance of the open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1 using different
languages (Dutch vs English translation) and few-shot prompting with different example selection strategies.
Performance was evaluated using balanced accuracy for categorical variables, accuracy and mean absolute error for
counts, and text similarity for free text. Metrics were computed across 10 random splits of the 947 reports.
Results LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated high zero-shot performance for visual rating scores (mean [95% CI]): medial
temporal atrophy: 0.90 [0.77–1.00] on the left and 0.96 [0.94–0.99] on the right, Global Cortical Atrophy: 0.87 [0.83–0.91],
and Fazekas: 0.94 [0.93–0.96]. Microbleed mentions were detected with 0.93 [0.92–0.95] accuracy, and infarct mentions
with 0.82 [0.80–0.84]. Text similarity for lesion location reached 0.95 [0.95–0.96]. Performance was lower for numerical
variables: 0.80 [0.78–0.82] for the number of microbleeds and 0.66 [0.63–0.68] for infarcts. English translation yielded
comparable results. Few-shot prompting improved performance for numerical variables, achieving 0.92 [0.90–0.93] for
microbleeds and 0.81 [0.77–0.85] for infarcts using structural similarity-based selection.
Conclusion LLaMA 3.1 shows strong potential for extracting data from Dutch neuroradiology reports. Few-shot
prompting enhances performance for numerical variables, whereas challenges remain for location-specific variables.
Key Points
Question The free-text format of radiology reports limits the accessibility of structured data; can LLM LLaMA 3.1
automatically structure free-text Dutch neuroradiology reports?
Findings LLaMA 3.1 accurately extracted 30 variables from Dutch neuroradiology reports, with few-shot prompting
significantly improving performance compared to zero-shot prompting, particularly with similarity-based example selection.

authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
Introduction
The rapid advancements of radiology techniques and their
growing accessibility have led to an increasing volume of
radiology reports, offering a rich resource for data-driven
medical research. However, their unstructured and free-
text format limits their usability, particularly in large-scale
analysis [1]. Although expert organizations such as the
European Society of Radiology (ESR) advocate for the
adoption of structured reporting (SR) in clinical practice,
its implementation remains limited [2]. This is primarily
due to technical barriers (e.g., incompatibility with radi-
ology information systems), challenges in documenting
complex cases, and resistance from radiologists to rigid
templates conflicting with their established workflow [3].
Currently,
extracting
structured
data
from
free-text
reports relies on manual annotation, which is time-
consuming and error-prone. This raises the need for
automated solutions, particularly for complex applica-
tions such as dementia, where reports often contain
detailed findings and specialized metrics [4].
Recently, ESR emphasized the potential of large language
models (LLMs), such as OpenAI’s Generative Pretrained
Transformer 4 (GPT-4), in automating the conversion of
free-text
reports
into
structured
formats
[5].
These
transformer-based models trained on extensive text corpora
can perform advanced language tasks with minimal anno-
tated data [6, 7]. Recent studies demonstrated their effec-
tiveness in extracting clinical information across diverse
languages and applications [4, 8]. For instance, Lehnen et al
[9] utilized GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to extract structured data
from stroke reports. Adams et al [10] evaluated GPT-4 for
standardizing German MRI/CT reports, and Sasaki et al
[11] applied GPT-4 to Japanese interventional radiology
reports. Cozzi et al [12] evaluated the performance of GPT-
3.5, GPT-4, and Bard in performing BI-RADS classification
in Italian, English, and Dutch reports. Despite their pro-
mising results, significant challenges remain in imple-
menting LLMs for
SR
[4]. Most
studies
relied
on
proprietary models like GPT-4, which require data transfer
to external servers, raising privacy concerns and limiting

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
clinical adoption [8]. Open-weight LLMs, which allow local
deployment, present a potential solution, though their
performance in specialized medical domains requires fur-
ther validation [13]. In this regard, Nowak et al [1] reported
that open-weight models achieve competitive performance
to private models in extracting variables from English chest
X-ray reports. Builtjes et al showed that open-weight
models outperform fine-tuned task-specific models on 28
extraction tasks from Dutch medical reports [14]. However,
benchmark analyses reveal that such models underperform
proprietary counterparts [15], particularly in non-English
languages and specialized domains, as their training pre-
dominantly relies on general-domain English data [16, 17].
While fine-tuning with domain-specific data can enhance
accuracy, hospital settings often lack the required compu-
tational resources and annotated datasets [13]. Few-shot
prompting, where models are given input-output pairs as
examples, emerges as a low-resource alternative that
showed promise in simpler tasks such as LI-RADS classi-
fication [18], yet its potential in radiology remains under-
explored [19, 20].
This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the
open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1 for structuring Dutch neu-
roradiology reports, encompassing 30 variables of diverse
types (categorical, numerical, and free-text). We first com-
pare its zero-shot performance to human raters using con-
sensus annotations and assess inter-rater reliability (IRR).
Next, we assess whether English translation of the input
reports improves performance. We also investigate few-shot
prompting as a resource-efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic
assessment of an open-weight LLM for structured radiology
reporting in Dutch using few-shot prompting, providing
critical insights into the feasibility of scalable, privacy-
preserving solutions for clinical deployment.

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
Materials And Methods
Dataset
The study was approved by the institutional Medical Ethics
Committee with a waiver of informed consent (METC-
2023-0569). It retrospectively included Dutch neuroradiol-
ogy reports from 947 patients who underwent brain MRI as
part of their diagnostic work-up at a tertiary memory clinic
between 2016 and 2021. We included all consecutive
patients with an MRI performed within three months of
their initial consultation. Reports were authored as part of
routine practice by different radiologists at the same clinic.
Of all 947 reports, 152 were drafted following a structured
template with predefined fields; the other 795 reports had
no predefined structure, leaving the outline of the report up
to the radiologist. Each report was manually annotated for
30 variables by one of three trained final-stage medical
students, using a structured template with standardized
guidelines that defined variable definitions, acceptable
values, and provided instructions for handling missing data
(See Appendix B for variable definitions and distributions).
The template included 24 clinical variables related to brain
atrophy and vascular lesions, and 6 internal quality control
(QC) variables. We applied Monte Carlo cross-validation
(MCCV) by generating 10 random splits of the dataset, each
with 50% training and 50% test data. Training sets were
used to select few-shot examples; test sets were used for
evaluation. To assess inter-rater agreement and compare
the model to human performance, a random subset of 100
reports was independently annotated by two raters, with
consensus reached in consultation with a neuroradiologist
(M.W.V., 15 years of experience).
LLM prompting
As LLM, we used LLaMA 3.1 (Meta, July 2024) [21], because:
(1) its open-weight nature allows local deployment, which
complies with hospital data governance requirements; (2) an
evaluation on a general-domain Dutch benchmark showed it
can process Dutch text, with no performance gain by fine-
tuning [22]; and (3) the availability of multiple model sizes
(8B, 70B, and 405B parameters) allows institutions to choose
models that fit their resources. We used the 8B and 70B
versions. The 405B version was excluded due to computa-
tional constraints.

followed Meta’s prompt engineering guidelines (https://
www.LLaMA.com/docs/how-to-guides/prompting/)
(Fig. 1). It included extraction guidelines, a JavaScript

authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
Experimental design
We perform the following analyses:
1.
Comparison to human performance and inter-rater
agreement: using the dual-annotated Dutch reports,
we evaluated the model’s zero-shot performance (i.e.,
its ability to extract information without task-specific
examples), compared to human performance. Model
outputs and individual human annotations were
compared to consensus labels as reference standard.
In parallel, we assessed IRR between the two
annotators.
2.
Impact of input language: we evaluated whether
translating
Dutch
radiology
reports
to
English
impacts the model’s zero-shot performance. Three
conditions were compared: original Dutch reports,
English translations generated by LLaMA 3.1, and
translations generated by a Helsinki NLP’s OPUS-MT
model [23]. For English inputs, extracted text fields
were back-translated into Dutch using LLaMA 3.1 to
maintain evaluation consistency. An author (K.M.)
rated translations of 50 reports as good, acceptable, or
poor, and repeated the ratings 8 months later to assess
consistency.
3.
Few-shot prompting: to evaluate the impact of few-
shot prompting, three example reports from the
training
set
with
their
manually
structured
counterparts were given in the input prompt to
guide output generation. Experiments were conducted
using the original Dutch reports. Four example
selection strategies were compared:
1.
Random selection: different examples are randomly
sampled from the training set for each report.
2.
Fixed selection: a manually curated set is selected
from the training set of each split, ensuring coverage of
commonly occurring values, rare cases, and reports
with missing information.

Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis
Variable-specific performance metrics were used. For
categorical variables, we used balanced accuracy to
account for class imbalance; missing was treated as a
separate class. For count variables, we used accuracy (i.e.,
percentage of model outputs matching the reference
annotation) and mean absolute error (MAE). For MAE,
entries marked as missing by either the model or the
annotator were excluded. For free-text fields, semantic
similarity was computed between model outputs and
reference annotations by calculating the cosine similarity
of sentence embeddings generated using Sentence-BERT
[24], with RobBERT-v2 (a Dutch transformer model) as a
backbone
[25].

[28]. Agreement levels for Kappa and ICC were defined
according to McHugh [29] and Koo and Li [30], respec-

sensitivity analysis is presented in Appendix E to assess

We evaluated the performance of LLaMA 3.1 in extract-
ing 24 neuroradiology report variables. For results related
to QC variables, see Appendix C. This section reports
results for the 70B version, which performs comparably or
significantly better than the 8B version for nearly all
variables (Appendix D). F1 scores for categorical variables
and Spearman’s correlation for numerical fields are pro-
vided as additional metrics in Appendix G. Tables in this
section are visualized as radar plots in Appendix J.
Comparison to human performance and IRR
Table 1 shows the results of the comparison with human
performance and IRR on the 100 double-annotated
reports.
LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated high performance on stan-
dardized visual rating scales, achieving balanced accuracy
of 0.98 for left medial temporal atrophy (MTA), 1.00 for
right MTA, 1.00 for Fazekas score, and 0.85 for overall
global cortical atrophy (GCA), all comparable to human-
level performance (p > 0.05). Detection of the mention of
brain infarcts (0.83) and microbleeds (0.86) was slightly
lower but remained on par with at least one annotator.
The model excelled in extracting lesion locations, with
high text similarities (0.95 for infarcts, 0.96 for micro-
bleeds). Numerical variables proved challenging, particu-
larly infarct counts, where extraction accuracy ranged
from 0.66 to 0.78, falling significantly below Annotator 1
(p < 0.05). The low MAE suggests that when numerical
values were extracted, they were mostly correct; and the
lower accuracy is due to confusion between true lesion
counts and cases where the count was missing from the
report. Performance was also lower for lobar GCA scores
and infarct subtypes. In 3 of the 24 variables (occipital
GCA, cerebellar infarcts, and splinter infarcts), the model
performed significantly worse than both human annota-
tors (p < 0.05). Notably, these variables were reported less
frequently (see Table S1). IRR varied, ranging from near-
perfect (κ = 0.99 for MTA) to poor agreement (κ = 0.39
for superficial siderosis). Considering variables with
moderate or higher agreement as reliable, most catego-

fields met this threshold, indicating satisfactory annota-
tion consistency. Bootstrapping results in Appendix E.1
further show that single-rater annotations yield compar-

This study evaluated the open-weight LLM LLaMA 3.1
for extracting structured data from Dutch radiology
reports in a tertiary dementia clinic. We first assessed
model performance compared to two human raters using
100 consensus-annotated reports. We then used the full
dataset of 947 reports to examine the impact of input
language and evaluate few-shot prompting with different
example selection strategies as a resource-efficient alter-

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
LLaMA 3.1 demonstrated promising zero-shot cap-
abilities in extracting 24 variables from Dutch brain MRI
reports, performing overall comparably to human raters.
We observed that the model shows excellent performance
on simple variables (e.g. standardized visual scales). Per-
formance was lower when extraction concerns specific
locations in the brain (e.g. lobar GCAs) or specific lesion
subtypes. Numerical variables pose additional difficulties,
often demanding arithmetic operations (e.g., summing
numbers of infarcts across different locations). Perfor-
mance was also lower for variables that were less fre-
quently reported by radiologists. Most variables showed
moderate to near-perfect IRR, with only a few displaying
poor agreement. Stratified analysis (Appendix E) found no
link between agreement level and model performance,
likely to reflect the sensitivity of IRR to class imbalance in
rare findings such as superficial siderosis. However, lower
agreement may introduce noise into the reference stan-
dard, so results for individual variables with weak agree-
ment should be interpreted cautiously. Despite this,
manual annotations remain the reference standard in
radiological AI.
No significant performance gain was observed from
translating the reports to English. Notably, the findings
suggest that using the original Dutch reports yields more
reliable results than using translations. A key challenge
was handling local terminology. For example, the Dutch
term “splinterinfarcten”, referring to small, linear, streak-
like cortical cerebellar infarcts, has no direct equivalent in
the English literature and was therefore consistently
mistranslated, leading to extraction errors. These infarcts
are distinct from typical territorial cerebellar infarcts as
their linear or radial configuration is consistent with the
involvement of small penetrating vessels or distal emboli,
aligning them more closely with small cortical infarcts
and microinfarcts [34]. This morphological distinction
motivated their separate analysis in our cohort. We
addressed the mistranslation by including terminology-
mapping in the translation prompt. This straightforward
approach can be applied to other datasets but requires
prior knowledge of local terms. Parameter-efficient fine-
tuning methods could enable LLMs to learn local termi-
nology and improve their domain knowledge directly
from data, though current evidence suggests they under-
perform in limited-data settings [35]. We observed

and process Dutch medical language, despite being pri-

We explored few-shot prompting as a resource and
data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning, which is often
impractical in clinical settings due to high computational
and annotation costs. Our results show that few-shot
prompting with curated example selection can sig-

initially showed low performance in the zero-shot setting
benefited most. Data extraction required less than 30 s

considered in the context of regulatory and safety fra-
meworks governing medical software. Tools that use
patient data or influence clinical workflows may be
subject to medical device regulations such as the Eur-
opean Union’s Medical Device Regulation [36]. Using
open-weight models that can be deployed on local
institutional hardware avoids sending protected health
information to external services and enables hospitals to
maintain control over data governance and audit logs,
potentially simplifying compliance with privacy and
security standards. Nonetheless, rigorous validation,
careful documentation of intended use, and adherence to
relevant regulatory requirements will be necessary for
any intended clinical deployment of LLM-based systems.
This study focused exclusively on extracting clinical
variables from Dutch radiology reports in a tertiary
memory clinic cohort using LLaMA 3.1. Although newer
open-weight LLMs exist, LLaMA 3.1 remains competi-
tive according to recent benchmarks (www.vellum.ai/
open-llm-leaderboard (Update of 19 November 2025)).
Medical-specialized LLMs can offer advantages in more
heterogeneous domains that require advanced clinical
reasoning, such as oncology, but evidence for their
consistent benefit in structured information extraction is
limited. For instance, Zhu et al showed that an oncology-
specific LLM outperformed LLaMA 3 in predicting
cancer progression [37], yet Liu et al [38] found that,
without
task-specific
fine-tuning,
general-purpose
LLaMA 3.1 8B outperformed Llama-3-8B-UltraMedical
on structuring radiology and pathology reports. In our
cohort, reports contained structured elements such as
visual rating scales, reducing the need for specialized
medical knowledge and making a general-purpose model
sufficient. A systematic comparison across newer general
and medical-domain LLMs for this specific task remains
an important direction for future work. The translation
quality assessment was limited by its single-rater design
and sample size (n = 50), although the consistency of the
observed differences and the downstream extraction

lacked external validation, which limits its general-

extend to diverse and less standardized clinical domains
to broaden the impact of these results. We employed

title: Automatic extraction of structured information from brain MRI reports using an open-weight large language model
authors: Kaouther Mouheb, Amos Pomp, Antoine Manenti, Romy de Haan, Farog Faghir, Joy Martens, Harro Seelaar, Francesco Mattace-Raso, Meike W. Vernooij, Frank J. Wolters, Stefan Klein, Esther E. Bron
text:
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the potential of open-weight
LLMs for extracting structured clinical information from
radiology reports. Few-shot prompting with informed
example selection significantly improves performance,
approaching human-level accuracy for most variables.
Although challenges persist for complex or ambiguous
cases, the model’s effectiveness in processing Dutch
medical text underscores the promise of LLMs as scalable
tools for post-hoc structuring of free-text reports. Future
work should validate this approach across models, extend
it to other clinical domains, and explore multimodal
integration to enhance its applicability across different
research settings.

Original Investigation
Comparative Evaluation of Open-
Weight Large Language Models for
Pathological Brain MRI Reports
Classification: From Prompts to a
Fine-Tuned Model
Claudio Demaria, MSc, Claudio Crema, PhD, Mario Verdicchio, PhD, Valentina Brancato, PhD,
Vincenzo Alfano, MSc, Luca Basso, MSc, Giuseppe Pontillo, PhD,
Damiano Archetti, MSc, Silvia Fostinelli, PhD, Silvia De Francesco, MSc, Michela Pievani, PhD,
Cesare M. Baronio, PhD, Alberto Boccali, MSc, Nicola Toschi, PhD, Arturo Brunetti, MD,
Alberto Redolfi, PhD, Marco Aiello, PhD
Rationale and Objectives: Automated semantic classification of radiology reports can enhance clinical workflows and research, but often
relies on language- and task-specific models, limiting scalability. This study aims to evaluate and improve the 0-shot baseline performance of
open-weight large language models (LLMs) in the semantic classification of free-text magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reports.
Materials and Methods: A corpus of 1385 reports from a single neuroradiology center was used to assess four LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B,
Magistral-Small-2509, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) of comparable scale (∼20-35B parameters). The brain MRI reports were
labeled as Pathological or Non-Pathological, with the Pathological ones further classified into five diagnostic categories (Neoformation,
Vascular, Inflammation/Infection, Neurodegenerative, Other). The LLMs were evaluated using zero- and few-shot prompting with ma­
jority-vote aggregation. Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning was then applied to the best-performing model across
multiple configurations. Performance was assessed using Macro F1, Micro F1, Precision, Recall, and Exact Match Accuracy.
Results: The binary classification task achieved a Macro F1 score of 0.84 on the best-performing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B model, while
multilabel classification reached 0.81. Majority voting (MV) outperformed individual-set predictions. QLoRA fine-tuning yielded a Macro
F1 score of 0.83 on the multilabel task; the improvement over the 0-shot baseline was statistically supported for Macro F1, Micro F1,
Macro Precision, and Exact Match, whose bootstrap 95% confidence intervals excluded zero, but not for Macro Recall. Fine-tuning and
few-shot prompting strategies are complementary, with neither consistently outperforming the other. Error analysis showed that the
models struggled with borderline annotation cases and often missed secondary labels.

Introduction
A
rtificial intelligence in radiology has traditionally fo­
cused on image-based approaches, leading to major
advances in classification, detection, and segmentation
of medical images. However, a complementary and increasingly
important direction involves extracting structured information
from radiology free-text reports. These narratives contain rich
clinical interpretations and diagnostic reasoning, but their un­
structured nature limits their utility for large-scale analysis, ret­
rospective studies, and clinical decision support.
Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), par­
ticularly large language models (LLMs), have enabled new ap­
proaches for converting radiology reports into structured
representations. In radiology, this has allowed LLMs to perform
information extraction, report summarization, and automated
classification across multiple imaging domains, especially when
adapted via fine-tuning or parameter-efficient strategies such as
low-rank adaptation (LoRA (1)) methods (2,3).
Despite these advances, several challenges remain that
limit their clinical translation. LLMs are sensitive to input
phrasing and dataset shifts, raising concerns about robustness
and generalizability across institutions and reporting style
interpretation (4). Moreover, hallucinations, prompt sensi­
tivity, and stochastic variability can cause inconsistency or
errors, limiting reliability in clinical environments (5). These
limitations are particularly relevant in neuroradiology, where
reports often describe complex and heterogeneous patholo­
gical patterns, including vascular, neoplastic, inflammatory,
infectious, and neurodegenerative conditions.
Additional concerns include privacy risks and the potential
memorization of sensitive patient information when models
are trained on institutional datasets (6).
To date, LLMs used in neuroradiology have focused on
narrow tasks, such as detecting specific acute findings (e.g.,
hemorrhage or stroke) or binary classification of studies as normal
or abnormal. More recent studies have explored information
extraction from brain imaging reports, but these remain limited
in scope, often relying on restricted datasets or single-center
cohorts, which limits generalizability and clinical applicability (2).
In radiology informatics, an additional emerging direction is
the use of LLMs for semantic search over radiology information
systems and picture archiving and communication systems

In radiology informatics, an additional emerging direction is
the use of LLMs for semantic search over radiology information
systems and picture archiving and communication systems
(PACS). Traditional keyword-based indexing is limited in cap­
turing the semantic richness of clinical narratives, often requiring
manually engineered queries that fail to reflect linguistic varia­
bility (7). Early studies suggest that LLM-based approaches may
enable natural language-driven retrieval of clinical cohorts, re­
presenting a shift toward semantic search paradigms for radiology
data access and reuse (8).
Meaningful automated magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) report interpretation requires moving beyond binary
classification toward multilabel representations that capture
the full diagnostic spectrum of brain findings. In this context,
structured information retrieval from radiology reports re­
mains an open challenge of high importance for clinical re­
search and data warehousing. LLMs offer a promising
solution for the semantic understanding of clinical narratives;
however, this area remains insufficiently explored.
To address this gap, we evaluated four open-weight
LLMs—GPT-OSS-20B (GPT-OSS) (9), Magistral-Small-2509
(Magistral-S) (10), Gemma-4-31B (Gemma-4) (11), and
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen3.5) (12)—on neuroradiological
MRI reports extracted from a tertiary care hospital PACS. We
assessed their performance on binary classification (Pathological vs
Non-Pathological) and multilabel categorization (Neoformation,

ditionally, we investigated the impact of different prompting
strategies and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Quantized
Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) (13) to evaluate the feasibility
of integrating LLMs into scalable semantic radiology data pi­

Data
A total of 80,000 consecutive radiology reports were retro­
spectively collected from the electronic health records and
PACS of IRCCS SYNLAB SDN, an Italian diagnostic and
research institute. The dataset included free-text Italian reports
from brain MRI examinations performed between January
2012 and December 2022. Only brain MRI studies acquired
with or without contrast medium were included. All reports
consisted of unstructured narrative texts generated during
routine clinical practice without auxiliary technologies such as
speech recognition or structured reporting systems.
For each report, authorship was traced to account for inter-
observer variability and differences in reporting style; the an­
notated corpus was authored by 14 reporting radiologists, with
a single radiologist accounting for the majority of reports. The
study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of
Helsinki and approved by the local Ethics Committee (CET
Campania 1; Protocol No. 1/24 OSS SDN) (14). Patients were
informed about the potential research use of their clinical data.
Reports were pseudonymized and processed exclusively on
institutional servers, without transfer to external services or
third-party application programming interfaces (APIs), in
compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation
(GDPR) and institutional privacy policies.
A subset of 1385 reports, uniformly sampled from the ori­
ginal dataset, was selected for annotation by three radiology
experts with over 10 years of experience. Annotators were
asked to: (i) assign a categorical label that served as ground-truth
for the classifier, (ii) provide a confidence score ranging from 1
to 5, and (iii) highlight keywords or phrases driving their de­
cision. For the analyses reported in this study, only the cate­
gorical labels and highlighted keywords/phrases were
considered, while confidence scores were collected for quality-
control purposes and were not included in the evaluation. To
ensure consistency across annotators, all raters followed an
agreed annotation protocol detailing the labeling criteria and
decision rules, and subsequently annotated the reports in­
dependently, without a consensus adjudication step. To stan­
dardize the workflow, annotations were performed using the
Label Studio platform ([labelstud.io] (http://labelstud.io)).

Experimental Setup
Models used in this study (Table 1) were selected according
to four criteria: (1) open-weight availability, enabling local
deployment without external API dependencies; (2) a small-
to-medium parameter scale (20-35B total parameters),
compatible with single-node institutional graphics processing
unit (GPU) infrastructure; (3) representation of major geo­
graphic ecosystems and leading LLM developers across the
U.S., China, and Europe; and (4) the opportunity to in­
vestigate how differences in pretraining data, model archi­
tectures, training procedures, and alignment strategies
influence performance on domain-specific NLP tasks. All
models were downloaded from the Hugging Face Model
Hub (15) under open-weight licenses.
All models were served locally using vLLM (16), which
provided compatible APIs for the four models tested, dy­
namic batching, and tensor parallelism across GPUs. No
inference-time quantization was applied, ensuring evaluation
at original model precision, except for the PEFT experiments
(section “PEFT”). All models support explicit reasoning or
“thinking” modalities. Only final structured outputs were
evaluated. Inference was deterministic across all experiments:
all models were decoded greedily (temperature 0), so that the
only source of variability across runs was the choice of few-
shot examples rather than stochastic sampling. Because de­
terministic decoding reproduces the same output on re-
query, outputs that could not be parsed were excluded rather
than resampled; such cases were rare (below 0.2% of pre­
dictions in every configuration). Additional details on soft­
ware, dependencies, and hardware configuration are
provided in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 and in
Supplementary Methods – Hardware Infrastructure.

For both binary and multilabel tasks, few-shot examples
were sampled from a task-specific held-out pool not used for
evaluation. For each shot, multiple independent example sets
were used to build separate prompts for the same LLM,
which classified the target report independently for each
prompt. To reduce dependence on the specific examples
included in the prompt, predictions from all sets within the
same shot configuration were aggregated using intrashot MV
(17). The number of sets per shot was kept odd to ensure a
unique majority: 11 for 5-shot, 5 for 10-shot, and 3 for
20-shot.
For the binary task, the final prediction was the class
(Pathological/Non-Pathological), receiving the majority of votes. For
the multilabel task, voting was performed separately for each
diagnostic category, and a label was included in the final output if
it was selected in more than 50% of the predictions. This ap­
proach preserved the multilabel structure while avoiding MV
over Label Powerset (LP) class combinations. Few-shot examples
were allowed to reappear across different sets.
Table 2 gives an overview of the experimental protocol
across the three classification tasks.
Binary Task
The aim was to classify reports automatically as Pathological or
Non-Pathological using 0-shot and few-shot prompting,
without any domain-specific training (18).
Each model received a system prompt and a user prompt
containing the full report text, which was inserted without
preprocessing, normalization, or translation. The reports
were retrieved from the institutional PACS and kept in their
original language, while the prompts were written in English
to reflect both a fixed clinical-data constraint and a cross-
lingual generalization setting.
We used four prompts, ranging from very concise to
highly informative; these are provided in the Supplementary
Material.
