few-shot and MV protocol, obtaining 20 inference runs per
prompt, namely: 1 0-shot, 11 five-shot, 5 ten-shot, 3
twenty-shot. This resulted in 80 total runs across the four
prompts.

effective test set of 1335 reports. These 50 reports were se­

formal selection rule was applied, and the residual depen­
dence on the specific examples chosen was mitigated by
sampling multiple independent example sets for each shot
configuration.
Multilabel Task
The aim was to automatically classify Pathological brain MRI
reports into five diagnostic categories. This was formulated as
a multilabel task, as each report could be assigned to one or
more labels. Each model received a system prompt and a user
prompt containing the full report text, optionally augmented
with few-shot examples. No preprocessing was applied to
the reports. The five diagnostic categories used for ground-
truth annotation were: (1) Neoformation (n = 163)—in­
tracranial neoplasms, cysts, and tumor-like lesions; (2)
Vascular (n = 611)—spontaneous (nontraumatic) intracranial
hemorrhages and intracranial vascular lesions (aneurysms,
vascular malformations, stroke, venous occlusions, vasculo­
pathies); (3) Inflammation/Infection (n = 227)—infectious and
noninfectious inflammatory diseases of the central nervous
system; (4) Neurodegenerative (n = 237)—diseases character­
ized by progressive neuronal loss; (5) Other (n = 563)—other
pathologies (e.g., trauma, malformations, toxic-metabolic
conditions). Annotations were performed at the level of
these five diagnostic categories, precluding reliable reporting
of case counts for individual diseases.
Annotators highlighted text spans within each report as ex­
plicit evidence supporting each assigned label. These spans served
as grounded justifications and were incorporated into two of the
four prompt variants. Four prompt templates were defined a
priori, reflecting the binary task design and varying along two
dimensions: verbosity (minimal vs detailed instructions with full
category definitions and output specification) and the inclusion of
evidence spans in few-shot examples.

PEFT
Qwen3.5 achieved the best overall performance on the
multilabel task—the task carried forward to fine-tu­
ning—attaining the highest Macro F1 across prompt and shot
configurations and leading in three of the five diagnostic
categories, and was therefore selected for fine-tuning. Its flat
performance trajectory across increasing shot counts sug­
gested that in-context learning had reached a ceiling, in­
dicating that further gains would require parametric
adaptation.
The fine-tuning set included 1153 pathological reports.
While the prompting experiments treated the task as true
multilabel classification, with each category predicted in­
dependently (sections “Experimental Setup” and “Multilabel
Task”), for fine-tuning, we deliberately adopted an LP for­
mulation, reframing the task as a 23-class problem by treating
each observed label combination as a separate class. This shift
rests on two interacting properties of the data: the labels were
strongly correlated, so only 23 of the 31 possible nonempty
combinations actually occurred (eight never appeared),
which makes a per-combination encoding compact; and the
strong class imbalance made a class-balanced weighting
scheme well defined once each report carried a single
powerset class (Supplementary Methods – Label Powerset

inference, the model output was parsed back to the five
diagnostic labels and scored with the same multilabel metrics
used for prompting (Supplementary Methods – Test-Phase
Decoding). Because evaluation was always performed at the
five-label level, the rare LP classes (≤4 samples) were con­
fined to training, so the prompting versus fine-tuning
comparison was made on the same five-label footing. The
data were split into training (80%, ≈922 samples), validation
(10%, ≈115 samples), and test (10%, ≈116 samples) sets using
stratified random sampling, with rare combinations retained
to preserve the original clinical distribution. We fine-tuned
the model with QLoRA, testing 10 predefined configura­

Results
Data
A subset of 1385 brain MRI reports was uniformly sampled from
the 80,000 consecutive examinations held in the IRCCS
SYNLAB SDN PACS, providing a representative cross-section
of routine neuroradiological reporting. The cohort had a mean
age of 50.5 ± 19.0 years and comprised 40.4% male and 59.6%
female examinations. Of these, 1153 (83.3%) were Pathological
and 232 (16.7%) Non-Pathological. Within the pathological set,
labels were unevenly distributed across the five diagnostic
categories—Vascular (n = 611; 53.0%), Other (n = 563; 48.8%),
Neurodegenerative (n = 237; 20.6%), Inflammation/Infection (n =
227; 19.7%) and Neoformation (n = 163; 14.1%)—with Vascular
occurring roughly 3.7 times more often than the rarest class,
Neoformation. Reports frequently carried co-occurring findings
(1801 label assignments; mean 1.56 labels/report): 53.8% had a
single label, 37.0% two, and 9.2% three or more. The most
frequent label pairs were Other+Vascular (n = 280) and
Neurodegenerative+Vascular (n = 179).

evaluation for Italian neuroradiology report classification.
This finding is consistent with recent evidence that gen­
erative models can reliably extract clinical information from
medical texts. For example, previous research showed that
open-weight LLMs performed competitively on a 28-task
Dutch clinical NLP benchmark, matching fine-tuned base­
lines on most tasks (22). Similarly, another study found that
providing domain-specific context in prompts with GPT-4
consistently improved radiology report labeling performance
(23). The high baseline performance in 0-shot settings sug­
gests that some models, such as Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4,
already possess strong prior alignment to the linguistic reg­
ister and output format. This is consistent with the ob­
servation that less recent LLMs, such as Magistral-S and
GPT-OSS, required minimal few-shot examples to match
the labeling task performance of newer LLMs.
Indeed, we observed differences in in-context learning tra­
jectories across models. Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 both plateaued
rapidly: on the binary classification task, they reached near-
ceiling performance at 0-shot, with little or no gain from ad­
ditional examples. This suggests that their pretrained knowledge
and instruction tuning already closely match our annotation
schema. In contrast, GPT-OSS showed the lowest 0-shot
performance but the largest gains from ensemble MV over
multiple prompt sets. Its predictions were more variable across
examples (high variance), so aggregating them via majority vote
produced a substantial Macro F1 boost. The 20-shot majority-
vote result represents an upper bound of the prompting para­
digm, as ensemble voting canceled many model-specific and
prompt-specific errors.
Gemma-4 showed no benefit from additional examples on
the multilabel task, with a slight decline under two of the four
prompt templates and near-identical performance in the 0-shot
setting. This could reflect the recently described over-
prompting phenomenon, in which providing too many in-
context examples paradoxically reduces LLM accuracy (24).
Furthermore, introducing more few-shot instances for our five-
label multilabel problem may have altered the model’s internal
representations without providing sufficient guidance on the
complex label combinations, thereby impairing its native clas­
sification ability. This contrasts with previous findings for GPT-
4 (23), where in-context prompts generally improved labeling.

and no report was hard in both the binary and the multilabel
formulations. This implies that “hard” cases depend on how
the task was defined and labeled, not solely on intrinsic re­
port ambiguity. Thus, they are influenced by three aspects,
namely: report content, task formulation, and annotation
uncertainty.
In the binary task, the most challenging cases were MRI
reports that combined negative language, such as “no sig­
nificant abnormalities”, with subtle incidental findings. All
LLMs consistently labeled these as normal (false negatives)
despite a positive ground truth. The linguistic profile of these
reports closely resembles that of reports labeled as Non-
Pathological, suggesting an annotation boundary effect: by
convention, they were labeled Pathological, but semantically
they are ambivalent. In other words, these MRI reports lie
near the decision threshold between “normal” and “ab­
normal,” and all models struggle similarly. Such consensus
errors suggest limitations in the label definition rather than
specific model bias.
In the multilabel setting, two confusion patterns have
emerged. First, diffuse white-matter changes caused ambi­
guity between Inflammation/Infection and Neurodegenerative
due to overlapping clinical terms (e.g., “lesion”, “hyper­
intensity”) and a lack of context. Second, small lesions were
mislabeled as Neoformation instead of Other. This reveals a
lexical bias where some terms trigger neoplastic associations.
Because the model could be penalized for these plausible
alternative interpretations, standard metrics such as Macro F1
may be insufficient, as they treat borderline or synonymous
assignments as outright errors.
A notable error pattern was the prevalence of partial
omission errors (false negatives on secondary labels). In the
multilabel task, the model almost always identified the pri­
mary (most salient) diagnosis correctly, but systematically
missed less prominent co-occurring labels. We refer to this as
a salience-driven anchoring effect (26): the model focuses on
the dominant finding and underweights subordinate clauses.
The Other category was most affected—it is a heterogeneous
residual label with no strong lexical triggers, often appearing
as a brief aside in the report (e.g.: “also noted...”). Consistent
with this, Other was the most frequently omitted true label in
both our 0-shot and fine-tuned results. This salience-driven,

The Other category was most affected—it is a heterogeneous

explicit signals. This suggests a structural limitation: when
one pathology dominates the text, models—in our experi­

and this was the largest of the four metric improvements
whose bootstrap confidence interval excluded zero, resulting
in more completely correct multilabel outputs. This is a
clinically meaningful gain, as capturing all diagnoses in a
report is crucial. Previous work similarly shows that QLoRA
can achieve expert-level performance in medical report tasks;
for example, QLoRA-tuned LLMs have been used to
summarize radiology reports (28), and open models have
been fine-tuned for diagnostic labeling with QLoRA to
good effect (4). In our case, QLoRA reduced the over­
prediction of Neurodegenerative labels, indicating better
alignment with our annotation criteria. However, this came
with a trade-off: Other became slightly overpredicted,
meaning the model learned some spurious co-occurrences.
Critically, the anchoring errors (missing secondary labels)
persisted after fine-tuning, confirming that learning the
combinatorial label structure is inherently difficult.
Despite these improvements, gains must be interpreted cau­
tiously given the data limitations (single-site, moderate corpora
size) and quantization. QLoRA’s 4-bit adapters enabled training
on modest hardware (4), but the fine-tuned model may still
underfit rare label combinations or learn dataset-specific patterns.
The multilingual setup also introduces noise: as others have
found (29), naively translating reports into the model’s pre­
training language can degrade performance. In our Italian setting,
using Italian MRI brain reports was essential, and the remaining
performance gap may partly result from language.
From a deployment perspective, our framework should be
regarded primarily as a semantic retrieval and information-
extraction tool. It is not intended for, and its current evi­
dence does not support, real-time diagnostic decision sup­
port. In retrospective PACS queries, omission of secondary
pathological findings may reduce cohort completeness and
limit identification of complex cases characterized by mul­
tiple co-occurring abnormalities. Therefore, configurations
that improve sensitivity for secondary labels may be prefer­
able, even at the cost of a moderate increase in false-positive
assignments. Even so, the overall performance achieved in­
dicates that open-weight LLMs might already provide useful
support for report-level triage and extraction of neuror­
adiologically relevant information. Moreover, the con­

mechanism for threshold adjustment and targeted human
review without requiring fine-tuning, although these scores
are self-reported rather than calibrated, and their reliability
was not evaluated here. Routing low-confidence cases for
human verification in this way also supports internal audit of
existing report archives and active-learning strategies, in
which the reports the model finds most uncertain are
prioritized for expert annotation. In this classification setting,
the principal reliability risks are not free-text hallucination in
the general sense but label hallucination, that is, the assign­
ment of categories not supported by the report, together
with overconfident outputs. The confidence-based routing
described above is a plausible safeguard against both.
Our study has some limitations that should be considered
when interpreting the results: i) single-center provenance,
which restricts generalizability across reporting styles and
scanner distributions; ii) a small labeled training set for fine-
tuning, as well as a small test set; iii) inter-annotator agreement
was not formally assessed, leaving annotation reliability un­
quantified, so part of the residual disagreement attributed to
the models may reflect noise in the reference standard; iv)
seven rare label classes (≤4 samples) were confined to training,

authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri
venue: Systems and Soft Computing, Volume 8, Article 200493
text:
Abstract
Brain tumors are among the most life-threatening neurological conditions, and effective therapy and patient
outcomes depend on accurate and timely diagnosis. This study proposes an interpretable and deployment-
oriented deep learning framework for multi-class classification of brain tumors using magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI). The framework employs a carefully designed lightweight CNN configuration that prioritizes
computational efficiency and robustness for practical clinical use. Evaluations on a publicly available MRI
dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving a classification accuracy of
99.54%. To enhance clinical trust, Grad-CAM visualizations were integrated to highlight class-discriminative
regions within MRI scans, providing transparent and interpretable predictions. In addition, the framework
was deployed within a user-friendly desktop application, enabling real-time diagnostic support. Comparative
analysis with state-of-the-art models shows that the proposed system achieves competitive or superior
performance while maintaining efficiency, making it a promising candidate for clinical decision support, subject
to further validation in real-world settings.

text:
Introduction
Brain tumors, which are characterized as a collection of abnormal
cells that develop within the brain’s tissues, are one of the main
causes of illness and death globally. The World Health Organization
(WHO) reports that brain tumors rank as the second most common
cause of death globally [1]. Brain tumors are generally classified into
two broad categories: benign and malignant. Benign tumors typically
develop more slowly and neither invade nor spread to neighboring
tissue. Malignant tumors, such as gliomas, on the other hand, have
the ability to spread into nearby tissues and organs, which can lead
to serious health problems. Early detection of brain tumors is crucial
to improve patient survival rates and outcomes [2,3].
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the primary imaging modality
for brain tumor detection due to its superior ability to visualize soft
tissue structures. However, manual interpretation of MRI scans is still
highly dependent on radiologists’ expertise and is prone to human
error, fatigue, and variability in judgment. Furthermore, brain tumors
often exhibit heterogeneous appearances in MR images, with over-
lapping morphological features that complicate accurate classification.
Biopsy procedures, although definitive, can be invasive and risky,
especially during the early stages of diagnosis [4].

authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri
venue: Systems and Soft Computing, Volume 8, Article 200493
text:
This study introduces an interpretable and deployment-oriented
deep learning framework for multi-class brain tumor classification us-
ing MRI scans. While several existing approaches focus on architectural
complexity or transfer learning, the proposed framework emphasizes
a balanced design combining accuracy, interpretability, and practical
usability. The key contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
• A carefully designed lightweight CNN configuration for four-class
brain tumor classification, achieving high diagnostic accuracy
while maintaining low computational complexity compared to
transfer learning and transformer-based approaches.
• A multi-level explainability strategy using Grad-CAM, including
layer-wise visualization and analysis of misclassified cases, pro-
viding deeper insight into the model’s decision-making process
beyond standard post-hoc explanations.
• The development of a fully offline, real-time desktop applica-
tion that integrates classification and visual explanation, facili-
tating practical deployment in clinical environments with limited
computational or network resources.
• Experimental evaluation demonstrating that a carefully designed
lightweight CNN can outperform or match more complex models
while offering improved interpretability and deployment readi-
ness.
By bridging the gap between research innovation and clinical ap-
plicability, this work contributes a significant step forward in making
AI-assisted brain tumor diagnosis more reliable and potentially useful
for clinical decision support.
This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work.
Section 3 details the proposed methodology. Section 4 presents experi-
mental results and clinical evaluation. Section 5 discusses key findings,
and Section 6 concludes the paper with future directions.

Related Work
This section reviews prior work on brain tumor classification, cov-
ering traditional machine learning methods, deep learning approaches,
and recent explainable AI techniques used in medical imaging. From a
clinical and imaging perspective, brain tumors present significant chal-
lenges in medical image analysis due to their varying types, locations,
and sizes [9]. Brain tumors must be classified accurately to prepare
a proper diagnosis and treatment plan. Researchers have employed
different techniques to enhance the performance of classifiers, such as
traditional machine learning and deep learning.
Traditional machine learning approaches have built on the founda-
tion of handcrafted features and standard classifiers. Gumaei et al. [10]
proposed a hybrid feature extraction technique combined with a Regu-
larized Extreme Learning Machine (RELM), achieving 94.23% classi-
fication accuracy. Similarly, Kaplan et al. [11] utilized Local Binary
Patterns (LBP and nLBP) with K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) for classifi-
cation, achieving 95.56% accuracy. Although these early approaches
demonstrated promise, their dependence on manually crafted features
restricted their scalability and ability to adapt to diverse datasets.
Deep learning methodologies, especially Convolutional Neural Net-
works (CNNs), have revolutionized medical image analysis and brain
tumor detection due to their automated feature extraction and superior
performance. CNNs excel in learning features directly from imaging
data, bypassing the need for manual feature design. Afshar et al. [12]
introduced a modified Capsule Network (CapsNet), emphasizing spatial
relationships among features and achieving 90.89% accuracy. Rasheed
et al. [13] proposed a CNN-based framework that incorporated Gaus-
sian blur-based sharpening and Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram
Equalization techniques, yielding a classification accuracy of 97.84%
across four brain tumor classes. Furthermore, data augmentation tech-
niques, such as scaling and rotation, have been incorporated to improve
the performance of deep learning models [14].
Transfer learning has further advanced this field by enabling the
reuse of powerful pre-trained models. Architectures such as VGG19,
ResNet-50, InceptionV3, and DenseNet have been fine-tuned on
domain-specific brain MRI datasets to achieve strong classification
performance. Zhu et al. [15] demonstrated the effectiveness of transfer

Materials And Methods
This section describes the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, model
architecture, and explainability strategy adopted in this study. Each
component is designed with consideration for classification accuracy,
interpretability, and practical usability.
While recent studies have explored optimization-assisted and
uncertainty-aware learning frameworks to enhance robustness, the
proposed methodology emphasizes training stability and generaliza-
tion through architectural design choices, regularization strategies,
and explainable visualization, prioritizing computational efficiency and
deployment simplicity.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri
venue: Systems and Soft Computing, Volume 8, Article 200493
text:
Brain tumor MRI dataset
The dataset employed in this study is a publicly available image-
level brain tumor MRI dataset obtained from Kaggle and curated by
Kadam et al. [34]. It integrates MRI scans from several publicly ac-
cessible repositories, including Figshare, SARTAJ, and Br35H, thereby
ensuring a diverse and representative collection of imaging data. It
consists of 7023 MRI images, divided into four categories: normal (no
tumor), pituitary tumors, meningioma tumors, and glioma tumors.
The dataset does not provide patient-level metadata (e.g., age,
sex, clinical history, scanner manufacturer, magnetic field strength, or
acquisition protocols), and subject identifiers are unavailable. Conse-
quently, annotations are provided at the image level rather than the
patient level. Labels were assigned by the dataset curators based on
expert-reviewed sources and have been widely used in prior brain
tumor classification studies. A sample of images from the dataset is
shown in Fig. 1.
The dataset was systematically partitioned into training, validation,
and testing subsets to ensure effective model development and evalua-
tion. Specifically, 4569 images were allocated for training, 1143 images
(20% of the training set) for validation, and 1311 images for testing.
This split preserves the overall dataset composition across the four
classes: no tumor (2000 images, 28.5%), pituitary tumors (1757 im-
ages, 25.0%), meningioma tumors (1645 images, 23.4%), and glioma
tumors (1621 images, 23.1%). The dataset exhibits mild class imbal-
ance, with the ‘no tumor’ class exceeding the smallest class (glioma)
by approximately 5.4 percentage points. To mitigate potential bias,
stratified splitting was employed to maintain class proportions across
all subsets. Macro-averaged evaluation metrics were used to ensure
balanced performance assessment, and data augmentation was applied
uniformly to the training set without introducing artificial rebalanc-
ing techniques such as oversampling or class weighting. The class
distribution and its preservation across splits are illustrated in Fig. 2.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri
venue: Systems and Soft Computing, Volume 8, Article 200493
text:
Data preprocessing
Effective image preprocessing plays a vital role in enhancing the
performance of deep learning models, especially in medical imaging
applications. To get the dataset ready for training, it is subjected to
various preprocessing steps. All images are resized to 125 × 125 pixels
in the first step. In the next step, pixel values are normalized by
dividing them by 255. This normalization step helps stabilize training
and improves optimization efficiency. The training data were ran-
domly shuffled to reduce sampling bias and improve generalization.
Class labels were one-hot encoded, which is required for multi-class
classification.

title: An interpretable CNN framework for multi-class brain tumor classification with visual explanation in MRI scans
authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri
venue: Systems and Soft Computing, Volume 8, Article 200493
text:
Data augmentation
The specialized nature of medical imaging datasets gives them high
value but also comes with several challenges. Accurate annotation
requires domain-specific expertise, while labeling inconsistencies can
result in negatively influence model training and predictive perfor-
mance [35]. In addition, when it comes to data privacy, the sensitive
nature of the data limits the accessibility and sharing of data. As
a result, it complicates the data gathering of sufficiently large and
representative datasets.
The limited size of labeled medical image datasets creates a se-
vere bottleneck to effective deep learning model development. To
avoid this problem, the image augmentation techniques have been
widely used to increase data diversity to improve model generalization
synthetically [36]. Consistent with prior brain tumor classification
studies, data augmentation has been extensively employed to mitigate
overfitting and enhance model robustness when training on publicly
available MRI datasets. Commonly adopted strategies in the litera-
ture include geometric transformations such as rotation, flipping, and
translation [37,38], while more advanced approaches have explored
GAN-based synthesis to generate realistic tumor variations [39,40].
Compared to these methods, our augmentation strategy prioritizes
computational efficiency and anatomical preservation. In this study,
data augmentation was employed to enhance robustness and improve
generalization under real-world variability. The augmentation strategy
included controlled geometric transformations with the following pa-
rameters: rotation range = 10, width shift range = 0.05, height shift
range = 0.05, and horizontal flipping. The rotation range introduces
random rotations up to ±10 degrees, while the shift parameters apply
minor horizontal and vertical translations of up to 5% of the image
dimensions. Horizontal flipping was applied with a probability of 0.5,
further increasing sample diversity. All augmentation operations were
applied exclusively to the training set, while validation and test data
were kept unchanged to ensure unbiased performance evaluation.
Fig. 3 illustrates the impact of data augmentation by presenting a
visual comparison between original and augmented MRI scans. The top
row displays four representative training images in their original form,
while the bottom row depicts the corresponding images following the
application of augmentation transformations.

Training configuration
The model’s hyperparameters were selected to balance classifica-
tion performance, generalization ability, and computational efficiency.
Hyperparameters were selected empirically through iterative experi-
mentation, where candidate configurations (learning rate, batch size,
dropout rates, and optimizer) were evaluated based on validation per-
formance and training stability. The reported settings represent the
best-performing combination among the tested configurations. The fi-
nal training configuration, chosen to facilitate exact replication, is
summarized in Table 1. The Adamax optimizer was selected for its
adaptive learning rate behavior in complex classification tasks [8]. The
dropout rates (0.25, 0.3, 0.4) and the 50-epoch training limit were
empirically validated to mitigate overfitting. A batch size of 8 ensured
stable training given the dataset size. Data augmentation was applied
exclusively to the training set to maintain unbiased evaluation on the
validation and test splits. All hyperparameters were kept fixed across
the cross-validation experiments and ablation studies to ensure a fair
and reproducible evaluation of the proposed architecture. Using this
fixed configuration, the final model was trained for a total duration
of approximately 32.5 min (1948 s) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU, with an
average training time of approximately 39 s per epoch.

Visualization of model decision-making using Grad-CAM
To examine model interpretability, Gradient-weighted Class Activa-
tion Mapping (Grad-CAM) was employed to visualize regions of the in-
put MRI scans that most influenced the model’s predictions. Grad-CAM
produces class-discriminative heatmaps that highlight salient image
regions without requiring architectural modifications. Fig. 9 illustrates
the evolution of model attention across multiple convolutional layers
for a correctly classified meningioma sample. Early layers exhibit dif-
fuse responses to general anatomical structures, while deeper layers
progressively focus on the tumor region. This coarse-to-fine local-
ization behavior is consistent with the hierarchical feature learning
characteristics of convolutional neural networks.
To further assess model explainability, Figs. 10 and 11 present Grad-
CAM overlays for both correctly classified and misclassified samples
across the four tumor classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and no
tumor. The top row in each figure illustrates accurate predictions, where
attention heatmaps are well aligned with the tumor mass. In contrast,
the bottom row highlights misclassified cases, revealing that the model
occasionally focuses on irrelevant anatomical structures (e.g., ventricles
or image borders), which may contribute to confusion between tumor
types. For instance, in Fig. 10, several no tumor cases are misclassified
as glioma, with Grad-CAM activations concentrated near artifact regions
or ambiguous tissue boundaries. Similarly, Fig. 11 shows that pituitary
tumors are misinterpreted as glioma or meningioma when the model’s at-
tention drifts toward peripheral features rather than the central lesion.
These observations demonstrate the utility of Grad-CAM not only for
validating correct predictions but also for diagnosing common failure
modes and potential model biases.
A layer-wise Grad-CAM analysis was further conducted on repre-
sentative correct and misclassified cases (Fig. 12). In the correctly
classified example, deeper-layer activations accurately localize the tu-
mor region, while earlier layers exhibit broader responses. In contrast,
misclassified cases show diffuse or misplaced activations and insuf-
ficient focus on diagnostically relevant regions at deeper layers. For

This provides quantitative evidence that the model’s decisions are

The Attention Focus Score (AFS) and Peak-in-Brain Ratio (PBR)
provide insight into whether the model’s attention is anatomically
consistent, which is a necessary, although not sufficient, condition for
trustworthy predictions. However, standard localization metrics such as
Dice or Intersection over Union (IoU) cannot be computed in this study
due to the absence of pixel-level tumor annotations. Consequently,
unlike Dice or IoU, the proposed metrics do not quantify overlap
with precise tumor boundaries, but instead evaluate attention at the
organ level (brain) rather than at the lesion level. These metrics are
therefore not intended to replace segmentation-based evaluation, but
to provide complementary insight under weakly supervised conditions.
Future work incorporating tumor segmentation datasets will enable
direct comparison with Dice/IoU and a more fine-grained assessment
of localization accuracy.

authors: Helala AlShehri, Luluh Almogbil, Jiyan Alrajhi, Lama Alosaimi, Jawlan Almarri

text:
Real-time brain tumor detection application
To demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed model, we
developed a user-friendly desktop application using Python, Tkinter,
and CustomTkinter for real-time brain tumor detection. The application
allows healthcare professionals to upload MRI scans, initiate model
inference, and receive classification results instantly—streamlining the
diagnostic workflow.
The system supports classification into four categories: no tumor,
pituitary, meningioma, and glioma. It provides both the predicted class
and the associated confidence score. To enhance interpretability, Grad-
CAM visualizations are incorporated to highlight the image regions
most influential in the model’s decision.
Fig. 13 illustrates the application interface. In Fig. 13a, the user has
uploaded an MRI scan and is prompted to classify it. Upon clicking
the ‘‘Classify Image’’ button, the application displays the predicted
tumor type (e.g., pituitary), the confidence score (e.g., 99.98%), and
a Grad-CAM overlay highlighting the tumor region (Fig. 13b).
To support interpretability and streamline clinical workflows, the
interface employs a color-coded scheme—green for no tumor, yellow
for pituitary, orange for meningioma, and red for glioma—allowing rapid
visual assessment. The design prioritizes simplicity and accessibility,
ensuring usability even for non-technical users. Additionally, the sys-
tem operates entirely offline, making it suitable for clinics with limited
internet connectivity or heightened data security requirements.
This application functions as a real-time decision support tool, help-
ing radiologists review cases efficiently and confidently, particularly in
resource-constrained or high-demand clinical settings.

Interpretation and advantages
The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of
99.54% while maintaining a lightweight design (5.37M parameters),
enabling real-time inference at approximately 0.66 ms per image
(pure model forward pass). Beyond accuracy, Grad-CAM visualizations
provided clinically meaningful validation through anatomically plau-
sible attention patterns, addressing the critical need for transparency
and interpretability in medical AI systems. Together, these results
demonstrate a strong balance between performance, efficiency, and
explainability, representing a practical step toward clinical integration.

text:
Clinical translation
The framework is designed as an offline decision-support tool,
supporting data privacy and usability in resource-limited clinical envi-
ronments. Its integrated explainability mechanisms facilitate clinician
trust and align with emerging regulatory expectations for transparent
AI-assisted diagnostics.
In real-world clinical settings, MRI data exhibit substantial vari-
ability due to differences in scanner manufacturers, magnetic field
strengths (e.g., 1.5T vs. 3T), and acquisition protocols (e.g., T1, T2,
FLAIR sequences). In addition, patient-specific factors such as age,
tumor characteristics, and anatomical variability further contribute to
data diversity. These factors can introduce domain shifts that may
affect model performance when deployed outside controlled experi-
mental conditions. For example, a model trained predominantly on
T1-weighted contrast-enhanced images may exhibit reduced sensitivity
when applied to non-contrast T2-weighted sequences. Furthermore,
real-world clinical populations may exhibit class distributions that
differ from those in benchmark datasets, which may influence model
calibration and decision thresholds.
Future multicenter validation and prospective clinical studies are
essential to address real-world challenges such as scanner variabil-
ity, protocol heterogeneity, and patient-level diversity, and to support
regulatory approval and clinical adoption.

text:
Limitations and future work
A key limitation of this study is the reliance on a single publicly
available dataset, which may not fully capture the diversity and vari-
ability encountered in real-world clinical environments. In particular,
the dataset is curated at the image level and lacks subject-level iden-
tifiers and detailed acquisition metadata (e.g., scanner type, imaging
protocols, and patient demographics), which prevents direct assessment
of cross-institutional generalization.
Although the proposed framework demonstrates strong and con-
sistent performance, including under stratified cross-validation, this
evaluation remains confined to a single data distribution. Consequently,
performance may vary when the model is applied to external datasets
with different imaging characteristics and acquisition conditions. Given
the high classification accuracy achieved, particular care was taken to
minimize the risk of overfitting and data leakage. The model exhibited
consistent performance across cross-validation folds, suggesting stable
learning behavior rather than overfitting to a specific data split.
To mitigate this limitation, strict experimental protocols were
adopted, including complete separation of training, validation, and test
sets, stratified cross-validation, and controlled data augmentation to
simulate real-world variability. Nevertheless, these strategies cannot
fully substitute for true external validation. The held-out test set was
fully isolated and was not used during preprocessing, augmentation, or
hyperparameter tuning. However, due to the absence of subject-level
identifiers, potential hidden correlations cannot be entirely ruled out
and should be considered when interpreting the results.
Future work will therefore focus on external validation using inde-
pendent and multi-institutional MRI datasets to assess robustness under
domain shifts. In addition, federated learning and domain adaptation
strategies will be explored to enable generalization across heteroge-
neous clinical settings while preserving data privacy.
Furthermore, robustness-enhancing strategies such as class-weighted
loss functions and imbalance-aware training schemes will be inves-
tigated to improve performance on rare tumor subtypes and highly
imbalanced data. Future work may also investigate the integration
of uncertainty-aware or adaptive optimization strategies to further
enhance robustness and interpretability under increased data variability,

Conclusion
This study presents an interpretable deep learning framework for
multi-class brain tumor classification from MRI scans. The proposed
model achieves high classification accuracy while maintaining compu-
tational efficiency suitable for practical clinical decision-support sce-
narios. Multi-level Grad-CAM analysis provides clinically meaningful
transparency, while the fully offline desktop implementation supports
potential use in resource-limited settings. While results under stratified
cross-validation demonstrate robust performance, external multicenter
validation remains necessary to further assess generalization across
diverse clinical imaging environments.

Abstract
Early detection and precise characterization of brain tu-
mors are critical for improving patient outcomes and sur-
vival rates.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) remains
a cornerstone modality in brain tumor diagnostics, offering
high-resolution, multi-sequence imaging essential for cap-
turing the complex structure and pathology of intracranial
abnormalities.
However, the process of diagnostic report
generation is labor-intensive, requiring meticulous review,
synthesis, and verification by clinicians. In this study, we
present a clinical data pipeline, named iReportMed, designed
for automated diagnostic report generation specific to brain
tumors. The framework consists of a two-phase model. In
the initial phase, multi-modality MRI scans are utilized for
comprehensive feature extraction and classification, leading
to subject-specific labeling. The second phase employ Large
Language Models (LLMs) to produce structured diagnostic
reports based on extracted features and identified labels. The
proposed framework is initially trained on the UCSF-PDGM
dataset and subsequently fine-tuned with real clinical data.
Results demonstrate that automated diagnostic reporting is
both feasible and potentially advantageous for integration
into routine clinical work-flows, offering a promising tool for
enhancing efficiency in healthcare settings.
Index Terms— Diagnostic reports, brain tumor, MRI,
LLMs

Introduction
Automatic generation of diagnosis reports is currently in
great demand due to the substantial amount of time required
to draft, edit, revise, and approve medical discoveries ob-
tained from medical images into well-reported documents.
The common clinical procedure addresses this problem in
two phases. The first phase involves medical image process-
ing and feature extraction to reach a diagnosis decision. The
second phase involves generating text that describes the find-
ings in detailed, accurate, and concise statements. Artificial
intelligence (AI) is now trending as a leading technology with
several contributions to different daily applications, achiev-
ing remarkable accuracy that is close to human cognition in
many clinical applications [1, 2]. Another important leading
technology is large language models (LLMs), which demon-
strate a significant improvement in generating human-like
conversations through publicly accessible online platforms
such as ChatGPT and Gemini. In early 2023, a few studies
evaluated the performance of chatbots in clinical applica-
tions, and the results demonstrated impressive performance,
attracting attention to their potential use in the healthcare
sector [3]. With the rapid progress of generative AI chatbots,
there is controversy regarding the impact of this technology
on the future of several healthcare clinical applications. A
comparative study evaluated the performance of different
LLM models in comparison to medical experts, considering
different summarization tasks, including medical reports, and
demonstrated the significant performance of the LLMs [4].
Surprisingly, the summarization ability of LLMs outperforms
medical experts. Another study evaluated the capabilities of
vision LLMs in generating diagnosis reports on computed to-
mography (CT) images [5]. Results demonstrate that GPT-4V
outperformed LLaVa-Med and RadFM in terms of Pearson’s
correlation with clinicians. Another study also investigated
report generation from CT images using LLaMA2-7B [6].

remarkable performance improvement in comparison with

layer.

text:
This study aims at the development of an interactive
framework, named iReportMed, for medical image diagnosis
using deep learning architectures with LLM assistance. The
multi-task image diagnosis models empower extended image
knowledge extraction, while LLM technology is used for the
generation of expert-like medical diagnosis reports. Without
losing generality, the scope of this study is the diagnosis of
brain tumors from multi-modality magnetic resonance imag-
ing (MRI). To achieve this goal, we collect data from online
resources and real clinical raw data to improve the robustness
of the proposed framework. Within this pipeline, two models
are combined to generate the diagnosis report. First, a multi-
modal deep learning neural network is employed to enable ef-
ficient knowledge extraction from MRI at different realization
scales. We consider a wider scope that includes abnormality
segmentation, target organ annotation, disease diagnosis, and
characterization. With the careful design of deep learning
architectures customized for mutual-attention multimodality
feature extraction, a remarkable improvement in automatic
diagnosis is expected. Second, an auto-regressive LLM is
used to combine images, image features, and text represent-
ing the initial diagnosis to generate a comprehensive medical
report. The output of the image diagnosis track will be con-
verted into a text prompt generator to enable communication
with chatbots for the automatic generation of diagnosis re-
ports. Up to the best of author’s knowledge, this is the first
study that proposed a method for automatic report generation
of brain tumor from multi-modality MRI.

Datasets

UCSF-PDGM, which consists of 542 subjects with differ-

acquired using a 3T scanner with different modalities such
as T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, etc. Images are co-
registered and resampled to the 3D space of the T2/FLAIR
with 1 mm resolution. The skull is stripped using publicly
available software.
Tumors are manually annotated using
automatic segmentation followed by manual correction by
two trained radiologists. A subset of 374 subjects is selected
where the diagnosis of Glioblastoma is confirmed. The im-

formats. All images are normalized to reduce inter-subject
variability using the normalization method detailed in [11].
Segmentation labels represent different tumor regions such
as enhancing tumor, necrotic tumor, and edema. For simplic-
ity, all the three regions are combined as abnormality. The
segmentation of parenchyma and the whole brain is available
as well. The dataset is associated with brief clinical meta-
data in CSV formats that is used to generate a synthetic brief

Image Perception Model
The Image Perception Model (IPM) is designed to extract ad-
ditional features to highlight different regions within an MRI
scan, such as the segmented brain region, segmented abnor-
malities, and the corresponding attention map. The proposed
IPM extends the well-known U-Net architecture to handle
multi-inputs with mutual attentions mechanism. It incorpo-
rates a general score attention layer and multiple encoders in-
stead of a single encoder, enabling feature extraction from
multi-modality images with mutual attention. Network archi-
tecture and other technical details of the IPM can be found
in [11].

Report Generation Model
The Report Generation Model (RGM) is a multimodal few-
shot learning architecture. An auto-regressive model with al-
ternative input of images and text is designed to incorporate
four MRI sequences with initial diagnosis reports from four
different clinical experts. This design enable multimodal set-
tings that enable feature extraction from images to highlight

An open source pre-trained LLM BioMistral-7B is utilized
as medical domain trained on PubMed Central [13]. The en-
coded images and text are embedded into a frozen LLM, al-
lowing the language model to generate comprehensive diag-
nosis reports using MRI images.

Evaluation metrics and assessment
The accuracy of the IPM is evaluated using segmentation
evaluation metrics such as dice coefficient (DSC) and Haus-
dorff Distance (HD). These metrics are computed for both
whole brain and abnormality segmentation. The evaluation
of medical diagnosis reports generated by LLMs is a chal-
lenging task as requires insightful evaluation from experts.
Following the same evaluation method in [4] we requested
two medical experts (not included in the initial report data
generation) to evaluate output reports in terms of complete-
ness, correctness and conciseness. Each expert independently
ranked the reports on a scale from 0 to 10 for each of these
three criteria, where 0 indicates the lowest quality and 10 sig-
nifies the highest quality. Completeness refers to the extent
to which all necessary and relevant information is included
in the report, ensuring that it provides a thorough account of
the patient’s condition. Correctness assesses the accuracy of
the medical information presented, verifying that diagnoses,
descriptions, and other medical details are precise and reli-
able. Conciseness evaluates how effectively the information
is communicated in a clear and succinct manner, avoiding un-
necessary verbosity while maintaining essential details. This
ranking system provided a quantitative measure to compare
the quality of the reports systematically.

Namya Musthafa$1, Mohammad M. Masud∗†, Qurban Memon$2, and Yauhen Statsenko#3

Abstract—Accurate tumor diagnosis from MRI, free from bias,
remains a major challenge in neuro-oncology, demanding reliable
detection, classification, and clinically meaningful interpretation.
In this work, we propose a unified framework that integrates
tumor diagnosis with automated report generation. Our method
couples a segmentation-integrated classifier—producing both
tumor labels and spatial masks—with radiomics features to
improve diagnostic robustness and interpretability. Furthermore,
we adapt large language models (LLMs) to generate structured,
human-readable reports consistent with radiology reporting stan-
dards. Experimental findings demonstrate that this fusion of
segmentation-classification, radiomics, and generative AI delivers
high diagnostic accuracy and produces coherent narrative re-
ports, advancing both diagnostic precision and clinical usability.
Index Terms—LLM, diagnosis report, radiomics data, Pre-
dicted mask, Region of interest.

Introduction
The diagnosis of brain tumors using magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) is both critical and highly challenging. Tra-
ditionally, this task has depended on manual interpretation
by radiologists—a process that is time-intensive, cognitively
demanding, and susceptible to human bias. In addition, the
manual preparation of MRI reports can be inconsistent and
frequently prolongs clinical decision-making.
In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has shown re-
markable promise in automating medical imaging analysis.
A wide range of AI-based techniques has been investigated
for both tumor classification and segmentation. Advances in
deep learning, in particular, have significantly enhanced brain
tumor analysis from MRI data. Convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) achieve state-of-the-art results in tumor classification,
while U-Net architectures and their variants are widely adopted
for precise lesion segmentation. Moreover, hybrid models that
jointly optimize segmentation and classification have further
strengthened diagnostic performance. Radiomics, which ex-
tracts quantitative imaging features that describe tumor pheno-
type, has also been explored as a complementary methodology,
providing additional insights beyond deep learning alone.
Despite these advances, there remains a lack of integrated
AI frameworks that not only detect and classify brain tumors
on MRI scans but also generate coherent, human-readable
diagnostic reports to support clinical workflows. To address
this gap, we propose a unified framework that combines tumor
segmentation, classification, and automated report generation.
Our approach leverages radiomics features alongside gener-
ative AI models to generate radiology-style reports directly
from imaging data, thereby enhancing clinical interpretability
and reducing the reporting burden. The resulting reports are
systematically evaluated using well-known natural language
processing metrics in conjunction with radiomics-informed
analysis to ensure higher diagnostic fidelity.

• Introducing a unified framework that integrates tumor
detection, classification, and automated report generation.
• Employing technique to guide large language models
(LLMs) toward producing clinically relevant outputs.
• Utilizing generative AI to create coherent, human-
readable MRI reports that support clinical workflows.

understanding. By exploiting the U-Net’s inherent multi-scale
feature representation along with the broad receptive field

B. Brain Tumor Classification
Conventional methods often address tumor segmentation
and classification as separate tasks—either performing seg-

a hybrid 3B-Net combined with EfficientNetB2, which first lo-

through heat-map visualizations while attaining an impressive
accuracy of 99.1%. Along similar lines, Khan and Auvee

a ResNet50 architecture augmented with Grad-CAM visual-

approach achieved over 98% accuracy, combining diagnostic

A. System Setup
The model was implemented in Python 3 within a Jupyter
Notebook environment, using PyTorch as the primary deep
learning framework with CUDA for GPU acceleration. Train-

with three NVIDIA GPUs (12 GB each), an Intel Xeon dual-
core processor, and 128 GB RAM, enabling parallel computa-

tasks without memory bottlenecks. The proposed approach
requires 4–5 GB of GPU memory, while the remaining re-

report generation, the system interfaces with Gemini 2.5 Flash
via Google SDKs under a strict response schema, ensuring
syntactically valid JSON aligned with predefined reporting
fields. Final reports are formatted into PDFs using ReportLab,
with all figures scaled to fit A4 dimensions while preserving
aspect ratio for visual fidelity.
B. Dataset Description
This study employs a publicly available dataset for training
and evaluation of the proposed framework. The **Brain Tumor
Segmentation Dataset (BraTS) [22] provides annotated brain
MRI slices with corresponding ground-truth masks, each in
grayscale format. All images were preprocessed in 2D and
resized to a resolution of 224×224 pixels as input for the Phase
1 segmentation module. In Phase 2, the classification head re-
ceives a fused representation of the MRI slice and its predicted
mask for multiclass classification. Finally, the predicted mask,
along with the corresponding MRI and classification output,
is used for radiomics feature extraction.
C. Evaluation Matrices
To assess alignment with expert-authored ground-truth nar-
ratives, each generated report is paired with its correspond-
ing reference report by case ID, normalized into canonical
text, and evaluated using ROUGE-1/2/L and BLEU metrics.
ROUGE measures reference-based text similarity, quantifying
content overlap through n-gram matches, longest common
subsequence (ROUGE-L), and related variants [23]. BLEU
evaluates text quality using clipped n-gram precision (com-
monly up to N=4), combined with a brevity penalty to
discourage overly short outputs, producing a single score that
correlates well with human judgments in tasks such as machine
translation and text generation [24].

segmentation-based classification, radiomics feature analysis,
and automated report generation. The evaluations reveal that
radiomics features alone are insufficient for highly reliable

Methodology
A. Environment setup
The proposed framework has been designed as an end-
to-end pipeline for automated radiological reporting of brain
tumors. The system accepts multi-modal MRI scans as
input, performs preprocessing, and applies a 3D U-Net
model for semantic segmentation of tumor sub-regions:
whole tumor (WT), tumor core (TC), and enhancing tumor
(ET).
Fig 1. AI-Based System for Brain Tumor Detection
Segmentation masks are used to extract quantitative
clinical metrics, including tumor volume, edema extent,
compactness, and midline shift. To provide anatomical
context, the segmented regions are mapped to a standard
brain atlas, after which the derived features are passed to a
large language model (LLM) such as Qwen3-Coder-30B-
A3B-Instruct. The LLM is guided by JSON-formatted
inputs to generate coherent, clinically relevant radiology
reports. Finally, the complete system is deployed as a web
application that enables MRI upload, automated analysis,
and structured report generation.

workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 3050 GPU (4

Discussion
The results confirm that combining deep learning
with LLMs provides a viable and scalable solution for
automated brain tumor reporting. Compared to manual

title: Boosting brain tumor detection with an optimized ResNet and explainability via Grad-CAM and LIME
authors: K. Afnaan, C. G. Arunbalaji, T. Singh, R. Kumar, and co-authors
text:
Abstract
Detecting Brain Tumors is essential in medical imaging, as early and accurate diagnosis significantly improves
treatment decisions and patient outcomes. Convolutional Neural Networks have demonstrated high efficiency
in this domain, but their lack of interpretability remains a significant drawback for clinical adoption. This study
explores the integration of Explainability techniques to enhance transparency in CNN-based classification and
improve model performance through advanced optimization strategies. The primary research question addressed is
how to improve the accuracy, generalization, and interpretability of CNNs for brain tumor Detection. While previous
studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of deep learning for tumor detections, challenges such as class
imbalance and overfitting of CNNs persist. To bridge this gap, we employ different dynamic learning rate modifiers,
perform architectural enhancements, and apply XAI techniques, including Grad-CAM and LIME. Our experiments
are conducted on three publicly available multiclass tumor datasets to ensure the generalizability of the proposed
approach. Among the tested architectures, the enhanced ResNet model consistently outperformed others across
all datasets, achieving the highest test accuracy, ranging from 99.36% to 99.65%. The techniques such as unfreezing
layers, integrating various blocks, pooling, and dropout layers enhanced feature refinement and reduced overfitting.
By incorporating XAI, we improve model interpretability, ensuring that clinically relevant regions in MRI scans
are highlighted. These advancements contribute to highly reliable AI-assisted diagnostics, addressing significant
challenges in medical image classification.

Methodology
The overall framework for brain tumor classification
involves multiple stages, including preprocessing, model
training, evaluation, and visualization of explainabil­
ity. Initially, MRI images undergo resizing and one-hot
encoding to standardize input for deep learning models.
The proposed approach leverages an improved ResNet
architecture with a squeeze-and-excitation block, global
average pooling, dropout, and fine-tuning of the last
ten layers to enhance feature extraction and classifica­
tion performance. The model is trained and evaluated
on multiple datasets, incorporating dynamic learning
rate optimization techniques to improve generalization.
Grad-CAM and LIME provide interpretability, high­
lighting the key regions influencing the model’s predic­
tions, and ensuring clinical reliability. Figure 1 is a visual
description of the detailed system flow. Figure 2 is the
pictorial description of the pipeline of the proposed
work.

text:
Model training
In this research, several deep learning architectures with
pre-trained models were utilized and trained to clas­
sify brain tumor types. Transfer learning was applied
using pre-trained models such as MobileNetV2, Effi­
cientNetV2-S, DenseNet-121, ResNet, and VGG-16. The
convolutional base of each model was frozen since it had
been trained on ImageNet to retain the learned feature
representations. A custom CNN model is designed to
contain multiple convolutional layers, batch normaliza­
tion, pooling, and dense layers for extracting hierarchical
features from the MRI scans.
The Adam optimizer with the categorical cross-entropy
loss function, combined with metrics of accuracy, pre­
cision, and recall, was used to compile these models, as
it may provide a fair measure of prognostic capability.
Training was conducted on Colab Pro GPU NVIDIA
A100 to accelerate computations, utilizing early stopping
and learning rate reduction to achieve optimal perfor­
mance. All the architecture performed well, as was evi­
denced by the efficacy of transfer learning and custom
CNN approaches in the classification of brain tumors
from MRI scans; most required fine-tuning: modifying
the last unfreezing in a limited fashion by returning from
4 to 10 layers based on architecture into training at low
learning rates. During training, the categorical cross-
entropy loss was monitored using an Adam optimizer in
the training environment, with accuracy, precision, and
recall metrics employed to track its efficacy. Each model
underwent training for 100 epochs, with a validation split
incorporated and ran on a GPU, thus providing a thor­
ough and systematic route to an effective multiclass brain
tumor classification engine.
ResNet is selected as the best-performing model based
on the results achieving high accuracy and efficiency.
Transfer learning is employed, loading the pre-trained
ResNet backbone with ImageNet weights and integrat­
ing its custom dense layers for classifying the images.
Residual skip connections have enabled efficient train­
ing of extremely deep models by mitigating challenges
such as the vanishing gradient problem. The framework
architecture relies on several residual blocks composed
of convolutional layers and skip connections, allowing for

In medical imaging, understanding model decisions
is crucial, particularly when dealing with critical tasks
such as brain tumor detection. To enhance the inter­
pretability of our optimized ResNet model, we employ
two prominent Explainable AI (XAI) techniques: Gra­
dient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM)
and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations
(LIME). These techniques provide insights into the mod­
el’s decision-making process by highlighting the regions
in the input image that contributed most to the model’s
prediction.

LIME: Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME)
is designed to explain predictions made by any black-
box machine learning model. Unlike Grad-CAM, LIME
focuses on approximating the model’s behavior in the
local region of a specific input instance. LIME provides
interpretable insights into complex model predictions
by implementing a simple surrogate model trained on a
small number of data samples[62].
The LIME methodology involves generating perturbed
samples x′

interpretable model g, such as a linear regression or deci­
sion tree, is trained on the perturbed data. The surrogate
model approximates the complex model’s behavior in the
vicinity of the input instance by minimizing the following
loss function:

The LIME-based explainability results illustrated in Fig­

different datasets for brain tumor detection. For each
dataset, LIME highlights regions of the MRI scans that
influence the classification of no tumor, meningioma, gli­
oma, and pituitary tumors. The visualizations show that
while LIME effectively identifies certain relevant regions,
the highlighted superpixels often appear to overlap
across different tumor types and healthy scans. This over­
lap indicates that LIME struggles to distinguish precise,
class-specific features, making it challenging to interpret
model decisions with clinical clarity.
In the first dataset, although some focused regions
align with the expected tumor locations, the highlighted
area s are not sharply defined and appear scattered. Simi­
lar patterns are observed in datasets 2 and 3, with LIME
outputs showing diffuse, broad regions of interest rather
than clear tumor boundaries. This lack of granularity
reduces the effectiveness of LIME in isolating subtle dif­
ferences between tumor types, which is critical in medi­
cal diagnostics.
The superpixel approach of LIME is beneficial in gen­
eral domains, but it does not offer the level of detailed,
localized explanation required for MRI-based tumor
classification. The highlighted regions are too coarse
and do not correspond to well-defined anatomical or
pathological structures, reducing the practical utility of
these explanations for medical professionals. As a result,
although LIME provides a surface-level understanding of
the model’s focus areas, it gives less precise, actionable
insights necessary for clinical interpretation.
For more meaningful and clinically relevant visual
explanations, techniques such as Grad-CAM, which
inherently utilize the neural network architecture to pro­
vide spatial precise and class-discriminative heatmaps,
may be better suited. In conclusion, while LIME contrib­
utes to basic interpretability, its current implementations
can be improved and enhanced in the future to meet the
standards demanded in medical imaging applications.

Discussion
The proposed SE-ResNet framework demonstrates out­
standing performance in brain tumor classification,
achieving accuracies exceeding 99% across three inde­
pendent MRI datasets. The ablation study (Table 4) shows
that each architectural refinement contributed incre­
mentally to performance. Unfreezing the last ten layers
improved transfer learning effectiveness, while the inte­
gration of Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) blocks enhanced
channel-wise feature representation, enabling the model
to focus on tumor-specific cues. Global Average Pooling
reduced parameter redundancy, Dropout alleviated over­
fitting and enriched feature interactions with additional
dense layers. The incorporation of an adaptive learning
rate strategy (LR Plateau) further stabilized training to
ensure consistent gains across datasets. Together, these
modifications elevated the baseline ResNet accuracy to
near-perfect levels. The strong performance across multi­
ple datasets highlights the robustness and generalization
of the proposed framework, distinguishing it from stud­
ies limited to single-dataset validation. Grad-CAM visu­
alizations confirmed that the model consistently attended
to clinically relevant tumor regions, reflecting structural
features commonly identified by radiologists. LIME pro­
vided complementary insights into feature importance,
though its coarser spatial resolution compared to Grad-
CAM suggests gradient-based methods may be more
effective for localized medical interpretability. The com­
bination of performance and explainability demonstrate
the potential of SE-ResNet as a clinically trustworthy
decision-support system.
At the same time, several limitations must be acknowl­
edged. Although the datasets used are more diverse than
in many prior works, they still represent curated MRI
collections with four classes, which may not capture
rare tumor subtypes or inter-institutional variability in
imaging protocols. Misclassifications, while minimal,
were most notable in meningioma cases, indicating that
irregular tumor boundaries remain challenging. The reli­
ance on 2D MRI slices resized to 250×250 pixels intro­
duce a trade-off between computational efficiency and
the preservation of fine-grained anatomical detail: future
extensions to 3D volumetric scans could provide richer
contextual information and improve tumor delineation.

Finally, while Grad-CAM and LIME enhance transpar­
ency, they provide post-hoc explanations that are inher­
ently qualitative and require clinical validation to ensure
interpretability in real-world practice.
It is also essential to consider the scope of this frame­
work beyond MRI. While SE-ResNet proved highly
effective for structural MRI, its direct application to
modalities such as positron emission tomography (PET)
are less straightforward. MRI provides high spatial reso­
lution and strong tissue contrast, whereas PET has lower
resolution and higher noise, while measuring func­
tional rather than structural information. Adapting this
framework for PET would therefore require substantial
modifications, including harmonization of resolution,
denoising, and normalization in preprocessing, as well as
adjustments to feature extraction layers to capture meta­
bolic rather than anatomical patterns. This highlights
that although the overall strategy is extensible, modality-
specific adaptations are essential for reliable performance
across different imaging domains.

authors: K. Afnaan, C. G. Arunbalaji, T. Singh, R. Kumar, and co-authors
text:
Conclusion
The study describes an improved systematic enhance­
ment of the SE-ResNet model to brain tumor classifi­
cation that reaches close to perfect accuracy in three
different MRI data sets. Through the successive stages of
refined architecture, including unfreezing of deeper lay­
ers, adding Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks, global aver­
age pooling, dropout, and dense layers, the model proved
to have an outstanding representation of features and
overall classification accuracy of above 99%. The combi­
nation of explainable AI techniques and the use of Grad-
CAM ensured the predictions were based on clinically
meaningful tumor areas, improving the interpretability
and confidence in the system. High predictive accuracy
and open-minded decision-making is the synergy that
makes the model potentially an important clinical deci­
sion support tool to reinforce confidence in its deploy­
ment to help radiologists.
Based on such positive findings, further studies will
aim at generalizing the framework to broader clini­
cal applicability and strength. This also involves train­
ing bigger and more heterogeneous datasets to capture
rare tumor types and different radiologic acquisitions
and expand the model to discuss 3D volumetric scans,
which provides more detailed spatial information. Inte­
gration Multi-modal integration, like the integration of
MRI with CT or PET can further enhance the represen­
tation of the features. The SE-ResNet framework can be
further adapted to classify tumor subtypes and capture
more subtle intra-tumoral characteristics. Achieving
this will require more granular datasets with detailed
subtype annotations, along with potential architectural
enhancements, such as multi-scale feature extraction and
attention mechanisms that focus on finer patterns. Incor­
porating advanced interpretability techniques beyond
Grad-CAM and LIME will provide more precise and
actionable explanations of model predictions. Ultimately,
the goal is to deploy this high-performing, interpretable
AI model into clinical workflows to assist the radiolo­
gist’s efficiency and support more confident, data-driven
decision-making.

title: AI-Assisted Brain Tumor MRI Reporting and Treatment-Planning Segmentation: A Retrospective Paired Workflow Evaluation
authors: Jia-Sheng Hong, Wei-Kai Lee, Jing-Jhong Chen, Yi-Chen Sun, Ying-Yi Hsu, Yung-Fa Lu, Ming-Hsi Sun, Kai-Lin Yang, Chia-Yu Lin, Hsiu-Mei Wu, Shu-Ting Chen, Wan-Yuo Guo, Hung-Chieh Chen, Weir-Chiang You, Yu-Te Wu
text:
Abstract
Background: Brain tumor magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reporting and tumor segmen-
tation for treatment planning are time-consuming and variable. This retrospective fixed-
sequence paired workflow study evaluates whether AI assistance is associated with changes
in efficiency, consistency, and reproducibility. Methods: Thirty MRI cases (10 vestibular
schwannomas, 10 meningiomas, 10 brain metastases) were assessed. Two neuroradiolo-
gists completed diagnostic reporting with and without AI assistance, and two physicians
completed tumor delineation with and without AI-generated preliminary contours after a
3-week washout. Results: Reporting time decreased from 42.94 to 27.90 min for Reader A
and from 101.04 to 80.47 min for Reader B, corresponding to median paired case-level re-
ductions of 40.39% and 11.51%, respectively; only Reader A reached statistical significance.
Sensitivity remained 97.73% and 100.00%, while precision was numerically higher after AI
assistance (89.58% to 97.73% and 83.02% to 91.67%). Report-similarity metrics increased
across ROUGE-L, BERTScore F1, and Sentence-BERT cosine similarity (all p < 0.001). Con-
touring time decreased from 54.63 to 4.93 min for Reader 1 and from 184.44 to 44.19 min
for Reader 2, with median paired reductions of 100.00% and 87.11%. Dice coefficients
were numerically higher after AI assistance (0.81 to 0.87 and 0.83 to 0.87). Conclusions:
AI assistance was associated with shorter task-completion times, higher report-similarity
metrics, and numerically higher contour-overlap measures. Prospective validation should
determine whether these workflow efficiency gains translate into broader clinical benefit.

text:
Introduction
Brain tumor management relies heavily on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) through-
out the clinical pathway, from initial detection to lesion characterization, response assess-
ment, and treatment planning. In neuro-oncology, standardized imaging frameworks
such as the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) criteria [1] and the RANO
criteria for brain metastases (RANO-BM) [2] emphasize consistent evaluation of lesion size,
enhancement pattern, multiplicity, and interval change. In parallel, structured reporting
frameworks such as the Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) have been
introduced to improve the consistency, completeness, and clinical usability of brain tumor
MRI reports [3,4]. Together, these developments highlight the need for imaging workflows
that are accurate, reproducible, and standardized across readers and clinical settings.
Brain tumor MRI interpretation remains labor-intensive. A prior time-motion analysis
of brain MRI interpretation reported that the total interpretation workflow, measured from
study opening to report signing, required approximately 10–18 min per case across reader
roles, with time distributed among image viewing, report transcription, obtaining clinical
data, education, and other related activities [5]. Prolonged reporting turnaround time
can affect departmental efficiency and may also influence downstream clinical operations.
Assistive artificial intelligence (AI), including structured reporting tools and large language
model (LLM)-based support systems, has therefore attracted interest as a means of im-
proving reporting efficiency, standardization, and quality [6,7]. Although recent studies
have reported favorable performance for AI-assisted reporting paradigms, their value in
disease-specific clinical brain tumor workflows remains to be validated.
Artificial intelligence (AI) includes conventional machine learning models and deep-
learning methods that learn imaging representations directly from data. These approaches
differ in data requirements, interpretability, and validation needs. Recent systematic re-
views in neurosurgical, neuroendocrine, and neuroimaging applications highlight rapid
growth of clinical AI while emphasizing heterogeneity and the need for external valida-
tion [8–10].
A similar challenge exists on the treatment side. Tumor delineation for surgery and ra-
diotherapy planning is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability, particularly

A similar challenge exists on the treatment side. Tumor delineation for surgery and ra-
diotherapy planning is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability, particularly
when lesions are multiple, irregular, or adjacent to critical neuroanatomical structures [11].
Recent reviews and clinical evaluations have shown that AI-based auto-segmentation
can reduce contouring burden and improve reproducibility when used under physician
supervision [12]. In brain tumor imaging, meta-analytic evidence suggests that deep learn-
ing models have demonstrated performance in detection and segmentation across brain
metastases, meningiomas, gliomas, and vestibular schwannomas, supporting their use as
assistive tools in treatment planning rather than as fully autonomous systems [13–16].
However, most prior studies have evaluated AI assistance for diagnostic reporting
and contouring separately. In brain tumor care, these processes are clinically connected:
diagnostic MRI interpretation informs follow-up decisions, multidisciplinary treatment
strategy, target delineation, and treatment delivery. AI-assisted tools may be useful not
only for isolated algorithmic tasks, but also for creating shared lesion-level information
that can be carried from diagnostic reporting into treatment planning. When lesions are
preliminarily marked by AI during image review, physicians may verify report content,

For physician-facing AI tools, workflow efficiency is a key clinical consideration.
Even if an AI model demonstrates acceptable standalone diagnostic or segmentation
performance, its clinical utility may be limited if its use increases reader workload, prolongs
reporting or contouring time, or disrupts routine practice. From this perspective, time
efficiency provides an appropriate primary endpoint for workflow evaluation: an AI-
assisted workflow should reduce, or at least not increase, the physician burden required
to complete clinical tasks. Measures of lesion detection, report consistency, segmentation
overlap, and volumetric agreement were therefore considered complementary outcomes to
determine whether any time savings were achieved without compromising output quality.
This rationale led to the present study, which evaluates whether AI assistance is associated
with changes in workflow efficiency, consistency, and reproducibility in two connected use
scenarios: brain tumor MRI report preparation and treatment-planning tumor delineation,
using controlled retrospective paired workflow testing (Figure 1).

authors: Jia-Sheng Hong, Wei-Kai Lee, Jing-Jhong Chen, Yi-Chen Sun, Ying-Yi Hsu, Yung-Fa Lu, Ming-Hsi Sun, Kai-Lin Yang, Chia-Yu Lin, Hsiu-Mei Wu, Shu-Ting Chen, Wan-Yuo Guo, Hung-Chieh Chen, Weir-Chiang You, Yu-Te Wu
text:
Study Design
This retrospective controlled study evaluated physician workflows with and without
AI assistance in two linked clinical tasks: diagnostic MRI reporting and treatment-planning
tumor delineation. The evaluation consisted of two stages: first, the establishment of a
consensus reference standard from 30 retrospective MRI cases by an independent three-
physician panel external to the study reader group; second, task-specific reader evaluations
using the same cases. The reference-standard physicians did not participate in the subse-
quent diagnostic reporting or treatment-planning delineation reader-evaluation sessions.
In both tasks, the AI-assisted session was performed first, followed by a 3-week washout
period and then the physician-only session. Although the same 30 cases were used across
sessions, case identifiers were de-identified and case presentation order was randomized
separately for each physician and each session to reduce case recognition, sequence effects,
and recall bias. The workflow condition order was fixed, with AI-assisted sessions per-
formed before physician-only sessions. This sequence was selected under the assumption
that any residual case familiarity after the washout would be more likely to benefit the
