where Ri is the relative workflow–time reduction for case i, TPO,i is the time required under
the physician-only condition, and TAI,i is the time required under the AI-assisted condition.
Because reliable prior estimates of the standard deviation of paired relative workflow–
time reduction were not available for this specific clinical setting, the sample size rationale
was based on a standardized paired-effect framework and estimation precision rather than
on a fixed absolute time-reduction threshold. With 30 paired cases, the study provides
approximately 80% power to detect a medium standardized paired effect size (dz = 0.53)
using a two-sided paired-comparison framework at alpha = 0.05 [17]. In this context, dz
represents the mean paired workflow–time difference divided by the standard deviation
of the paired differences; it is a standardized measure of paired workflow change rather
than a percentage time reduction. In addition, 30 paired cases allow the mean paired
relative workflow–time reduction to be estimated with a 95% confidence interval half-
width of approximately 0.37 standard deviations, providing a precision-based rationale for
estimating the workflow–time effect and its variability. The same sample size also allowed
balanced representation of the three target tumor categories. Therefore, 30 retrospective
paired cases were included, with 10 cases each of vestibular schwannoma, meningioma,
and brain metastasis. Lesion-level sensitivity, precision, report consistency, Dice coefficient,
and volumetric agreement were treated as secondary descriptive performance measures
and were not used as the basis for sample size determination.

Study Population and Image Acquisition
This retrospective study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB; proto-
col code SE24344C; approval date: 23 July 2024), and informed consent was waived because
only de-identified retrospective imaging data were analyzed. Cases were retrospectively
selected to provide 10 cases in each target tumor category and required diagnostic-quality
contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and T2-weighted imaging; the cohort was not intended to
represent a consecutive or population-based sample. This study included MRI data from
a total of 30 clinical cases, comprising 10 vestibular schwannomas, 10 meningiomas, and
10 brain metastases. The patient cohort consisted of 21 females and 9 males, with a mean
age of 60.2 ± 13.1 years (range: 32–84 years).
All imaging data were acquired using either 1.5 Tesla (1.5 T; n = 18, 60.0%) or 3.0 Tesla
(3.0 T; n = 12, 40.0%) MRI systems to reflect real-world clinical heterogeneity. Examinations
were performed on multi-vendor platforms, including GE Healthcare scanners (Signa HDxt
and Optima MR450w; n = 19), Siemens Healthineers scanners (MAGNETOM Verio and
Lumina; n = 6), and Philips Healthcare scanners (Ingenia Elition X; n = 5).
The standard imaging protocol for all cases included multi-contrast sequences, specif-
ically incorporating both contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging (CE-T1WI) and T2-
weighted imaging (T2WI). Detailed acquisition parameters varied according to institutional
protocols and scanner models. Slice thickness ranged from 0.9 mm to 3.0 mm, with 3.0 mm
being the most prevalent value (66.7%).

the study interface also displayed structured lesion-level information derived from the

were conducted using the same reader interface in 3D Slicer (version 5.8.0). This controlled

generated outputs, and physician-generated outputs, and to record task-timing procedures
across reference-standard generation, AI-assisted sessions, and physician-only sessions.

text:
Diagnostic Reporting Outcomes
The diagnostic reporting evaluation included reporting efficiency, lesion-level diagnos-
tic performance, and report consistency. Reporting efficiency was assessed using the total
report generation time across the 30 cases for each reader. Diagnostic performance was
assessed using lesion-level sensitivity and precision against the reference standard. Report
consistency was assessed using Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation-Longest
Common Subsequence (ROUGE-L), BERTScore, and Sentence-BERT (SBERT) cosine simi-
larity to quantify structural and semantic similarity between reports generated by different
readers. ROUGE-L was used as a lexical and structural overlap metric based on the longest
common subsequence between reports [18]. BERTScore F1 was used to quantify token-
level semantic similarity using contextual BERT embeddings [19]. SBERT cosine similarity
was used to compare sentence-level embeddings as a global semantic similarity measure
between reports [20].

Treatment-Planning Outcomes
The treatment-planning evaluation included contouring efficiency, volumetric agree-
ment, lesion-level contouring performance, and segmentation overlap. Contouring effi-
ciency was assessed using per-lesion delineation or contour-editing time across the 30 cases
for each reader, with lesion-level times summed within each case for paired case-level
workflow–time comparisons. Volumetric agreement was assessed by comparing tumor
volumes among AI contours, manual physician contours, and AI-assisted physician con-
tours. Lesion-level contouring performance was assessed using sensitivity and precision,
and segmentation overlap was evaluated using the Dice coefficient.

For workflow–time analyses, case-level paired observations were used. Report gener-
ation time was analyzed at the case level. For tumor delineation, the raw time unit was
the individual lesion; when a case contained more than one lesion, all lesion-level edit
times within that case were summed to obtain case-level contouring time before paired
comparison. Paired workflow–time comparisons between AI-assisted and physician-only
conditions were performed using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Case-level relative
workflow–time reductions were calculated for each paired case and summarized using
median and IQR.
Cross-reader report-similarity metrics (ROUGE-L, BERTScore F1, and SBERT cosine
similarity) were compared between physician-only and AI-assisted reports using paired
two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across cases. Lesion-level sensitivity, precision,
and Dice coefficient were summarized descriptively without formal hypothesis testing or
confidence-interval-based inference. These metrics were considered secondary descriptive
performance measures. Tumor volume differences across standalone AI contours, manual
physician contours, and AI-assisted physician contours were assessed using the Kruskal–
Wallis test.
Linear least-squares regression analysis was performed to examine the relationship
between tumor volume and manual contouring or editing time, and regression results were
reported using fitted equations and coefficients of determination (R2). A p-value < 0.05 was
considered statistically significant. No formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was
applied; therefore, p-values for non-primary analyses should be interpreted cautiously.
All statistical analyses were performed using Python (version 3.12.12). Data handling
and numerical calculations were performed using pandas (version 2.3.3) and NumPy
(version 2.3.5). Statistical testing and regression analyses were performed using SciPy
(version 1.16.3) and statsmodels (version 0.14.6). Report-similarity metrics were calculated
using rouge-score (version 0.1.2) for ROUGE-L, bert-score (version 0.3.13) for BERTScore,
and sentence-transformers (version 5.1.2) with scikit-learn (version 1.7.2) for Sentence-BERT
cosine similarity. Figures were generated using Matplotlib (version 3.10.8) and seaborn
(version 0.13.2).

text:
Relationship Between Tumor Size and Contouring Time
Manual contouring time increased with tumor volume, indicating greater physi-
cian burden in larger lesions. On lesion-level regression analysis, manual edit time in-
creased with tumor volume for both contouring readers: Reader 1 showed a fitted rela-
tionship of y = 15.00 x + 31.88 s (R2 = 0.82), and Reader 2 showed a fitted relationship of
y = 26.28 x + 156.95 s (R2 = 0.57), where x represents tumor volume in cubic centimeters.
In contrast, AI inference time showed minimal dependence on tumor volume, with fitted
relationships of y = 0.02 x + 4.42 s (R2 = 0.03) for Reader 1 cases and y = 0.02 x + 4.43 s
(R2 = 0.04) for Reader 2 cases. These findings suggest that AI support may mitigate the
volume-dependent workload associated with manual delineation, particularly for larger or
more complex lesions. The volume–time relationship is shown in Figure 5d.

Discussion
In this study, we evaluated the workflow effects of AI assistance across two connected
tasks in brain tumor care: MRI reporting and tumor delineation for treatment planning.
AI assistance was associated with shorter task-completion times in both settings, higher
report-similarity metrics, and numerically higher contour-overlap measures. These find-
ings suggest that the value of AI in this setting should be assessed not only by standalone
algorithmic performance but also by its ability to support physician-supervised, standard-
ized clinical workflows. This interpretation is consistent with prior work emphasizing
structured reporting in neuro-oncology, LLM-supported radiology reporting, and AI-based
segmentation as tools for workflow standardization rather than replacements for physician
judgment [3–7,12].
The clinical contribution of AI differed between the diagnostic and treatment-planning
settings. In the diagnostic workflow, the main observed benefit was shorter reporting time
and higher inter-reader report-similarity metrics rather than increased sensitivity. This

and emphasis. By providing structured lesion-level information and preliminary anno-
tations, the AI-assisted workflow appeared to reduce inter-reader variation and promote
more standardized reporting. However, higher similarity does not necessarily indicate
better clinical report quality and may partly reflect anchoring to AI-derived structured
information. This finding is aligned with the rationale of BT-RADS and structured report-
ing frameworks, which aim to improve clarity, completeness, and actionability of brain
tumor reports [3,4]. Broader structured-reporting evidence similarly suggests that reporting
support may add value by improving completeness, consistency, and usability rather than
by replacing expert interpretation [21,22].
In the treatment-planning task, AI assistance reduced contouring burden while pro-
ducing numerically higher overlap metrics relative to the reference standard. Manual
delineation is labor-intensive and depends on lesion complexity, imaging quality, and
physician experience; interobserver variability in brain tumor gross tumor volume delin-
eation has been documented even when MRI information is available [11]. In this study,
AI-generated preliminary contours shifted physician work from full manual segmenta-
tion toward review-and-edit behavior, which likely explains the observed reduction in
annotation time. For Reader 1, the median AI-assisted edit time was 0.00 min, indicating
that in many cases the physician accepted the AI-generated contour after review without
additional manual modification; these zero-time observations therefore reflect contour
confirmation rather than missing measurements. These findings are consistent with recent
deep learning applications in MRI-guided radiotherapy and brain tumor segmentation,
where AI supports segmentation while preserving physician oversight [12–16,23–27]. Clin-
ical implementation studies of auto-segmentation also emphasize that physician review,
local validation, editing burden, and clinical acceptability should be evaluated alongside ge-
ometric metrics such as the Dice coefficient [28–30]. Nevertheless, geometric metrics do not
fully establish clinical acceptability, and AI contours require physician review, particularly
near critical neurovascular structures.

These workflow effects may also be relevant to radiology turnaround time, although
turnaround time is influenced by more than the time needed to compose a report. In
routine practice, overall turnaround time can be affected by case arrival and worklist
position, prioritization or triage, the interval before a physician opens the examination,
image interpretation, report generation, finalization, notification of actionable findings, and
clinician review of the report [32,33]. In this context, AI assistance could affect different
components of the pathway: automated triage or notification could help identify brain tu-
mor cases requiring earlier physician attention, whereas AI-derived structured lesion-level
information may support report preparation once the case is opened. These possibilities
should be examined in future studies that integrate AI-assisted reporting with worklist
prioritization and notification systems.
Taken together, prior evidence indicates that AI assistance in radiology and radio-
therapy is most informative when evaluated as part of a physician-supervised workflow
rather than as an isolated algorithmic output. Current guidance for clinical AI evaluation
emphasizes human–AI interaction, the intended setting of use, workflow integration, error
analysis, external validation, and outcome-oriented assessment [34–40]. The present work
extends this perspective by measuring reporting time, report consistency, contouring time,
lesion-level detection performance, volumetric agreement, and Dice overlap in the same
paired evaluation framework. Prior reader-assistance, reporting, and auto-contouring
studies have reported reductions in reading, reporting, segmentation, or contouring work-
load, but the magnitude of benefit varies across task definitions, measurement methods,
and clinical settings [41–43]. By evaluating two connected clinical nodes, this study high-
lights the potential role of AI assistance in linking diagnostic report preparation with
treatment-planning tumor delineation.

ited to vestibular schwannoma, meningioma, and brain metastasis; therefore, the findings
should not be generalized to gliomas or other tumor types without further validation.
The sample size was planned for a paired workflow–time evaluation with power and
precision considerations, and the cohort was balanced across the three target tumor cate-

diagnostic accuracy, segmentation performance, or downstream clinical outcomes. Second,
the workflow order was fixed, with AI-assisted sessions performed before physician-only
sessions; recall, learning, fatigue, and workflow-adaptation effects cannot be excluded.
Third, only two readers performed each task, so reader-level results may reflect individual
practice patterns. The inclusion of one more experienced and one less experienced reader
in each task provides preliminary observations across experience levels, but the study
was not powered to formally test reader–experience interactions. Fourth, reporting and
contouring times were controlled task-completion times rather than full clinical turnaround
or treatment-planning workflow times. The diagnostic reporting experiment measured
report preparation for a single MRI examination under a controlled study setting. In routine
clinical practice, physicians often review prior imaging examinations, compare interval
changes, consult clinical history, and incorporate information from the medical record be-
fore finalizing a brain tumor MRI report. Therefore, the absolute reporting times observed
here should not be interpreted as the full clinical reporting time required in routine practice.

text:
Conclusions
This retrospective paired workflow evaluation suggests that AI-assisted workflows
are associated with shorter task-completion times, higher report-similarity metrics, and
numerically higher contour-overlap measures in brain tumor MRI reporting and treatment-
planning delineation. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary workflow
evidence from a small fixed-sequence retrospective cohort rather than as validation of
standalone AI diagnostic or segmentation performance.
Future prospective multicenter studies with randomized or counterbalanced workflow
order, broader representation of tumor types including gliomas, independent external vali-
dation, and clinically relevant endpoints such as turnaround time and treatment-planning
impact will help determine the extent to which these observed workflow efficiency gains
translate into broader clinical benefit.

authors: Md Rakhibul Hasan, Shrawman Majumder Rudra, Nayon Karmoker, Mohammad Abu Yousuf, Jesmin Akhter, Asmaa Soliman Al-Moisheer, Salem A. Alyami, Mohammad Ali Moni
venue: Expert Systems with Applications, Volume 315, Article 131513
text:
Abstract
Timely and accurate identification of brain tumors is crucial for optimizing patient outcomes, guiding surgi-
cal planning, and determining appropriate treatment strategies. Despite the advancements in MRI-based tumor
detection and artificial intelligence, developing reliable and clinically applicable models remains challenging,
particularly in contexts where robustness, interpretability, and consistency are critical. Existing approaches often
lack advanced 3D imaging capabilities and robust Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, which limit their diagnostic
utility and clinical adoption. To address these limitations, this study proposes a robust deep learning architecture
that incorporates the improved EfficientNet B7, Xception, and ResNet152 architectures. We further proposed a
novel classification model incorporating enhanced data augmentation and histogram equalization to automati-
cally classify brain MRI images into four diagnostic categories. Three distinct datasets, one segmented dataset,
and a merged dataset combining all sources were used to train and evaluate the models. The proposed models
achieved accuracies in the range of 97-99%, demonstrating consistent and strong performance across datasets.
To enhance diagnostic transparency, XAI techniques, including Grad-CAM and LIME, were employed to provide
visual insights into the system’s decision-making processes. Additionally, this study incorporated a novel 3D
reconstruction approach across the sagittal, coronal, and axial planes, providing a comprehensive view that sup-
ports improved diagnostic accuracy and precise clinical interpretation. Overall, this study demonstrates a novel
unified framework integrating classification, segmentation, XAI, current gaps in brain tumor diagnostics and
holding significant potential to enhance clinical reliability, transparency, and precision, ultimately improvinge
clinical reliability, interpretability, and precision, ultimately supporting better patient outcomes.

are known for their complex presentation and severe implications for pa-

gliomas, meningiomas, or pituitary adenomas, each of which presents
unique challenges in terms of diagnosis and treatment. Gliomas, orig-
inating from glial cells, are particularly aggressive and frequently as-
sociated with poor prognoses. Meningiomas, although usually benign,
can cause significant complications because of their location and poten-

Literature Review
Although brain tumor classification has seen notable advancements,
several challenges persist, including limited dataset size, overfitting,
and poor generalization across diverse clinical data. Several models
aimed to improve efficiency and accuracy, but encountered trade-offs.
Aggarwal et al. (2023) introduced a lightweight model that reduced
computational costs but sacrificed accuracy. Shah et al. (2022) fine-
tuned EfficientNet-B0 on 3060 MRI images and achieved high accuracy,
yet it struggled to generalize to new datasets. Ghassemi et al. (2019)
utilized GANs to enhance training and optimized fully connected layers,
but the approach remained sensitive to small sample sizes. Mehnatkesh
et al. (2023)introduced an evolutionary deep residual learning frame-
work for MRI-based brain tumor classification in which an improved
ant colony optimization algorithm enhanced with differential evolution
and multi-population strategies automatically designs an optimization-
driven ResNet architecture. Although the research did not specifically
address flaws or limitations in external validation, the system demon-
strated strong performance in automated architecture search and tumor
classification, achieving an accuracy of 98.69%. Kurdi et al. (2023) ap-
plied HHOCNN, focusing on edge loss minimization, though overfitting
limited its broader applicability. Tandel et al. (2020) implemented a
five-class classification system, yet the small dataset constrained perfor-
mance beyond controlled experimental settings. These limitations high-
light the need for architectures that not only extract robust and general-
ized features from MRI images but also stabilize deeper representations
and improve tumor subtype discrimination, which is directly addressed
in our proposed approach.

multiscale feature extraction, while Sultan et al. (2019a) used CNNs

Dataset and methodology
Classification and segmentation techniques were applied to the five
datasets. For classification, three separate datasets and one combined
dataset were considered. A merged dataset was created by combining
these three datasets. The proposed models were validated using differ-
ent datasets, including segmented data with a mask. The input images
were gathered from the dataset and then forwarded to the preprocess-
ing stage. In the preprocessing step, data augmentation was applied to
increase the dataset’s variability and improve the model’s generaliza-
tion. Preprocessing methods such as rotation, cropping, flipping, scaling,
zooming, and resizing are employed during data augmentation. CLAHE
was applied to enhance image contrast and improve the visibility of tu-
mor locations. The proposed model and pre-trained architectures were
used independently on the classification datasets, and each model cate-
gorized the MRI images into four groups. In Fig. 1, the complete working
model for classifying tumors is displayed. Fig. 1 shows that the MRI im-
ages were augmented, and then they were sent out for preprocessing
purposes. Subsequently, the MRI scans were sent to the proposed and
pre-trained models separately to classify the images as glioma, menin-
gioma, pituitary, or no tumor. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, includ-
ing Grad-CAM and LIME, were incorporated to ensure interpretability
of the models. Grad-CAM provides visual explanations by highlight-
ing important regions in the input images, whereas LIME offers local
approximations of model predictions. Additionally, generating 3D im-
ages in the sagittal, coronal, and axial planes provides a comprehensive
view of the tumor location and structure. The pre-trained and proposed
model’s classification and segmentation performance was compared us-
ing a range of measures.

Classification datasets
To assess the robustness and generalizability of the proposed models,
five datasets were employed: three publicly available individual datasets
(Bhuvaji et al., 2020; Nickparvar, 2021; Pradeep2665, 2022),a merged
dataset, and a segmentation dataset(Akter et al., 2023). The individ-
ual datasets (Dataset 1, Dataset 2, and Dataset 3) collectively contained
20,286 MRI images across four tumor classes: glioma, meningioma, pi-
tuitary, and no tumors. Dataset 1 comprises 10,000 balanced images
(Pradeep2665, 2022), Dataset 2 includes 3264 images with training
and testing subsets (Bhuvaji et al., 2020), and Dataset 3 contains 7022
images divided into training and testing partitions (Nickparvar, 2021).
These datasets were further combined to construct the Merged Dataset,
yielding 20,286 images distributed as 5047 glioma, 5082 meningioma,
5158 pituitary, and 5000 non-tumor cases. Integration requires prepro-
cessing steps, such as normalization and histogram equalization, to re-
duce variability across acquisition protocols. Nevertheless, challenges
related to scanner heterogeneity, privacy, and workflow integration re-
main important considerations for future deployment. Additionally, a
Segmentation Dataset (Akter et al., 2023) of 4237 MRI images with
corresponding masks (649 glioma, 999 meningioma, 994 pituitary, and
1595 non-tumor) was utilized to support tumor detection and delin-
eation. While balanced datasets (Dataset 1 and the Merged Dataset) pro-
vided controlled conditions for model evaluation, imbalanced datasets
(Dataset 2 and the Segmentation Dataset) reflected real-world clinical
variability. This combination ensures a comprehensive assessment un-
der both ideal and practical diagnostic scenarios. A summary of the
dataset composition is shown in Fig. 2.

Image resizing
Standardizing image dimensions is essential for consistency across
datasets and computational efficiency in model training. In this prepro-
cessing phase, all MRI images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels, ensur-
ing uniform input dimensions while retaining the essential features of
the brain tumor regions. This resized format preserves the anatomical
details necessary for effective tumor detection while maintaining man-
ageable memory and processing requirements. Uniform resizing further
reduces the variability in the input shape, streamlines the training pro-
cess, and aids the model by focusing on the relevant tumor features
across various cases.

Contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization
Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) is ap-
plied as a preprocessing technique to enhance image quality and im-
prove the visibility of tumor regions in MRI scans. CLAHE works by
equalizing the histogram in localized sections of an image, rather than
globally, effectively enhancing contrast without amplifying noise in ho-
mogeneous areas. By limiting contrast amplification to small regions,
CLAHE highlights subtle features in MRI images that are essential for
accurate tumor detection, particularly in low-contrast areas. This en-
hancement step contributes to more robust model training and improved
segmentation accuracy.

3.3.4.3. Training Strategy.
The models were trained for a maximum of 30 epochs with a batch size
of 16. Early stopping was employed with a patience of three epochs,
monitoring the validation loss to prevent overfitting, and ensuring that
training stopped once convergence was achieved. To further enhance
the convergence stability, a ReduceLROnPlateau learning rate sched-
uler was used, which dynamically reduced the learning rate when the
validation loss plateaued. Additional regularization techniques, includ-
ing dropout layers, data augmentation, and histogram equalization,
were applied to improve model generalization. The performance of the
models was evaluated across five datasets, including three individual
datasets, one merged dataset, and one segmentation dataset, to ensure
that the high accuracies achieved (ranging from 97% to > 99%) re-
flected true generalization rather than overfitting.
3.3.4.4. Model Summary.
In summary, the proposed model leverages the strengths of EfficientNet-
B7 for efficient feature extraction, Residual and Xception Blocks for
deeper and refined learning, and SE Blocks for adaptive attention. By
combining these components with regularization techniques, the archi-
tecture achieves robust performance while maintaining computational
efficiency, and its modular design allows scalability to other medical
imaging tasks.

Implementing XAI techniques
Explainable AI (XAI) is essential because it provides transparency in
the decision-making processes of AI models, allowing clinicians to un-
derstand and trust a model’s predictions. This transparency enhances di-
agnostic reliability and ensures that AI-driven decisions are confidently
integrated into clinical practice.

text:
Grad-CAM
A powerful method for deciphering and visualizing the decisions
made by deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural net-
works (CNNs), is gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-
CAM). It produces a heat map that shows the areas of the input image
most influencing the model prediction, utilizing the gradient informa-
tion fed into the last convolutional layer of the CNN. Grad-CAM can offer
essential insights into the regions of MRI images that the model uses to
make classification decisions in Context for brain tumor detection. By
visualizing these regions, medical professionals can better understand
the factors that influence the model’s forecasts, facilitating the identifi-
cation and analysis of brain tumor characteristics.

LIME
The local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) method
provides an interpretable local surrogate model approximation for
machine-learning model predictions. By altering the input data and
tracking the ensuing modifications in the projections, locally accurate
explanations were generated, enabling users to understand how the
model responds to specific situations. LIME can shed light on MRI char-
acteristics that matter most when identifying the existence or absence
of a tumor in the context of brain tumor identification. By generating
explanations at the local level, LIME enhances physicians’ ability to as-
sess the model’s reliability and understand specific predictions, thereby
increasing their trust and confidence in the diagnostic procedure.
3.5. 3D Reconstruction of brain tumor images
Three-dimensional (3D) imaging is a vital component of medical
imaging, providing comprehensive visualization of anatomical struc-
tures. In the context of brain tumor detection, 3D reconstruction en-
ables clinicians to examine tumors from multiple perspectives, including
sagittal, coronal, and axial planes, providing unique insights critical for
accurate diagnosis and effective treatment planning. It facilitates pre-
cise quantification of tumor volume, accurate localization for surgical
planning, and assessment of potential risks to adjacent brain structures,
thereby supporting safer and more individualized interventions.
Complex imaging modalities, computer algorithms, and specialist vi-
sualization tools are used in the precisely planned, multistep 3D brain
tumor reconstruction process from MRI data. Owing to this approach,
clinicians may assess changes before and after therapy, monitor tumor
progression over time, and efficiently share findings with multidisci-
plinary teams. This method enhances clinical decision-making and pa-
tient management by integrating 3D reconstruction into the diagnostic
workflow, thereby improving spatial comprehension of tumor anatomy.

Results And Discussion
The experiments were structured into several sections encompass-
ing comparative analysis and individual outcomes. The performance of
each deep learning model was independently assessed, and evaluations
were conducted for each epoch. Five datasets were utilized for training
and testing, including three individual classification datasets: Dataset
1 (Pradeep2665, 2022), Dataset 2 (Bhuvaji et al., 2020), and Dataset
3 (Nickparvar, 2021), one merged classification dataset, and a sepa-
rate segmentation dataset (Akter et al., 2023). Three transfer learning
models and the proposed model were trained and tested across all clas-
sification datasets. The experiments evaluated the impact of different
datasets, the utility of the segmentation dataset, and comparisons with
state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, separate results are presented
for explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including LIME and LIME, and for
the 3D reconstruction process, thereby offering comprehensive insights
into the robustness and interpretability of the proposed methodology. It
is crucial to acknowledge the practical considerations related to the sug-

Comparison with pre-trained classification models
The performance of the proposed classification model was compared
with that of three pre-trained models, EfficientNetB7, ResNet152, and
Xception, on the merged dataset. The results demonstrate that the pro-
posed model outperformed all pre-trained models across key evalua-
tion metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. For
the merged dataset, the proposed model achieved a testing accuracy of
97.4, a precision of 98.4, a recall of 97.2, and an F1 score of 97.5, sur-
passing the respective scores of EfficientNetB7 (95.3, 96.1, 96.2, 96.5),
ResNet152 (93.2, 93.6, 93.3, 93.3), and Xception (95.5, 95.2, 95.5,
95.3). The improvement in accuracy highlights the model’s superior gen-
eralization capabilities, whereas higher precision and recall indicate its
ability to handle class imbalances and minimize false positives and neg-
atives. Table 3 clearly illustrates the consistent performance advantages
of the proposed model over the pretrained models, particularly in han-
dling diverse features within the merged dataset.
A similar trend was observed when the models were compared with
the segmentation dataset. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of
99.88, precision of 97, recall of 97, and F1 score of 97, outperforming
EfficientNetB7 (98.2,98.2,98.3,98.4), ResNet152 (98.3,98.3,98.2,98.4),
and Xception (98.4,98.4,98.2,98.5). The segmentation dataset, enriched
with pixel-level annotations, allowed the proposed model to achieve ex-
ceptionally high precision and recall, reducing both misclassifications
and missed tumor regions. The confusion matrices for the segmentation
dataset further underscore the minimal errors made by the proposed
model compared with the pretrained ones. As shown in Table 4, the
proposed model’s ability to leverage segmentation details enables it to
achieve state-of-the-art performance, emphasizing its robustness and ef-
fectiveness over existing pre-trained models.
Similarly, for the individual datasets (Datasets 1, 2, and 3), it was
evident that the proposed classification model performed better than
the pre-trained model. Tables 5-7 present the comparisons.

LIME
LIME is a model-agnostic technique that explains predictions by per-
turbing the input data and observing the resulting changes in the model
output. It generates interpretable visualizations by segmenting the im-
age into superpixels and identifying the regions that contribute the most
to the prediction. In this study, LIME was applied to a set of MRI scans
representing gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors. The LIME-
generated visualizations shown in Fig. 16 illustrate the superpixel re-
gions that played a crucial role in the classification. By highlighting
these regions, LIME complements Grad-CAM analysis by offering an al-
ternative perspective on the model’s interpretability.
4.9. 3D reconstruction
Three-dimensional (3D) visualization provides a comprehensive per-
spective of brain tumor structures and their spatial relationships within
the brain. 3D reconstructions across the sagittal, coronal, and axial
planes provide volumetric insights that can support surgical planning,
radiological assessment, and personalized treatment strategies, enabling
better integration into clinical workflows. This section details two ap-
proaches to 3D visualization: constructing entire tumor regions us-
ing segmentation masks and visualizing MRI scans across different
planes.
4.9.1. Reconstruction of 3D tumor regions
In this approach, the marching cubes algorithm was used to con-
struct three distinct 3D tumor regions based on segmentation masks
from the MRI scans of three different patients. This method is crucial
because it provides a detailed 3D representation of the tumor, allow-

Multi-Plane visualization across MRI modalities
MRI scans of the same patient were visualized using four different
modalities: T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR, to gain a comprehensive under-
standing of the tumor characteristics. These modalities offer varied con-
trasts, highlighting the diverse anatomical and pathological features of
tumors. The tumor was visualized in the coronal, sagittal, and axial
planes, offering a multidimensional perspective that facilitated in-depth
analysis. For instance, the coronal plane provides a frontal view, the
sagittal plane offers a side view, and the axial plane presents a top-down
view of the tumor structure. This approach enables detailed comparisons
of tumor appearance across modalities, which is crucial for identifying
its boundaries, internal composition, and potential infiltration into sur-
rounding tissues. Such visualizations are pivotal for enhancing diagnos-

Conclusion
This study presents a comprehensive framework for the automated
classification and analysis of brain tumors, addressing the critical limi-
tations of existing methodologies. The proposed approach significantly
improved the accuracy and reliability by introducing a novel classifi-
cation architecture alongside robust CNN models, including Efficient-
NetB7, ResNet-152, and Xception. The integration of advanced 3D imag-
ing techniques provides detailed spatial insights that can support diag-
nostic precision, treatment planning, and educational use when embed-
ded into appropriate clinical viewers. Furthermore, the inclusion of Ex-
plainable AI techniques such as Grad-CAM and LIME enhances the trans-
parency and interpretability of model predictions, fostering greater clin-
ical trust. The framework demonstrated robust generalizability and di-
agnostic effectiveness across five distinct datasets - three individual, one
merged, and one segmented - illustrating its versatility in diverse scenar-
ios. Overall, the proposed framework advances AI-driven brain tumor
classification by combining high accuracy, interpretability, and 3D vi-
sualization, thereby offering significant potential for real-world clinical
applications. A few practical considerations remain, such as optimizing
the computational load of the hybrid architecture and 3D reconstruc-
tion workflow, ensuring robustness across varying MRI quality, and con-
ducting prospective, multi-center evaluations to support broader clini-
cal integration. At the same time, its current form should be viewed as a
validated prototype that requires further clinical evaluation, workflow
integration, and safety assessment before adoption in real-world prac-
tice. Future work will focus on streamlining the pipeline for smoother
deployment, incorporating more diverse imaging data, and performing
workflow-based studies to further demonstrate the system’s value in sup-
porting radiologist decision-making.

title: Toward interpretable multiclass semantic intelligence: explainable brain tumor segmentation and automated grade stratification
authors: S. Berlin Shaheema, Suganya Devi, J. Jasper, R. Murugan, and co-authors
venue: Egyptian Journal of Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, Volume 57, Article 201
text:
Abstract
Purpose Accurate brain tumor grade classification from magnetic resonance imaging is essential for diagnosis, treat-
ment planning, and prognosis assessment. Although deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance,
many lack clinical validation, robustness across datasets, and interpretability for decision support. This study proposes
an explainable hybrid deep learning framework that integrates tumor segmentation, feature optimization, grade clas-
sification, and model attribution for high-grade and low-grade gliomas, with evaluation across multiple MRI datasets
under controlled experimental conditions.
Methods The proposed framework, Towards Interpretable Multiclass Semantic Intelligence: Explainable Brain Tumor
Segmentation and Automated Grade Stratifi cation, integrates brain tumor segmentation, optimized feature selection,
and discriminative classifi cation to support automated tumor analysis and grade stratifi cation. Tumor regions are segmented
using a Path Aggregation Network (PANet) integrated with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) and ResNet-50
to preserve relevant structural characteristics. From the segmented tumor regions, shape, texture, and Histogram of Oriented
Gradients (HOG) features are extracted to characterize morphological and visual patterns. A modified Reptile Search Algo-
rithm (RSA) is then employed to select discriminative features, aiming to reduce feature redundancy and mitigate over fitting.
The selected features are subsequently classified using DenseNet-201 within a Siamese architecture to enhance robustness
to inter-patient variability. Model interpretability is incorporated through Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-
CAM), which provides visual explanations of the regions contributing to model predictions. The framework is evaluated using
the BraTS 2019, BraTS 2020, and BraTS 2021 datasets, together with additional MRI datasets.

Introduction
Brain tumors are among the most life-threatening dis-
eases and represent a significant cause of cancer-related
mortality worldwide [1]. According to the American
Cancer Society, approximately 25,400 new cases of
malignant brain and spinal cord tumors were diagnosed
in the USA in 2023, with nearly 18,760 associated deaths
reported during the same year [2]. Accurate identifi-
cation and classification of brain tumors are therefore
essential for effective treatment planning, prognosis esti-
mation, and improvement of patient survival outcomes in
clinical practice [3–5]. Advances in computer vision and
machine learning have significantly transformed medical
image analysis, enabling the early detection of diseases
and improving diagnostic accuracy.
Brain tumor classification (BTC) aims to categorize
tumors based on grade and severity. According to the
World Health Organization (WHO) grading system, glio-
mas are classified into Grades I–IV, where Grades I and
II correspond to low-grade gliomas (LGGs), and Grades
III and IV correspond to high-grade gliomas (HGGs)
[6]. Accurate differentiation between LGG and HGG
is crucial for treatment planning, chemotherapy and
radiotherapy selection, and predicting patient survival
[7]. Although LGG tumors generally grow more slowly,
delayed treatment may lead to malignant progression
into HGG.
Deep learning (DL) has significantly advanced brain
tumor classification (BTC) using magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), consistently outperforming traditional
machine learning approaches by automatically learn-
ing hierarchical and discriminative features from raw
data. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been
extensively employed for BTC, with architectures such
as DenseNet, ResNet, and custom CNN variants achiev-
ing strong performance on benchmark datasets. Recent
explainable CNN-based frameworks further enhance clini-
cal interpretability by highlighting tumor-relevant regions
using techniques such as Grad-CAM and SHAP, thereby
supporting clinical decision-making. However, purely
CNN-based models often exhibit limited generalization
across heterogeneous MRI datasets due to variations in
tumor appearance, size, and acquisition protocols [8].
DL techniques have demonstrated effectiveness across
multiple medical imaging applications, including brain
tumor classification and skin cancer detection [9, 10].

Methodology
The suggested methodology is comprised of five phases,
namely preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction,
feature optimization, and classification. Figure 1 illustrates
the overall architecture of the brain tumor classification
model. Multimodal MRI images are gathered and split into
training, validation, and testing datasets. Next, the images
are preprocessed through augmentation, resizing, and bias
field correction (BFC). Further, the tumor is segmented
by means of the proposed Panoptic Tumor Segmentation
Network that incorporates the use of PA-Net, GCNN, and
ResNet-50. The output obtained from the process is used
to segment the tumor region. Afterward, Radiomic fea-
tures such as shape-based and texture-based features are
extracted from the segmented tumor region. Statistics of
mean, entropy, and kurtosis are later on analyzed to find dis-
criminative tumor properties. The modified reptile search
algorithm (mRSA) is used to remove any redundant infor-
mation from the features obtained. The selected features are
provided to the classifier called DenseNet-201. Lastly, the
DenseNet-201 classifies tumors according to their grades
and, in other words, divides the MRI images into low-grade
glioma (LGG) and high-grade glioma (HGG).

The publicly available multimodal MRI brain tumor data-
sets BraTS 2019 [29–31], BraTS 2020 [32], BraTS 2021
[33, 34], and Brain Tumor MRI Dataset [35] were used to
train and assess the technique. The MRI sequence for the
LGG and HGG is illustrated in Fig. 1. The MRI images
of the LGG and HGG from the BraTS 2019 dataset are

and independent evaluation are summarized in Table 1.
The available evaluation includes public benchmark MRI

These datasets provide useful evidence of performance

Patient‐level cross‐validation strategy
To prevent data leakage and ensure a fair evaluation, all
dataset partitioning procedures were performed strictly
at the patient level. Since each BraTS subject consists of
a complete 3D MRI volume containing multiple 2D slices
across four modalities (T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR), all
slices belonging to a given patient were treated as a single
entity during data splitting.
For the tenfold cross-validation experiments, patients
rather than individual slices were randomly assigned to
one of the tenfold. Consequently, all slices from a par-
ticular patient were included exclusively in either the
training or validation fold during each iteration and
never appeared simultaneously in both sets. This patient-
level stratification ensured that no information from a
patient’s MRI volume was shared across folds.
Furthermore, the class distribution of low-grade glioma
(LGG) and high-grade glioma (HGG) cases was main-
tained across folds to preserve class balance throughout
the cross-validation process. This evaluation protocol
eliminates inter-patient data leakage and provides a real-
istic estimate of the generalization performance of the
proposed framework.
Data partitioning and model validation procedure
In order to carry out a strict assessment and avoid data
leakage, all data partitioning steps were done in the con-
text of patient-level splitting. All slices from one BraTS
subject were included exclusively in one dataset parti-
tion. BraTS 2019 dataset was used to develop our model,
which included training, validation, feature selection, and
hyperparameter tuning. In BraTS 2019 dataset, patients
were split into train (70%), validation (15%), and test
(15%) sets via patient-level stratified sampling in order to
maintain the proportion of low-grade glioma (LGG) and
high-grade glioma (HGG).
In order to check the stability of our model, tenfold
patient-level cross-validation was performed using BraTS
2019 development dataset. In each fold, preprocessing,
feature extraction, mRSA-based feature selection, and
classification model training were done using only the
training part of this fold. Validation set from each fold
was used for performance estimation purposes only. Fol-

the proposed framework was tested on BraTS 2020 and

Performance evaluation
Statistical analysis and uncertainty
The evaluation was performed at the patient level to
avoid treating multiple slices from the same subject as
independent observations. Accuracy, sensitivity, speci-
ficity, precision, F1-score, AUC/ROC, and confusion
matrices were used as primary performance measures.
Where patient-level prediction outputs were available,
uncertainty should be summarized using patient-level
resampling rather than slice-level resampling. Formal
comparisons with selected baseline methods should use
paired patient-level predictions and a predefined sig-
nificance threshold. The manuscript does not introduce
numerical confidence intervals, calibration estimates,
decision-curve results, or ROC-comparison statistics
that are not explicitly supported by the source data sup-

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Abstract
The diagnosis of brain tumors by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is still a difficult task because of the
tumor heterogeneity, low tumor contrast, imaging artifacts and differences between tumor types. Deep learning
methods commonly used today lack explainability, tolerability to corrupted imaging conditions and the ability
to interpret the complex structures of tumors. To overcome these challenges, the study introduces a Promptable
Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explainable Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification with
the recent BRISC 2025 dataset. The proposed framework leverages diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foun­
dation-based feature representation learning, prompt-based attention mechanisms, and explainable dual-task
intelligence to achieve simultaneous tumor segmentation and classification. A diffusion enhancement module
is used to enhance the visibility of the tumor boundaries and to minimize the imaging artifacts before extract­
ing features. Then, a pre-trained foundation encoder extracts strong semantic representations, and the adaptive
localization of the tumor areas is achieved by prompt-guided attention. The framework jointly segments and
classifies with an enhanced interpretation of the result with attention visualization and attention-based explana­
tion maps. Experimental results showed that the classification accuracy of 98.1%, Dice score of 93.2%, and
AUC of 99.0% were achieved, which is more superior than the conventional CNN and the transformer-based
methods. The proposed framework also demonstrated high robustness in the presence of imaging noise and
low MRI contrast conditions, which would be important for the clinical robust and interpretable analysis of
brain tumors.
Keywords Brain tumor analysis · Diffusion enhancement · Foundation models · Prompt-guided learning ·
Explainable medical AI

Introduction
Brain tumors are one of the most severe neurological diseases and can have a high mortality and morbidity in the
world. Early and precise diagnosis of a brain tumor is vital for proper treatment planning, surgery and patient sur­
vival. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one of the most popular imaging techniques employed for assessing

pretation of MRI scans is still time-consuming, subjective and highly reliant on radiological expertise. Tumors
can also be of varying shapes, sizes, textures, intensities, and edge characteristics, adding to the complexity of
accurately analyzing a tumor [2].
Deep learning has recently seen many developments that have greatly enhanced the field of automated brain
tumor diagnosis. CNNs have been shown to have superior performance in effectively learning local spatial infor­
mation for tumor classification and segmentation [3, 4]. Later on, transformer architectures were developed and
integrated into the field of global contextual learning and long-range dependency modelling, thus enhancing
representation learning in medical imaging applications [5]. However, many existing methods have several limi­
tations such as vulnerability to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) noise, poor accuracy of boundary delineation,
lack of explainability, and low cross-ability to tumor patterns [6, 7].
Foundation models and prompt-guided learning have been identified as potential areas for medical AI advance­
ments in recent years [8]. The feature understanding using prompt-based learning can be adaptive and task aware,
and the foundation encoders with large-scale visual data give strong semantic representation. Likewise, the diffu­
sion models have demonstrated excellent results in image enhancement, denoising and artifact rejection, making
them well-adapted for medical imaging applications [9]. However, the combination of diffusion enhancement,
foundation representation learning, prompt-guided attention, and explainable dual tasks intelligence in brain
tumor analysis is relatively under-researched.
To overcome these limitations, the current study aims to develop a Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Founda­
tion Framework for Explainable Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification with the latest BRISC 2025 data­
set. The proposed framework is designed to achieve a better segmentation and classification results by combining
diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foundation-driven feature extraction, and prompt-guided attention learning.
Moreover, an explainability module has been included for generating attention maps that are clinically meaning­

set. The proposed framework is designed to achieve a better segmentation and classification results by combining
diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foundation-driven feature extraction, and prompt-guided attention learning.
Moreover, an explainability module has been included for generating attention maps that are clinically meaning­
ful, and enhance the interpretability of the model. The framework simultaneously segments and classifies tumors
in a single model, to provide powerful and secure brain tumor intelligence.
The architectural novelty of the proposed framework does not arise from introducing diffusion models, foun­
dation encoders, prompt learning, or explainability as independent techniques. Instead, it lies in the task-coupled
interaction among these components. Unlike conventional sequential pipelines in which enhancement, segmenta­
tion, classification, and explanation are performed independently, the proposed framework introduces prompt–
image cross-attention before shared feature formation. The encoder-derived visual features and prompt-refined
representations are adaptively fused into a common tumor-aware representation that simultaneously supports
pixel-level segmentation and image-level classification. Joint optimization allows segmentation supervision
to reinforce spatially meaningful features used for classification, while classification supervision encourages
diagnostically discriminative representations within the shared feature space. Thus, the contribution is a unified
prompt-conditioned dual-task architecture in which enhancement, semantic guidance, localization, and diagnosis
interact during representation learning.
The study investigates whether diffusion-based MRI enhancement, prompt-guided semantic learning, and joint
segmentation–classification can improve tumour-boundary localization, diagnostic reliability, robustness under
degraded imaging conditions, and interpretability. By integrating these functions within a shared learning archi­
tecture, the framework aims to produce accurate and clinically meaningful tumour analysis while maintaining
performance across different MRI datasets.

1. A diffusion-enhanced preprocessing module is introduced to improve MRI quality, suppress imaging artifacts,
and enhance tumor boundary visibility.

authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Review of literature
Recent studies show that deep learning has become central to MRI-based brain tumor analysis, particularly for
tumor detection, classification, and segmentation. Reviews by Bouhafra et al. [10], Dorfner et al. [11], Fahim et
al. [12], and Verma et al. [13] indicate that CNNs, hybrid CNN-transformer models, and attention-based segmen­
tation networks have improved automated tumor assessment, but challenges remain in boundary precision, model
explainability, robustness, and generalization.
CNN-based and hybrid deep learning approaches have achieved strong performance in classifying glioma,
meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor MRI classes. Ahmed et al. [14] proposed a hybrid ViT-GRU frame­
work for MRI brain tumor detection and classification, while Musthafa et al. [15], Disci et al. [16], Lu et al. [17],
Ali et al. [18], Gundogan et al. [19], and Younis et al. [20] further demonstrated the usefulness of pretrained and
hybrid deep models for multiclass brain tumor diagnosis. However, many of these studies mainly focus on clas­
sification accuracy and provide limited integration between segmentation, robustness, prompt-based learning,
and clinical explainability.
Recent advances in medical image segmentation have increasingly focused on improving boundary delinea­
tion, multiscale feature representation, attention-based feature selection, and robustness to subtle intensity varia­
tions. Arshad et al. [21] proposed RaNet, a residual attention network for prostate segmentation in T2-weighted
MRI, which integrates a DilatedContextNet encoder, Multi-Scale Attention Fusion (MSAF), and a Feature Fusion
Module (FFM) to capture hierarchical contextual information and refine spatially relevant features. Evaluations
on the PROMISE12 and ProstateX datasets demonstrated Dice scores of 98.61% and 96.57%, respectively, high­
lighting the benefit of residual learning, multiscale attention, and feature fusion for precise boundary delineation
and robustness to MRI variability.
Similarly, another study introduced PZSNet, a U-shaped hybrid transformer framework designed to address
the challenging problem of similar signal intensities and subtle textures in prostate MRI [22]. The framework
incorporates an Adaptive Boundary Fusion Module (ABFM), Dynamic Feature Injection Module (DFIM), and
Feature Enhancement Module (FEM) to integrate local details with broader contextual information and improve

explainable semantic segmentation and Bayesian learning for brain tumor MRI analysis. These works highlight
the value of combining segmentation and classification, but existing systems still struggle with low-contrast
tumor boundaries, irregular tumor morphology, and uncertain attention localization.
Foundation models have recently changed the direction of medical image analysis. Ma et al. [26] introduced
MedSAM as a universal medical image segmentation foundation model, showing the potential of promptable
segmentation across diverse medical imaging tasks. Huang et al. [27] reviewed the application of SAM in medical
imaging and noted that medical segmentation is more difficult than natural-image segmentation due to complex
boundaries, modality variation, and anatomical ambiguity. Noh et al. [28], Timilsina et al. [29], and Hussain et al.
[30] further emphasized that foundation models offer strong generalization potential, but their trustworthy adap­
tation to medical imaging still requires improvements in robustness, explainability, and task-specific prompting.

authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Proposed methodology
This section puts forward the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explainable
Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification. The proposed framework aims to tackle the major drawbacks
of the previous brain tumor analysis techniques, such as low robustness in MRI noise, inaccurate delineation
of tumor boundaries, low semantic understanding, and low clinical interpretability. This framework combines
diffusion-based MRI enhancement, foundation-driven semantic representation learning, prompt-guided cross-
attention refinement, and explainable dual-task intelligence, all within a single, end-to-end framework.
The proposed methodology starts with a preprocessing and diffusion enhancement of the MRI to enhance the
quality of the images and make the tumor visible. The enhanced MRI images are then fed into a pretrained medi­
cal foundation encoder to obtain powerful multi-scale semantic representations. A semantic attention mechanism
with prompt guidance is integrated into the framework to enhance adaptive localization and clinically relevant
feature learning. The semantic representations extracted are further refined by combining features together and
they are also used for tumor segmentation and multiclass classification. Furthermore, the explainability engine
creates attention visualization and saliency maps for enhancing transparency and clinical trustworthiness.
The proposed framework is tailored to optimise the segmentation accuracy, the classification reliability, the
robustness under degraded MRI conditions and the explainability performance simultaneously. The overall archi­
tecture and major components of the proposed framework are discussed in the following subsections.

Overall framework architecture
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework aims to be a single multi-task framework
that segments and classifies brain tumors in MRI simultaneously. It integrates a diffusion-based enhancement, a
foundation-based semantic representation learning, a prompt-based cross-attention refinement, and explainable
prediction generation into a single end-to-end learning system. As shown in Fig. 1, the architecture is composed
of sequential stages such as MRI preprocessing, diffusion enhancement, foundation encoding, prompt-guided
semantic alignment, shared feature fusion, segmentation decoding, classification prediction, and explainability
generation.
The technical innovation of the proposed framework lies in the way semantic prompting and dual-task super­
vision are incorporated into shared representation learning. Unlike conventional pipelines that apply enhance­
ment, segmentation, classification, and explanation as independent stages, the proposed architecture introduces
prompt–image cross-attention before shared feature formation. The visual representation produced by the

Firstly, the input MRIs are preprocessed by normalizing, resizing, stripping the skull and correcting the intensi­

The preprocessed MRI images then go to the diffusion enhancement module, where latent diffusion learning is

The enhanced MRI images are then processed through a pre-trained medical foundation encoder which is
built based on MedSAM and DINOv2 architectures. Semantic representation learning is used by the foundation
encoder to learn both local tumor properties and global contextual relationships by contrast to the traditional con­
volutional models that mostly learned local spatial representations. The encoder can generate multi-scale feature
representations to keep fine-grained information of the tumor with different spatial resolutions.
A cross-attention mechanism is introduced in the framework to enhance the semantic understanding with
the help of prompts. Using a bio-clinical language encoder and cross-attention learning, clinically meaningful
prompts are encoded by a bio-clinical language encoder and aligned with image representations. This semantic
interaction allows for adaptive localization of clinically relevant tumor regions and better feature discrimination
and task-aware representation learning.

saliency representations, and confidence-aware localization maps, to enhance interpretability and transparency
in the clinical context. The fused semantic representations from the prompt-guided feature refinement process
are fed into the explainability engine. These representations of the semantic representations are used to produce
heatmaps and attention activation maps for regions that are essential to the final prediction that are specific to the

Experimental setup and performance evaluation
In this section, the experimental setup, the description of the dataset, the implementation details and the evaluation
metrics adopted to validate the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explain­
able Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification are summarized. The BRISC 2025 dataset was extensively
used to assess segmentation accuracy, classification performance, robustness to poor MRI quality and explain­
ability quality.

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Dataset description
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework was tested on the recently released expert-
annotated brain tumor segmentation and multiclass classification benchmark dataset named BRISC 2025. Some
of the most prominent shortcomings in earlier brain tumor MRI data sets were inconsistency in the way they
were annotated, lack of tumor diversity, class imbalance, and poor tumor segmentation quality, all of which were
addressed by the development of this data set. The BRISC 2025 database offers high-quality MRI scans along
with pixel-level tumor masks and multiclass diagnostic labels, which is ideal for assessing explainable dual-task
medical AI approaches.
The official BRISC 2025 partition contains 5000 training images and 1000 independent test images. To create
a validation set without accessing the official test data, 20% of the official training partition was selected through
stratified sampling based on tumour class and anatomical plane. Consequently, 4000 images were used for train­
ing, 1000 for validation, and 1000 for final testing. The same partitions were used for the proposed framework
and all comparison methods. The validation set was used for hyperparameter tuning, early stopping, and check­
point selection, whereas the test set was reserved exclusively for final evaluation. Data augmentation was applied
only to the training partition.
The data set contains two major tasks—Classifications and Segmentation. The subset of classification consists
of MRI images that are classified into four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Accurate
lesion localization and structural delineation is provided by the corresponding tumor masks in the segmentation
subset. The dataset contains various types of tumor appearances with significant differences in tumor size, shape,
texture, edema distribution, visibility of the contrast, and irregularity in the boundary. The variations make the
data appropriate for assessing the ability of the model to be robust and generalizable, further establishing the
complexity of automated tumor analysis.
The MRI scans have been acquired and annotated by experts in the medical field to maintain consistency in the
structures and to have reliable ground-truth labelling. The segmentation masks precisely localize tumor regions
and edema structures, which allows for a proper assessment of the segmentation performance. The previous

Implementation details
The proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework was put into practice with Python and
the PyTorch deep learning framework. All experiments were performed in a GPU-enabled environment with the
CUDA acceleration support to enable efficient training of the diffusion enhancement module, the transformer-
based foundation encoder and the prompt-guided semantic attention mechanism. The complete architecture was
trained in an end-to-end manner for simultaneous segmentation and multiclass classification.
First, all of the MRI images were resized to a fixed spatial resolution and normalized to achieve structural
uniformity in MRI acquisitions. After that, the normalized MRI representations were passed to the diffusion
enhancement module prior to the semantic feature extraction. Post diffusion reconstruction of the enhanced MRI
was then passed to the pretrained foundation encoder for hierarchical semantic representation learning.
The proposed framework employed a transformer-based semantic encoding that was able to model local tumor
structures and global contextual relationships. The semantic representations extracted were further improved by
the cross-attention learning strategies using prompts, and then fused into the shared feature fusion module. Both
the fused semantic representations were used concurrently for segmentation and classification.
The framework parameters were optimized using the Adam optimizer because of its adaptive learning capabil­
ity and stable convergence behavior in deep neural networks. The parameter update rule during optimization is

Evaluation metrics
The performance of the proposed framework was assessed based on standard classification and segmentation
metrics to fully cover the assessment of prediction accuracy, segmentation quality, robustness and semantic
consistency.
The accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under curve (AUC) were used for the classification evalua­
tion. Accuracy is the overall correctness of the predictions of tumors, while precision is the reliability of the posi­
tive predictions. Recall refers to how well the framework performs in correctly recognizing the tumor samples,

Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Intersection over Union (IoU) were used to evaluate the segmentation
by calculating the overlap between the predicted tumor masks and ground truth annotations. The Dice and IoU
values increase as the localization and delineation performance of the tumor improve.
Robustness analysis has been performed in addition to quantitative evaluation, under degraded MRI condi­
tions such as Gaussian, motion blur and low-contrast imaging conditions. Explainability performance was quali­
tatively assessed with the help of Grad-CAM visualization, transformer attention maps, saliency overlays, and
confidence-aware localization representations. These evaluation strategies allowed for a comprehensive evalua­
tion of segmentation quality, the reliability of the classification and the robustness of the framework, as well as
its clinical interpretability.

title: Promptable diffusion-enhanced foundation framework for explainable brain tumor segmentation and classification
authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Results And Discussion
The experimental results and detailed analysis of the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation
Framework for Explainable Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification is presented. The framework was
tested on the basis of classification accuracy, segmentation accuracy, explainability, robustness analysis, abla­
tion study, computational efficiency and cross-dataset generalization. The achieved performance of the proposed
technique proves that the combination of diffusion enhancement, pretrained foundation representation learning,
prompt-guided semantic attention, and explainable feature fusion has an extremely positive effect on segmenta­
tion and multiclass classification tasks.

combining the diffusion enhancement, semantic prompt learning and explainable attention refinement.

Segmentation performance analysis
The segmentation results of the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework were assessed
with the metrics of Dice Score, Intersection over Union (IoU), Sensitivity, Specificity and Hausdorff Distance.
The framework was evaluated and benchmarked against several state-of-the-art segmentation methods, such as
U-Net, Attention U-Net, TransUNet, MedSAM and Diffusion-Enhanced U-Net. The comparative segmentation
performance results are shown in Table 2.
The proposed framework outperformed other methods on all metrics under evaluation. The Dice score of
93.2% obtained suggests high level of accuracy in the overlap between the predicted tumor masks and manually
annotated ground-truth regions. Likewise, the IoU score of 89.4% shows better structural agreement and better
ability to localize the lesions. The proposed framework showed a substantial improvement of 6.8% in Dice score
compared to the conventional U-Net architecture, validating the effectiveness of incorporating diffusion enhance­
ment, semantic prompt learning, and explainable attention refinement.
A high sensitivity of 94.1% indicates that the framework is effective at correctly highlighting the areas of tumor
and excluding false negatives. The specificity value of 98.9% suggests that the technique has good false-positive
suppression in healthy brain tissues. The reduced Hausdorff Distance value of 5.21 indicates a better delineation
of the boundary and preservation of the structure, especially in regions with edema in the tumor and irregular
contours.

The framework also shows enhanced uniformity of the segmentation in cases of low contrast and structurally

To strengthen the comparison with contemporary medical-segmentation methods, nnU-Net [41], Swin UNETR

evaluated using the same prompt-generation procedure for all test images. This controlled evaluation allowed the
proposed framework to be compared with self-configuring segmentation, transformer-based medical segmenta­
tion, and promptable medical foundation-model approaches.
Among the recent baseline methods, SAM-Med2D achieved the strongest segmentation performance, with a
Dice score of 92.7% and an IoU of 88.8%, followed by Swin UNETR and nnU-Net. The proposed framework
achieved a Dice score of 93.2%, an IoU of 89.4%, and the lowest Hausdorff distance of 5.21. The improvement
suggests that diffusion-based refinement and prompt-conditioned shared feature learning provide complementary
benefits beyond self-configuring, transformer-based, and promptable segmentation baselines.
The segmentation results obtained from the proposed framework are also shown to be more stable over dif­
ferent types of tumors, such as glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor and small and difficult tumors. The frame­
work’s ability to incorporate explainable semantic attention allows it to reject unwanted background activations

The segmentation results obtained from the proposed framework are also shown to be more stable over dif­

An additional error analysis was conducted to examine the principal failure conditions of the proposed frame­
work. Misclassifications occurred mainly between glioma and meningioma cases with similar intensity patterns
and between low-contrast pituitary tumours and no-tumour images containing high-intensity anatomical struc­
tures. For segmentation analysis, tumours were grouped according to their relative mask area as small (< 1% of
image pixels), medium (1–5%), and large (> 5%). The corresponding mean Dice scores were 88.4%, 93.0%, and
95.2%, respectively, indicating that small lesions were more difficult to delineate. Tumour size showed a moder­
ate positive correlation with Dice score (Spearman’s in l ine-eq-IEq119, in l ine-eq-IEq120). Peripheral tumours located close to the
skull achieved a lower mean Dice score of 90.6%, compared with 94.1% for centrally located tumours, while
low-contrast lesions achieved a mean Dice score of 89.8%. The principal failure modes were therefore small
lesion size, weak tumour-to-background contrast, irregular or infiltrative boundaries, peripheral location, imag­
ing artefacts, and visual similarity between tumour categories. These findings suggest that future improvements
should focus on scale-aware feature learning, boundary-sensitive loss functions, and stronger modelling of low-
contrast lesions.

Statistical significance analysis
To assess the consistency and statistical reliability of the reported improvements, each method was independently
trained and evaluated over ten runs using different random seeds. The same training, validation, and test partitions

Explainability analysis
In medical imaging systems, especially in the field of brain tumor diagnosis, reliability and transparency of the
system are crucial, and interpretability is an indispensable requirement in planning treatment. The explainability
capability of the proposed framework was assessed by using comparative analysis of the proposed visualizations:
Grad-CAM, transformer attention maps, localization consistency and semantic attention interpretability. The
results of the Explainability evaluation are presented in Table 6 below.
The proposed framework had the best tumor localization accuracy of 93.4% and attention consistency value of
91.7%, better than traditional explainability methods which showed interpretability and semantically meaningful
localization. In all cases the attention maps generated were tightly correlated to clinically relevant tumor regions
and attenuated irrelevant background regions.
The increased explainability performance can be explained by the incorporation of prompt-guided semantic
learning and explainable attention fusion. In contrast to the traditional Grad-CAM approaches that often result
in diffuse activation localization and low localization consistency, the proposed framework is able to provide
semantically informative distribution maps of attention regions that are coherent with tumor structures and edema
regions.
Figure 8 shows qualitative explainability comparisons for various tumor types, such as irregular glioma,
edema-rich lesions, low contrast tumors and small difficult lesions. Conventional Grad-CAM visualizations suf­
fer from background activation leakage and incomplete tumor localization, while transformer attention maps
provide relatively more diffuse and less accurate attention regions.
The proposed explainability mechanism, on the other hand, yields more acute and focused attention maps to
diagnose important regions of tumors. The generated attention overlays exhibit better structural consistency, bet­
ter lesion boundaries and better semantic localization capability in all the evaluated tumor conditions.
This framework also exhibits better stability of explainability in difficult MRI environments. The proposed
attention mechanism maintains focused activations around clinically meaningful areas while reducing activations
that fall on non-relevant areas in healthy tissues, even for low-contrast lesions and structurally complex tumor
boundaries.

Discussion
The experimental results show the proposed Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework’s effec­
tiveness on various tasks of brain tumor MRI analysis, including classification, segmentation, robustness, and
explainability. By combining these components, the framework can overcome multiple challenges that traditional
CNN and transformer-based medical imaging models encounter, such as ambiguous object boundaries, noisy or
corrupted input data, and uncertainty regarding what to focus on.
The proposed framework shows superior explainability performance, semantic localization capability and seg­
mentation consistency when compared to the existing literature. It has been recently observed that the traditional
CNN architecture-based segmentation models tend to fail in capturing the irregular boundaries of the tumor, low
contrast lesions and in learning the contextual representation in the heterogeneous MRI environments [1, 44].
Recent explainable AI research also revealed that many deep learning models suffer from fragmented activations
and low interpretability of clinical actions, which hinders the real-world use of these models in medical deci­
sion support systems [45, 46]. Likewise, diffusion models have been recently found to benefit the preservation
of the structures and the refinement of their boundaries in complex medical imaging tasks [35, 36, 47]. These

The applications of this research are of great importance for intelligent clinical decision support system. The
suggested framework can help radiologists to accurately segment tumors, reliably classify tumors into more than
one class, and generate attention visualizations that are clinically interpretable. Additionally, the explainability
mechanism enhances transparency by identifying diagnostically relevant regions of tumors, thereby boosting the
clinical trustworthiness and aiding in treatment planning. The framework’s performance in these MRI conditions
with noise and distortion also suggests it can be adapted to work well in a realistic clinical MRI setting with
