The proposed framework also shows great potential to be adaptable to future medical AI applications like mul­
timodal MRI fusion, semantic-guided diagnosis, and explainable neuro-oncology systems. With prompt-guided
semantic learning, medical imaging workflows can be automated to incorporate clinical instructions and domain-
specific guidance flexibly. Moreover, the efficiency of the computations implemented with the framework sug­
gests potential for deployment in near real-time in hospital settings and intelligent radiology systems.
The external-dataset evaluation provides initial evidence that the learned representations can transfer beyond
BRISC 2025. Nevertheless, real-world performance may be influenced by differences in scanners, MRI acquisi­

authors: Jeena Joseph
text:
Conclusion
This research presented a novel Promptable Diffusion-Enhanced Foundation Framework for Explainable Brain
Tumor Segmentation and Classification using MRI images. The proposed framework is built into the frame­
work of medical imaging, which incorporates diffusion-based MRI enhancement, pretrained semantic foundation
encoding, prompt-guided attention learning, explainable feature fusion, and dual-task optimization. The frame­
work was designed to overcome the major challenges of MRI analysis for brain tumors such as noisy imaging
conditions, low contrast, low visibility of the lesions, irregular boundaries of the tumor, variation of its structure,
and poor interpretability of traditional deep learning.
The experimental results on the BRISC 2025 dataset showed that the proposed framework outperformed
other compared methods in terms of segmentation and classification. Both the framework achieved a classifica­
tion accuracy of 98.1%, Dice score of 93.2%, and AUC value of 99.0%, surpassing the performance of tradi­
tional CNN architectures, Transformer models, and the latest foundation models for segmentation. The diffusion
enhancement module contributed greatly to the improvement of the MRI quality and structural preservation, and
the prompt guided semantic attention mechanism contributed to the adaptive localization of clinically relevant
tumor regions.

Vinayaka R. Srinivas and Ramasubramanian Parvathi *†
School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India
Introduction: Brain tumors are among the most aggressive forms of cancer,
requiring precise diagnosis and treatment planning to improve patient outcomes.
This study aims to develop an efficient deep learning-based framework for the
classification of brain tumors using MRI data.
Methods: The methodology employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
to accurately classify tumors into four categories: normal, glioma, pituitary, and
meningioma. Key preprocessing techniques, including noise reduction,resizing,
and data augmentation, were applied to enhance the robustness of the model.
Advanced architectures such as DenseNet50, VGG19, and other transfer
learning models, along with CNN variants, were trained and evaluated for their
performance. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including Grad-CAM, LIME, and
feature map visualizations, played a crucial role in providing better visualizations
of the model’s decision-making process and identifying areas of improvement
during model training and to establish a better model.
Results: The best-performing model, a 4-conv-1-dense-1-dropout CNN,
achieved a classification accuracy of 95.86%, outperforming deeper architectures
and transfer learning approaches. The findings underscore the potential of deep
learning models for reliable and efficient brain tumor classification. This work
concludes with recommendations for real-time deployment in clinical settings
and explores future integration with Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate
detailed diagnostic reports.
KEYWORDS
brain tumor classification, convolutional neural networks, data augmentation, deep
learning, explainable AI, feature visualization, medical imaging, MRI

title: Explainable AI-driven MRI-based brain tumor classification: a novel deep learning approach
authors: Vinayaka R. Srinivas; Ramasubramanian Parvathi
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Volume 8, Article 1700214
text:
Objective
The primary objective of using the Tumor dataset (Crystal Clean
MRI dataset) is to develop machine learning models capable of
accurately classifying and segmenting brain tumors from MRI images.
This involves distinguishing between different types of brain tumors,
such as gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors, or distinguishing
between tumor and non-tumor cases. Early and accurate tumor
classification is critical for effective diagnosis and treatment planning.
To achieve this, the project aims to design a deep learning-based
model, such as a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), that
significantly improves classification accuracy. The model will leverage
techniques like data augmentation and preprocessing to enhance
generalization, enabling it to perform effectively on real-world medical
datasets. Moreover, exploring multimodal MRI data will further
optimize classification performance, addressing the computational
challenges posed by the high-dimensional nature of MRI scans.
In addition to improving accuracy, the project emphasizes reducing
overfitting and optimizing computational efficiency. Overfitting, that
limits a model’s ability to generalize to new data, will be mitigated using
data augmentation, regularization methods, and cross-validation
techniques. To enhance computational efficiency, strategies such as
dimensionality reduction, region of interest (ROI) detection, and model
pruning will be explored, minimizing memory usage and processing time
while maintaining accuracy. The ultimate goal is to create a scalable and
deployable solution for clinical use. The model will be designed to adapt
to larger datasets, different MRI machines, or imaging centers. By being
integrated into medical software or platforms used in hospitals, this
solution could help healthcare professionals diagnose brain tumors more
effectively and efficiently.

Dataset
The Crystal Clean Brain Tumor MRI Dataset is a comprehensive
collection of high-resolution MRI scans designed to support precise
brain tumor classification. The dataset consists of detailed MRI images
that capture intricate brain structures, making it invaluable for
distinguishing subtle features across various tumor types. The Crystal
Clean Brain Tumor MRI dataset used in this study was obtained from
a publicly available Kaggle repository.1 The dataset contains
T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI scans categorized into four
classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and normal. Initially, the
dataset comprised 3,264 images—826 glioma, 822 meningioma, 830
pituitary, and 786 normal images. Following data augmentation
(including rotation, flipping, and brightness variation), the dataset
expanded to 13,056 images to balance class distribution and improve
model generalization. The data were split into 80% for training and
20% for testing, ensuring class balance across both subsets.
Each image is meticulously annotated to indicate the presence or
absence of a tumor (refer Figure 1), with tumor types labeled as
glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, or no tumor cases. These high-
quality images, paired with accurate annotations, serve as a robust
foundation for training machine learning models, enabling researchers
to achieve precise tumor identification and classification.

Augmentation
To enhance the robustness of the dataset and improve the model’s
ability to generalize, several data augmentation techniques were
employed. The distribution of data across the four classes—Normal,
Glioma, Pituitary, and Meningioma—is shown in Figure 3.
Salt and Pepper Noise introduces random noise to the images by
setting pixels to white (salt) or black (pepper) at specific intensities.
This technique simulates real-world imperfections, such as sensor
noise or transmission errors, which often occur in medical imaging.
By exposing the model to noisy data, it becomes more resilient in
handling distorted or degraded images, thereby improving its
performance in practical scenarios.
Histogram Equalization was applied to improve image contrast by
redistributing pixel intensity values. This method enhances subtle
details in images that may appear washed out or underexposed. For
MRI scans, this is crucial as it brings out intricate patterns and
features, enabling the model to better differentiate between tumor and
non-tumor regions.
Rotation involved altering the orientation of images by rotating
them clockwise or counterclockwise. This augmentation accounts for
the slight variations in orientation that can occur during MRI scans.
By diversifying the dataset with rotated images, the model learns to
identify tumors regardless of the alignment of the image, improving
its adaptability to real-world data.
Brightness Adjustment simulated varying lighting conditions by
increasing or decreasing the image intensity values. Since MRI images
might differ in brightness due to variations in equipment or imaging
protocols, this technique ensures the model can handle such
discrepancies. Training on images with varied brightness levels
improves the model’s ability to make accurate classifications under
diverse imaging conditions. Lastly, Horizontal and Vertical Flipping
created mirror images of the data, effectively doubling the dataset size
and introducing spatial orientation variability. For symmetrical
structures like the brain, flipping helps the model recognize tumors
regardless of their location within the brain’s symmetry as seen in
Figure 4. This augmentation increases data diversity and helps the
model generalize better between different spatial configurations. This
constitutes a large dataset of 22,000 MRI images which is used for the
training process.

Justification for using CNNs, transfer
learning, and explainable AI
The choice of CNN-based models and transfer learning
architectures over more complex state-of-the-art models was driven
by practical considerations such as hardware limitations,
computational efficiency, and accessibility for smaller research
environments or medical institutions with limited resources. While
transformer-based architectures and advanced deep learning models
like Vision Transformers (ViTs) or hybrid networks have shown
promising results in medical imaging, they demand extensive
computational power, large-scale labelled datasets, and specialized
hardware such as high-end GPUs or TPUs. Many small-scale
healthcare facilities, startups, and research groups lack the
infrastructure to deploy such resource-intensive models in real-world
clinical applications.

Load Data: The first step is loading the MRI images needed for

it is clean and consistent. Common preprocessing steps might include
resizing images, normalizing pixel values, removing noise, and data
augmentation techniques to increase the dataset’s diversity and
robustness. Proper preprocessing is essential to improve model

Model development
Feature Extraction: After the data is prepared, it is followed by
feature extraction, where meaningful characteristics or patterns are
extracted from the images. For MRI data, features could include pixel
intensities, textures, shapes, or tumor-specific markers. These features
help the model distinguish between different types of tumors or
between tumor and non-tumor cases.
Design Model: In this step, a deep learning or machine learning
model architecture is chosen and designed based on the project
requirements. Common architectures for image classification tasks
include Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) or other neural
network models optimized for visual data processing.
Run Model: After designing the model, it is trained on the
preprocessed dataset. During this phase, the model learns from the
features to differentiate between tumor types or identify the absence
of a tumor. Training involves adjusting model parameters to minimize
errors and improve classification accuracy.
Establish Performance Metrics: As the model trains, performance
metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, or AUC (Area
Under the Curve) are calculated to evaluate the model’s effectiveness.
These metrics help assess whether the model is learning effectively and
can generalize well to new, unseen data.

Model evaluation
Evaluate Training Set: After completing the training, the model is
assessed on the training set to determine if it is overfitting or
underfitting. Overfitting happens when the model excels on the
training data but fails on new data, whereas underfitting indicates that
the model is not effectively identifying the underlying patterns in
the data.
Establish Metrics: After evaluating on the training set,
performance metrics are recalculated to ensure consistency and
validate the model’s effectiveness. This step might also include testing
the model on a separate validation or test dataset to gauge its real-
world applicability.

Save Model: Once the model performs satisfactorily, it is saved for
deployment. This saved model can then be loaded in a production
environment where it can be used for real-time tumor classification.

users to interact with the model easily. Streamlit is a popular
framework for creating web applications for machine learning models,
making it simple to create a user-friendly frontend.

uploaded image, performs the tumor classification, and returns the
result to the user. The result, including predicted tumor type and any
other relevant metrics or visualizations, is displayed on the frontend
for easy interpretation.

The DenseNet50 architecture, known for its efficient feature reuse
and gradient propagation, was fine-tuned on the MRI dataset to assess
its classification capability. Dense connections between layers enable
strong feature retention, reducing redundant computations while
improving learning efficiency. The model achieved 90.04% validation
accuracy, indicating strong feature extraction capabilities. However,
fluctuations in validation loss suggested potential overfitting, despite
the model’s ability to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem. While
DenseNet50 provided high accuracy, its complex connectivity and
depth required extensive hyperparameter tuning to stabilize loss and
enhance generalization. The results indicate that while the model
effectively distinguishes tumors, it requires regularization strategies
such as dropout and data augmentation to improve its robustness for
clinical applications.

VGG19, a deep sequential convolutional architecture, was
implemented for its structured feature extraction process, making it
well-suited for hierarchical feature learning in MRI scans. Fine-tuning

applied to optimize classification performance. The model yielded a
95.92% validation accuracy, the highest among the transfer learning
architectures. However, overfitting was evident, with near-perfect
training accuracy and a significant discrepancy between training and
validation loss. The model’s depth and high parameter count, while
beneficial for feature extraction, contributed to its over-reliance on
training data, reducing generalization capacity. Despite its strong
classification accuracy, lighter architectures with regularization
mechanisms may offer more balanced performance for deployment in

types in MRI scans. The model was fine-tuned by freezing initial layers
and adjusting learning rates to adapt to the dataset. The results showed

large-scale classification tasks, appears to have contributed to slower
convergence and limited feature specialization for this medical
imaging dataset.

Xception, an extension of the Inception architecture using depth

computational efficiency while retaining strong feature extraction
capabilities. The model was fine-tuned by adjusting batch
normalization parameters and dropout rates to optimize learning.
While achieving 76.17% validation accuracy, the model exhibited
inconsistencies in validation loss, suggesting difficulties in
generalization. The high-capacity nature of Xception, designed for
complex feature hierarchies, resulted in overfitting to training data,
limiting its effectiveness for MRI-based classification. These findings
indicate that while Xception offers strong pattern recognition
capabilities, its architectural complexity and computational demands
may not be ideal for small-scale, domain-specific medical
imaging datasets.

Comparative study of the XAI methods
In the context of Explainable AI (XAI) for brain tumor
classification, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-
CAM) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME)
serve as two widely used techniques for visualizing model decision-
making. Both methods aim to enhance model transparency, enabling
clinicians to understand how the deep learning model arrives at a
specific classification. A comparative analysis of Grad-CAM and
LIME, based on the results and visual interpretations, reveals distinct
strengths and limitations in their applicability to medical imaging
(Table 7).
Grad-CAM generates class-specific heatmaps by computing the
gradient of the predicted class score concerning the final convolutional
layer, highlighting salient regions in the image that contribute most to
the model’s decision. The generated heatmaps in our study showed
that Grad-CAM effectively highlights tumor regions with high spatial
precision, making it particularly useful for radiologists to verify
whether the model is focusing on the correct anatomical structures.
In cases where the model predicted glioma or meningioma, the
heatmaps consistently activated around the tumor mass, reinforcing
the model’s interpretability.
In Figure 21, the Grad-CAM heatmap visualizes the regions of the
brain MRI that contributes to the prediction of the model. The
highlighted regions in red and yellow represents the regions with
higher model attention, indicating potential tumor regions. By
applying grad-cam in the early stages of the model development. it
ensures that researchers can interpret how the model focuses on
relevant anatomical structures instead of background details. This
interpretability helps in refining the model architecture, adjusting
hyperparameters, and understanding potential biases.
However, there are limitations to these visualizations. As you can
see in Figure 22, the Grad-Cam’s resolution is might often be coarse,
meaning it may produce vague boundaries and in some cases, missing
fine details. Additionally, Grad-CAM does not provide quantitative
measure of uncertainty, which limits its decisions in cases where
confidence assessment is necessary. Also, Grad-CAM is inherently
limited by its dependency on convolutional layers, which makes it less
effective for fully connected architectures.

In Figure 23 and 24, the LIME visualizations highlight regions of

predictions, its explanations can vary based on the sampling process
and parameter choices. Additionally, it may sometimes highlight
non-tumor regions, especially in noisy or complex medical images. The
localized nature of LIME explanations also means it might miss broader
contextual insights that global interpretability methods could provide.
When comparing the two methods, Grad-CAM proves to be more
effective for global interpretability, allowing domain experts to visualize
the primary decision-making areas at a glance. This is crucial in
confirming clinical validity, as a well-trained model should consistently
focus on the tumor region across different images. LIME, in contrast,
is more suitable for local interpretability, as it helps identify specific
features and potential biases influencing the model’s classification. Its
ability to provide fine-grained attributions makes it valuable for
understanding misclassifications and edge cases in medical imaging.

Conclusion
The brain tumor classification project achieved its goal by
developing and deploying deep learning models to accurately classify
brain tumors from MRI data. Various architectures, such as
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformer-based
models, were designed, trained, and evaluated for their effectiveness
in handling medical imaging data. The CNN models excelled in
feature extraction and classification tasks, reaching an accuracy of up
to 98.65%, making them valuable tools for medical practitioners in
detecting and diagnosing brain tumors. While Transformer models
showed potential, they required more computational resources and
fine-tuning to improve their efficiency for real-time deployment.
To ensure accessibility, the project deployed the best-performing
models through web interfaces using frameworks like Streamlit and
Gradio. These interfaces allowed for seamless real-time image uploads
and classification, providing an intuitive experience for users. The
deployment demonstrated the practical application of deep learning in
medical diagnostics, supporting radiologists and healthcare professionals
in identifying brain tumors early. The project highlights the potential of
deep learning in medical image classification and lays the foundation for
future advancements, evolving into a more powerful tool for early tumor
detection and diagnosis. Looking ahead, there are areas for improvement
and expansion in the brain tumor classification project.
Future work will involve refining advanced models with improved
attention mechanisms and feature extraction techniques, enhancing
the ability to detect subtle tumor features. An exciting prospect is the
integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) after the classification

findings and provide insights into tumor characteristics and
recommended actions. This integration would enhance the
interpretability and usefulness of the model’s output, bridging the gap
between predictions and clinical insights.

Introduction
Despite achieving high performance on benchmark datasets in brain tumor
segmentation and classification, many deep learning (DL)-based neuro-oncology systems
remain insufficiently validated for routine clinical deployment. The major barriers limiting
clinical translation include poor interpretability, weak external generalization, dependence
on centralized datasets, and increasing concerns regarding patient data privacy under
regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. Consequently, recent neuro-oncology research has
gradually shifted from performance-oriented AI toward the development of trustworthy
AI frameworks capable of ensuring transparency, robustness, privacy preservation, and
clinically reliable decision support.
Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a critical component of trustworthy neuro-
oncology systems because clinicians require biologically meaningful reasoning rather than

(SHAP), and saliency-based visualization are increasingly used
to identify whether neural networks focus on clinically relevant
pathological regions such as enhancing tumor cores, necrosis, and
peritumoral edema instead of imaging artifacts. Simultaneously,
Federated Learning (FL) has gained considerable attention as a
privacy-preserving collaborative learning paradigm that enables
multi-institutional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis
without direct data sharing. The convergence of XAI and FL
therefore represents an important step toward secure, transparent,
and clinically adaptive neuro-oncology AI systems. In parallel,
recent advances in architectural design have accelerated the
evolution of brain tumor analysis frameworks from conventional
neural network-based models toward Vision Transformers (ViTs)
(Dosovitskiy, 2020), hybrid attention-driven systems, and State
Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba, which are capable of
modeling long-range spatial dependencies in high-dimensional
multi-modal MRI volumes (Gu and Dao, 2023). Moreover, the
increasing integration of multimodal MRI, radiogenomics, digital
pathology, and clinical metadata has expanded the role of AI
beyond tumor detection toward prognosis prediction, treatment
planning, and personalized neuro-oncology.

• Detailed analysis of translational barriers that hamper real-
world applications such as data dependence, insufficient
external validation, limited explainability, computational
complexity, and regulatory issues.
• A holistic view on future trustworthy AI systems for neuro-
oncology, integrating explanations, federated intelligence,
multimodal reasoning, and clinical validation approaches.
The rest of the paper is outlined as follows. In Section II, the
background and preliminaries of trustworthy AI-based brain tumor
detection using technologies such as explainable AI, Federated
Learning, and multimodal MRI analysis are presented. Section III
outlines the method for literature review, specifically the study
selection criteria following the PRISMA guidelines and the thematic
evaluation criteria adopted for this survey. In Section IV, a detailed
thematic analysis is provided about deep learning approaches for
brain tumor analysis including CNN, transfer learning, explainable
AI, multimodal/radiomics frameworks, robust learning techniques,
workflow-based clinical solutions, and optimization-based neuro-
oncology solutions. In Section V, we discuss some of the major
barriers to the adoption of trustworthy AI-based brain tumor
detection, whereas emerging research directions are discussed in
Section VI.

text:
Explainable AI (XAI)
Conventional deep learning models often operate as black-
box models, limiting clinical confidence despite achieving high
predictive
performance.
In
brain
tumor
segmentation
and
classification, XAI methods such as Gradient-weighted Class
Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) (Selvaraju et al., 2017), SHapley
Additive exPlanations (SHAP) (Lundberg and Lee, 2017), Local
Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) (Ribeiro et al.,
2016), and saliency mapping are increasingly used to associate
model activations with anatomically meaningful tumor regions.
Such
explainability
mechanisms
are
particularly
important
for differentiating true tumor progression from treatment-
related pseudoprogression and for improving clinician trust in
automated neuro-oncology systems. However, many current
explainability approaches remain post-hoc visual approximations
without biologically validated causal interpretation. To maintain
conceptual consistency throughout the review, explainability-
related methods are distinguished according to the type of
information they provide and the degree of validation they receive.
Feature attribution refers to methods that estimate the contribution
or importance of input features to a model prediction, including
SHAP and LIME. Saliency visualization refers specifically to
spatial or feature-level visual representations of model sensitivity,
such as Grad-CAM, CAM, saliency maps, and attention maps.
These visualizations indicate regions or features associated
with a prediction but do not, by themselves, establish that the
highlighted regions are biologically causal. Intrinsic interpretability
refers to models whose decision mechanism is designed to
be interpretable as part of the model architecture or learning
process, rather than applying an explanation after prediction. In
contrast, post-hoc explanation refers to methods applied after a
model has generated a prediction to approximate or visualize the
factors associated with that prediction. Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME,
and conventional saliency-based methods are therefore treated
primarily as post-hoc explanation or attribution approaches unless
the reviewed study explicitly integrates them into the learning
process. Counterfactual explanation considers how a prediction
would change under a specified change in the input or relevant
feature, thereby providing an alternative form of explanation
based on hypothetical modifications. Causal explanation requires

the reviewed study explicitly integrates them into the learning

would change under a specified change in the input or relevant
feature, thereby providing an alternative form of explanation
based on hypothetical modifications. Causal explanation requires
stronger evidence than attribution or visualization because it
seeks to establish whether a feature or biological characteristic
has a causal influence on the prediction, typically requiring an
intervention-based, mechanistic, or otherwise causally grounded
evaluation. Consequently, an attention map, saliency map, or
feature-attribution score is not interpreted as evidence of biological
causality unless such causal validation is explicitly demonstrated.
Finally, clinician-validated explanation refers to explanations that
have been evaluated by domain experts, such as radiologists,
pathologists, or neuro-oncology specialists, for clinical relevance,
anatomical plausibility, or agreement with established diagnostic
evidence. Clinical trust is treated separately from these explanation
types because it represents a broader outcome or property of an
AI system rather than a specific explanation mechanism. Similarly,
visualization describes the presentation format of an explanation
and should not be treated as synonymous with explainability
or interpretability.
Accordingly, throughout this review, XAI methods are
described using the most specific applicable category: feature
attribution, saliency visualization, intrinsic interpretability, post-
hoc explanation, counterfactual explanation, causal explanation,
or clinician-validated explanation. This taxonomy is used to
distinguish what an explanation method computes from how the
explanation is presented and whether its clinical or biological
validity has been demonstrated.

Federated Learning (FL)
Large-scale centralized collection of MRI data is generally
hindered by stringent healthcare data protection policies such
as General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Federated
Learning provides an opportunity for collaborative learning in
multiple institutions through sharing model updates rather than
patient images. In such a decentralized approach, access to
diverse neuroimaging data is ensured without compromising data
ownership at institutions. However, federated approaches are still
plagued by several problems of non-IID (non-independent and
identically distributed) data distribution, communication costs,
utility-privacy trade-offs, and robustness issues in a heterogeneous
clinical setting. Decentralized privacy-preserving techniques and
interpretability of AI models in clinical context is theoretically
represented in Figure 1.

Synergy of multi-modal MRI sequences
Multimodality is an intrinsic quality of brain tumor analysis
with MRI. For example, T1-weighted (T1), T1 contrast-enhanced
(T1c), T2-weighted (T2), and fluid attenuated inversion recovery
(FLAIR) images are indispensable in order to have an adequate
characterization of a tumor. More specifically, FLAIR is more
prone to detecting peritumoral edema, whereas T1c images
are more informative in identifying the core and necrosis
of enhancing tumors. Thus, contemporary trustworthy neuro-
oncology systems tend to incorporate image fusion approaches into
their algorithms.

Methodology
This systematic literature review (SLR) was undertaken by
adhering to the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) approach in
order to ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility
(Page et al., 2021). The main aim of this review was to explore
recent advancements in brain tumor MRI analysis across five
primary research themes: (i) Explainable AI (XAI), (ii) Deep
Learning Frameworks, (iii) Privacy and Federated Learning, (iv)
Advanced Architectures (Transformers/Mamba), and (v) Multi-
modal MRI Integration. The process of literature search entailed
several stages including database searching, filtering based on
metadata, logical screening and manual verification of articles.
All retained studies were manually reviewed to confirm thematic
relevance and methodological alignment with the objectives of
trustworthy brain tumor detection using AI systems.

authors: Uthra B; Sivashankari R
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Volume 9, Article 1959004
text:
Research questions
To guide the systematic synthesis, this review addresses three
research questions:
• RQ1: What are the major methodological trends in brain
tumor MRI analysis using deep learning, Explainable AI
(XAI), Federated Learning (FL), advanced architectures, and
multimodal approaches?
• RQ2: How are explainability and privacy-preserving learning
addressed in the reviewed literature, and to what extent are
XAI and FL integrated within the same brain tumor MRI
analysis frameworks?
• RQ3: What are the major limitations and research gaps
concerning
interpretability,
privacy,
data
heterogeneity,
validation, evaluation, and clinical applicability of trustworthy
AI for brain tumor MRI analysis?
The intersection of XAI and FL is examined by distinguishing
studies that address XAI and FL separately from studies that
incorporate both components within the same framework. For
studies involving both components, the review considers how
interpretability and privacy-preserving collaborative learning are
jointly addressed, together with the reported challenges related to
data heterogeneity, robustness, and clinical validation.

Early researches in brain tumor detection through deep
learning techniques mainly relied on the CNN architecture and
transfer learning methods for detecting tumors, classifying multiple
classes, and segmenting tumors. Pretrained backbone networks,
including ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet, and YOLO, were used

Explainable and interpretable deep learning
models
In order to boost the level of trust in clinicians and enhance
decision-making, the latest research has adopted an approach
involving the incorporation of XAI methods like SHAP, LIME,
Grad-CAM, CAM, and neuro-fuzzy reasoning in deep learning
workflows. The goal was to detect biologically relevant tumor areas
and generate explainable interpretations along with predictions.
These studies, (Saeed et al., 2023; Hardani et al., 2024; Zheng et al.,
2023a; Valerio et al., 2025; Šefˇcík and Benesova, 2023; Gaur et al.,
2022; Mayeta-Revilla et al., 2025; Mazhar et al., 2026; Jahan et al.,
2025; Gao et al., 2025) together show that there is an increasing
trend toward moving away from accuracy-driven deep learning
models for the application of brain tumor detection using AI
toward explainable and biological models. Many of these papers
adopted techniques like Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, CAM, neuro-
fuzzy reasoning, or explanation-guided learning methods to ensure
better explainability and provide better insight into tumor-related
areas of interest. Although the MGMT methylation paper cast
serious doubt on the explainability techniques used today due
to the poor correlation of model attention with biologically
interesting tumor characteristics, frameworks like CSF-Glioma
and explanation-guided learning tried to achieve explainability
during the model learning process itself rather than relying
on post-hoc techniques. At the same time, segmentation-to-
explanation models extended explainability further by integrating
large language models for human-comprehensible reporting,
while histopathology-based frameworks like PGE-Net and diffuse
glioma classifier models took pathological cues and multi-
scale explainability techniques to enhance explainability in
WSIs. Nevertheless, despite significant developments in the
implementation of Explainable AI in these models, several major
issues remain outstanding within the frameworks. For example,
most of the methods for generating explanations are post-hoc
visualizations that are not rigorously validated from a biological
or clinician-oriented perspective, meaning that it is not always
clear whether the highlighted portions correspond to causative
features or accidental imaging patterns. Additionally, combining
various explainability tools, such as SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM,
and fuzzy inference systems, results in considerable computational

Beyond architectural innovations in image-based analysis,
recent studies increasingly emphasize multi-modal and multi-
omics integration to capture the biological heterogeneity of brain
tumors. Hamid et al. (2026) propose a correlation-based Graph
Attention Network (BioGAT-LGG) that incorporates various omics
information to classify the subtypes of lower-grade gliomas. This
addresses the biological heterogeneity that imaging-based models
may not be able to capture. However, the model’s dependence on
limited data sets and the interpretability of the attention mechanism
also point to the difficulties that arise in biological validation.
Ramasamy et al. (2026) propose the MM-3DAttNet model, which
is a multi-modal 3D attention network that incorporates various
MRI sequences such as T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR to predict the
methylation status of the MGMT gene. The weak supervision at
the patient-label level and the lack of uncertainty calibration also
present difficulties.
Recent
developments
in

and
hybrid

more context-aware learning frameworks for brain tumor analysis.
There is a consensus among Maria Nancy and Sathyarajasekaran

To address the issue, researchers are shifting toward hierarchical

the continued reliance on skip connections reflects architectural
dependencies inherited from earlier segmentation frameworks.
One of the key points that have been observed from the works of

Bridging the trust gap: Explainable AI
(XAI) in brain tumor detection
Approaches such as the combination of convolutional neural
networks and explanation methods like Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME,
and attention visualization aim to highlight tumor-relevant areas
and help clinicians better understand the decisions made by the
models (Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2025; Pongphaw and Buaphan,
2026;
Srinivas and Parvathi,
2025;
Shaheema et al.,
2025;
Samara and Harry, 2025), Saleem et al. (2021), and Safarpour et al.
(2026). Though these approaches improve the interpretability of
the diagnostic results, many of these approaches are still based
on saliency map-based methods, which are not always reliable.
Other approaches focus on the development of hybrid approaches
for feature engineering and explanation methods, where machine
learning classifiers are combined with feature selection methods
and explanation methods like Boruta, LASSO, and SHAP to
improve the selection of clinically meaningful radiomic features
(Rohan et al.,
2025;
Hosny et al.,
2025;
Rahman et al.,
2024;
Song et al., 2022; Hosny and Mohammed, 2025; Mushgil et al.,
2025; Aksoy et al., 2025). Though these approaches improve
the interpretability of the diagnostic results, they are still based
on carefully curated data, which may not be applicable to all
situations. Recent approaches have been made to improve the
interpretability of the diagnostic results by developing explanation
methods for segmentation and multi-task approaches, where
tumor localization, segmentation, and classification are combined
to improve the interpretability of the results for better tumor
characterization in MRI scans (Andrianos et al., 2025; Ali et al.,
2025; Cao et al., 2023; Dasanayaka et al., 2022; Ayaz et al., 2024;
Bhaskaran and Datta, 2025). These methods have shown better
interpretability of the diagnosis but often come with the cost of
higher computational complexity and large amounts of annotated
data like BraTS. Another direction that is currently being explored
is the fusion of explainable AI with more powerful deep learning
architectures like ensemble methods, transformer networks, and
multimodal methods for more reliable predictions (Gagliardi et al.,
2025;
Alyatimi et al.,
2025;
Akgündo ̆gdu and Çelikba ̧s,
2025;

2025; Haque et al., 2024; Abdulateef, 2025; Charaabi et al., 2025;

in this domain still grapples with a fundamental trade-off:
while the introduction of privacy-preserving noise (e.g., Laplace

section_heading: Privacy risks beyond federated data locality
text:
Privacy risks beyond federated data locality
Although Federated Learning avoids direct exchange of raw
MRI data, it should not be regarded as a complete guarantee of
patient privacy. The model updates exchanged during federated
optimization may themselves contain information about local
training samples. Gradient leakage or gradient inversion attacks
can exploit shared gradients or model updates to reconstruct
sensitive characteristics of training images, while model inversion
attacks can use model outputs or updates to infer representative
features of the underlying data (Zhu et al., 2019). Membership
inference attacks pose a different risk by determining whether a
particular patient or MRI sample contributed to model training
(Shokri et al., 2017; Nasr et al., 2019). These threats are particularly
relevant in neuro-oncology because MRI data contain highly
sensitive patient-specific anatomical and pathological information.
Therefore, privacy protection in federated brain tumor analysis
requires safeguards beyond data locality.
Additional
privacy-preserving
mechanisms
can
be
incorporated to mitigate these risks. Differential Privacy (DP)
limits the contribution of individual records by perturbing model
updates or gradients with controlled noise, thereby reducing the
risk of information disclosure (Abadi et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2020).
However, excessive noise may reduce the sensitivity required for
detecting subtle tumor characteristics and can introduce a privacy–
utility trade-off. Secure Aggregation can further protect client
updates by ensuring that the aggregation server receives only an
aggregate of participating updates rather than directly inspecting
individual client updates (Bonawitz et al., 2017). Consequently,
future XAI-FL frameworks for brain tumor MRI analysis should
evaluate not only whether raw data remain decentralized, but
also the resistance of shared model updates to gradient leakage,
model inversion, and membership inference attacks, together
with explicit assessment of differential-privacy parameters and
secure-aggregation mechanisms.

text:
Data heterogeneity and domain shift in federated
learning
A major challenge in federated brain tumor MRI analysis
is the non-IID nature of institutional data. Differences in
scanner manufacturers and field strengths, acquisition protocols,
voxel spacing, MRI sequences, patient demographics, disease
distributions, and annotation practices can cause substantial
variation in the local data distributions across participating
institutions.
Such
heterogeneity
can
produce
client-specific
optimization objectives and gradient divergence, causing a globally
aggregated model to perform inconsistently across institutions.
Domain shift can further arise when a model trained collaboratively
across participating centers encounters an unseen institution with
different imaging characteristics or patient populations. Therefore,
evaluation of federated brain tumor models should extend
beyond aggregate global performance and include client-level
performance, cross-institutional validation, and explicit assessment
of robustness under domain shift. Approaches such as FedProx,
adaptive client selection, personalized Federated Learning, and
other non-IID-resilient optimization strategies may help reduce
the effects of distributional divergence, but their effectiveness
should be evaluated under realistic multi-institutional MRI
heterogeneity rather than only under artificially homogenized
data splits.

authors: Uthra B; Sivashankari R

text:
Multimodal and multi-omics
frameworks
In brain tumor research, multimodal learning has gained
popularity as a result of its capacity for integrating complementary
features extracted from different imaging sequences, heterogeneous
clinical data, and multi-omics data sources. As opposed to
traditional monomodal models, multimodal techniques seek
to increase accuracy, improve segmentation quality, enhance
interpretability, and boost robustness by fusing distinct feature
spaces into one coherent learning framework. Nevertheless,
although multimodal methods have achieved impressive results
in many recent publications, significant variation exists in aspects
related to the fusion mechanism, architectural design, explanation
capacity, computational considerations, and experimental validity.
This paper therefore provides a critical evaluation of the discussed
multimodal and multi-omics research papers by contrasting
their methodologies, interpretability techniques, computational
challenges, and generalizability problems instead of merely
highlighting their results.

in Rawas and Samala (2024), Maqsood et al. (2022), Coupet et al.

can be found in the literature review is Coupet et al. (2022). This
paper provides focused research into the effects of different MRI

of a particular combination determines the performance level
significantly and that T2-FLAIR proved to be the best modality used
individually. Moreover, excluding certain pairs of MRI sequences
demonstrated that their fusion adds complementary information.
On the other hand, Zhang et al. (2025) transcend the realm of
structural imaging by introducing the use of MOFNet for multi-
omics classification of cancer subtypes. Unlike spatial fusion
approaches which capitalize on the notion of anatomical continuity,
MOFNet uses genomics, transcriptomics, and epigenomics data via
Similarity Graph Pooling (SGO) and decision-level fusion using
the View Correlation Discovery Network (VCDN). Unfortunately,
despite the novel design of the proposed architecture, Zhang et al.’s
(2025) study is only confined to three TCGA datasets without
showing how robust the model would be among other clinical
samples or other omics modalities. As such, although the model
introduces an interesting expansion of multimodal fusion, its
practicality remains unproven.
4.5.2 Architectural sophistication vs.
computational efficiency
The studies reviewed here show an evident compromise
made between the architectural sophistication of the models
and the ability to computationally optimize them. Coupet et al.
(2022) use several complex pretrained models, specifically,
VGG19, InceptionV3, ResNet50, DenseNet169, EfficientNet-B6,
and UNET-3D. The described architectures are powerful from the
viewpoint of representation learning; however, their optimization
is rather problematic. Particularly, the authors note problems with
the performance of UNET-3D due to convergence issues and local
minima. Additionally, they report significant overfitting without
using dropout regularization, where some models demonstrate
close to perfect training accuracy but fail at validation. It
adds validity to the results presented in the paper since the
authors do not ignore limitations associated with the complexity
of deep neural networks for medical data. Kesav and Rajini

end approach for learning features, their architecture incorporates
Discrete Orthogonal Stockwell Transform (DOST), in addition
to hand-engineered features like entropy, variance, and contrast,
in classification. Likewise, Maqsood et al. (2022) have used a
light-weight variant of the MobileNetV2 network with multiclass
SVM classifiers and feature selection using entropy. Despite the
very high accuracy levels of these simpler frameworks being
well above 98%, it would be prudent to treat these assertions
with some caution. With respect to Kesav and Rajini (2024),
the design of the experiment relies on a very limited set of
data that significantly raises the chances of overfitting and
skewed accuracy levels. Thus, such a high level of accuracy
achieved by the authors might not represent generalization
but rather a case of memorizing the limited dataset used. In
addition, even as complexity simplification reduces neural net
size, it increases computation during data preprocessing and
feature engineering.

authors: Uthra B; Sivashankari R
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Volume 9, Article 1959004
text:
Explainability and clinical interpretability
challenges
sExplainability remains one of the most important unresolved
issues across the reviewed studies. Kesav and Rajini (2024) apply
the Class Activation Mapping (CAM) technique for pointing
out relevant tumor locations, and Coupet et al. (2022) rely on
three techniques including LRP, Deep Taylor decomposition, and
Guided Backpropagation for visualizing the feature relevance. In
this regard, both methods increase explainability because they
show the relevance of predictions to particular image areas.
Nevertheless, due to their mathematical complexity, visualization
techniques need further explanation, and it is not easy to
provide a clinical understanding of the generated explanations
through the heatmaps. To solve this problem, Rawas and Samala
(2024) implement a novel approach for linking the CNN
model and ChatGPT to create a conversational explanation
tool based on human-language input and output. Although this
method increases usability and also interactive experience, the
study fails to prove causality between the chatbot responses
and the operations of the neural network. This introduces
an important clinical concern. Large language models can
generate fluent but potentially inaccurate explanations, creating
a risk of overreliance by clinicians. Therefore, although the
integration of generative AI is innovative, the interpretability
benefits remain preliminary and require stronger validation before
clinical deployment.

generalizability
One of the consistent drawbacks found in almost all reviewed
papers is the lack of validation scale and poor proof of
clinical applicability. This issue is addressed by Kesav and Rajini
(2024). Despite the fact that the model is described as having
a 98.99% accuracy and a specificity of 99.76%, it was tested
on just 32 patients and evaluated through just five images
for assessing features. A study of this small size cannot
provide sufficient statistical evidence to claim robustness or
applicability. Coupet et al. (2022) clearly state the problem of
overfitting with regard to limited training data in medicine.

Critical synthesis of trustworthiness,
generalizability, and clinical translation
challenges
One of the key insights derived from the above analysis is that
AI research in brain tumor detection is moving beyond simple
accuracy-driven learning models to more trustworthy intelligent
systems for clinical use. Although previous research efforts focused
mostly on achieving high accuracy results by using neural networks
for segmentation purposes and optimizing Dice-score values,
today’s research tends to pay more attention to explainability,
data privacy protection, multimodal reasoning capabilities, and
distributed learning strategies. As depicted in our framework of
the systemic architecture transition (Figure 9), it appears that
improvements in architectural design have been outpacing those in
other areas significantly.
Among the clear trends that have emerged from reviewing the
literature in this area is the reliance on post-hoc interpretability
frameworks such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, LayerCAM, Guided
Backpropagation, and attention visualization. These techniques
have been incorporated extensively into CNNs, Transformers,
and multimodal architectures to provide visual indications of
regions or features associated with model predictions. However,
the review indicates that the availability of an XAI visualization

Moreover, the review emphasizes the methodological gap

development of privacy-preserving approaches to collaborative
learning. While most of the relevant research is dedicated to
the topic of explainability, less attention is paid to the topics of

highlights one of the critical deployment issues faced by clinical
brain tumor detection. Since the disease under study implies
multi-institutional learning because of the rarity and diversity of
patients’ cases, centralized training is limited by GDPR, HIPAA,
and the principle of institutional data sovereignty. One important
trade-offthat emerges frequently in the FL body of work is the

configurations, voxel spacing, missing modality information, and
variable annotations. While methods like FedProx, dynamic
collaboration schemes, adaptive client selection strategies, and

The 61-study subset was selected because these studies

The 61-study denominator was applied consistently to all metric

Figure 12 and Table 18 together show an evident tendency

evaluation studies. The accuracy metric is used in 45 papers, which

reported metric despite all the drawbacks inherent in such an
approach. Multiple studies report classification accuracies higher

text:
Trustworthiness and clinical validation
gap
In addition to being effective predictors, trustworthy AI
needs to be reliable, well-calibrated, robust, and clinically useful.
Yet, the evaluation of the reviewed papers shows an obvious
disparity between performance-related and trustworthiness-related
approaches to assessing these models.
As seen from Table 19, traditional performance indicators
like accuracy, Dice, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-scores prevail
in research; calibration indicators, metrics related to uncertainty
estimation, and clinical usefulness criteria are mentioned quite
rarely. Calibration measures like Brier Score, Expected Calibration
Error (ECE), Maximum Calibration Error (MCE), and Negative
Log-Likelihood (NLL) can be found in less than 7% of the reviewed
works. This problem is especially pertinent since the accuracy of a
model does not imply its trustworthiness. A system can have great
benchmark scores but at the same time can have poor-calibrated
confidences or be unreliable in distribution shift situations. Thus,
performance scores alone are not enough for assessing the
clinical readiness of a model. Fortunately, some promising recent
works started to use the analysis of the calibration, uncertainty
quantification, external validation cohorts, and decision-curve
analysis which shows that there is already a move toward the
trustworthy evaluation of AI. However, these approaches still are
exceptions rather than the rule.
Overall, these results expose an underlying imbalance within
modern neuro-oncology AI research. As is clear from the extensive
use and reporting of performance metrics, there has been far less
focus on developing reliable evaluation methodologies. Thus, many
state-of-the-art algorithms show excellent performance metrics but
lack adequate validation for their calibration, uncertainty handling,
robustness to distributional shifts, or practical applicability in
clinical settings. It is therefore imperative that future research
efforts emphasize both innovative validation methods along with
algorithm design.

text:
Unified benchmarking of trustworthiness: It is highly necessary
to develop standardized benchmarking protocols that would
cover all aspects of trustworthiness assessment in the context
of AI applications to brain tumor detection. In addition to
accuracy, future frameworks should be evaluated based on their
performance in terms of explanation, uncertainty handling,
fairness, computational efficiency, and repeatability.
In order to consolidate the results of this review, Table 20
demonstrates a thematic synthesis of selected collaborative and
multimodal AI models designed for brain tumor detection. The
table provides an overview of the fundamental structure used in
the framework of each research paper, the major metrics used
to demonstrate the performance of these models, the nature of
datasets used, the methods of interpretability used in each case, and
a critique of the reliability of these measures.
Concluding, it becomes apparent that the future of brain tumor
imaging is less likely to be about reaching higher accuracy rates
than about creating explainable, privacy-preserving, biologically
interpretable, efficient, and clinically relevant AI systems.

text:
Open challenges
However, despite all the advances in brain tumor detection
research that can be considered trustworthy, there is still a
set of crucial obstacles impeding the reliable implementation of
such technologies in practice. For instance, one of the major
drawbacks of neuro-oncology AI is its high dependence on
benchmark datasets such as BraTS, TCGA, TCIA, and Figshare.
As a result, models trained on such datasets may demonstrate
their inefficiency in real-life settings due to lack of generalization.
Furthermore, despite the availability of explainable AI technologies
(Grad-CAM, SHAP, and saliency mapping), the biologically causal
explanation and physician-oriented assessment of AI frameworks
remain problematic.
As demonstrated in Figure 13, current limitations associated
with trustworthiness in brain tumor detection using AI go
beyond merely being linked to predictive capabilities and include
several interlinked challenges pertaining to dependency on
datasets, reliability of explanation methods, scalable computation,
robust Federated Learning, variability in images, and translating
regulations. These limitations illustrate how the aforementioned
challenges prevent the experimental implementation of AI from
becoming practical in neuro-oncology. Despite the presence
of external testing and some multi-institutional evaluations,
prospective
multi-center
clinical
validation
and
systematic
clinician-in-the-loop assessment remain limited. In particular,
independent clinical testing, radiologist comparison, prospective
evaluation, and workflow-based assessment are not yet consistently
incorporated into the validation of brain tumor AI systems.

architectures
in

transformer,
and
optimization
approaches.

such

improving

of reproducibility, and challenges in implementation due to
the limited resources in healthcare institutions. Additionally,

communication overhead, and poor results achieved under strict
privacy conditions. Issues regarding missing modalities, artifacts,
scanner heterogeneity, calibration of uncertainty, and robustness to

text:
Future directions
In terms of trustworthy brain tumor detection using AI,
future research directions include improving the clinical utility,
robustness, and biological plausibility of DL methods. The
potential approach that could address these needs is developing
the concept of radiology foundation models using large pre-
trained models based on multi-center MRI data sets to reduce the
reliance on benchmark datasets, like BraTS. Moreover, combining
Explainable AI and Federated Learning approaches can provide
an effective privacy-preserving way of distributed learning while
preserving clinically useful explanations of the decision process.
Multimodal and radiogenomic intelligence can be considered
as another key aspect of future developments as they may allow
analyzing MRI, histopathology, genomic features, and clinical data
simultaneously in order to provide personalized predictions of
disease progression. Future work should also aim at developing
and
applying
rigorous
trustworthiness
evaluation
protocols
including the analysis of predictive uncertainty, adversarial
robustness,
calibration,
and
clinician-centered
explainability.
Additionally, it might be worthwhile exploring lightweight
architectures and continual learning approaches as well as
developing hybrid models based on transformers and other
DL approaches.

title: A paradigm shift toward explainable and federated intelligence for brain tumor MRI analysis
authors: Uthra B; Sivashankari R
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Volume 9, Article 1959004
text:
Conclusion
This systematic review synthesized 146 studies published
between 2020 and 2026 to examine the evolution of trustworthy
AI for brain tumor MRI analysis across five primary research
themes: Explainable AI (XAI), Deep Learning Frameworks,
Privacy
and
Federated
Learning,
Advanced
Architectures
(Transformers/Mamba), and Multi-modal MRI Integration. The
quantitative thematic analysis showed that Explainable AI (XAI)
was the most represented research theme, with 55 studies (37.7%),
followed by deep learning frameworks with 51 studies (34.9%).
Privacy and Federated Learning were represented in 20 studies
(13.7%), while advanced architectures based on Transformers and
Mamba accounted for 15 studies (10.3%). Multi-modal integration
was represented in 5 studies (3.4%). Each study was assigned to one
primary research theme according to its dominant methodological
focus, and the five categories therefore collectively represent all
146 included studies. These findings indicate that explainability
and conventional deep learning frameworks constitute the
largest thematic groups in the reviewed literature, whereas
privacy-preserving, advanced-architecture, and multimodal studies
represent smaller primary thematic groups.
The publication trend further demonstrated a substantial
concentration of recent research. The reviewed studies comprised
2 publications in 2020, 2 in 2021, 9 in 2022, 11 in 2023, 31 in
2024, 77 in 2025, and 14 in 2026. Thus, 122 of the 146 included
studies (83.6%) were published during 2024–2026, indicating a
marked recent expansion of research on trustworthy AI for brain
tumor MRI analysis. Dataset analysis also revealed substantial
dependence on established benchmark resources. BraTS was
the most frequently reported dataset, occurring in 63 of the
146 included studies (43.2%). Because individual studies could
report multiple datasets, dataset frequencies were not mutually
exclusive and were therefore not expected to sum to 146. The
dataset–task analysis further showed that dataset utilization varied
across segmentation, classification, prognosis, and molecular
characterization tasks. For these analyses, the individual study
was used as the counting unit; within each task category, a study
was counted once for each distinct dataset it reported, irrespective
of repeated use of that dataset across experiments. Studies
addressing multiple tasks were counted in each applicable task

text:
lization varied
across segmentation, classification, prognosis, and molecular
characterization tasks. For these analyses, the individual study
was used as the counting unit; within each task category, a study
was counted once for each distinct dataset it reported, irrespective
of repeated use of that dataset across experiments. Studies
addressing multiple tasks were counted in each applicable task
category, and therefore task-specific frequencies and denominators
were not mutually exclusive. The review also identified an
imbalance between conventional performance evaluation and
trustworthiness-oriented evaluation. Accuracy-based metrics were
reported in 73.8% of the representative studies analyzed, while
F1-score and Dice-based measures were reported in 27.9% each. In
contrast, calibration, clinical utility, and uncertainty measures were
comparatively uncommon, reported in 6.6%, 3.3%, and 1.6% of
the representative studies, respectively. This quantitative evidence
indicates
that
predictive
performance
remains
substantially
more established than systematic evaluation of calibration,
uncertainty, and clinical usefulness. Overall, the reviewed evidence
demonstrates measurable progress toward trustworthy AI for
brain tumor MRI analysis, particularly in explainability and the
adoption of emerging architectures. However, the relatively limited
representation of Federated Learning, multimodal integration, and
trustworthiness-oriented evaluation, together with dependence
on benchmark datasets, highlights persistent gaps in privacy-
preserving collaboration, external validation, clinical validation,
and robust assessment. These findings support the need for future
studies to complement predictive performance with externally
validated,
clinically
grounded,
and
quantitatively
assessable
measures of trustworthiness.

of the brain for precise identification and characterization of
neoplasms, aids in formulating the most suitable therapeutic
strategy, serves as a navigational aid for neurosurgeons during
procedures, and is employed post-therapeutically to monitor the
neoplasm’s response to treatment and detect any early signs of
recurrence.
Patient
management
decisions
require
balancing
potential benefits and risks. Effective coordination among team
members
ensures
accurate
data
interpretation,
streamlined
workflows, and timely decision-making.
Recent progress in artificial intelligence (AI) related to
neuroimaging makes the application to neuro-oncology timely
and
promising
(1).
AI
technology
can
support
healthcare
professionals in making clinical decisions for neuro-oncology
patients by providing evidence-based information and patient-
specific tools (1). It thus promises to improve patient care by
reducing diagnostic variation, preventing unnecessary treatments
and surgeries, and decreasing associated healthcare costs (1, 2).
Lack of clarity regarding how AI systems operate has been one of
the reasons why the clinical translation of AI tools has been
limited so far. Explainable AI (XAI) methods aim to produce
explanations
that
improve
trustworthiness,
informativeness,
confidence, fairness, and interactivity (3, 4). Given the varying
criteria that constitute a good explanation, the success of XAI
methods depends on considering the specific context and goals
of end-users (clinicians) and their individual preferences (5).
Additionally, clinical translation of XAI systems will require
usable and familiar interfaces to clinicians (6).
User-Centered Design (UCD) is an iterative design process
where designers prioritize user needs in every phase. It involves
users
throughout
the
process to
create highly
usable
and
accessible products. A UCD framework ensures that usability
goals, user characteristics, environment, tasks, and workflow are
given extensive attention at each stage. Previous studies on XAI
to support MRI interpretation related to CNS tumors have lacked
a direct and intentional focus (7). Theoretical solutions often
adjust existing XAI solutions in a way that does not fit the
clinical context. For instance, tasks like distinguishing between
tumor tissue and healthy tissue or between brain metastases and

When designing and evaluating AI tools to support clinical
decision-making, it is crucial first to determine which UCD
framework best suits your specific circumstances, such as team size
and meeting frequency. Next, we must determine the details
regarding patient care trajectories and clinical workflows within
which the AI system will be deployed. By adhering to UCD
principles, we can rigorously define the task specifications for the
XAI interface by working directly with the target user groups. Finally,
we can determine the specifications for the underlying AI models to
optimize for factors like cost, time, and explainability. These pilot
systems can then be evaluated in terms of clinical beneficence and
usability via user studies before scaling to clinical settings. Because
this process is iterative, the system can be constantly scrutinized and
improved. Overall, UCD ensures that the software meets the
expectations of providers, users, and affected patients and is aligned
with software outputs and clinician expectations.

and describes the inability of a user or programmer to identify the

create highly accurate predictive models. However, there are limits
to our understanding of how the prediction was made and the
associated uncertainty. Therefore, the translation of AI into clinical
settings has been limited because of the ethical and legal need for
clinicians to have a reliable understanding of the information they
utilize in making patient care decisions and recommendations.
XAI methods broadly fall into two main categories: ante hoc
and post hoc. Ante hoc methods involve the construction of AI
models that are inherently interpretable but may sacrifice some
degree of accuracy. On the other hand, post hoc methods
generate explanations after the model has been trained.

and

for

For

model’s accuracy is relatively low (38). This implies that AI, even
with limited accuracy, can be beneficial by enhancing human
performance through attention direction. However, it’s important
to note that this approach can lead to false positives, disrupting
workflow by requiring additional time to investigate non-existent

others, potentially harming patients by necessitating unnecessary
procedures. Despite these challenges, visual analytics methods
specifically designed for clinical settings are still in their infancy

statistical methods, with only a few catering to predictive
modeling. This presents an opportunity to develop AI tools that
support clinical decision-making while minimizing risks like

Factors to consider in tailoring UCD
guidelines for neuro-oncology
There is an increasing demand for guidelines to help direct the
design of XAI systems that support decision-making in clinical
neuro-oncology
practice
(12,
47).
Meeting
this
demand
necessitates the inclusion of UCD in the development of XAI
(48). Although specific XAI design guidelines for clinical neuro-
oncology remain to be defined, some prospective elements have
been described.
One of the most directly applicable resources is the INTRPRT
framework, a set of UCD guidelines specific to medical imaging AI
(12). These guidelines are relevant to neuro-oncology because
clinical image analysis and interpretation are the most common
AI applications in neuro-oncology (39, 49). Like DoReMi,
INTRPRT emphasizes the importance of formative user research,
empirical user testing, general assessment of model transparency,
and XAI systems for diverse stakeholders. Notably, the authors
emphasize that these guidelines are a starting point and must be
adapted
and
refined
to
the
individual
context
of
an
AI
application to ensure it is tailored to the clinical end-user’s
needs. This requirement for refinement and adaptation asserts
that the successful implementation of XAI in neuro-oncology (or
any specific field) merits customized UCD.
From the clinical provider perspective, we can abstract clinical
decision-making into two steps: gathering high-quality information
and aggregating that information to make decisions (50). For AI to
gather high-quality information, the interface between the AI and
humans must be designed to ensure that the information is
accessible and understandable to the expected clinical user (6, 48,
51). AI can also assist with information aggregation to reduce
diagnostic error and cost, improve electronic health record data
collection and interpretation, and potentially help make advanced
technologies more available in geographic areas without specialized
medical facilities (36, 52–61). To leverage this potential, AI
technologies must establish trust with clinical decision-makers and
demonstrate greater intuitive usability for clinicians (62).

Enhancing patient outcomes through AI
in neurosurgery
AI applications are rapidly adopted in neurosurgery, offering a
variety
of
clinical
advantages
such
as
enhanced
lesion
characterization, predictions of surgical outcomes and potential
complications, and projecting healthcare costs (80). AI has made
a significant impact in preoperative neurosurgical planning and is
expected to continue to do so to enhance the care and outcomes
of patients in this area. During pre-operative stages, AI has been
employed to assess overall health, select the appropriate operative
approach, and inform patients of the risks involved in the
procedure. Intraoperatively, AI is commonly used to aid with
vital sign monitoring. For example, radiomics and AI are used to
forecast intraoperative changes in visual evoked potentials or
cerebral spinal fluid leaks, as well as the estimated total expense
(81, 82). Surgical planning tools have largely been built on
population-scale data but have yet to be implemented on an
individual patient level. For many patients with a CNS tumor,
there is an opportunity for improved AI solutions to contribute
to personalized decision-making around calculating surgical risk
and operative approach (83). Furthermore, there is increasing
interest in using AI in neurosurgical training, and further
research is needed (84). AI enhances neurosurgical outcomes,
and
incorporating
user-centered
design
ensures
these
advancements
meet
the
specific
needs
of
patients
and
healthcare providers.

Radiation therapy is an essential tool for treating cancer. AI-

Implementing clinical AI for MRI interpretation in neuro-
oncology patient management requires standardized imaging
protocols,
data
sharing
for
generalizability,
and
federated
learning. Standardization ensures consistency and accuracy in
images acquired across different settings. Generalizability allows
for inferences for a large population by studying a smaller
sample, while federated learning enables collaboration on model
training without sharing sensitive patient data.
Clinical AI applications have the potential to introduce bias
into medical decisions, impacting accuracy, fairness, and patient
safety. Bias stemming from data, algorithmic, and human factors
can lead to skewed AI results. It is important to consistently
review and update datasets to mitigate bias and uncertainty in AI
and
ensure
diversity,
representativeness,
and
transparency.
Moreover, it is crucial to critically examine AI to prevent the
perpetuation
of
existing
inequalities
and
to
offer
clear
explanations for AI decisions accessible by clinicians, thus
mitigating concerns about bias. However, this is only part of
the solution.

incorporate
AI
information
into
their
decision-making,
sometimes
over-
or
underweighting
predictive
information,

and usability. Time efficiency measures the time required for

User-centered XAI tools aim to improve

Contrary to the prevailing notion in many studies, we believe AI
is not meant to replace human experts in radiology but to enhance
their capabilities. AI should empower experts to make more
informed, efficient, and accurate decisions. Guided by UCD, AI
applications can be tailored to specific clinical decisions, improving
patient management. It is critical to fully assess the risks associated
with AI errors within the human expert’s workflow.
Generative AI systems are being studied for their benefits in
ambient audio and video recording within clinical settings,
enhancing

and

decision-making

text:
Designing XAI systems for clinical
decision-making involves navigating the
trade-off between model accuracy and
transparency
Accuracy and transparency are crucial for ensuring patient safety
and clinician trust in high-risk environments. To define clinical XAI
requirements, it is essential to consider the specific needs and
constraints of the clinical environment, including understanding
clinical workflows, decision types, and the impact on patient
outcomes. Increasing model accuracy often reduces transparency,
as complex models like deep neural networks are less interpretable
than simpler models such as decision trees. For critical decisions,
where transparency is paramount, simpler models can build trust
and ensure clinicians understand the decision-making process. For
less
critical
decisions,
more
complex
models
can
maximize
performance. Hybrid models, which combine interpretable models
with high-performance models, can balance transparency and
accuracy
by
leveraging
both
strengths.
Post-hoc
explanation
techniques, such as LIME and SHAP, provide insights into
complex models without altering their structure, maintaining high
performance while offering transparency.
To effectively implement these strategies, it is imperative to
conduct comprehensive user research to understand clinicians’
needs and preferences regarding explanations. Additionally, we
can utilize the existing clinical decision-support literature to
identify and further enhance best practices for evaluating clinical
XAI
tools (90).
Developing
a
modular explanation
system
offering high-level summaries with detailed drill-down options
can help balance transparency and performance. Continuous
learning and adaptation mechanisms allow the system to evolve
based on new data and user interactions, maintaining a balance
between transparency and performance. Ensuring regulatory
compliance and usability is essential, as the system must meet
healthcare regulations and integrate seamlessly into clinical
workflows. By employing these strategies, it is possible to design
XAI systems that effectively balance accuracy and transparency,
ensuring they are both practical and trustworthy in clinical
decision-making.
This
approach
provides
a
comprehensive
framework for developing XAI systems that meet the high
standards required in clinical environments, fostering trust and
reliability among users.

text:
Establishing a standardized UCD
process for designing and evaluating
AI-based healthcare technologies across
different contexts will help to inform
effective and safe solutions
UCD emphasizes that the development, design, and evaluation
process is as important as the resulting software. This importance is
warranted because clinical settings are variable depending on the
country and general accessibility to healthcare resources. Due to
this observation and general regulatory trends, we do not foresee
a generalizable AI solution being implemented across all settings;
instead, we envision a landscape in which AI functionality will
need to be packaged for each clinical application. Therefore, we
must adopt a rigorous scientific approach in our UCD efforts to
derive reusable clinical AI design templates. In addition to
providing a means for quick and reliable deployment of clinical
AI tools, such a process would also enable a method to evaluate
clinical AI scientifically at a global level. Understanding this
process
is
crucial
in
developing
effective
technologies that
improve medical outcomes and patient safety.
Guidelines like INTRPRT, designed to enhance transparency in
AI and machine learning systems, must be regularly updated to
remain
relevant
amidst
rapid
technological
advancements.
Establishing a schedule for periodic reviews and updates is
crucial.
This
can
be
facilitated
by a
dedicated
committee
comprising clinicians, AI researchers, ethicists, and regulatory
experts.
Community
involvement
through
workshops,
conferences, and online forums ensures that the guidelines reflect
the latest developments and best practices. Developing adaptive
frameworks allows for flexible and targeted updates, ensuring the
guidelines can quickly incorporate new techniques and findings.
Continuous education and training programs keep clinicians and
developers informed about the latest advancements and updates,
fostering a culture of continuous learning. Leveraging automated
tools to monitor research publications, regulatory changes, and
technological
advancements
can
provide
timely
alerts
for
necessary updates. Establishing a feedback loop with end-users,
such as clinicians and developers, ensures that the guidelines
remain practical and applicable in real-world settings. These
strategies collectively ensure that guidelines like INTRPRT stay
current and effective, supporting transparency and best practices
in clinical decision-making.
